## #6677 — daemon/reth: pciAddrToEnp ignores ARI, so the derived name diverges from systemd for any ARI-enabled NIC [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

## Summary

`pciAddrToEnp` (`pkg/daemon/daemon_reth.go`) derives a predictable interface name
from a PCI address alone. For an **ARI-enabled** device that derivation is wrong,
because ARI reinterprets the slot and function fields together as a single 8-bit
function number and `pciAddrToEnp` treats them as separate.

systemd's `net_id` builtin does:

```
if (ari_enabled)
        func += slot << 3;
```

So a device at `0000:03:01.2` with `ari_enabled=1` has combined function
`1 << 3 | 2` = **10**, and systemd names it accordingly. `pciAddrToEnp` derives
`enp3s1f2` — a name udev never assigns. The RETH member's `OriginalName=` lookup
then fails to match and that NIC is neither renamed nor bound.

## Verified on this host

```
$ strings /usr/bin/udevadm | grep -E '^%x:%x:%x\.%u$|^ari_enabled$'
%x:%x:%x.%u
ari_enabled

$ for d in /sys/bus/pci/devices/*/; do [ "$(cat $d/ari_enabled 2>/dev/null)" = 1 ] && basename $d; done
0000:65:00.0
0000:65:00.1
0000:65:00.2
0000:65:00.3
0000:67:00.0
0000:67:00.1
```

ARI-enabled devices are present on ordinary hardware, so this is not exotic.

## #6678 — daemon/device-map: deviceMapOriginalNameFor falls back to the LOGICAL name on an empty derivation, persisting an OriginalName= udev never presents [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

## Summary

`deviceMapOriginalNameFor` (`pkg/daemon/device_map.go:121`) calls
`deriveKernelNameFn` and, when that returns `""`, falls through and returns
`currentNIC`. In the branch that matters — the "NIC already wearing its logical
name but missing its `.link`" recovery case — `currentNIC == logical`, so the
**logical** name is persisted as `OriginalName=` through the mapped-name apply
path (`device_map.go:209`).

The function's own documentation states that udev will never present that logical
name. So the written `.link` cannot match on the next boot, and boot-time
persistence silently fails.

## Why it is a latent rather than live bug

An empty derivation is currently hard to produce from a genuine kernel sysfs
address: `pciAddrToEnp` returns `""` only for a malformed address, and real
addresses are well-formed. Every other consumer treats `""` as a clean skip —
`ensureRethLinkOriginalName` (`daemon_reth.go:39`) returns immediately without
rewriting the RETH `.link`, which is the correct posture.

So this is the one non-skip fallback in the call graph, and it converts "I could
not derive a name" into "here is a name" rather than "do nothing". Whenever a
future change widens the set of inputs that fail to derive, this turns into a
silent boot-persistence failure rather than a loud one.

## Why it is worth fixing now rather than when it bites

The failure is silent and deferred: the bad `.link` is written at apply time, and
the consequence appears at the *next boot*, on a machine the operator is not
watching, as a NIC that did not get its name. Correlating that back to an empty
derivation hours earlier is expensive.

Declining to write a `.link` at all is strictly better — it leaves the NIC under
its kernel name, which is at least a state the rest of the daemon understands.

## Fix direction

Return an explicit "no name derivable" signal rather than `currentNIC`, and have
the apply path skip writing `OriginalName=` for that NIC — matching what

## #6680 — test: afxdp::ha poisoned-shared-mutex tests fail on origin/master, with a varying failing set run to run [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-07)

## Summary

The `afxdp::ha::tests::*poisoned_shared_mutex*` family fails on **unmodified
`origin/master`**, and **which** members of the set fail varies run to run.

Verified in a detached worktree at `origin/master`: fails **3/3 runs**,
identically to how it fails on a feature branch. Not caused by any PR in flight.

## Why it needs its own issue

A test that fails on master is worse than a missing test, for two reasons:

1. **It burns reviewer time on every PR that touches userspace-dp.** Each round,
   someone has to re-establish that the failure is pre-existing rather than
   theirs — which means running master in a detached worktree to compare. That
   has now happened repeatedly across this campaign.
2. **A varying failing set defeats the usual defence.** An allowlist or a
   "known-failing" note keyed on test names does not hold when the names change
   between runs, so there is no cheap way to filter it out.

It also erodes the signal the whole gate depends on: the discipline here is that
a red is an assertion until proven otherwise, and a permanently-red suite trains
the opposite reflex.

## What is known

- Family: `afxdp::ha::tests::*poisoned_shared_mutex*`
- Reproduces on `origin/master`, 3/3
- The failing subset is not stable across runs — suggesting ordering or shared
  state between tests rather than a single deterministic assertion

A varying set under a name containing "poisoned shared mutex" points at exactly
what it says: one test poisons a mutex that another observes, so the outcome
depends on execution order. If so the fix is isolation — a fresh lock per test,
or serialising the family — rather than changing any assertion.

## #6681 — userspace-dp: per-interface queue binding raises the binding count from min(queues)xN to sum(queues) — eight downstream systems assume the old count [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-21)

## Summary

Fixing the #5173 queue mis-steer requires the planner to bind **each interface's
own queues** instead of the global minimum across interfaces. That changes the
binding count from `min(rx_i) x interfaces` to `sum(min(rx_i, 16))` — on the test
box, **3 to 17**. At least eight downstream systems were written against the old
count and do not hold at the new one.

Recorded so none is lost while the shim half and the planner half are sequenced.
The shim half (identity queue coordinate + read-side stride bound) is safe on its
own and is tracked at #5173/PR #6676; **this issue is the planner half.**

## The items, ranked

**1. Heartbeat slots are only partially zeroed.** `maps_sync.go:1831-1836`
zero-inits `workers*32` leading slots (`heartbeatSlotsPerWorker = 2*16`), but the
binding count is now decoupled from `workers`. With `workers=1` and 3 interfaces
x 16 queues = 48 bindings, **slots 32-47 are never zeroed** and retain whatever
the previous load left. The comment at `:1809-1812` states the per-worker bound
the new planner does not honour. Correct bound is `len(status.Bindings)`.

**2. Worker threads grow 1 -> 8, busy-polling.** `worker_id = queue_id % workers`
(`planning.rs:556`) and `plan_workers` groups by it, so spawned threads are
`min(configured_workers, max_queue_count)`. On an asymmetric box
`max_queue_count` was 1, so exactly one thread ran regardless of config. Default
poll mode is `PollMode::BusyPoll` (`lifecycle.rs:485`) — this is 1 to 8 spinning
cores on upgrade with no config change.

**3. UMEM is eagerly committed and scales linearly.** `umem/mmap.rs:43-56`,
`:74-83` map with **MAP_POPULATE** on both the hugetlb and fallback paths, so it
is RSS rather than virtual. ~40 MiB per non-virtio binding, ~48 MiB virtio: 3 ->
17 bindings is ~130 MiB -> **~690 MiB**, and at `ring-entries 8192` the repo's own
note (`schema_validators_system.go:151-160`) gives ~96 MB per binding -> **~1.6
GiB**. `MaxRingEntries` was sized against the OLD product. Shared UMEM does not
help: `create_shared_binding_group` sizes the group as the SUM of members.

**4. All-or-nothing readiness gates gain 5.7x the blast radius.** The #5143
barrier requires `bound == planned` per worker (`bringup.rs:41,54-60,100-117`), so
one failed XSK bind returns `WorkerBindIncomplete` and `snapshot.rs:354-396` turns
that into "dataplane down, snapshot not persisted". A queue that sysfs reports but

## #6682 — userspace-dp: an unzoned ifindex resolves to zone 0 and matches from-zone-any/to-zone-any rules with no zone guard [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

## Problem

An ingress interface that is in **no security zone** resolves to `zone_id = 0` and is then
adjudicated against wildcard policy rules as if zone 0 were a real zone. A
`from-zone any to-zone any permit` rule matches it. The result is that traffic on an
interface with no zone membership can be **permitted** and forwarded, with screen checks
skipped.

This is independent of any particular config-compiler bug — it is the runtime's own
treatment of a missing zone. Filed separately from #6525 (which is the compiler-side cause
of one way an interface ends up unzoned) so it is not silently absorbed into that fix.

## Evidence (traced on `ebe370701`)

**Zone miss becomes zone 0** — `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/forwarding/mod.rs:83-90`:

```rust
let from_id = ingress_zone_override
    .or_else(|| forwarding.ifindex_to_zone_id.get(&ingress_ifindex).copied())
    .unwrap_or(0);
let to_id = forwarding.egress.get(&egress_ifindex)
    .map(|iface| iface.zone_id).unwrap_or(0);
```

That pair reaches `evaluate_policy_result_with_icmp`
(`afxdp/poll_descriptor/mod.rs:2054`, pair built at `:3386`). There is no `from_id == 0`
guard on this path; the only such check in `policy.rs` is at `:2984` inside
`evaluate_junos_host_policy`, a different function.

**The both-any tier has no zone guard at all** — `userspace-dp/src/policy.rs:2764`:

```rust
for &idx in &state.both_any_indices {
    match try_match_rule(&state.rules[idx], ...)
```

No comparison against `from_id` / `to_id`. Any `from-zone any to-zone any` rule is tried
for every flow, including one whose zone pair is `(0, 0)` because the interface is in no
zone. A permit there permits the flow.

## #6683 — config: compact 'ids-option <p> icmp ping-death;' compiles the screen check DISABLED — silent screen fail-open [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

## Problem

The compact (packed one-liner) spelling of a screen ids-option compiles the check
**disabled**, with no error and no warning. The nested spelling of the same intent enables
it. A screen/IDS protection the operator configured is silently absent.

## Measured on `ebe370701`

Same intent, two spellings, both commit clean:

| spelling | compiled `ScreenProfile.ICMP.PingDeath` |
|---|---|
| `security { screen { ids-option s1 { icmp { ping-death; } } } }` | **`true`** |
| `security { screen { ids-option s1 icmp ping-death; } }` | **`false`** |

Both produce a profile named `s1`, so the profile exists and can be bound to a zone — it
simply enforces nothing. Zero errors, zero warnings in both cases.

## Why it matters

This fails **OPEN** in the security direction: the operator writes a screen profile,
attaches it to a zone, and receives no protection from the check they named. Unlike a
dropped address or port, there is no downstream symptom — traffic flows normally, which is
exactly what a working screen profile looks like until an attack arrives.

`ping-death` is used here only as the probe; the same packed descent almost certainly
affects the other checks under `icmp`/`ip`/`tcp`/`udp`/`limit-session`. **Whoever fixes
this must enumerate all 16 screen checks in both spellings rather than fixing the one
named above** — a fix that closes only `ping-death` leaves the same fail-open on fifteen
siblings.

## Root cause

Same class as #6525 / #6526 / #6662: a compact leaf's trailing tokens land on the node's
`Keys` rather than as `Children`, and the compiler descends only into `Children`. See
CLAUDE.md "Parser Dual AST Shape" — the compiler must handle both shapes.

Note the asymmetry that makes this hard to notice: the profile NAME survives (so the
config looks present in `show configuration` and binds successfully to a zone) while the
CHECK is lost.

## #6684 — config: compact 'syslog host <ip> any any;' compiles the host with ZERO facilities — logs silently not shipped [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

## Problem

The compact spelling of a syslog host compiles the host entry with an **empty** facility
list, so nothing is shipped to it. The nested spelling of the same intent compiles one
facility/severity pair. No error, no warning.

This is the `syslog host` half of #6662, which I noted there as untested; it is now
measured.

## Measured on `ebe370701`

| spelling | compiled |
|---|---|
| `system { syslog { host 10.0.0.1 { any any; } } }` | `addr="10.0.0.1" facilities=1` → `{Facility:any Severity:any}` |
| `system { syslog { host 10.0.0.1 any any; } }` | `addr="10.0.0.1"` **`facilities=0`** |

The host entry exists with the right address in both cases — only the selector is lost.

## Why it matters

Fails toward **silence**. The operator configures remote logging, `show configuration`
displays a syslog host, the daemon holds a host entry — and no events are exported. The
failure is invisible until someone needs the logs, which is the moment they are least
recoverable. For an audit or incident-response posture this is a meaningful gap even
though it is not itself a traffic-path fail-open.

Related: #5797 (per-facility severity selectors) is about which selector survives; this is
about none surviving.

## Root cause

Same class as #6525 / #6526 / #6662: compact-leaf trailing tokens land on `Keys`, the
compiler descends only `Children`.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Compact spelling compiles identically to nested, or is REJECTED at commit.
- [ ] Cover the other packed forms under `host` (`source-address`, `port`,
      `allow-duplicates`) — enumerate them, do not fix only `any any`.
- [ ] Test asserts the compiled facility/severity pair, not just that a host exists.

## #6685 — config: compact 'term <t> then discard;' compiles the firewall filter term with an EMPTY action [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

## Problem

The compact spelling of a firewall filter term's action compiles `Action` to the **empty
string**. The nested spelling compiles `"discard"`. The term still exists and still
matches — it just no longer does anything.

## Measured on `ebe370701`

| spelling | compiled |
|---|---|
| `filter f1 { term t1 { then { discard; } } }` | `terms=1`, `term="t1" action=discard` |
| `filter f1 { term t1 then discard; }` | `terms=1`, `term="t1"` **`action=""`** |

Both commit clean with no warning. The filter and the term both exist, so the config reads
as present and the filter binds to an interface normally.

## Why it matters

Fails **OPEN**. A `discard` term is a drop rule; compiling it to no action means traffic
the operator intended to drop is not dropped by that term. Because the term still exists
and still matches, it also shadows nothing and reports nothing — there is no counter
anomaly to notice, and `show configuration` shows the discard the operator wrote.

`FirewallFilterTerm.Action` is documented as `"accept", "reject", "discard", ""`, so an
empty action is a representable state rather than something a type check would catch.
Whoever fixes this should also state what an empty action means at enforcement time — if
an empty action falls through to the filter's implicit default, the direction of the
failure depends on that default and should be recorded explicitly.

## Root cause

Same class as #6525 / #6526 / #6662: compact-leaf trailing tokens land on `Keys`; the
compiler descends only `Children`.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Compact spelling compiles identically to nested, or is REJECTED at commit.
- [ ] Cover `accept` and `reject` as well as `discard`, and the packed `then` forms that
      carry an argument (`count`, `log`, `forwarding-class`, `dscp`) — enumerate them.
- [ ] Test asserts the compiled `Action` value, not that the term exists.

*(truncated — 44 lines total)*

## #6686 — config: policy-options as-path regex multi-token spelling compiles to '.*' — a from as-path term accepts every BGP path [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

## Problem

`policy-options as-path AP1 ".* 65000 .*"` written in its multi-token spelling compiles
`Regex` to `".*"` — the whole-path wildcard — instead of the authored pattern. A
`from as-path AP1; then accept` term therefore accepts **every** BGP path rather than only
those transiting AS 65000.

Verified in both spellings; both commit clean with 0 warnings.

## Location

`pkg/config/compiler_routing.go:632-650`.

There is no validator over `ASPaths` and no reference gate on `from as-path`, so nothing
downstream catches the widened pattern.

## Why it matters

Fails **OPEN** in the routing-policy direction and silently: the operator's intent is "only
paths through AS 65000"; the compiled result is "any path". A route-acceptance policy that
was meant to be selective becomes unconditional, which is a route-leak / hijack-acceptance
exposure rather than a cosmetic parse bug. Nothing in `show configuration` reveals it — the
authored regex is displayed back correctly.

## Root cause

Single-value accessor reading only the first token of a multi-token leaf. Same root cause
family as #6659 / PR #6673 (which fixes five sibling arms but not this one).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The multi-token spelling compiles the full authored regex, or is REJECTED at commit.
- [ ] Add a validator over `ASPaths` so a malformed or empty regex cannot reach the FRR
      render silently.
- [ ] Test asserts the compiled `Regex` STRING, not that an as-path object exists.
- [ ] Mutation proof: revert, build + vet clean, the specific test reds as an assertion.

Found by independent enumeration during the hostile review of PR #6673.

## #6687 — config: vlan-id-list bracketed list skips validation past slot 0 — '[ 10 99999 ]' and '[ 10 notanumber ]' commit clean [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-21)

## Problem

`vlan-id-list [ 10 99999 ]` and `vlan-id-list [ 10 notanumber ]` **commit clean**. The
identical bad value placed in slot 0 is correctly REJECTED. Validation only ever examines
the first element.

## Location

`pkg/config/compiler_services.go:1940`.

## Why it matters

This is the same gate-escape shape that PR #6673 fixes for `flow traceoptions flag` — but
on a leaf whose *idiomatic Junos spelling is the bracketed list*. Practically every real
`vlan-id-list` in the wild is written as a list, so the unvalidated path is the common
path, not the exotic one. An out-of-range (99999 > 4094) or non-numeric VLAN id reaches the
compiled config unchecked.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Every element of the list is validated, not only slot 0.
- [ ] Tests cover a bad value in slot 1 AND slot 0, asserting the SPECIFIC validator's
      message — a bare `err != nil` cannot distinguish which gate fired and would pass even
      if the widened check never ran.
- [ ] Check the tolerant/lenient load path separately; a strict gate firing first can mask
      an unvalidated tail.
- [ ] Mutation proof with build + vet clean.

Found by independent enumeration during the hostile review of PR #6673.

## #6688 — config: source-NAT 'port range [ 1000 2000 ]' compiles a ONE-PORT pool; out-of-range and non-numeric slots commit clean [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-21)

## Problem

A source-NAT pool's `port range [ 1000 2000 ]` compiles to `PortLow == PortHigh == 1000` —
a single-port PAT pool instead of a 1001-port range. Additionally `[ 1000 99999 ]` and
`[ 1000 notaport ]` commit clean, passing `validateSourceNATPoolStrict`.

## Location

`pkg/config/compiler_nat_source.go:409` and `parseSourcePoolPortRange` at `:257`.

## Why it matters

Two distinct harms from one defect:

1. **Port exhaustion / connectivity outage.** A pool the operator sized at 1001 ports
   provides one. Under any real translation load the pool exhausts immediately, and the
   symptom (intermittent NAT failures under load) points nowhere near the config that
   caused it.
2. **Unvalidated values reach the compiled config**, since the upper slot is never checked
   at all — the strict pool validator does not see it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `[ low high ]` compiles `PortLow=low, PortHigh=high`.
- [ ] Both slots validated for range (1-65535) and numeric form; `high >= low` enforced.
- [ ] Tests assert the compiled `PortLow`/`PortHigh` PAIR, and assert the specific
      validator message for the rejection cases.
- [ ] Verify the tolerant/lenient path separately.
- [ ] Mutation proof with build + vet clean.

Found by independent enumeration during the hostile review of PR #6673.

## #6689 — config: 'from { protocol { bgp; ospf; static; } }' compiles only [bgp] — a then-reject term silently stops filtering the rest [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-21)

## Problem

A routing-policy `from { protocol { bgp; ospf; static; } }` block compiles to `[bgp]` only
— a first-child-only descent. A term written to reject three protocols rejects one.

## Location

`pkg/config/compiler_routing.go:773-777`.

## Why it matters

Fails **OPEN**. With `then reject`, the operator's intent is to filter BGP, OSPF and static
routes; the compiled policy filters BGP alone, so OSPF and static routes the operator meant
to exclude are accepted and installed. This is a silent route-acceptance widening with no
diagnostic — the authored config renders back intact.

Note this is the *nested-block* multi-child shape, distinct from the bracketed-list shape:
a fix that only handles `protocol [ bgp ospf static ]` will not close this. Both spellings
need covering.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] All children of a `from { protocol { ... } }` block accumulate.
- [ ] Cover BOTH the nested-block spelling and the bracketed-list spelling, and state the
      enumeration.
- [ ] Test asserts the compiled protocol SLICE contents, not its length alone.
- [ ] Mutation proof: revert, build + vet clean, the specific test reds as an assertion.

Found by independent enumeration during the hostile review of PR #6673.

`system { ntp { server { a; b; } } }` compiles **zero** NTP servers and the commit is
green. The nested-block spelling loses everything.

`pkg/config/compiler_system.go:67-71`. The already-correct `name-server` sibling is
**two lines above** at `:65` — the fix pattern is immediately adjacent, which is why this
is worth closing now rather than in a general sweep.

Fails toward **silence**: the operator configures time sync, `show configuration` displays
the servers, and the daemon has none. Clock drift then degrades anything that depends on
time — certificate validity windows, IPsec rekey scheduling, log correlation across an HA
pair, and scheduler-based policies. The failure surfaces far from its cause.

This is the mirror direction of the defect PR #6673's own commit message warns about, on a
leaf that PR did not touch.

- [ ] The nested-block spelling accumulates all servers; the compact and bracketed
      spellings too — enumerate all three and state which were checked.

      the same first-child-only descent, and report the scope of that check rather than
      claiming a general sweep.

## #6692 — config: five system-stanza multi-value leaves drop everything past slot 0 (archival, ssh key-exchange, api-key, shared-umem) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-21)

## Problem

Four `pkg/config/compiler_system.go` arms read only the first element of a bracketed
multi-value leaf. Two are security-relevant.

| leaf | site | authored | compiled |
|---|---|---|---|
| `system archival configuration archive-sites [ scp://backup-a/cfg scp://backup-b/cfg ]` | `compiler_system.go:203` | 2 sites | first only |
| `system services ssh key-exchange [ diffie-hellman-group14-sha1 curve25519-sha256 ]` | `compiler_system.go:412` | 2 methods | **first (weaker) only** |
| `system services web-management api-auth api-key [ keyA keyB ]` | `compiler_system.go:487` | 2 keys | `["keyA"]`, keyB silently lost |
| `system dataplane shared-umem interface [ eth1 eth2 ]` | `compiler_system.go:1054` | 2 ifaces | `["eth1"]` |

## Why these matter

- **`ssh key-exchange`** — the operator lists algorithms in preference order and the
  compiler keeps only the first. If that first entry is the weaker legacy method (as in the
  example, `diffie-hellman-group14-sha1` before `curve25519-sha256`), the box is pinned to
  the weaker KEX and the modern one the operator added is silently discarded. A hardening
  change that appears applied but is not.
- **`api-key`** — a second API key is silently dropped, so a credential the operator
  believes is provisioned does not authenticate. Fails toward lockout, but it also means
  key rotation (add new, then remove old) silently fails to add the new key.
- **`archive-sites`** — config backups go to one destination when two were configured; the
  redundancy is absent exactly when it is needed.
- **`shared-umem interface`** — dataplane memory topology differs from what was authored.

## Root cause

Single-value accessor on a schema-declared multi-value leaf; the bracketed list collapses
onto the node's `Keys` and only `Keys[1]` (or the first child) is read. Same family as
#6659 / PR #6673.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] All four leaves accumulate every element, in both the bracketed and repeated-child
      spellings.
- [ ] Tests assert the compiled SLICE contents, not its length.
- [ ] For `ssh key-exchange` and `api-key`, add a validator over every element — a widened
      read with an unwidened validator turns a silent truncation into silent propagation of
      an unvalidated value.

## #6693 — config: five NAT match-address arms drop the second prefix in the mixed Keys/child AST shape [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

## Problem

Five NAT `match` arms use an either/or reader (`Keys` OR children) rather than accumulating
both, so in the mixed AST shape — first value on the node's `Keys`, remainder in the child
tail — every prefix past the first is dropped.

| site | leaf | compiled |
|---|---|---|
| `compiler_nat_source.go:683` | source-NAT `match source-address [ 10.0.0.0/8 192.0.2.0/24 ]` | `["10.0.0.0/8"]` |
| `compiler_nat_source.go:706` | source-NAT `match destination-address [ 203.0.113.0/24 198.51.100.0/24 ]` | first only |
| `compiler_nat_destination.go:118` | dest-NAT `match destination-address [ 203.0.113.10/32 203.0.113.11/32 ]` | first only |
| `compiler_nat_destination.go:148` | dest-NAT `match source-address [ 10.0.0.0/8 192.0.2.0/24 ]` | first only |
| `compiler_nat_static.go:762` | static-NAT `match source-address [ 10.0.0.0/8 192.0.2.0/24 ]` | first only |

## Why it matters

A NAT rule's `match` is a selector. Dropping alternatives makes the rule **narrower** than
authored, so traffic the operator intended to translate is not translated — it either
egresses untranslated (a source-address leak, or an asymmetric path that breaks the
session) or misses a destination-NAT and is delivered/forwarded to the wrong place.
Narrowing a NAT match is not fail-closed in any useful sense: it silently changes which
flows get translated, and the symptom appears far from the config.

Note this is the MIXED shape specifically (`Keys` carries the first value, children carry
the tail), which is distinct from the pure-bracketed and pure-nested shapes. A fix that
handles only one shape leaves the others — cover all three and state the enumeration.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] All five arms accumulate `Keys[1:]` AND `Children` (use the `firewallMatchValues`
      pattern rather than a new either/or reader).
- [ ] Cover the pure-bracketed, pure-nested, and mixed Keys/child shapes for each.
- [ ] Tests assert the compiled prefix SLICE contents.
- [ ] Widen the corresponding validators in the same change, and check the tolerant path
      separately — a strict gate firing first can mask an unvalidated tail.
- [ ] Mutation proof with build + vet CLEAN and the specific test redding as an assertion.

Found by the independent Codex enumeration on PR #6673 (MAJORs 13, 14, 15, 16, 17).

## #6694 — config: fab0 fabric-options member-interfaces packed leaf compiles to EMPTY — HA fabric loses its members [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-21)

## Problem

`pkg/config/compiler_interfaces.go:149` reads only `Children` for
`fabric-options { member-interfaces ... }`. In the packed-leaf shape the node has no
children — the members sit on its `Keys` — so:

```
interfaces { fab0 { fabric-options { member-interfaces [ ge-0/0/0 ge-0/0/1 ]; } } }
  -> FabricMembers = []          (expected: both members)
```

## Why it matters

This is the **chassis-cluster fabric**. `fab0` carries session sync, config sync, IPsec SA
sync, and the cross-chassis forwarding path that keeps TCP alive across a VRRP failback
(`docs/fabric-cross-chassis-fwd.md`). A fabric with zero compiled members is a fabric that
cannot form.

The failure is silent at commit and its symptom appears only under HA: sync never
establishes, or the fabric redirect for peer-owned sessions has no interface to use. On a
two-node cluster that is a split-brain / dual-primary risk rather than a cosmetic config
bug, and per CLAUDE.md any change touching cluster/session-sync/failover must pass
`make test-failover` — which means this defect can also make that gate misleading if the
config under test uses the packed spelling.

Note the bracketed spelling used above is the idiomatic Junos one for a two-member fabric,
so this is the common spelling, not an exotic one.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The packed/bracketed shape accumulates all members; cover the nested-block spelling
      and the flat-set spelling too, and state the enumeration.
- [ ] Test asserts the compiled `FabricMembers` SLICE contents.
- [ ] Consider REJECTING a `fab0` with zero compiled members at commit — a fabric with no
      members is never a valid intent, so this should not be representable silently.
- [ ] Mutation proof: revert, confirm build + vet CLEAN, confirm the specific test reds as
      an assertion.

## #6695 — config: RA dns-server-address multi-value drops every RDNSS server past the first [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-21)

## Problem

`pkg/config/compiler_protocols.go:918` reads only the first value:

```
set protocols router-advertisement interface ge-0/0/0 dns-server-address [ 2001:db8::53 2001:db8::54 ]
  -> compiles 2001:db8::53 only
```

The second RDNSS server is never advertised.

## Why it matters

RDNSS redundancy is the entire point of configuring two resolvers. Hosts on the link learn
one server; when it goes away they have no fallback and IPv6 name resolution fails for the
whole segment. The operator's `show configuration` displays both, so the missing
redundancy is invisible until the primary resolver fails — i.e. exactly when the fallback
was supposed to matter.

xpf sends RAs from its own embedded sender (`pkg/ra/`, replacing radvd), so there is no
external daemon that would re-read the config and behave correctly.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] All addresses accumulate, in the bracketed and repeated-child spellings.
- [ ] Test asserts the compiled address SLICE contents and that the emitted RA option
      carries both.
- [ ] Validate every element, not only the first — a widened read with an unwidened
      validator propagates a malformed address into the RA sender.
- [ ] Mutation proof with build + vet CLEAN.

Found by the independent Codex enumeration on PR #6673 (MAJOR 6).

## #6696 — config: dhcp-local-server group interface and pool dns-server drop everything past slot 0 on the tolerant path [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

## Problem

Two `pkg/config/compiler_services.go` arms keep only the first element, observed on the
TOLERANT load path:

| site | authored | compiled |
|---|---|---|
| `compiler_services.go:414` | `system services dhcp-local-server group g interface [ ge-0/0/0.0 ge-0/0/1.0 ]` | `group.Interfaces=["ge-0/0/0.0"]` |
| `compiler_services.go:437` | `... group g pool p dns-server [ 192.0.2.53 198.51.100.53 ]` | first only |

## Why it matters

- **`group interface`** — the DHCP server serves only the first interface in the group. The
  second segment gets no leases at all, and the failure looks like a network problem rather
  than a config one. A group listing several interfaces is the ordinary way to write this.
- **`pool dns-server`** — clients receive one resolver where two were configured, so the
  redundancy is absent (same shape as the RA RDNSS case).

That this reproduces on the TOLERANT path matters specifically: the tolerant path is what a
persisted config and an HA peer-sync take, so a node can come up serving a narrower DHCP
scope than the config on disk describes — and the two cluster nodes can disagree if one
loaded strictly and the other tolerantly.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Both arms accumulate every element, on the STRICT and TOLERANT paths, checked
      separately.
- [ ] Tests assert the compiled slice contents on both paths.
- [ ] Validate every element; a widened read needs a widened validator.
- [ ] Mutation proof with build + vet CLEAN and the specific test redding as an assertion.

## #6697 — config: CoS DSCP and IEEE classifier code-points read no child values — authored code-point entries vanish [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-21)

## Problem

Two classifier arms in `pkg/config/compiler_class_of_service.go` read no child values, so a
`code-points` block written with children compiles empty:

| site | authored | compiled |
|---|---|---|
| `:1147` | DSCP classifier `code-points { ef; cs1; }` | entry lacks the authored `[46, 8]` |
| `:1204` | IEEE classifier `code-points { 3; 5; }` | both values lost |

The classifier itself survives if another valid entry exists (e.g. `code-points default;`
or `code-points 0;`), so the compiled classifier is present but silently missing the
authored mapping.

## Why it matters

A classifier that keeps its name but loses a code-point mapping is worse than one that
fails to compile: it binds successfully to an interface and misclassifies traffic. Packets
the operator mapped to a priority forwarding class fall to whatever the remaining entry or
the default resolves to, so QoS silently degrades — the shaped classes do not receive the
traffic intended for them.

This is hard to notice because `show class-of-service` renders the authored config and the
interface binding succeeds. It surfaces only as unexplained latency/loss under congestion,
and the CoS smoke matrix would only catch it if it happens to exercise the affected class.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Both arms read child values as well as `Keys[1:]` and accumulate.
- [ ] Cover the nested-block, bracketed, and flat-set spellings; state the enumeration.
- [ ] Tests assert the compiled code-point set per entry, not merely that the classifier
      exists — an existence assertion is what let this hide.
- [ ] Mutation proof: revert each arm SEPARATELY, confirm build + vet CLEAN, confirm the
      specific test reds as an assertion.

Found by the independent Codex enumeration on PR #6673 (MAJORs 11, 12).

## #6700 — userspace-dp: make IPsec secure tunnels (xfrmi) first-class dataplane interfaces so decrypted plaintext is zone-adjudicated [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

The open half of #5619. PR #6691 fixed the netdev-name drift and made the
dataplane's exclusion of secure tunnels explicit; PR #6698 tells the operator
about it at commit. **This issue is the work that would lift that exclusion.**

## The gap

Route-based IPsec decrypts in the **kernel** XFRM stack. `xfrmi_rcv_cb`
(`net/xfrm/xfrm_interface_core.c`) sets `skb->dev` to the xfrmi, then
`xfrm_input` tunnel-mode does `gro_cells_receive` (`net/xfrm/xfrm_input.c:734`)
→ `__netif_receive_skb_core`. The plaintext then traverses Linux routing.

xpf does not adjudicate it:

- the xfrmi ifindex is not in `userspace_ingress_ifaces`, so the shim takes
  `cpumap_or_pass` → `XDP_PASS` (`userspace-xdp/src/lib.rs:1139-1147`);
- xpf installs only `type filter hook input` nftables chains —
  `grep -rn "hook forward"` over the whole repo returns **zero** hits;
- `ip_forward` and `ipv6.conf.all.forwarding` are force-enabled
  (`pkg/daemon/daemon_system.go:618-629`).

So decrypted transit plaintext is forwarded by the kernel with **no zone
policy, no session, no NAT and no screen**.

The mechanism to adjudicate it does exist — generic XDP runs on
`skb->dev->xdp_prog` at `net/core/dev.c:5958`, and by then `skb->dev` is the
xfrmi. What is missing is everything around it.

Measured on PR #6691's branch with `buildLinkSnapshot` stubbed so `st0.0`
resolves:

```
ingress ifindexes (name unfixed): [11]        <- LAN only; xfrmi invisible via ifindex 0
ingress ifindexes (name fixed):   [11 42]     <- the xfrmi ENTERS
```

## #6702 — userspace-dp: plan per-interface RX queues — the binding-count half of #5173 (capacity, UMEM, and 8 downstream assumptions) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

Split out of #5173 / PR #6676, which shipped only the **shim half** (the queue coordinate is never transformed, plus a read-side stride bound). This issue is the **planner half**: making queues above the global minimum actually *work*.

## Why this was split rather than shipped

#6676's shim half stops the mis-steer. What it does **not** do alone is give those queues somewhere to go — an interface's queues above the global minimum get no binding and are dropped explicitly, where before they were silently mis-steered onto a socket `xsk_rcv_check()` then rejected. Same outcome, legible instead of silent. That is a shippable increment.

Making them *work* means changing the planner from `min(rx_queues) × interfaces` to `Σ min(rx_queues, 16)` — and that changes the binding **count**, which at least eight things downstream assume. The old under-provisioning was accidentally also a **cap**; removing it removes a limit nobody chose but which was doing load-bearing work.

### The number that decided the split

On the real asymmetric topology (fxp0 virtio 1q + fabric parent virtio 1q + LAN mlx5 16q + WAN mlx5 16q):

| | bindings | pinned UMEM |
|---|---|---|
| today (`min × n`) | 4 | ~176 MiB |
| per-interface (`Σ`) | **34** | **~1.34 GiB** |

…and **4× that again** at the permitted `--ring-entries 16384`. Each binding is an independent `MmapArea` registered as its own UMEM, mapped with **`MAP_POPULATE`** — so this is **resident**, not virtual. Shared UMEM does not help: `create_shared_binding_group` sizes a group as the **sum** of its members. `MaxRingEntries` (#2524) caps `ring_entries` only; nothing caps the product, and this change multiplies the other factor.

## Blockers — must be resolved before the count changes

**1. XSK / heartbeat maps are hard-capped at 4096 while the plan is not.** `userspace-xdp/src/lib.rs:335,338`. 257 interfaces (256 × 16q + one × 1q) plans **4,097** slots including invalid slot 4096. XSK registration then propagates the map-update failure (`worker/mod.rs:638`) and readiness reports the shortfall (`bringup.rs:1034`). Per `snapshot.rs:355` this **can fail an apply after the previous dataplane is already torn down** — a config that planned fine under the old scheme ends with **no dataplane**. Must fail at PLAN time with a message naming the limit; a loud refusal to plan is recoverable, a half-torn-down dataplane is not.

**2. Heartbeat slots are only partially zeroed.** `pkg/dataplane/userspace/maps_sync.go:1831-1836` zero-inits `workers * heartbeatSlotsPerWorker` (2×16) leading slots, but the binding count is no longer a function of `workers`. With `workers=1` and 3 ifaces × 16q = 48 bindings, **slots 32-47 are never zeroed** and retain whatever the prior load left. The comment at `:1809-1812` states the per-worker bound the new planner would not honour. Correct bound is `len(status.Bindings)`. This is stale state, not a capacity note.

**3. Worker threads 1 → 8, busy-polling.** `worker_id = queue_id % workers`; `plan_workers` groups by it, so spawned threads are `min(configured_workers, max_queue_count)`. On the asymmetric box `max_queue_count` was 1, so exactly one thread ran regardless of config — it becomes up to 8, and the default is `PollMode::BusyPoll`. That is 1 → 8 spinning cores on upgrade with no config change.

**4. All-or-nothing gates get 5.7× the blast radius.** The #5143 readiness barrier requires `bound == planned` per worker (`bringup.rs:41,54-60,100-117`); one failed XSK bind → `WorkerBindIncomplete` → `snapshot.rs:354-396` → "dataplane down, snapshot not persisted". Any queue that sysfs reports but that cannot accept an AF_XDP bind becomes a total outage rather than a non-event. Same shape in `standbyBindingsReadyLocked` (`manager_ha.go:450-466`) and `allBindingsBound` (`maps_sync.go:438-455`).

**5. Auto-rebind recovery can no longer fire.** `hasBusyBindingsWedgeLocked` (`maps_sync.go:1431-1452`) requires `bound == 0 && ready == 0`. With 17+ bindings the realistic failure is PARTIAL (16 bind, 1 EBUSY), so `bound != 0` and recovery never triggers. That gate was written for an era when the binding set was small and failed together.

**6. Slot identity is no longer stable.** `replan_bindings_from_candidates` carries prior state forward keyed by SLOT (`planning.rs:499-501,547`), retaining `registered`/`armed`/`last_error`. With queue-major ordering plus per-row skipping, changing ONE interface's queue count reshuffles which `(iface, queue)` owns which slot in every row above it: `[A(rx=4), B(rx=2)]` has slot 5 = `(A,q3)`; after `ethtool -L B combined 4`, slot 5 = `(B,q2)`. So `binding slot 5 unregister` silently retargets a different interface — and since the shim no longer reduces the coordinate, that queue's packets then have nowhere to go. Under `min()` the slot prefix was stable.

**7. RSS pins RX to `[0, workers)`.** `pkg/daemon/rss_indirection.go:244-280` does this whenever `workers < queues`, so bindings for queues ≥ workers are bound, ready, heartbeating and holding ~40 MiB each **while receiving nothing**. Also `process_napi.go:96-102` sends a hard-coded 30 probes while its comment claims "~2× the queue count" — coverage per queue thins as the live set grows, and a zero-copy queue that never gets its first NAPI event never posts fill-ring WQEs.

**8. Go-side accepts the binding list with almost no validation.** `maps_sync.go:690-745` checks only `QueueID >= bindingQueuesPerIface` and `idx >= BindingArrayMaxEntries`. No count limit, no slot uniqueness, no duplicate `(ifindex, queue)` detection, and **no check that `binding.Slot` is inside the 4096-entry XSK/heartbeat map** before writing it. A duplicate would last-wins and silently orphan an XSK. Go-side complement to blocker 1.

## Confirmed NOT affected

The binding array itself (1,048,576 entries, both dimensions correctly guarded), `WorkerBindingLookup` / `MirrorTargetMap` (unbounded `FastMap`s), the cold-path zone slots, `summarize_queues` and the Go renderers (ragged-safe), Prometheus cardinality, the control-socket payload, and `ctrl.queue_count` — which the shim deliberately no longer reads after #6676.

## #6703 — security: secret-bearing URLs (DDNS Server/URLTemplate/CheckIPURL, FeedServer.URL) render cleartext — type- and keyword-based redaction both miss them [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

## Defect

Two independent redaction mechanisms both miss a class of value that is secret **by
content** rather than by type or by keyword, so credentials embedded in URLs render in
cleartext on config-read surfaces.

| field | type | reached by redaction? |
|---|---|---|
| `DDNSProvider.Password` | `config.Secret` | yes — `Secret.MarshalJSON` |
| `DDNSProvider.Server` (`types_system.go:273`, documented *"or full base URL"*) | plain `string` | **no** |
| `DDNSProvider.URLTemplate` (`:282`) | plain `string` | **no** |
| `DDNSProvider.CheckIPURL` (`:303`) | plain `string` | **no** |
| `FeedServer.URL` (`types_security.go:65`) | plain `string` | **no** |

## Why both mechanisms miss

- `Secret.MarshalJSON` (`pkg/config/secret.go:141`) is **type**-based. These fields are
  plain `string`, so it never applies.
- `secretIndices` (`pkg/config/ast_redact.go:103`) is **keyword**-based — it matches
  `pre-shared-key`, `password`, `community` and similar, disambiguated by required ancestor
  context. A leaf named `url`, `server` or `url-template` matches nothing.

A URL is secret-*bearing* without being a secret:
`https://user:pass@ddns.example/update` — dyndns2 uses HTTP Basic by protocol — or a threat-feed
URL carrying `?token=…`. Both are the ordinary way these two features are configured.

## Exposure

On the default loopback bind with no api-auth configured, the REST **read** surface is
unauthenticated (42 GET routes — see #6660), so `GET /api/v1/config` renders these fields
verbatim to any local caller. `GET /api/v1/config/export` and `/show` should be checked in
the same pass, along with supported archival inline passwords, which `secretIndices` also
does not classify.

Note the CLI has an analogous exposure surface: `showConfigRedacted`
(`pkg/cli/permissions.go:93`) returns false for an unset login class, and #6662/#6701 both
produce an unset class from a valid-looking config.

## #6704 — userspace-xdp: shim resolves an L4 for a NON-FIRST IPv6 fragment and can key a session from payload bytes (pre-existing, not from #4555) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

**Pre-existing. NOT introduced by #4555 / PR #6655** — found while building that PR's executable parity corpus, which is why it is filed separately rather than folded in.

## Defect

The AF_XDP shim resolves a terminal L4 for a **non-first IPv6 fragment** and hands the resulting offset to `parse_l4`, which reads the bytes there as a TCP/UDP header. For a non-first fragment those bytes are **payload, not an L4 header**, so the shim can form a session key from attacker-influenced payload bytes. `userspace-dp` refuses to build a session from the same packet.

## Concrete input

```
IPv6(next=Fragment) -> Fragment(next=TCP, frag_off=0x0008) -> <payload bytes>
```

| | disposition |
|---|---|
| shim (`userspace-xdp/src/ipv6_ext_walk.rs`, Fragment arm) | walks past the Fragment header, returns `L4(48, TCP)`; `parse_l4` then reads offsets 48.. as TCP source/dest ports |
| userspace-dp (`walk_ipv6_ext_chain`, `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/frame/inspect.rs`) | records the sighting in `ExtChainWalk.non_first_fragment_offset_seen`; the session path declines to construct a session (`inspect.rs:1428`) |

Both agree on `.outcome`. The divergence lives entirely in the fragment state, which is why a corpus comparing only outcomes stayed green — see #6655, where the compared unit was widened to carry it.

## Why it matters

The shim's session lookup can only HIT an entry userspace INSTALLED, and userspace never installs one from a non-first fragment. So this is not a path to a session of the attacker's choosing. The concern is narrower and still real: the 5-tuple synthesised from payload bytes may **coincide with a legitimate existing session**, in which case the fragment takes that session's fast path — forwarded on a decision made for a different flow, with no policy evaluation of its own. An attacker who can send fragments to the box controls those bytes.

Severity is bounded by needing a collision with a live session's exact key, and by the fragment being forwarded rather than delivered. It is a fail-open shape rather than a demonstrated bypass, which is why it is filed for assessment rather than as an incident.

## Why it is not a small fix

The shim's walk (`walk_ipv6_ext_headers`) returns `(offset, protocol)` and carries no fragment state, because nothing downstream of it in the shim consumes any. Closing this means:

1. teaching the walk to carry a non-first-fragment flag — the Fragment arm already reads all 8 bytes, so testing `(frag_off & 0xFFF8) != 0` is cheap;
2. propagating it into `ParsedPacket`;
3. having the session path honour it — decline the lookup, or route to userspace, rather than forming a key from payload.

Step 3 is a shim **behaviour** change and needs its own review. All three carry BPF verifier cost against the 1M processed-insn cap, which the shim has repeatedly bumped against (#1864); the current object sits at 947,188 / 5.28% headroom, so any addition here must be measured through `make generate`'s verify-then-install gate, not estimated.

## Acceptance criteria

1. A test that sends the input above and asserts the shim does **not** synthesise an L4 key from post-fragment bytes — behavioural, not a source-text check.
2. Parity with `walk_ipv6_ext_chain`'s disposition for the same packet, verified by the executable corpus in `tests_shim_ext_parity.rs` with the fragment fields compared on the resolved-L4 path.
3. A measured verifier figure through `make generate` before and after, with headroom stated.

The #5575 `LenientContentDropped` poison is honoured by the **userspace dataplane** but not
by the **kernel host-inbound actuator**. `junos_host_deny.go` -> `daemon_nft.go:418` never
consults the flag — it is the flag's only non-test consumer that ignores it.

Consequence, measured: a `to-zone junos-host` permit whose match dimension carries no value
**erases the entire host-inbound DROP program**:

```
before:  RulesV4:[{Src:[10.0.9.0/24] PermitSubtract:[10.0.1.50/32]}]
after:   RulesV4:[]
```

and it **still marks the deny "rendered"**, so the #4168 warning that would have flagged the
missing enforcement is suppressed. The operator gets neither the protection nor the
diagnostic.

## Reachable through a CLEAN STRICT COMMIT on master

This is the part that makes it urgent rather than a tolerant-path curiosity. The **omitted**
form produces the byte-identical erasure, and on current master that reaches the erasure
through a clean strict commit **with the policy unpoisoned** — no lenient load, no peer sync,
no malformed config. The blast radius is wider than the #5575 framing implies.

## Why the poison does not save it

For the userspace dataplane, a poisoned policy is forced to the
`unsupportedApplicationSentinel`, so the Rust integrity preflight rejects the whole snapshot
(previous-good retained; fresh-boot default-deny) — an action-agnostic fail-closed. That
mechanism is sound and is not in question here.

The kernel actuator simply does not read the flag. So the same config that is fail-closed in
one plane is fail-open in the other, and the plane that fails open is the one enforcing
host-inbound admission.

consequences of that rejection have never been traced, and all three are live on master.

**These are pre-existing.** Discriminator run on current master, hierarchical parser:

| `match` form | strict compile | lenient poisoned |
|---|---|---|
| `source-address 10.0.0.0/8;` | ACCEPTED | no |
| `source-address;` (valueless) | REJECTED | **YES** |
| **omitted entirely** | REJECTED | **YES** |

The **omitted** form — which predates any recent work — reaches the poison on the tolerant
path exactly as the valueless form does. So everything below is reachable today.

`pkg/dataplane/userspace/manager_compile.go:350`/`:438`, `maps_sync.go:230`,
`process_status.go:153`.

For a policy-only same-plan update, the helper rejects before mutation and retains its old
snapshot — but Go disables `userspace_ctrl.Enabled`. **Neither snapshot forwards transit**
until the next one-second status poll restores maps from `m.lastSnapshot`; a poll failure
extends the outage.

On a **fresh start** it is worse: bootstrap sets `Enabled=0`, the helper has `snapshot=None`,
and the rejection returns before `m.lastSnapshot` is advanced or the status loop is started.
No policy configuration ever becomes active and transit stays dropped.

## #6710 — userspace-dp: negative-neighbor cache (3s TTL) may fast-fail a PERMITTED LAN->tunnel flow instead of reinjecting; xfrmi has no resolvable lladdr [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

## Summary

An xfrmi (secure tunnel) netdev has **no resolvable link-layer address**, so a
LAN→tunnel packet that reaches the FIB's neighbor lookup resolves to
`MissingNeighbor` and the `pending_neigh` path times out. That timeout arms the
**negative-neighbor cache (3 s TTL)**.

The open question: once that cache is armed, does a **permitted** LAN→tunnel
flow fast-fail against the cached negative entry instead of falling through to
the reinject gate? If it does, a policy-permitted flow is dropped for up to 3 s
at a time, repeatedly, on a tunnel that is otherwise healthy.

Surfaced while gating PR #6691 (issue #5619). It is **not** introduced there:
at that PR's merge-base, the canonical bare spelling `bind-interface st0`
already resolved `MissingNeighbor`, so the interaction predates the change.
What #6691 does is **extend its reach to the dotted spelling** `st0.0`, which
previously resolved `NoRoute` and never reached the neighbor lookup at all.

So: pre-existing mechanism, wider blast radius. That is a follow-up, not a
merge blocker for #6691, and #6700 does not cover it.

The engineer on #6691 was explicit that this was read from source plus the
pinned `is_slow_path_eligible` table and that **the worker loop was not
executed**. It is recorded as unverified rather than asserted in either
direction. Do not treat the framing above as established — the first task here
is to settle it by execution.

## What would settle it

1. Execute the worker loop (not read it) for a LAN→tunnel packet on an xfrmi
   with a `from-zone <lan> to-zone <tunnel-zone>` **permit** in place, across
   the window where the negative cache is armed.
2. Determine whether the permitted flow reaches the reinject gate or fast-fails
   against the cached entry.
3. If it fast-fails: decide whether the negative-neighbor cache should be

## #6711 — cluster/heartbeat: a SINGLE >1h backward wall-clock step regresses the sender boot epoch and gets the node refused by its peer — the documented 'both terms must fail together' margin does not hold [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

## Summary

A single backward wall-clock step larger than `bootEpochMaxSkew` (one hour),
**with persisted state intact**, causes the sender's boot epoch to regress. The
regressed value **overwrites the higher persisted one**, and the peer then
refuses this node until wall time recovers.

The design documents this class as requiring **two** simultaneous faults. It
does not. One fault is sufficient, and it was reproduced.

## Why this is filed separately

Found during the round-4 hostile re-gate of PR #6669 (issue #6169). It
**pre-dates that PR's fold round** and is not introduced by it, so it is not a
merge blocker for #6669 — but it invalidates three places in that branch's own
documentation, which are listed below so they get corrected together with the
fix rather than drifting further.

## What it contradicts

- `pkg/cluster/README.md:339-341`
- The same README's **residual 3**, which states *"Both terms must fail
  together"*
- The justification at `pkg/cluster/heartbeat_epoch.go:494-497`, which states
  *"nothing is locked out"*

All three describe a two-fault safety margin that the reproduction shows is a
one-fault path. A documented margin that does not exist is worse than no margin
documented, because it suppresses exactly the review that would have caught
this.

## Mechanism, as reproduced

1. Node's wall clock steps backward by more than one hour. Persisted boot-epoch
   state is intact — no corruption, no missing file, no dead RTC.
2. The sender derives a boot epoch from the stepped-back clock, producing a
   value LOWER than the persisted one.
3. That lower value overwrites the higher persisted value.
4. The peer, holding the higher floor, refuses this node's frames until wall
   time climbs back past the old value.

## Summary

`populate_egress` (`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/forwarding_build/interfaces.rs:302-307`)
requires a MAC to build an `EgressInterface`. An xfrmi (IPsec secure tunnel)
**never has one** — it is `ARPHRD_NONE`. The tunnel is therefore absent from
`state.egress`, and the `MissingNeighbor` arm reads its to-zone from exactly
that map (`forwarding/mod.rs:84-89`, `.unwrap_or(0)`).

The result: a LAN→tunnel packet is adjudicated against zone pair **`(lan, 0)`**
instead of `(lan, vpn)`. Policy evaluation deliberately refuses to match any
exact, wildcard, or global rule when either zone id is zero
(`policy.rs:2645`, `:2679`), so **no operator-authored permit can match** — not
`from-zone lan to-zone vpn permit`, not `global ... permit`. The packet reaches
default deny, becomes `PolicyDenied`, and exits before reinjection
(`poll_descriptor/mod.rs:4241`, `:4290`).

**This is live on master today** for `bind-interface st0`: 8 of 12 measured
next-hop × destination cells drop traffic the operator explicitly permitted.

## Measured, not inferred

Chain driven: real Go snapshot (`buildSnapshotWithSchedulerStateAndNATCounters`)
→ real `build_forwarding_state` → real FIB → real policy evaluator.

- `state.egress.contains_key(&42)` is **false** in all 24 measured cells.
- All three MAC fallbacks fail, unconditionally, for every secure tunnel:
  - `hardware_addr` is `""` — verified in a **private netns** through the exact
    `netlink.LinkByName` path `buildLinkSnapshot` uses: `hw_len=0`,
    `hardwareAddr=""`, `encap_type=none`. Not a test-stub artefact.
  - `mac_by_ifindex[bind_ifindex]` is absent — the parent is itself a MAC-less
    xfrmi.
  - `iface.tunnel` is `false` — `Tunnel` means a Junos `tunnel {source
    destination}` stanza, which `st0` does not have.
- Measured zone pair: `(50675,trust) -> (0,<none>)`. The tunnel **is** correctly
  zoned in `ifindex_to_zone_id` (`Some(60779)` = `vpn`); the to-zone read simply
  does not consult that map.
- Disposition with an explicit permit and default-deny: **action Deny**,
  `policy_id=4294967295` (`DEFAULT_POLICY_SENTINEL_ID`).

## #6714 — config: three more multi-value leaf readers still drop authored values (nested-bracket tails, proxy-ARP after a range, repeated 'commands' leaves) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-21)

## Summary

Three compiler arms still read a `multi: true` leaf incompletely and silently
drop authored values. Same root cause and same fix pattern as the arms widened
in #6659 / PR #6673 — these three were confirmed during that work but were
deliberately left out of scope rather than folded in.

Grouped because they are one shape with one remedy, not because any is
individually trivial: each is a **silent value drop**, where the operator
authored something the compiler never installs and nothing warns.

## The three

1. **Nested-bracket tails inside a hierarchical value block are one-sided.**
   `firewallMatchValues` reads only `vn.Keys[0]` per child, so a bracketed list
   nested inside a hierarchical block contributes only its first element.

2. **Proxy-ARP list/range mixtures drop everything after a range.** An authored
   list that mixes discrete addresses and a range stops contributing at the
   range.

3. **`FindChild("commands")` reads only the first repeated `commands` leaf.**
   Repeated `commands` statements silently collapse to the first.

## Why these matter individually

Each drops configuration the operator wrote, with no diagnostic. For (1) and
(2) the consequence is a firewall/NAT match or a proxy-ARP set narrower than
authored — which, depending on which value survives, is either an unintended
narrowing or an unintended broadening of what the rule covers. For (3) it is a
remediation action that does not run.

The #6659 cohort has repeatedly shown that these read as cosmetic and are not:
the same class of defect produced a static-NAT selection flip and two
fail-closed→fail-open conversions in PR #6673 alone.

**MEDIUM.** No attacker needed — an ordinary authored config triggers it, in
the bracketed and repeated spellings the schema explicitly permits. Blast

## #6715 — config: forwarding-table dangling-reference warning claims load-balancing 'would be silently disabled' when the valid scalar still renders [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

## Summary

`pkg/config/compiler_validate_strict_routing.go:207-219` warns that
load-balancing "would be silently disabled" when a `routing-options
forwarding-table export` names an undefined policy. That is false whenever a
**valid** scalar is also present: only the non-selected token is ignored, and
the valid policy still renders and still load-balances.

## Why this is worth its own issue rather than a comment tweak

It is the same falsity class that PR #6673 corrected on the NAT side, and the
reason it matters is not tidiness. A diagnostic that overstates the
consequence sends an operator to fix something that is not broken — and, worse,
teaches them that this warning does not mean what it says, which is how a
later true instance gets ignored.

After PR #6673's fold this is, as far as that work established, the **only
known-false diagnostic left in this cluster**. The NAT-side equivalents were
corrected there (`emitMatchAddr` now picks the tolerant-path suffix per value,
so the message distinguishes the selected value — which really does drop the
rule — from a non-selected one, which never reaches the dataplane and leaves
the rule translating).

## Fix direction

Mirror the NAT-side fix: decide per value whether the reference is the one that
actually renders, and word the consequence accordingly. Concretely, the warning
should distinguish:

- the dangling reference **is** the selected/rendering value → load-balancing
  really is disabled, current wording is correct;
- a valid scalar renders and the dangling reference is a non-selected token →
  say the token is ignored, and name the policy that **does** take effect.

The second form is the one an operator can act on, because it tells them
whether their traffic is currently balanced.

## #6716 — daemon: DHCP/feed callbacks capture ActiveConfig BEFORE applySem — a queued apply overwrites a newer commit and republishes a revoked api-auth credential [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

Found by an independent Codex review of #6645 (the #5561 REST authorization PR). **Pre-existing on `master`** — `pkg/daemon/daemon_dhcp.go`, `daemon_feeds.go` and `daemon_apply.go` are byte-identical on `origin/master` and on that branch, so this is not introduced by the REST-auth work. Filed separately rather than folded, because it is a daemon apply-serialization defect, not a request-path one.

## Defect

The background apply callbacks read `d.store.ActiveConfig()` **before** acquiring `applySem`, and then apply that captured pointer under the semaphore. A commit that lands in between is silently overwritten by the older config in every subsystem `applyConfigLocked` reconciles.

- `pkg/daemon/daemon_dhcp.go` `onDHCPAddressChange` — `activeCfg := d.store.ActiveConfig()` then `d.applyConfig(activeCfg)`.
- `pkg/daemon/daemon_feeds.go` `ensureFeedManager`'s `onUpdate` — `activeCfg := d.store.ActiveConfig()` then `d.applyConfigResult(activeCfg)`.
- The semaphore is taken only inside `pkg/daemon/daemon_apply.go` `applyConfig` / `applyConfigResult`.

## Trigger (credential republish — the sharp edge)

1. Active config A carries `system services web-management ... api-auth` secret `old-secret`.
2. A commit of config B (rotating to `new-secret`) acquires `applySem`.
3. While the store still holds A, a DHCP lease change or a feed refresh fires and captures A, then blocks on `applySem`.
4. B is promoted and applied; `reconcileWebManagement` publishes `new-secret` via `managementReconciler.reconcileTo` -> `srv.ReplaceAuth`.
5. The callback wakes and applies A. The same reconcile republishes `old-secret`.
6. `store.ActiveConfig()` still reports B, but the live listener honours the **revoked** `old-secret` until some later reconcile happens to run.

The same inversion re-applies any other A-vs-B difference (bind address, TLS, and everything else `applyConfigLocked` touches), so the credential case is the sharpest instance of a general defect, not the whole of it.

## Second half: a false applied-stamp

`applyConfig` calls `d.store.MarkActiveApplied()` after the apply returns. On the inverted path it stamps **B** as applied while **A** is what was actually applied. `handleConfigSync`'s #4957 converged shortcut then skips re-applying B on a peer sync, so the divergence can persist across a reconnect.

## Suggested shape

Read `ActiveConfig()` **inside** the semaphore. The callbacks want "apply whatever is active now", not "apply what was active when I woke up" — so `applyConfig`/`applyConfigResult` could take a `func() *config.Config` (or a nil-config sentinel meaning "re-read under the lock") rather than a pre-captured pointer. The re-read also makes `MarkActiveApplied` honest by construction.

A guard should drive a real inversion: hold a fake apply, fire a callback that captures A, land a commit of B, release, and assert the live auth snapshot (and the applied digest) reflect B.


---

## #6717 — api/daemon: publishing a nil auth snapshot races the ASYNC retirement of the old routable listener — an unauthenticated read window on the retiring socket [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-21)

Found by an independent Codex review of #6645 (the #5561 REST authorization PR). **Pre-existing on `master`**: `pkg/api/listener.go` is untouched by that branch, and the nil-auth publish in `pkg/daemon/management.go` sits in the same place, behind the same gate, as it does on `origin/master` (#6645 moved only the *non-nil* publish earlier). Filed separately rather than folded.

## Defect

Retiring a listener leg is **signalled, not awaited**, while the auth snapshot every leg shares is swapped to `nil` synchronously.

- `stopLegLocked` (`pkg/api/listener.go`) closes a channel and returns; the actual `Shutdown` + listener close run in a goroutine.
- `ReconcileHTTP` / `ReconcileHTTPS` therefore return with the old leg possibly still accepting and serving.
- All legs read one `s.auth` pointer (`dynamicAuthMiddleware`, `pkg/api/server.go`), and a nil snapshot is a **pass-through**.

## Trigger

1. A routable HTTPS/HTTP management listener is live with `api-auth` configured.
2. A commit moves the bind to loopback (or disables the leg) **and** removes `api-auth` — a legitimate pairing, since the #4047/#5127 clamp only requires the credential off-loopback.
3. The reconcile rebinds, the fingerprints advance, the nil-auth gate passes, and `m.srv.ReplaceAuth(nil)` stores nil.
4. The old routable socket has not finished shutting down. A request that reaches it takes the nil branch and is served **unauthenticated**.

Mutating requests still fail #5561's principal guard, so the exposure is **reads**: config export, sessions, events, logs — i.e. an unauthenticated disclosure window on an address that was reachable off-box a moment ago.

## Suggested shape

Make the nil (loosening) direction wait for the retiring legs it is loosening. The tightening direction can stay where it is — #6645 already argues that applying a stricter snapshot to whatever is live cannot fail open. Options: have `stopLegLocked` return a drain handle the nil publish joins before storing nil, or publish nil only once every retired leg's serve goroutine has exited.

A guard needs a leg whose shutdown is held open (an injectable drain), a nil publish committed while it is, and an assertion that a request landing on the retiring socket is still challenged.

## #6718 — daemon: first-commit-confirmed rollback (prevCfg==nil) never reconciles web management — the abandoned commit's listener and api-auth credential stay live [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

Found by an independent Codex review of #6645 (the #5561 REST authorization PR). **Pre-existing on `master`**: `pkg/daemon/daemon_apply_commit.go` and `pkg/daemon/bootstrap.go` are untouched by that branch. Filed separately rather than folded.

## Defect

The first-commit `commit confirmed` timeout path reverts the store but never reconciles web management, so the listener and credential the abandoned commit created stay live.

In `pkg/daemon/daemon_apply_commit.go`, the rollback timer callback calls `d.store.PromoteRollback(gen)`. When `prevCfg == nil` (the #1922 Item 1b case — a *first* commit on a fresh store), it runs `d.enterBootstrapMode()` and **returns**. Only the non-nil branch below reaches `d.applyConfigLocked`, which is the sole caller of `reconcileWebManagement`. `enterBootstrapMode` (`pkg/daemon/bootstrap.go`) deliberately preserves "the management lifeline" and does not touch `d.mgmt`.

## Trigger

1. Fresh appliance, empty store, bootstrap mode.
2. First `commit confirmed` enables routable `system services web-management` with `api-auth` credential B.
3. The operator never confirms; the timer fires.
4. `PromoteRollback` returns `prevCfg == nil`. The store is back to the empty tree and marked never-committed; interface/FRR/dataplane takeover is unwound.
5. The listener stays bound where the abandoned config put it, and B keeps authenticating. Under #5561 B still yields a full-power credential principal — authorised by a config that is no longer active, and that the box has formally abandoned.

The management endpoint the *empty* config implies is the flag-default loopback bind with no credential; the box is left serving the abandoned commit's endpoint instead.

## Tension to resolve, not just a missing call

"Keep the management lifeline" is the reason this branch skips the reconcile, and it is a real requirement: reverting to bootstrap must not strand the operator. But *lifeline* and *the abandoned commit's off-box bind plus its credential* are not the same thing. The right shape is probably an explicit bootstrap-management reconcile — revert to the flag-default (loopback) endpoint and drop the abandoned credential — rather than either skipping the reconcile or running the generic one.

A guard needs a first-commit-confirmed timeout over a fixture whose commit enabled a credentialed off-box bind, asserting the live auth snapshot and bind afterwards.

## #6719 — daemon: HA startup can install a STALE management auth snapshot (start derives ActiveConfig outside m.mu), and d.mgmt is published without synchronization [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

Found by an independent Codex review of #6645 (the #5561 REST authorization PR). **Pre-existing on `master`**: `pkg/daemon/daemon_run.go` and `daemon_run_servers.go` are untouched by that branch, and `managementReconciler.start`/`startTo` are byte-identical to `origin/master`. Filed separately rather than folded.

## Two defects, one ordering

### 1. `d.mgmt` is published without synchronization

`d.mgmt = newManagementReconciler(...)` is a plain field write in `startHTTPServer` (`pkg/daemon/daemon_run_servers.go`). Cluster comms are started **earlier** in `Daemon.Run` (`pkg/daemon/daemon_run.go`, `d.startClusterComms(ctx)`), and the peer-sync apply path reads `d.mgmt` in `reconcileWebManagement` (`pkg/daemon/management.go`). There is no happens-before edge between the write and that read — a data race on a pointer that gates the management auth reconcile. Worth confirming under `-race` with a peer sync driven during startup.

### 2. A stale auth snapshot can win the startup race

`managementReconciler.start` derives `m.desired(m.d.store.ActiveConfig())` **before** `startTo` takes `m.mu`. So:

1. Startup reads active config A (with credential A).
2. A peer sync promotes B, which rotates/revokes A's credential, and calls `reconcile`.
3. That reconcile takes `m.mu` first, finds `m.srv == nil` (nothing started yet), and returns a no-op.
4. `startTo` then takes `m.mu` and installs the server built from the **stale** A.

Credential A stays accepted until some later reconcile or a restart. Same window applies to the bind address and TLS.

## Suggested shape

Read `ActiveConfig()` **under** `m.mu` inside `startTo` (or move the derive inside the lock), so a reconcile that loses the race to the lock is re-read rather than dropped; and publish `d.mgmt` before cluster comms start, or behind the same mutex/atomic its readers use. Ordering the two `Run` phases is the blunter fix and may be the right one — the reconciler has no dependency on the cluster runtime.

A guard can hold `m.mu` from a test seam, drive a reconcile that no-ops on `m.srv == nil`, release, and assert the started server carries the *newer* snapshot.

## #6720 — daemon/cluster: tolerant peer sync PROMOTES a config then skips its management reconcile on a topology/identity backstop — a synced api-auth revocation never reaches the listener [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

Found by an independent Codex review of #6645 (the #5561 REST authorization PR). **Pre-existing on `master`**: `pkg/daemon/daemon_apply_commit.go` is untouched by that branch. Filed separately rather than folded.

## Defect: a strict-vs-tolerant outcome difference

On the peer-sync path, `d.store.SyncApply(...)` **promotes** the peer config to active first, and only afterwards do the two fail-closed backstops run:

- `clusterTopologyCommitPreflight` (#5840 standalone<->cluster transition)
- `clusterIdentityCommitPreflight` (#6192 node-id / cluster-id change)

Both `return nil, err` **before** `applyConfigLocked`, which is the only caller of `reconcileWebManagement`. The strict operator path checks the same two transitions **before** promotion (earlier in the same file), so the two paths diverge in outcome, not just in ordering.

## Trigger

A divergent or older peer pushes config B that carries **both** a topology (or cluster-identity) transition **and** a revocation of `api-auth` credential A.

1. `SyncApply` promotes B: `ActiveConfig()` is now B, and the store is persisted.
2. The topology/identity backstop rejects the live apply and returns.
3. The management reconcile never runs, so the listener keeps honouring **A** — a credential the now-active config has revoked — until a restart or some later successful apply.

The backstops are correct to refuse to arm the dataplane (the HA runtime is boot-only). The bug is that they also skip the *authorization* reconcile, which has no such constraint: `reconcileWebManagement` deliberately runs early in `applyConfigLocked` precisely so a committed revocation survives an apply that aborts later.

## Suggested shape

Run the management reconcile for the promoted config **before** the topology/identity backstops return — or hoist those checks above the `SyncApply` promotion so the tolerant path matches the strict one and nothing is promoted that will not be reconciled. The second is the larger change but removes the divergence rather than patching one consequence of it.

A guard needs a tolerant sync of a config that both trips a backstop and revokes a credential, asserting the live auth snapshot no longer honours the old secret.

## #6721 — daemon/api: a BOOT management bind failure is never retried — m.srv stays nil so every later reconcile no-ops, and an initial HTTPS failure records its fingerprint as converged [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-21)

Found by an independent Codex review of #6645 (the #5561 REST authorization PR). **Pre-existing on `master`**: `managementReconciler.start`/`startTo`/`reconcileTo`'s `m.srv == nil` early return and `pkg/api/listener.go` are byte-identical to `origin/master`. Availability only — no authorization consequence. Filed separately rather than folded.

## Defect: the documented retry does not happen

Two places state that a failed management bind is retried by the next commit:

- `managementReconciler.startTo` — "A bind failure is returned (the caller logs it non-fatally); the next commit retries."
- `startHTTPServer` (`pkg/daemon/daemon_run_servers.go`) — "the next commit's `reconcileWebManagement` retries the bind."

Neither holds for a failure at **boot**.

### HTTP

`startTo` returns on `srv.Start(ctx)` error **before** assigning `m.srv`. Every later `reconcileTo` begins with `if m.srv == nil { return nil }`, so no reconcile ever retries. The listener is dead until a daemon restart, and `show system services` reports it Failed (#6401) forever regardless of what the operator does.

### HTTPS

An initial HTTPS bind/cert failure is swallowed inside `pkg/api/listener.go`, while `startTo` still records the desired TLS fingerprint as converged (`m.cur = endpointOf(next)`). A subsequent reconcile sees the fingerprint already at the desired value and skips the rebind, so there is no retry debt for the HTTPS leg either — the opposite of the day-2 path, which deliberately leaves the fingerprint unrecorded on failure so the next commit retries.

## Trigger

Boot with the management port held by another process (or a bind address not yet present). Release the port and make an unrelated commit: nothing rebinds. Only `systemctl restart xpfd` recovers.

## Suggested shape

The day-2 path already has the right pattern — retain, do not record the fingerprint, retry on the next reconcile. Boot should join it rather than have its own: keep the `api.Server` object on a boot bind failure (so `m.srv` is non-nil and reconciles are live) and leave the failed leg's fingerprint unrecorded, letting the existing retry-debt logic do the work. The HTTPS half needs its swallowed error surfaced to `startTo` so the fingerprint is not recorded as converged.

Guards: a boot bind failure followed by a reconcile must bind; and an initial HTTPS failure must leave the TLS fingerprint unconverged so the next reconcile retries.

## #6723 — docs(daemon): deletedPolicyRuntimeIDs still calls the policy-rematch half 'deferred' after it shipped [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

## Gap

`pkg/daemon/daemon_policy_invalidate.go`, in the header of `deletedPolicyRuntimeIDs` (~line 20):

> Only DELETED policies are reported. A policy whose match/action CHANGED but whose zones+name are unchanged keeps the same stable key, is present in both maps, and is therefore NOT reported here — that in-progress re-evaluation is **the deferred #4234 modified-policy (policy-rematch) half, intentionally out of scope** for the Junos-default deletion-clear.

The first half is still correct and worth keeping: `deletedPolicyRuntimeIDs` genuinely does not report changed policies, and the stable-key reasoning explains why. The stale part is "**the deferred** #4234 … half". It is not deferred — `changedPolicyRuntimeIDs` in the same file implements it, gated on `newCfg.Security.PolicyRematch`, and `clearSessionsForPolicyChanges` runs it on every commit alongside the deletion-clear.

## Why it matters

This is the first comment a reader hits when tracing commit-time session invalidation, and it points at an issue number that is now closed as implemented. Anyone following the pointer concludes a shipped, security-relevant behaviour (in-progress sessions re-evaluated against a tightened policy) is missing — and either re-implements it or, worse, tells an operator xpf does not do it.

## Fix

Reword to say the changed-policy case is handled by `changedPolicyRuntimeIDs` / `clearSessionsForModifiedPolicies` under `policy-rematch`, and keep the stable-key rationale for why THIS function does not report it. Check the sibling comments in the same file for the same phrasing while there.

Found while triaging #4234 to closure (2026-08-01). Doc-only: no runtime behaviour is wrong.
