## #6724 — cluster/heartbeat: the boot-epoch flock orders lock acquisition, not incarnations — an older overlapping xpfd can strand the surviving newer one below its peer's floor [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

`withEpochFileLock` (`pkg/cluster/heartbeat_epoch.go`) serializes the boot-epoch
read-modify-write across processes, but it does **not** order incarnations: it
serializes by lock ACQUISITION, and there is no happens-before edge from daemon
start — or from survivorship — to that acquisition. `heartbeatBootEpoch`
publishes the wall-clock seed and starts emitting *before* its worker reaches
the lock, deliberately (a storage fault must not take a healthy node off the
air), so the two orders are independent.

Reachable because nothing in xpf enforces a single daemon instance: there is no
pidfile, and the gRPC listener sets `SO_REUSEPORT` (`pkg/grpcapi/server.go`), so
a second `xpfd` does not fail on a port collision.

Schedule:

1. Older incarnation A publishes seed `a`; its refine worker is delayed.
2. Newer incarnation B publishes seed `b > a`, acquires the lock first, persists `b`.
3. A acquires the lock second, reads `b`, and raises **itself** to `b+1`, then persists that.
4. The peer's floor latches `b+1` — the OLDER incarnation — and refuses B at `b`.
5. A exits; B survives, and every frame B sends is below the peer's floor.

Measured on `fix/6169-heartbeat-boot-epoch-v2`
(`TestConcurrentIncarnationsAreOrderedByLockAcquisition_6669`).

**Why it cannot be closed with this file alone.** Refinement only matters when
the persisted value exceeds our own seed — and "a predecessor wrote it after a
backward clock step" and "a concurrent newer incarnation wrote it" leave the
identical file. Separating them needs state the design does not keep: a
lifetime-held liveness lock (so a refiner can tell another incarnation is alive),
or a writer identity persisted alongside the epoch. Both are larger changes than
the epoch itself.

**What #6669 already did.** The unrecoverable half is closed: refinement is now
re-run on every later heartbeat start (`Manager.refreshBootEpoch`, wired through
`initHeartbeatEpochState`), so the stranded incarnation climbs back above the
file at the next `StartHeartbeat` — a DHCP-triggered VRF rebind or the HA comms
restart. Before that, `sync.Once` made the state last for the life of the
process: the peer refused the node until a full daemon restart, even after the
other incarnation had exited.

**What remains.** Between the mis-ordering and that next heartbeat start, this

## Gap

`pkg/config/schema_walk.go`, in the `walkSchemaNode` doc block (~line 297) and the open-world branch (~309-315):

> `closed:` closed-world enforcement flag (#4313). … Inherited from any ancestor subtree whose `schemaNode.closedWorld` is set; **false (open-world) everywhere in production today.**
> … Only a subtree that opted in … reaches this branch; **no production subtree does so today.**
> … Open-world (the default for every production subtree) … Behaviour here is **byte-identical to pre-#4313.**

All three claims are false on current master. Ten production subtrees set `closedWorld: true`:

- `pkg/config/schema_security.go` — 9: `nat … then` (:538), `nat64` (:614), `natv6v4` (:628), IKE `proposal` (:907), IKE `dead-peer-detection` (:985), IPsec `proposal` (:1039), IPsec `dead-peer-detection` (:1114), `vpn-monitor` (:1188), `traffic-selector` (:1215)
- `pkg/config/schema_system.go` — 1: `master-password` (:133)

and the reject branch is exercised by dedicated tests (`schema_closedworld_nat64_4313_test.go`, `schema_closedworld_ike_proposal_4313_test.go`, `schema_closedworld_ipsec_4313_test.go`, `schema_closedworld_ipsec_proposal_4313_test.go`), which assert the typo is rejected AND that valid config still commits clean.

## Why it matters

Reading it, an engineer concludes the gate is inert — and either re-implements it, "enables" something already on, or tells an operator that IPsec/NAT64 typos still commit silently when they now fail commit. It is also what made #4313 look unstarted during triage.

State that the flag is opt-in per subtree, that ten subtrees currently opt in (or point at the schema files rather than enumerating, so it cannot rot again), and that the open-world branch is the default for subtrees that have NOT opted in — dropping the "no production subtree" and "byte-identical" claims.

Second instance of this pattern found today; see #6723 for the same class in `pkg/daemon/daemon_policy_invalidate.go`. Doc-only: no runtime behaviour is wrong.

## #6726 — test(ddns): TestRFC2136ReplaceOwnedAdoptsOwnNameOnReadd binds a fixed ephemeral port and flakes under concurrency [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-02)

## Symptom

`pkg/ddns` `TestRFC2136ReplaceOwnedAdoptsOwnNameOnReadd` fails intermittently:

```
backend_rfc2136_test.go:792: tcp listen: listen tcp 127.0.0.1:60670: bind: address already in use
```

Observed twice today on unrelated PRs (#6645 and #6722), both of which touch **zero** Go files under `pkg/ddns`. Re-runs pass: 3 targeted, plus full-package, plus full `go test ./...`.

## Why it matters more than an ordinary flake

This produces a **false red that mimics a real test failure**, in a package the failing PR did not touch. On a box running several build agents concurrently the ephemeral-port range gets contended and the collision becomes likely rather than rare. The cost is not the re-run — it is that a reviewer or an automated gate reads `FAIL pkg/ddns` and either blames the diff under review or, worse, dismisses a genuine failure elsewhere in the same run as "that flaky ddns thing".

## Cause

The test binds a specific port rather than asking the kernel for a free one, so two concurrent runs — or one run racing anything else on the box — collide.

## Fix

Listen on `127.0.0.1:0` and read the assigned port back from `l.Addr().(*net.TCPAddr).Port`, threading it into wherever the fixed constant is used. If a fixed port is genuinely required by the DNS-update protocol path under test, retry the bind on a fresh port rather than failing the test, and skip with a clear message if no port can be obtained.

Check the rest of `pkg/ddns` for the same pattern while there — a fixed-port listener in one test usually has siblings.

Found while triaging concurrent agent runs (2026-08-02). Not caused by either PR that surfaced it.

## #6727 — security/zones: xpf zones the BASE interface when the operator zones a UNIT — Junos zones logical units [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

## Gap

`set security zones security-zone vpnb interfaces st0.1` also zones **`st0`** in xpf's model. `pkg/dataplane/userspace/zones.go:68-79`:

```go
iface := config.CanonicalInterfaceUnitRef(rawIface)
if _, exists := out[iface]; !exists { out[iface] = zoneName }
if base, unit, ok := strings.Cut(iface, "."); ok && base != "" {
    if _, exists := out[base]; !exists { out[base] = zoneName }   // base inherits the UNIT's zone
    if unit != "" { continue }
}
```

Combined with `snapshotLinuxName`'s unit-0 collapse (`pkg/dataplane/userspace/interfaces.go:444-446` — `if unit.Number == 0 { return config.LinuxIfName(ifName) }`), the base row and unit 0 share one ifindex. So a zone the operator placed on unit 1 lands on the ifindex **unit 0 forwards out of**.

Measured (`buildInterfaceZoneMap` + `buildInterfaceSnapshots`, `buildLinkSnapshot` mocked; config = `st0` units 0 and 1 with the zone on `st0.1` only):

```
zoneByInterface = {"st0":"vpnb", "st0.1":"vpnb", ...}
snap name="st0"    linux="st0"    ifindex=42  parent=0   zone="vpnb"
snap name="st0.0"  linux="st0"    ifindex=42  parent=42  zone=""
snap name="st0.1"  linux="st0.1"  ifindex=43  parent=42  zone="vpnb"
```

Consequence: traffic egressing `st0.0` — a logical unit the operator deliberately left in **no** zone — adjudicates against `(lan, vpnb)`, and a `from-zone lan to-zone vpnb permit` matches with a real rule index rather than the default-policy sentinel.

## Why this is a parity gap and not a bug in one code path

**Junos zones logical units.** `st0.0` and `st0.1` are different units and can be in different zones, or one can be in none. xpf's model collapses them, and it does so *consistently* — the ingress half resolves the same ifindex to the same inherited zone (`userspaceSkipsIngressInterface` returns false for the base row precisely because its zone is non-empty). That consistency is why it is defensible as current behaviour, and why fixing only the egress half would be worse than leaving it: it would make a packet arriving on `st0.0` be from-zone `vpnb` while one leaving resolves to-zone 0.

So the fix is not a one-sided guard. It needs the unit/base distinction carried across the Go→Rust boundary on **both** halves — e.g. an `InterfaceSnapshot.ZoneInherited bool` set by `buildInterfaceSnapshots` when the zone came from the propagation above rather than a direct reference, with ingress and egress both honouring it.

## Provenance

Surfaced while gating PR #6722. That PR attempted a Rust-side scoping fix (`ifindex_own_zone_id`) and it is **inert**: the distinction does not survive the Go→Rust boundary, because Go has already propagated. #6722 is being closed on the smaller, honest option — accept the propagated behaviour and document it — with this filed as the Junos-correct follow-up. Do not confuse the two: nothing in #6722 addresses this.

Severity: this changes which policy adjudicates real forwarded traffic, and an operator reading their config would not predict it. Not a fail-open in the sense of bypassing policy — a permit still has to be authored for the inherited zone pair — but the zone pair is not the one the config describes.

`pkg/routing/xfrm.go` creates the device as `LinuxIfName(vpn.BindInterface)`

## #6734 — api: authSlot is substituted for nil in two places; a future nil-nil call site would pin a slot the handler never reads [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

`pkg/api` substitutes a fresh `authSlot` for a nil in **two independent places**,
so a future call site that passes nil to BOTH would give the handler one slot and
the leg a different one — and the retirement pin would silently become a no-op.

- `Server.listenerHandler` (`pkg/api/server.go:724-731`) substitutes when
  building the handler, and the handler closes over whatever it substituted.
- `Server.serveLegLocked` (`pkg/api/listener.go:62-65`) substitutes again when
  registering the leg, and the leg's `slot` is what `trackRetiring` pins.

If both substitute, the leg is pinned to slot Y while every request on that leg
is judged by slot X. `authSlot.pin` / `tighten` then operate on an object nothing
reads, so a retired listener keeps following the server-wide snapshot — exactly
the #5561 round-14 defect the pin exists to prevent (a credential committed for
the NEW address becoming valid on the address the same commit RETIRED).

## Not currently reachable

All four production leg-construction sites thread ONE non-nil slot through both
layers, verified during the #6645 round-16 review:

- `NewServer` HTTP (`server.go:645`) and HTTPS (`server.go:651`)
- `ReconcileHTTP` (`listener.go:250`)
- `ReconcileHTTPS` (`listener.go:296`)

So this is latent, not a live bug. It is filed rather than fixed inside #6645
because closing it properly means changing ownership — the leg should own its
slot and hand it to the handler, or a single constructor should return
`(*http.Server, *authSlot)` together — which touches all four sites, and #6645
deliberately kept its runtime delta to the one real regression it was fixing.

Note the possibility is NEW relative to `origin/master`: master had no per-leg
slot at all (every leg read one shared snapshot), so the divergence could not
exist there.

## Suggested fix

Make the substitution impossible rather than defensive: one constructor that
allocates the slot and returns it alongside the server, with `listenerHandler`
and `serveLegLocked` both taking a slot they are not allowed to replace. A guard
test should assert that a leg's `slot` is the same pointer the handler reads —

## #6736 — config: the PACKED per-interface host-inbound body under `security zones ... interfaces <if>` compiles to NO override — silent admission loss [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

## Problem

The per-interface `host-inbound-traffic` override under
`security zones security-zone <z> interfaces <if>` is compiled only when the
body arrives as a **child node**. In the hierarchical **packed** spelling the
body sits on the member's own `Keys`, and the override is **silently dropped**:

```
security {
    zones {
        security-zone trust {
            interfaces ge-0/0/0.0 host-inbound-traffic system-services ssh;
        }
    }
}
```

`parseHostInboundNode` (`pkg/config/compiler_security_zones.go:10`) switches on
`hit.Name()` over `n.Children`; the packed form has no such children.
`compileZones` reaches it via `iface.FindChildren("host-inbound-traffic")`
(`compiler_security_zones.go`, the `case "interfaces":` arm), which finds
nothing, so `hib` stays nil and no `InterfaceHostInbound` entry is recorded.

This is the same #2419 packed-body class as #6525 / #6694 / #6672 / #6665 /
#6662, on a different dimension: #6525 fixed the **membership** side of this
exact stanza (and stopped the packed tokens being compiled as phantom interface
names); the **admission** side is untouched.

## Measured (at `fix/6525-zone-compact-leaf`, i.e. after the #6525 fix)

Same authored intent, three spellings:

| authored | membership | per-interface override |
|---|---|---|
| `set security zones security-zone Z interfaces ge-0/0/0 host-inbound-traffic system-services ssh` | `[ge-0/0/0]` | `hib[ge-0/0/0] = {SystemServices:[ssh]}` |
| `interfaces ge-0/0/0.0 { host-inbound-traffic { system-services ssh; } }` (hierarchical, body as child) | `[ge-0/0/0.0]` | `hib[ge-0/0/0.0] = {SystemServices:[ssh]}` |
| `interfaces ge-0/0/0.0 host-inbound-traffic system-services ssh;` (hierarchical, PACKED) | `[ge-0/0/0.0]` | **absent** |
| `interfaces { ge-0/0/0.0 host-inbound-traffic system-services ssh; }` (block with a packed child) | `[ge-0/0/0.0]` | **absent** |

## #6737 — config/userspace-dp: an in-range st<N> PHYSICAL interface silently loses transit zone adjudication [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

An interface name is wildcard-authorable and there is no reserved `st` namespace, so an operator
can legitimately name a physical NIC `st5`. PR #6691 adds an exclusion keyed on the interface
NAME rather than on the presence of a VPN, and an in-range `st<0..65535>` name is classified as a
secure tunnel whether or not any `bind-interface` names it.

**Reachable, verified rather than assumed.** `config.ValidateDeviceMapLogicalName("st5", nil)`
returns nil — the validator accepts bare alphanumeric forms
(`pkg/config/schema_validators_devicemap.go:88-109`) — and grepping for a reservation in
`pkg/config/schema_interfaces.go` finds only a VLAN-4095 comment.

```
set chassis device-map interface st5 pci 0000:09:00.0
set interfaces st5 unit 0 family inet address 10.9.9.1/24
set security zones security-zone trust interfaces st5.0
```

A probe on this configuration gives `snapshotLinuxName=st5.0`, `skipUnit=true`, `skipBase=true`:
the NIC is dropped from the ingress-adjudication map, the AF_XDP binding plan and the RSS
allowlist. Its transit traffic then takes the kernel/FRR path with **no xpf zone policy** — a
silent transit-policy bypass on an interface `origin/master` adjudicated normally.

Bounded: host-inbound denies still cover it (`junosHostScope[trust]` contains `st5` and `st5.0`),
so the bypass is **transit-only**, not host-inbound.

**Sites:** `pkg/dataplane/userspace/maps_sync.go:1681`
(`case config.IsSecureTunnelIfName(base):`) and
`userspace-dp/src/server/helpers/planning.rs:310`. Differs from master, which had no `st` arm in
`userspaceSkipsIngressInterface` at all.

**This is disclosed, not hidden** — `userspace-dp/src/server/README.md` states the exclusion keys
on the name and that authoring an `st`-named interface without a route-based VPN is not a
supported topology. The boundary is defensible: in-range `st<N>` is exactly the set that could
collide with a VPN binding the same name, and out-of-range never can.

The gap worth closing is that the failure is **silent**. A supported-topology boundary should be
enforced, not assumed. Candidate fix: a commit-time reject, or a #4168-style warning, for an
in-range `st<N>` interface with no matching `bind-interface` — turning a silent transit bypass
into a loud error at the point the operator can act on it.

## #6738 — dataplane: buildInterfaceNetworkdModels reconstructs the xfrmi name from the ref, so a bare bind-interface st0 unit address is never programmed [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-21)

Follow-up to #6729, which covers `resolveInterfaceRef` reconstructing a secure-tunnel name from
the ref. The second non-adopter has **two** defects and only the first is filed.

`pkg/dataplane/compiler_iface.go:754-757` — `buildInterfaceNetworkdModels`:

```go
unitName, _ := config.XFRMIfNameAndID(fmt.Sprintf("%s.%d", ifName, unitNum))
if _, err := result.cachedInterfaceByName(unitName); err != nil { continue }
```

#6730 covers the over-match (the raw prefix branch dropping every unit of `start0`). This is the
other half: line 757 **reconstructs the device name from the ref** instead of resolving it from
the authored `bind-interface`.

Under the canonical bare `bind-interface st0`, `unitName` becomes `st0.0` while the device
created is `st0`. `cachedInterfaceByName` misses, the unit gets no `ManagedInterfaces` entry, and
its configured address (e.g. `10.5.5.1/30`) is **never programmed on the kernel device**.

Confirmed nothing else programs it: `pkg/routing/xfrm.go` contains no address handling at all
(grep for `Addr|address` is empty), and `mapZoneInterface`'s `reconcileInterfaceAddresses` is
soft-skipped on the same missing-device path.

**Not a regression** — the code is untouched by #6691, so this does not block it. It is filed
because #6691's README scope table offers the per-site disposition as evidence that its claim is
no broader than its sweep, and for this row the disposition column lists only the over-match.
#6729 is scoped to `resolveInterfaceRef` and does not cover this site.

Fix shape: resolve through `Config.SecureTunnelUnitNetdev`, the single resolver #6691 introduced,
rather than reconstructing `<base>.<unit>`.

Note this does not affect #6691's FIB measurement: the snapshot merges configured addresses with
live ones at `pkg/dataplane/userspace/interfaces.go:289`, so the connected prefix reaches the FIB
regardless.

Found by the hostile review of #6691 at `0403fa089`.

## #6740 — dataplane: guard the 1 Hz status-path XDPLinks/VlanSubInterfaces reads with m.mu [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

## Problem

Pre-existing fatal-crash-class race named honestly by the #2114 research (r71 Codex m1 / r72 Codex m1, adjudicated r73-r74 as OUT of the A3 pre-arm scope): the 1 Hz userspace status path ranges the root Manager's `xdpLinks` Go map (`pkg/dataplane/userspace/maps_sync.go` status snapshot path) while `CompileUserspaceShim` can mutate it before taking the userspace `m.mu` — and the same shape applies to the exported `VlanSubInterfaces` Go map (read during the swap path at `loader.go`'s `swapXDPEntryProg` and by the status helper, written by `CompileUserspaceShim` at `loader.go:201`). A concurrent map read/write here is a fatal runtime.throw.

This is a POST-arm Compile-vs-status race with no Start-window overlap, so it is NOT part of #2114's A3 admission gate (which scopes to the pre-arm window). PR #2114 does not worsen it; the gate's uniform registry rule deliberately does not cover the Go link maps.

## Proposed fix (cheap, per the r73 adjudication)

A one-field guard: take `m.mu` (or a dedicated small mutex) around the `xdpLinks`/`VlanSubInterfaces` reads in the 1 Hz status path and the writers in `CompileUserspaceShim`/`swapXDPEntryProg`. The #2114 A3 test seams (registryLookupHook-style lock-ownership legs) give a ready pattern for the regression test: hold the writer's section and assert the status reader blocks.

## Acceptance

- `-race` regression covering the status-path read vs the compile/swap write.
- No lock held across netlink/BPF syscalls (scoped sections only).

Refs: #2114 (research §10 residual), follow-up context in #6739.

## #6741 — dataplane AC2: Close/Teardown cannot drain an in-flight registry operation (lease/refcount design item) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-28)

## Problem

Two pre-existing dataplane-lifecycle hazards named (not fixed) by the #2114 research, assigned to their own follow-up per r77 Codex m2 (they are broader than #6739's FirstCommit+cluster scope):

1. **Retained-generation confusion on the recurrence paths.** `bootstrap.go`'s enterBootstrapMode Teardown-RETAINs the Manager; `Cleanup` removes the pin tree (`loader.go`'s Cleanup) but Teardown does not close the `m.maps`/`m.programs` FDs, so the retained handles reference LIVE FD-BACKED OBJECTS OF AN OBSOLETE FORWARDING GENERATION while a re-`Start` creates FRESH maps (`loadOrCreatePinnedShimMap`). A retained-proceed method (the #2114 A3 two-state rule deliberately preserves master's proceed-on-retained behavior) can then mutate the obsolete object — a mutation that SUCCEEDS yet never reaches the live generation — and multi-map readers can report a mixed old/new generation. The standalone first-commit timeout path (`daemon_apply_commit.go`) Teardown-retains and re-arms the same way, so this is not cluster-specific.

2. **Teardown close-in-use.** cilium/ebpf documents "It is not safe to close a map which is used by other goroutines" (`map.go`). The #2114 A3 `Close()`-entry `Store(false)` narrows the loaded-check set's admission window but deliberately claims no drain: an operation that already observed armed can still be inside a map syscall when Close/Teardown runs. The shutdown-window link-map race (a late-admitted attach writing the Go link maps while `Close` ranges them, after the scheduler stop's unbounded applySem acquisition releases) is the exact-schedule instance.

## Proposed direction

A dataplane-lifecycle redesign: generation-tagged registry handles (a retained handle refuses to mutate once a new generation publishes) and/or a lease/refcount + drain discipline for Close/Teardown. This is a design item, not a point fix — candidate for a /research pass first.

## Acceptance

- No retained handle can mutate an obsolete map generation (mutation fails loudly or is a verified no-op with a metric).
- Close/Teardown cannot run concurrently with an in-flight registry operation (drain or fenced admission).

Refs: #2114 (research §10 residuals), #6739 (the FirstCommit+cluster-scoped recurrence terminator), #6740 (the Go link-map sibling).

## #6745 — A1-b1: Per-session close deletes a shared reverse-NAT steering key [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

## Problem

Per-session close deletes a shared reverse-NAT steering key (opus-review-001 root R01, severity Medium).

## Evidence (re-derived and VERIFIED at `39f1f8b93`)

> The original body cited `/tmp/opus-review-001.md`, which does not exist, and a base
> (`ad9591177481`) whose line numbers have since rotted. Located by SYMBOL and re-pinned
> below so the next reader does not have to re-derive it.

**Graded REAL.** The steering key omits the remote endpoint, so two sessions can share one map row, and per-session close deletes it unconditionally.

- `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/checksum.rs` — `dnat_v4_key_bytes` / `dnat_v6_key_bytes` build the key from `key.protocol`, the SNAT source address and the SNAT source port only. **The remote endpoint is absent.**
- `userspace-dp/src/nat/allocator.rs` — `AddressOnlyReverseKey` enforces uniqueness on a key that DOES include `dst_ip`/`dst_port`, so under address-only SNAT (`port no-translation`) two flows differing only in remote are both admitted and collide on one `dnat_table` key. Plain static SNAT claims no occupancy bit at all.
- `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/checksum.rs` — `delete_dnat_table_entry` has no read-before-delete, no value comparison, no refcount and no holder set.
- `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/session_delta.rs` — the `SessionDeltaKind::Close` arm calls it for every close.
- `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/shared_ops.rs` — `remove_shared_session` likewise removes without checking the entry belongs to the closing session, while the INSERT side (`record_shared_nat_displacement`) does exactly that comparison to count 1:N collisions.

**Why the holders/refcount work does NOT already fix this** (this is the trap): `#6211 F2` / `#6522` added `LiveAllocation::holders: u128` so a synced NAT **port reservation** is freed only on the last release. That refcounts the allocation LEASE. The steering MAP ROW is a different resource and is not refcounted. Separately `#4399`/`#4438` made the worker-local `nat_reverse_index` a 1:N multimap with a per-handle bucket remove — the project fixed exactly this shape in ONE of the three places and left the shared map and the BPF table single-valued. The `#1758`/`#1760` line of work ended at a telemetry counter (`NAT_REVERSE_KEY_SHARED_DISPLACEMENTS`), not a fix.

## Fix direction

maintain coordinator-side holders/refcounts per steering key, publish on `0 -> 1`, delete on `1 -> 0`, include HA imports/resync, and preserve static-DNAT ownership; alternatively redesign the map identity without losing embedded-ICMP lookup capability.

Refs: /tmp/opus-review-001.md (root R01, source batch opus-A1-b1.md).

## #6747 — A1-b1: Full IKE exchange table serializes admitted initiations through an O(4096) eviction scan [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

## Problem

Full IKE exchange table serializes admitted initiations through an O(4096) eviction scan (opus-review-001 root R03, severity Medium).

## Evidence (re-derived and VERIFIED at `39f1f8b93`)

> The original body cited `/tmp/opus-review-001.md` (gone) and base `ad9591177481`, whose line
> numbers have rotted. Re-located by SYMBOL below.

**Graded REAL.**

- `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/forwarding/ipsec.rs` — `IKE_EXCHANGE_TABLE_CAP = 4096`; the table is a single `Mutex<FastMap<IkeExchangeKey, u64>>`.
- `IkeExchangeTable::seed` — on a full table the victim is chosen by `entries.iter().min_by_key(|(_, seen)| **seen)`, a **full traversal of all 4096 entries** (plus empty hashbrown slots), followed by a key `clone()` and a second hash lookup for `remove`. There is no free list, ring index, LRU head, generation counter or amortised reap anywhere in the file.
- `lock_entries()` — the guard is taken on the first line of `seed` and held across the whole scan. The same lock is taken by `matches()`, which is on the hot admission path for every Responder-SPI IKE packet, and the table is `Arc`-shared by every packet worker (`worker/launch.rs`, with an `assert!(Arc::ptr_eq(...))`). So one worker's scan blocks the others.
- Idle reaping happens only in `matches()`, never in `seed()` — a table full of stale entries is not compacted by the seed path, it scans anyway.
- No eviction counter or telemetry, so the condition is unobservable.

**Narrowing, in fairness to whoever fixes this:** the scan is a cold branch. `entries.get_mut(&key)` short-circuits O(1) for any key already present (retransmits, rekeys, DPD), and the scan cannot run until 4096 **distinct** live exchanges are resident. Reaching it requires 4096 distinct `(initiator_spi, peer_ip, local_ip)` keys, each admitted through the host-inbound gate on an IKE-permitting zone to a firewall-owned address. The in-code claim that "the stage-10 udp-flood screen is the rate limiter" does not hold unconditionally: `stage_screen_check` returns immediately when no screen profile is configured, and `udp_flood_threshold: 0 = disabled`.

Cite hygiene: of the seven original refs, the four `ipsec.rs` ones still land on the named symbols; `poll_stages.rs:1086`/`:1144` now land inside doc-comment prose and `poll_descriptor/mod.rs:230` lands on an unrelated IPv6-ext-header drop.

## Fix direction

use an O(1) generational FIFO/LRU discipline or a bounded auxiliary age queue with stale-generation checks; shard only if global exchange semantics remain correct.

Refs: /tmp/opus-review-001.md (root R03, source batch opus-A1-b1.md).

## #6748 — A1-b2: Native GRE decapsulation promotes bytes outside the outer IP datagram [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

## Problem

Native GRE decapsulation promotes bytes outside the outer IP datagram (opus-review-001 root R04, severity Medium).

## Evidence (re-derived and VERIFIED at `39f1f8b93`)

> The original body cited `/tmp/opus-review-001.md` (gone) and base `ad9591177481`, whose line
> numbers have rotted. Re-located by SYMBOL below.

**Graded REAL — but the mechanism is NOT the one the title implies, and that matters for the fix.**

REFUTED: decap does not use the frame length as the inner end. `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/gre.rs` computes `inner_len` via `packet_trimmed_len(inner_packet, inner_family)`, which reads the **inner** IP header's own declared length (IPv4 Total Length / 40+IPv6 Payload Length) and fails closed when it exceeds the slice. Ethernet min-frame padding is therefore already trimmed and is NOT promoted.

HOLDS: the inner length is bounded by `frame.len() - inner_offset`, **never by the OUTER IPv4 Total Length / IPv6 Payload Length**. There is no cross-check that the inner extent stays inside the outer datagram. A peer that appends a trailer past the outer datagram AND inflates the inner IP Total Length to cover it has those out-of-datagram bytes promoted into the decapsulated packet. Narrower than "any trailer" — it needs a lying inner header, and the frame must first pass `match_tunnel_endpoint` (configured tunnel src/dst + GRE key).

**The asymmetry is the strongest evidence this is an oversight, not a design choice.** In the SAME FILE, `gre_checksum_region` DOES bound by the outer IP length, and its docstring says so explicitly — "bounded by the OUTER IP length (IPv4 Total Length, IPv6 Payload Length) so trailing Ethernet min-frame padding is excluded". So the outer-length concept exists here and is applied to the checksum but not to payload promotion. Consequence: checksummed GRE gets an incidental outer-length sanity check that non-checksummed GRE does not.

No earlier clamp exists: `raw_frame` comes straight from the AF_XDP descriptor length; `classify_metadata` validates snapshot/config-gen/fib-gen/addr-family and performs **no length validation at all**; and the XDP shim declares `tot_len`/`payload_len` in its header structs but never reads either (repo-wide, those are the only two occurrences in `userspace-xdp/`).

The issue's own fix direction — compute one authoritative outer end and extract on `frame[..outer_end]` — is correct. GRE option-field parsing (checksum/key/sequence skips) is also frame-bounded and should move inside the same bound. The identical `packet_trimmed_len` pattern is used by the WireGuard decap path, which is worth checking in the same work.

## Guidance for whoever fixes this

**Do not bound against the frame length.** Implementing this issue from its title alone would
produce exactly that, and it would look correct while fixing nothing — `packet_trimmed_len`
already keeps the inner extent inside the frame. The missing bound is against the **outer IP
datagram**.

**Reuse the bound this file already has.** `gre_checksum_region` computes the authoritative outer
end (IPv4 Total Length, or 40 + IPv6 Payload Length, checked against `frame.len()`) and its
docstring states the reason. The codebase already knows the answer and applies it in one place
only. Extract that computation and use it for payload promotion and for the GRE option-field
skips, rather than writing a second, possibly divergent, notion of "outer end".

## Fix direction

compute one authoritative outer end from IPv4 total length or IPv6 payload length, reject declarations shorter than required headers/options, and perform checksum, option parsing, and inner extraction only on `frame[..outer_end]`; add v4/v6 and checksum/no-checksum tail regressions.

Refs: /tmp/opus-review-001.md (root R04, source batch opus-A1-b2.md).

## #6751 — A1-b4: Interface SNAT admits indistinguishable no-PAT return tuples and sends replies to the first session [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-27)

## Problem

Interface SNAT admits indistinguishable no-PAT return tuples and sends replies to the first session (opus-review-001 root R08, severity High).

## Evidence (re-derived and VERIFIED at `39f1f8b93`)

> The original body cited `/tmp/opus-review-001.md` (gone) and a ~3-week-old base whose line
> numbers have rotted. Re-located by SYMBOL below.

**Graded REAL. High severity is justified — replies reach the wrong internal host.**

1. **Interface mode preserves the source port unconditionally.** `userspace-dp/src/nat/source.rs` — the `if rule.interface_mode` branch returns a `NatDecision` with `rewrite_src: Some(egress)` and leaves `rewrite_src_port` at `None`; `checksum.rs` then uses `rewrite_src_port.unwrap_or(key.src_port)`, so the wire keeps the original port. **There is no PAT branch in interface mode**, and the branch is evaluated before `rule.pool_mode`.
2. **No admission check.** The interface branch never touches `rule.pool_allocator`. The occupancy structure that would catch this DOES exist — `allocator.rs` `address_only_owners: FxHashMap<AddressOnlyReverseKey, SourceNatFlowKey>`, whose contract is that *"a genuinely-colliding second flow (same identity) is DENIED as exhaustion ... rather than receiving an unowned duplicate whose replies the reverse (1:N) index cannot disambiguate"* — but it is minted only by the POOL-mode address-only path (`reserve_address_only_*`). Interface mode gets none of it. The only response to an interface-SNAT collision is telemetry: `nat_reverse_key_collisions` and `xpf_userspace_session_nat_reverse_key_shared_displacements_total`.
3. **The reverse-index validation cannot disambiguate.** `session/lookup.rs` `find_forward_nat_match` walks the 1:N bucket and returns the first candidate passing `reply_matches_forward_session`, which is `reverse_wire_key(fwd, nat) == reply || reverse_canonical_key(fwd, nat) == reply` (`session/key.rs`). For interface SNAT `wire_dst = nat.rewrite_src.unwrap_or(...)` = the **egress** address — the original internal `src_ip` never appears in the reverse key. Two flows differing only in internal source produce **byte-identical** reverse keys, so BOTH candidates validate. The validation is a stale-index guard, not a disambiguator.

**The existing test pins the ambiguity as accepted behaviour**, which is why this has not been caught. `session/tests.rs` `nat_reverse_1n_collision_preserves_displaced_return_path`, fixture `iface_snat_decision` with `10.0.0.1:5555` and `10.0.0.2:5555` to the same server:

```rust
// A reply on K resolves to a LIVE forward session. Both validate — the
// wire tuple is genuinely ambiguous under no-PAT interface SNAT — so the
// multimap returns the first-installed S1 deterministically instead of
// "whatever was written last".
```

The tests assert determinism, **not** that replies reach the correct internal host. Pre-#4399 was worse (single-valued index, the earlier session was displaced and stranded); the current code preserves both and makes the winner deterministic — an improvement that does not make the tuple unambiguous.

**Extra finding, worth folding into the fix:** the per-worker and shared/HA paths disagree about WHICH session wins. `find_forward_nat_match` yields the FIRST-installed; the shared-scope index (`shared_ops.rs` `lookup_shared_forward_nat_match`) is a plain single-valued map `get`, i.e. **LAST-published wins**. So the same ambiguous tuple resolves differently depending on which path handles the reply.

No commit since 2026-06 addresses interface-mode collisions; all the collision work in `nat/source.rs` (#5269, #6041, #6226, #5338) is pool-mode address-only. The only interface-mode commit in range is #5688, which added the no-egress-address fail-closed.

## Fix direction

reserve translated tuples at install and PAT later colliders using existing allocator discipline, or reject the later flow atomically if interface mode must remain no-PAT; do not add a longer packet-path scan.

Refs: /tmp/opus-review-001.md (root R08, source batch opus-A1-b4.md).

## #6752 — A1-b4: A SYN-ACK without the final ACK retains a half-open flow for the established timeout [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

## Problem

A SYN-ACK without the final ACK retains a half-open flow for the established timeout (opus-review-001 root R09, severity Medium).

## Evidence (re-derived and VERIFIED at `39f1f8b93`)

> The original body cited `/tmp/opus-review-001.md` (gone) and base `ad9591177481`, whose line
> numbers have rotted. Re-located by SYMBOL below.

**Graded REAL.**

- Classes: `DEFAULT_TCP_OPENING_TIMEOUT_NS = 20 s`, `DEFAULT_TCP_SESSION_TIMEOUT_NS = 300 s` (`userspace-dp/src/session/mod.rs`). `session_timeout_ns` selects on `!established`.
- **Promotion is on the SYN-ACK, not the final ACK.** `userspace-dp/src/session/lookup.rs`:
  ```rust
  let promote_from_reverse = is_tcp && is_syn_ack(tcp_flags) && entry.metadata.is_reverse;
  if promote_from_reverse { entry.established = true; }
  ```
  and the deadline is re-stamped immediately after with the new flag, so the reverse entry jumps to the 300 s class the moment the SYN-ACK is seen.
- `propagate_tcp_state_to_companion` sets the forward half's flag only, with the comment: *"We deliberately do NOT extend its expiry here so a handshake the client never completes still reaps on the short opening window."*
- **That stated intent is no longer what the code does.** The #4380 companion probe (`companion_keeps_alive`, `userspace-dp/src/session/expire.rs`) is protocol- and handshake-agnostic — it compares `now - companion.last_seen` against `companion.expires_after_ns` and never consults `established`. So at the forward half's 20 s deadline the probe sees the reverse half alive on its new 300 s window, keeps the forward half, re-stamps its `last_seen` and re-buckets it. Both halves persist ~300 s from the SYN-ACK. #4380 (2026-07-07) landed AFTER #4109 (2026-07-04) wrote that comment.
- No flow-level handshake object exists; `established` is per-`SessionEntry`, and both halves are installed from the same first packet.
- No concurrent half-open cap exists anywhere in `userspace-dp/src/` (`max_half_open` — no such thing). The SYN-flood screen is a per-second RATE limiter, off unless `syn_flood_threshold > 0`, not a concurrency cap. The only bound is the global session table cap.

**The cited "behavior pin" does not pin this.** `tcp_handshake_promotes_opening_to_established` asserts the `established` FLAG on both halves after the SYN-ACK, then sends the final ACK and only afterwards asserts `expires_after_ns == tcp_established_ns`. It **never asserts the reverse entry's `expires_after_ns` after the SYN-ACK**. `forward_ack_without_reverse_synack_stays_opening` covers only the no-SYN-ACK case, and the #4380 companion tests install with `TCP_ACK` (both halves already established). **No test covers SYN → SYN-ACK → no final ACK.**

Partial refutation worth recording: a bare forward ACK does NOT promote (#4109 restricted promotion to a reverse SYN-ACK), so the broader "any second packet promotes" reading is false.

## A second defect: the comment is now false, in the safe direction

`propagate_tcp_state_to_companion` still carries #4109's rationale — *"We deliberately do NOT
extend its expiry here so a handshake the client never completes still reaps on the short opening
window."* That was **true when written** (2026-07-04) and was **falsified three days later** by
#4380's companion probe (2026-07-07), which is handshake-agnostic and re-stamps the forward half
off the reverse half's fresh 300 s deadline.

Neither change was wrong. The comment simply stopped describing the system, and **nobody
re-examined it because it overstates safety** — a comment claiming the conservative behaviour is
one readers stop checking. This is the same shape as #7409's `"NoRoute drops anyway"`, which was
false the same way and for the same reason.

## #6753 — A10-b1: Local CLI config load allocates or blocks on an unbounded file before the 16 MiB store gate [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

## Problem

Local CLI config load allocates or blocks on an unbounded file before the 16 MiB store gate (opus-review-001 root R10, severity Medium).

## Evidence (re-derived and VERIFIED at `39f1f8b93`)

> The original body cited `/tmp/opus-review-001.md` (gone) and base `ad9591177481`, whose line
> numbers have rotted. Re-located by SYMBOL below.

**Graded REAL.**

- `pkg/cli/cli_config.go` — `handleLoad`'s file branch is a bare `os.ReadFile(source)` where `source` is `args[1]` verbatim. No `os.Stat`, no `Mode().IsRegular()`, no `io.LimitReader`, no path restriction. `string(data)` then COPIES, so peak is 2x the file.
- `pkg/configstore/store.go` — `MaxConfigSize = 16 << 20` and `checkConfigSize(content string)` take an **already fully materialised string**. It is a post-read length check, not a read bound, so it cannot fire until the CLI has allocated the whole file.
- Non-regular inputs are not rejected: a FIFO blocks in the read until a writer closes; `/dev/zero` or a FUSE-backed file streams unbounded and grows the slice to OOM, never reaching the gate; symlinks are followed silently.
- A second, independent copy of the same pattern is in the REMOTE CLI binary, `cmd/cli/main.go` `handleLoad` — same `os.ReadFile`, feeding a gRPC `LoadRequest`.

**The decisive evidence is that this repo already fixed exactly this hazard, elsewhere.** `cmd/xpfd/main.go` has `readBoundedFile` — `os.Open`, `Stat`, `!fi.Mode().IsRegular()` reject, then `io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(f, max+1))` — introduced by #4909 with a comment describing the identical TOCTOU: *"an adversarial or FUSE-backed file can under-report its size to Stat and then stream an unbounded body to ReadFile"*. Both helpers are unexported in `package main` and are used only by `check-config`. Nothing in `pkg/cli` or `cmd/cli` references them.
- The NETWORK ingress paths are bounded (`pkg/api/config.go` `MaxBytesReader` → 413; `pkg/grpcapi/server.go` `maxRecvMsgSize = 16 << 20`). Only the two file-reading CLI surfaces are unbounded.

**Severity bound, stated honestly:** the path is operator-gated — `load` dispatches inside config mode behind `checkPermission` → `config.PermConfig`. Note `checkPermission` returns `nil` outright when no RBAC is configured, and the in-process console runs INSIDE xpfd, so the `os.ReadFile` executes with the daemon's privilege on an operator-supplied path.

No commit on `pkg/cli/cli_config.go` since 2026-06 adds a size guard, stat precheck or limit reader.

## The fix is to REUSE the existing helper, in TWO places

`cmd/xpfd/main.go` already contains `readBoundedFile` — `os.Open`, `Stat`, reject
`!fi.Mode().IsRegular()`, then `io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(f, max+1))` with an over-cap check —
added by #4909 with a comment describing the identical TOCTOU. It is unexported in
`package main` and its only caller is `check-config`.

So this is not "write a bounded reader": it is "call the one that already exists, from the two
places that do not". Both surfaces need it:

- `pkg/cli/cli_config.go` `handleLoad` (in-process console, runs with the daemon's privilege)
- `cmd/cli/main.go` `handleLoad` (remote CLI, feeds a gRPC `LoadRequest`)

The helper will need lifting somewhere both can import.

**Scope note:** the network ingress paths are already bounded — `pkg/api/config.go` via
`MaxBytesReader` (413 on over-size) and `pkg/grpcapi/server.go` via

## #6754 — A10-b2: HTTP DDNS cache ignores a changed resolved bind device [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

## Problem

HTTP DDNS cache ignores a changed resolved bind device (opus-review-001 root R11, severity Medium).

## Evidence (re-derived and VERIFIED at `39f1f8b93`)

> The original body cited `/tmp/opus-review-001.md` (gone) and a ~3-week-old base whose line
> numbers have rotted. Re-located by SYMBOL below.

**Graded REAL, and narrowly scoped: only the `destination-interface` arm is exposed.**

- `pkg/ddns/backend_http.go` — the cache is `httpClientCache{clients map[string]*http.Client}` keyed by `bindCacheKey(p)` = `p.SourceAddress + "\x00" + p.DestinationInterface + "\x00" + p.RoutingInstance` — the **raw Junos config leaves**.
- `clientFor` resolves the real bind config on EVERY call and then discards it on a hit:
  ```go
  b, err := resolveProviderBindConfig(p, firstResolver(resolveIf))
  key := bindCacheKey(p)
  if cl, ok := c.clients[key]; ok { return cl, nil }   // b is DISCARDED
  cl := newHTTPClientBound(b)
  ```
- The resolved device comes from `backend_bind.go` `resolveBindConfig` → `resolveIfKernelName` → `config.(*Config).ResolveKernelIfName`, whose output is a function of the **whole committed config** — `ResolveReth` (reth to physical member), the tunnel name map, the IRB-to-bridge map, `SecureTunnelUnitNetdev`, unit-vs-vlan-id. So the resolved device can change while all three key leaves stay byte-identical.
- The code states the split deliberately: *"The cache KEY stays the raw binding leaves (bindCacheKey) so the #2956 reap stays consistent; only the bound client's SO_BINDTODEVICE target is resolved."* The hazard is the consequence of that choice, not an accident of it.
- No outer invalidation exists. The only eviction is `reap`, and `surface_a.go` builds its `live` set from `bindCacheKey` of the configured scopes + catalog — so an unchanged config keeps the key in `live` and the entry is **explicitly preserved** (*"A key still in live ... is preserved — only an actual key change is superseded"*). Every non-test reference was enumerated: construction once in `NewSurfaceAManager`, two `clientFor` call sites, one `reap`. No generation counter, no per-apply rebuild, no `CloseIdleConnections` outside `reap`.
- `validateDevice` fails loudly on a MISS but is not re-run on a hit.

**Partial refutations — do NOT widen the fix beyond the destination-interface arm:**
- `source-address` changes ARE covered: `SourceAddress` is in the key verbatim.
- `routing-instance` is effectively covered: `diagcmd.VRFDeviceName` is a pure string transform of `RoutingInstance`, which is in the key.
- RFC 2136 is unaffected — `pkg/ddns/manager.go` rebuilds per pass with no cache.

Test gap: **no test threads a resolver into `clientFor`** — every call site in `surface_a_httpcache_reap_2956_test.go` and `redirect_crosshost_6545_test.go` is resolver-less, so the resolved-device path is untested end to end. No commit since 2026-06 touches the cache key (the post-June churn on this file is all URL-scrub and redirect work).

## Fix direction

key entries and the reconcile live set by a canonical resolved `bindConfig`, or retain resolved metadata beside each client and close/replace the transport atomically on any difference.

Refs: /tmp/opus-review-001.md (root R11, source batch opus-A10-b2.md).

## #6756 — A10-b3: Malformed or zero-length RFC 3442 option presence falls through to the forbidden Router option [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

## Problem

Malformed or zero-length RFC 3442 option presence falls through to the forbidden Router option (opus-review-001 root R13, severity Medium).

## Evidence (re-derived and VERIFIED at `39f1f8b93`)

> The original body cited `/tmp/opus-review-001.md` (gone) and base `ad9591177481`, whose line
> numbers have rotted. Re-located by SYMBOL below.

**Graded REAL.**

- `pkg/dhcp/dhcpv4.go` — `leaseFromACKv4` selects the gateway purely on the third return of `classlessStaticRoutes(ack)`:
  ```go
  if classless, defGW, present := classlessStaticRoutes(ack); present { ... }
  else { routers := ack.Router(); ... }   // option 3
  ```
- `classlessStaticRoutes` derives `present` **only** from `len(libRoutes) != 0`. So all three of "option 121 absent", "option 121 zero-length", and "option 121 malformed" return `(nil, {}, false)` and take the identical fall-through to the Router option. **The caller cannot distinguish absent from present-but-unparseable.** RFC 3442 requires option 3 to be ignored whenever option 121 is RETURNED.
- Malformed option 249 is worse — its parse error is explicitly discarded: `if err := r.FromBytes(raw); err == nil { libRoutes = r }`.
- The library discards the WHOLE option on any per-entry error (`ClasslessStaticRoute` maps any error to `nil`), including a trailing-short entry after N good ones, and `maskSize > 32`.

**Refutation checks, both negative:**
- No presence check exists — `grep -rn 'OptionClasslessStaticRoute|Options.Has|\.Has(' pkg/dhcp/` returns **zero hits**. The library DOES expose `Options.Has`, which returns true for a zero-length option because the map key is created. It is simply not used.
- The library does NOT shield xpf from present-but-malformed. `Options.fromBytesCheckEnd` fails the packet only when the declared option length exceeds the remaining packet bytes. An option that is self-consistent at the DHCP framing layer but internally short at the RFC 3442 layer parses fine there and fails later in `Routes.FromBytes` — so xpf can and does observe it. Zero-length is likewise reachable on the wire.

**One sub-case IS refuted and should not be fixed:** a VALID option-121 carrying only specific routes and no `0.0.0.0/0` already suppresses option 3 correctly (`present=true`, `defGW` invalid), pinned by `TestLeaseFromACKv4ClasslessOnlySpecificNoDefault` in `pkg/dhcp/classless_routes_test.go`.

Test gap: `classless_routes_test.go` has **no** malformed-option or zero-length-option case.

Fix shape: return presence from an explicit `Options.Has(121) || Options.Has(249)` check, independent of parse success, and decide deliberately whether a malformed option means "no gateway" (RFC-strict) or a logged fallback — but not silently the latter.

## Fix direction

(per the root section — see link)

Refs: /tmp/opus-review-001.md (root R13, source batch opus-A10-b3.md).

## Problem

Config-drive secrets are exposed with umask-derived permissions for the duration of ISO construction (opus-review-001 root R21, severity Medium).

## Evidence (re-derived and VERIFIED at `39f1f8b93`)

> The original body cited `/tmp/opus-review-001.md`, which does not exist, and a base
> (`ad9591177481`) whose line numbers have since rotted. Located by SYMBOL and re-pinned
> below so the next reader does not have to re-derive it.

**Graded REAL, but NARROWED — one of the three original cites refutes the issue's own framing.**

REFUTED: the staging directory is **not** umask-derived. `scripts/image/make_config_drive.py` and `scripts/deploy/xpf-deploy.py` both use `tempfile.mkdtemp()`, which is 0700 by construction and umask-independent. No `os.makedirs`/`os.mkdir` is used for day-0 staging in either script, and neither calls `os.umask`. The staged `xpf.conf` has a sub-millisecond 0644 window from `shutil.copyfile` before its `chmod(0o600)`, but it sits inside that 0700 dir and is unreachable by other UIDs.

ALSO REFUTED: the cited `scripts/deploy/xpf-deploy.py:224-227` is not ISO-construction code at all — it is a path-containment `die()` message with no permission logic.

HOLDS, and is what the title actually describes: **the output ISO**. `xorriso`/`genisoimage` writes it under the process umask (~0022 → 0644, world-readable) and `os.chmod(out, 0o600)` runs only AFTER `subprocess.run` / `run_capture` returns — so the artifact embedding every day-0 secret (root-authentication hash, IKE PSK, SNMP community, DDNS tokens) is world-readable **for the duration of ISO construction**, in CWD. Both scripts have the same shape and both in-code comments acknowledge it.

The two cited tests (`scripts/image/test_make_config_drive_mode.py`, `scripts/deploy/test_xpf_deploy_iso_mode.py`) already pin the END state (0600) and even simulate the hostile umask — they do not pin the absence of the window. Prior work `b4019c6ec` (#4586) and `9cdf4016f` (#4905-C) tightened the end state, not the race.

## #6765 — A2-b1: Changed SNAT/NAT64 pools reissue live translated tuples on retained addresses [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-23)

## Problem

Changed SNAT/NAT64 pools reissue live translated tuples on retained addresses (opus-review-001 root R22, severity High).

## Evidence (re-derived and VERIFIED at `39f1f8b93`)

> The original body cited `/tmp/opus-review-001.md` (gone) and a ~3-week-old base whose line
> numbers have rotted. Re-located by SYMBOL below.

**Graded REAL. The exposed case is precisely a PARTIAL-OVERLAP pool change — and that is the one case no test exercises.**

1. **Carry-over is keyed on the full address list.** `userspace-dp/src/nat/source.rs` `SourceNatPoolAllocatorKey { pool_name, pool_addresses_v4: Vec<Ipv4Addr>, pool_addresses_v6, port_low, port_high }`. `Vec` equality is order-sensitive and whole-list, so **adding one address to a pool of ten changes the key**, the reuse lookup misses, and `PortAllocator::new` builds a fresh allocator for the whole pool — including the nine RETAINED addresses.
2. **Occupancy is rebuilt from scratch, never reconciled against live sessions.** `allocator.rs` `AddressOccupancy` is all-zero with `cursor: AtomicU32::new(0)`, and the bitmap is the SOLE arbiter of ownership (*"The set bit is the ownership token: a held bit cannot be re-claimed, so no separate owner-identity check is needed"*). `claim()` hands out ascending offsets from the cursor, i.e. `port_low` first. So the next new flow on a retained address is issued `(retained_addr, port_low)` — a tuple a pre-change live session may still hold, with the bit that would have blocked it now zeroed.
3. **The snapshot refresh does not help.** `coordinator/snapshot_refresh.rs` rebuilds forwarding state and hot-swaps it with live workers retained; the only session purge on that path is `tunnel_remap_purge_ids`. Nothing NAT-related.
4. **NAT64 has the identical shape.** `nat64.rs` `reuse_allocator` matches on `prefix_bytes == * && pool_v4.as_slice() == pool_v4`, else a fresh `PortAllocator::new`. Note the asymmetry inside the same constructor: the fragment-association cache gets a `build_generation` stamp (#5624), the port allocator gets none.
5. **No re-seed, no generation gate, no drain-before-swap.** The `reserve_synced_source_nat_allocation*` / `reserve_nat64_pool_port` entry points exist but every caller is an **HA session-import** path (`ha/session_import.rs`, `session_glue/commands/upsert_synced.rs`, `session_glue/promote.rs`), never a config apply. `source_nat_runtime_compatible` would compare pools but is `#[allow(dead_code)]` and off the apply path.

The code acknowledges the class: *"carries allocators over keyed on `allocator_key()` alone, so an edit that reshuffled which rule a session matched could strand a flow in a carried-over allocator"* and *"A config change does not rebuild the allocator either ... so the very edit that flips pass 1's outcome preserves the leak."*

**Why this survived — the test pins the reset using a DISJOINT pool.** `nat64_tests.rs` `nat64_4518_pool_change_resets_allocator` swaps `198.51.100.1` for `203.0.113.9` and asserts the fresh allocator starts at the low port. With the address itself changed, reissuing `port_low` is not a tuple collision — so the test pins the reset as CORRECT and never touches the retained-address case. On the SNAT side there is **no** test that reloads with a changed pool plus a retained address: every `parse_source_nat_rules_with_previous` test passes either `None` or the identical snapshot.

**Cases that are genuinely safe and should stay that way:** an unchanged pool (the reused `PortAllocator` shares its `Arc<PortAllocatorShared>`, so bitmap, cursor, `live_by_flow` and persistent leases all carry across — pinned by `tests_pool.rs` `pool_snat_persistent_compatible_refresh_preserves_lease_state`); a fully-disjoint swap; and a cold start, which resets deliberately rather than *"replaying unproven translated tuple ownership"*.

## #6767 — A3-b1: Wildcard `apply-groups` cloning bypasses the expansion work budget and can build a quadratic AST [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

## Problem

Wildcard `apply-groups` cloning bypasses the expansion work budget and can build a quadratic AST (opus-review-001 root R24, severity Medium).

## Evidence (re-derived and VERIFIED at `39f1f8b93`)

> The original body cited `/tmp/opus-review-001.md` (gone) and base `ad9591177481`, whose line
> numbers have rotted. Re-located by SYMBOL below.

**Graded REAL.**

- `pkg/config/ast_groups.go` — the budget is `maxGroupExpandDepth = 64` and `maxGroupExpandWork = 100000`, checked in exactly two places, both inside `expandGroupsRecursive`: the depth test, and `budget.work++` / `if budget.work > maxGroupExpandWork` inside `for _, name := range applyNames`. So **one unit of work is charged per `apply-groups <name>` reference resolved** — not per node cloned or merged.
- `mergeNodes(dst *[]*Node, src []*Node, ancestorPath [][]string)` **takes no budget parameter and has no counter of any kind.** Verified exhaustively: every reference to `maxGroupExpandWork` / `maxGroupExpandDepth` / `groupExpandBudget` in `pkg/` lives in `ast_groups.go`'s budget block, the two checks in `expandGroupsRecursive`, and the test — none in `mergeNodes`, `cloneNodes` or `walkGroupToContext`.
- The wildcard branch is the fan-out: for a src whose keys contain `<*>` it iterates **every** matching dst container and calls `cloneNodes(s.Children)` per match, then recurses. The non-wildcard container path finds the FIRST match and `break`s (1→1), so wildcard is the only D-way multiplier. A second `<*>` level inside `s.Children` multiplies again.
- Structural bypass: `expandGroupsRecursive` charges 1 work unit, then hands the body to `mergeNodes`; everything from that point — including the D-way fan-out and its recursion — is uncounted. A config with a **single** `apply-groups` statement consumes `budget.work == 1` of 100000 while performing O(D x S) clones. The depth cap does not apply either: `mergeNodes` has no depth parameter.

**Outer bounds do not save it.** `MaxConfigSize` (16 MiB) and `maxParseDepth` (256) bound the INPUT; there is no post-expansion node cap, tree-size cap or memory quota (`countNodes`/`nodeCount`/`TotalNodes` — no such thing in `pkg/config` or `pkg/configstore`), and `compileExpanded` runs straight into the pre-walk gates. With D and S each O(n) in input bytes, the permitted ceiling is **quadratic in 16 MiB**.

**Provenance makes the gap unambiguous:** `c386e1ada` (#5194) is the commit that ADDED the budget specifically to bound apply-groups expansion — it instrumented `expandGroupsRecursive` and did not touch `mergeNodes`. And `maxGroupExpandWork` has **zero test references anywhere in the repo**: `apply_groups_depth_5194_test.go` pins DEPTH only (chain of `maxGroupExpandDepth+40`, asserts the error contains "depth"), with a shallow negative control. Nothing pins work, node count, output size or the wildcard fan-out.

This is production syntax, not a corner case — `set groups <g> security policies from-zone <*> to-zone <*>` appears throughout `pkg/config/parser_ast_test.go` — and the path runs on every commit, HA config sync, and `| display inheritance`.

## Why this survived: the bound is on the wrong quantity, and nothing tested it

`c386e1ada` (#5194) added `maxGroupExpandWork` **specifically** to bound apply-groups expansion.
It instrumented `expandGroupsRecursive` and never touched `mergeNodes`, which is where the
wildcard D-way fan-out lives. So the budget is not a weak bound — it is a bound on the wrong
quantity: it counts *references resolved*, while the blowup is in *nodes cloned*. One
`apply-groups` statement spends `budget.work == 1` of 100000 while performing O(D x S) clones.

And `maxGroupExpandWork` has **zero test references anywhere in the repo**. The #5194 test pins
DEPTH only. The budget itself was never bound by anything, which is why it could be measuring the
wrong thing for as long as it has.

A fix should charge work where the allocation happens (per node cloned / merged), not per
reference, and add a test that pins the work budget rather than only the depth budget.

## #6782 — A5-b2: Invalid RETH redundancy-group values commit as non-HA addresses owned by both nodes [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-23)

## Problem

Invalid RETH redundancy-group values commit as non-HA addresses owned by both nodes (opus-review-001 root R41, severity High).

## Evidence (re-derived and VERIFIED at `39f1f8b93`)

> The original body cited `/tmp/opus-review-001.md`, which does not exist, and a base
> (`ad9591177481`) whose line numbers have since rotted. Located by SYMBOL and re-pinned
> below so the next reader does not have to re-derive it.

**Graded REAL.** Every step of the chain verified.

1. **Untyped schema leaf** — `pkg/config/schema_interfaces.go`, `redundant-ether-options` → `redundancy-group: {desc: ..., args: 1}`. No `valueType`, no `validator`, no `keyValidator`. `pkg/config/schema_walk.go` gates on `isTypedLeaf() && (validator != nil || treeValidator != nil)`, so `SchemaValidate` never inspects this token. Contrast siblings in the same file that ARE typed: `mtu`, `native-vlan-id`, `unit`.
2. **Parse error discarded** — `pkg/config/compiler_interfaces.go:139`:
   ```go
   if v, err := strconv.Atoi(nodeVal(rgNode)); err == nil {
       ifc.RedundancyGroup = v
   }
   ```
   Non-integer / missing → `err` discarded, field stays 0. `0` parses to 0. **Negative parses SUCCESSFULLY and is stored verbatim.**
3. **The validator does not cover it** — `pkg/config/compiler_validate_strict_reth_vrrp.go` `validateRethVRRPGroupIDStrict` `continue`s on `RedundancyGroup <= 0` (no lower bound anywhere) AND returns early when `PrivateRGElection` — which `pkg/config/compiler_system.go` sets as the **DEFAULT**. So on a default cluster config the gate returns before the loop. It is a one-sided upper bound (`> 155`) only. No validator requires a reth to have an RG or cross-references `cfg.Chassis.Cluster.RedundancyGroups`.
4. **Downstream becomes a static address** — `pkg/dataplane/compiler_iface.go` sets `isReth` from `RedundancyGroup > 0`; with 0 the `!isDHCP && !isReth` branch runs `reconcileInterfaceAddresses`, writing the reth's configured address onto the physical device. The networkd model computes `isVRRPReth = RedundancyGroup > 0 && clusterNodeID >= 0`, so the `169.254.x.y/32` link-local substitution does not fire and the REAL address is written with `KeepAddresses:false`. Both nodes run the same synced config, so both write it.
5. **Empirically it commits** — `pkg/daemon/vip_readiness_test.go` authors `set interfaces reth0 redundant-ether-options redundancy-group 0` and `Commit()` succeeds.

An AST gate for exactly this failure mode already exists for the sibling slot — `pkg/config/compiler_chassis_identity.go` `validateChassisClusterIdentitiesAST` — whose header explains the identical mechanism ("on parse FAILURE, LEAVES the field at its zero default") and whose stated scope covers only the two chassis-cluster instance-name slots. The interface leaf is not in it.

## Fix direction

Make the schema argument integer-typed and require a contextual
RETH group in the valid range starting at 1. Preserve parse errors explicitly. Any
leniently imported invalid value must suppress service-address installation until
repaired rather than silently becoming static.

Refs: /tmp/opus-review-001.md (root R41, source batch opus-A5-b2.md).

## #6792 — A7-b1: DNS ownership failures are warning-only, so a successful commit can leave stale or dual resolvers [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-23)

## Problem

DNS ownership failures are warning-only, so a successful commit can leave stale or dual resolvers (opus-review-001 root R51, severity Medium).

## Evidence (re-derived and VERIFIED at `39f1f8b93`)

> The original body cited `/tmp/opus-review-001.md`, which does not exist, and a base
> (`ad9591177481`) whose line numbers have since rotted. Located by SYMBOL and re-pinned
> below so the next reader does not have to re-derive it.

**Graded REAL.**

- `pkg/daemon/daemon_dns.go:205` — `slog.Warn("DNS: failed to disable+mask systemd-resolved; it may remain a second resolver owner")`, then **falls through** to the render and write. No `return`.
- Two further warn-only points in the same function: stale drop-in removal, and the `atomicWrite` failure (which warns and returns, leaving `/etc/resolv.conf` stale).
- `reconcile` and `reconcileDNSLocked` both have **no return value**, so nothing can propagate.

**The asymmetry is the evidence.** In `pkg/daemon/daemon_apply_tail.go`, `applyLo0Filter` and `applyHostInboundFilter` are both captured and joined into the commit result. `reconcileDNSLocked` sits between them as a bare statement and is the **only** reconciler in that function whose error is not joined. Two siblings doing the opposite in one function is an inconsistency, not a documented tradeoff.

**Reachable end states:** dual resolver (mask fails, resolved keeps running, xpf still writes resolv.conf — and xpf's own networkd `.network` files carry `UseDNS=yes`, so a live resolved is independently fed DHCP nameservers); and stale resolv.conf (write fails after the mask and drop-in removal have already run).

No retry, no ticker, no metric. `pkg/daemon/daemon_dns_test.go` stubs `disableMaskResolved` to always return `nil` — **no test covers any failure path**.

## #6802 — A7-b2: Failed host-inbound conntrack revocation has no retry trigger [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-26)

## Problem

Failed host-inbound conntrack revocation has no retry trigger (opus-review-001 root R63, severity Medium).

## Evidence (re-derived and VERIFIED at `39f1f8b93`)

> The original body cited `/tmp/opus-review-001.md`, which does not exist, and a base
> (`ad9591177481`) whose line numbers have since rotted. Located by SYMBOL and re-pinned
> below so the next reader does not have to re-derive it.

**Graded REAL.**

- `pkg/daemon/host_inbound_conntrack_flush.go:287` — `flushDeniedHostInboundConntrack` has **no return value**. On failure it `slog.Warn`s and `continue`s to the next address family.
- `pkg/daemon/daemon_nft.go` — the call site is a bare statement; no assignment, no `errors.Join`. Contrast the siblings in the same function: `InstallHostInbound` failure returns an error, the gap fence is joined, teardown failure returns an error.
- No dirty flag, no pending-revocation set, no failure counter. Compare the nft-side state the same function DOES keep (`d.hostInboundEnforced`, `d.hostInboundCoveredAddrs`).
- No periodic reconcile: every ticker under `pkg/daemon/` was enumerated (DDNS, RPM, HA fabric, HA, IPsec rebind, DHCP lease sync, neighbor, proxy-ARP, archive, kernel self-recover) — **none** re-runs `applyConfig`, `applyHostInboundFilter`, or the flush.
- No metric: `grep -riE 'conntrack_flush|host_inbound_conntrack' pkg/` returns nothing outside the file and its test.
- `pkg/daemon/host_inbound_conntrack_flush_5566_test.go` — the `conntrackDeleteFilters` stub always returns `(0, nil)`; **no test exercises the delete-error path**.

**The failure direction is what makes this a defect rather than a tradeoff.** The stale entry rides the chain's leading `ct state established,related accept`, so a now-DENIED host-inbound flow keeps working — it fails OPEN. The in-code rationale ("failing the commit would roll back correct enforcement over a transient error") justifies not failing the commit; it does not address the absence of any retry, signal or test. The only re-attempt is the next externally-triggered apply, itself gated on `InstallHostInbound` succeeding.

## #6811 — A9-b1: Multi-family sampling instance cross-fans each family's flows to the other family's collectors [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-26)

## Problem

Multi-family sampling instance cross-fans each family's flows to the other family's collectors (opus-review-001 root R72, severity Medium).

## Evidence (re-derived and VERIFIED at `39f1f8b93`)

> The original body cited `/tmp/opus-review-001.md`, which does not exist, and a base
> (`ad9591177481`) whose line numbers have since rotted. Located by SYMBOL and re-pinned
> below so the next reader does not have to re-derive it.

**Graded REAL.**

- `pkg/config/types_system.go` — `SamplingInstance` keeps the families separate (`FamilyInet`, `FamilyInet6`, each with its own `FlowServers`).
- `pkg/flowexport/manager.go` — `collectInstanceVersionCollectors` loops both families and appends into ONE `collectors` slice, collapsing family to two booleans (`servesInet`, `servesInet6`) that are then stamped onto every group.
- `pkg/flowexport/manager.go` — `CollectorConfig` has **no family field** (`Address`, `SourceAddress`, `Template` only), and `groupCollectorsByTemplate` keys on template name alone.
- `pkg/flowexport/manager.go:664` — `ServesFamily` is evaluated **per INSTANCE**, not per collector. With both families configured both booleans are `true`, so it returns `true` for either family and never narrows the socket set.
- `pkg/daemon/daemon_flowexport.go` — `lead.ServesFamily(sd.IsIPv6)` is the single family gate; the loop then fans to **every** group of that instance.
- `pkg/flowexport/netflow.go` / `ipfix.go` — downstream, family selects only the template/field layout (`fieldsV6`/`templateIDv6`); the write is `e.conns.writeAll(pkt, ...)`.
- `pkg/flowexport/transport.go` — `writeAll` iterates every conn unconditionally (the only skip is the #4423 unhealthy backoff). `dialCollectors` opened one UDP conn per entry of the merged slice, with no family notion.

So an instance with `family inet { flow-server A }` and `family inet6 { flow-server B }` sends IPv4 flows to BOTH A and B.

The commit-time validator `validateSamplingInstanceConflictsStrict` only rejects TWO DIFFERENT instances claiming the same `(version, family)`; it explicitly permits one instance holding both families. `pkg/flowexport/instance_isolation_test.go` exercises only family-DISJOINT instances — **no test configures a single instance with both families**, which is consistent with this going unnoticed.

## Fix direction

## #6813 — audit cohort: up to 38 bounded low-materiality groups, routing stale (opus-review-001) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-27)

## Problem

The opus-001 review's cohort audit reconciled 53 source rows to 40 source-declared groups; 38 remain bounded COHORT groups (2 exact dups of #6566/#5523, others belong as acceptance-criteria additions to existing issues). The remaining 24 unowned bounded groups form this one cohort tracking issue — defense-in-depth, test-coverage, observability-precision, lenient-path, and display-only classes.

## Evidence

docs/reviews/recovered/opus-review-001.md — 'Consolidated cohort issue' + 'Surviving cohort groups' sections (opus-cohort-audit.md embedded). Each group carries file:line evidence and a one-line reason at base ad9591177481.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] **Pass 1 (mechanical):** re-derive each of the 38 groups against current master. Every row carries file:line evidence at `ad9591177481` and master is thousands of commits ahead, so some will have been fixed incidentally. Per-row grep, not judgement.
- [ ] **Pass 2 (mechanical):** for the 16 routed groups, read what the now-closed target issue actually did. Covered by it -> close the group with a cite. Dropped when it closed -> it joins the real backlog.
- [ ] **Then** triage only what survives: fix, fold into an existing issue as acceptance criteria, or document as accepted-residual.
- [ ] The class breakdown (defense-in-depth / test-coverage / observability / lenient / display) is reflected in linked fixes.

Refs: docs/reviews/recovered/opus-review-001.md, #6566, #5523

---

## CORRECTION (2026-08-27): the population is up to 38, not 24, and the routing is entirely stale

Measured before starting work, rather than triaging against the stated number.

**"24" is not reproducible.** From the source document's "Surviving cohort groups" table:

| fact | count |
|---|---|
| surviving cohort groups in the table | **38** |
| route column names an existing issue | 16 |
| route column names none | 22 |
| of those 22, explicitly "material-support alias — do not file separately" | 8 |

38 is a hard count. **24 is not derivable from it** by any mechanical rule — not by subtracting routed groups (-> 22), nor routed plus material-support aliases (-> 14). The prose reads *"Material-support groups and several survivors belong as acceptance-criteria additions to existing issues; the remaining 24"*, and "several survivors" is a judgement, not a rule. The 24 is an artifact of a human pass that cannot be re-run.

**And the reduction rested on routing that has since gone stale in full.** All **23** distinct issues those 16 groups were routed to are now **CLOSED** (`CLOSED=23, OPEN=0`). So each routed group is now one of two things, and only reading the closing work tells you which:

- **covered** by what that issue shipped, or
- **dropped** when it closed.

Neither is "owned". That is why the two mechanical passes above come before any triage: the acceptance criterion "each of the 24 groups triaged" named a set that does not exist.

## #6817 — config: login-user `authentication` compact-leaf spelling silently drops the credential (#2419 class) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-26)

## Defect

`pkg/config/compiler_system.go` compiles a login user's `authentication` stanza by iterating **only** `prop.Children`:

```go
case "authentication":
    for _, authChild := range prop.Children {
        switch authChild.Name() {
        case "encrypted-password":
            user.EncryptedPassword = Secret(nodeVal(authChild))
        case "ssh-ed25519", "ssh-rsa", "ssh-dsa":
            ...
```

It never reads `prop.Keys[1:]`. This is the #2419 dual-AST-shape class documented in `CLAUDE.md`: the same operator intent produces two different node shapes, and a `prop.Children`-only reader sees exactly one of them.

The hierarchical **block** spelling puts the credential in a child:

```
system { login { user ops { authentication { encrypted-password "$6$..."; } } } }
```

The hierarchical **compact** spelling — equally legal, and what a flattened or hand-edited config often carries — puts it on the stanza's own `Keys`:

```
system { login { user ops { authentication encrypted-password "$6$..."; } } }
```

In the compact spelling the loop body runs **zero times**. `user.EncryptedPassword` and `user.SSHKeys` are left at their zero values, and the config compiles cleanly with no error and no warning.

## Verified

Confirmed on `origin/master` at `ad9591177` by reading `pkg/config/compiler_system.go` around the `case "authentication":` arm. The reader is `prop.Children`-only; there is no `prop.Keys[1:]` accumulation and no fallback.

Surfaced while reviewing PR #6735 (the same defect class in `compiler_security_zones.go`), which enumerated this site among roughly thirty `prop.Children`-only arms in the config compiler.

## What has to be determined before fixing

The mechanism is certain; the **direction** is not, and it decides the severity:

## #6818 — config/OSPF: interface `authentication` compact-leaf spelling silently drops authentication — adjacency forms unauthenticated (#2419 class) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-27)

## Defect

`pkg/config/compiler_protocols.go` compiles interface `authentication` for OSPF by iterating **only** `prop.Children`:

```go
case "authentication":
    for _, authChild := range prop.Children {
        switch authChild.Name() {
        case "md5":
            iface.AuthType = "md5"
            ...
        case "simple-password":
            ...
```

It never reads `prop.Keys[1:]`. This is the #2419 dual-AST-shape class from `CLAUDE.md`.

The block spelling compiles correctly:

```
protocols { ospf { area 0.0.0.0 { interface ge-0/0/0.0 {
    authentication { simple-password "secret"; }
} } } }
```

The compact spelling — equally legal — puts the value on the stanza's own `Keys`, so the loop runs **zero times**:

```
protocols { ospf { area 0.0.0.0 { interface ge-0/0/0.0 {
    authentication simple-password "secret";
} } } }
```

`iface.AuthType`, `iface.AuthKey`, and `iface.AuthKeyID` stay at their zero values. The commit succeeds with no error and no warning, and FRR is rendered with **no authentication on an interface the operator authenticated**.

## Why this direction is fail-open

Unlike a dropped address or a dropped counter, the failure here removes a control rather than adding one. The adjacency still forms — it forms *unauthenticated*, on a link the operator explicitly configured to require authentication. An attacker on that segment can inject LSAs that a correctly-compiled config would have rejected. The configuration on disk and `show` output both continue to claim authentication is present, so the gap is invisible from the box.

## #6819 — test/ha: five ha_tests share two process-global stale-ignored counters — cross-test race fails the suite ~60% of runs [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-06)

Five `#[test]` fns in `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/ha_tests.rs` use the SAME two **process-global** `AtomicU64` counters as a before/after baseline, with no serialization between them. Cargo runs them concurrently in one process, so one test's intentional stale-generation install/delete bumps the global another test is asserting UNCHANGED.

The counters are process-global, not per-`Coordinator`:

```

## #6821 — config: security-log `transport` compact-leaf spelling silently drops the TLS profile — audit logs ship unprotected (#2419 class) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-27)

## Defect

`pkg/config/compiler_security_log.go` compiles a security-log stream's `transport` stanza by iterating **only** `prop.Children`:

```go
case "transport":
    for _, tc := range prop.Children {
        switch tc.Name() {
        case "protocol":
            stream.Transport.Protocol = nodeVal(tc)
        case "tls-profile":
            stream.Transport.TLSProfile = nodeVal(tc)
        }
    }
```

It never reads `prop.Keys[1:]`. This is the #2419 dual-AST-shape class documented in `CLAUDE.md`.

The block spelling compiles correctly:

```
security { log { stream audit {
    host 192.0.2.10;
    transport { protocol tls; tls-profile secure-logs; }
} } }
```

The compact spelling — equally legal — puts the value on the stanza's own `Keys`, so the loop runs **zero times**:

```
security { log { stream audit {
    host 192.0.2.10;
    transport tls-profile secure-logs;
} } }
```

`stream.Transport.Protocol` and `stream.Transport.TLSProfile` are both left empty. The stream is still installed — the guard immediately below is only `if stream.Host != ""` — so the config commits cleanly with no error and no warning, and the stream ships with **no TLS profile selected**.
