## #6875 — config: `security log stream <name> source-interface <x>` is accepted and silently discarded — and a #3349 test asserts the no-op commits [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-27)

## Summary

`set security log stream <name> source-interface <interface>` **commits clean and does nothing.**

`source-interface` is modelled only as a child of `security log` (top level) at `pkg/config/schema_security.go:670`, with `ValidateSyslogSourceInterface` attached. There is **no** `source-interface` leaf under the `stream` subtree, and the schema is open-world there, so a per-stream spelling parses as an unmodelled keyword and is accepted.

Nothing consumes it. `pkg/config/types_security.go:274` — `type SyslogStream struct` has **no `SourceInterface` field** (verified: zero matches in the struct body). The only read is `pkg/config/compiler_security_log.go:31`, which populates `SourceInterface` on the top-level `LogConfig`.

So the operator writes a per-stream source interface, sees a clean commit, and the stream sources from whatever the global setting is — or from nothing.

## A test currently asserts that the no-op commits

`pkg/config/log_stream_config_3349_test.go:83` includes

```
"set security log stream s2 source-interface reth1.100",
```

in its **valid** list, and `pkg/config/parser_security_test.go:3347` carries the same shape. So the suite is pinning "this commits clean" for a statement that has no effect — which is worse than no coverage, because it makes the behaviour look deliberate.

This is the #2008 `profile`-stanza class: a leaf accepted by an open-world subtree, compiled by nothing, and blessed by a happy-path test.

## Decide the disposition, then make the tests say it

Two defensible answers, and the choice is a real one:

1. **Reject at commit.** If a per-stream source interface is not supported, model it as an error rather than letting it parse. Junos-compat argues against a hard reject if real vSRX configs carry it.
2. **Accept and implement.** Add `SourceInterface` to `SyslogStream`, compile it, and have the stream bind that source — with the top-level value as the fallback.

If neither is wanted, the third option is the project's existing convention for inert knobs: keep it in the schema and mark it **accepted for Junos compatibility; no runtime effect** (as `control-link-recovery` and `nat-state-synchronization` do), so it is visibly inert rather than invisibly so.

Whichever is chosen, the #3349 test's valid-list entry must change to match — either move it to the rejected list, or assert the compiled per-stream value. Leaving it asserting a clean commit for a no-op is the part that must not survive.

## Why it needs its own issue

Surfaced during re-verification of audit cohort **#6218**, but it is not one of that cohort's members — it is a new finding. Filing separately so it is individually assignable and does not close when the cohort does.

## Provenance

Found by a lane writing a subtest to assert the stream-level unit was bounded. The subtest failed, and the reason was that the feature does not exist. It removed the subtest rather than leave it asserting a property nothing implements — which is how the discard surfaced at all.

## #6878 — daemon: the #5078 step-20 subtests bind teardown and a cfg-derived decision, not restart completion [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-27)

Split out of the PR #6865 gate so the residual is tracked rather than buried in a comment. Both escapes below were **measured**, not reasoned.

## What is bound today

`TestKeyCommitDoesNotRestartCommsAtTheCallSite_5078` drives `applyTailReconciles` and observes `clusterCommsGen` across three subtests. That genuinely binds the step-20 decision against the mutation it was written for — suppressing the restart whenever the candidate config carries an auth key REDs `keyed_endpoint_change_must_still_restart`, and the pre-fold test file was green under the same mutation.

## Escape 1 — a store-derived keyed check is invisible

The subtests bind a keyed decision derived from the **candidate** `cfg`. Deriving it from `d.store.ActiveConfig()` instead leaves the entire `pkg/daemon` package green:

```go
keyed := <read the auth key from d.store.ActiveConfig()>
if !keyed && d.activeClusterTransport != (clusterTransportKey{}) && newTransport != d.activeClusterTransport {
```

The fixture's store deliberately holds **no committed cluster config** — that is what makes `startClusterComms` early-return so a unit test need not stand up heartbeat/sync sockets. But a real commit promotes the new config *before* apply (`store_commit.go` → `daemon_apply.go`), so in production a store-derived check would see the key and suppress the restart. Same deadlock, different spelling, no red.

## Escape 2 — the subtests prove teardown, not restart

All three observe `clusterCommsGen`, which `stopClusterComms` bumps **first**. Deleting `d.startClusterComms(d.daemonCtx)` from step 20 leaves `go vet` and the whole package green. A build that tears comms down on every endpoint change and never brings them back up passes the suite — while every endpoint move would silently leave the cluster with no session-sync.

`startClusterComms` also returns before opening an epoch when the store has no cluster config, which is why its absence is unobservable in this harness.

## Fix direction

Both escapes have the same root: the fixture has no committed cluster stanza. A harness where the store holds a real keyed cluster config, and where `startClusterComms` does not early-return, would bind:

- a keyed decision derived from **either** the candidate or the promoted store, and
- restart **completion** (comms back up), not merely teardown.

That likely needs a fake/injected comms starter rather than real sockets, so it is a fixture change rather than another assertion — which is why it is filed instead of folded.

## Do not

Do not "fix" this by deleting or weakening the three subtests. They bind the decision this PR exists to protect; these are gaps *beside* them, not defects *in* them.

Found by the Codex leg of the #6865 gate. The scope comment on `keyed_endpoint_change_must_still_restart` points here.

## #6879 — logging: RFC 3164 facility/severity numeric constants are a wire contract with no golden test [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-27)

Split out of the #6829 gate. Pre-existing, low severity, but it is a **wire-format contract** and nothing pins it.

## The gap

`FacilityAuth = 4`, `FacilityLocal0 = 16` and the rest are RFC 3164 numeric codes. `pkg/logging/syslog.go` computes the wire priority as `priority := s.Facility*8 + severity`, so those integers go out on the wire verbatim to a third-party collector.

Measured: changing `FacilityAuth` from `4` to `9` leaves the suite **fully green**. Every table-driven test references the constants symbolically on both sides of the assertion, so it is comparing a value to itself. The mapping-table and corpus tests added by #6829 have the same shape — they bind *which names map*, not *what they map to*.

## Failure scenario

A refactor renumbers or reorders the constants (a plausible edit: sorting them, or aligning them with a different vendor table). xpf keeps parsing and rendering consistently, all tests pass, and every syslog record silently arrives at the collector filed under the wrong facility. Downstream routing rules, retention policies and alerting keyed on facility all misfire, with nothing on the appliance indicating a change.

This is the same class as the #5797 misrouting #6829 exists to close, one layer down: there, an unmapped *name* fell through to local0; here, a correct name maps to a wrong *number*.

## Fix direction

A golden test asserting the literal integers against RFC 3164 §4.1.1, independent of the constants:

```go
// Not FacilityAuth -- the literal, so renumbering the constant REDs this.
{"auth", 4}, {"kern", 0}, {"user", 1}, {"daemon", 3}, {"syslog", 5},
{"local0", 16}, ... {"local7", 23},
```

Same for severities. Assert against `ParseFacility`'s output so the test binds the mapping end to end rather than the constant's spelling.

Worth pairing with a check that `priority = facility*8 + severity` yields the RFC's expected byte for a couple of known pairs, since that arithmetic is the actual wire value.

## Provenance

Found while gating #6829 (facility parsing hardening). Reported by the implementing lane rather than dropped; it declined to widen its own PR's scope, correctly.

## #6881 — docs/cluster: three sync_auth.go comments and the README rollout section describe dual-accept, removed by #5078 [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-27)

Inherited residuals surfaced by two rounds of the #6865 gate. All comment/doc only — no runtime effect — but they describe a mechanism that no longer exists, and one of them now sits ~500 lines below a section that says the opposite.

## The sites

- **`pkg/cluster/README.md` "Rolling it onto a live unkeyed cluster"** — the procedure asks the operator to commit the key on the *other* node. A seated RG0 secondary returns `ErrClusterReadOnly`; and if sync drops before that step, the keyed side rejects the unkeyed reconnect. PR #6865 marked this section STALE inline and pointed at the correct recovery enumeration, but the step-by-step itself still needs rewriting to the post-#5078 reality.
- **`pkg/cluster/sync_auth.go:327`** — claims `performSyncHandshake` returns an optional legacy first frame. Its signature does not.
- **`pkg/cluster/sync_auth.go:401`** — labels the keyed-local / unkeyed-peer case "Dual-accept", immediately before `syncAuthDecision` rejects it (line 299).
- **`pkg/cluster/sync_auth.go:433`** — describes a removed sticky guard and a `pending` result that no longer exist.

## Why it is worth a ticket rather than a drive-by

A reader hitting `sync_auth.go:401` sees "Dual-accept" three lines above a rejection and has to decide which is true. The #5078 work made the rejection unconditional; the comments were not swept with it. The same reader in a maintenance window follows the README rollout steps and finds step 2 refused on the standby.

None of this is reachable as a bug — the code is correct, the prose is not — so it is filed rather than folded into #6865, whose diff is already carrying its own corrections.

## Fix direction

Sweep the four sites against what `syncAuthDecision` actually returns today, and rewrite the README rollout section around the one recovery path that works (controlled RG0 promotion: stop `xpfd` on the keyed primary, the secondary promotes and `applyRG0OwnershipTransition` clears its read-only gate, commit the key there, restart the old primary).

## Provenance

Flagged by the Codex leg of the #6865 gate across rounds 2 and 3; present at every revision reviewed, so genuinely inherited rather than introduced.

## #6883 — userspace-dp: test fixtures set pkt_len = frame.len() - 14 while the shim stamps the full frame length [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-27)

Tree-wide test-fixture drift, surfaced while verifying #6304. **Not a runtime defect** — filed so it is tracked rather than rediscovered per-PR.

## The drift

`test_meta`-style helpers across the AF_XDP fixtures construct metadata with:

```rust
pkt_len: frame.len() - 14
```

i.e. frame length minus the Ethernet header. The shim stamps the **full frame length**. So every fixture using this convention feeds the dataplane a `pkt_len` 14 bytes short of what production supplies.

## Why it has not bitten

On the paths currently exercised, `pkt_len` feeds byte counters and nothing that steers a decision. Specifically on the #6304 flow-cache-hit path it cannot reach the mirror admission decision at all, which is why the new guard there binds correctly despite the drift.

## Why it is still worth fixing

The value is wrong in a consistent direction across many fixtures, so:

- any future assertion on a **byte counter** computed from a fixture is off by 14 per packet, and will look like an off-by-N bug in production code rather than in the fixture;
- any future code that gates on `pkt_len` (MTU comparison, segmentation threshold, a length-derived hash) will be exercised at the wrong boundary, and a fixture that sits exactly on a threshold in the test will sit 14 bytes off it in production;
- because the convention is repeated verbatim across siblings, a lane copying an adjacent fixture inherits the drift silently.

That is the shape that produces a guard which passes for the wrong reason.

## Fix direction

Decide which the fixtures mean to model and make it uniform:

- if `pkt_len` is the **frame** length as the shim stamps it, drop the `- 14`;
- if some call sites genuinely want an L3 length, give that its own named field or helper rather than overloading `pkt_len`.

Then grep the tree for the `- 14` idiom and convert together, since a partial conversion is worse than either consistent state.

## Provenance

Disclosed by the lane that verified the #6304 salvage, as a residual it deliberately did not close because it is out of that issue's scope and tree-wide.

## #6884 — userspace-xdp: shim is at 99.08% of the eBPF verifier instruction cap (990,796 / 1,000,000) — one toolchain bump from unbuildable [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-27)

Measured while driving #4555. Filed separately because this is a standing build-availability risk independent of that issue.

## The number

| | insns | headroom |
|---|---:|---:|
| tracked shim object at `86927d23c` | **990,796** | **9,204 (0.92%)** |
| verifier cap | 1,000,000 | — |

`make generate` runs a kernel-verifier gate, and `build-userspace-xdp.sh` correctly refuses to install an object the verifier rejects. So the failure mode is not a bad object shipping — it is **`make generate` starting to fail**, blocking any change that touches the shim, including changes unrelated to the extension-header walk.

## Why 0.92% is thin

The cost of a single structural change dwarfs the remaining budget. From the #4555 measurements, one additional extension-header iteration costs **87,000–106,000 instructions** — roughly **10× the entire headroom**. Anything with comparable footprint hits the wall.

More to the point, the margin is hostage to codegen. Measured on this tree:

| variant | insns | Δ vs master |
|---|---:|---:|
| master | 990,796 | — |
| master + widened EH-type match arm (#4517 types) | 874,873 | **−115,923 (−11.7%)** |

Widening an 8-value `u8` match *reduced* cost by 11.7%, almost certainly because LLVM lowers it as a table rather than a compare chain and the verifier's state pruning copes far better. That swing is larger than the entire current headroom — **in either direction**. A Rust/LLVM pin bump that flips that lowering the other way pushes master itself over the cap with no source change at all.

## Why it is not urgent-but-is-real

Nothing is broken today: the object builds, the gate passes, the dataplane runs. The risk is that the next person to touch `userspace-xdp` — for any reason — discovers the budget is gone, and the fix is a refactor they did not sign up for.

## Fix direction

PR **#6676** (open, head `4de0f9319`) already demonstrates the shape: a runtime `binding_slot` extraction that measures at **797,849 insns / 202,151 headroom (20.22%)** — it frees 192,947. If it merges, this issue is largely addressed and should be re-measured.

If it does not, the same move applies elsewhere: pull work out of the verifier's reach by making it runtime-data-driven rather than branch-structural.

**Do not chase the 11.7% match-arm saving as a fix.** It is codegen luck tied to the toolchain pin, not a structural property, and relying on it makes the pin load-bearing in a way nothing records.

## Suggested guard

Whatever restores headroom, consider having the build gate **report** the instruction count rather than only pass/fail, and fail on a *threshold* (say 90% of cap) rather than at the cliff. A gate that only fires at 1,000,001 gives no warning that 990,796 was ever reached — which is why this went unnoticed.

## #6885 — userspace-dp: screen/extract.rs comment claims MAX_EXT_HDRS=8 parity with the BPF parser — the parser bounds at 6 and no such constant exists [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-27)

`userspace-dp/src/screen/extract.rs:204`:

> `// We bound the walk to MAX_EXT_HDRS=8 like the BPF parser.`

Both halves are false, verified on `origin/master` (`86927d23c`):

```
$ git grep -n "MAX_EXT_HDRS" origin/master -- 'bpf/' 'userspace-xdp/'
bpf/headers/xpf_common.h:35:#define MAX_EXT_HDRS    6
userspace-xdp/src/lib.rs:33:const MAX_EXT_HDRS: usize = 6;
```

The BPF/shim parser bounds at **6**, not 8, and **no constant named `MAX_EXT_HDRS` equals 8 anywhere in the tree**. (The userspace walker's bound is `MAX_IPV6_EXT_HEADERS = 8` in `afxdp/frame/inspect.rs:31` — a different constant with a different name.)

## Why this is worth fixing rather than shrugging at

The comment does not merely state a wrong number. It **asserts the exact parity that #4555 exists because we do not have** — the shim stopping at 6 while userspace walks 8 is the divergence #4555 tracks. A reader here concludes the two planes agree and stops looking, which is the opposite of true.

That makes it actively load-bearing in the wrong direction: it would have told someone screening #4555 that the issue was already resolved.

## Fix

State the bound this walk actually uses, and if the parity claim is worth keeping at all, name the two constants separately and say they **differ** — with a pointer to #4555 for why. Do not write a number that has to be kept in sync by hand across two planes; that is how this one rotted.

## Provenance

Found while measuring #4555 (a lane went to the shim expecting parity, per this comment, and found 6 vs 8). Same class as the stale comment on #4313's own mechanism: a comment describing a mechanism's coverage, never re-checked as the mechanism moved.

## #6886 — userspace-xdp: classify_native_gre_inner_ipv6 EH bail-out set omits the #4517 types — builds a session key on protocol=135 instead of bailing [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-27)

`userspace-xdp/src/lib.rs:914`, in `classify_native_gre_inner_ipv6`:

```rust
let protocol = ip6[6];
match protocol {
    NEXTHDR_HOP | NEXTHDR_ROUTING | NEXTHDR_DEST | NEXTHDR_AUTH | NEXTHDR_FRAGMENT => {
        return 0;
    }
    _ => {}
}
let mut key = UserspaceSessionKey {
    addr_family: AF_INET6,
    ...
```

The bail-out set is `HOP | ROUTING | DEST | AUTH | FRAGMENT`. It omits the extension-header types added by **#4517** — MOBILITY (135), HIP (139), SHIM6 (140), and the experimental 253/254.

So a GRE-encapsulated inner IPv6 packet whose next header is, say, **135** falls through to the `_ => {}` arm and **builds a session key with `protocol = 135`** — an extension-header type in the protocol field — instead of bailing out the way the other EH types do.

## What is NOT yet established

**Whether such a key is ever installable, or whether it merely misses.** Post-#4517 the userspace walker walks past 135, so the expectation is that the shim-built key never matches anything userspace installs → miss → XSK redirect → full userspace policy → fail-closed, same as #4555's over-limit case.

That is the *expectation*, not a measurement. It has been verified at the level of code shape only. **Someone should trace it before anyone calls it harmless**, specifically:

1. Can a session ever be installed under a key whose `protocol` is an EH type? If yes, a shim-built `protocol=135` key could match it, and the packet takes the fast path on a mis-parsed identity.
2. If it always misses, the cost is a fast-path miss on GRE-inner-v6-with-mobility traffic — LOW/parity, same class as #4555, and it should be recorded as such rather than left ambiguous.
3. Does the same omission exist in the non-GRE inner path, or is the main `parse_l4` walker already consistent with #4517?

## Why it matters that #4517 was an evasion fix

#4517 added those types because a chain using them was parsed differently by the two planes — an IDS-evasion shape. This site was not swept when that landed, so the shim's GRE-inner path still has the pre-#4517 view. Even if the outcome is fail-closed today, the divergence is the same one #4517 closed elsewhere.

## Provenance

Found while measuring #4555. Reported as a code-shape observation with the trace explicitly **not** done, rather than asserted as harmless.

## #6888 — cluster: heartbeat readLoop discards the UDP source address — no pin to the configured peer [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-27)

Split out of #5086, whose titled defect (A→B→A session rollback) is fixed and closed. This was the second clause of that issue's fix direction and was never done.

## The site

`pkg/cluster/heartbeat.go`, in the receiver's read loop:

```go
r.conn.SetReadDeadline(time.Now().Add(r.interval))
n, _, err := r.conn.ReadFromUDP(buf)
```

`ReadFromUDP` returns the sender's address; it is discarded into `_`. Nothing compares it to the configured peer address for the cluster control link.

## What this does and does not mean

**It is not an authentication bypass.** Heartbeat frames are MAC-verified, and `heartbeatAuthReplay.admit` is documented as callable only after that verification — so an attacker without the control-link PSK cannot get a frame admitted, whatever source address it carries. This is **defence in depth**, not a hole.

What the missing pin costs:

- **Off-path spoofing is not filtered at the cheapest possible point.** An attacker who can reach the control-link port makes the node do MAC verification work on every forged frame. That is a small CPU amplification on a path that runs at 200ms intervals with a threshold of 5, i.e. it is latency-sensitive.
- **A misconfiguration is silent.** If a third node is accidentally pointed at this cluster's control link, its frames are read, MAC-checked and dropped with no signal that traffic is arriving from an unexpected source. A source pin would make that visible as a counted rejection rather than an invisible drop.
- **It is the layer that survives a key compromise partially.** With a leaked PSK, a source pin still constrains where forged frames can originate from.

Severity: **LOW**. Filed for accuracy rather than urgency — #5086 should not have stayed open carrying a claim that was mostly fixed.

## Fix direction

Capture the address and compare it to the configured peer for this cluster:

```go
n, src, err := r.conn.ReadFromUDP(buf)
...
if !r.peerAddrMatches(src) { /* count and drop before MAC verification */ }
```

Two things to get right, and they are the reason this is not a one-liner:

1. **Where in the order.** Dropping before MAC verification is the point (it saves the work), but it must not become a way to *skip* replay-state updates for genuine frames — check the interaction with `admit`.
2. **What "matches" means.** The control link may be configured by interface plus address, addresses can be v4 or v6, and a node can legitimately source from a link-local address on the control interface. A pin that is too strict breaks a working cluster on upgrade, which is far worse than the gap it closes. Consider warn-and-count first, reject second — the same strict-at-the-boundary / tolerant-on-the-live-path asymmetry used elsewhere in `pkg/cluster`.

## #6889 — cluster: a dropped RG0 transition event leaves the manager PRIMARY while the config store stays read-only [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-27)

Found while verifying a documentation claim about recovery paths for #5078. Verified firsthand on `origin/master`.

## The gap

`pkg/cluster/manager.go`, `sendEvent`:

```go
select {
case m.eventCh <- ClusterEvent{GroupID: groupID, OldState: oldState, NewState: newState}:
default:
    slog.Warn("cluster: event channel full, dropping event", ...)
```

Transition events are delivered **non-blockingly** and dropped when the channel is full.

The only production caller of `applyRG0OwnershipTransition` — the function that clears the config-store read-only gate — is the event consumer in `pkg/daemon/daemon_ha.go`:

```go
// RG0-specific: config ownership and IPsec SA re-initiation.
if ev.GroupID == 0 {
    d.applyRG0OwnershipTransition(ev.NewState)
}
```

There is a dropped-event fallback, and it performs generic RG reconciliation — but it **never reconciles `Store.ClusterReadOnly`**.

## Consequence

If the RG0 `StatePrimary` event is dropped, the node ends up in a split state:

- the cluster manager reports RG0 **primary**, so `IsLocalPrimary(0)` passes and the gRPC layer admits the operator;
- the config store is still **read-only**, so `EnterConfigureSession` returns `ErrClusterReadOnly`.

The operator sees a node that says it owns config and refuses to be configured, with no indication why. The only trace is a `slog.Warn` about a full event channel, which does not mention config ownership.

Worse, it is self-healing only by luck: nothing re-drives the gate until the *next* RG0 transition, so a node can sit in this state indefinitely after a single burst of events.

## Why this matters beyond the annoyance

`SetClusterReadOnly` is the authority boundary for who may write config in a cluster. A mechanism that sets it via a **droppable** channel means the boundary's state can diverge from the state that decides it. Today the divergence fails *closed* (refuses a legitimate primary). The same missing reconciliation is what would let it fail *open* if a demotion event were dropped instead — worth checking as part of the fix.

## #6890 — cluster/api: a cold-start standby never gets SetClusterReadOnly(true), and REST exposes commit without an RG0 check [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-27)

Found while verifying a documentation claim for #5078. Verified firsthand on `origin/master`.

## Two facts that compose badly

**1. The store starts writable and a cold-start standby may never be told otherwise.**

A new RG is constructed already in the secondary state (`pkg/cluster/group_state.go`):

```go
State:  StateSecondary,
```

`SetClusterReadOnly(true)` is called from the RG0 **transition** handler. A node that comes up as standby and stays there — non-preempt cold start, no peer flap — never experiences a transition, so the call never happens. The config store remains **writable** on a seated secondary.

**2. The REST config path has no RG0 check.**

`pkg/api/config.go` enters a configure session directly:

```go
if err := s.store.EnterConfigureSession(sessionID); err != nil {
    writeError(w, http.StatusConflict, err.Error())
    return
}
```

It relies entirely on the store gate. The interactive CLI has an independent check (`pkg/cli/cli_dispatch.go`, "node is not primary for RG0"), and gRPC checks `IsLocalPrimary(0)` — REST has neither.

## Consequence

On a cold-start standby with the REST API enabled, an operator can enter a configure session and **commit** on the node that is not the config authority. Config-sync from the real primary will later overwrite it, so the likely outcome is a silently discarded change — and, in the window before that, two nodes with divergent candidate config and no indication which one is authoritative.

This is the mirror of #6889: there the gate is set but not reconciled after a dropped event; here it is never set at all.

## Why the CLI being safe is not enough

The three config entry points do not share a check. Two implement their own; one delegates to a store gate that is not reliably armed. That is the shape where a future entry point inherits the weakest of the three by default — and it means the store gate cannot be described as the boundary "however the operator reached the box", which is how it is currently documented.

Two independent halves, and both are worth doing:

## #6892 — userspace-dp: NAT64 synced reserve has the same first-prefix-whose-pool-contains selection that #6211 fixed for source NAT [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-28)

Found by the #6876 gate as the symmetric surface. Out of that PR's scope and correctly not overclaimed there, so filed separately.

## The mirror

`#6211` established that selecting a source-NAT rule on a standby by *"the first pool-mode rule whose pool contains `rewrite_src`"* can pick a different rule than the active chose, because two differently-scoped rules can share a pool address. The fix narrows selection using the synced zone pair and the post-DNAT destination before falling back.

`userspace-dp/src/nat/nat64.rs`, `reserve_synced_nat64_allocation`, has the **identical** selection shape: first prefix whose `pool_v4` contains `snat_v4`. And each `Nat64Prefix` owns its **own** `port_allocator`, so two prefixes sharing a v4 pool address hit exactly the same wrong-allocator divergence #6211 exists to close.

## Why it is worth fixing rather than noting

The consequence is the same class: the standby reserves the flow in a different allocator than the one the active used. On its own that is an accounting divergence. Combined with the release path — which scans and stops at the first allocator reporting the flow released — it is also the precondition for the leak found in #6876: if the same session is re-synced and selection resolves differently across the two upserts, two allocators hold the flow and teardown frees one.

HA session-sync re-upserts a live session on reconnect bulk-sync and on `forceResync` after a delete-journal overflow, so "selection resolves differently at two different times" is not hypothetical.

## The information needed is already available

The standby **can** narrow here, and more cheaply than for source NAT: the synced v6 destination is `key.dst_ip`, already present on the entry. So a prefix whose v6 range does not contain the session's destination can be excluded without any new wire field.

## Fix direction

Mirror #6211's shape:

1. narrow candidate prefixes by the synced v6 destination before the pool-address test;
2. keep the unfiltered scan as a strict fallback, so the outcome can only improve on the current behaviour, never refuse a reservation the current code would have made;
3. bind the **production call site**, not just the helper — the #6876 gate found that PR's equivalent call site completely unbound (disabling the feature left 4366/4366 green), which is the recurring failure mode in this area.

Whatever the fix, the release path must be checked at the same time: if two reservations can ever coexist, a release that stops at the first hit leaks the second. See #6876.

## Provenance

Enumerated during the #6876 completeness audit as the one mirror surface not covered: source-NAT port-bearing and address-only arms are both narrowed and both bound, v4/v6 both handled, Go/Rust needs no change — NAT64 is the gap.

## #6893 — config/dataplane: a VLAN sub-interface that fails to be created is soft-skipped, and the firewall filter for it is then silently not assigned [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-27)

Fail-open on a security surface, reachable on current master, independent of #4960 (found while scoping it).

## The two soft skips

`pkg/dataplane/compiler_iface.go`, in `mapZoneInterface`:

- if `ensureVLANSubInterface` fails → `slog.Warn("VLAN sub-interface failed, skipping"); return nil`
- ~20 lines earlier, if the physical interface is missing → `slog.Warn("interface not found, skipping"); return nil`

Both return `nil`, so **`compileZones` succeeds** even though the sub-interface does not exist.

## What that composes into

`compileFirewallFilters` later resolves the same sub-interface by name (`fmt.Sprintf("%s.%d", physName, vlanID)`), misses, logs a warning, and `continue`s. **The configured firewall filter is silently not assigned to that interface.**

Net effect: the operator commits a config containing a filter binding, the commit **reports success**, and the filter is not applied. The only trace is two `slog.Warn` lines. Port mirroring has the same shape.

## Reachability

Any condition that makes VLAN creation fail while leaving the rest of the apply viable:

- a transient netlink failure
- a name collision with an existing device
- a parent interface that is itself down, missing, or was skipped by the sibling soft-skip above

None of these is exotic, and none of them fails the commit.

## Why this is a fail-open rather than a fail-closed

The interface still exists in the zone from the operator's point of view — or does not exist at all, in which case traffic is not forwarded and the failure is loud. The dangerous case is the one where forwarding works and the *filter* is the thing that quietly went missing. A filter that is absent permits what it was configured to deny.

## Relationship to #4960

Same root cause, second reachability path. #4960 is about phases 3-11 aborting *after* `compileZones` already mutated the host; this is about `compileZones` **succeeding** while having failed to create something a later phase depends on.

The connection is worth recording because it is what makes the naive fix for #4960 dangerous: reordering the fail-capable phases ahead of `compileZones` would make these lookups miss *by construction* on every apply, turning an occasional fail-open into a universal one. That is why #4960's fix has to be additive rather than a reorder.

## #6895 — cmd/cli: the remote CLI cannot distinguish an idle zone from one whose counters are unavailable [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-27)

Surfaced during the #6843 re-gate as a **pre-existing** gap — not introduced by that PR, so it is filed rather than folded. Verified firsthand on `origin/master` at `86927d23c`.

## The gap

`cmd/cli/show_security.go:255-259` — the remote `cli` binary that CLAUDE.md tells operators to use — renders zone traffic from the structured `GetZones` proto and simply omits the section when both counters are zero:

```go
if z.IngressPackets > 0 || z.EgressPackets > 0 {
	fmt.Println("  Traffic statistics:")
	fmt.Printf("    Input:  %d packets, %d bytes\n", z.IngressPackets, z.IngressBytes)
	fmt.Printf("    Output: %d packets, %d bytes\n", z.EgressPackets, z.EgressBytes)
}
```

`ZoneInfo` in `proto/xpf/v1/xpf.proto` carries `ingress_packets` / `egress_packets` and **no availability flag** — nothing mirroring REST's `PerZoneCountersAvailable`. So the client has no way to tell the two cases apart:

- the zone is genuinely **idle** — zero is the truth; and
- the zone's counters are **unavailable** — no slot, no apply result, a pre-#3651 helper — where zero is the absence of an answer.

Both render as a silently missing section.

## Why it matters

The other two operator surfaces already distinguish these. The local CLI (`pkg/cli/cli_show_security_zones.go`) and the gRPC text renderer (`pkg/grpcapi/server_show_zones_text.go`) both print an explicit "Traffic statistics: not available" line with the reason, and #6843 is currently tightening exactly that wording on both. REST exposes `PerZoneCountersAvailable`. The remote `cli` binary — the one an operator is most likely to be holding — is the only surface with no signal at all.

The concrete case #6843's own rationale describes applies verbatim here: with 64+ zones, slot exhaustion means `show security zones` prints real byte counts for slotted zones and nothing for overflowed ones. On the local CLI that reads as a labelled "not available". On the remote `cli` it reads as "this zone has no traffic" — which is a wrong answer, not a missing one.

## Fix sketch

Add a per-zone availability field to `ZoneInfo` (mirroring REST's flag, and ideally carrying the reason rather than a bare bool), populate it in `pkg/grpcapi/server_show_zones.go` from the same `{!loaded, cr == nil, !ok, ErrCounterNotPopulated}` membership set the Prometheus gauge and REST already agree on, and render the "not available" line in `cmd/cli/show_security.go` instead of omitting the section.

Wire-protocol note: this is a proto field addition, so both sides need to land together — a one-sided field is the #1961-class no-transit risk. The Go client and Go server are the only consumers here, but the field number must not collide with anything in flight.

## Provenance

`cmd/cli/show_security.go:255-259`, `proto/xpf/v1/xpf.proto` (`message ZoneInfo`), `pkg/api/security.go` (`PerZoneCountersAvailable`), `pkg/cli/cli_show_security_zones.go`, `pkg/grpcapi/server_show_zones_text.go`. Found while reviewing PR #6843 at `e08a3c74f`; that PR fixes the two labelled surfaces and does not touch this one.

## #6896 — docs: three docs outside pkg/cluster still assert that a cluster secondary rejects all config mutations [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-21)

Split out of the #6865 / #5078 documentation sweep so a round-7 PR does not widen into three unrelated doc trees. Verified on `origin/master` at `86927d23c`.

## The refuted premise

Several docs assert, categorically, that a cluster secondary cannot be configured. That is the **design intent**, and it holds wherever the store's read-only gate is armed — but arming is not universal:

- `SetClusterReadOnly(true)` has exactly one production caller path: `applyRG0OwnershipTransition` (`pkg/daemon/daemon_ha.go`), driven by an RG0 **transition event**. There is no startup arming and no reconcile that re-derives the flag.
- A redundancy group is constructed already in `StateSecondary` (`pkg/cluster/group_state.go`) and emits no event; every `sendEvent` call site accompanies a real state change.
- `Store.clusterReadOnly` is a plain `bool` with no constructor initialisation, so it starts `false`.

So a node that cold-starts, seats as RG0 secondary and never transitions has a **writable** store. And `pkg/api/config.go` enters a configure session with no RG0 check, where `pkg/grpcapi/server_config.go` guards on `IsLocalPrimary(0)` and `pkg/cli/cli_dispatch.go` has its own check.

The underlying gaps are already filed: **#6890** (cold-start standby + REST with no RG0 check) and **#6889** (a dropped transition event leaves the manager primary while the store stays read-only).

## Sites still to fix

These are in packages that #6865 does not touch:

- `pkg/configstore/README.md` — "the secondary is read-only and receives config only via `SyncApply`"
- `docs/feature-coverage.md` — REST has "full gRPC parity", followed by configure mode being "blocked on secondary cluster nodes". Both halves cannot be true: REST is precisely the surface with no RG0 check.
- `docs/phases.md` — "Secondary nodes operate in read-only mode, rejecting all config mutations."

`pkg/cluster/README.md`, `pkg/cluster/sync_auth.go` and `pkg/daemon/cluster_transport_key_5078_test.go` are being corrected in #6865 and are **not** part of this issue.

## Fix

State the mechanism with its precondition rather than the conclusion: the gate covers every entry point *once armed*; arming comes from an RG0 transition; a cold-started standby and the REST path are the two holes, tracked as #6890 and #6889 and being closed. Describe the intent and name the hole — do not assert the hole away.

## Method note, because it is the reusable part

A symbol grep finds none of these. The premise is restated in different words at every site, so it has to be searched as a **claim** ("secondary", "read-only", "rejects", "only writer", "blocked on secondary") rather than as an identifier. The #6865 round-6 edit corrected exactly one row and left nine other restatements standing — including the section title seven lines below the fix, and three citations of `Daemon.applyHAState`, a symbol that does not exist anywhere in the tree (`grep -rn 'func.*applyHAState' pkg/` returns nothing; the real one is `applyRG0OwnershipTransition`). Whoever takes this should grep the three files above for the claim, not for a name, and check the surrounding paragraphs rather than the matched line.

## #6897 — test/incus: test-failover.sh silently emits NO cell when iperf3 throughput is sub-Gbit, and the session-count floor fails on master [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

Two defects in `test/incus/test-failover.sh`, both found while attributing a smoke failure on PR #6862. Both measured on the loss userspace cluster today.

## 1. A sub-Gbit run silently drops the throughput cell

```bash
throughput=$(incus exec "$CLUSTER_LAN_HOST" -- grep '\[SUM\].*sender' /tmp/iperf3-failover.log 2>/dev/null \
	| grep -oP '[\d.]+\s+Gbits' | grep -oP '[\d.]+' || echo "0")
...
if [[ -n "$throughput" ]] && awk "BEGIN{exit !($throughput >= $MIN_THROUGHPUT)}"; then
	pass "iperf3 throughput: ${throughput} Gbps (>= ${MIN_THROUGHPUT} Gbps)"
elif [[ -n "$throughput" ]] && [[ "$throughput" != "0" ]]; then
	fail "iperf3 throughput too low: ${throughput} Gbps (expected >= ${MIN_THROUGHPUT} Gbps)"
fi
```

The parse only matches **`Gbits`**. When iperf3 reports the `[SUM] … sender` line in `Mbits/sec`, `throughput` becomes the literal `"0"` — and then *neither* branch fires. There is no `else`. The run emits **no cell at all**: not a pass, not a fail, nothing in the summary.

Measured, same commit range, same harness (`md5sum` identical between the two worktrees), differing only in cluster state:

| run | CoS | `[SUM]` unit | throughput cell | summary |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| PR #6862 | applied (`scheduler-100m`, `output bandwidth-output` on `reth0 unit 80`) | Mbits | **absent** | `12 passed, 1 failed` |
| `origin/master` `86927d23c` | wiped by deploy | Gbits | `PASS … 22.9 Gbps` | `13 passed, 1 failed` |

So a shaped run and an unshaped run produce different *cell counts*, and the only tell is comparing the two summary lines side by side. A reader looking at one run sees a clean-looking `12 passed, 1 failed` and has no way to know a gate did not execute. Silence is indistinguishable from success — and this is the exact case the harness most needs to catch, since a sub-Gbit result is what a throughput regression looks like.

**Fix:** add the missing `else` and fail loudly, e.g. `fail "iperf3 throughput unparseable from the [SUM] sender line (got '$throughput') — was the class shaped?"`. Better, parse the unit as well as the number and normalise Mbits/Gbits, so a shaped class produces a real measurement instead of a hole. Either way the cell must always be emitted.

## 2. The established-session floor fails on unmodified master

```
FAIL  fw0 has only 0 established sessions (expected >= 4)
```

Reproduced at `origin/master` `86927d23c` with **13 passed, 1 failed** — no PR applied. On PR #6862 the same assertion reported `1` (also below the floor), so #6862 is not the cause; if anything it scores marginally higher.

Note the internal inconsistency in the same run: `fw0 has only 0 established sessions` immediately followed by `PASS fw1 has 9 synced sessions`. The primary reports zero established while nine sessions synced *from* it to the peer. So either the count the assertion reads is not the count the sync path uses, or the check runs before the `-P8` streams reach the state it filters on. Either way the floor as written does not measure what its message claims.

**Fix direction:** decide what the assertion is for. If it is "traffic is flowing before we crash the node", the synced-session count on the peer already proves that and is passing. If it is genuinely about `fw0`'s established table, the check needs to poll with a timeout rather than sample once, and should print what it actually counted so a failure is diagnosable.

## #6899 — firewall filter + DNAT: two codex-180 survivors — stale non-SYN doc claim, and a silently-swallowed unparseable destination-prefix [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-28)

Split from **#5583** (codex-review-180 survivors) after a full 4-of-4 sweep against `origin/master` `e80db2eae`. Two shipped; these two are live.

### 1. `C180-021` — the packet-processing doc still asserts a shim drop that no longer happens

`docs/afxdp-packet-processing.md:48-49` still says non-SYN TCP without a live entry in the `userspace_sessions` BPF map is dropped. That describes the retired eBPF pipeline. The session-miss guard now lives in the userspace dataplane and behaves differently — transit dispositions drop a bare RST/FIN (#4400), while the host-inbound LocalDelivery path declines to *cache* a session off a non-SYN first packet but **still delivers** the packet to the local stack (#4539), specifically so a peer teardown for a firewall-originated flow is not lost.

The doc as written would lead an operator to expect a drop where the packet is delivered. Fix is to restate it against the current guard, including the transit-vs-host-inbound split.

### 2. `C180-023` — an unparseable `destination_prefix` with a valid base address falls through silently

`userspace-dp/src/nat/destination.rs:322-324`. A non-empty but unparseable `destination_prefix` combined with a **valid** base address still reaches `Ok(ip) => DnatDest::Host(ip)` with no error recorded — the misconfiguration is swallowed and DNAT quietly targets the base address.

**This one has a decoy three lines away, and it is the sharpest trap found in this sweep.** A `record_parse_error` call *does* exist just below, so grepping `record_parse_error` in this file returns a hit that looks exactly like the fix. It is not: that call fires only when the prefix **and** the address both fail to parse — the #4718 both-unparseable drop. The single-unparseable case this item names is untouched.

Anyone re-checking this should verify by constructing the input (non-empty garbage prefix + parseable address) rather than by finding the neighbouring symbol.

### Why #5583 can now close

4 of 4 checked, with current-master evidence:
- `C180-024` **SHIPPED** — `pkg/config/tcp_flags.go:245-249` rejects `)` at depth 0, `:305` rejects nonzero depth at end, `:155` covers empty/misordered groups, with mirror guards at `:161-170` and `:223`. Broader than the item asked for.
- `C180-026` **SHIPPED** via #6383 — `pkg/snmp/traps.go:395` now documents exact accounting (`accepted == delivered + trapsDropped`).
- `C180-021`, `C180-023` — tracked here.

## #6901 — test: the GC-reap source-NAT release call site is unbound — deleting it leaves the whole package green [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-28)

Found while gating PR #6876 (#6211). Pre-existing and unrelated to #6211 — filing rather than folding, per the "do not put a second unrelated production claim under one title" rule.

## The gap

`release_source_nat_allocation` has four production call sites. Deleting the call at each, whole package, `cargo test --release --no-fail-fast --test-threads=1`:

| call site | exit | failures | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| `session_glue/promote.rs:194` | 101 | `purge_translated_synced_hit_releases_source_nat_reservation_5295` | BOUND |
| `session_glue/mod.rs:563` | 101 | `delete_terminal_filtered_session_releases_companion_and_allocator_5622` | BOUND |
| `session_glue/commands/delete_synced.rs:38` | 101 | only `shared_cos_lease::…v8_epoch_seqlock…` + `wg::engine::…install_session_serializes…` (known-flaky #6657 / #6157 / #6294) | UNBOUND |
| **`worker/loop_body/mod.rs:1625`** (`reap_expired_sessions`) | **0** | **none** | **UNBOUND** |

`delete_synced.rs:38` is being bound in PR #6876 (it is the #6211-relevant teardown). **This issue tracks the remaining one: the GC reap.**

## Why it matters

`reap_expired_sessions` is the ordinary inactivity-timeout teardown — the path that frees a source-NAT pool port for the overwhelming majority of sessions, which age out rather than being explicitly deleted. Deleting its `release_source_nat_allocation` call would leak a pool port per reaped translated session until `AllocatorExhausted`, and nothing in the suite would notice.

Note the baseline discipline this needs: scoring the `delete_synced` cell by exit code alone would have marked it BOUND. The full suite at the same head had **zero** failures, which is what makes attributing those two to flake rather than to the mutation airtight.

## Fix direction

A test driving `reap_expired_sessions` with an expired translated session and asserting the pool port is returned — `source_nat_pool_statuses(...)[n].used_ports` goes 1 → 0. The sibling #5295 / #5622 tests are the shape to copy.

Same check is probably worth running for `release_nat64_allocation`, whose call sites sit alongside all four of these.

## #6904 — api: REST ping/traceroute accept unbounded per-field diagnostic args; gRPC bounds them at 512 [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-27)

### Summary

`pkg/api/system.go` (REST) passes operator-supplied diagnostic arguments into
`exec` argv with **no per-field length bound**. The gRPC sibling for the same
operation enforces `maxDiagArgLen = 512`. One surface was hardened and the other
was missed.

### Verified on current master (`dd23119aa`)

```
$ git show origin/master:pkg/api/system.go | grep -c 'maxDiagArgLen\|checkDiagArg'
0
$ git show origin/master:pkg/grpcapi/server_diag_ping.go | grep -n maxDiagArgLen
20:// maxDiagArgLen bounds each operator-supplied diagnostic argument
29:const maxDiagArgLen = 512
35:     if len(v) > maxDiagArgLen {
```

The REST path reaches exec unbounded — `pkg/api/system.go`:

```go
var diagRun = func(ctx context.Context, argv []string) (string, error) {
	c := exec.CommandContext(ctx, argv[0], argv[1:]...)
	c.WaitDelay = requestExecWaitDelay
	out, err := c.CombinedOutput()
	return string(out), err
}
```

`pingHandler` checks only `req.Target == ""`, clamps `count` to [1,100], then
`buildPingArgv(req, count)` → `diagRun`. No length check on `Target` or any
other string field.

### Severity: MEDIUM, not HIGH

The source review rated this High. Downgrading, with the bounding factors named:

- **Not command injection.** `exec.CommandContext(argv[0], argv[1:]...)` passes
  an argv vector with no shell, so a long or metacharacter-laden argument is one
  opaque argument, not a second command.

## #6905 — userspace-dp: neg_neigh overflow clears the whole suppression cache, so a multi-hop scan disarms dead-host suppression for every hop [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-28)

### Summary

`neg_neigh_record` evicts the negative-neighbor suppression cache **wholesale**
when it reaches `MAX_NEG_NEIGH_CACHE`. Traffic to many distinct unresolvable
next-hops therefore does not merely fail to be suppressed itself — it discards
the suppression state protecting every *other* hop, re-arming resolver work for
destinations that were already known dead.

### Verified on current master (`dd23119aa`)

`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/neg_neigh.rs`:

```rust
/// Record a dead-host drop at `now_ns`. Bounded by `MAX_NEG_NEIGH_CACHE`: on
/// overflow (and only when inserting a genuinely new key) the map is cleared
/// wholesale. `clear()` retains capacity, so this is allocation-free.
pub(super) fn neg_neigh_record(cache: &mut NegNeighCache, key: (i32, IpAddr), now_ns: u64) {
    if cache.len() >= MAX_NEG_NEIGH_CACHE && !cache.contains_key(&key) {
        cache.clear();
    }
    cache.insert(key, now_ns);
}
```

Still present 32 commits after the review base.

### Why this is a defect and not just a documented choice

The comment records **what** the code does ("cleared wholesale", "allocation-free")
but not the consequence that makes it interesting: the eviction victim set is
chosen by the *arriving* key, not by age or usefulness. A host sweeping distinct
next-hops controls when the clear fires and thus destroys unrelated suppression
entries at will. The module's own header says the mechanism exists because a
multi-hop scan "could saturate the bounded queue (cap `MAX_PENDING_NEIGH`) and
starve" resolution — the clear-on-overflow behaviour partially undoes the very
defence the module is documented to provide.

Any bounded-eviction policy (LRU, random victim, or simply refusing the new key)
loses at most a small share of entries per overflow instead of all of them.

## #6906 — cluster: a session-sync connection established BEFORE the PSK was committed stays unauthenticated forever [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-06)

### Summary

Session-sync verification is gated **per-connection** on `ac.authed()`. A
connection established while both nodes were unkeyed holds `authConn{key:nil}`
and keeps that state for its entire lifetime. Committing the PSK afterwards does
not re-handshake it, so every frame in both directions continues to be accepted
with **no HMAC and no sequence check**, indefinitely.

An attacker holding a connection to the node while it was unkeyed therefore
keeps it across keying — literally "an unauthenticated peer's frames are
accepted on a keyed node", which is the condition #5078 exists to prevent.

### Status: PRE-EXISTING, not a regression

`origin/master` persists the same connection identically. This is filed
separately from PR #6865 for that reason. What #6865 changes is the
*surroundings*: it **pins** the non-restart with two new tests
(`TestAuthKeyChangeDoesNotRestartClusterComms_5078`,
`TestKeyCommitDoesNotRestartCommsAtTheCallSite_5078`) and **prescribes** this
exact rollout in a shipping code comment — while the same comment asserts,
unqualified, that "a node must POSSESS the key to join a keyed cluster".

### Trace

1. Two unkeyed nodes connected, holding `authConn{key:nil}`.
2. Operator commits the key on the primary. `daemon_apply_tail.go` →
   `UpdateConfig` sets `m.controlAuthKey`.
3. The transport-key comparison deliberately excludes the auth key — both new
   tests exist to keep it that way — so comms do not restart.
4. Config-sync carries the key to the secondary over that same connection; the
   secondary likewise does not restart.
5. Both nodes are now keyed. The connection is **still** `authConn{key:nil}`.
6. `ac.authed()` gates verification per-connection, so frames stay unverified.

Nothing re-handshakes: the read deadline sends a keepalive and continues. Only a
process restart, link failure, or write error drops the connection.

## #6908 — cluster: lastRecvConfigGen has the same unserialised race on the ENQUEUE side — manual-failover readiness can stick at applied < received [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-28)

### Summary

#6900 serialises the config-apply **publish** side: `publishAppliedConfigGenIfCurrent`
holds `configNamespaceMu` across re-test-supersession → publish-high-water, and
`resetRecvGen` holds the same mutex across clear-watermarks → claim-namespace.

`lastRecvConfigGen` has the same class of race on the **enqueue** side and is NOT covered
by that fix.

### Mechanism

The `syncMsgConfig` handler raises `lastRecvConfigGen` monotonically on the **old**
connection's receive loop. That goroutine can run *after* `resetRecvGen` has cleared the
watermarks for a new peer incarnation.

The payload itself is then correctly dropped as superseded — so there is **no config
divergence**, which is why this is a different bug from #6900 and not a gap in it. But
`received` stays HIGH while `applied` lands LOW.

### Impact

The #5563 manual-failover readiness gate compares `applied <= received`. With `received`
stuck above whatever `applied` reaches, that gate can report **"transfer not ready"
indefinitely** — an operator attempting a planned failover is blocked with no self-clearing
path short of a process restart or another reconnect that happens to reorder favourably.

Distinct from #6900 in symptom (stuck readiness, not stale config applying), in code path
(receive/enqueue rather than post-apply publish), and in test shape.

### Why it is filed rather than folded

Found by the engineer during the #6900 fold and deliberately scoped out — correctly. It
needs its own regression test driving the enqueue-side interleaving, and folding it would
have widened a concurrency fix that already carries two production test seams.

### Fix direction

Bring the `lastRecvConfigGen` raise under the same `configNamespaceMu` discipline #6900
established, or make the readiness gate tolerant of a received-watermark belonging to a
superseded incarnation. Prefer the former for consistency — #6900 deliberately left the

## #6910 — cluster: a peer reboot entering through an EMPTY alternate fabric slot is indistinguishable from routine second-fabric-up (needs #6669's boot epoch) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-28)

### Summary

`installConn` classifies a new connection by **local slot occupancy**. When a rebooted peer
connects on a fabric whose slot is *empty*, that classification is indistinguishable from a
second fabric coming up routinely — so incarnation is not advanced, the corpse is not
evicted, capability is not cleared, and cold-prime is not armed.

Found by the hostile gate on PR #6825 at `562799c95`, after that PR had already closed two
*other* holes in the same area (generation-aware selection, and eviction of a
superseded-stamp connection). This is a third, distinct path.

### Reachable sequence

1. Old peer A has `conn0`; `conn1` is already down/empty.
2. A hard-reboots, leaving `conn0` half-open locally.
3. Replacement A′ connects first or exclusively on **fabric 1**.
4. `installConn` sees a non-empty registry but an **empty target slot**, so
   `wasDisconnected=false` and `supersededCurrent=false`. It does not advance the
   incarnation, evict `conn0`, clear capability, or arm cold-prime.
5. A′'s `conn1` receives the **same incarnation stamp** as dead `conn0`, so
   `preferredFabricLocked` chooses dead fabric 0 over live fabric 1.
6. When `conn0` eventually drops, `conn1` keeps `connected=true`, so the full-disconnect
   path never runs and cold-prime is never armed. Incremental sync may resume, but A′ never
   receives the survivor's pre-existing session table. **The next failover can blackhole
   established sessions.**

With a modern ack-capable peer the corpse may clear after two read deadlines; with a
legacy/no-ack peer it can persist until TCP or write failure. **Neither path repairs the
missing authoritative bulk.**

### Why this cannot be fixed locally — and what it needs

> Without a peer boot-incarnation signal, it is indistinguishable from the reboot case.

PR #6825's own tests, `TestSecondFabricComingUpIsNotEvicted_5718` and
`TestRoutineInstallDoesNotReArmColdPrime_5718`, deliberately enforce the routine-recovery
classification — and they are **right** for the routine case. The two cases present
identically to a local observer. Any further local heuristic must break one to fix the
other.

## #6911 — daemon: renameRethMember cycles a RETH member link with no AF_XDP worker join (#5103 mirror) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-28)

Surfaced by the hostile gate on #6871 (the #5103 worker-join ordering fix). Filed separately because it is pre-existing and out of that PR's scope.

## What

`renameRethMember` (`pkg/daemon/daemon_reth.go:213`) performs a **second** `setDown` -> `setUp` cycle on a RETH member link, in the same loop as `programRethMAC`, with **no AF_XDP worker join** before the DOWN.

That is the identical hazard #5103 fixed in `programRethMAC`: worker threads live across the link DOWN, touching UMEM pages the NIC unmaps as it tears down its queues. #6871 added a `beforeCycle` hook that joins workers before `setDown` and aborts the cycle if the join fails. `renameRethMember` has no such hook.

## Why it was not folded into #6871

The reviewer established it is **not currently reachable with live bindings**, so this is a latent symmetry gap rather than an active defect:

- `renameRethMember` only runs when `LinkByName(linuxName)` fails, and
- it matches candidates by the **virtual** MAC — so if it finds one, `programRethMAC` then early-returns, and
- the dataplane could not have resolved a binding to a name that did not exist.

The chain holds today. It rests on three separate properties of unrelated code, none of which is asserted anywhere, which is what makes it worth tracking rather than dismissing.

## Suggested work

1. Decide whether the reachability argument should be **enforced** rather than merely true — e.g. a guard or assertion that `renameRethMember` cannot run with live bindings, so a future change to any of the three properties fails loudly instead of silently reopening #5103.
2. Or give it the same `beforeCycle` join hook, which is cheap and makes the two cycle sites symmetric without depending on the argument at all.

Option 2 is likely correct: the hook is idempotent (`stop_workers` always ACKs `ok`) and never fires at all on IFF_LIVE_ADDR_CHANGE drivers such as the mlx5/virtio NICs the loss cluster runs, so the cost on the reference deployments is zero.

## Provenance

- `pkg/daemon/daemon_reth.go:213` (`renameRethMember`)
- `pkg/daemon/daemon_reth.go:282-287` (the `beforeCycle` hook site added by #6871)
- Related: #5103, #5134, PR #6871

## #6912 — networkd: a successful EXTERNAL networkctl reload lets the next unchanged Apply skip its activation tail [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

Proved by the Codex gate on PR #6825, and **reproduced identically on `origin/master`** — this is pre-existing, not introduced by that PR. Filed separately so it is not misattributed.

## The gap

`Apply`'s activation tail does two things only `Apply` can do: the per-interface `networkctl reconfigure` that applies bond/VLAN addresses, and `restoreSlowPathRPFilter`, which re-disables `rp_filter` on the userspace dataplane's slow-path TUN after networkd resets it. Both sit behind:

```go
// pkg/networkd/networkd.go:434
if needReload || reconfDebt || activationOwed {
```

pkg/daemon is a second `networkctl reload` owner. On the live day-2 path it runs `teardownUnmappedManaged` **before** `networkd.Apply` (`pkg/daemon/daemon_apply_dataplane.go:198`); the teardown removes stale files and reloads successfully (`pkg/daemon/device_map.go:723`). That success is recorded only as the **global** reload result:

```go
// pkg/daemon/linksetup.go:544
epoch := networkd.BeginReload()
out, err := execCommand("networkctl", "reload")
networkd.NoteReloadResult(epoch, err)
```

The following `Apply` then has `changed=false`, no global debt, and no `activationPending` — so it skips the whole block and returns nil. The kernel really did re-read the directory, so the reload obligation was genuinely discharged. But the addresses were never reconfigured and `rp_filter` is left at networkd's default, which silently drops locally-originated traffic via the TUN.

An external owner discharged a postcondition it cannot perform.

## Reproduction

An isolated regression set `rp_filter` to `"2\n"` to model the successful external reload, reported that success, then called an unchanged `Apply`. At **both** PR #6825's head and `origin/master`, it made no reconfigure call and left `rp_filter` at `"2\n"` (exit 1).

## Relationship to #5718 / PR #6825

#6825 fixes the adjacent but **narrower** interleaving where `Apply`'s OWN reload failed first — it returns early before the tail, records no reconfigure debt, and a later external success clears the only remaining signal. That case is now covered by `TestApplyTailSurvivesExternalDebtDischarge_5718`.

This issue is the standalone case: no failed Apply at all, just a successful external reload followed by an unchanged Apply. The existing debt mechanism has nothing to carry, because nothing failed.

## Suggested direction

The tail is owed whenever *anyone* reloads, not only when Apply itself does or when a previous Apply failed. Options worth weighing:

- have `NoteReloadResult` on a SUCCESS also arm an activation debt for the Manager, so the next Apply runs its tail even with unchanged files;
- or make `restoreSlowPathRPFilter` idempotent and unconditional at the end of every Apply, decoupling it from `needReload` entirely — it is a cheap procfs write.

## #6914 — networkd: three wrong-interface regressions on the activation tail remain unbound [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

Surfaced and mutation-proven during the #5718 / PR #6825 gate. Filed separately because closing them needs fixture work beyond that PR's scope, and because leaving it implicit would let the argv assertion read as broader coverage than it has.

## What is bound today

`pkg/networkd/activation_tail_5718_test.go` asserts the FULL argv of the activation tail's `networkctl reconfigure` call, not just the call count. Its local `activationTailIfaces()` fixture adds a bond MEMBER (`lag0m`, `BondMaster: "ae0"`) specifically so the exclusion at `pkg/networkd/networkd.go:461` is load-bearing:

```go
if !ifc.Unmanaged && !ifc.Disable && ifc.BondMaster == "" {
    reconf = append(reconf, ifc.Name)
}
```

Deleting `&& ifc.BondMaster == ""` reds both activation-tail tests with `[reconfigure trust0 lag0m]` against `[reconfigure trust0]`. That arm is genuinely closed.

## What is NOT bound — each proven by mutation to exit 0

1. **A hardcoded interface name.** Replacing the accumulated list with a literal `"trust0"` passes, because the fixture's expected argv IS `["reconfigure", "trust0"]`.
2. **Removal of the unmanaged / disabled filtering.** The fixture contains no `Unmanaged` and no `Disable` interface, so dropping either predicate changes nothing it can observe.
3. **Reversed multi-interface accumulation or ordering.** Only one interface is ever eligible, so order is unobservable.

An inverted predicate is a separate case and IS caught — it produces zero calls, which the pre-existing count assertion already flagged. The gap is specifically **deletion** and **ordering**.

## Why this matters

`networkctl reconfigure` on the wrong interfaces leaves the real ones' addresses unapplied while still making a call that looks correct. The count-based assertion could not see that at all, which is why the argv assertion was added; the argv assertion sees only the dimension the fixture varies.

## Suggested fix

Extend `activationTailIfaces()` to carry, alongside the existing managed interface and bond member:

- an `Unmanaged: true` interface,
- a `Disable: true` interface,
- a SECOND managed non-member interface, so accumulation and order are both observable.

Then assert the exact multi-element argv. Keep the expectation spelled out rather than derived by filtering the fixture with the production predicate — deriving it would make the assertion true by construction.

`debtTestIfaces()` is deliberately shared with the reload-debt tests and should stay as it is; the richer fixture belongs local to the activation-tail file, which is where it already lives.

## #6915 — daemon: a failed cycled-MAC write drops RETH VIPs with no reconcile (step 2.6b is gated on linkCycled) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-28)

Surfaced during the #5103 / PR #6871 work and deliberately left open there, since it is **identical on `origin/master`** and closing it needs a change to step 2.6b's gate rather than to the worker-join fix.

## The gap

`programRethMAC`'s non-`IFF_LIVE_ADDR_CHANGE` fallback does DOWN -> set MAC -> UP. When the **cycled** `setHardwareAddr` fails (`pkg/daemon/daemon_reth.go:290-292`), it does a best-effort `ops.setUp(link)` and returns `linkCycled=false`.

But the link really did go DOWN, and a DOWN removes every kernel address on it — including the VRRP VIPs and the stable RETH link-local.

Step 2.6b's recovery (`ReconcileVIPs` / `addStableRethLinkLocal`) is gated on `needLinkCycleRecovery`, which is driven by `linkCycled`. So on this path the reconcile is **skipped for a cycle that actually happened**:

- addresses removed by the DOWN,
- `linkCycled=false`, so nothing re-adds them,
- the member comes back UP with no VIPs.

## What PR #6871 does and does not change

#6871 reworked the abort path to key on whether the worker join RAN rather than whether it FAILED, which closes the **rebind** half — `NotifyLinkCycle()` now fires on this path, so AF_XDP workers are re-armed.

It does **not** close the VIP half, because that is a separate gate. The outcome table added to `docs/reth-mac.md` in that PR records the carve-out so it is not silently inherited.

## Why it matters

VIPs are how the RETH presents itself to the LAN. Losing them without a reconcile means the node holds the VRRP role while carrying none of the addresses that role is supposed to answer for — and the failure is silent, because the MAC-write error is warn-only on this branch.

## Suggested direction

The real condition for step 2.6b is "did the link go DOWN and back UP", not "did the MAC program succeed". Options:

- have `programRethMAC` report the cycle separately from success — e.g. return `linkCycled=true` whenever `setDown` succeeded, regardless of what failed afterwards, and let the caller decide about the MAC error; or
- give step 2.6b its own signal set by the DOWN itself.

The first is closer to what `linkCycled` already means everywhere else and would also make the `setUp`-failure path consistent. Check both against `TestRethMACNoRollbackWhenJoinSucceeds_5103` and the other #5103 over-reach guards before changing the return contract — several tests read `linkCycled` directly.

## Provenance

- `pkg/daemon/daemon_reth.go:290-292` (the cycled-MAC failure return)
- `pkg/daemon/daemon_apply_dataplane.go:394-406` (`needLinkCycleRecovery`, step 2.6b/2.6b2)
- `docs/reth-mac.md` outcome table (added by #6871)
- Related: #5103, #5134, PR #6871

## #6917 — dataplane: compiler.go:474 reads ParentIndex for the VLAN generic-attach decision without proving kind or namespace [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-28)

`pkg/dataplane/compiler.go:474` reads `link.Attrs().ParentIndex` to decide whether a
VLAN child should take a generic XDP attach, and uses that value without first
establishing that the device is actually an 802.1Q VLAN whose parent is local.

This is the identical aliasing exposure that #5275 PR1 (PR #6864) closed inside the
arm-coverage proof, in two rounds:

1. **Wrong kind.** vishvananda/netlink maps `IFLA_LINK` into `LinkAttrs.ParentIndex`
   for EVERY link kind, not just VLANs. A veth's `ParentIndex` is its PEER's ifindex;
   a macvlan's is its lower device. `ensureVLANSubInterface`
   (`compiler_iface.go:113-121`) adopts ANY existing device found at `<phys>.<vid>` on
   `LinkByName` success without inspecting its kind, and the unmanaged sweep skips
   names whose prefix before `.` is managed — so a squatter at that name survives.
   PR #6864 fixed its own read by gating on `lnk.Type() == "vlan"` first.

2. **Foreign namespace.** Even for a genuine vlan, if the real_dev has been moved to
   another network namespace the child keeps its kind and keeps a `ParentIndex` that
   now refers to an ifindex in the FOREIGN namespace. A hostile review of #6864
   reproduced this across three namespaces and showed the orphan is NOT inert: it is
   un-`up`-able only while the foreign real_dev is down, and once that device is up in
   its own namespace the local child comes up (`LinkSetUp` rc=0, `oper=up`) and
   forwards. PR #6864 closed this by additionally requiring `Attrs().NetNsID == -1`.

`compiler.go:474` was verified UNCHANGED by PR #6864 (`git diff origin/master...HEAD --
pkg/dataplane/compiler.go` does not touch it), so it still carries both exposures.

## Why this is filed separately rather than folded

It is a different decision surface. #6864's read fed a diagnostic COUNT (an under-count
hides a live forwarding surface from a report). This one feeds an ATTACH decision — the
consequence of aliasing here is choosing generic vs native XDP attach for the wrong
device, which is a forwarding-path effect, not a reporting one. It deserves its own
analysis of what the wrong branch actually does rather than being assumed symmetric.

## What to establish

- What does taking the wrong branch at `compiler.go:474` actually cause? Trace both
  directions (treated-as-VLAN-child when it is not, and vice versa).
- Does the same `Type() == "vlan"` + `NetNsID == -1` pair close it, or does this call
  site need the CONFIGURED parent rather than the netlink-reported one?


A map entry present with a **nil** `*ZoneConfig` value makes `ok` true, so the guard falls

`pkg/dataplane/compiler_iface.go:412-417` guards precisely this, and its comment states the

```go
// SSOT already defends, e.g. userspace/zones.go). Skip it — every
// deref below (ScreenProfile, HostInboundTraffic, Interfaces)
```

That site names the tolerant/programmatic and HA-peer-sync config paths as where a nil zone

always assigns `&ZoneConfig{...}` — so this is a defensive-guard gap on the non-parser entry
points, consistent with what `compiler_iface.go` already assumes.

PR #6894 adds a validate-before-mutate pre-pass, which reorders when this panic occurs. Its

## #6923 — userspace-dp: the shim's over-limit ext-header refusal is conditional on every session-map writer declining the tuple [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-28)

## Summary

The XDP shim's refusal to fast-path an **over-limit IPv6 extension-header chain** is not a property of the shim. It is a property of the *session map*, which userspace writes — so it holds only for as long as every writer declines to mint the key the shim probes.

Surfaced while gating #6655 (advances #4555). Filed separately because the invariant spans the shim, the packet path and the HA import path, and because several code comments now cite it by number.

## Mechanism

`userspace-xdp/src/ipv6_ext_walk.rs` walks extension headers up to a fixed limit. Exhausting the loop is deliberately **not** an error: the walk returns the last declared next-header value, which is an extension-header type rather than a real L4 protocol, and `parse_l4`'s catch-all then yields ports `0/0`.

The intended consequence is that the session lookup misses and the packet is redirected to userspace. But the lookup only misses while nothing has published

```
(AF_INET6, <a next-header this walk traverses>, src, dst, 0, 0)
```

into the session map. If any writer publishes that tuple, the **next** packet of the same over-limit chain HITS and takes the fast path — the refusal stops holding, silently, with no code change anywhere near the shim.

That was reachable before the fix: `metadata_tuple_complete` accepted the tuple on the packet path, an `application any` permit matched a flow that has no ports to fail on, and the key was installed.

## Current state

Both known writers now decline it:

- `metadata_tuple_complete` — packet path (`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/frame/inspect.rs`)
- `build_synced_session_key` — HA import path (`userspace-dp/src/server/helpers/session_sync.rs`)

The shim's doc comment records that the refusal is conditional on exactly those two, rather than restating it as unconditional.

## Why this stays open as its own issue

The fix is an **enumeration**, and an enumeration is only as good as its completeness. It is correct today because there are two writers. It becomes wrong the moment a third appears — a CLI-driven install, a NAT or tunnel path minting its own key, a bulk-sync path, or a test helper promoted to production — and nothing mechanical will catch that. The doc comment says "do not add a third writer without extending them", but a comment is not a gate.

**What would close this properly:** a single chokepoint that all session-key publication goes through, so the refusal is expressed once and cannot be bypassed by a new caller; or a compile-time/structural check that fails when a session key is constructed outside the sanctioned constructors. Either replaces "we checked, there are two" with something that stays true.

## Provenance

Found by a hostile review leg on PR #6655 at `42b2c8733`, which established the reachability rather than asserting it. The fix and its tests are on that PR.

## #6924 — config: `tunnel mode` accepts any value — the schema leaf has no validator and the gate keys on the literal "ipip" [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-28)

## Summary

`set interfaces <if> tunnel mode <anything>` commits green for an arbitrary value. The schema leaf has no validator, and the compiler's deadness gate keys on the literal string `"ipip"` while the dataplane's own predicate is the complement of a known-good set. So `tunnel mode banana` is accepted, builds a kernel GRE device, and carries no traffic — exactly the condition #4785 exists to reject, reached by a different route.

Surfaced by a hostile review leg on PR #6861 (#4785 half 1) as a pre-existing gap, not introduced by that PR.

## The two halves

**No validator on the leaf.** `"mode"` in `pkg/config/schema_interfaces.go:420` is a plain typed leaf with no value validation, so `commit check` accepts any token.

**The gate and the dataplane disagree on what "dead" means.** The commit-time gate added for #4785 keys on `Mode == "ipip"`. The dataplane's deadness predicate is `tunnel_mode_kind` in `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/forwarding_build/tunnels.rs:163-169`, which classifies as carrying traffic only `gre`, `ip6gre` and `wireguard` — everything else is dead. `ipip` is one member of that complement; the complement is unbounded.

**What the operator gets.** `pkg/routing/tunnel.go:656` creates a kernel GRE device regardless, so an unrecognised mode produces a visible interface with nothing routed through it — the same "an interface an operator can see that carries no traffic" symptom #4785 documents, with none of the #4785 diagnostics, because those are keyed on the `ipip` string.

## Fix

Validate the leaf against the set the dataplane actually implements, so the accepted values and the carrying-traffic values are one list rather than two that can drift. Then the `ipip` rejection becomes one case of a general rule instead of a special case, and a future mode added to the dataplane cannot be silently unaccepted, nor an unimplemented one silently accepted.

Note for whoever takes this: #1960 no-brick applies. A config already persisted with an unrecognised mode must still BOOT — the strict rejection belongs on the commit path, with the load/sync path staying lenient and warning, exactly as #4785 half 1 arranged it.

## Provenance

Hostile review of PR #6861 at `ecd1f60ce`, reported as one of two lesser observations alongside the review's MERGE-READY verdict. Both pre-existing on `origin/master`.
