## #6925 — userspace-xdp: classify_native_gre_inner_ipv6 uses a narrower ext-header reject set than the canonical one [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-07)

## Summary

`classify_native_gre_inner_ipv6` (`userspace-xdp/src/lib.rs:931`) rejects only HOP / ROUTING / DEST / AUTH / FRAGMENT. For an inner next-header of 59 (No-Next), 135, 139, 140, 253 or 254 it does not walk and does not refuse — it builds a fixed `inner IPv6 + 40` key using the extension value AS the protocol, with ports 0/0.

Split out of PR #6655 (#4555) on the fold lane's recommendation, which I endorse. Recording the reasoning because it is the useful part.

## Why this is a SPLIT and not a defect left open

The *reachable* bad outcome is already closed. The only branch that did not end at userspace was an exact `PASS_TO_KERNEL` row returning the whole outer native-GRE packet to the kernel (`lib.rs:666`/`:683`). That value is published only through `uses_kernel_local_session_map_entry`, which requires `origin.is_peer_synced()` — so a synced LocalDelivery row was the sole route, and #6655's fix now rejects exactly that import (`build_synced_session_key` declines the traversable-extension protocol set). For 135/139/140/253/254 the classifier's probe now misses and falls through to XSK. 59 is not a defect at all: it is a terminal verdict on both sides, and the key it builds is the one userspace installs for that inner packet.

So what remains is an **inconsistency**, not a live fail-open: the classifier's reject set is narrower than the canonical class set the rest of the code uses.

## Why it needs its own change

Widening the reject set to the canonical set, or folding in the shared walker, is a shim **codegen** change — it produces a different `.o`, which owes a loss-userspace cluster smoke. Shipping a changed dataplane object unsmoked inside a lane that could not run the smoke was the wrong trade.

**Verifier headroom, measured rather than assumed, for whoever takes this: 947,188 / 1,000,000 processed insns — 5.28% free, against a 3% floor.** That is the budget available for a wider reject set or the shared walker.

## Fix

Use the canonical non-terminal class set (or call the shared walker) in `classify_native_gre_inner_ipv6`, so the shim has one definition of "this next-header is an extension header" rather than two that can drift. Re-measure headroom after, and run the loss-userspace smoke because the object changes.

## Provenance

Codex review of PR #6655 at `42b2c8733`, finding 5. The fold lane traced the reachability, closed the live half via the #6923 producer-side fix, and recommended the split with the headroom measurement above.

## #6929 — userspace-dp: per-worker WorkerCommand queues have no capacity bound, drop counter, or loss-of-sync latch [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-28)

## Summary

The per-worker `WorkerCommand` queues are `Arc<Mutex<VecDeque<WorkerCommand>>>` with **no producer-side cap and no drain-side backpressure**. Every producer calls a bare `push_back`. If a worker stops draining — a stall, a panic before respawn, a demotion, or simply a consumer slower than a sustained producer — its queue grows until memory is exhausted.

Surfaced by the #4800 connection-rate instrumentation lane (PR #6927), which declined to fix it in scope and reported it. Verified against `origin/master` (`d77583fe5`).

## Evidence

Unbounded producers, all bare `push_back`:

- `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/ha/session_import.rs:272` and `:274` — `UpsertSynced` for the forward entry and its reverse companion
- `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/ha/session_import.rs:378` — `DeleteSynced`
- `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/ha/export.rs:53` — `ExportOwnerRGSessions`
- `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/cos/cross_binding.rs:140` — `EnqueueShapedLocal`

Queue construction carries no capacity: `coordinator/reconcile/bringup.rs:426-427`.

## The contrast — this codebase already knows the right pattern

`BindingLiveState::push_session_delta` (`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/binding_state/session_delta.rs:12-24`) does all three things the `WorkerCommand` path does none of:

```rust
if pending.len() >= MAX_PENDING_SESSION_DELTAS {
        self.session_delta_dropped.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed);
        // #5290: a dropped RPC-fallback delta is a HA-relevant open/close the
        // standby will never observe — the fallback stream just went lossy.
        // Latch loss-of-sync so the owning worker forces a full owner-RG
        // resync (table-truth rescan), mirroring SessionTable::push_delta.
        self.delta_loss_pending.store(true, Ordering::Relaxed);
        return;
}
pending.push_back(delta);
```

It **caps** (`MAX_PENDING_SESSION_DELTAS = 4096`, `afxdp/mod.rs:411`), **counts** the drop, and **latches a recovery obligation** so the loss is repaired rather than silently absorbed. That third part is the important one: a bounded queue that drops silently trades an OOM for a correctness hole. The `WorkerCommand` path needs the same three properties, not just the cap.

## Why it matters more under connection-rate load

The HA producers above run per synced session. `session_import.rs:272`/`:274` push **two** commands per imported session — forward and reverse. A bulk sync or a sustained new-flow rate therefore drives this path hard, which is precisely the regime PR #6927 exists to measure. Its new `session_replication_queue_depth_max` gauge makes the growth **observable for the first time**; before that, a queue heading for OOM looked like nothing at all.

## #6930 — userspace: heartbeatZeroSlots caps the slot count AFTER a uint32 multiply that can wrap to zero [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-28)

## Summary

`heartbeatZeroSlots` (`pkg/dataplane/userspace/maps_sync.go:1855-1866`) computes the slot count as `uint32(effectiveWorkers(...)) * 32` **before** applying the `slots > mapCap` cap. On a sufficiently large worker count the multiply wraps to 0, the cap never fires, and the zeroing loop iterates zero times — silently skipping the heartbeat zeroing the A6-b01-C1 fix exists to perform.

**Unreachable today**, with a named precondition. Filing it because the precondition is a property of a constant in a different crate, and the doc sentence describing the guard is not literally true.

## Mechanism

`effectiveWorkers` skips its high clamp when `maxW == 0`, which happens when `heartbeatMapCap < 32`. With a sub-32-entry heartbeat Array and a worker count around `1<<27`, `workers * 32` overflows `uint32` to 0. Because the cap is applied to the already-overflowed product rather than to the operand, `slots > mapCap` is false and the loop body never runs.

## Why it cannot happen now

The shim declares the heartbeat Array with 4096 entries (`userspace-xdp/src/lib.rs:335`), so `maxW = 128` and the high clamp in `effectiveWorkers` always binds long before the multiply can overflow. Both halves of the precondition — a sub-32-entry map AND an enormous worker count — are unreachable against the current shim.

## Why it is still worth fixing

The safety here rests on a constant in `userspace-xdp` rather than on anything at the arithmetic site. Nothing at `maps_sync.go` would notice if that Array were resized, and the failure mode is silent: the loop simply does nothing, which reads identically to "there was nothing to zero".

Also, the `effectiveWorkers` doc claims *"heartbeatZeroSlots caps the resulting SLOT count at mapCap for that degenerate case"*. That is not literally true for a large enough input — the cap is applied after the product, so an overflowed product is capped to itself. The comment describes the intent rather than the code.

## Fix

Apply the bound to the operand rather than the product — clamp the worker count before multiplying, or compute in a width that cannot wrap and clamp after. Then correct the `effectiveWorkers` doc sentence to say what the guard does.

## Provenance

Free-hunt finding from a hostile review of PR #6825 at `9ab2fbd21`, which returned MERGE-READY overall; reported as a NIT with the unreachability established rather than assumed. Not introduced by that PR.

## #6931 — userspace-dp: the HA delete verb refuses the same ext-header keys it can no longer create, so a stale pre-upgrade row cannot be removed [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-28)

## Summary

`build_synced_session_key` now returns `Err` for an IPv6 key whose protocol is a traversable extension header (the #6923 refusal). `server/handlers/sync_session.rs:29` routes the HA **`delete`** verb through that same constructor — so a peer can no longer instruct this node to REMOVE such a row.

The refusal is right for `upsert`. On `delete` it is backwards: the keys most in need of removal are exactly the ones now un-removable.

## Reachability — narrow, and stated honestly

On a fully-upgraded node no such row can be created, and a mixed-version peer's `upsert` is refused too, so the node never holds the row to begin with. The only shape that bites is a row created **before** the upgrade surviving in the pinned map across a helper restart, where the in-memory table no longer owns it — leaving an entry nothing can delete.

Against `origin/master` the packet path could re-mint that row at will, so the PR that introduced this asymmetry (#6655, advancing #4555) **strictly reduces** exposure. This is a residual, not a regression.

## It is a considered choice, not an oversight

`userspace-dp/src/main_tests.rs:2464` frames the delete-side refusal deliberately — "the upsert path must refuse the same key the delete path refuses". Symmetry between the two verbs was the intent. Filing because the symmetry argument is weaker for `delete` than for `upsert`: refusing to CREATE a dangerous key is fail-closed, while refusing to DESTROY one is fail-open in the small.

## Fix

Let `delete` construct the key without the traversable-protocol gate, or give it a gate-bypassing constructor, so a stale pre-upgrade row can always be removed. Keep `upsert` refusing. Add a test that a row which cannot be created can still be deleted.

Worth pairing with #6923, which tracks the broader invariant: the refusal holds only because every session-map writer declines the tuple, with nothing mechanical to catch a third writer.

## Provenance

Non-blocking NIT from a hostile review of PR #6655 at `89bcf6ddb`, which returned MERGE-READY overall. The reviewer established the reachability rather than asserting it, and explicitly declined to inflate it.

## #6932 — config: the ipip unit-branch advisory hard-codes WireGuard as the suppressing mode, with only a comment guarding it [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-28)

## Summary

The unit-branch anchor-only advisory names `tunnel mode wireguard` as the specific cause that suppresses a complete unit-level `ipip` endpoint. That is **correct today and measured**, but nothing mechanical pins it. If a future interface-level mode gains a short-circuit, units under that mode would receive the WireGuard wording — the same wrong-cause defect one layer in — and the existing test would still pass, because it drives WireGuard.

The only guard is a comment: *"If another mode ever gains a short-circuit, this wording needs revisiting with it."*

## Why it is correct today, established by measurement not inspection

The mode space is exactly three values — `gre`, `ipip`, `wireguard` (`pkg/config/compiler_interfaces.go:161`/`:261` default to `gre`, or `ipip` for `ip-*`). A hostile review swept every interface-level shape against every unit topology, 12 cells, and recorded which COMPLETE unit-level `ipip` records go unemitted:

| interface stanza | units | suppressed |
|---|---|---|
| tunnel nil | [3], [1 3] | none |
| gre complete / incomplete | [3], [1 3] | none |
| ipip complete / incomplete | [3], [1 3] | none |
| **wireguard** | [3] | **[3]** |
| **wireguard** | [1 3] | **[1 3]** |

12 of 12: only WireGuard suppresses. So naming it is right for the whole branch, not a guess from the one case that was found.

## The residual

`ipipAnchorOnlyText`'s unit branch hard-codes the WireGuard explanation. A fourth mode, or a change making `gre` short-circuit the way WireGuard does, silently produces a wrong cause with a green suite. That is precisely the shape PR #6861 was folded to fix for the interface-vs-unit case — a call site inheriting a message written for a different situation.

## Fix

Derive the suppressing mode rather than hard-coding it: the emitter knows which interface-level stanza took the endpoint slot, so the advisory can name it. Failing that, add a test that enumerates the mode space and asserts every short-circuiting mode is named by the branch — so adding a fourth mode without updating the wording reds something instead of shipping a wrong cause.

## Provenance

Non-blocking NIT from a hostile re-gate of PR #6861 at `0cf212602`, which returned MERGE-READY. The reviewer measured the 12-cell sweep rather than asserting the enumeration, and explicitly classified this as a future risk rather than a present defect.

## #6933 — HA: syncPeerBulkPrimed survives a peer incarnation change because its clear is gated on the never-cleared bulkEverCompleted [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-06)

## Summary

`syncPeerBulkPrimed` retains its value across a **peer incarnation change**, because the two sites that clear it are themselves gated on a flag that is never cleared. Its consumers are bulk-prime retry-loop stop conditions, so a NEW incarnation's retry loop can stop early on the strength of the PREVIOUS incarnation's ack.

Same lost-obligation shape as the #5718 `needColdPrime` defect, one belt out. Pre-existing; surfaced while re-gating PR #6825.

## Trace

1. `bulkEverCompleted` is sticky for the process lifetime — set at `pkg/cluster/sync_conn_read.go:245` and `:275`, cleared nowhere.
2. `pkg/daemon/daemon_ha_sync.go:66` and `:118` gate the **clearing** of `syncPeerBulkPrimed` on `bulkEverCompleted`.
3. So once any bulk has ever completed, neither clear can fire again.
4. `syncPeerBulkPrimed` therefore survives a peer incarnation change.
5. Its three consumers — `pkg/daemon/daemon_ha_userspace_readiness.go:172`, `daemon_ha_sync.go:216`, `daemon_ha_sync.go:276` — are all retry-loop **stop conditions** for bulk priming.

Net: the daemon's bulk-prime retry loop can conclude a new incarnation is primed because the previous one was.

## Severity — a degraded belt, not a lost obligation

Deliberately not filed as a blocker on #6825, and the distinction is the useful part. In the `needColdPrime` case no other path existed, so the obligation was genuinely lost. Here the retry loop is a **second belt** over `pkg/cluster`'s own re-drive, and #6825's arming-on-supersession (`pkg/cluster/sync_conn.go:620`) plus its widened gate repair the primary path. So the obligation is still discharged; only its backstop is degraded.

That is materially weaker, and it is why this is its own issue rather than a fold.

## Fix direction

**Do not de-stick `bulkEverCompleted`.** Its #466 semantics genuinely want "has this daemon ever primed" — that is what the flap suppression is for, and clearing it would reintroduce the storm it exists to prevent.

Key the `syncPeerBulkPrimed` clear on the **incarnation** instead, the way `needColdPrime` now is after #6825. The obligation belongs to an incarnation, so its state should be scoped to one.

## Adjacent, worth knowing before anyone touches this pair

`syncBulkPrimed` — the OUTBOUND twin of `syncPeerBulkPrimed` — has **no consumer at all**. It is written at `daemon_ha_sync.go:69`, `:91` and `:120` and read only in log lines. Half of the pair is inert. Anyone "fixing" its stickiness would be maintaining a variable nothing reads; either give it a consumer or delete it, but decide deliberately rather than mirroring whatever is done to the peer half.

## Provenance

Hostile re-gate of PR #6825 at `86a5c3130`, which returned MERGE-READY. The reviewer traced past the point the fold lane's own survey stopped — that survey had classified these two `pkg/daemon` readers as "outside this diff", which is true and is not the same as safe.

## The symptom (unchanged, and still unexplained)

On `loss:xpf-userspace-fw0/fw1`, after a manual RG failover, IPv6 blackholed for ~60s while IPv4 recovered in seconds:

```
v4: 10 packets transmitted, 9 received, 10% packet loss      (recovers in seconds)
v6: 10 packets transmitted, 0 received, 100% packet loss     (blackhole)
```

After ~60s with no intervention, IPv6 recovered on its own. An `iperf3` started during the window hung rather than failing fast.

**The unsolicited-NA burst works.** Failing over **RG2** — the redundancy group that actually owns `reth1`, the interface carrying the affected VIP — with simultaneous captures on sender and receiver:

| | sender (`fw1 ge-7-0-1`) | receiver (LAN `eth0`) |
|---|---|---|
| unsolicited NA (dst `33:33:00:00:00:01`) | **96** | **96** |
| broadcast ARP | **96** | **96** |

Zero loss, carrying the exact VIP and the new primary's MAC:

```

  2001:559:8585:ef00::1 > ff02::1: ICMP6, neighbor advertisement,
  tgt is 2001:559:8585:ef00::1, length 32
```

**The burst's address coverage is complete.** The LAN host's v6 default route is `via fe80::bf72:16:2` (proto ra); the burst announces exactly that address plus the VIP. There is no announced-address gap.

**The `Override=0` theory** was already false and remains so — `garp.go` sets `0xA0` (Router+Override). The doc comment that contradicted the code is fixed in #7769.

## #6935 — userspace-xdp: non-first IPv6 fragments are parsed as L4 and dropped — the shim never reads the fragment offset [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-08)

## Summary

The XDP shim's IPv6 extension-header walk steps past a Fragment header taking
only its next-header byte, and never consults the **fragment offset**. It
therefore returns the original L4 protocol (e.g. TCP) for a NON-FIRST fragment,
whose bytes at that offset are datagram payload, not an L4 header. The caller
parses them as L4, the parse fails for most payloads, and the packet is dropped
before it ever reaches userspace.

The result is **payload-dependent loss on non-first IPv6 fragments**.

## Evidence on `origin/master` (verified at `04ef2c5a1`)

The fragment arm, `userspace-xdp/src/ipv6_ext_walk.rs`:

```rust
EH_CLASS_FRAGMENT => {
    let frag = read_bytes(data, data_end, offset as usize, 8)?;
    protocol = frag[0];
    offset = offset.checked_add(mem::size_of::<FragHdr>() as u16)?;
}
```

Only `frag[0]` (next header) is read. The offset/flags field at `frag[2..4]` is
never examined, so a non-first fragment is indistinguishable from a first
fragment here and the walk falls out at `Some((offset, protocol))` with
`protocol` still naming the upper-layer protocol.

The field exists and is simply unused. `frag_off` is declared in **two** places
and read in neither:

- `userspace-xdp/src/ipv6_ext_walk.rs:108` — `pub frag_off: u16,`
- `userspace-xdp/src/lib.rs:280` — `frag_off: u16,`

`git grep frag_off -- userspace-xdp/` returns exactly those two declarations and
no reads.

On L4 parse failure the shim takes `userspace-xdp/src/lib.rs:442`:

## #6939 — cluster: fabric RPC auth rejects on clock skew with an undiagnosable "invalid auth token" — blocks manual failover [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-28)

## What happened

On the `loss:xpf-userspace-fw0/fw1` cluster, **every cross-node fabric RPC failed**, in both directions:

```
error: rpc error: code = Unavailable desc = cannot connect to peer on any fabric address:
  rpc error: code = Unauthenticated desc = fabric RPC authentication failed: invalid auth token
```

Listener side logged the matching rejection:

```
level=WARN msg="fabric gRPC listener rejected call: authentication failed"
  method=/xpf.v1.BpfrxService/GetStatus reason="invalid auth token"
```

**Impact: `request chassis cluster failover` is impossible**, so `make test-failover` and every HA smoke target are non-functional. That is how I found it — an unrelated investigation could not force a transition.

## Root cause — clock skew, not a key problem

The fabric token is time-windowed (`pkg/grpcapi/fabric_auth.go`):

```go
fabricAuthWindowSeconds = 30
func fabricAuthWindow(t time.Time) int64 { return t.Unix() / fabricAuthWindowSeconds }
// computeFabricAuthToken = HMAC-SHA256(key, domain || window)
```

and `verifyFabricAuthToken` accepts `{now, now-1, now+1}` — a **±60 second** tolerance.

Measured on the cluster:

```
node0 epoch: 1786031353.90
node1 epoch: 1786031554.04     -> 200.14 s skew
NTPSynchronized = no    on BOTH nodes
```

200 s against a ±60 s window: the two nodes compute non-overlapping window indices, so the HMACs can never match.

## #6940 — [cohort] config compiler: 13 typed integer leaves discard the strconv.Atoi error, so malformed values silently become 0 [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-28)

## Summary

Thirteen typed integer leaves in the config compiler parse with the error discarded:

```go
opts.MinimumLinks, _ = strconv.Atoi(v)
```

`strconv.Atoi` returns `0` alongside its error, so a malformed value does not fail the commit — it silently compiles to **zero**. For several of these leaves zero is not a harmless default but a meaningful setting, which makes this a quiet semantic change rather than a parse nuisance.

## The 13 sites, measured at `origin/master` `b8b39a16a`

```
pkg/config/compiler_interfaces.go:130   opts.MinimumLinks
pkg/config/compiler_interfaces.go:390   opts.LeaseTime
pkg/config/compiler_interfaces.go:394   opts.RetransmissionAttempt
pkg/config/compiler_interfaces.go:398   opts.RetransmissionInterval
pkg/config/compiler_interfaces.go:519   dc.PrefixDelegatingPrefixLen
pkg/config/compiler_interfaces.go:524   dc.PrefixDelegatingSubPrefLen
pkg/config/compiler_system.go:74        sys.NTPThreshold
pkg/config/compiler_system.go:192       sys.Archival.TransferInterval
```

(plus the remainder of the 13 — full list via `git grep -nE ', _ = strconv\.Atoi\(' -- pkg/config/`)

## Why it matters, per leaf shape

- **`MinimumLinks`** — a LAG minimum-links of 0 is not the same as an unset one. The operator writes a link-count floor, the compiler stores "no floor", and nothing reports the discrepancy.
- **`LeaseTime`, `RetransmissionAttempt`, `RetransmissionInterval`** — zero-valued timers/counters on DHCP paths.
- **`PrefixDelegatingPrefixLen` / `SubPrefLen`** — a zero prefix length is a distinct and wrong prefix, not an absent one.
- **`NTPThreshold`, `TransferInterval`** — zero thresholds/intervals change scheduling semantics.

In every case the operator's intent (a typo, a unit suffix, a `${var}` that did not expand) is converted into a valid-looking configuration rather than rejected.

## Relationship to existing issues

**#6587** already covers this shape for the RA prefix-length leaves ("prefix-length leaves take an unbounded Atoi"). This cohort is the remaining instances of the same defect elsewhere in the compiler. They are filed together because the fix is one mechanism applied N times, not N designs; splitting into 13 issues would be overfiling.

Note the two halves are separable: #6587's concern includes *unbounded* values (a parse that succeeds but yields an out-of-range number). This cohort is specifically the *discarded error* half. A leaf can have both problems and needs both fixes.

## #6941 — tunnel: routing and the dataplane disagree on which Linux device an interface-level WireGuard tunnel lives on (wg0 vs wg0uN) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-28)

## Summary

With an interface-level `wireguard` tunnel and a unit carrying its own tunnel stanza, two subsystems resolve the WireGuard tunnel to **different Linux devices**:

- **Routing** creates `wg0` for the WireGuard record.
- **The dataplane** binds the WireGuard endpoint to `wg0u3` (the unit's own device).

Both then operate on their own device believing it is the tunnel.

## The dataplane side — verified here against `origin/master`

`pkg/dataplane/userspace/interfaces.go:424` `snapshotLinuxName` resolves a unit through the tunnel name map:

```go
if unit != nil {
    if tunnelNames := cfg.TunnelNameMap(); len(tunnelNames) > 0 {
        ref := fmt.Sprintf("%s.%d", ifName, unit.Number)
        if linuxName, ok := tunnelNames[ref]; ok && linuxName != "" {
            return linuxName
```

So `wg0.3` maps to `wg0u3`, that lands in `InterfaceSnapshot.LinuxName`, and `buildTunnelEndpointSnapshots` reads that field. The dataplane's device for this endpoint is `wg0u3`.

Note the sharp edge that makes this easy to get wrong: for `wg0.3` the **emitter's** `ep.Tunnel.Name` is `wg0` (it carries the interface-level object) while `TunnelNameMap` says `wg0u3`. Those are different questions, and keying off `ep.Tunnel.Name` is the plausible-looking wrong answer.

## The routing side — attributed, not independently verified here

Reported from the #6861 (issue #4785) fold lane, which traced it while working on the IPIP anchor advisory: routing creates `wg0` for the WireGuard record. I confirmed the dataplane half above by reading `snapshotLinuxName`; I did **not** independently trace the routing creation path, so treat that half as a lead to confirm rather than an established fact. `pkg/routing/tunnel.go` is where the WG link lifecycle lives (see the `#1919` address-prune and `#5120` removal-path comments around `:296` and `:1136`).

**First thing to do on this issue is settle that half**, because it decides whether this is a real split or a misreading.

## Why it matters if confirmed

Two subsystems disagreeing about a device identity is the shape that produces symptoms nobody can attribute: addresses pruned from one device while traffic uses the other, a link kept alive by one owner and torn down by the other, or a WireGuard peer bound to a device that carries no routes. It is also exactly the class the #6861 fold just closed one instance of — an advisory keyed on the wrong notion of device identity — which is why it surfaced.

## Provenance and scope

Found by the #6861 fold lane while establishing that `cfg.TunnelNameMap()` is the production authority for endpoint→device binding. **Deliberately left out of that PR** — it is a pre-existing divergence in a different subsystem, and widening the fold's diff to chase it would have made an already-large review harder to gate. #6861's own conclusion does not depend on it: `wg0u3` is claimed by something live either way.

Not caused by any PR in flight.

## #6942 — logging: ResolveSyslogSourceAddr silently binds unit 0 on a unit it cannot parse, and skips the TrimSpace its validator applies [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-28)

## Summary

`ResolveSyslogSourceAddr` (`pkg/config/syslog_source.go:23`) and its schema validator `ValidateSyslogSourceInterface` (`pkg/config/schema_validators_logging.go:18`) disagree about the same string in two ways. The validator rejects; the resolver silently substitutes a default. On the strict commit path the validator masks it — on the **lenient** path it does not, and that is where it bites.

## Defect 1 — an unparseable unit silently becomes unit 0

```go
base, unitStr, hasUnit := strings.Cut(srcIface, ".")
unitNum := 0
if hasUnit {
    if n, err := strconv.Atoi(unitStr); err == nil {
        unitNum = n
    }
}
if ifc, ok := cfg.Interfaces.Interfaces[base]; ok && ifc != nil {
    if unit, ok := ifc.Units[unitNum]; ok && unit.PrimaryAddress != "" {
```

The error is checked, but the failure path keeps `unitNum = 0`. So `reth1.abc` — or a unit that overflows `int` — resolves to **`reth1` unit 0** rather than failing. If unit 0 has a `PrimaryAddress`, syslog binds its source address to the **wrong logical unit**, silently and plausibly.

This is a distinct instance from #6940's cohort: there the error is *discarded*, here it is *checked and then ignored*. Same outcome, different code shape, so a sweep for `, _ = strconv.Atoi(` does not find it.

## Defect 2 — the resolver does not TrimSpace, the validator does

The validator normalises first (`schema_validators_logging.go:19`):

```go
trimmed := strings.TrimSpace(raw)
...
base, unit, hasUnit := strings.Cut(trimmed, ".")
```

The resolver cuts the raw argument. So a leading/trailing space means the resolver's `base` (`"reth1 "` or `" reth1"`) misses the `cfg.Interfaces.Interfaces` lookup, falls through to the kernel path, and `net.InterfaceByName(srcIface)` — also un-trimmed — fails too, even when the interface exists. The result is an empty source address where the operator configured a valid one.

## Why the validator does not save it — the reachability argument

`ValidateSyslogSourceInterface` genuinely rejects both cases (`:28-30` returns an error for a non-numeric or negative unit). That closes the **strict** commit path.

It does not close the **lenient** path. `compileTreeLenient` is used by `Store.Load` on disk boot and by `SyncApply` on HA peer sync, where validation failures are warnings rather than rejects (the #1960 no-brick posture). A config that a strict commit would refuse can therefore reach the resolver — from a persisted config written by an older build, from a hand-edited DB, or from a peer.

## #6944 — config: tunnel `mode` is an unvalidated free-form leaf — every unrecognised mode commits green and blackholes both directions [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-07)

## Summary

`set interfaces <if> [unit N] tunnel mode <anything>` commits successfully for **any** string. Only three values mean something to the dataplane; every other value maps to `TunnelKind::Unknown`, which neither decaps nor encaps. The result is a tunnel the operator configured, the commit accepted, and that silently carries no traffic in either direction.

## Measured on `origin/master`

The Rust mapping recognises exactly three modes (`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/forwarding_build/tunnels.rs:163-169`):

```rust
pub(in crate::afxdp) fn tunnel_mode_kind(mode: &str) -> TunnelKind {
    match mode {
        "gre" | "ip6gre" => TunnelKind::Gre,
        "wireguard" => TunnelKind::WireGuard,
        _ => TunnelKind::Unknown,
    }
}
```

Decap indexing is gated on `== TunnelKind::Gre` (`tunnels.rs:130`); egress returns `None` for `Some(TunnelKind::Unknown) | None` (`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/frame/mod.rs:421`). So `Unknown` is a two-way blackhole.

And the config leaf has no validator at all (`pkg/config/schema_interfaces.go:420`):

```go
"mode": {desc: "Tunnel mode", args: 1, placeholder: "<mode>", children: nil},
```

No `validator` field, so `SchemaValidate` has nothing to enforce. Every one of these commits green, emits an endpoint, and blackholes:

```
mode=ip6ip6   COMMITS GREEN; emitted=1
mode=IPIP     COMMITS GREEN; emitted=1
mode=vxlan    COMMITS GREEN; emitted=1
mode=typo     COMMITS GREEN; emitted=1
```

`ip6ip6` and `vxlan` are especially bad: both are real, plausible mode names an operator would reasonably try. `IPIP` is worse still — it is the *correct* feature name in the wrong case.

## Relationship to #4785 / PR #6861

PR #6861 adds a commit-time rejection for `mode ipip` specifically, because IP-IP is unimplemented. That is correct and this issue does **not** block it — the blackhole class described here is pre-existing on master, and #6861 does not widen it.

## #6945 — test: two concurrency tests flake under full-suite load (install_session_serializes_with_reconcile_removal reproduced 1-in-5 at master) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-28)

## Summary

Two unrelated concurrency tests have been observed failing under full-suite load on the same machine within one session. One reproduces at master and is therefore not attributable to any PR; the other did not reproduce and is recorded here only so a third sighting is not mistaken for a first.

Filing because a flaky concurrency test is worse than an ordinary flake in this project: the merge gate treats a RED as evidence, and an unattributed failure costs a round to disprove every time it appears.

## 1. `afxdp::wg::engine::engine_internal_tests::install_session_serializes_with_reconcile_removal` — REPRODUCES

Measured with like-for-like full-suite runs:

- **master `a26509a6f`: 1-of-5 FAIL**
- PR head under test (`e8c2403a5`): 0-of-5 FAIL
- isolated at that head: 0-of-10

So it fails at master and not under the PR — the PR is exonerated, and the flake is a master property. Load/ordering sensitive: it only appears under the full suite, never isolated.

## 2. `afxdp::types::shared_cos_lease::tests::v8_epoch_seqlock_snapshot_never_tears_tag_grace` — DID NOT reproduce

Seen failing once during a full-suite run. Follow-up: **5/5 clean at the PR head, 5/5 clean at the unmodified base**. A CoS seqlock test, unrelated to the diff it appeared under.

**This is explicitly NOT being claimed as proven pre-existing.** One sighting with ten clean re-runs is a sighting, not a characterisation. It is recorded so the next person who sees it knows it is the second occurrence rather than the first, and can go straight to a higher trial count instead of re-deriving that it is not reproducible at n=5.

## Why the pair is worth an issue rather than two notes

Two *different* concurrency tests flaking under full-suite load on one box in one session suggests the possibility of a shared cause — scheduling pressure, thread-count interaction, or a resource the suite contends on — rather than two independent bugs. That may be wrong; it is a hypothesis, not a finding. But it is cheap to check once and expensive to keep re-discovering.

Suggested first step: run the full suite at high repetition and record which tests fail and at what rate, rather than chasing either test individually. If the failures correlate with concurrency level or with each other, that is the signal; if `install_session_serializes_with_reconcile_removal` is simply flaky on its own, the second one drops out.

## Impact on the merge gate

Until this is characterised, a full-suite RED in either test is not automatically attributable to the PR under review. The gate discipline that applies:

- A RED here requires a **like-for-like** re-run at the merge base before it is attributed to the diff — same scope, same concurrency, `-count` high enough to matter. A single run at the PR head proves nothing either way.
- "It's a known flake" is not a disposition on its own; the base-run measurement is what makes the claim checkable.

## Provenance

Both sightings from review lanes on PR #6835 during the 2026-08-06 campaign. The `install_session…` measurement (1-of-5 at master, 0-of-5 and 0-of-10 at head) was taken deliberately as a like-for-like comparison; the seqlock sighting was incidental and its re-runs were done specifically to avoid reporting an unreproduced failure as a finding.

## #6946 — userspace-dp: bound the per-zone counter accumulators with a touched-slot bitmask (both ZonePending and FloodPending) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-28)

Follow-up surfaced during the #3651 flood-counter review (non-blocking N1 there). Filed as ONE issue covering BOTH accumulators, because they must move together — see "Why one issue" below.

## What

`ZonePending` (`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/zone_counters.rs`) and `FloodPending`
(`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/flood_counters.rs`) are per-worker thread-local
coalescers with dense slot-indexed arrays and a single `touched: bool`. Two
consequences on the per-RX-batch path:

- **`reset()` clears the whole array whenever anything was touched.**
  `ZonePending` clears 4 x `[u64; 64]` = 2048 B; `FloodPending` clears
  3 x `[u64; 64]` = 1536 B. Typically ONE slot was actually touched (the zone
  carrying traffic, or the single zone under attack).
- **`fold_pending()` scans every slot every flush** — `ZONE_COUNTER_SLOTS` (64)
  iterations, each checking the cached `Arc` and 4 (resp. 3) pending values,
  to fold what is usually one slot.

The cycle cost is small next to the work already on that path. The cache cost is
the real one: 24-32 dirtied cache lines per flush per worker, per batch.

## Why it matters more for flood than traffic

The flood accumulator is fed from the screen DROP path. A SYN flood is the
primary `screen_drops` trigger, so during exactly the event the counter exists
to measure, that path is hot on every worker at once — see the #1187 note in
`stage_screen_check` and the `flood_counters.rs` module header. Traffic is
steady-state hot; flood is hot precisely when it is being read.

## Proposed fix

Replace `touched: bool` with `touched_slots: u64` (a bitmask — both modules cap
at 64 slots, and `FLOOD_COUNTER_SLOTS == ZONE_COUNTER_SLOTS` is already pinned
by a `const _: () = assert!(...)`, so a `u64` covers both exactly).

- `record_*` sets `touched_slots |= 1 << slot`.
- `fold_pending` iterates set bits instead of `1..SLOTS`.
- `reset` zeroes only the set slots, then clears the mask.

Both the reset AND the fold scan shrink from O(64) to O(touched), so it is one
change with two wins, applied twice.

## #6947 — userspace-dp: the two per-zone status blocks emit an empty array every poll; Go already omits it (add skip_serializing_if to both) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-28)

Surfaced while quantifying the status-poll cost of #3651 (PR #6938). Wire-payload
hygiene, not correctness. Filed separately from #6946 — that one is about the
per-zone *accumulators*; this is about the *wire*.

## The asymmetry

The two per-zone `ProcessStatus` blocks disagree with their Go mirrors on how an
EMPTY block is represented:

| Side | `zone_traffic_counters` | `zone_flood_counters` |
|---|---|---|
| Rust (`protocol/control.rs`) | `#[serde(rename=..., default)]` — **emits `[]`** | `#[serde(rename=..., default)]` — **emits `[]`** |
| Go (`protocol_status.go`) | `json:"...,omitempty"` — **omits** | `json:"...,omitempty"` — **omits** |

Neither Rust field carries `skip_serializing_if = "Vec::is_empty"`, so the helper
puts `"zone_traffic_counters":[]` and `"zone_flood_counters":[]` on the wire on
EVERY status poll, forever, on a firewall that has never populated either. Their
sibling scalars (`*_counter_layout_version`, `*_counter_overflow_active`) DO carry
`skip_serializing_if` and are correctly omitted — so the omission is inconsistent
even within the same block.

Cost is small and entirely idle-state: 24 bytes/poll for the flood block, similar
for traffic, at 1/s, unconditionally. Measured from
`tests/fixtures/protocol_wire_v1.json` (the ProcessStatus specimen contains both
`[]` entries).

## Why it is worth fixing

Not the bytes. Two reasons:

1. **The control socket is shared** with the status poll, HA sync, session
   installs, snapshot sync and forwarding sync (see CLAUDE.md). Unconditional
   payload on the 1/s poll is the one thing on that socket nobody chose to send.
2. **The two sides disagree about what "empty" looks like on the wire.** Today
   that is benign — Go decodes an absent key and `[]` identically — but it is a
   latent inconsistency in a wire contract that is otherwise byte-specified, and
   the golden fixture enshrines it.

## #6948 — policy: commit-time deletion-clear can over-clear a live session whose policy inherited the deleted policy's id [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-28)

Found while researching #4626 L01 (`docs/research/4626-l01-policy-id-zero/plan.md`
on branch `research/4626-l01-policy-id-zero`). This is a **separate, live defect
on master**, independent of #4626's id-0 overload, and it affects every policy
**except** the first.

## The defect

Runtime policy ids are **positional** (`policySetID*MaxRulesPerPolicy +
ruleIndex`, `pkg/dataplane/userspace/policies.go:63`), so deleting a policy
renumbers every later one. The commit path activates the new policy set **before**
the invalidation scan runs:

```go
applyErr := d.applyConfigLocked(d.applyCancelCtx(), compiled)
...
clearErr := d.clearSessionsForPolicyChanges(oldActive, compiled)
```
`pkg/daemon/daemon_apply_commit.go:245-262` — and the in-tree comment states the
ordering as intent: *"Runs under d.applySem (the caller holds it), after the
dataplane apply so the new policy set is already live."*

The deletion set is computed from the **old** config's numbering
(`PolicyIDsByStableKey(oldCfg)`), but between activation and the scan the
dataplane admits sessions under the **new** numbering. When the deleted policy's
id is reassigned to a surviving policy, those fresh sessions match the sweep set.

## Worked example

```
C1 = [A, B, C]   ->  A=0, B=1, C=2
delete B
C2 = [A, C]      ->  A=0, C=1
deletion set     =   { B's old id } = { 1 }
```

A `C` session admitted after the apply and before the scan carries `policy_id 1`
and is swept as though it were `B` — a live, correctly-permitted session dropped
by an unrelated policy's deletion. `d.applySem` serialises applies, not dataplane
admission, so nothing in the current structure closes the window.

## #6949 — userspace-dp: JSON/RPC session-delta fallback drops policy_id, policy_counter_idx and app timeout [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-28)

Found while researching #4626 L01 (`docs/research/4626-l01-policy-id-zero/plan.md`
on branch `research/4626-l01-policy-id-zero`). Live on master, independent of
#4626's outcome.

## The defect

The Go side declares and consumes three per-session policy metadata fields on the
session delta:

```go
PolicyID          uint32 `json:"policy_id,omitempty"`
PolicyCounterIdx  ...
AppTimeout        ...
```
`pkg/dataplane/userspace/protocol_ha.go:93` (and `:162` for the sync request).

The Rust producer for the **JSON/RPC fallback** carries none of them.
`SessionDeltaInfo` (`userspace-dp/src/protocol/binding.rs:1147`) has no
`policy_id` field at all — it carries `ingress_zone`, `egress_zone`, the NAT
fields, `fabric_ingress`, `log_session_init`, `log_session_close` and so on, but
no policy attribution — and its constructor
(`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/session_delta.rs:200`) never sets one.

This is not a cold path. The Go fallback loop drains that queue **every 100 ms
while the event stream is disconnected and every 5 s even while connected**
(`pkg/daemon/daemon_ha_userspace_stream.go:254`).

## Impact

Every session learned through the fallback is converted with `PolicyID = 0`,
`PolicyCounterIdx = 0` and no application timeout. Consequences:

- **Attribution.** The session renders `unattributed` on `show security flow
  session`, REST and gRPC (correct-looking, because #6851 renders 0 that way —
  which is exactly why this has been invisible), even though a real policy
  admitted it.
- **Invalidation.** It is exempt from the commit-time deletion-clear and the
  policy-rematch (#4234), because id 0 is excluded there
  (`pkg/daemon/daemon_policy_invalidate.go:72-77` and `:443-447`). A session the
  operator intended to drop keeps forwarding.

Observed during `make test-rust` on 2026-08-06 while several parallel
release builds were running on the box.

```
afxdp::wg::engine::engine_internal_tests::install_session_serializes_with_reconcile_removal
panicked at userspace-dp/src/afxdp/wg/engine_tests.rs:872:5:
  reconcile loop must have completed at least one full add/remove cycle
```

## Why it fails

The test spawns two threads. Thread A installs `iterations` sessions then
sets `stop`; thread B loops `reconcile_peers(&[])` / `reconcile_peers(&cfg)`
until `stop` is set, counting iterations. The post-join assertion is

```rust
assert!(
    reconcile_iters >= 1,
    "reconcile loop must have completed at least one full add/remove cycle"
);
```

That is a **liveness** assertion on the scheduler: thread B must be
scheduled at least once before thread A finishes its whole install loop.
Under CPU contention B can get zero iterations, and the test fails
without anything being wrong with the code under test.

## Evidence it is non-deterministic, not a regression

- Re-running the **identical** `make test-rust` on the **identical
  tree and commit** passes: exit 0, 4253 passed / 0 failed.
- 20/20 isolated runs of the single test pass on an unloaded box.
- It surfaced on a branch (`refactor/4408-waterfill-split`, PR #6950)
  whose diff touches only `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/cos/queue_service/`
  and docs — `git diff origin/master...HEAD -- userspace-dp/src/afxdp/wg/`
  is empty, so the WG code under test is byte-identical to master's.

## #6953 — config/event-options: a flat-set `commands` added onto a PERSISTED packed leaf is silently dropped (FindChild is singular) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-28)

Surfaced during the #6673 hostile review (F3). **Pre-existing — not a regression from #6673**, but that PR is the first tree on which it becomes operator-visible, which is why it is worth filing now.

## Defect

`pkg/config/compiler_services.go:2064` reaches the leaf with `ccNode.FindChild("commands")` — **singular**. When a `change-configuration` stanza carries two sibling `commands` nodes, only the first is read and every command on the second is silently discarded.

## How two siblings arise

Not from either parser alone — `SetPath` merges repeated flat-set statements into one node's children, and the hierarchical parser produces one node. The sibling appears in the **persisted-packed + flat-set overlay** path: a config stored in the packed spelling, then amended with a `set` line.

## Runnable repro (measured)

Start from a persisted hierarchical config:

```
commands "set system host-name foo";
```
→ `ThenCommands = ["set system host-name foo"]`

then overlay a flat-set line:

```
set event-options policy p then change-configuration commands "delete system host-name"
```

The AST now holds **two sibling `commands` nodes**:

```
#1  Keys=["commands","set system host-name foo"]
#2  Keys=["commands"]  child ["delete system host-name"]
```

and the compiled result is unchanged:

```
ThenCommands = ["set system host-name foo"]     <- the new command is dropped
```

## #6954 — api/authz: the per-permission body-budget ladder cannot deliver its stated guarantee under CUSTOM login classes [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-28)

Surfaced during the #5561 round-19 fold (PR #6645) and confirmed by refuting a proposed fix. Filed separately because it is a limitation of the mechanism's *shape*, not a bug in its current values, and no ceiling assignment repairs it.

## The stated guarantee

`mutationBodyTierCeilings` (`pkg/api/authz.go`) partitions the mutation body budget by the permission a route requires, so that exhausting the budget "is not a way to deny someone more privileged than you". Each ceiling is tested against the aggregate, giving a one-directional property: a tier is protected from every tier strictly below it. The ordering is derived by `strictlyBelow`, which iterates `config.LoginClassPermissions` — the **system-defined** classes.

Among built-ins that ordering is real: `read-only` ⊂ `operator` ⊂ `super-user`.

## Why it does not survive custom classes

`mapJunosPermissions` (`pkg/config/types_system.go`) maps each Junos permission token through its own arm, and `compiler_system.go` folds a custom class's tokens into `MappedPermissions`. So an operator can author a class holding **any single coarse permission alone**:

```
set system login class netops permissions configure
set system login user alice class netops
```

→ `MappedPermissions = [PermConfig]` — configure without view.

Once such classes exist, the coarse permissions are **not ordered by subset at all**. `PermView ⊄ PermClear`, because a class can hold clear without view. Every `strictlyBelow` pair becomes false.

That has two consequences, and the second is the one that makes this unfixable in place:

1. **Feeding the ordering derivation a custom-class config makes the guard vacuous, not stronger.** `strictlyBelow` returns an empty step set, so every requirement in `authz_bodybudget_fairness_5561_test.go` passes for want of anything to check — including the `view < clear` step that round 18's finding 1 was specifically about. This was proposed as a fix during the fold and refuted before implementation; recording it here so it is not proposed again.

2. **The denial primitive is reachable and no ceiling assignment removes it.** A `permissions configure`-only class floods the configure tier to its 48 MiB ceiling. A holder of `configure` + `view` — strictly *more* privileged — is then refused. The flooder holds a strict subset of the victim's permissions and denies them anyway. Reordering or re-sizing the ceilings cannot fix this, because the ladder is a total order over single permissions and the real lattice is a partial order over permission *sets*.

## Scope, stated honestly

- Not exploitable by an unauthenticated caller: the flooder must hold a real login class and authenticate.
- Not currently reachable through built-in classes, which are genuinely nested.
- Requires an operator to have authored a custom class carrying a single high permission without the lower ones — unusual, but expressible and committable today.
- Bounded by the aggregate budget: the flooder cannot exceed its own tier's ceiling.

So: a real gap in a stated security property, narrow in practice, and mis-described rather than absent. The mechanism protects against the built-in class hierarchy and says so only in prose.

## What the fix would have to look like

## #6955 — dataplane: a BARE `bind-interface st0` never gets its authored address — the networkd model looks for `st0.0` [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-28)

Surfaced during the #6691 hostile review (F2). **Pre-existing, not introduced by #6691.** Filed because #6691's audit table records only the *over-match* half of this function's defect and leaves the under-match half unrecorded — so a reader of that table would conclude the site is fully characterised.

## Defect

`buildInterfaceNetworkdModels` (`pkg/dataplane/compiler_iface.go:757`) derives the netdev name from the unit **ref**, building `"<ifName>.<unit>"`. For a secure tunnel that name is wrong whenever the operator used the bare spelling.

The xfrmi reconciler materialises the device under the **authored** `bind-interface` string:

- `bind-interface st0.0` → a netdev literally named `st0.0`
- `bind-interface st0`   → a netdev named `st0`

and the unit ref is `st0.0` in **both** cases. So with the bare spelling the reconciler creates `st0`, the networkd model looks for `st0.0`, misses, and `continue`s. The authored `family inet address` is never applied.

The bare spelling is the canonical one — it is the form `ValidateSecureTunnelBindInterface`'s own error message advertises first.

## Why nothing else covers it

Verified on the #6691 head, each with a positive control:

- **`pkg/routing/xfrm.go` applies no addresses itself** — zero `AddrAdd` occurrences. (Control: `pkg/routing/tunnel.go` has 3, so the query and pathspec work.) The reconciler creates the link and nothing more.
- **`networkd.Apply` is the only applier** — one non-test call site, `pkg/daemon/daemon_apply_dataplane.go:239`, fed from `applyResult.ManagedInterfaces`.
- `mapZoneInterface`'s address reconcile is skipped for the same name-mismatch reason.

So there is no second path that quietly supplies the address.

## Consequence

A route-based VPN authored with the canonical bare spelling comes up with a tunnel device that has **no IP address**, and therefore no connected prefix. Everything downstream that depends on a tunnel address — a connected route, a next-hop resolution, anything expecting the interface to be addressable — is affected, and the operator sees a device that exists and is up.

## Related, and why this matters beyond the address

This also makes one measured baseline in #6691 a lab-only result. That PR repeats, in `interfaces.go`, `maps_sync.go`, the `server/README.md` and its PR body:

> `bind-interface st0` : MissingNeighbor before AND after

That holds under the tests' stubbed `buildLinkSnapshot`. On a real box the bare spelling has no tunnel IP and therefore no connected prefix either, so the "master already did MissingNeighbor for bare" framing does not hold in the field. #6691's *convergence* conclusion survives — this defect hits both spellings identically at its head — but the framing should not be relied on.

## Scope of what IS already filed

## #6956 — config: `system host-name fw1;` on the system line compiles to an EMPTY host name, silently [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-28)

Found during the #6706 round-11 fold and **verified firsthand on `origin/master`**, with the nested spelling as a control.

## Measured

Driving `CompileConfig` on `origin/master`:

```
system host-name fw1;        err=<nil>  host=""     <- DROPPED, commits clean
system { host-name fw1; }    err=<nil>  host="fw1"  <- control, works
```

Same statement, two spellings, and the flattened one compiles to an empty host name with **no error and no warning**.

## Why it happens

Same mechanism as the `system login` path defect fixed in #6706: the compiler's walk expects to descend into a nested block at each step, so a `system` node carrying `host-name fw1` on its own `Keys` has zero children, and the child walk that would read `host-name` never runs. The statement is not rejected — it is simply not seen.

## Why it is filed separately from #6706

#6706 closes the `system login` path specifically, because that one is an RBAC fail-open: it compiles `System.Login == nil`, which downstream reads as "no RBAC configured" and yields allow-everything. The host-name case has no such privilege consequence, so it was deliberately kept out of that diff rather than widening a security fix.

But it is the same root cause, and it means the packed-path defect is **not confined to `system login`** — any `system` child statement written on the ancestor line is at risk. The `login` case was the one someone happened to look at.

## Consequence

An operator who writes the flattened spelling — which the `display set` output format encourages, and which appears in migration paths from vSRX configs — gets an appliance with no configured host name and no indication anything was ignored. Everything keyed on host name is affected: the management TLS certificate's subject, syslog's origin field, the CLI prompt.

## What to check when fixing

Do not fix `host-name` alone. Enumerate every direct child statement of `system` and determine which are reachable only through the nested walk; the fix should be at the walk, not per-statement. #6706's gate rejects the flattened `system login` path rather than compiling it — decide whether the same disposition (reject at commit) or the more forgiving one (compile it correctly) is right here, and apply it consistently. Rejecting is safer for a security-relevant stanza; for `host-name` compiling it correctly is arguably better, and the two choices should be made deliberately rather than by which code path someone touched.

Guard whatever ships with the flattened spelling as the fixture, since the nested spelling passes today and is what every existing test uses.

## #6957 — config: two sibling `login` blocks under one `system` reduce to the LAST — the first block's users are silently lost [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-28)

Found during the #6706 round-11 fold and **verified firsthand on `origin/master`**, with the single-block form as a control.

## Measured

Driving `CompileConfig` on `origin/master`:

```
system {                              err=<nil>  users=1   <- alice is LOST
  login { user alice { class read-only; } }
  login { user bob   { class operator;  } }
}

system {                              err=<nil>  users=2   <- control, both present
  login {
    user alice { class read-only; }
    user bob   { class operator;  }
  }
}
```

Two sibling `login` blocks under one `system` compile to **one** user. No error, no warning. The first block's contents are discarded.

## Why it matters for RBAC specifically

The lost block is the *first* one. An operator appending a second `login { … }` stanza — a natural thing to do when adding an account, and something a generated or concatenated config does routinely — silently deletes every account defined in the earlier block. The result commits clean.

Combined with how `pkg/daemon` reconciles accounts, the compiled set is authoritative: `reconcileAbsentLoginUsers` deprovisions xpf-managed accounts not present in it. So the earlier block's users are not merely absent from the running config, they are removed from the box.

## Scope — this is probably not confined to `login`

The mechanism is last-writer-wins on same-named sibling containers during the AST walk, not anything specific to `login`. Any stanza that can legitimately appear twice under one parent is a candidate. Worth an audit rather than a point fix.

Note: #6706 makes this **unreachable via one particular route** (a packed `login` prefix beside a well-formed block now rejects at commit), but that is incidental — it closes one spelling that could produce the shape, not the underlying merge behaviour. Two properly-nested sibling blocks, as measured above, still lose data.

## Expected behaviour

Sibling same-named containers should MERGE, which is what Junos does and what this codebase already does elsewhere — `mergeNodes` coalesces fragments of one named object across repeated group roots under `apply-groups`. The compiler having two different behaviours for the same shape depending on which walk reaches it is the actual defect.

```rust

root.waterfill_epoch_wrap_pending = true;

has **zero binding coverage**. Deleting all three writes leaves the entire

- **W3** — delete the three writes: `test result: ok. 4254 passed; 0 failed`.

  which reaches the tail incidentally and asserts nothing about its effects.
  So the tail is reached once and checked never.
- **N1 negative control** — reorder the three independent writes (semantically

  reporting "everything fails".

returns `None` on every call until the 200 µs `COS_GUARANTEE_VISIT_NS` tick.

compares a unit's *derived* `uN` device name against an authored
interface name.

`pkg/routing` keys its desired tunnel set by `TunnelConfig.Name`
(`pkg/routing/tunnel.go`), so two records with one Name are one device with
two conflicting intents — here an `ipip` interface-level record and a `gre`

## #6967 — cluster: refineBootEpoch cannot distinguish a corrupt persisted epoch from an intact one read by a backward-stepped clock [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-28)

## The information problem

`refineBootEpoch`'s `!epochOrderable` branch is reached by **two situations it
cannot tell apart from inside**:

1. a **year-2191 file with a correct clock** — corrupt state that *should* be
   healed by writing over it;
2. an **intact file written by a correctly-clocked predecessor**, read by a node
   whose clock has stepped **backward** (e.g. 2h) — which *must not* be written
   over.

Both present identically as "the persisted value is far beyond my forward
bound". Healing necessarily writes **down**; protecting necessarily **refuses**
to. No predicate over the currently available inputs separates them — this is
an information problem, not a logic bug.

## Consequence today

A backward clock step emits and persists a **lower** epoch, which strands the
live sender and lets an archived higher epoch poison fresh receivers.

## Why it is not a patch

The obvious fix — stop `refineBootEpoch` overwriting an intact higher persisted
epoch with a lower wall-clock seed — was implemented and **broke two tests and
hung a third**, because the codebase deliberately asserts the healing side:

> `TestRefinementSamplesTheClockAfterLoadingPersistedState_6669` —
> *"Declining to chain also HEALS the file"*

So closing this means **changing persistence semantics** and re-deciding that
test's expectation. PR #6669's own comment already says the matter is "tracked
there rather than papered over here" — a deliberate deferral, not an oversight.

## Suggested direction

Persist an extra bit that distinguishes **"written by a previous incarnation of
me"** from **"garbage"** — e.g. a writer/incarnation tag alongside the epoch.
With that, the two situations above stop being indistinguishable: an intact tag
means protect, a missing or foreign tag means heal.

## #6968 — cluster: a forged heartbeat is reported as "stale nonce (replay)" — heartbeatAuthDecision's bad-MAC arm is unbound [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-28)

## Summary

`heartbeatAuthDecision` attributes a **forged or tampered** heartbeat to
`"stale nonce (replay)"`. The frame is still rejected — this is **not** a
fail-open — but the operator-facing reason names the wrong cause, and no test
can currently detect the mislabel.

**Pre-existing #4107 code. Non-blocking for #6669** — that PR touches neither
this function nor its truth table (body is byte-identical to `origin/master`).

## The mutation

In `pkg/cluster/heartbeat.go`, `heartbeatAuthDecision`:

```go
if !macOK {
    return false, "hmac verification failed"
}
```

Change `if !macOK` to `if false` and **the whole `pkg/cluster` suite stays
GREEN** (`go vet` rc=0 first, so this is not a build break).

## Mechanism — why it still rejects

`nonceFresh` is computed by the caller as `macOK && r.auth.admitAuthed(...)`.
So whenever `macOK` is false, `nonceFresh` is false too. With the `!macOK` arm
disabled the frame falls through to the next arm:

```go
if !nonceFresh {
    return false, "stale nonce (replay)"
}
```

Admission is therefore unchanged — a bad-MAC frame is still refused. What
changes is the reason the operator sees: a **forged/tampered** frame (wrong
key, flipped byte, active on-link attacker) is reported as a **replay**.

## #6969 — cluster: epoch admission treats "cannot safely raise the floor" as "reject the frame", stranding genuine live peers (findings 3/4/5/7) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-28)

## One root, four symptoms

The heartbeat epoch gate added in #6669 treats **"I cannot safely raise the
floor"** as **"reject the frame"**, and gives a genuine live peer no way to make
progress once it is at or below a saturated floor. Four reviewed findings are
the same defect seen from four angles:

- **F3 — the third genuine reconnect at an unchanged epoch is rejected forever.**
  `heartbeatEpochSessionsPerEpoch` is a hard cap of 2 with no refill, so a
  genuine successor is permanently excluded. It needs eviction or
  liveness-based refresh, not a larger constant.
- **F5 — a healthy peer with a correct clock is rejected when the receiver is
  more than an hour slow.** The implementation rejects the whole frame, while
  the comment three lines above says the bound "gates ONLY the irreversible
  operation — raising the floor". The implementation is wider than its own
  stated intent.
- **F7 — overlapping xpfd incarnations can strand the surviving newer process
  indefinitely.** B sits below the floor with no periodic re-read; it needs a

## #6974 — api: the accept-time peer-lookup budget is process-global and spent pre-authentication [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-28)

Split out of PR #6645 (#5561) review round 20. The cap itself is **accepted** there and is not a regression to revert — this issue tracks the refinement that removes its cost rather than bounding it.

## What exists today

`pkg/api/authz.go`:

- `:236` `const maxConcurrentPeerLookups = 1024`
- `:241` `var peerLookupSlots = make(chan struct{}, maxConcurrentPeerLookups)`
- `:356` `case peerLookupSlots <- struct{}{}:` — the acquire, inside `connContext`
- `:358` `defer func() { <-peerLookupSlots }()` — the release

A slot is taken at **accept**, and past the cap the connection resolves immediately to an unattributable local identity, which denies.

## Why it is accepted as-is

The wedge being bounded is inside `localAddrsFn()` holding `localAddrCache.mu`. A context cannot unblock a goroutine parked on a mutex, so cancellation is unavailable and admission control is the only lever. Without the cap, connections against a wedged enumeration accumulate goroutines and their captured addresses without limit on the management plane, driven by an unauthenticated caller. Bounded denial beats unbounded growth.

## The costs the refinement should remove

1. **Spent pre-authentication.** The slot is taken before authentication and before any HTTP byte is read, so an unauthenticated client consumes the budget by opening TCP connections alone.
2. **Process-global.** HTTP, HTTPS, retiring and rebound listeners and every `api.Server` share one pool, so saturation on any listener denies on all of them.
3. **Denies rather than queues.** Requests that would have completed become denials under load.

## Proposed direction

- Acquire the slot **after** authentication, so an unauthenticated caller cannot spend it; and/or
- make the budget **per-listener** rather than package-global, so one saturated leg cannot deny on another.

Either change needs to preserve the property the cap exists for: no unbounded goroutine accumulation when `localAddrsFn` is wedged. A fix that simply raises or removes the cap reintroduces the original defect.

## Existing coverage to build on

`TestPeerLookupSlotsAreReturned_5561` (`pkg/api/authz_freshness_5561_test.go`) already pins acquire / release / refusal accounting through production `connContext`, and fails when the release defer is removed. Any refinement must keep it green.

Split out of PR #6645 (#5561) review round 21. Codex found these as MINOR 2 and MINOR 3; they are one class — **an assertion that reads asynchronously-produced state without an edge that proves the state is the assertion's own** — and they are the leading explanation for a real, observed, unreproduced `pkg/api` test failure.

Deliberately NOT fixed in #6645: it is work across several files and that PR is 21 rounds deep.

## A. The body-window waiter edge can be consumed by the wrong test

`mutationBodyWaitersInFlight` is a package-global counter. The wait helper accepts **any** global count `> 0` (`pkg/api/authz_freshness_5561_test.go:608-613`) rather than a delta attributable to the calling test.

Meanwhile `TestNoBodyRouteIsNotBufferedByTheGate_5561` returns with its final control request still parked (`pkg/api/authz_bodywindow_5561_test.go:291-299`), and cleanup closes the connection without joining the handler (`:169`, `pkg/api/config_authz_5561_test.go:85-87`).

So under `-shuffle=on`, a following test can mistake the previous test's stale waiter for its own and proceed before its own request has parked. Affected observers named by the review:

- `TestNoBodyRouteIsNotBufferedByTheGate_5561`
- `TestLocalCallerCredentialIsRevalidatedAfterTheBody_5561`
- `TestAuthorizationIsRemadeAfterTheCallerSuppliesItsBody_5561`

## B. Exact resolver counts are checked while the lookup is still running

`TestPeerIdentityIsResolvedAtAccept_5561` asserts exact resolver invocation counts immediately (`pkg/api/config_authz_5561_test.go:738,753`), but the peer lookup runs asynchronously (`pkg/api/authz.go:388-394`) and safe requests bypass the mutation wait (`:761-764`). **Response completion does not imply resolver completion**, so the count can be read early.

Related, same file: `p.done` is closed **before** the admission token is returned (defer order at `authz.go:391-392`), so a test that immediately fills the global pool can observe a preceding lookup's transient token.

## Why this is the leading flake explanation

A `pkg/api` run failed **once** and has never reproduced. Investigation history:

- 1 failure in ~20 subsequent executions of the same scope.
- `-count=5` (4365 test runs): clean.
- `-race -count=2`: clean, no data race — consistent with these being *ordering* defects on atomics, not memory races.
- `-shuffle=on` x3: clean.
- The failing test name is **unrecoverable** (output was truncated before it was read).

A separate hypothesis — that a counter was incremented twice and decremented once — was **refuted** three ways: all four counted resources have exactly one increment and one decrement site, each `defer`-balanced; both test-side direct manipulations of `peerLookupSlots` balance; and a probe running last in the binary measured `goroutines=2 slots=0 bodybytes=0`, identical across three full iterations, so nothing accumulates.

These defects fit every one of those observations: nothing leaks (so the residue probe is clean), there is no data race (so `-race` is clean), and the failure needs one specific interleaving or predecessor (so it reproduces rarely and survives short repeat runs).

## The claim

`pkg/dataplane/types.go:110-112` and `userspace-dp/src/session/README.md:1090-1094`

string it leans on (`pkg/dataplane/loader_userspace_shim.go:52-53`) says
"stop xpfd so the old pin is released".

## Why that is imprecise

Stopping the process does **not** release a bpffs pin. A pin under
`/sys/fs/bpf/xpf` outlives the process that created it — that is what pinning
is for. What actually releases it is `xpfd cleanup`
(`cmd/xpfd/main.go:213` -> `dataplane.Cleanup()` -> `os.RemoveAll("/sys/fs/bpf/xpf")`,
`pkg/dataplane/loader.go:1260`), or a reboot.

The raw deploy path already does the right thing: `test/incus/cluster-setup.sh:898-899`
runs `systemctl stop xpfd` and then `xpfd cleanup`. But the **#1917 in-place
`xpfd upgrade`** path does not appear to call `Cleanup()`. If that is right,
then an in-place upgrade across an ABI flag day leaves the old pin in place.

## Why this is bounded, not urgent

The failure is fail-CLOSED, not fail-open. `loadOrCreatePinnedShimMap`
(`loader_userspace_shim.go:621-639`) refuses on `ErrMapIncompatible` before the
friendly pre-flight even runs, so a new daemon never reads stale rows of the old
size — it declines to start the dataplane instead. Precedent exists: #5460 moved
the same struct sizes 128 -> 136.

So the consequence is a failed upgrade requiring manual `xpfd cleanup`, not
silent corruption. Still worth closing, because the operator-facing text tells
them to do something that will not work.

## #6979 — nat: synced source-NAT reservation lifecycle — occupancy-dependent selection, lost deletes, and allocator carryover (split from #6876) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-31)

Split out of PR #6876 (issue #6211) during its round-7 gate. These six are
**pre-existing on master** — #6876 neither introduces nor is required to close
them — so they are tracked here rather than billed to that PR. #6876 keeps only
its own debt (the missing multi-worker refcount, the NAT64 release's first-hit
`break`, a false invariant, two stale citations).

The scoping decision was verified against master rather than inferred from the
PR's diff. That check is recorded under F1 below because it is the one that
decides the split.

## F1 — occupancy-dependent selection, and install-with-no-reservation

The synced-session reserve does not reserve on *the matched rule*; it reserves
on the first candidate whose allocator **currently accepts** the tuple. A
refusing rule falls through to the next, and if every rule refuses the session
installs with **no reservation at all**.

**Verified pre-existing.** `git show origin/master:userspace-dp/src/nat/source.rs`
— the loop at `892-951` has four `continue`s past refusing rules and `break`s
only on success. Master's own comment at `:892` says a collision "leaves the
rule untouched and **tries the next**". So on master a transient collision
already installs unreserved, and which allocator holds a flow already depends on
occupancy rather than on `rules` alone.

Concrete failure: one rule A with pool `203.0.113.10:20000`; synced flow F
translated to that tuple; standby currently has unrelated flow G holding it when
F arrives; G retires before failover. F is installed but unrecorded, G's release
frees `20000`, and after failover a new A flow is issued `20000` while F is
still live. With an overlapping later rule B the standby records F in B instead,
so allocator selection differs across HA nodes under identical configuration,
zones and tuple.

Fix direction: on refusal, either retry the *matched* rule after a bounded
backoff, or record the intended (rule, tuple) so the reservation can be
completed later — installing an unrecorded session is the state to eliminate.

matter.

## #6982 — nat64: PortAllocator built with no aggregate budget — same exhaustion vector #6812 caps for SNAT [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-28)

Split out of PR #6815 (issue #6812) after a lane verified the coverage gap by measurement rather than folding it into an already-large PR.

## The gap

There are exactly **two** production `PortAllocator::new` call sites in the tree:

- `userspace-dp/src/nat/source.rs:540` — gated by #6812's apply-boundary aggregate budget.
- `userspace-dp/src/nat64.rs:940` — **gated by nothing.**

NAT64 builds one allocator per prefix sized `pool_v4.len() × (NAT64_PORT_HIGH 65535 − NAT64_PORT_LOW 1024 + 1)` = `len × 64512` slots. The port range is a **fixed constant**, so unlike the SNAT path every NAT64 pool address costs the maximum — there is no narrow-range case. There is no aggregate budget and no pool-count bound on the `'rules:` loop.

The same ~1.48 GiB allocation scenario #6812 exists to prevent is therefore reachable through the NAT64 path with #6812 fully in place.

## It is uncovered on the Go side too

The #5877 strict-commit gate body (`pkg/config/compiler_validate_strict_nat.go:2440-2600`) contains **no `nat64` reference at all** — grepped against the body specifically, not the file. So NAT64 sits outside the strict commit gate *and* outside the apply-boundary cap. Both planes, same gap.

## Missed, not deliberate

Nothing in #6815's docs, comments, or commit messages claims NAT64 is covered, and nothing argues it is out of scope. There is no recorded decision to exclude it. Treat it as an omission.

## Fix

Mirror `resolve_pool_allocators`: charge NAT64 prefixes against an aggregate budget at the apply boundary before any allocator is constructed, and refuse the snapshot fail-closed when the budget is exceeded. Genuinely separate code on a separate wire path from the SNAT allocator, which is why it wants its own PR rather than doubling #6815's diff.

Two things the fix should carry, learned from #6815's own review:

1. **Bind the production wiring, not just the budget arithmetic.** #6815's cap logic was fully tested while its production wiring was not: substituting an infinite budget into the production call left the suite at 273 passed / 0 failed. A test that injects a scaled-down budget does not bind the real one. Drive the real production entry point.
2. **Cross the budget by pool count or the saturating-charge path, not by port capacity.** A fixture that genuinely materialises 2^33 port slots is a test that gets deleted for being slow, and a deleted guard is no guard.

## Explicitly NOT in scope

The address-vector pre-expansion (`pool_addresses_v4/v6`, bounded per-pool by `MAX_POOL_PREFIX_HOSTS = 65536` but not aggregated) is **not** the exhaustion vector and should not be bundled here. Measured comparison for a full-range /16 pool: 65536 × 4 B ≈ **262 KB** as addresses versus 65536 × 64512 bits ≈ **528 MB** as bitmap — roughly 2000×. Bounding it means restructuring the parse loop for negligible gain. Recorded here so the next reader does not re-derive the concern; #6815 carries a doc sentence to the same effect.

Observed and deliberately not folded during PR #6938 (issue #3651), because it is pre-existing on master and outside that PR's diff.

## The shape

#6938 closed a gap where `flush_recorded_flood_counters` had **13 direct test call sites and one production call site**, and that production line was observed by nothing — deleting it left the whole suite green. The fix bound the real worker-loop fold and the status publication.

The traffic-counter fold on the line immediately **above** it has the identical shape: all of its non-production call sites are direct unit tests, and its production call site is equally unbound. Sever it and nothing reds.

## Why the test count is evidence against coverage, not for it

This is worth stating because it inverts the usual reading. Every one of those unit tests calls the helper *itself*, so none of them exercises the single production line that reaches it. The count does not merely fail to cover the caller — it **actively disguises the gap**, because both coverage tooling and human review read "well-tested". A high ratio of direct test callers to production callers is a flag, not a comfort.

The discriminating question: *does any test reach the helper WITHOUT the test body invoking it?* If every test supplies its own call, the caller is unbound by construction.

## Fix

Bind it the way #6938 bound its sibling, and reuse that PR's structure directly:

- Drive the **real control-socket dispatcher** (`handle_stream` via `run_request`) so the assertion rides the production use rather than a helper call. `ping` works as the driver — the dispatcher's post-match block runs `refresh_status` for every non-export verb.
- Assert on the **wire payload the reply carries**, not on in-memory state.
- Carry a precondition (status starts empty) so a fixture that never reaches the hook fails loudly instead of passing vacuously.
- Add an over-reach control in its own body. Note the specific hazard here: loosening a source-pin needle to `flush_recorded_` would match the *flood* fold four lines away and keep the binder green with the traffic fold deleted. The control must also assert the needle DOES match a body containing it, so it cannot pass by matching nothing.

## Known limit, inherited

`worker_loop` takes five heavyweight parameters and is spawned only from coordinator bringup against real AF_XDP sockets. #6938 found no real seam above it and pinned that half **structurally** rather than behaviourally, labelling it as such. Inventing a seam would be the extraction trap — moving the unbound boundary upward and arriving wearing the evidence of a fix. Expect the same limit here, and label it the same honest way rather than manufacturing a testable wrapper.

Provenance: reported by the #6938 lane rather than folded, since it is master code outside that PR's range.
