## #6984 — conntrack ABI: the C mirror is pinned by a comment — a C-only field transposition is undetectable [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-28)

Split out of PR #6928 (issue #4983) rather than grown into its diff. Two independent reviewers reached this conclusion by different routes in the same round.

## The gap

Three artifacts mirror the same conntrack session struct layout:

- **Rust** — `offset_of!` assertions. A Rust-only transposition fails the **build**.
- **Go** — an explicit mirror. A Go-only transposition is **caught** by test.
- **C** — `bpf/headers/xpf_conntrack.h`. Pinned by a **comment** at `:90`, and a comment cannot fail.

A **C-only** transposition of the two fields moves VLAN to offset 136/184 and ifindex to 140/188 — and because both are within the same alignment run, `sizeof` stays at **144/192**. Every executable guard stays green. `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/bpf_map_tests.rs:193` compares against **literals**, so it agrees with itself; nothing in the tree compiles the header and compares `offsetof`.

## The constants are correct today — that is not the issue

Two independent derivations agree, neither by reading the comment that states them:

| method | v4 | v6 |
|---|---|---|
| standalone `gcc` probe | `ifindex=136 vlan=140 size=144` | `ifindex=184 vlan=188 size=192` |
| Clang BPF-target record layout dump | `136 / 140 / 144` | `184 / 188 / 192` |

Derivation for v4: fields reach the end of `fib_gen` at 136, the aligned `u32` lands at 136 and the `u16` at 140, then 142 rounds up to the struct's 8-byte alignment giving 144. v6 is analogous from 184.

So this is **not** a live wrong-offset defect. It is that the third mirror has no executable guard, and the claim "three sides now agree" (commit `37776a107`) is true about present values while being unenforced going forward.

## Why it is worth closing

A silent ABI divergence between the C header and the Rust/Go mirrors mis-reads every session row's ingress interface and VLAN — wrong interface attribution in session display and filtering, and wrong data crossing HA session sync. The shape that produces it is exactly the one the existing guards cannot see: a transposition that preserves total size.

## Fix

Add a test that **compiles the header and compares `offsetof`** against the shipped constants, rather than restating literals. It needs a C toolchain, so gate it the way other tool-dependent legs in this repo are gated (SKIP when absent, and make the skip visible rather than silent — a guard that quietly never runs is the same as no guard).

Alternatively, generate the constants from the header so there is one source rather than three mirrors. That is the stronger fix and the larger change; either closes the gap.

## Note for whoever takes it

`bpf/headers/*.h` is retained after the #1476 eBPF source deletion specifically because the Rust AF_XDP shim build and the userspace-dp parity tests consume it — so this header is **live**, not retired-path. Do not close this as stale on the strength of the #1373/#1476 retirement.

## #6985 — flaky: wg engine install_session_serializes_with_reconcile_removal fails under machine load [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-28)

Costing gate cycles. Not a regression — it fails on load, not on code.

## Symptom

`afxdp::wg::engine::engine_internal_tests::install_session_serializes_with_reconcile_removal`

```
panicked at src/afxdp/wg/engine_tests.rs:872:5:
reconcile loop must have completed at least one full add/remove cycle
```

## Measured, 2026-08-12

Observed once in a full `cargo test --release` (4342 passed / 1 failed, **0 build errors**) on a box concurrently running several other cargo builds at 250%+ CPU. Re-run four times in isolation on the same tree:

| run | result |
|---|---|
| 1 | ok |
| 2 | ok |
| 3 | **"has been running for over 60 seconds"** |
| 4 | ok |

Three of four pass. Run 3 did not fail but did exceed 60s, which is the same underlying condition one notch short of the assertion. The tree under test touches NAT (`nat/source.rs`, `nat/mod.rs`, a new NAT budget test) and does not touch WireGuard at all, so the failure has no causal path from the change it appeared under.

## Why it matters

The assertion is that a background reconcile loop completed **at least one** full add/remove cycle within the test's observation window. That is a wall-clock race against a scheduler, so under CPU contention the loop legitimately has not run yet and the test reports a failure that says nothing about correctness.

The cost is not the red itself — it is that a load-induced red is **indistinguishable at a glance from a real one**, so every gate that hits it spends a cycle re-running and attributing before it can proceed. This campaign has now spent that cycle at least once, and the "pre-existing flake" reflex it encourages is exactly what lets a genuine failure through.

## Fix direction

Replace the implicit wall-clock wait with an explicit **quiescence edge**: have the reconcile loop signal cycle completion (a counter the test can poll to a target, or a channel/notify the test can await with a generous timeout), and assert on that signal rather than on "enough time has probably passed".

If a timing bound is genuinely part of the contract being tested, say so in the test body and make the bound explicit and generous, so a reader can tell a timing assertion from a correctness one. Right now the message reads like a correctness claim.

Same class as the process-global test-synchronisation items found on #6645 in the same round: a test whose synchronisation is implicit rather than explicit will eventually observe someone else's timing. Worth checking whether this is the flaky-test name this campaign lost track of earlier.

## #6986 — userspace: neighbor/fabric lockstep generation advance can swallow an unpublished Compile snapshot [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-28)

Found while tracing the #6871 lease release contract. **Pre-existing, independent of #6871, not fixed there** — filed rather than widening that diff.

## The shape

`Compile()`'s `pendingXSKStartup` branch stores `m.lastSnapshot = snap` **without publishing it** (`manager_compile.go`, the "deferring snapshot publish during XSK startup" path). That leaves `m.publishedSnapshot < m.lastSnapshot.Generation`, which is the level-triggered predicate the status tick uses to drive `syncSnapshotLocked` later.

Two other producers advance `m.generation`, `m.lastSnapshot.Generation` and `m.publishedSnapshot` **in lockstep to the same value** after their own successful publish:

- `RegenerateNeighborSnapshot()` (`manager_neighbor.go`) — after a successful `update_neighbors`
- `persistResolvedFabricsLocked()` (`manager_ha.go`, via `SyncFabricState`) — after a successful `update_fabrics`

Neither publishes an `apply_snapshot`. So if either runs while a Compile-deferred generation is outstanding:

```
before:  lastSnapshot.Generation = 10   publishedSnapshot = 7   (gen 10 content NEVER sent)
regen:   generation++ -> 11; lastSnapshot.Generation = 11; publishedSnapshot = 11
after:   publishedSnapshot == lastSnapshot.Generation  -> the tick's gate is FALSE
```

The full snapshot content (policies, routes, interfaces, NAT) that Compile deferred is never `apply_snapshot`'d. The helper received only the neighbor replace or the fabric update. The manager's bookkeeping says it is published.

## Reachability

`RegenerateNeighborSnapshot` is driven by the daemon's `RTM_NEWNEIGH`/`DELNEIGH` listener plus a 60s safety tick, and it early-returns only when `neighborsEqualForwarding` holds. A link DOWN/UP flushes the kernel neighbor table for that link, so the diff is non-empty and it publishes — i.e. it is *especially* reachable during exactly the RETH MAC link cycle #6871 is about. `SyncFabricState` runs on the daemon's ~30s post-`refreshFabricFwd` cadence.

Both take `m.mu` and can land between any two status ticks, so this does not depend on the #6871 lease. What the lease does is widen the window by roughly one tick period for the duration of a cycle, because the tick that would otherwise have serviced the pending publish is suppressed. That trade is deliberate and favourable — publishing mid-cycle is the worker-restart race #6871 closes — but the underlying swallow is worth fixing on its own.

## Suggested direction (not a decision)

The two writebacks conflate "I published my own partial update" with "the full snapshot is published". Candidates: keep a separate `publishedFullSnapshot` high-water that only `apply_snapshot` paths advance; or have the writebacks advance `lastSnapshot.Generation` **without** touching `publishedSnapshot` when it was already behind. Either needs a look at the content-hash dedup (`lastSnapshotHash`) at the same time, since both writebacks refresh it.

Refs #5103, PR #6871.

## #6987 — session filter: a recycled ifindex renders one confident WRONG interface name [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

Found while narrowing a documentation claim on PR #6928 (issue #4983), and deliberately **not** fixed there — correcting it changes behaviour, so it belongs in its own change.

## The mechanism

`resolveIngressIfaces` (`pkg/cli/session_filter.go:456`) returns a single interface name on a hit in `ifaceNamesByKey`, and otherwise falls back to listing the zone's interfaces.

The map is rebuilt **per query**, from the **current** config and the **current** kernel ifindex. The session row's ifindex was recorded **at install**. Everything below lives in that gap.

## Why this one is different from the other two gaps

The sibling gaps — an unnameable ifindex, and a unit whose map key disagrees with the wire VID — both **miss** the map and fall back to the zone. That is *approximate*, and an operator can see it is approximate.

A recycled ifindex does not miss. The kernel reassigns ifindex N to a different interface over the node's lifetime, the stale N **hits** the rebuilt map, and the CLI renders **one confident interface name that the session never arrived on**. There is nothing in the output to distinguish it from a correct answer.

Concretely: an operator filtering sessions by interface gets rows for traffic that never touched that interface, and misses rows that did. On a long-lived node with interfaces created and destroyed — tunnels, VLAN units, XFRM interfaces, GRE — recycling is normal, not exotic.

## Severity reasoning

Display and filtering only; it does not affect forwarding, policy, or NAT. But it is worse than the usual display bug because **the wrong answer is indistinguishable from the right one**. A fallback to a zone list is visibly imprecise and an operator treats it accordingly. A single confident name gets believed, and it is the input to operational decisions during an incident — "which sessions came in on the tunnel" is exactly the question asked when something is wrong.

## Fix direction

The row needs enough identity to detect that its recorded ifindex is stale, rather than trusting a bare integer across time. Options, roughly in increasing cost:

1. **Record a generation/epoch** alongside the ifindex at install, bumped whenever the interface table changes, and treat a mismatch as a miss (falling back to the zone — the honest answer).
2. **Record the resolved name at install** rather than resolving at query time, accepting that a renamed interface then shows its old name — which is at least *true of when the session started*.
3. **Validate the hit** against something stable about the interface captured at install (permanent MAC, or the config name), and fall back when it disagrees.

Option 1 is the smallest change that makes the failure mode honest. Option 2 arguably matches what an operator means by "which interface did this session arrive on", since that is a fact about the past.

Whichever is chosen, the guard should be bound by a test that installs a row, recycles the ifindex to a different interface, and asserts the render does **not** produce the new interface's name.

## Provenance

The two adjacent gaps were closed as documentation on #6928 at `f43e31db3` — the claim that locally-owned rows carry an exact identity was narrowed to what actually holds. This one was left open because it is not a documentation defect.

## #6989 — flake: install_session_serializes_with_reconcile_removal fails ~1-in-3 under --test-threads=1 [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-28)

`afxdp::wg::engine::engine_internal_tests::install_session_serializes_with_reconcile_removal`
(`engine_tests.rs:872`) fails intermittently under `cargo test --release
--test-threads=1`, asserting `reconcile_iters >= 1`.

Measured during the #6882 gate at `78f1239f9`:

- `--test-threads=1` run 1: FAILED at that assertion.
- `--test-threads=1` runs 2 and 3: rc=0, 4283 passed / 0 failed / 2 ignored.
- That test alone, single-threaded: 6/6 pass.
- Parallel `cargo test --release`: rc=0, consistently.

Roughly a 1-in-3 failure rate single-threaded.

**Cause:** the assertion requires thread B (the reconciler) to be scheduled at
least once before thread A finishes its iteration loop and sets `stop`. That is a
pure scheduling race with no time budget — single-threaded execution makes the
interleaving far less likely, which is why it only shows up there.

**Not a #6882 regression.** That PR's entire production diff is a 9-line
`#[cfg(test)]` mod registration and it touches no WireGuard code. Last substantive
changes to this area were #6157 / #6315.

**Suggested fix:** give the reconciler a bounded wait rather than relying on the
scheduler — e.g. have thread A wait on a signal that the reconciler has completed
at least one iteration before setting `stop`, with a generous timeout, so the
assertion tests serialization rather than scheduling luck.

Worth fixing because a 1-in-3 single-threaded flake makes `--test-threads=1` runs
unusable as a gate, and single-threaded runs are exactly what reviewers reach for
when chasing cross-test interference.

## #6990 — refactor: pkg/dataplane/userspace/maps_sync.go crossed the 2000-line REFACTOR tier (2076) in #6691 [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-28)

`pkg/dataplane/userspace/maps_sync.go` crossed the 2,000-line REFACTOR threshold in
PR #6691 (issue #5619 PR1): 1,953 -> 2,076 lines. The regenerated heatmap row now
reads `[REFACTOR] 2076`.

Verified:

```
git show origin/master:pkg/dataplane/userspace/maps_sync.go | wc -l   -> 1953
git show 0e807ec1a:pkg/dataplane/userspace/maps_sync.go   | wc -l   -> 2076
```

Filed separately rather than folded into #6691, for the same reason as #6988: a
tier crossing is a structural decision, not a defect in that PR's correctness fix,
and expanding a fold round into a module split is scope creep.

**The decision:** split `maps_sync.go` into a module directory, or accept it above
the threshold with a recorded rationale. Prefer a pure code-motion split — it has
no architectural premise to fail, which is the cheapest shape to review.

### How this was found, which is the more useful part

`TestHeatmapNotStale` had been failing on that branch since round 5 and nobody saw
it, because **round 5's gate run was scoped to three packages and never covered
`pkg/refactoraudit`.** The check that would have caught the growth was excluded by
the same round that caused it.

That is a general hazard worth guarding: a package-scoped test run cannot observe a
repo-scoped invariant. Any gate that scopes `go test` to the packages a PR touches
will systematically miss `TestHeatmapNotStale`, and any other whole-repo assertion,
precisely on the PRs most likely to trip them. Either run `./...` before declaring
a round green, or explicitly include `pkg/refactoraudit` in every scoped run.

every reader loses the race to be scheduled for the whole writer loop,
`total_checked` is 0 and the guard correctly reports the run as vacuous.

## #6992 — config: duplicate user names — configuredClass reads the first block, applySystemLogin applies the last [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

Found during the #6838 re-gate, **pre-existing and untouched by that PR** — filed
separately rather than expanding its scope.

For a config with the same **user** name in two `system login user` blocks, two
readers disagree about which block wins:

- `configuredClass` returns the **first** block that has a non-empty class.
- `applySystemLogin` applies **all** blocks in order, so the OS state that lands
  comes from the **last**.

So the class the daemon believes a user has, and the account state actually
provisioned, can be sourced from different blocks of the same config.

This was **not driven to a runtime conclusion** — it is a read of the two call
sites, not a measured end-to-end trace. Someone taking this should first establish
whether the divergence is reachable with a strictly-committable config and what the
observable consequence is, rather than assuming it mirrors the class-name case.

**Why it is worth its own issue:** it is the third instance of one defect class in
this area. #6861 keyed an advisory on a name the runtime resolved differently;
#6838 keyed a fold on a class name the runtime picked differently (first-vs-last,
a real tolerant-path fail-open, now fixed by narrowing the whole same-named
cohort); this is the same shape for user names. The established fix pattern is to
make the outcome **independent** of which reader picks — not to teach one reader to
imitate the other's tie-break, which is a proxy that rots the day the other reader
changes.

Adjacent to the #6645 duplicate-UID work, which merged today.

## #6995 — userspace: a REJECTED forwarding build leaves residue in the policy and NAT counter stores; the NAT half reaches the operator status surface [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-28)

## Symptom

A forwarding build that is **rejected** by one of the late fallible belts still
leaves blocks in two live shared counter stores, keyed by the *rejected*
snapshot's own ids.

Measured with a rejecting build (candidate zones `{100,300}` over live
`{100,200}`, rejected by the last belt) against a live carried-forward store:

```
PROBE zone_residue   = [100, 200]          <- correct, this is what #6832 fixed
PROBE policy_residue = ["default-policy", "zone100->zone300/probe-rule"]
PROBE nat_residue    = [4242]
```

## Mechanism

`build_fallible_forwarding_state` (`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/forwarding_build/mod.rs`)
calls, on the **live** stores both production call sites pass in:

- `counter_store.rule_hit_counter(...)` — get-or-create on the shared
  `PolicyCounterStore` (`policy.rs:1858`, `policy.rs:2158`; store at
  `policy.rs:730-746`), reached at `mod.rs:324`
- `nat_counters.rule_counter(...)` — get-or-insert on the shared
  `NatCounterStore` (`nat/static_nat.rs:440`, `:467`, plus the DNAT and
  source-NAT siblings; store at `nat/mod.rs:261-272`), reached at
  `mod.rs:385-391`

Three fallible belts fire **after** those and can reject the build: NPTv6
(`mod.rs:423`), filter (`mod.rs:465`), CoS (`mod.rs:478`).

This is the same residue class that #6832's
`rejected_build_does_not_create_zone_blocks_in_the_live_store` forbids for the
zone-counter store — the sibling stores in the same function are not covered.

## Why the NAT half is worse than the zone half

`NatCounterStore::snapshots()` emits one row per stored id *"regardless of

(`pkg/daemon/daemon_apply_dataplane.go:300`), with **no AF_XDP worker join**
around it.

That is the same class #5103 closes for `programRethMAC`: `PrepareLinkCycle`'s
contract is that no thread touches UMEM once it returns, so it must precede a
NIC queue/link teardown. PR #6871 routes the *MAC-programming* cycle through
`programRethMACWithWorkerJoin` and takes the link-cycle lease around it; the
*rename* cycle, four lines earlier in the same loop, still cycles the link with
workers potentially live.

- Found during the round-11 hostile review of PR #6871. It is **unchanged by
  that PR** — pre-existing on `master`, neither introduced nor fixed there.
- **Reachability is explicitly not claimed.** `renameRethMember` runs only when
  `netlink.LinkByName(linuxName)` fails, i.e. the member is not yet present
  under its configured name. Whether AF_XDP workers can be bound to that
  interface *at that moment* — under its old kernel name — is the open question,
  and nobody has measured it. If they cannot be, this is a no-op and the issue
  should be closed with that measurement recorded.

  carries its own evidence.

1. Determine reachability first: can a binding exist on the pre-rename kernel
   name while step 2.6 runs? `pkg/dataplane/userspace` binding table +
   `enumerateAndRenameInterfaces` ordering are the places to look.
2. If reachable, the join belongs in the same place it does for the MAC cycle —
   after the decision to cycle is unavoidable, before the first mutation
   (`setDown`) — and it must take the same lease, since the 1 Hz reconcile is
   the thing being protected from.
3. If not reachable, record the measurement and close.

Refs #5103, #6871.

Two production calls in the flow-cache-hit path can be **deleted outright** and the entire
`userspace-dp` crate stays green — 4264 passed / 0 failed on each:

  TCP-flags and DSCP capture that the `SESSION_CLOSE` RT_FLOW record carries (#2501, #2749)
- `sessions.touch_if_stale(..)` — session liveness refresh (#918)

Both were measured by single-line deletion with the whole crate run unfiltered, not inferred.

## Why it matters

`account_packet` is not only a counter. The RT_FLOW `SESSION_CLOSE` record's byte/packet
totals and its TCP-flags/DSCP fields come from this accounting, so a regression here is
invisible in the dataplane and shows up as **wrong data in the security log** — the surface
an operator uses after the fact, where a silent wrong number is worse than a missing one.

`touch_if_stale` governs whether a live session is kept fresh; a regression expires sessions
that are still carrying traffic.

Neither is hypothetical breakage — the point is that nothing in the suite would notice.

A cell that drives a flow-cache hit and asserts, on the session itself:

- byte and packet counters advanced by the amount the packet actually carried, not merely
  that they are non-zero (a count assertion cannot see an identity change);
- the captured TCP flags and DSCP match the packet's, so the `SESSION_CLOSE` fields are
  bound at their source rather than at the record renderer;
- the staleness timestamp moved, with a negative control that it does *not* move when the
  session is already fresh — otherwise the assertion is satisfied by any write.

was covered by a test whose assertions were **all negative**, so severing the production line
satisfied them. A cell for this gap must assert a positive change, and must red when the call

member is itself an unbindable device, the refused netdev lands in the

category that sweep covered. Filed rather than folded, consistent with how #6997 was handled.

## The gap

Deleting **both** cached filter-LOG emissions from `stage_flow_cache_hit` —
`emit_cached_input_filter_log(..)` and `emit_cached_output_filter_log(..)` — leaves the
**entire crate green**: 4289 passed / 0 failed / 2 ignored, all six integration binaries
green, `FULL_RC=0`. Measured by severance on an unfiltered whole-crate run, not inferred.

## Why it matters

These are per-packet observable side effects. If they regress, firewall-filter `then log`
and the RT_FLOW records stop **for every cached flow** — that is most packets of every
long-lived permitted flow. The dataplane keeps forwarding correctly and the operator's log
simply goes quiet, which is the same silent-observability failure #2573 and #3777 were
filed for, on the log side rather than the counter side.

`emit_cached_output_filter_log` additionally carries `output_reject_reply_enqueued`, the
#3615 truthful DENY-vs-REJECT action, so a regression there also makes the logged action
disagree with what the dataplane did.

## Why the earlier sweep missed it

The swept set was calls named `record_*`; #6997 added the two `sessions.*` calls. These two
are neither. `docs/userspace-dataplane-gaps.md` scopes its residual sentence to
"accounting" calls, so it is not false — but it reads as an exhaustive enumeration of what
is left at that call site, and a merge reader will take it that way. There are at least
**four** residuals there, not two.

## What a fix looks like

A cell that drives a flow-cache hit with a filter carrying `then log` and asserts on the
emitted record — not merely that a log call happened, but that the record's fields match
the packet, since the neighbouring counter site was already found bound by a test asserting
the *wrong property* (suppression, counted as replay). For the output side, assert
`output_reject_reply_enqueued` reflects the action actually taken.

Both must red when the corresponding emission is deleted.

## #7003 — test canary: worker-count clamp-helper prohibition matches only call.Fun.(*ast.Ident), so a method value evades it [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-28)

`TestWorkerCountSingleSource_5718` (`pkg/dataplane/userspace/worker_count_single_source_5718_test.go`)
contains two distinct guards. One is safe by construction; the other has a method-value
bypass.

## The hole

The clamp-helper prohibition matches only `call.Fun.(*ast.Ident)` — i.e. it recognises a
prohibited helper only when it appears as the **direct callee identifier** of a call
expression. So this evades it entirely:

```go
f := heartbeatZeroSlots
f(...)
```

The prohibited helper is invoked, but the only reference to its name is an assignment RHS,
which `call.Fun.(*ast.Ident)` never inspects.

The sibling guard in the same test — the `cfg.Workers` count — is **position-free**: any
read in any position counts. That is the safe direction and needs no change.

## Why this is being filed rather than fixed in place

Found while auditing sibling canaries during PR #6871 round 13, which fixed the identical
family in `link_cycle_acquisition_site_6871_test.go`. There the escape was **compiled and
measured**: `take := m.acquireLinkCycleLease` inside the allowlisted function, then
identifier calls elsewhere, passed both static guards while creating a self-renewing lease
outside the deferred-abandon extent.

This is the same *family* — a matcher keyed on a NAME where the property is about a
POSITION — but a different property, a different issue, and a different owner. #6871 did
not change it, correctly.

## Suggested fix

Mirror the shape #6871 landed: classify references into **calls** (the selector/ident is
the callee of a `CallExpr`, after unwrapping `ParenExpr` / `IndexExpr` / `IndexListExpr` so
`(f)()` and `f[T]()` are not misclassified) and **escapes** (every other reference form),
and report escapes as violations regardless of enclosing declaration.

## #7004 — test canary: shim-loader boundary guard greps function source text, so a method value and any argument respelling evade it [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-28)

`shim_loader_boundary_test.go` enforces a #1476 boundary property by running
`strings.Contains` over **function source text**, looking for call forms such as `.Load()`
and `.Compile(cfg)`.

## The hole

A text match on `.Load()` cannot see a method value:

```go
load := x.Load
load()
```

The call happens; the literal `.Load()` never appears in the source. The same applies to
`.Compile(cfg)` and to any argument spelling that differs from the one hard-coded in the
matcher — a renamed local, a different variable name, or a call through a wrapper.

Being text-level rather than AST-level makes this a strictly weaker instance than the
AST-based canaries: it is defeated not only by a method value but by ordinary refactoring
that changes the spelling of an argument.

## Why filed rather than fixed in place

Found while auditing sibling canaries during PR #6871 round 13, which fixed the same family
in `link_cycle_acquisition_site_6871_test.go` after the escape was **compiled and
measured**. This guards a different property (the #1476 shim-loader boundary), belongs to a
different issue, and #6871 correctly did not touch it.

## Suggested fix

Parse rather than grep. Walk the AST for the guarded methods and classify each reference as
**callee position** vs **any other position**, reporting the latter as a violation. That
also removes the argument-spelling fragility for free, since an AST matcher keys on the
callee rather than on the rendered call text.

Prove it with a planted method value: current guard GREEN, fixed guard RED, and an adjacent
ordinary call still GREEN.

## #7005 — api,daemon: a self-terminated HTTP leg is a permanent dead end on an unchanged config [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-28)

## Summary

The HTTP management leg has the same dead-end that #6827 round 6 identified as a blocker
for HTTPS and round 7 fixed there. A self-terminated HTTP leg is a **permanent** dead end
for the life of the process on an unchanged configuration.

This is the primary management plane.

## Provenance

Found while reviewing #6827 round 7 (head `e63e7144d`). The lane verified it by reading
both gates and correctly declined to widen an eight-file, seventh-round PR to cover it.
The symmetric fix belongs on its own change with its own binders.

## The two gates, at `e63e7144d`

- `pkg/api/listener.go:393` — `ReconcileHTTP`'s same-address no-op tests
  `s.httpLeg != nil && s.httpLeg.srv.Addr == addr`. It consults neither `serving()` nor
  `dead`, so a dead leg at the right address looks like a healthy one and reconcile
  returns early.
- `pkg/daemon/management.go:437` — the daemon's HTTP arm fires only when
  `next.Addr != m.cur.addr`. On an unchanged bind, `ReconcileHTTP` is **never called at
  all**, so even a correct no-op gate would not be reached.

Nothing else reads `httpLeg.dead` except `EffectiveHTTPAddr`, which is reporting only —
`show system services` says Failed and nothing acts on it.

Compare the HTTPS side after #6827 round 7: the reconciler's `!HTTPSServing()` arm fires on
every commit while the leg is dead, which is what makes recovery reachable on the common
path.

## Severity: availability, not a credential leak

Worth being precise, because #6827's HTTPS version of this *was* a credential issue and
this one is not. After #6827's B1 fix, a dead leg's accepted connections are **drained**
rather than left serving under a stale pin — `drainLeg` runs on all three exit paths. So a
dead HTTP leg fails closed. The consequence here is that the management plane stays down
until the process restarts or the operator changes the bind address, not that a revoked
credential keeps working.

## #7007 — dataplane: the link-cycle lease releases at the FIRST repair, not the last (multi-member RETH) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-28)

## Summary

The link-cycle lease is released at the **first** repair rather than the last. On a
multi-member RETH apply where an early member cycles cleanly and a later one aborts, the
aborted member's rollback releases a lease the earlier member still depends on.

This is **not a regression** — master has no lease at all — and it is **not** fixable by
refcounting. It is a deliberate design boundary that deserves its own change and its own
smoke.

## Provenance

Surfaced during #6871 round 14 review (a hostile reviewer measured the trace) and analysed in
round 15. I prescribed "refcount the lease, or record it as a known gap"; the lane confirmed
the premise and **refuted the refcount branch by reading the loop boundaries**, which is why
this is filed rather than folded.

## Why a refcount is the wrong fix

Acquisitions and releases do not pair:

- **acquire is per MEMBER** — inside the per-member loop.
- **release is per REPAIR** — one per aborted member, plus at most one for the whole apply at
  step 2.6b2, which sits **outside** the per-member loop
  (`pkg/daemon/daemon_apply_dataplane.go:341` versus the loop ending at `:317`) and is gated on
  `needLinkCycleRecovery`.

So two members both cycling is **two acquires and one release**. A refcount would sit at 1 on
the most ordinary multi-member commit, strand the lease to the apply-wide deferred abandon, and
make that backstop emit its "leaving with a RETH link-cycle lease still held" ERROR on every
such commit — turning a genuine bug report into routine log noise. That is worse than the gap.

## Why the current early release is nonetheless safe

The rebind is helper-**global**, so a cycled member's torn-down state is repaired by the aborted
member's rollback as well. The residual, documented at the release site and in
`docs/reth-mac.md` as of #6871 round 15: a rollback whose rebind itself **fails** has already
released — on a path where the commit fails regardless.

## #7009 — pkg/ddns: tests fail with bind: address already in use under parallel load (2 independent reports) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

## Summary

`pkg/ddns` fails under parallel load with `bind: address already in use` and passes cleanly in
isolation. Two independent lanes on two unrelated PRs have now reported it, so it is a property
of the package rather than of either change.

## Evidence

- **#6820 round 3** — an intermediate `go test ./...` returned `FULL_RC=1` on three `pkg/ddns`
  cases, all `bind: address already in use`, in a package that PR does not touch.
  `./pkg/ddns/` alone was rc 0 and the full re-run was `FULL_RC=0`.
- **#6691 rounds 10 and 11** — 61 of 62 packages green, `pkg/ddns` failing only under parallel
  load and clean in isolation. Recorded across two rounds.

Both lanes correctly reported it rather than omitting it, and both correctly declined to treat
it as a finding against their own change.

## Mechanism

Ephemeral-port collisions. The tests bind fixed or ephemeral ports and, on a host running
several concurrent `go test` invocations, two runs race for the same port. The host in question
was carrying roughly a dozen concurrent cargo/go runs at the time.

## Why it is worth fixing rather than tolerating

It is a **false red in the exact place a false red is most expensive** — a full-suite
`go test ./...` at the end of a round, where a lane is deciding whether its change is green.
A lane that trusts it wastes a round chasing an unrelated package; a lane that learns to
discount it acquires the habit of discounting reds, which is worse.

It also degrades the value of every `FULL_RC` figure this campaign reports, because each one
now needs a caveat.

## Fix

## #7010 — userspace: policy and NAT hit counters are pruned outside a commit point (the destructive half of #6995) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-28)

## Summary

The policy and NAT **hit counters** are destroyed outside a commit point, the same defect
#6832 fixed for the zone counters — `reconcile/snapshot.rs:562` and `:564-566`.

## Provenance

Found during the hostile review of #6832 at `cb65e9686`, and correctly kept out of that round.

## Why this is not #6995

#6995 covers the **additive** residue a rejected build leaves in the policy and NAT counter
stores. This is the **destructive** half: a prune that runs before the apply has committed, so
a build that is subsequently rejected has already destroyed live counter state.

They are two halves of the same store and they need separate fixes:
- #6995 — a rejected build leaves blocks it created (residue).
- this — a rejected build removes blocks it should not have touched (destruction).

## Why it matters

Identical to #6832's zone case: `show` surfaces serve from a store the failed build already
pruned, so an operator reads counters that do not reflect the running configuration. The
difference is only which counters.

## Fix

The shape is already established by #6832 and should be copied rather than re-invented: make
the attach path **additive only**, move the destructive prune into a `commit_*_prune` called by
each apply path at its own commit point — reconcile only when `bringup_result.is_ok()`, refresh
at its `self.forwarding` swap.

## Binder requirements

From #6832's experience, three things that are easy to get wrong:

- **Bind each call site separately.** #6832's three cells are mutually exclusive, so each
  production line has exactly one assertion. A single test covering both apply paths cannot
  tell you which one you broke.
- **The two bring-up arms are not interchangeable.** `WorkerBindIncomplete` calls

## #7011 — pkg/api: retire the hijacked-connection drain exception instead of enumerating hijackers [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-28)

## Provenance

PR #6827 round 9 hostile review. Two separate rounds of that PR have now been spent patching a
tripwire that enumerates hijacking handler types, and the enumeration has been defeated twice.

## The defect in the current approach

`pkg/api/drain_scope_6827_test.go` maintains a map of hijacking types and asserts they are not
reachable from `pkg/api`, so that `drainLeg`'s guarantee can carry a "modulo hijacked
connections" caveat. The map's comment claims it lists "the ones reachable from this module
today".

That claim cannot be maintained, and the reason is structural rather than an oversight:

- **Both escapes came from one module.** `golang.org/x/net` (a direct dependency, `go.mod:16`)
  vends *both* `websocket` (already mapped, caught round 8) and `http2/http2/h2c` (missed,
  caught round 9). `h2c` hijacks at `http2/h2c/h2c.go:136,171`.
- **Neither required a `go.mod` change.** A version bump of an *existing* dependency can begin
  vending a new hijacking subpackage with nothing in the module file to notice, so any review
  reflex keyed on "did dependencies change" is blind to it.
- The local AST walk itself is sound — it was verified to catch
  `http.NewResponseController(w).Hijack()`, method values, and aliased import paths. The hole is
  entirely "a handler from another package", which a package-local walk cannot see by
  construction.

## The fix

**Retire the exception rather than re-key the guard.** If hijacked connections are drained, the
caveat disappears and the tripwire has no job to do.

`drainLeg`'s own doc already writes the recipe: `ConnState` reaching `StateHijacked` hands you
the `net.Conn`. The hook slot is one field off the existing `ConnContext` wiring. The reviewer's
estimate is ~15 lines to make `drained` true outright, with no "modulo hijacked connections"
qualifier anywhere.

That change is deliberately **not** being made in #6827: it is new production mechanism on the
connection-draining path, it needs its own binding and review pass, and #6827 is at round 10 with
its gate nearly closed. #6827 instead adds `h2c` to the map and rewrites the comment to state its
derivation (the grep predicate plus the dependency version) rather than asserting completeness.

## #7012 — pkg/daemon: d.mgmt is published under staleCertMu on the write side only [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-28)

## Provenance

PR #6827 round 9 hostile review, reported as informational. Not a defect at that PR's head and
explicitly self-disclosed there; filed so it is tracked rather than resting on a comment.

## The finding

`pkg/daemon/daemon_run_servers.go:475-481` publishes `d.mgmt` under `staleCertMu`. Three reads
are **not** under that lock:

- `pkg/daemon/management.go:813`
- `pkg/daemon/management.go:816`
- `pkg/daemon/daemon_run_servers.go:46`

A mutex held on one side of a publish establishes no happens-before for a reader that does not
take it. The write-side lock therefore orders nothing with respect to these three.

## Why it is not urgent

- The one read #6827 claims to fix — the diagnosis delivery at `management.go:672` — genuinely
  **is** under the lock.
- `daemon.go:288-296` says so in terms: *"Do not read this as 'mgmt is guarded'; it is not."*
  The narrower claim is accurate and the wider one is explicitly disclaimed.
- `go test -race` over the 6827/5719/5561/5866/6401 cells in `pkg/api` and `pkg/daemon` is clean.

## Why it should still be closed out

A partial lock is the shape that invites a later reader to assume the field is guarded and add a
fourth read without taking it — at which point the disclaimer comment is the only thing standing
between the codebase and a real race, and comments do not fail builds.

## Fix options

1. Take `staleCertMu` on all three reads, making the field genuinely guarded and letting the
   disclaimer be deleted.
2. Or leave the reads unlocked and make the *absence* of a guarantee structural rather than
   documented — e.g. by not exposing the field directly, so an unlocked read is not spellable.

Option 1 is the smaller change. Option 2 is the one a comment cannot regress.

## #7013 — config: repeated same-mode NAT actions collapse silently and commit under strict [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-28)

## Provenance

Found and measured during PR #6820 round 5, which fixed the *cross-mode* packed contradiction
(`destination-nat off pool p1`). This is the same-mode sibling, deliberately scoped out of that
round because closing it needs state the typed struct does not carry.

`docs/reviews/archive/codex-review-182.md:14550` already documented this path.

## The defect

Repeated actions of the **same mode** collapse to the last one and commit under STRICT, in both
the hierarchical and the packed spelling:

```
destination-nat { pool PD; pool PD2; }      ->  Pool:"PD2"   ACCEPTED
destination-nat pool PD pool PD2            ->  Pool:"PD2"   ACCEPTED
```

The operator authored two pools; one is silently discarded, and nothing rejects.

## Why the #6820 fix does not cover it

`validateNATTerminalActionCardinalityStrict` counts **modes**, not authored occurrences. Two
`pool` clauses are one mode, so the cardinality counter sees `n == 1` and the gate does not fire.
And `NATThen.PoolName` is a **scalar**, so by the time validation runs there is only one value —
the earlier one is already gone.

Round 5's accumulation fix reads `Keys[1:]` and `Children` and accumulates *distinct actions*,
which is what makes `off pool p1` countable as two. It does not and cannot make `pool PD pool PD2`
countable as two, because the destination it accumulates into holds one pool name.

## What closing it requires

Occurrence state the typed struct does not carry today. Options, roughly in increasing cost:

1. Count authored occurrences during lowering and hand that count to the cardinality gate
   alongside the resolved `NATThen` — the gate then rejects on `occurrences > 1` for any mode,
   without changing the resolved type.
2. Make the affected fields carry their multiplicity (slice, or a small "authored twice" flag) so
   the discard is representable and therefore checkable.

## #7014 — config: fully-compact 'then <action>;' compiles to zero actions and is rejected [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-28)

## Provenance

Found while reproducing the packed-contradiction defect for PR #6820 round 5. **Pre-existing and
unchanged by that round** — recorded so it is tracked rather than rediscovered.

## The defect

The fully-compact authoring, where every token lands on the `then` node itself, compiles to **zero
actions** and is refused by the zero-action arm:

```
then source-nat off;              ->  0 actions  ->  REJECTED
then { source-nat off; }          ->  1 action   ->  accepted
```

Both compilers look for a `source-nat` / `destination-nat` **child** of `then`, so when the tokens
pack onto the `then` node there is no child to find and the action set comes back empty.

Flat-set is unaffected: `SetPath` builds the child, so `set … then source-nat off` produces the
hierarchical shape.

## Why it is low severity but still worth closing

It **fails closed** — a legitimate single-action config is refused with a diagnostic, rather than
being silently misread. Nobody's traffic is mishandled. But it is a real Junos-syntax authoring
form that this parser accepts structurally and then rejects semantically, and the rejection message
will point at "no terminal action" for a stanza that visibly has one, which is a confusing place for
an operator to land.

## Fix sketch

The `then`-node iteration needs to read tokens packed onto `then` itself, the same way round 5
taught `applyNATThenActions` to read `Keys[1:]` on the action leaf. The parse shape is the one
documented in `docs/config-schema.md` under multi-value leaves and bracketed lists (#2419) — this
is the same family one level up the tree.

Note the interaction with #6820 round 5: once `then` node tokens are read, the packed-contradiction
accumulation must apply there too, or `then source-nat off pool P;` becomes a new instance of the
defect round 5 just closed one level down.

## #7015 — userspace-dp: bind the zone-counter prune obligation with a prune-debt receipt [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-28)

## Problem

The zone-counter prune is an obligation that exists only on a control-flow branch, and nothing binds it. `commit_zone_counter_prune` must be called on the `bringup_result.is_ok()` path after forwarding state is published; both current commit points do call it (`reconcile/mod.rs:417`, `snapshot_refresh.rs:388`, both bound by fail-on-revert cells in #6832), but a **third** apply path added later would skip it silently.

## Why this cannot be a type-level fix

Established during #6832 round 7, and worth recording so it is not re-litigated:

1. **The value is published BEFORE the obligation site, and must be.** In `reconcile/mod.rs` the state reaches `self.forwarding` inside `apply_snapshot` (`reconcile/snapshot.rs:610`), then `bring_up_workers` runs at `:391`, and only then does the prune fire at `:417`. In `snapshot_refresh.rs` it is `self.forwarding = new_forwarding` at `:380`, prune at `:388`. A `#[must_use]` value or a linear token would have to be consumed at the move into the field — which happens *before* the obligation exists — so by the time the obligation is live there is no unused value left for anything to fire on.
2. **"Make the un-pruned state unrepresentable" contradicts the design.** That state must be live and observable during bring-up: a build that succeeded but whose workers failed is deliberately NOT committed, and `show security zones` keeps reporting from that store. A sealed constructor or a builder that cannot complete would forbid the state the design exists to preserve.
3. **The obligation is control-flow-shaped, not ownership-shaped.** It is "on the `is_ok()` branch, this call happens" — typestate over program points, which Rust's type system does not express.

So it is **unenforced, not unenforceable**.

## Options, ranked

1. **(preferred) A prune-debt receipt.** `attach_zone_counters` records "prune owed for generation N" on the store. A new build's additive half finding a prior generation's debt still outstanding *is* the defect — surface it as a debug assertion and/or a status counter. Catches a third apply path at runtime and in any test that drives it, and needs **no exemption list**.
2. **A structural guard test**: any function that publishes forwarding state or calls `bring_up_workers` must contain a `commit_zone_counter_prune` call. Enforceable today and cheap, but it needs an exemption list — the publish population is `snapshot_refresh.rs:380` and `reconcile/snapshot.rs:610`, plus two non-applies (`reconcile/mod.rs:315` builder staging, `coordinator/mod.rs:715` teardown reset). This board has repeatedly been bitten by exemption lists going stale or vacuous, which is what ranks it below (1).
3. **Funnel both commit points into one method** — readable, but it *renames* the obligation rather than binding it. A third path can still skip the funnel. Not recommended as the fix.

## Scope

Both current commit points are genuinely covered today, so this is not a live defect — it is a guard against the third one that does not exist yet. Provenance: analysis performed under #6832 round 7 at `62c7938a2`; deliberately not implemented there because that round was scoped to tests and claims.

## #7017 — Standalone daemon never re-installs userspace event-stream callbacks on a replaced stream instance [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

## Summary

On a STANDALONE (no-cluster) daemon the userspace event-stream
callbacks are installed exactly once and never re-installed if the
helper's `EventStream` instance is REPLACED. The clustered path was
fixed for this in #6743 r6-F4 (`es != wired` re-install inside
`eventStreamFallbackLoop`); the standalone arm never runs that loop.

The gap is stated honestly in-tree at
`pkg/daemon/daemon_ha_userspace_stream.go:96-115` ("KNOWN GAP (#6743
r2-N5)"). Filing it so it is tracked somewhere a work queue can see,
rather than only in a comment.

## Mechanism

`daemon_run.go:373` starts `runUserspaceEventStream(ctx)` only when
`d.cluster == nil`. That function takes its standalone arm:

```go
if d.cluster == nil || d.getSessionSync() == nil {
    d.wireUserspaceEventStreamCallbacks(ctx)
    return
}
```

`wireUserspaceEventStreamCallbacks` re-reads the #2114 cell every
500 ms until it finds a provider with a non-nil stream, calls
`installEventStreamCallbacks(es)`, and **returns**. The arm returns
with it. Nothing watches for a later stream instance.

The clustered path instead runs `eventStreamFallbackLoop`, which
per tick does:

```go
if es != nil && es != wired {
    d.installEventStreamCallbacks(es)
    wired = es
}
```

`pkg/dataplane/userspace/fabric_verdict_scope_6691_test.go` carries a scope caveat naming **two** unsingle-sourced axes between the probe and production. 2. `ifindex > 0` — **three** literals: the probe at `:312`, production at `ingress_exclusions.go:754` **and** `:781`. Named, but "this probe's own literal" reads as "production has no counterpart"; it has two.
3. `name != ""` — production `:746`, `:789`. Named.
4. **`vote.role == netdevVoteFallback` (`fabric_verdict_scope_6691_test.go:316`)** — a re-typed ROLE-axis literal inside `countedVotes`, four lines below the sentence claiming the role axis cannot drift. **Not named.**
5. `vote.unbindable` / `tally.refused()` unanimity — the probe never models the decision. Not named.

Plus the `redirects` closure at `:335`, re-typing `userspaceOwnsItsNetdev || Ifindex<=0 || ParentIfindex<=0` from `maps_sync.go:1596/1627`.

The Codex leg added the sharper wording: **"ROLE axis" is too broad** — only counted-versus-not-counted is single-sourced; fallback classification remains a separate literal.

## Fix

Re-derive the caveat from the predicates rather than the axes, and state item 4 explicitly. Do NOT just re-count the quantifier — the enumeration is a floor, so bind the predicate.

## #7020 — userspace: TestEveryNetdevProducerIsEnumerated's producer sweep is bounded to resettable slice fields with a differing cardinality [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-28)

Filed from the #6691 Codex leg at `76045dfae`. **Non-blocking — this bounds a diagnostic, it does not make the guard vacuous.**

## What is wrong

The producer sweep in `pkg/dataplane/userspace/fabric_verdict_scope_6691_test.go` enumerates a snapshot field as a "producer" only when

    Kind() == reflect.Slice && CanSet() && len(E(nil field)) != len(E(base))

so it misses:

* **non-slice producers** — a producer reached through a scalar or map field is never nilled, so the sweep cannot observe it;
* **equal-cardinality membership substitutions** — a field whose nilling swaps *which* netdevs are emitted without changing *how many* passes the `len(...) != len(...)` test and is not reported.

## Why it is not blocking

The primary assertion (`E ⊆ C-or-valid-redirect`) is type-independent, so a producer the sweep never names is still covered by the membership assertion. What the bound costs is the DIAGNOSTIC: the sweep is what tells a future reader "here is the complete set of fields that produce emitted netdevs", and that list is a floor, not a census. Codex separately verified every substantive assertion in the file has a production mutation that reds it (eleven listed), so the guard is not vacuous.

## Fix

Either widen the sweep (walk maps and scalars; compare emitted SETS rather than lengths) or state in the doc that the enumeration is a floor and name what it cannot see.

## #7023 — userspace: snapshotLinuxName resolves a secure-tunnel unit to a netdev that does not exist (st0.0 -> st0), so the unit reports ifindex 0 / MTU 0 / no addresses [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-21)

Scoping issue for the defect PR #6691 fixes, split out of #5619 so that PR has a terminal record of its own. #5619 stays open for PR2 (#6698) and the remaining dataplane ownership work (#6700).

## The defect

`snapshotLinuxName` (`pkg/dataplane/userspace/interfaces.go`) resolved a secure-tunnel unit ref through the generic unit-0 collapse, so `st0.0` became `st0` — a name that exists on no box when the operator authored `bind-interface st0.0`. The unit row therefore reported **ifindex 0, MTU 0 and no live addresses**, and fell out of every ifindex-keyed dataplane set.

`Config.ResolveKernelIfName` already carried an `st<N>` rule *and* a doc comment saying "Keep in sync with `snapshotLinuxName`". Nothing enforced it, and the dataplane copy silently lacked the resolution rule.

## Why the name cannot be reconstructed

A bare `bind-interface st0` and an explicit `bind-interface st0.0` derive ONE `if_id` under two DIFFERENT device names (`st0` vs `st0.0`, see `pkg/routing/xfrm.go` and `pkg/config/xfrmi.go`), while the unit ref is `st0.0` in both. Synthesising `"<ifName>.<unit>"` is right for the dotted spelling and wrong for the bare one. The device name is `LinuxIfName(bind-interface)` — whatever the operator authored — and must be read back from the config, which is what `Config.SecureTunnelNetdevForRef` does by joining on `if_id`, with `XFRMIfNameAndID` as the single source of truth for both halves.

## Scope

Resolving the name also admits the tunnel's connected prefix to the FIB (the Rust `populate_interfaces` gate is `ifindex > 0`), which moves a LAN→tunnel forwarding disposition from `NoRoute` to `MissingNeighbor` for the dotted spelling — converging it onto what the bare spelling already did. The consequence of that adjudication is the pre-existing MAC-less-xfrmi egress defect, #6713, fixed by #6722. **#6722 must merge before #6691.**

Fixed by #6691.

## #7024 — userspace: the two zone maps CAN disagree about a base reference, and the #6722 agreement guard does not cover the shape [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-28)

Filed from the #6722 final gate at `413c6818c`. **Non-runtime** — the divergence
fails CLOSED, so nothing forwards wrongly. What is wrong is the recorded claim
and the guard that is supposed to hold it.

## The claim

`TestAuthoredAndDerivedZoneMapsAgreeOnEveryAuthoredRef_6722`
(`pkg/dataplane/userspace/egress_zone_identity_6722_test.go`) asserts
`buildInterfaceZoneMap[ref] == authoredZoneRefs[ref]` for every ref the authored
map holds, over a 6-shape corpus, and `docs/userspace-dataplane-architecture.md`
records it as a load-bearing property ("the two zone maps must not disagree").
It was the round-12 answer to review finding F2.

## The counterexample

`buildInterfaceZoneMap` fans a unit-suffixed reference UP to the base
(`out[base] = zoneName`, first-write-wins over sorted zone names).
`authoredZoneRefs` deliberately does not. So a base name claimed by a bare
reference in one zone AND reached by a dotted reference's fan-up from an
alphabetically earlier zone gets two different answers.

Measured through `compileWithStubbedLinks6722(..., lenient=true)` at
`413c6818c` (strict `CompileConfig` rejects the doubly-claimed interface with a
multi-zone error, so this is the tolerant load / HA config-sync path — the same

so `EgressInterface::zone_id` was the egress-zone answer. #6722 moved the answer
into `state.ifindex_unambiguous_zone_id` and pointed both `egress_zone_id` AND
`populate_egress` at that ledger, so the field is now a copy of a value nothing
reads through the struct.

Enumerated at `413c6818c` — every non-test caller of `forwarding.egress.get(...)`
(`icmp.rs`, `icmp_ptb.rs`, `forwarding/nat.rs`, `frame/wg.rs`,
`session_glue/mod.rs`, `coordinator/inject.rs`, `forwarding/local_delivery.rs`,
`forwarding/mss.rs`, `tx/dispatch/mod.rs`, `tx/tcp_segmentation.rs`,
`frame/tcp_segmentation.rs`) uses `bind_ifindex` / `vlan_id` / `mtu` / `src_mac`
/ `primary_v4` / `primary_v6`. The only remaining reader of `.zone_id` is the
`#[cfg(feature = "debug-log")]` dump at `forwarding_build/mod.rs:533-547`, which
is compiled out of a normal build.

Mutation that stays green: delete the `zone_id` field from `EgressInterface` and
its initializer in `populate_egress` (keeping the debug dump's use behind a
`0`), and the cargo suite is unaffected on the production side.

Either drop the field (and render the debug line from
`state.ifindex_unambiguous_zone_id`), or keep it and say in its doc that it is a
debug-only mirror of the ledger so a future reader does not take it for a second
opinion.

give the int a consumer (naming the unit in a warning would be the obvious one,

    && next.addresses <= budget.max_addresses
    && next.port_capacity <= budget.max_port_capacity)

That `<=` is the exact-fit contract, and it is the half that must agree with the

install, not fail closed.

**port-capacity** axes are unbound: narrowing either boundary from `<=` to `<`
leaves the whole `nat::` module green.

-            && next.port_capacity <= budget.max_port_capacity)
+            && next.addresses < budget.max_addresses
+            && next.port_capacity < budget.max_port_capacity)
```

## #7033 — config/nat: a cross-mode packed `then` contradiction commits under strict — an authored `off` EXEMPTION is dropped and a TRANSLATION published in its place [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-30)

## Provenance

Measured firsthand while driving PR #6820 round 7. Filed rather than folded because it
**reproduces identically on `origin/master`** — it is pre-existing, not introduced by that PR.

Related but distinct: #7013 (repeated **same-mode** actions) and #7014 (fully-compact
`then <action>;` compiling to zero actions). This is the **cross-mode** packed case.

## The defect

`validateNATTerminalActionCardinalityStrict` (#5628) is meant to reject a NAT `then` block
carrying two mutually-exclusive translation actions. When the two actions are **packed as
tokens on one node** rather than lowered as two separate fields, the compiler lowers only
ONE of them, the cardinality counter sees `n == 1`, and the contradiction commits under
STRICT with no diagnostic.

Measured through the public `CompileConfig` pipeline at `origin/master` (1dd8db158):

| authored | shape | strict result | resolved | dropped |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `then { source-nat off pool P; }` | root-packed | **ACCEPT** | `{Off:true}` | `pool P` |
| `then { source-nat pool P off; }` | root-packed | **ACCEPT** | `{PoolName:"P"}` | **`off` — the EXEMPTION** |
| `then { source-nat { pool P off; } }` | child-packed | **ACCEPT** | `{PoolName:"P"}` | **`off`** |
| `then { destination-nat { pool PD off; } }` | child-packed | **ACCEPT** | `{PoolName:"PD"}` | **`off`** |
| `set … then source-nat pool P off` | flat-set | **ACCEPT** | `{PoolName:"P"}` | **`off`** |
| `set … then source-nat off pool P` | flat-set | **ACCEPT** | `{Off:true}` | `pool P` |

The rows in bold are the ones that matter: the operator authored a no-NAT **exemption** and
the compiler publishes a **translation** instead — the exact inverse of the authored action,
which is the outcome the #5628 gate's own rejection text says it prevents.

## Why nothing catches it

- `parseKeys` retains every token (`pkg/config/parser.go`), so the tokens are present in the AST.
- Schema validation deliberately ignores leftover container keys (`pkg/config/schema_walk.go`),
  and the source-NAT `then` subtree is deliberately **open-world** per #4313, so
  `SchemaValidate` returns nil for every source-NAT row above.
- Both lowering paths read `Keys[1]` alone (`compiler_nat_source.go`, `compiler_nat_destination.go`),
  so only one action is ever lowered.
- The cardinality counter counts lowered **fields**, so it sees `n == 1`.

## #7038 — api: a stale mgmt TLS cert after `set system host-name` is diagnosed nowhere [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-21)

Split out of the **#5719** cohort so PR #6827 can carry a `Closes` keyword
without closing the cohort, which still has an unfixed item (the applied-nft
truth projection — analysis in
https://github.com/psaab/xpf/issues/5719#issuecomment-5193689327).

## The gap

The durable management cert (#1916 D6) bakes TWO identities into its SANs at
first generation — the HTTPS bind host and the kernel host name — and is
deliberately never re-minted (a re-mint churns remote clients' TOFU pins).
#6378 closed the diagnostic silence for the **bind host** only.

A later `set system host-name` leaves the cert's DNS SAN naming the OLD host.
Renaming a firewall does not move its management IP, so the bind-host check
does not fire either. An operator connecting by the new name gets a bare
`x509: certificate is not valid for any names` with **nothing in the log**.

Two independent reasons the existing load-path diagnostic could never see it:

1. **Reachability** — the HTTPS leg is rebuilt only when the TLS flag or the
   HTTPS bind address changes, so a rename on an unchanged endpoint reloads
   nothing.
2. **Ordering** — `reconcileWebManagement` runs early in `applyConfigLocked`
   while `applyHostname` runs in the apply tail, so even a commit that DID move
   the bind would have diagnosed the OLD kernel name.

## Scope

- `pkg/api`: a shared `certCoversHost`/`certHasNoSANs` classification on the
  load path, a terminal no-SANs diagnostic, and
  `Server.WarnStaleMgmtCertForHostName` reading the LIVE HTTPS leg.
- `pkg/daemon`: a fenced rename (`renameHostNotingStaleMgmtCert`) plus a
  generation-fenced debt ledger delivered at the rename and re-attempted at the
  boot management start and every web-management reconcile.

Fixed by PR #6827.

`set system services web-management https` **with no `interface`** resolves to
`127.0.0.1:443` (`pkg/daemon/daemon_run_servers.go` `resolveAPIBinds`:
`httpsBindIP := "127.0.0.1"` unless an interface is named, and
`resolveInterfaceAddr` itself falls back to `127.0.0.1`). On that plane no
remote client exists, so no client can verify by host name.

The **bind-host** half of this very diagnostic knows that:
`bindHostWarnable("127.0.0.1")` is `false` (`pkg/api/server.go:1154-1162`), so
`warnStaleBindHost` stays silent for a loopback bind by design.

The **host-name** half on the rename path has no equivalent gate.
`warnStaleHostName` (`pkg/api/server.go:1401-1415`) gates on
`hostnameSANWarnable(hostName)`, `hostName == bindHost`, and — only for
`hostNameInferred` — `hostNameLikelyAccessIdentity`. Nothing looks at whether
the LISTENER is loopback-only. `Server.WarnStaleMgmtCertForHostName` passes
`hostNameOperatorSet`, which skips gate 3, so every `set system host-name` on a
loopback-bound management plane emits a WARN about remote clients that cannot
exist.

## Measured

Probe over the package's own fixtures (`mintCert` / `legServing` /
`captureWarn`), run at head `0cc7dd908`:

```
PROBE P1 loopback-bind rename warn output =
  level=WARN msg="loaded management TLS cert does not cover the current host-name;
  clients verifying by host-name will fail — if this device is reached by host-name,
  remove /etc/xpf/tls to re-mint (the SANs below are the identities it does cover)"
  host_name=new-fw cert_dns_sans="[localhost old-fw]" cert_ip_sans="[127.0.0.1 ::1]"
PROBE P1 RESULT: WARN FIRES on a loopback-only mgmt bind
PROBE P1 bindHostWarnable(127.0.0.1)=false  cert DNS=[localhost old-fw] IP=[127.0.0.1 ::1]

`ZoneCounterSlotMap::build` (`zone_counters.rs`):

let mut ids: Vec<u16> = zone_ids.iter().copied().filter(|&z| z != 0).collect();

for zid in ids {
    if next_slot > ZONE_COUNTER_ASSIGNABLE_SLOTS {
        overflow_active = true;
        break;                       // <- stops; remaining configured zones get NO block

    ...
    slot_totals[next_slot] = Some(store.zone_totals(zid));   // <- the only get-or-create

So a config carrying zone id 0, or more than `ZONE_COUNTER_ASSIGNABLE_SLOTS`
zones, resolves a block for a **strict subset** of what it configures.

- `web-management listener reconcile incomplete; retaining previous listener(s)`
  (from `reconcileTo`), plus
- `web-management listener reconcile did not converge; retrying on next commit`
  (`pkg/daemon/daemon_apply.go:211`).

Before #6827 the reconcile was skipped entirely once the fingerprint matched, so
none of these repeated.

From the hostile review of PR #6827 at head `5deefb242` (28-cell deletion sweep
over the PR's `pkg/api` delta: 24 RED, 4 GREEN). **Non-runtime** — the code is
correct; nothing binds it.

`pkg/api/server.go:1481-1484`, inside `Server.WarnStaleMgmtCertForHostName`:

```go
leaf, err := x509.ParseCertificate(cert.Certificate[0])
if err != nil {
	// A live leg is serving a certificate we cannot parse. The question WAS
	// reached; re-parsing it later will fail identically, so report it
	// answered rather than making the caller retry forever.

}
```

**Mutation:** `return true` → `return false`.

```
go test -count=1 ./pkg/api/     rc=0   GREEN
go test -count=1 ./pkg/daemon/  rc=0   GREEN
```

Total survivor in both packages. The comment two lines above states the contract
the flip violates: with `false`, `deliverStaleMgmtCertDiagnosis`
(`pkg/daemon/management.go:698`) never clears `staleCertPending`, so the daemon
re-attempts the delivery at every web-management reconcile forever, re-parsing a
certificate that will fail identically each time.

returned value that decides a caller's retry loop, with the caller's behaviour
unasserted. That instance was closed; this one is in the same PR and was not.

**Minimum cell:** drive a serving HTTPS leg whose `TLSConfig.Certificates[0]`
carries an unparseable DER blob, note a rename debt, call the delivery, and
assert `staleCertPending` is `false` afterwards.

## #7047 — docs(api): a "up to legDrainTimeout" finite gloss survives at README:1307, and serveBound's doc over-scopes the 5s close_notify to the HTTP leg [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-28)

From the hostile review of PR #6827 at head `5deefb242`. **Non-runtime** — two
prose slips in the direction of *more* boundedness than exists.

### 1. A surviving finite gloss

`pkg/api/README.md:1307`:

> `Shutdown`, and already-accepted requests drain for **up to `legDrainTimeout`**

That is the exact finite gloss #6827 round 11 set out to remove, in one of the
two files that round names, while the same file says at `:1124` that
`legDrainTimeout` bounds neither phase in wall-clock terms.

Sweep predicate — `grep -rn "up to .legDrainTimeout"` over `pkg/api/` and
`pkg/daemon/` `.md` and non-test `.go` — returns exactly two hits at that head;
the other one self-corrects six lines later.

### 2. A scoping slip in `serveBound`'s doc

`pkg/api/server.go:1008-1012` and its README mirror:

> one stalled peer costs up to five seconds, then the next, **in each phase of
> each server**

The counts (2 phases × 2 servers) are right, but the five seconds attaches only
to the **HTTPS** server: `s.httpServer` runs through plain `Serve`, so its
`c.rwc` is a `*net.TCPConn` whose `Close` sends no TLS alert and carries no
`close_notify` write deadline. And "both phases put serial closes in front of it"
is not coherent for phase 2, since `http.Server.Close` takes no context at all.

Both slips point toward *more* unboundedness, and the load-bearing sentence
("has no fixed ceiling") re-scopes correctly, so neither is falsifying. Two
caveats are worth a sentence each while someone is in there: the 5 s is an
unexported `crypto/tls` detail rather than an API guarantee, and
`(*tls.Conn).Close` skips `close_notify` entirely when a Write is in flight — so
it is paid by idle/stalled connections, not by one mid-Write.

## #7054 — userspace-dp/nat64: widened frag key multiplies keys per shard while the shard digest stays coarse — live-association eviction is silent [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-29)

## Observation

`nat64_frag_shard_index` (`userspace-dp/src/nat64.rs:578-600`) hashes only
`(addr_family, src, dst, ident)`. `Nat64FragKey` since #5798 also carries
`protocol` and a 4-field `FragAuthority`, both deliberately excluded from the
shard digest (documented at `:565-577`).

Membership is decided by full-key equality inside the bucket, so the exclusion is
correct for CORRECTNESS — a cross-domain fragment lands in the same shard, finds
no equal key, and misses fail-closed. What it changes is CAPACITY pressure: one
`(family, src, dst, ident)` digest can now map to many distinct keys
(`protocol` x `authority`) competing for one `NAT64_FRAG_CAP_PER_SHARD = 64`
bucket, where pre-#5798 it mapped to exactly one.

## Eviction mechanism

`Nat64FragAssoc::install` (`nat64.rs:668-717`) on a full shard first prunes
expired entries, then `shard.remove(0)` — the oldest LIVE entry. A sender able to
install first-fragment associations that hash into a given shard can therefore
evict a live association belonging to another flow; its non-first fragments then
miss and are dropped fail-closed (`nat64_frag_dropped` /
`nat_frag_untranslated_dropped`).

## Pre-existing

This reproduces identically on `origin/master`: the shard digest there is the
same four fields, and an attacker varying `ident` lands ~1/16 of first fragments
in any chosen shard, so 64 live installs into one bucket was already reachable.
#5798 does not create the eviction path; it raises the number of distinct keys
that can occupy one bucket. Classified non-blocking on PR #6835 for that reason.

## Worth considering

- Mix `protocol` and `authority` into the shard digest and accept losing the
  single-shard co-location property the comment values, or
- keep the digest and bound per-`(src,dst,ident)`-digest occupancy so one
  datagram identity cannot monopolise a bucket, or
- at minimum count evictions of LIVE entries so the condition is observable
  (today an eviction is silent and shows up only as a downstream fragment drop).

## #7056 — userspace-dp/nat64: #5798 residuals — modular fragment_assoc/ component and the distinct cross-domain fail-closed counter [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-29)

## Context

#5798 (fragment-association hit is not ingress-domain scoped) is closed by
PR #6835, which implements the plan's Path A+: the ingress authority + upper-layer
protocol in `Nat64FragKey`, one SSOT resolver (`frag_ingress_authority`) for both
install and consult, and the interface input filter + PBR discard re-run on the
association-HIT arm.

Two of #5798's six "Required fix" items were explicitly held out of that PR and
are tracked here so they are not lost.

## 1. Required-fix #1 — modular `fragment_assoc/` component (Path C)

> Put the association in a modular `fragment_assoc/` component shared by NAT64
> and ordinary NAT only after the relevant designs converge.

Today the cache lives in `userspace-dp/src/nat64.rs` (key, entry, shards,
install/lookup) with the call-site helpers in
`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/poll_descriptor/frag_assoc.rs`, and it is shared by the
cross-family NAT64 arm and the same-family SNAT/DNAT/static-NAT/NPTv6 arm
(#5689) through a `decision.nat.nat64` discriminator on the cached value. The
#5689 miss-classifier and the Path C refactor were deferred as "a large refactor
that should not gate an open HIGH".

## 2. Required-fix #5 — distinct cross-domain fail-closed counter

> Ambiguous dual-direction or cross-domain matches fail closed and increment a
> distinct counter.

The fail-closed half is delivered (a cross-domain fragment builds a different key,
misses, and dies on the Pref64 gate or the #6122 discriminator). The DISTINCT
counter is not: a cross-domain miss is indistinguishable from a reorder, a TTL
straddle, a shard eviction or a config-generation bump — all of them land on
`nat64_frag_dropped` / `nat_frag_untranslated_dropped`. The plan classes this as
observability-only ("forwarding behavior is identical either way"); it needs a
Rust counter plus Go `protocol_binding.go` plumbing.

Because the shard digest deliberately keeps same-datagram candidates co-located
(`nat64.rs:565-577`), a cross-domain probe is a single-shard scan — the counter is
cheap to add where it is.

## #7057 — docs/comments: the #5831 repair-floor premise cites a daemon_run.go loop that no longer exists [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-29)

## What

The #5831 repair-floor design (PR #6838) rests on one load-bearing premise: **the
console `root` operator can be bound to a custom `system login class`**, so a
view-only collapse would strand the box. The premise is stated in three places by
quoting code that no longer exists:

- `pkg/config/compiler_login_deny.go:223-226`
- `pkg/config/login_class_deny_5831_test.go:301`
- `pkg/cli/permissions_login_deny_fold_5831_test.go:23`
- (and the PR #6838 body)

all say:

> `pkg/daemon/daemon_run.go` assigns the CONFIGURED class to any OS user whose name
> matches a `system login user` (`if u.Name == osUser { shell.SetUserClass(u.Class) }`)

That inline loop is gone. It survives only as a *historical* quote in
`pkg/daemon/cli_rbac.go:26`. The live mechanism is:

`pkg/daemon/daemon_run.go:742` → `applyCLILoginClass` (`pkg/daemon/cli_rbac.go:85`)
→ `cli.ResolveLoginClass` (`pkg/cli/identity.go:127`) → `configuredClass`
(`pkg/cli/identity.go:230`)

which is **not** a bare `u.Name == osUser` equality: it walks `candidateNames(id)`
(passwd aliases included) and returns the **first** user block carrying a
*non-empty* class; a root that is listed with **no** class takes
`ClassRootDefault` ("super-user") rather than an empty class.

`pkg/daemon/cli_rbac.go` was already present at PR #6838's merge-base
(`edefb7570`), so the citation was stale when written — it is not merge rot.

The same staleness appears for the reader side: `docs/system-login.md:483` still
says "`pkg/cli/permissions.go` `resolveClassPerms` walks the class list and
returns the first entry whose name matches". Since #5561 the walk lives in
`config.ResolveClassPermissions` (`pkg/config/login_perms.go:29`) and
`resolveClassPerms` is a store-bound adapter. PR #6838's round-4 sweep retargeted
this citation in the code it touched but not at `docs/system-login.md:483`,
`:558`, `:582`, `:208`, `:234`, `:358`.

## What

```
thread 'afxdp::types::shared_cos_lease::tests::v8_release_unused_v8_concurrent_preserves_ledger_invariant'
  panicked at src/afxdp/types/shared_cos_lease/shared_cos_lease_tests.rs:2395:5:
assertion `left == right` failed: no tag-checked-rollback exhaustion expected under this contention
  left: 1
 right: 0

test result: FAILED. 4337 passed; 1 failed; 2 ignored
```

Hit once during a full `cargo test -- --test-threads=1` run while several other
build/test jobs were saturating the machine.

## Why this is the #7001 class, not a defect

Same file and same shape as #7001 (`v8_epoch_seqlock_snapshot_never_tears_tag_grace`),
but a **different test and a different assertion**, so it is filed separately for
the same reason #7001 was split out of the closed #6657 rather than reopening it.

The assertion is **calibrated to a contention level**, not to a correctness
invariant: it asserts that *zero* tag-checked-rollback exhaustions occur "under
this contention". One occurred. Rollback exhaustion is a legitimate fallback, so
observing one on a loaded box is the harness's premise failing, not the ledger
invariant failing — the ledger invariant itself did not fire.

   `1 passed`, three consecutive runs.
3. **No plausible coupling.** #6815's production diff is confined to
   `userspace-dp/src/nat/{source,allocator,status,mod}.rs`; nothing in
   `shared_cos_lease`.

Follow-up from the #6858 hostile round-3 pass on PR #6858 (`show class-of-service rewrite-rule`, closes #6848). Filed rather than folded: the command answers from CONFIG, and closing this gap needs state the config alone does not carry.

## What is wrong

`cosRewriteRuleEnforcement` (`pkg/dataplane/userspace/format/cos_show.go`) answers `Enforced: yes` for a `dscp` rewrite rule as soon as a CONFIGURED logical interface unit binds it. #6858 round 3 made that predicate mirror `buildInterfaceSnapshots`, so a binding on an interface/unit that does not exist now reports `not bound`.

What it still cannot see is the helper's own admission gate. `build_cos_iface_config` (`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/forwarding_build/cos.rs`) computes:

```rust
let dscp_rewrite_targets_iface_class = dscp_rewrite_rule
    .map(|r| r.dscp_by_fc_lp.keys().any(|(fc, _lp)| iface_classes.contains(&fc.as_str())))
    .unwrap_or(false);
let contributes_usable_cos_state = iface.cos_shaping_rate_bytes_per_sec > 0
    || scheduler_map_resolved_to_queues
    || dscp_classifier_targets_iface_queue
    || ieee8021_classifier_targets_iface_queue
    || dscp_rewrite_targets_iface_class;
if !contributes_usable_cos_state { return Ok(None); }
```

and then builds the rewrite matrix only over the queues the interface materializes:

```rust
for queue in &cfg.queues {
    for lp in 0..COS_LOSS_PRIORITY_LEVELS {
        if let Some(&dscp) = rule.dscp_by_fc_lp.get(&(queue.forwarding_class.clone(), lp)) { ... }
    }
}
```

So a rule whose forwarding-classes do not intersect the interface's materialized classes rewrites nothing, while the command says `Enforced: yes`.

## #7064 — config: a `class-of-service interfaces <if>` stanza for an interface that is not configured commits with no warning [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-21)

Found during the #6858 hostile round-3 pass on PR #6858. Filed rather than folded: pre-existing on `origin/master` and not introduced by that PR.

## What is wrong

This commits clean — no error, no warning:

```
set class-of-service forwarding-classes queue 0 best-effort
set class-of-service rewrite-rules dscp rw-dscp forwarding-class best-effort loss-priority low code-point be
set class-of-service interfaces ge-9-9-9 unit 0 rewrite-rules dscp rw-dscp
```

There is no `interfaces ge-9-9-9` stanza anywhere. Every CoS knob written under that stanza — shaping-rate, scheduler-map, classifiers, rewrite-rules, traffic-control-profile — is dead: `buildInterfaceSnapshots` (`pkg/dataplane/userspace/interfaces.go`) walks `cfg.Interfaces.Interfaces` and reads `cfg.ClassOfService.Interfaces[name].Units[unitNum]` off each REAL logical unit, so a stanza with no counterpart there is never read.

The same holds for a UNIT mismatch: `class-of-service interfaces ge-0-0-1 unit 0 ...` while `interfaces ge-0-0-1` declares only `unit 100`.

## Why it matters

The `class-of-service interfaces ...` unit loop in `validateClassOfServiceWarnings` (`pkg/config/compiler_validate_warn.go`, ~:1600-1665) already warns about every dangling reference INSIDE the stanza — undefined scheduler-map, undefined output-traffic-control-profile, undefined dscp/ieee-802.1 classifier, undefined dscp/ieee-802.1 rewrite-rule. It does not warn about the stanza's own subject not existing, which silently voids all of them at once. A single typo in an interface name silently disables an entire interface's CoS.

`applyCoSInterfaceLevelBindings` (`pkg/config/compiler_class_of_service.go:798`) already documents the consequence for the interface-level form — "An interface with an interface-level binding but no configured logical unit contributes no unit here" — so the condition is known; it is just not surfaced to the operator.

## Suggested fix

Add a warning in the same loop, in the shape of its siblings:

```
class-of-service interfaces %s is not a configured interface; its class-of-service bindings have no effect
class-of-service interfaces %s unit %d is not a configured logical unit; its class-of-service bindings have no effect
```

WARN, not reject: peer-synced / older-binary configs must still load (#1960 no-brick).

## Downstream

#6858 round 3 made `show class-of-service rewrite-rule` report such a rule as `not bound` and name the dead reference, so the show command no longer lies about it. That is a display fix over the same condition; the commit-time warning is the one that catches it when the operator types it. See also #7063 and the phantom-interface display issue filed alongside this one.
