## #7065 — cos: `show class-of-service` renders a phantom interface for a CoS stanza whose interface is not configured [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-29)

Found during the #6858 hostile round-3 pass on PR #6858. Filed rather than folded: pre-existing since the #4228 Gap 7 CoS show work, reproduces identically on `origin/master`, and not touched by that PR.

## What is wrong

`configuredCoSInterfaceViews` (`pkg/dataplane/userspace/format/cos_sections.go:388`) builds the `show class-of-service` interface list by iterating `cfg.ClassOfService.Interfaces`:

```go
for ifName, iface := range cfg.ClassOfService.Interfaces {
    for unitNum, cosUnit := range iface.Units {
        logicalName := fmt.Sprintf("%s.%d", ifName, unitNum)
        ...
        var interfaceUnit *config.InterfaceUnit
        if cfg.Interfaces.Interfaces != nil {
            if intf := cfg.Interfaces.Interfaces[ifName]; intf != nil && intf.Units != nil {
                interfaceUnit = intf.Units[unitNum]
            }
        }
        views = append(views, cosInterfaceView{ ... interfaceUnit: interfaceUnit ... })
    }
}
```

`interfaceUnit == nil` is carried into the view but never used to qualify the row. An interface that exists ONLY as a `class-of-service interfaces` stanza — no `interfaces` stanza at all, which commits clean (see the sibling issue on the missing commit warning) — renders as a fully-fledged `Interface: ge-9-9-9.0` block with its configured shaping rate, scheduler-map and classifier bindings, indistinguishable from a real interface whose CoS is live.

The dataplane never sees any of it: `buildInterfaceSnapshots` (`pkg/dataplane/userspace/interfaces.go`) walks `cfg.Interfaces.Interfaces`, so a CoS stanza with no counterpart there contributes nothing to the snapshot.

## Repro

```
set class-of-service forwarding-classes queue 0 best-effort
set class-of-service schedulers be transmit-rate 15m
set class-of-service scheduler-maps sm forwarding-class best-effort scheduler be
set class-of-service interfaces ge-9-9-9 unit 0 scheduler-map sm
set class-of-service interfaces ge-9-9-9 unit 0 shaping-rate 100m
```

then `show class-of-service`. The block renders; no configured interface named `ge-9-9-9` exists.

## #7071 — daemon: setActiveTransportIfCurrent's drop signal is discarded at the call site while both sibling publishers gate on theirs [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-29)

Follow-up from the hostile review of PR #6869 (#6290). **Not a runtime defect** — no behaviour is worse than master, which had no gate at all. Filed rather than folded per the current campaign policy.

`setActiveTransportIfCurrent` was modelled on the #4958 publishers, and both of those gate control flow on the returned bool:

```go
if !d.publishSessionSyncIfCurrent(gen, ss) { ... }
if !d.publishFabricRefreshChansIfCurrent(gen, ch0, ch1) { ... }
```

The new one does not. `pkg/daemon/daemon_ha_sync.go:706`:

```go
commsCtx, commsGen := d.beginClusterCommsEpoch(ctx)
d.setActiveTransportIfCurrent(commsGen, clusterTransportFromConfig(cfg))
```

A `false` return means the epoch this `startClusterComms` invocation is bringing up has already been superseded — yet the function then goes on to resolve the VRF device, wire the heartbeat and launch the session-sync constructor for that dead epoch. The later publishes are themselves epoch-gated and will drop, so nothing incorrect is installed, but the work is known-wasted at the point the bool is discarded.

Why this is not a blocker: on master the write was unconditional, so the same invocation ran the same way with no signal available at all. The gate is a strict improvement; only the unused signal is new.

Worth deciding deliberately: either return early on a drop (matching the siblings) or add a comment at `:706` saying the drop is intentionally advisory, so the divergence from the two functions it mirrors is not read as an oversight.

## #7072 — daemon: stopClusterComms leaves activeClusterTransport naming a torn-down transport [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-29)

Observed while reviewing PR #6869 (#6290). **Pre-existing on master, not introduced by #6869**, and unreachable today. Filed for the record per the current campaign policy.

`stopClusterComms` (`pkg/daemon/daemon_ha_sync.go`) bumps the epoch and clears `clusterCommsCancel`, `clusterCommsCtx`, `sessionSync`, `fabricRefreshCh`, `fabricRefreshCh1` — but not `activeClusterTransport`. After a teardown the field still names the transport of the epoch that was just torn down, so `activeTransport()` reports a live-looking key for comms that are stopped.

Why it is unreachable today: the only `stopClusterComms` call site is `pkg/daemon/daemon_apply_tail.go:258`, which is immediately followed on the same goroutine by `d.startClusterComms(d.daemonCtx)` at `:259`, and that always republishes. There is no stop-without-start path, so no reader ever observes the stale value.

It becomes reachable the moment anyone adds a stop-only path — a shutdown sequence, a "cluster disable" commit, an error path that tears comms down and returns. Step 20 would then compare the next commit against a dead baseline and skip a restart it should perform.

Fix direction: clear the field inside the same `clusterCommsMu` section that nils `sessionSync` and the fabric channels, so the whole epoch tuple is torn down together.

Note this is the one asymmetry left in the #6290 fold: the field now joins the epoch on the publish side but not on the teardown side.

## #7077 — userspace-dp/nptv6: parse_prefix accepts a '+'-prefixed mask length that no Go parser does — tighten the Rust grammar (Go side now works around it) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-29)

Found while driving PR #6894 (#4960 validate-before-mutate pre-pass). Measured
firsthand at PR head `6eb35c749`; not folded into that PR because the correct
fix is on the Rust side and would make a Go-only PR owe a cluster smoke.

## The divergence

The two planes parse an NPTv6 prefix with different grammars for the mask
token:

| plane | parser | `"2001:db8::/+48"` |
|---|---|---|
| Go `pkg/dataplane.compileNPTv6` / `pkg/config.validateNPTv6Strict` | `net.ParseCIDR` (mask via `dtoi`, digits only) | **error** |
| Rust `userspace-dp/src/nptv6.rs::parse_prefix` | `parts[1].parse::<u8>()` (Rust `u8::from_str` accepts a leading `+`) | **accepts, prefix_len = 48** |

Differential over 21 candidate strings (leading `+`/`-`/whitespace/tab, leading
zeros, `_` separators, non-ASCII digits, embedded IPv4, host bits set,
non-48/64 lengths): **exactly one disagreement**, the `+`-prefixed mask.
Everything else agrees, and there is **no** case where Go accepts and Rust
rejects — so the pre-pass is not more permissive than the backend here.

Reproduce the Rust half standalone (`parse_prefix` is private, so this is a
verbatim copy of its body):

```rust
use std::net::Ipv6Addr;
fn parse_prefix(s: &str) -> Option<([u16;4], usize)> {
    let parts: Vec<&str> = s.split('/').collect();
    if parts.len() != 2 { return None; }
    let prefix_len: u8 = parts[1].parse().ok()?;
    let prefix_words = match prefix_len { 48 => 3, 64 => 4, _ => return None };
    let addr: Ipv6Addr = parts[0].parse().ok()?;
    let seg = addr.segments();
    if seg[prefix_words..8].iter().any(|&w| w != 0) { return None; }
    let mut p = [0u16;4]; for i in 0..prefix_words { p[i] = seg[i]; }
    Some((p, prefix_words))
}
fn main() { println!("{:?}", parse_prefix("2001:db8::/+48").is_some()); } // true
```

Go: `net.ParseCIDR("2001:db8::/+48")` -> `invalid CIDR address`.

   `CompileConfig`.

Only after all three does it reach
`CompileConfig(compilerDP, cfg, m.lastCompile != nil)`, which is where the
#4960 pre-pass lives.

So an apply rejected by the pre-pass — the case #6894 adds — still leaves the
host with its XDP link pins, legacy TC link pins and legacy-only map pins

bpffs pin does **not** detach the running XDP program. A rejected apply
therefore does not take forwarding down on the spot.

## What

`collectCoSINetPrecedenceCodePoints`
(`pkg/config/compiler_class_of_service.go`) accepts DECIMAL 0..7 only. Junos
spells `classifiers inet-precedence` code-points as 3-bit BINARY (`000` ..
`111`) or as an IP-precedence alias (`net-control`, `internet-control`,
`critical-ecp`, `flash-override`, `flash`, `immediate`, `priority`).

Measured against the branch head:

| written | result |
|---|---|
| `code-points 5` | accepted, precedence 5 |
| `code-points 000` | accepted, precedence 0 (`Atoi("000")`) |
| `code-points 001` | accepted, precedence 1 |
| `code-points 010` | REJECTED: `code-point 10 is out of range (must be 0..7)` |
| `code-points 101` | REJECTED: `code-point 101 is out of range (must be 0..7)` |
| `code-points net-control` | REJECTED: `code-point "net-control" is not a valid 0..7 value` |

So a vSRX config imported verbatim fails at the classifier line for every
precedence above 1.

## Not a silent-misclassification risk

Worth stating explicitly, because it is the failure mode that would make this
urgent and it does not occur: no 3-bit binary string aliases onto a DIFFERENT
valid decimal in 0..7. `000`/`001` happen to parse to the value they denote;
`010` and up all land outside 0..7 and are rejected loudly. There is no input
that quietly selects the wrong traffic class.

The sibling `collectCoS8021CodePoints` is decimal-only for the same reason

## #7088 — test: cold_path_hist snapshot_under_concurrent_writer_never_tears is load-sensitive and reds under a busy machine [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-28)

Environment/test-harness flake, observed while validating PR #6877. Not a
product defect and unrelated to that PR's diff (it touches no
`cold_path_hist` file).

## Observed

`cargo test --manifest-path userspace-dp/Cargo.toml -- --test-threads=1` on a
machine running several other agents' cargo/codex builds:

```
---- afxdp::cold_path_hist::tests::snapshot_under_concurrent_writer_never_tears stdout ----
thread '...' panicked at src/afxdp/cold_path_hist_tests.rs:824:5:
only 61/1000 snapshots coherent — retry budget may be too low
test result: FAILED. 4346 passed; 1 failed; 2 ignored
```

Re-run of the same test in isolation on the same tree: **3/3 pass**. The
durations are the tell — 51.36s, 24.32s, 85.77s for the identical single test,
a 3.5x spread driven purely by machine load.

The test asserts a COHERENT-SNAPSHOT COUNT (`>= N of 1000`) against a
seqlock-style reader that retries on an odd generation. That count is a
function of how often the reader is descheduled mid-read, which is a property
of the machine, not of the code under test. Under CPU starvation the writer
advances between the reader's two generation reads far more often, and the
retry budget runs out.

## Suggested shape of a fix

Assert the INVARIANT rather than a rate: every snapshot that is returned must
be internally coherent (never torn), and `snapshot()` returning `None` after
exhausting its retry budget is a legitimate outcome, not a failure. If a
throughput floor is genuinely wanted, it belongs behind an ignored/`--nocapture`
bench-style gate, or should loop the writer until the reader signals done and
report a rate instead of asserting a fixed count against a fixed iteration
budget.

Same family as the CoS-lease contention assertion (#7062).

## #7092 — userspace-dp: a dead or retired worker's NAT holder bit is never cleared, stranding the pool port permanently [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-30)

**Severity: Medium — a NEW under-release (leak) vector introduced by the #6211 F2 holder mask in PR #6981.**

Since #6211 F2 (`userspace-dp/src/nat/allocator.rs`), a source-NAT / NAT64 reservation carries a `LiveAllocation.holders: u128` bitmask, one bit per `worker_id`, and `drop_holder_locked` frees the port only when clearing this holder's bit empties the mask:

```rust
fn drop_holder_locked(live, flow, existing, holder) -> bool {
    if existing.holders == 0 { return false; }          // untracked -> free
    let remaining = existing.holders & !holder.bit();
    if remaining == 0 { return false; }                 // last holder -> free
    live.live_by_flow.get_mut(flow).map(|s| s.holders = remaining);
    true                                                // survive
}
```

A bit is set only in `handle_upsert_synced` (`afxdp/session_glue/commands/upsert_synced.rs`), and cleared only when that same worker later runs a release. **If a worker that holds a bit never runs its release, the port is stranded for the life of the allocator.**

That is reachable:

1. **Worker panic.** `spawn_supervised_worker` (`afxdp/coordinator/supervisor.rs`) catches the unwind, writes `panic_slot`, and sets `runtime_atomics.dead = true`. The only consumer of `.dead` is `coordinator/status.rs` — the worker is *reported* dead, not respawned. Its `SessionTable` dies with the thread, so it never reaps and never drops a bit. Every peer-synced reservation it held is stranded.
2. **Worker-count change.** `worker_id` is minted as `queue_id % workers` (`server/helpers/planning.rs:805`). A replan that shrinks the worker set retires ids that still have bits set in `live_by_flow`. The allocator itself survives the reload — `parse_source_nat_rules_with_previous` carries it forward — so nothing clears them.

**Differential vs master:** on master `release_flow` removed the record on the first tuple-matching release, so *any surviving worker's* reap reclaimed the port. With the mask, the dead worker's bit is permanent and no surviving worker can empty it.

**Consequence:** the pool addresses' occupancy bitmap never gets those ports back. On a busy standby carrying thousands of synced sessions, one worker panic strands one port per synced pool-SNAT session, and SNAT for new flows eventually fails with `AllocatorExhausted`.

**Direction is deliberate**, and it is the safe one — PR #6981 argues explicitly that an under-release (a bounded, observable leak) is preferable to an over-release (a live worker's `(pool_addr, port)` handed to a new flow). Filing it because it is a real new failure mode with no reclaim path, and it is *not* bounded in the way the PR's wording implies ("an under-release leaks a bounded, observable pool port"): there is no sweep, no TTL, and no reconcile that clears a dead worker's holder bit.

**Suggested fix:** clear a retired worker's bit across the whole allocator when the coordinator observes `runtime_atomics.dead`, or when a replan retires a worker id — e.g. a `PortAllocator::retire_worker(worker_id)` that walks `live_by_flow`, ANDs out that bit, and frees any record whose mask empties. That is the same operation the last-holder release already performs, applied to a worker that will never call it.

**Found by:** first-pass hostile review of PR #6981 (drive-to-merge campaign), head `ff54471ca`.

## #7093 — userspace-dp: the "a local NAT allocation has a single holder by construction" premise is false — siblings OR their bits into it [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-29)

**Severity: Low — a false premise stated in three places, which is the reason #6522 stays open.**

PR #6981 (#6211 F2) states, in `userspace-dp/src/nat/allocator.rs` (the `LiveAllocation.holders` doc comment, the `NatHolder::Untracked` doc comment, and five `holders: 0` initialiser comments), in `docs/session-sync-architecture.md` ("Per-worker holder set (#6211 F2)"), and in the PR body:

> `holders == 0` — an untracked **local** allocation. RSS steers a 5-tuple to exactly one worker, so a local allocation has a single holder by construction; first release frees, bit-identical to today.

**Both halves are false for a locally-born pool-SNAT flow.**

A local allocation does not stay untracked, and it does not have a single holder:

1. The RSS owner allocates through `allocate_translation`, which stores `holders: 0`.
2. `replicate_session_upsert` (`afxdp/session_glue/mod.rs`) then fans the entry out over `peer_worker_commands`. That slice is built in `afxdp/coordinator/reconcile/bringup.rs` as
   ```rust
   worker_command_queues.iter().filter(|(id, _)| **id != worker_id)
   ```
   — **the owner is excluded.**
3. `synced_replica_entry` re-tags the replica via `worker_replica_origin()`, which maps a local origin to `SessionOrigin::WorkerLocalImport`. `WorkerLocalImport::is_peer_synced()` returns **true** (`session/entry.rs`).
4. So each sibling's `handle_upsert_synced` passes the `entry.origin.is_peer_synced() && !metadata.is_reverse` gate and calls `reserve_synced_source_nat_allocation_for_worker(..., worker_id)`, which reaches `reserve_flow`'s idempotent early return and ORs **that sibling's** bit into the owner's record.

The record therefore ends up with `holders == {siblings}` and **the owner's bit absent** — the opposite of "untracked, single holder". The runtime consequence (the last sibling's reap frees a port the owner is still forwarding through) is #6522 and is tracked there; this issue is about the claim, which is what will mislead the next reader of this code into believing the case cannot arise.

Two secondary consequences worth fixing in the same pass:

- **`local_allocation_still_frees_on_first_release_6211_f2`** (`nat/tests_pool.rs`) is described as the "over-reach guard — a local allocation must NOT become refcounted". It only holds because the fixture never lets a sibling reserve. It binds a strictly weaker property than its name and comment claim.
- `nat/allocator.rs`'s `drop_holder_locked` doc says the `holders == 0` arm is "the pre-#6211-F2 contract, bit-identical". True for the record's *initial* state only.

**Suggested fix:** state what is actually true — a record starts untracked and *acquires* holder bits from every sibling that imports a replica of it, and the owner is never among them — and either re-scope the "over-reach guard" test's name/comment or extend it to a fixture that includes a sibling reserve.

**Found by:** first-pass hostile review of PR #6981 (drive-to-merge campaign), head `ff54471ca`.

## #7095 — session sync: the #4983 ingress-interface identity is not carried to the HA peer, so after a failover every session degrades to the zone approximation [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-29)

Split out of PR #6928 (#4983). **Not a defect introduced by that PR** — it is the
half of #4983's own stated scope that PR deliberately does not implement, and
until now it had no issue number. The PR has been HELD as a draft since
2026-08-06 for exactly this decision, with the reasoning recorded only in a PR
comment, which is not a pointer anyone can follow.

## What is missing

#4983's scope reads: *"Record the true ingress interface per session in the
dataplane session metadata (userspace-dp), **sync it**, and surface it to the
CLI filter."* #6928 does the first and the third (console CLI only). It does
**not** sync it, by design:

`userspace-dp/src/server/helpers/session_sync.rs:237-249` sets both fields to 0
on every peer import, and no field is added to the cluster wire
(`pkg/cluster/sync_protocol.go` decodes field-by-field at fixed offsets and
never reads one; `userspace-dp/tests/fixtures/protocol_wire_v1.json` is
unchanged).

## Why the PR made that choice, and it is the right choice as scoped

An ifindex is **node-local**. Node 0's `ge-0-0-1` and node 1's `ge-7-0-1` are
different numbers for the same logical RETH member, so shipping the
originating node's value would render a confidently **wrong** interface name on
the importing node — strictly worse than approximating. Zero is the honest
answer, and the Go consumer falls back to the #4792 zone approximation.

## Why it still needs closing

Every peer-synced session lands in the absent-field branch, so **after a
failover the new master degrades to exactly the pre-#4983 zone approximation**
— the diagnostic stops working in the case where diagnostics matter most. On a
two-node cluster that is not an edge case; it is half the sessions on the box
at all times, and all of them immediately after an RG transition.

## The fix shape that was already identified

Carry a **cluster-stable** identity instead of a node-local one.
`docs/ha-cluster-userspace.conf` binds its zones to `reth0.50` / `reth0.80` /
`reth1` — byte-identical strings on both nodes — while only the members differ

## #7096 — session filter: a fabric-redirected session records the LOCAL fabric member as its ingress identity while its zone names the peer's real ingress — latent confident-wrong-name [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-29)

Found in the hostile pass over PR #6928 (#4983). **Latent, not live** — it does
not reproduce on any shipped configuration, so it is filed rather than folded.

## The mechanism

For a packet redirected from the HA peer across the fabric link, the two halves
of the session's ingress record come from **different** sources and deliberately
name different interfaces:

- the **zone** is overridden to the peer-encoded ORIGINAL ingress zone —
  `stage_classify_fabric_ingress` (`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/poll_stages.rs:391`)
  returns `ingress_zone_override`, and `zone_pair_ids_for_flow_with_override`
  (`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/forwarding/mod.rs:89`) prefers it. Correct: the flow
  logically arrived on the peer's WAN.
- the **#4983 ingress identity** is `meta.ingress_ifindex`, which the XDP shim
  sets from `ctx->ingress_ifindex` (`userspace-xdp/src/lib.rs:454`) and which
  **nothing in production ever rewrites** — verified by sweep: the only
  `meta.ingress_ifindex = ...` assignments in the tree are in `#[cfg(test)]`
  fixtures. So it is the LOCAL fabric member's netdev.

`sessionFilter.resolveIngressIfaces` (`pkg/cli/session_filter.go`) then looks up
`{that local ifindex, wire vlan}` in `ifaceNamesByKey`.

## Why it is inert today, and why that is fragile

`buildSessionEgressIfaces` (`pkg/cli/session_display.go:44`) only creates a key
for a config interface that has at least one **unit**. On the shipped wiring
(`docs/ha-cluster-userspace.conf`) the fabric member `ge-0/0/0` has no
`interfaces { ge-0/0/0 { ... } }` stanza at all — it appears only inside
`fab0 { fabric-options { member-interfaces { ge-0/0/0; } } }` — so the lookup
misses and the CLI falls back to the zone, exactly as before #4983.

The trigger is one config line. Add `set interfaces ge-0/0/0 unit 0 ...` and
every fabric-redirected session starts resolving to a **confident wrong
interface name**: `show security flow session interface ge-0/0/0` selects flows
that arrived on the peer's WAN, and `interface reth0.50` no longer selects them.
Being a `clear` filter too, that is a wrong-session deletion, in the same family
as #6975 and #6987 but reached from a different direction.

Note `fab0` itself is NOT the trigger: even with a unit on `fab0` the map key

## #7098 — flaky: cold_path_hist snapshot_under_concurrent_writer_never_tears fails its Sanity-4 coherent-snapshot calibration under machine load [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

**Severity: Low — a flaky calibration guard, not a real tearing regression. Same class as #7062.**

`afxdp::cold_path_hist::tests::snapshot_under_concurrent_writer_never_tears` (`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/cold_path_hist_tests.rs`) fails under machine load:

```
thread 'afxdp::cold_path_hist::tests::snapshot_under_concurrent_writer_never_tears' panicked at
  src/afxdp/cold_path_hist_tests.rs:824:5:
only 7/1000 snapshots coherent — retry budget may be too low
test result: FAILED. 4437 passed; 1 failed; 2 ignored
```

**The assertion that fired is Sanity-4, not the test's namesake property.** The no-tear property held for every coherent snapshot; what failed is the meta-guard immediately above it:

```rust
// Sanity-4: at least 10% of snapshots must have been coherent;
// if EVERY snapshot exhausted retries the test is meaningless.
assert!(
    coherent_snapshots >= 100,
    "only {coherent_snapshots}/1000 snapshots coherent — retry budget may be too low"
);
```

That is a precondition on how much of the seqlock reader loop got scheduled, so it is a direct function of CPU contention. On a box running several parallel build/test lanes the reader is descheduled inside the seqlock window often enough that 993/1000 reads exhaust their retry budget.

**Evidence it is load and not code:**

- The file is byte-identical to `origin/master` (`git diff origin/master HEAD -- userspace-dp/src/afxdp/cold_path_hist*` is empty).
- The same test passed in a full-suite run of the same branch ~30 minutes earlier on a quieter box (4407 passed, 0 failed).
- Re-running it alone immediately after the failure passes: `cargo test --manifest-path userspace-dp/Cargo.toml snapshot_under_concurrent_writer_never_tears -- --test-threads=1` → rc **0**.

**Suggested fix:** make Sanity-4 load-tolerant the way a contention-calibrated guard has to be — scale the required coherent count against observed `writer_iters` / elapsed wall time, or retry the sampling loop once before failing, or downgrade it to an `eprintln!` diagnostic so a starved scheduler does not red the suite while the property under test is still green.

**Found by:** first-pass hostile review of PR #6981 (drive-to-merge campaign).

## #7106 — io_uring teardown: optionally close the ceiling-during-teardown residual by retaining unproven buffers (#6168 follow-up) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-29)

Split out of #6168, which fixed the **docs-contract** half (the docstrings
claimed the ring-fd close was a synchronous kernel cancel+wait; it is not —
`io_uring_release` queues `io_ring_exit_work` asynchronously). #6168 recorded
the remaining residual as **ACCEPTED** rather than hardened. This issue keeps
the hardening option on the board so it is not lost when #6168 closes.

## The residual

`InflightRegistry::drain_for_teardown` is the synchronous proof: it blocks on
each target write's terminal CQE before freeing that write's buffer. If it
cannot prove an entry terminal — its `MAX_WAIT_RETRIES` ceiling of 4096
consecutive failed waits was hit, or the ring is fatally dead — the entry is
RETAINED, and is then freed when `InflightRegistry` drops.

`RingWriter`'s field order puts that registry drop after the ring fd close, so
the kernel's teardown is *started* first. But `close()` does not wait for
`io_ring_exit_work`, so a write already executing in io-wq can still be
dereferencing that buffer at the instant it is freed. Field order narrows the
window; it is not a barrier.

Reaching it requires a pathological ceiling-during-teardown storm, and even
then it is strictly better than pre-#5800 (which freed on EVERY retry ceiling
with no drain at all). That is why #6168 accepted it.

## The available hardening

Give `InflightRegistry` a `Drop` that **leaks** (`mem::forget`) any entry the
drain could not prove terminal, instead of freeing it. That makes the #5800
buffer-lifetime invariant hold unconditionally, with no dependence on kernel
teardown timing at all.

The trade: an unconditional bounded leak on a path that has already failed,
versus a narrow, hard-to-reach lifetime hazard. Weigh:

- how many entries can actually be live at teardown (`reap_ready` runs at the
  top of every write, so the steady-state answer is 0)
- whether a leak on the state-writer ring differs from the slow-path ring
- whether the leak should be counted/logged rather than silent

## #7109 — debian: #DEBHELPER# inside a prose comment splices the generated block mid-sentence — 'apt-get install ./xpf_*.deb' FAILS on every fresh install (exit 127) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-21)

## Impact first: fresh package installs are broken

`apt-get install ./xpf_*.deb` fails to configure the package on **any fresh
install** — which is the #1917 appliance install path:

```
/var/lib/dpkg/info/xpf.postinst: 148: starts: not found
dpkg: error processing package xpf (--configure): ... exit status 127
```

## Mechanism

`debian/xpf.postinst:48` contains the token inside a **prose comment**:

```sh
# Seed the versioned runtime layout BEFORE #DEBHELPER# starts
# the unit: copy staged/* -> versions/<v>/, set versions/current
```

debhelper substitutes **every** occurrence of `#DEBHELPER#`, not just the one on
its own line. So the generated `dh_installsystemd` block is spliced into the
middle of that sentence, inside the first-install branch — and the tail of the
comment line, a bare ` starts`, is left behind as a **top-level command**.

Confirmed at `origin/master`:

```
$ git grep -n '#DEBHELPER#' origin/master -- 'debian/*'
debian/xpf.postinst:48:   # Seed the versioned runtime layout BEFORE #DEBHELPER# starts   <-- prose
debian/xpf.postinst:286:  #DEBHELPER#                                                     <-- intended
debian/xpf.postrm:330:    #DEBHELPER#
debian/xpf.preinst:274:   #DEBHELPER#
```

Introduced by `723427b1e` *"#1964: seed versioned runtime from the postinst on
first install"* (2026-06-17). The author wanted to *reference* debhelper's
behaviour in a comment; the token cannot be mentioned, only used.

## #7120 — bake.py's pinned Ubuntu 26.04 base digest is stale after a Canonical respin — every make image aborts [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-21)

`scripts/image/bake.py`'s `PINNED_BASE_SHA256["26.04"]` no longer matches

before it customizes anything:

does NOT match the pinned digest 3ee4f67f322abb2d1d1f0fffc957f7411404ad6635dd35b026c8ff05ac6e534c

cause is the benign one the error message itself names: **Canonical respun

Automatic Signing Key `D2EB44626FDDC30B513D5BB71A5D6C4C7DB87C81`. Fetching
the release directory's `SHA256SUMS` + `SHA256SUMS.gpg` and verifying the
detached signature against that key:

$ gpg --verify SHA256SUMS.gpg SHA256SUMS
gpg: Signature made Tue 04 Aug 2026 01:46:14 PM PDT

## #7121 — config: routing-policy `from protocol` value domain is unvalidated at commit — an unknown token reaches FRR `match source-protocol` and degrades the whole managed reload [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-29)

## Summary

The routing-policy leaf `policy-options policy-statement <p> term <t> from protocol
<token>` has **no value-domain check at commit in any spelling**. Whatever the operator
types is compiled into `PolicyTerm.FromProtocols` and rendered verbatim (after
`sanitizeFRRValue`) as an FRR ` match source-protocol <token>` line by
`pkg/frr/policy_render.go`.

FRR rejects an unknown `source-protocol`, and per the note already in
`pkg/frr/redistribute.go` **one rejected line degrades the WHOLE managed reload**
(#1880/#2223). So a single typo in a routing policy — `from protocol ospv;` — is a
green commit that can take down the managed FRR section.

## Why the identically-named sibling leaf IS gated

`firewall filter ... term ... from protocol <token>` is checked: `filterProtocolResolvable`
(`pkg/config/compiler_validate_strict_filter.go`) resolves the token through the
centralized protocol SSOT and the strict gate rejects an unresolvable one — the #3723 M01
partial-list case is explicitly covered there. The routing-policy leaf shares the spelling
and has no equivalent.

## Sites

- Schema: `pkg/config/schema_routing.go` — `"protocol": {args: 1, multi: true, children: nil}`,
  no `validator`, no `valueType`.
- Read: `pkg/config/compiler_routing.go` `collectProtocolList`, single caller in
  `parsePolicyTermChildren`.
- Render: `pkg/config/../pkg/frr/policy_render.go` ` match source-protocol %s`, and
  `pkg/frr/redistribute.go` `resolveRedistribute` for the export path.

## Provenance and scope note

Split out of #6689 rather than bundled into it. #6689 fixed a *read* defect — the nested
block spelling `from { protocol { bgp; ospf; static; } }` compiled to `[bgp]` alone while
the other four spellings compiled all three. Per the
`docs/config-schema.md` "widening a multi-value READ requires widening its VALIDATOR in
the same change" rule (#6659), that fold was checked for a validator to widen and there
was none to widen — the gate is absent for **every** spelling, before and after. Widening
the read therefore made five spellings agree rather than opening a new path, and adding a
value domain is a new commit REJECTION rather than a bug fix, so it is filed here.

## #7126 — config: a compiler that reads Keys[0] of each child still drops a flat-set bracket list on any leaf setSchema does NOT mark multi (rib-groups import-rib, event-options events) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-21)

## The predicate

This is not two isolated value drops. It is one mechanical predicate, and it holds for
every leaf that satisfies both halves:

> A leaf declared `children: nil` and **NOT** `multi: true` in `setSchema`, read by a
> compiler that takes `Keys[0]` / `Name()` of each child, drops every value past the first
> when the operator authors a bracket list through the flat-set path (`set`, `load set`,
> the CLI).

Both readers below already obey the documented rule in `CLAUDE.md` and
`docs/config-schema.md` — *"a compiler reading a multi-value leaf MUST read
`child.Keys[1:]` AND `child.Children` and accumulate"*. They read **both** sides. They
still drop, because reading `Children` is not the same as reading **every key of** each
child.

### Why `multi: false` is the discriminator

`SetPath` files a bracket list differently depending on the flag:

| schema | `set ... <leaf> [ v1 v2 ]` becomes |
|---|---|
| `multi: true, children: nil` | `Keys=["<leaf>","v1","v2"]`, no children — the tail absorber runs |
| **`multi: false, children: nil`** | `Keys=["<leaf>"]` with **ONE child** `Keys=["v1","v2"]` |

In the second row every value sits on one child's Keys, so `child.Name()` (== `Keys[0]`)
returns `v1` and silently discards the rest. The hierarchical parser is unaffected — it
puts the list on the node's own tail — which is why these survive every brace-authored
test and only bite the flat-set path.

Measured AST, at `b954d9ab1`:

```
set routing-options rib-groups rg1 import-rib [ inet.0 inet.2 ]
  Keys=[routing-options] -> [rib-groups] -> [rg1] -> [import-rib]
    child Keys=[inet.0 inet.2]   children=0      <-- both values on ONE child
```

This is the same mechanism as #6694 (`fabric-options member-interfaces`), which was fixed
by giving that leaf a reader that descends the subtree and takes every key. These two

## #7132 — config: model per-value MODIFIER keywords in setSchema — the promotion half of the #2419 class is undecidable without it, and every affected leaf currently needs a hand-written option table [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-29)

## The proof this rests on

Measured at `f1662d119`:

```
routing-options { static { route 10.9.0.0/16 discard; } }
  -> [{"Destination":"10.9.0.0/16","NextHops":null,"Discard":true,"Reject":false,"Preference":5,...}]

routing-options { static { route [ 10.9.0.0/16 discard ]; } }
  -> [{"Destination":"10.9.0.0/16","NextHops":null,"Discard":true,"Reject":false,"Preference":5,...}]
```

**Byte-identical.** The lexer strips `[` and `]` before any consumer sees the tokens
(`lexer.go` just advances and recurses), so *"the operator wrote a per-value modifier"* and
*"the operator wrote a two-element list"* arrive as the **same token stream**. There is no
observable in the AST, in the compiled config, or anywhere downstream that separates them.

This is not "we need a better heuristic". It closes a question: **no detector — lint,
differential, or otherwise — can decide the promotion direction of the #2419 class.** Only
knowledge of the individual leaf's Junos grammar can, and that knowledge exists in this
codebase in exactly one place today: hand-written tables.

## Why this matters now

The #2419 multi-value-leaf class has two directions:

| direction | defect | decidable? | status |
|---|---|---|---|
| **DROP** — the reader misses an authored value | a list compiles short, or to nothing | yes, behaviourally | **gated** by #7128 (`TestSchemaSpellingDifferentialGate`, merged `f1662d119`) |
| **PROMOTION** — the reader swallows a token that is not a value | a modifier keyword compiles as a value | **no**, per the proof above | unaddressed, and unaddressable as things stand |

#7128 closed the decidable half and says so in its own header. This issue is about the other
half. #7126 records the predicate for a related drop sub-class and is separate.

## The measurement that shows the remedy works

Sweeping `setSchema` at `f1662d119` for nodes that have **both** a value slot (`args >= 1`,
no `midKeyword`) **and** modeled childless modifier children:

## #7139 — userspace helper: resolve socket paths through a trusted directory, not by path string (#5839 residual) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-29)

Follow-up to #5839, which hardened the stale-socket unlink itself
(`removeStaleUnixSocket`, `pkg/dataplane/userspace/stale_socket.go`): it now
refuses a non-socket, refuses a socket a live listener holds, and never
discards an unlink failure. Two residuals from #5839's "Fix direction" were
deliberately NOT attempted there, because both are a redesign rather than a
bounded fix.

## 1. The liveness probe is path-STRING based

`unixSocketPathActive` compares the configured path string against the path
column of `/proc/net/unix`. A live socket reached through a DIFFERENT SPELLING
of the same file is therefore not recognised as active:

- a symlinked parent directory (`/run/xpf` -> `/var/run/xpf`) — the kernel table
  lists the path the listener bound, which need not be the spelling xpf holds;
- any non-canonical spelling of the same file.

In that case the socket passes the liveness check as "stale" and is unlinked
while its listener is alive. #5839 closed the common case (the typed
`control-socket` leaf now rejects `.`/`..` components at strict commit, so the
hand-written traversal spelling cannot be committed), but a symlinked parent
still aliases, and the tolerant load path accepts a stale value that never
passed a strict commit.

## 2. There is no TOCTOU-safe trusted directory

Validation and the unlink are separate syscalls on a path, so the target or its
parent can be swapped in between. #5839's fix direction asks for the unlink to
be performed relative to an opened trusted directory (`openat2` with
`RESOLVE_BENEATH`/`RESOLVE_NO_SYMLINKS`), with the runtime root pinned or
allowlisted, rather than validated as a string.

## What is required

- Open the runtime directory once and operate on it with `unlinkat`/`openat2`
  under `RESOLVE_BENEATH`, so neither the parent nor the target can be
  re-pointed between the check and the unlink.
- Key the liveness decision on something stronger than the path string — e.g.
  compare the socket inode from `Lstat` against the inode column in
  `/proc/net/unix` rather than the path column.

## #7147 — HA peer fencing: no fence acknowledgement exists on the wire, so takeover cannot be gated on one [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-29)

Split out of #72 proposal item 3 ("Optionally gate full active ownership until
fence acknowledged (policy-dependent)"). #72's mechanism and observability are
done; this is the remaining, unbounded piece.

## What is actually there today

At `a77d5568c`:

- `Manager.handlePeerTimeout` (`pkg/cluster/heartbeat_manager.go`) marks the
  peer lost, clears ManualFailover on every RG, calls `m.electSingleNode()`,
  and only THEN attempts the fence when `peerFencing == "disable-rg"`.
- The fence itself is `SessionSync.SendFence` (`pkg/cluster/sync_failover.go`):
  it takes `writeMu`, does one `writeMsg(conn, syncMsgFence, nil)`, bumps
  `FencesSent`, and returns.

## Why this is not a reordering fix

There is **no fence-ack message on the wire**. `SendFence` returns nil as soon
as the write reaches the socket; the peer's receive path
(`pkg/cluster/sync_conn_read.go`, `syncMsgFence` -> `OnFenceReceived` ->
`d.fenceAllRedundancyGroups`) sends nothing back. So:

- A successful `SendFence` does NOT mean the peer disabled its redundancy
  groups. Gating takeover on it would gate on a socket write, not on the
  property that matters.
- A failed `SendFence` means the sync channel is down — which is the common
  case when the peer is genuinely dead, i.e. exactly the split-brain scenario
  fencing exists for. Gating takeover on send success would convert a dead
  peer into a total outage.

Implementing "gate ownership until fence acknowledged" therefore requires a new
`syncMsgFenceAck` message, an HA protocol version bump, both-node compatibility
handling for a mixed-version cluster, and a bounded timeout policy for what to
do when the ack never arrives (which must not be "never take over"). That is a
protocol change, not an ordering change, and it owes a cluster smoke.

Note the `LastFenceSeq` / `LastFenceAckAt` fields in `SyncStats` are the
**bulk-sync install barrier** (`pkg/cluster/sync_bulk.go`), an unrelated
mechanism — they are not a peer-fence acknowledgement and cannot be reused as
one.

## #7153 — session filter: the CLI interface-name map keys a unit under its NUMBER while the session row carries the WIRE VID — an untagged unit N>0 never resolves [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-29)

Found while determining whether **#4983**'s own scope is fully carried by its
tracked remainders (#7095, #6960, #6975, #6965, #6987, #7096, #7097). This one
is covered by none of them.

## The divergence

`pkg/cli/session_display.go` builds the `{ifindex, vlanID} -> interface name`
map that BOTH the `If:`/`Out:` display columns and the #4983 ingress filter
resolve through (`buildSessionEgressIfacesWithLookup`, keyed by
`sessionDisplayVLANID`):

```go
func sessionDisplayVLANID(unit *config.InterfaceUnit) uint16 {
	if unit.VlanID > 0 { return uint16(unit.VlanID) }
	if unit.Number > 0 { return uint16(unit.Number) }   // <-- the fallback
	return 0
}
```

The session row, by contrast, carries the VID **observed on the wire**
(`SessionValue.IngressVlanID`, stamped by the helper from the frame).

`pkg/config/compiler_interfaces.go` populates `unit.VlanID` **only** from an
explicit `vlan-id` statement. So the two keys agree in the common cases and

## #7156 — userspace-dp neighbor: pending_neigh sweep is O(all-keys) per poll — replace with a bounded deadline queue (#1771 remainder) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-29)

Split out of #1359's sibling track — this is the **only live remainder** of #1771 (#1769 §10a), which is closed against this issue.

## Defect (verified at `origin/master` `9710cfd13`)

`retry_pending_neigh` sweeps **every** unresolved-neighbour key on **every binding poll**, allocating a fresh `Vec` each time, with no budget, no cursor, and no deadline ordering.

`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/neighbor_dispatch.rs:204` (function spans `:156-414`):

```rust
let keys: Vec<(i32, IpAddr)> = binding.pending_neigh.keys().copied().collect();
for key in keys { ... }                                    // :205
```

- The **only** bound is the empty-map early-out at `:175-177` (`if binding.pending_neigh.is_empty() { return; }`).
- Grep of the whole file for `timer.wheel|deadline|budget|cursor|BinaryHeap|BTreeMap<u64` → **zero hits**. `pending_neigh` is an unordered `FastMap<(i32, IpAddr), PendingNeighPacket>` (`worker/mod.rs:152-153`), so no deadline ordering exists even in principle; timeouts are found by a per-key `now_ns.saturating_sub(queued_ns)` comparison *inside* the loop.
- Cap: `MAX_PENDING_NEIGH = 4096` — `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/mod.rs:466`. Worst case is 4096 keys × (2 map lookups + a `probe_due` evaluation) per sweep.
- Called **twice per poll iteration** — `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/worker/lifecycle.rs:148` (inside the RX-empty `if available == 0 {` branch at `:141`, comment: *"Check pending neighbor buffer even when RX is empty"*) and `:317` (post-batch).

So an idle binding holding 4096 stale next-hops burns the full sweep on every idle spin. An attacker who can fill the distinct-hop cap consumes a worker core on control bookkeeping even after the packets are already being dropped and negatively cached, degrading unrelated forwarding.

## Required completion

Replace the full-map poll with deadline-driven bounded work:

- an intrusive deadline queue / timer wheel / min-heap keyed by the existing `(ifindex, next_hop)` map key;
- a strict per-poll budget with a cursor/debt carried across polls;
- no per-poll allocation;
- preserve one representative packet per key, oldest-packet semantics, timeout accuracy, the probe schedule, the negative-cache transition, and descriptor recycling;
- a just-resolved key must be woken promptly by resolver/monitor notification, not queued behind thousands of future deadlines;
- backlog / deadline-lag / budget-exhaustion telemetry;
- the auxiliary structure must stay consistent with the authoritative map under replace/remove/timeout and must not admit attacker-driven unbounded tombstones.

## RED acceptance (all constructible without a cluster except the last)

1. 4096 unresolved keys with **no due deadline** ⇒ O(budget) work and **zero allocation** per poll.
2. Due keys beyond the first budget make bounded forward progress without starvation.
3. A just-resolved tail key is dispatched promptly.
4. Timeout/probe ordering correct across wraparound and same-deadline keys.
5. Removal and duplicate replacement leave no stale deadline entry and no double recycle.
6. Criterion/load leg: bounded poll latency while forwarding unrelated packets.

## #7158 — WireGuard: peer endpoint must be an IP literal — a DDNS hostname is a hard commit reject, so the dynamic-WAN topology is unauthorable (#1703 remainder) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-29)

Split out of #1703 (Ubiquiti WireGuard interop), which is closed against this issue. #1703's remaining engineering work is this one gap; the rest of it was vendor-hardware verification with no hardware.

## Defect (verified at `origin/master` `9710cfd13`)

A WireGuard peer `endpoint` must be an **IP literal**. A DDNS hostname is a **hard reject at commit**, so the documented UniFi One-Click topology — which is the whole point of the interop track — is unauthorable, hardware or not.

`pkg/config/compiler_validate_wireguard.go:283-286` (`endpointIsV6`):

```go
ip := net.ParseIP(host)
if ip == nil {
    return false, fmt.Errorf("host %q is not an IP literal (a WireGuard endpoint must be a numeric address, not a hostname; the dataplane does not resolve DNS)", host)
}
```

Commit error produced for `endpoint unifi.example.ui.com:51820`:

```
wireguard wg0: peer "b2b2...": has an invalid endpoint "unifi.example.ui.com:51820":
  host "unifi.example.ui.com" is not an IP literal (a WireGuard endpoint must be a
  numeric address, not a hostname; the dataplane does not resolve DNS)
```

## Why this matters

#1703's own grounding from UniFi Network 10.4 screenshots states the requirement: *"WAN IP is dynamic → UniFi pushes DDNS / 'Alternate Address' hostname, so xpf's peer endpoint must support hostname + periodic re-resolution (roaming), not just a static IP."* Any lab slot booked against real Ubiquiti hardware is wasted on a static-IP-only subset until this is built. This is also the generic NAT-traversal / dynamic-WAN case, not a vendor quirk — it applies to every WG peer behind a dynamic address.

## Constraint that must be preserved

The reject is **deliberate**, tightened by #5182 to uphold: *every endpoint the strict commit ACCEPTS hydrates to a real `SocketAddr` and can therefore INITIATE.* The Rust hydrate is `wg_endpoint.parse::<SocketAddr>()` — it does **not** resolve DNS and rejects a missing/zero port. So this is **not** a validator relaxation. It needs:

- a resolver in the WG control thread that keeps the peer's `SocketAddr` fresh (periodic re-resolve on a bounded schedule, with the last-good address retained across a failed lookup);
- the hydrate invariant restated in terms of "resolves to a `SocketAddr` at the time of use" rather than "is a literal at commit";
- interaction with the already-shipped authenticated-datagram endpoint roaming (`coordinator/wg_control/dispatch.rs`) — a re-resolve must not fight a learned roam, and the precedence rule must be explicit;
- family classification: `endpointIsV6`'s bool return feeds the one-UDP-socket mixed-family gate, so a hostname that resolves to both families needs a defined rule;
- commit-time behaviour for a hostname that does not resolve at commit (accept-and-retry vs reject) — pick one and state it.

## Acceptance

1. A peer endpoint authored as `host:port` with a DNS hostname **commits clean**.

## What is being measured

Under the reduced 100E100M matrix, strict-exact CoS passes the p99.9 mouse-latency gate while surplus-sharing fails it by 4.4-6.5x. That dichotomy was last reproduced on `loss:xpf-userspace-fw0/fw1` at build `g00346ec1a` (2026-06-10), recorded in `docs/pr/1829-p2/evidence.md` with two Codex KILL-SOUND reviews and a Claude hostile SMR:

|---|---|---|---|---|
| surplus-loaded | 58 205 us | 1.27 Gb/s | **0.00 ms** | q2 **0.01 ms**, q0 0.00 ms |
| surplus-loaded | 56 112 us | 1.26 Gb/s | 0.00 ms | q2 0.01 ms |
| surplus-loaded | 38 989 us | 1.27 Gb/s | 0.00 ms | q2 0.01 ms |
| exact-loaded (pass control) | 9 530 us | 0.95 Gb/s | 0.06 ms | q2 16.96 ms |

The load-bearing negative result: **queue residence is excluded by measurement.** The failing surplus cells show no queue residence at any granularity — surplus borrowing (1.27 G against a 1.0 G configuration) drains the queues *faster* than the offered load, and the correlation is inverted: standing queues correlate with **passing** probes, empty queues with **failing** ones. Siblings in the same window: T-6(b), T-6(a), #4265/R-2, #4253.

Both lineage issues that would otherwise own this are now closed (#1743, #1829), so this measurement has no other home.

## #7160 — Decide the #2387 posture: VRF-aware session key (HA wire bump) vs the shipped loud-warning status quo — cross-VRF session reuse is live under PBR then routing-instance [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-30)

Split out of #2387, which is closed against this issue. #2387 was a broad "session identity omits logical ingress" umbrella; its record and surface halves shipped (#6928) and its remaining sub-surfaces are filed individually (#7095, #6960, #6975, #6965, #6987). What is left is **one posture decision**, stated here so it can be answered without re-deriving 900 lines of thread.

This is a **maintainer risk-appetite call**, deliberately not made by an agent: the only complete fix bumps the HA protocol version, which makes a release non-rolling-upgradable.

## The defect, verified at `origin/master` `9710cfd13`

`userspace-dp/src/session/key.rs:10-17` is still the bare 5-tuple:

```rust
pub(crate) struct SessionKey {
    pub addr_family: u8,
    pub protocol: u8,
    pub src_ip: IpAddr,
    pub dst_ip: IpAddr,
    pub src_port: u16,
    pub dst_port: u16,
}
```

No ingress ifindex, no VLAN unit, no zone, no routing-instance. Two flows in **different** routing-instances that share a 5-tuple collide in the conntrack map. The collision is **live** under PBR `then routing-instance`: the established-session fast path short-circuits before `ingress_route_table_override` (`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/poll_descriptor/mod.rs:1335`), so flow 2 in tenant-b inherits flow 1's cached egress / NAT / **policy** decision. Wrong-VRF forwarding and a policy bypass across tenants. Reachable, proven, unfixed.

## Interim mitigation — SHIPPED, so this is not silent

`pkg/config/compiler_validate_vrf_overlap.go` (Track A.1) raises a commit **warning** naming both routing-instances and the overlapping prefix, wired through `compiler_tailgates.go:98`, guarded by `compiler_validate_vrf_overlap_2387_test.go` (which also pins that the PBR-term `then routing-instance` source feeds the overlap set). The operator is told the topology is not session-isolated; the config still commits.

## The question

**Option A — hard-reject.** Refuse overlapping L3 across routing-instances at commit. No hot-path cost, no wire change, driveable to a merge as a rejection plus a migration note. **The code argues against it in its own comments** (`compiler_validate_vrf_overlap.go:48-56`): *"overlapping-subnet multi-tenant VRF via PBR is a legitimate, working forwarding design, so hard-rejecting it would break a valid deployment to work around a fast-path bug."* Overlapping address space across VRFs is the primary reason VRFs exist. A narrower variant — reject only the **combination** (overlapping L3 *and* PBR `then routing-instance`), leaving plain VRF overlap alone — is the defensible form of A, since that combination is the only one that is currently broken.

**Option B — widen the key.** Add a symmetric routing-domain `u32` to `SessionKey`. Preserves every working config and is the only complete fix. The discriminator is already available and cheap: `StableRoutingInstanceTableID(name)` (`pkg/config/routinginstanceid.go:48`) is a pure FNV-1a function of the instance **name**, backed by a strict commit-time collision gate at `:126` — config-derived, therefore identical on both HA nodes by construction.

## Why Option B is the reserved call

It bumps the HA wire, which trips two **exact-equality** gates:

- `parseHAProtocolCompatible` — `pkg/upgrade/cluster_cli.go:241`
- `HAProtocolVersionMismatch` — `pkg/cluster/peer_state.go:107`

plus the readiness path. Per `docs/in-place-upgrade.md:820-833`, a release that bumps `CurrentHAProtocolVersion` is **not rolling-upgradable** and the incompatibility is detected only on the second node. That is an upgrade-posture decision, not an engineering one.

## #7163 — cluster: session-sync proof carries no role/identity/transcript and derives an undirected frame key (vector B two-connection oracle) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-29)

Split out of #5078. **Vector A** of that issue (reflected / degenerate handshake
nonce) is closed by PR #7152; **vector B** is what remains, and it is a wire
flag-day, so it is filed on its own rather than left attached to a mostly-fixed
issue.

## The remaining defect

`syncAuthProof(key, challenge)` is `HMAC(key, tag ‖ challenge)`. It carries **no
initiator/responder role, no node or endpoint identity, and no transcript**, and
`syncDeriveFrameKey` (`pkg/cluster/sync_auth.go:228-240`) canonically SORTS the
two nonces, so the derived frame key is **undirected** — both directions use one
key and one counter space.

That leaves the **two-connection proof oracle**: an attacker with no PSK opens a
second keyed connection and relays a proof computed over connection α's local
nonce onto connection β. The two nonces on each individual connection differ, so
#7152's equal-nonce rejection never fires. Because both cluster nodes share one
PSK, the oracle can be the **peer node itself**, which no per-node nonce
bookkeeping can observe.

Impact is unchanged from #5078: a PSK-less fabric attacker is accepted as the
authenticated peer, can displace the real connection, disclose session/config
state, refresh sync liveness, and feed signed frames into peer-state handlers.

## What closing it requires

The proof must be bound to protocol version + cluster/node identity +
endpoint/fabric identity + an explicit initiator/responder role over the full
transcript, and the two directions must derive **independent** keys and
counters. That is a new proof construction on the wire — every node in a cluster
must change together, so it is a flag-day with a fail-closed rollout, not an
additive check.

## Status: blocked on a decision the maintainer has explicitly held

A converged PLAN-READY doc exists on branch `research/5078-syncauth-reflection`
(`docs/research/5078-syncauth-reflection/plan.md`, plus the Claude-SMR / Codex /
AGY round-1 hostile reviews alongside it). It is **held pending a transport-fork
decision**: extend the custom handshake in place, or replace it with a standard

committed-but-unapplied values on a `Heartbeat pending restart:` line. That
makes the divergence correct-by-construction wherever it is *consumed*, and
visible to the operator — it does not make the commit take effect.

Adding an auth-key digest to `clusterTransportKey` restarts comms on a PSK

## Item 1 — actionless SNAT rule disposition: fall-through vs terminal-exempt

**Status: LIVE, and it is a migration-contract decision, not a mechanical fix.**

A leniently-loaded SNAT rule with **zero** actions is not inert. The Go snapshot
builder emits the rule, and the Rust matcher's `else` arm continues, so matched
traffic falls through to a later broader rule and is translated by **that** rule.
The `#5628` gate's own zero-action rejection text describes this as a fail-open.

PR #6820 (merged 2026-08-21) did the driveable part: it **pinned today's
behaviour** on both sides of the language boundary so it cannot drift silently.
The pins live in `userspace-dp/src/nat/tests_source.rs`:

- `off_wins_over_contradictory_interface_action_5717`
- `off_wins_over_contradictory_pool_action_5717`
- `actionless_rule_falls_through_to_later_broader_rule_5717`
- `actionless_rule_with_no_later_rule_passes_untranslated_5717`

The first two also fixed a real gap: the pre-existing
`off_rule_short_circuits_translation` did **not** bind the `off`-precedence claim
— its rule sets `off` alone, so it survives a mutation that lets `interface`
win. Relocating the `off` check below `interface_mode` reds the new tests while
that one stays green.

**What remains is exactly one question:** should an actionless rule become
TERMINAL (exempt) instead of falling through?

Why it was not decided in a test/comment PR, and why it still should not be
decided casually: making it terminal would newly **exempt** traffic that
already-deployed configs currently **translate**. That is a behaviour change that
lands on upgrade, on boxes whose operators did not ask for it — the class the
#1960 no-brick posture exists to protect. It is also coupled to the Go↔Rust
precedence question (DNAT decides in Go, SNAT in Rust), so it is not contained
inside `pkg/config`.

## #7167 — userspace-dp: bounded logical-tunnel-ingress — adjudicate decapped WireGuard + IPsec plaintext through the AF_XDP zone-policy pipeline [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-02)

Successor to **#5618** (WireGuard) and **#5619** (IPsec/XFRM). Both were filed
by codex-review-181 as separate High findings; both are the same defect wearing
two protocol costumes, and both issues' own research comments say so
("same architectural class", "the shared architectural opportunity is a single
bounded logical-tunnel-ingress abstraction"). Carrying them separately means
solving the hard part twice.

## The single root

Tunnel plaintext that terminates **on the firewall** reaches the Linux kernel
FIB without ever being adjudicated by the xpf AF_XDP zone-policy engine. There
is no bounded path to hand a decapped inner frame back INTO the worker pipeline,
so `evaluate_policy` never runs on it: no zone policy, no session, no NAT, no
screen, no filter/PBR.

The kernel then forwards it: xpf force-enables `ip_forward=1` /
`ipv6.conf.all.forwarding=1` (`pkg/daemon/daemon_system.go`), and
`grep -rn "hook forward"` returns **zero** hits repo-wide — the nftables tables
xpf installs are `hook input` only.

An SA or a WireGuard AllowedIPs entry authenticates a **peer**. Neither
authorizes an inner **from-zone → to-zone flow**. They are not substitutes for
policy.

## The two capture points

### WireGuard — `wgN` TUN write from the control thread
`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/coordinator/wg_control.rs`: after `WgEngine::try_decap`
authenticates and enforces AllowedIPs, and after ECN combination,
`dispatch_inbound` calls `slowpath::write_packet_nonblocking(tun_fd, plaintext)`.
The in-source comment states the defect affirmatively: *"the kernel
routes/firewalls it (NOT the AF_XDP policy engine — the AllowedIPs gate inside
try_decap is S2a's inner-src control)"*. There is no zone lookup, session
create, route/PBR/filter/NAT evaluation, zone counter, policy-deny event, or
worker submission between authentication and that write. `WorkerCommand` carries
session/CoS commands only — there is no bounded logical-ingress packet command
the control thread could use instead.

This is a documented #1432-S2a boundary (`wg_control.rs` header: *"the kernel
routes inner traffic to/from it; xpf does not re-implement inner routing or

## #7169 — userspace-dp: NAT reverse-canonical index matches a pre-NAT 5-tuple on the main packet path and installs a reverse session with no ingress revalidation [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-29)

Escalated out of the **#5557** audit cohort (claude-review-003, area A1). The
cohort filed this as low-materiality on an explicit condition — *"verify the
canonical fallback is gated to identity-NAT flows"*. A firsthand trace at
`origin/master` **9710cfd13** shows **that gating does not exist**. The
disposition rested on a fact that is false, so the disposition has to be redone
rather than carried.

## What the code does

`reverse_canonical_key(key, nat)` (`userspace-dp/src/session/key.rs:19-26,143-157`)
computes the **pre-NAT** (private-side) reverse tuple for a session.

`index_forward_nat_key_parts` (`userspace-dp/src/session/mod.rs:1957-1966`)
pushes that canonical key into the shared `nat_reverse_index` multimap **whenever
it differs from the forward key** — which is true for essentially every NAT'd
flow, translating or identity, not just identity-NAT.

On the main packet path, `lookup_forward_nat_across_scopes` →
`find_forward_nat_match` (`userspace-dp/src/session_glue/mod.rs:1416`) consults
that index. This is the ordinary forwarding path, **not** only the
ICMP-embedded-error callers the low-materiality reading assumed.

On a match, `install_reverse_session_from_forward_match` /
`build_reverse_session_from_forward_match`
(`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/.../shared_ops.rs:732-960`) synthesizes a reverse
session from the **stored forward session's metadata**, with
`ingress_ifindex: 0` and **no revalidation against which interface or zone the
matching packet actually arrived on**.

## Why that shape matters

A packet whose observed 5-tuple equals a live session's pre-NAT tuple is
accepted as that session's reply and gets a reverse session installed carrying
the original flow's zone/NAT/forwarding metadata — decided entirely by tuple
equality, with the arrival interface discarded. That is the structural shape of
a session-hijack / reply-spoof primitive against translating NAT flows.

*"Either (1) enforce the regex contract at every operational and configuration

`foldLoginClassDenyToRepairableFloor`.

- coarse permission must first authorize the command family;

## #7173 — [cohort] 11 verified-live survivors from #5609 (claude-spark-review-001) — incl. zeroize skipping a custom archive dir [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-29)

Successor to the **#5609** audit cohort (claude-spark-review-001, 15 enumerated
items + 2 body-claimed-fixed). The cohort had **zero** comments — it had never
been swept. It has now been swept firsthand at `origin/master` **9710cfd13**:
**4 FIXED, 11 LIVE, 0 MOOT, 0 UNVERIFIED**. This issue carries the 11 live rows,
with loci re-measured at that head.

Nothing here is a policy bypass. Every row is a defense-in-depth gap, an
observability gap, or a deliberate fail-closed/fail-safe availability trade-off —
which is exactly what the cohort claimed, now with evidence rather than
assertion.

## Do this one first — zeroize can leave prior config text and PSKs on disk

`pkg/configstore/factory_reset.go:73-90` (`FactoryResetArchiveDir`).

The cohort filed this UNVERIFIED because it cited a path that does not exist
(`pkg/config/factory_reset.go:60`). The correct file was located and the finding
**confirmed**: `FactoryResetArchiveDir` deliberately **skips erasure** when the
archive dir is not the xpf-owned default, logging
`slog.Warn("zeroize: skipping config archive directory with unproven…")`.

So an operator who configured a custom archive directory and then ran zeroize
has prior configuration text — and any PSKs in it — still on disk. The skip is a
defensible choice on its own terms (do not erase a directory whose ownership
cannot be proven), but "zeroize completed" plus a warning line is a weak signal
for a secrets-destruction operation. Sibling: **#5520** (zeroize misses the root
account key).

Decide one of: refuse the zeroize outright when an unproven archive dir is
configured; erase it under an explicit operator confirmation; or keep the skip
and make the incompleteness a first-class, non-log-line result the CLI reports.
Any of those is better than today. This should not stay a `slog.Warn`.

Successor to the **#5649** audit cohort (codex-review-181, 19 items). The cohort

## Start here — C19 is the only wrong-answer bug in the set

**`userspace-dp/src/filter/engine/matching.rs:178-230`** (`term_matches_v4`,
mirrored in `term_matches_v6`).

`port_match` on source/destination port runs **unconditionally, before**
`per_packet_l4_matches`. `per_packet_l4_matches` correctly gates tcp-flags,
icmp-type, icmp-code and is-fragment on `l4_present` — but it never gates
**ports**. So a non-first fragment's *synthetic* port is matched against a real
`source-port` / `destination-port` term, and in particular against a
`*-port-except` term, where a spurious match or miss inverts the verdict.

Every other row below is availability, observability, hardening, or test
tooling. This one produces a **wrong filter decision** on a real packet. It is
narrow (it needs fragments and a port-bearing term) and the original codex-181
panel downgraded it from MATERIAL for lack of demonstrated production-scale
impact — but it is the only row here where the firewall answers incorrectly
rather than merely suboptimally or silently.

Fix direction: gate the port comparison on `l4_present` the same way the sibling
L4 predicates already are, and add a fail-on-revert test for a non-first
fragment against a `destination-port-except` term in both v4 and v6.

## #7175 — cluster: a truncated-but-framed session-sync record decodes ok=true and installs a session with zeroed policy/zone/NAT fields [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-29)

Escalated out of the **#5523** audit cohort (codex-review-179, item C179-074).
The cohort's framing — "low-materiality by design; the real Mediums were split
into #5517-#5522" — holds for most of its rows. It does not hold for this one:
this is forwarding-plane **state correctness** on the HA session-sync wire, not
observability.

## The defect

`pkg/cluster/sync_protocol.go:374-497` (`decodeSessionV4Payload`).

A session-sync record that is **framed correctly but truncated mid-block** still
returns `ok=true`. The partially-decoded session is then installed on the
receiving node with `SessionID`, `PolicyID`, ingress/egress zones and NAT fields
all left at **zero**.

Verified firsthand at `origin/master` **9710cfd13**.

## Why this is more than cosmetic

A zeroed policy id, zeroed zones and zeroed NAT metadata are not "missing" — they
are *values*, and the standby will forward against them. Zone id 0 in particular
is not inert: a `from-zone any to-zone any permit` rule matches zone-pair (0,0)
with no zone guard (#6682). So a truncated frame does not degrade to "no
session"; it can seed a session that a wildcard rule affirmatively permits, with
no NAT and no policy attribution, and that session survives until it ages out.

It then becomes the **live** forwarding state on the next failover.

## Reachability, stated honestly

The precondition is a malformed frame that no legitimate encoder emits — so this
needs corruption on the fabric link, a version-skewed or buggy peer, or a
compromised peer. It is narrow. It is also exactly the class where fail-open
decoding is worst, because the receiving node has no other check: the sibling
`#5875`-era work made the *count* clamp reject an allocation DoS, but a
mid-block truncation still decodes "successfully".

The cohort's sibling row **C179-075** (`sync_protocol.go:1052-1055`) is the same
shape on the DHCP full-set path: a malformed frame silently replaces the peer
lease set with an empty or prefix set. Fix them together — one decode contract,

## Dataplane / forwarding-adjacent (userspace-dp, userspace-xdp — Rust)

**M04 — Output-filtered Time Exceeded still consumes the (now per-zone) diagnostic token before output-filter classification.**
Locus: `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/icmp.rs:266,294` + `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/icmp_ratelimit.rs:284-311`.
`allow_generated_error_zoned` (token consume) still runs BEFORE `classify_generated_reply` (the output-filter drop check). Prior #5856 narrowed the shared bucket from process-global to per-ingress-zone, reducing blast radius, but an output-filtered reply on one interface can still exhaust ITS zone's bucket and starve other same-zone interfaces before being dropped.
Fix direction (from the original finding): classify before consuming the token; consume only after the output-filter/policy gate passes.

**M05 — TUN EAGAIN backpressure still spins up to 1,025 immediate syscalls with no poll/backoff.**
Locus: `userspace-dp/src/slowpath.rs:803-895` (`write_packet_atomic_nonblocking`, `NONBLOCK_WOULDBLOCK_RETRY_BUDGET = 1024`).
The `WouldBlock` arm still does a bare `continue` (tight retry loop) instead of registering for `POLLOUT`/yielding/enqueuing. Under sustained TUN backpressure this can burn up to 65,600 syscalls across one WG_RX_BURST(64) on the shared per-tunnel control thread.
Fix direction: cap immediate retries very low (1-2), then return to the poll loop / a bounded pending queue.

**M13 — HA-reserved NAT ports remain in the recycle FIFO, causing repeated full-range scans after role churn.**
Locus: `userspace-dp/src/nat/allocator.rs:696-742` (`claim`), `~1983` (`reserve_flow`).
`claim` still drains+restores the entire recycle queue on every call once the fresh cursor is spent; `reserve_flow`'s `occupancy.reserve()` never invalidates the port's queued FIFO entry. After an HA promotion with prior port churn, a connection flood can repeat an O(64,512) scan + heap allocation per claim under the per-address mutex.
Fix direction: track queue membership/generation so `reserve_flow` invalidates a recycled token, or bound the scan with a persistent cursor.

**C19 — Flowless filter port-except evaluates the synthetic port on a non-first fragment before the `l4_present` gate.**
Locus: `userspace-dp/src/filter/engine/matching.rs:178-230` (`term_matches_v4`, mirrored in `term_matches_v6`).
`port_match` on src/dst port runs unconditionally before `per_packet_l4_matches`; the latter gates tcp-flags/icmp-type/icmp-code/is-fragment on `extra.l4_present` but never gates ports. A non-first fragment (no real L4 header) can therefore wrongly match/miss a `destination-port-except`/`source-port-except` term. Bounded like the existing #4569/#5467 first-fragment family.
Fix direction: gate the two `port_match` calls in `term_matches_v4`/`term_matches_v6` on `extra.l4_present`, matching the pattern already used for tcp-flags/icmp.

**C03 — `read_bytes` remains a safe fn with an unconstrained lifetime (memory-safety hardening, no live bug).**
Locus: `userspace-xdp/src/ipv6_ext_walk.rs:136-140` (moved from `lib.rs`; only a "# Safety" doc comment was added since the original finding, no type-level fix).
All current call sites are sound (each consumes the slice within one XDP invocation), so this is preventive hardening against a future unsafe caller, not a demonstrated bug.
Fix direction: bind the lifetime to an XDP-context-backed `PacketView<'ctx>` guard, or mark the fn `unsafe` with a documented invocation-lifetime obligation.

## Go control-plane (each needs a real design decision, not a mechanical fix)

**C06 — Journal fsync can outlive its segment's retained pathname under concurrent rotation.**
Locus: `pkg/configstore/journal/journal.go:255-286` (`Log`, fsync runs with `j.mu` released), `358-384` (`maybeRotateLocked`, unconditional remove/rename with no in-flight-fd awareness).
Needs: per-segment in-flight-sync reference tracking (or an equivalent lifetime guard) before eviction — a genuine concurrency-design change, not a one-line fix.

**C08 — gRPC policy/zone counters serialize "dataplane unavailable" as an indistinguishable scalar zero.**
Locus: `pkg/grpcapi/server_show_zones.go:152-158,228-236`; `proto/xpf/v1/xpf.proto` `PolicyRule`/`ZoneInfo` messages (no availability field; REST already has this pattern via `hit_counters_unavailable`).
Needs: a new proto field (`hit_counters_available`/`traffic_counters_available`) + codegen + both RPC handlers set it — a wire/API surface change, not mechanical.

## #7178 — cluster: a node whose dataplane failed to arm still holds RG mastership and advertises routes [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-29)

Split from **#5275**, whose title named two consequences of one dataplane arm
failure. The forwarding half — a failed arm leaving the kernel routing transit
with `ip_forward=1` and no policy — is fixed under #5275. This issue carries the
**ownership** half.

## The situation

When `rt.Start()` fails at bring-up outside bootstrap mode
(`pkg/daemon/daemon_run_bringup.go`), the daemon logs a warning, calls
`setDataplane(nil)`, and continues into `d.applyConfig(cfg)`. That apply
configures interfaces, VRFs, FRR and — on a cluster node — leaves the node
eligible to hold RG mastership and to advertise routes.

So a node with **no forwarding dataplane** can:

- win or retain VRRP mastership for a redundancy group, taking ownership of the
  RETH VIPs away from a peer that *does* have a working dataplane; and
- keep injecting/advertising routes through FRR, so upstream neighbours keep
  steering traffic at it.

With the #5275 fix in place this is no longer a *policy bypass* — the node stops
forwarding transit. It is now an **availability** defect, and a sharper one: the
node becomes a black hole that actively attracts traffic. Before #5275 it
forwarded unpoliced; after #5275 it drops. Neither is what an operator wants from
a node that failed to arm, and in a cluster the correct answer is obvious —
**let the peer have it**.

## Why it was split rather than folded in

Three reasons, and they are about verification, not scope creep:

1. It is HA-coupled. Changing when a node is eligible for mastership touches the
   #2082 peer-priority gate, the #1960 fail-closed family, and the sync-hold
   preempt path. Those interact.
2. It **owes `make test-failover`** (and plausibly `test-ha-crash`), which the
   forwarding fix does not. Bundling would have gated a bounded, provable
   sysctl fix behind a cluster smoke.
3. A wrong answer here causes a split-brain or a failover storm. The forwarding
   fix fails safe by construction; this one does not.

## #7179 — dataplane: make the forward/reverse session pair one helper-local transaction (half-pair survives a failed second RPC) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-31)

Split from **#5698**. The Go-side interleaving window — a concurrent
session-socket mutation landing between a pair's forward and reverse transmit —
is closed under #5698 by holding `m.sessionMu` across the pair. This issue
carries the half that lock cannot reach.

## The residual

`syncSessionPairLocked` makes the pair's transmit **contiguous**. It does not
make it **atomic**. Two requests are still two fallible RPCs:

- If the forward upsert succeeds and the reverse then fails at the transport
  layer, the helper is left holding a half-installed pair. Nothing rolls it back.
- The same applies in reverse on the delete path.
- Non-socket coordinator callers in Rust (purge, replay, reconciliation) mutate
  the same synced-session authority without passing through the Go lock at all,
  so the Go-side lock is not a global linearization point for that state.

The `#5698` research comment says this plainly: holding a lock across two RPCs
"closes only the Go interleaving window and would still permit
first-success/second-failure state."

## The approved architecture

A full design already exists on #5698 (comment of 2026-07-14, *"Architecture
proposal: one forward wire mutation, one helper-local pair transaction"*) and was
left at **READY FOR ANTAGONISTIC DESIGN REVIEW**. Do not re-derive it. In outline:

- Go sends exactly **one forward** upsert. Rust validates the forward DTO,
  derives the reverse key/decision/metadata **before** mutating, and commits both
  as one helper-local pair operation. Rust **rejects** an explicit
  `is_reverse=true` upsert — a reverse entry is derived state and can never be
  standalone authority.
- Delete is symmetric: accept either half's key, identify the stored companion,
  remove both in one operation, with the generation guard applied to the **pair**.
- No new wire field and no protocol version bump: the semantic unit of the
  existing `sync_session` verb becomes the pair.

The proposal includes a field-by-field comparison of the explicit Go reverse
against the Rust-synthesized one across reverse identity, NAT decision, zones,
egress/FIB, fabric/tunnel, owner RG, NAT64 reverse BIB, logging/policy,

Successor to #5797, carrying the part of it that is an architecture rather than
a bug. PR #7183 landed the bounded half — a selector is now scoped to the
facility its host's client actually stamps, so `daemon info; authorization
critical` filters daemon records at info instead of critical, and `daemon info;
authorization none` no longer silences the destination outright. #5797 is closed

A `SyslogClient` carries **one** facility (`pkg/logging/syslog.go`,
`priority = Facility*8 + severity`), and every record the daemon forwards
through `SyslogSlogHandler.Handle` gets that one facility, because the record
itself carries no facility — only a `slog.Level` mapped to a severity.

So a host naming two mappable facilities can still only honor the one it stamps:

```

    daemon info;
    auth warning;      # mappable, and still selects nothing
}

`auth warning` is now correctly ignored for the daemon-stamped stream and
warned about at apply time (`"selector names a facility this host's client does
not emit"`), but xpf still emits no `auth`-facility record for it to select,
and which of the two is stamped depends on **selector order** —
`host.Facilities[0]` in `applySystemSyslog`. That is invariant 1 of #5797,
unfixed.

The blocker is not the selector evaluation, it is that **forwarded records carry

`docs/research/5275-arm-failclosed/plan.md` §6 specifies a fuller barrier. What
shipped is the sysctl leg alone. Still wanted:

  prose line in `pkg/config/README.md`), so `ip_forward` is the *only* thing
  standing between an unarmed box and kernel routing. A single sysctl that any
  future code path, an operator, a `sysctl.d` drop-in, or a systemd unit can
  raise is a thin barrier for a security posture.

  all, so a bridged topology is not covered by what shipped.
- a **flowtable disable** — an established flowtable offload can keep forwarding
  independently of the sysctl.

no adjudication — the same class of hole #5275 closed, one layer down. This is

#6312 is the shape of the recurrence: `rt_flow_session_id` was added to the
binary leg in #5212 and only reached the JSON leg in #6312, one issue later.
Every field added to one transport is a candidate for the same gap.

## Item 1 — one canonical schema, both transports derived

Define the session-open record once, and generate or mechanically check both the
binary codec and the JSON `SessionDeltaInfo` against it, so a field cannot exist
on one leg and not the other. The minimum viable version is not codegen: it is a
**golden equivalence test** that enumerates the canonical field set and fails
when either transport omits one — the enumeration being the SSOT, so adding a
field to the binary codec without the JSON producer reds the suite instead of
shipping.

That test is the load-bearing artefact. Codegen is an optimisation on top of it.
