## #7198 — userspace-dp NPTv6: embedded-ICMP reverse lookup uses the physical ifindex, not the logical VLAN unit — PMTUD black-hole on VLAN-trunked NPTv6 flows (4th instance of the #3021/#3022/#3026 class) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

## Defect

`match_outer_v6` (`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/icmp_embed/nat_match_v6.rs:33-37`) — the
IPv6-outer branch of the embedded-ICMP NAT match — resolves the ingress zone for the
NPTv6 reverse translation by keying `ifindex_to_zone_id` on the **raw physical**
`meta.ingress_ifindex`, without first resolving the logical VLAN sub-interface:

```rust
let ingress_zone = ctx
    .forwarding
    .ifindex_to_zone_id
    .get(&(meta.ingress_ifindex as i32))     // <-- PHYSICAL parent ifindex
    .and_then(|id| ctx.forwarding.zone_id_to_name.get(id))
    .map(|s| s.as_str())
    .unwrap_or("");
let mut emb_src_lookup_v6 = hdr.src_wire;
let _nptv6_reverse = ctx
    .forwarding
    .nptv6
    .translate_inbound(&mut emb_src_lookup_v6, ingress_zone);
```

The site's own comment states the intent it fails to implement:

> #5176: the reverse translation is zone-scoped like every NPTv6 lookup. ... the error
> returns ingressing on that same external interface, so gate on **THIS packet's
> ingress zone** (the inbound-direction zone per the #5176 invariant).

On a VLAN trunk, "this packet's ingress zone" is the **logical unit's** zone
(`ge-0/0/2.50`), not the physical parent's (`ge-0/0/2`). Those are different zones,
and the parent frequently has no zone at all — in which case `unwrap_or("")` yields
the wildcard-empty zone and the scoped rule silently fails to match.

## Consequence

An ICMPv6 error (notably **Packet-Too-Big**, i.e. PMTUD) arriving on a VLAN
sub-interface for a flow whose source was NPTv6-translated outbound is attributed to
the wrong zone. The zone-scoped `translate_inbound` then misses, so the embedded
source is not reversed to the internal client, the embedded-ICMP session match fails,
and the error is not delivered back to the originating host.

## #7201 — userspace-dp: worker command ingest drains an unbounded batch with no budget or ring yield — a full RG-activation burst stalls forwarding at failover [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-29)

Escalated out of the **#5189** "warmed-path allocation/contention LOW cohort"
(codex-review-177 A1-b4-F6). The cohort filed this as an allocation nit. It is
not: it is an **availability defect on the failover path**, and the forwarding
stall is reachable. Verified firsthand at `origin/master`.

## The mechanism

`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/session_glue/mod.rs`:

- `:703` — `core::mem::take(&mut *pending)` captures the whole shared pending
  deque (and leaves a zero-capacity `VecDeque` the producers must regrow).
- `:740` — `for cmd in pending` drains the **entire** captured batch in one
  uninterrupted loop, with **no per-loop command budget, no time budget, and no
  yield back to the AF_XDP RX/TX rings**.

Each command is a session-table mutation plus a BPF-map publish syscall. The
worker does not touch its rings until the whole batch is done.

## Nothing bounds the batch — and the burst arrives exactly at failover

Every push site is a bare `push_back` on an unbounded `VecDeque`. There is **no
producer-side cap anywhere**.

The producers that matter are the HA ones, and they fan out per entry to every
worker:

- `activate_owner_rgs_prewarm` (`shared_ops.rs:444,481`) enqueues one
  `UpsertSynced` per forward **and** per reverse synced entry, to **every** worker
  queue, in one pass.
- `replay_synced_sessions` (`coordinator/mod.rs:835`) does the same per synced
  entry.

The documented entry ceiling is `2 * worker_count * DEFAULT_MAX_SESSIONS`
(`coordinator/status.rs:281`; `DEFAULT_MAX_SESSIONS = 131072`,
`session/mod.rs:60`) — so O(10^5–10^6) commands, drained in one uninterrupted
loop, **at RG activation**. That is the moment the node has just become
forwarding-authoritative and its rings most need servicing.

## A1-b6-F4 — non-CoS backup drain loses its persistent allocation and allocates a fresh retry deque per batch

**Locus:** `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/tx/drain/mod.rs:577-585`
(`take_pending_tx_requests`), `tx/drain/phase_backup.rs:164`, `:205`.

`take_pending_tx_requests` does `mem::take`, leaving a **zero-capacity** deque in
the worker that producers must regrow. `phase_backup` allocates a fresh
`retry = VecDeque::new()` per batch. On **full success** the restore is skipped
(`:205` is `if !retry.is_empty()`), so both deques are dropped and re-allocated on
the next successful non-CoS backup batch — i.e. the allocation happens on the
*good* path, every time.

Sibling of #4973 but a distinct path and function.

**Fix direction:** keep a persistent worker-owned retry deque as a
`WorkerTxPipeline` scratch field, and always return the emptied pending
allocation to `pending_tx_local` on success — not only on the partial-failure
path.

**Gate:** this is the TX hot path. Rust change ⇒ helper binary moves ⇒ cluster
smoke owed.

## #7205 — linksetup: positional naming has no transaction — no live-name verification, a collision break that can fail into phase 2, and a dropped protected set (the #5842 remainder) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-30)

Successor to #5842. PR #7203 landed its bounded half — the error channel — so
positional naming now fails when it does not converge instead of returning nil.
#5842 is closed against this issue.

## What is left

#5842 asked for more than an error channel. Two of its items are unaffected by
#7203 and are genuine, and they share one root: **the positional path has no
notion of a naming transaction.**

### 1. Nothing verifies the LIVE names after the pass

`renamePositional` reports what it attempted. It does not read back the
interface list and confirm that each NIC now wears the name its `.link` claims.
A rename that returns success but does not take effect — a `networkctl reload`
that partially applied, a udev race, a NIC that vanished mid-pass — leaves the
box running under names the config does not reference, with a clean return
value.

The device-map path has the identity half of this (`enumerateAndRenameMapped`
refuses a binding when the PCI address matches but the permanent MAC differs —
a swapped card is never silently hijacked). Positional mode has no equivalent
because it has no stable identity to verify against; positional index *is* the
identity. A live-name verification pass is the substitute, and it is what would
turn "I attempted the rename" into "the box is named correctly".

### 2. `breakNameCollisions` leaves the box worse on a failed temp rename

`breakNameCollisions` (`linksetup.go`, shared by BOTH the positional and
device-map paths) warns and `continue`s on a failed temp rename. That NIC stays
occupying a desired final name, so phase 2's stated premise —

> Collisions are already broken, so no EEXIST here.

— is false for that name. Phase 2 then attempts a rename that EEXISTs.

After #7203 that EEXIST is at least reported rather than swallowed, so this is
no longer silent. But the correct behaviour is not to report it: it is not to
enter phase 2 with a broken premise. Either the collision break is a
transaction that rolls back, or phase 2 re-checks occupancy per name instead of

## #7210 — cmd/cli: remote pipe filter buffers full output before filtering (unbounded client-side memory on large piped output) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-29)

## What

The remote CLI client (`cmd/cli` — the `cli` binary that connects to `xpfd` over
gRPC) buffers a piped command's ENTIRE output in memory before applying the
`| match` / `| except` / `| find` / `| count` / `| last` / `| no-more` filter. The
equivalent local in-process CLI path (`pkg/cli`) streams instead; the remote client
was never brought in line.

`cmd/cli/shared.go`, `dispatchWithPipe`:

```go
outputCh := make(chan []byte, 1)
go func() {
        output, _ := io.ReadAll(r)                     // <-- unbounded
        r.Close()
        outputCh <- output
}()
cmdErr := c.dispatch(cmd)
w.Close()
os.Stdout = origStdout
output := <-outputCh
lines := strings.Split(string(output), "\n")           // <-- materialized AGAIN
applyPipeFilter(lines, origStdout, pipeType, pipeArg)
```

A command with very large output (`show log messages | match error` against a large
syslog buffer, `show route | count` on a big table) materializes the full output
once as a `[]byte` and again as a `[]string` before the filter ever runs.
`applyPipeFilter` is a faithful reimplementation of the local filter semantics, but
it operates on the already-fully-buffered slice.

## Blast radius — read this before triaging severity

**This affects only the `cli` client PROCESS, on whatever host the operator runs it
from. It does NOT touch `xpfd` or the dataplane.** The daemon-side gRPC handler
streams normally; the unbounded buffering happens entirely in the client's own
memory after it has received the output. An operator piping a large `show` through
a filter on a memory-constrained jump host can OOM-kill their own CLI session — not
the firewall. Stated explicitly so this is not mis-read as a dataplane risk.

## #7212 — userspace-dp: revalidate established sessions against a changed static input filter, stamped by filter generation (the #5858 dataplane half) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-30)

Successor to #5858. That issue's `/research` converged to PLAN-DEFERRED because
the bounded fix was proven unsafe and the correct fix is a multi-subsystem
dataplane feature. PR (see #5858's close comment) landed the operator-truth half
— a commit that attaches or tightens an input filter that can deny now says so,
and names the `clear security flow session interface <name>` remedy. #5858 is
closed against this issue.

## The gap

`poll_descriptor/filter.rs` re-evaluates an established session's input filter
only behind `interface_input_filter_varies_per_packet` — DSCP or per-packet L4
match terms. A purely static address/protocol/port `then discard` attached after
session creation is never rechecked, so the flow forwards until it idles out.
The rotation purge is gated on the same predicate
(`has_dscp_match_terms || has_per_packet_l4_match_terms`), so a purely static
filter change matches neither and triggers no purge either.

Junos firewall filters are stateless and evaluated on every packet. This is a
parity gap as well as a revocation gap.

## The mechanism, decided

#5858 left this as an A/B product decision. Deciding it, because the two
candidates are not equally defensible:

**Rejected — widen the existing family purge.** Killed with evidence in #5858's
research and re-verified: the family purge drops *permitted* flows, and a purged
permitted SNAT flow reinstalls on a different translated port (the
non-persistent PAT allocator hands out a fresh monotonic-cursor port and only
drains the recycle FIFO once the fresh range is spent), so it breaks. It also
carries a one-iteration flow-cache bypass (`validation` and `forwarding` are
separate ArcSwaps) and unreliable HA delete propagation (a large family purge
overflows the 4096-entry per-worker Close ring against up to 131072 sessions).
Not shippable, and this is settled — do not re-propose it.

**Chosen — lazy per-tuple revalidation, stamped by filter generation.** For a
purely STATIC filter the verdict is a function of (ingress interface, family,
5-tuple), all of which are constant for the life of a session. So the verdict
does not need re-deriving per packet — only when the filter snapshot changes:

## Measured

At `bf10c6b7c`, over the same base config #7145 used, with the probe value
`10.0.0.0/33` — an out-of-range mask, so the value parses as neither an
`IpNet` nor an `IpAddr` on the Rust side:

| kind | `match source-address` | `match destination-address` |
|---|---|---|
| `security nat source` | rejected (#7145) | rejected (#7145) |
| `security nat destination` | rejected (#7145) | **accepted** |
| `security nat static` | rejected (#7145) | rejected (#3206 host-mask arm) |

So after #7145 the destination-NAT `match destination-address` slot is the only
one of the six that still accepts an out-of-range mask.

## Why it matters

That slot's gate is `validateDestinationNATAddressesStrict`
(`pkg/config/compiler_validate_strict_nat.go`). Its predicate is
`natCIDRIPPart(raw)` + `net.ParseIP` — it strips everything after the first `/`
and parses only the address part, so `10.0.0.0/33` reads as the perfectly good
`10.0.0.0` and passes.

Its own consumer is stricter. `dnatDestinationParts`
(`pkg/dataplane/userspace/nat_destination.go`) calls `net.ParseCIDR` on any
value carrying a `/`, and returns `ok == false` when that fails — the entry is
SKIPPED and never reaches the wire. So this is a validator/builder divergence
inside one gate: the commit gate accepts a value its own snapshot builder then
silently drops, which is the exact silent-drop class #2396(c) created this gate
to close.

The comment on that gate says the acceptance "MUST match the builder's exactly".
It does not.

## Suggested fix

Make the #3228 loop's predicate the builder's own — the same `net.ParseCIDR`
then `net.ParseIP` pair `natMatchPrefixParses`
(`pkg/config/compiler_nat_helpers.go`, #7145) already implements for the other
four slots — so the six agree on this value class too.

## Measured

At `bf10c6b7c`, over the same base config #7145 used, with the probe value
`""` — an explicitly quoted empty value, e.g.
`set security nat static rule-set RT rule R1 match destination-address ""`:

| kind | `match source-address` | `match destination-address` |
|---|---|---|
| `security nat source` | rejected (#7145) | rejected (#7145) |
| `security nat destination` | rejected (#7145) | rejected (#3228) |
| `security nat static` | rejected (#7145) | **accepted** |

## Why it matters

`compileNATStatic` selects `rule.Match` from the authored value, so a quoted
blank makes `rule.Match == ""`. `buildStaticNATSnapshots`
(`pkg/dataplane/userspace/nat_static.go`) lowers it as
`StaticNATRuleSnapshot.ExternalIP = ""`, and the Rust `parse_nat_prefix`
(`userspace-dp/src/nat/static_nat.rs`) returns `None` on it, so
`from_snapshots` `continue`s and drops the WHOLE static-NAT mapping. The
operator authored a rule that does not exist at runtime, with no commit error
and no warning — the #3206 silent-drop, reached through the blank rather than
through a typo.

The #3206 arm of `validateNATHostMaskStrict` skips it explicitly
(`if addr == "" { continue }`). That skip is not accidental: #6673 gave an empty
slot in `MatchAddresses` a deliberate meaning — an authored BLANK SELECTION,
which is how `destination-address 192.0.2.1/32` followed by
`destination-address [ ]` is modelled, and counting or rejecting raw empties
there would invent a rejection the multi-value gate was never meant to make.

So this is not a one-line widening: closing it means separating "a blank the
multi-leaf machinery produced as a selection artifact" from "a blank the
operator typed as the rule's only external prefix", and only rejecting the
second. The #6673 rationale on `validateStaticNATMatchAddressesStrict` and
`multiLeafAuthoredValues` is the required reading.

Note the multi-value gate ALREADY handles one adjacent shape: with two or more
prefixes where the selected slot is the blank, it rejects with "...the selected
value is EMPTY, so NONE of them takes effect and the dataplane drops the rule".

## #7223 — eventengine: a within-clause trigger-on crossing is suppressed depending on clause ORDER [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

**Defect**

`withinMatches` (`pkg/eventengine/engine.go`) decides the `within { trigger on N }`
edge latch from **inside** the loop that walks a policy's within clauses,
returning `false` from the middle of that walk. `within` clauses are ANDed
(#4423 M3), so with more than one `trigger on` clause the verdict depends on the
**order the operator wrote the clauses in**, and in one ordering a genuine
threshold crossing is **silently suppressed**.

Sequence, with the policy already latched from a previous crossing:

1. The walk reaches the LONG-window clause first. Its in-window count is still
   at or above its threshold, so it falls through to the latch check and
   `return false`.
2. The SHORT-window clause — whose count has decayed **below** its threshold,
   and which is therefore the clause that should have executed
   `rt.onLatched[eventName] = false` and RE-ARMED the latch — is never reached.
3. The ANDed condition went false (the short clause was below threshold) and
   then true again. That is a real crossing. The policy does not fire.

Written in the other order the identical config re-arms and fires correctly.

## #7227 — userspace manager: expose the helper crash record and a named crash-loop state [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-29)

Successor to #5838, which shipped the process-lifecycle half (single generation-fenced waiter, reap, fail-closed teardown, bounded-backoff restart) in PR for `fix/5838-helper-supervisor`.

## What #5838 deliberately did NOT ship

#5838's acceptance list had one bullet the PR does not satisfy:

> Operational status exposes exit code/signal, restart count, last exit/restart timestamps, backoff deadline, and crash-loop reason.

The data now EXISTS — `helperCrashState` in `pkg/dataplane/userspace/process_supervisor.go` records `Detail` (exit status or signal), `PID`, `At`, `Restarts` and `NextRestart`, and `Manager.HelperCrashState()` returns it — but **no `show` command renders any of it**. An operator whose helper is crash-looping sees `journalctl` lines and nothing in the CLI.

That is the same defect shape as #7059/#5804: a field populated in the control plane that no operator surface reads, so the box knows something it never tells anyone.

## Also not shipped: a named state machine

#5838's fix direction asked for explicit states — `starting`, `ready`, `stopping`, `exited`, `backoff`, `crash-loop`. What shipped is a boolean (`helperCrash.Crashed`) plus a restart counter. That is sufficient for the fail-closed property and is what the tests bind, but it cannot distinguish "backing off, will retry in 8s" from "crash-looping, 14 consecutive failures" in a way a status renderer or an alarm could key on. There is no crash-loop THRESHOLD at all: the backoff is bounded at `helperRestartBackoffMax` and retries forever, which is the right availability behaviour but never raises a distinct condition.

## Scope

- [ ] Render the crash record in `show system dataplane` (or the nearest existing helper-status surface) and in the gRPC/REST status projection, so the remote CLI sees it too — both surfaces, per the #7059 lesson that a remote operator must not read a weaker claim than an on-box one.
- [ ] Promote `helperCrash.Crashed` to a named state with an explicit `crash-loop` threshold, and decide whether crossing it should raise a chassis alarm / CF monitor failure rather than only backing off.
- [ ] Expose it in the Prometheus collector (a restart counter and a "helper down since" gauge are the two an operator would actually alert on).

## Explicitly out of scope / already done in #5838

- Reaping, the single waiter, and generation fencing.
- Fail-closed teardown on an unexpected exit, including `TakeoverReady()` going false.
- Bounded exponential backoff restart through the ordinary bring-up path.
- The forwarding posture itself: a post-crash node blackholes rather than routing unadjudicated packets, enforced by three independent degraded-path gates in `userspace-xdp/src/lib.rs` (binding not ready, heartbeat stale within 5s, XSK redirect error). No work is needed there and this issue must not re-litigate it.

## #7230 — userspace-dp/WireGuard: a zero-length keepalive never roams a peer endpoint on a multi-peer interface (and the comments calling attribution ambiguous are wrong) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-27)

Split from the **#5191** protocol-fidelity cohort, which is closed. The two
mechanical rows (ICMP identifier restore + TCP segmentation fidelity) are fixed
in PR #7229. This row needs a decision, not a patch, and it comes with a
correction to the source comments that currently justify the behaviour.

## What is broken

A zero-length authenticated WireGuard **keepalive** does not roam a peer's
endpoint on any **multi-peer** interface.

- `try_decap` returns `Err(MalformedInner)` for a zero-length authenticated
  keepalive (`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/wg/engine.rs:1567-1570`), which **discards
  the peer identity** along with the error.
- `coordinator/wg_control/dispatch.rs:228-250` then tries to recover the identity
  via `single_peer_pubkey()`. On any interface with more than one peer that
  returns `Unauthenticated`, so **no endpoint roam happens**.

Consequence: a peer behind a NAT that rebinds, or a roaming client whose only
traffic is keepalives, is blackholed until its next handshake. Bounded at roughly
**120-180 s**, not indefinite — stating that plainly because it is the difference
between "degraded" and "outage", and the issue should not be oversold.

## The source comments justifying this are WRONG, and that is the finding

The comments in that path claim multi-peer attribution is ambiguous — that xpf
cannot know *which* peer sent the keepalive. That is false, and it is checkable:

- `try_decap` resolves the session **by receiver index, BEFORE any crypto**
  (`wg/engine.rs:1434-1440`).
- It then uses that same `session.peer_pubkey` **four times** after AEAD success.

So the identity is in hand, and it is provably unique, at the moment the error is
constructed. Nothing is ambiguous; the identity is simply thrown away with the
`Err`. A future reader who takes those comments at face value will conclude there
is nothing to fix here — which is presumably what happened already.

## Why it is a decision, not a mechanical fix

Three things make this more than a patch:

## #7233 — userspace-dp: a dead constant's doc comment claims the shim XDP_PASSes transit when the heartbeat is absent — it drops [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

## Defect

`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/mod.rs:392-395` documents `HEARTBEAT_GRACE_PERIOD_NS` with:

> Grace period after binding before writing heartbeat. During this window **the XDP shim sees no heartbeat → XDP_PASS → kernel forwards packets** AND NAPI bootstraps the NIC's XSK receive queue from the fill ring. After this period, heartbeat is written and the XDP shim redirects to XSK.

**Both halves are wrong at HEAD.**

1. **The shim does not `XDP_PASS` on an absent heartbeat — it DROPS transit.** At `588d94dff5351c9a9b403cbf0b57eefa569a7eaf`, `userspace-xdp/src/lib.rs:530` is `return drop_degraded_transit(ctrl, USERSPACE_FALLBACK_REASON_HEARTBEAT_MISSING);` and `:560` the same for `..._HEARTBEAT_STALE`. `drop_degraded_transit` returns `XDP_DROP` unconditionally. Only proven local/control traffic passes, via `is_degraded_local_or_control` -> `pass_local_control`.
2. **The grace period it describes does not exist.** `HEARTBEAT_GRACE_PERIOD_NS` is `#[allow(dead_code)]` and `grep -rn HEARTBEAT_GRACE_PERIOD_NS --include=*.rs userspace-dp/src/` returns **exactly one hit — its own declaration at mod.rs:399**. Nothing reads it. The live cadence constant is a different one, `HEARTBEAT_UPDATE_INTERVAL_NS` (250 ms), consumed by `maybe_touch_heartbeat` in `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/bpf_map/ha.rs:79`.

## Why this is worth an issue rather than a drive-by comment fix

This is the single most load-bearing sentence in the tree for the question *"what does the dataplane do when the helper stops heartbeating?"* — which is exactly the question asked when reasoning about a helper crash (#5838), an unarmed boot (#5275/#7189), or the residual attach case (#7191). It answers **"the kernel forwards packets"**, i.e. it tells a reader the box **fails OPEN**, when the code fails **closed**.

Same defect shape as #7059 and #5804 — a claim in the tree the code does not implement — except the subject here is a security posture and the claim points in the dangerous direction. A reader who trusts it would either (a) believe a nonexistent forwarding hole and spend a cycle "fixing" it, or worse (b) design around a guarantee of pass-through that is not there.

It nearly did exactly that: I hit this comment while confirming the three degraded-path gates for #5838 and had to go read the shim to establish it was stale.

## Fix

- Delete `HEARTBEAT_GRACE_PERIOD_NS` (dead — one declaration, zero uses; the `#[allow(dead_code)]` is what has been suppressing the compiler's own report).
- If any prose is retained about the post-bind window, it must state the ACTUAL behaviour: a binding whose heartbeat slot has never been written reads as `Some(0)`, and `now_ns.wrapping_sub(0) > timeout_ns` is true, so it classifies **STALE and drops transit** — it does not pass. The NAPI/fill-ring bootstrap concern the comment was written for is real, but it is handled by the Go-side ctrl enable delay and the `bootstrapNAPIQueuesAsyncLocked` broadcast pings, not by a shim pass-through.

## Acceptance

- [ ] `grep -rn HEARTBEAT_GRACE_PERIOD_NS` returns nothing.
- [ ] No comment in `userspace-dp/` or `userspace-xdp/` claims the shim passes transit to the kernel on a missing or stale heartbeat. A grep-based guard for `XDP_PASS` near `heartbeat` would keep it from coming back.
- [ ] `cargo test -- --test-threads=1` clean (parallel deadlocks this crate).

Comment-only plus a dead-constant removal, so no `.text` change and no cluster smoke is owed.

## #7239 — session identity: a kernel ifindex recycled WITHIN one zone still corroborates and names the wrong sibling [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-31)

Residual left open deliberately by #6987 (PR #7238), measured there and named in
the code comment on `sessionFilter.ingressIfaceIdentity`
(`pkg/cli/session_filter.go`) and its `pkg/grpcapi` / `pkg/api` mirrors.

## What #6987 closed, and what it could not

A session's recorded ingress `{ifindex, VLAN}` is stamped at install; the
`{ifindex, VLAN} -> interface-name` table is rebuilt from the current config and
current kernel ifindexes on every query. A RECYCLED ifindex therefore HITS the
rebuilt table and names an interface the session never arrived on.

#6987 corroborates the hit against the row's own recorded ingress ZONE — the one
other identity recorded at the same instant, with a name-derived id that is
stable across commits (`assignZoneIDs`). A disagreement is a miss on the filter
and prints no interface name on the reported column.

**That check is blind to a recycle within one zone.** If interface A (zone Z) is
destroyed and interface B — a different PARENT netdev, also in zone Z — is
created and handed A's ifindex, the hit corroborates and the surfaces report B,
confidently, for a session that arrived on A.

Note the case does NOT arise for two VLAN units of one trunk: those share the
parent ifindex and the map key carries the VID, so the units do not alias. It
needs two distinct parent netdevs in one zone — e.g. two GRE tunnels or two XFRM
interfaces bound to the same `vpn` zone, one torn down and one created after.

## Why it was not fixed there

The row carries no third identity to check against. Closing it needs one of:

1. an install-time **generation/epoch** stamped alongside the ifindex on the
   session row, bumped whenever the interface table changes, with a mismatch
   treated as a miss — the option #6987 lists first, and a **dataplane wire
   change** (`SessionValue` layout, the ABI-asserted 144/192 sizes, and the
   helper side in `userspace-dp/src/session/entry.rs`);
2. the resolved **name** recorded at install rather than at query time, which
   has the same wire cost;
3. a daemon-side ifindex→name binding HISTORY sampled continuously, with a
   session whose `Created` predates the last observed rebinding of that ifindex
   treated as stale. No wire change, but it is sound only as far as its sampling

## #7240 — session identity: the EGRESS FIB ifindex is not corroborated — same recycle hazard as #6987 [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-30)

Found while fixing #6987 (PR #7238) and deliberately left out of it to keep that
change scoped to the ingress side the issue was filed against.

## The mechanism, unchanged from #6987

`resolveSessionEgressIfaces` / `egressIfaceDisplay` resolve a session's EGRESS
interface from `{FibIfindex, FibVlanID}` — recorded at install — through the
`{ifindex, VLAN} -> interface-name` table, which is rebuilt from the current
config and current kernel ifindexes on every query. A RECYCLED kernel ifindex
hits the rebuilt table and names an interface the session never left on.

The ingress side now corroborates that hit against the row's own recorded
ingress zone (#6987). **The egress side does not**, on any of the three
surfaces:

- `pkg/cli/session_filter.go` — `resolveEgressIfaces`, `egressIfaceDisplay`
- `pkg/grpcapi/server_sessions.go` — `resolveSessionEgressIfaces`,
  `sessionEgressIfaceDisplay`
- `pkg/api/sessions.go` — the same two mirrors

So a filtered `show`/`clear` can still reach a session through its EGRESS arm on
a name it never used, and the `Out: ... If:` column can still print one
confident wrong name.

## The symmetric check exists

`val.EgressZone` is recorded at the same instant as `FibIfindex` and is derived
from the same FIB result, so the two agree by construction — exactly the
relationship the ingress check relies on. `zoneBindsIface(zoneIfaces[EgressZone],
name)` is the whole fix, mirroring `sessionIngressIfaceIdentity`.

## Why it was not just done

Unverified: whether every EgressZone value the dataplane stamps is a zone that
actually binds the FIB-resolved interface. Fabric and tunnel egress paths carry
zone-encoded overrides (`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/forwarding/fabric.rs`,
`resolve_fabric_redirect`), and an egress zone that is a fabric/override marker
rather than a config zone would fail the check for every such row and silently
degrade a correct answer to the zone approximation. That population needs to be
enumerated before the check is applied, which is more than the #6987 change

## #7250 — userspace manager: no operator surface renders the helper crash/restart state (#5838 successor) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-29)

Successor to #5838, closed by PR #7228 (supervisor) + PR #7242 (the
restart-after-teardown fence). The supervisor RECORDS the state this issue is
about; nothing renders it, and two of the fields cannot be rendered as they
stand.

#5838's last acceptance bullet — *"operational status exposes exit code/signal,
restart count, last exit/restart timestamps, backoff deadline, and crash-loop
reason"* — is the part still open. #7228's own commit message says so
("helperCrashState records the exit disposition, pid, restart count and backoff
deadline but no `show` command renders them yet, and there is no named
crash-loop state").

## What exists at HEAD

`helperCrashState` (`pkg/dataplane/userspace/process_supervisor.go`) holds
`Crashed`, `Detail`, `PID`, `At`, `Restarts`, `NextRestart`, read through
`Manager.HelperCrashState()`.

## The four items

1. **`HelperCrashState()` returns an UNEXPORTED type** (`helperCrashState`). An
   out-of-package caller — which is what any status surface is — can hold the
   value but cannot name its type, so it cannot declare a variable, a struct
   field, or a function parameter for it. Exporting the struct is a rename and
   is a prerequisite for the rest.

2. **Exit code and signal are folded into one `Detail` string** ("exit status
   101" / "killed by signal killed"). The acceptance bullet asks for them
   separately, and a renderer cannot reliably re-split that string. They are
   both available at the source (`describeExit` already inspects
   `syscall.WaitStatus`), so carrying them as typed fields alongside the
   human-readable detail costs nothing.

3. **No crash-loop state is named.** The backoff caps at
   `helperRestartBackoffMax` and retries forever, which is the right runtime
   behaviour, but there is no predicate an operator or a health surface can read
   as "this helper is not coming back". A derived one — e.g. restarts beyond a
   threshold, or a backoff that has been at the cap for some period — needs
   deciding, not just plumbing.

## #7253 — refactoraudit: the heatmap freshness gate reds authors for growth they did not cause — regenerated twice in an hour, for different files each time [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

`pkg/refactoraudit`'s `TestHeatmapNotStale` gate reds on master repeatedly, for changes the failing author did not make. It has now been regenerated twice within an hour (#7235, #7252), each time for a *different* file, and it will go stale again.

## The measurements

**Round 1** — `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/frame/tcp_segmentation.rs` crossed the 1500-LOC floor (1475 → 1582) in PR #7229. Regenerated in #7235.

**Round 2**, at `origin/master` `e5403832e`, with #7235 already landed:

```
entered the audit (now >=1500 LOC):
  [WATCH]    pkg/dataplane/types.go
changed tier (crossed 2000 LOC):
  pkg/grpcapi/server_sessions.go: [WATCH] -> [REFACTOR]
```

`pkg/dataplane/types.go` is **1501** lines — it crossed the floor by **exactly one line**. `pkg/grpcapi/server_sessions.go` reached **2197** after `0053f3533` (+251/-47). Both sizes verified directly, not taken from the assertion text.

## Why this is a gate-design problem, not a sequence of authoring mistakes

The artifact is a generated snapshot of a **repo-global** property. It is only valid for the tree it was generated from. On a board landing several PRs an hour, a PR that regenerates it correctly **at its own base** can still land stale because a sibling PR grew a different file in between. #7235 was authored against a head that no longer existed by the time it merged.

The consequence is that the gate reds an author for a file they never touched, and the remedy — regenerate again — is itself immediately perishable. That is a gate that costs attention without buying a decision.

**This has been diagnosed once before, in the same file.** #6617 relaxed the gate from a byte-for-byte compare to an audit-content compare after measuring master byte-stale in **26 of 40** first-parent commits, and after #6602 and #6613 *both* regenerated the artifact at their own base and *both* still landed red — each disagreeing only on `pkg/snmp/agent.go`, a file neither PR touched. The reasoning recorded there is exactly right:

> A gate that reds when the author did everything right is noise.

The content compare is **narrower** than the byte compare, so #6617 was a real improvement. But it is the same shape one level up: any file crossing 1500 or 2000 anywhere in the tree flips it globally, and threshold crossings are frequent on a repo this active. A one-line addition to an unrelated file is sufficient.

## What the gate is actually for

Worth separating, because the answer shapes the fix. The valuable signal is *"this file is growing past the point where it should be split"* — a **modularity** signal aimed at the author of the growth. The current mechanism instead delivers *"the committed snapshot disagrees with the tree"* — a **freshness** signal aimed at whoever merges next. Those are different properties and only the first is worth interrupting someone for.

## Options

1. **Regenerate at merge time** rather than in the PR. The artifact stops being something an author can get wrong, and becomes a derived product of the merge — the same reasoning that moved `_Log.md` resolution to the merge gate.
2. **Tolerate a bounded lag** — allow the artifact to be N commits behind, or compare only against files the PR actually touched, so an author is only ever gated on growth they caused.
3. **Split the two signals**: keep a hard gate on *"a file YOU touched crossed a threshold"* (actionable, local, correct to interrupt for) and demote the global-snapshot freshness check to a periodic job that regenerates and commits on its own.

Option 3 most directly matches what the gate is for; option 1 is the smallest change that removes the treadmill.

## #7268 — cleanup: retire the DataPlane eBPF NAT write surface itself (maps_nat.go writers, compileNPTv6's nptv6_rules, the now-defensive shim overrides) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-30)

Follow-up to #6420 / PR #7267, which deleted the dead eBPF NAT **record construction** in `pkg/dataplane/compiler_nat.go` (`compileNAT` / `compileStaticNAT` / `compileNAT64`) while deliberately leaving the `DataPlane` NAT **interface surface** and its implementations in place. That surface is now provably unreached and is what this issue tracks.

## What #6420 established (traced, in the PR body)

`SetSNATRule`/`SetDNATEntry` and their siblings have three implementations:

- `userspaceShimCompileDataplane` (`loader.go`) — `return nil`; the only production compile path (`Manager.CompileUserspaceShim`).
- `discardingDataPlane` (`compiler_validate_4960.go`) — the #4960 validate pre-pass; discards by contract.
- `(*Manager)` (`maps_nat.go`) — the real eBPF map writers, reachable **only** through `Manager.Compile` → `CompileConfig(m, ...)`, which no production caller reaches: nothing registers a non-userspace backend, `NewDataPlane`/`NewRuntimeDataPlane` hard-reject `TypeEBPF` (#1373/#1476), the sole `dataplane.New()` is `userspace.New()`'s `bpfShim`, and `LegacyDataPlaneAdapter` shadows `Compile`/`ApplyConfig` with the userspace ones.

## Scope

1. **`compileNPTv6`'s `nptv6_rules` writes.** `SetNPTv6Rule` / `DeleteStaleNPTv6` are the last remaining NAT-family writes in `compiler_nat.go`, and `nptv6Adjustment` (plus its RFC 6296 vectors in `nptv6_test.go`) exists only to fill `NPTv6Value.Adjustment`; the Rust helper computes its own (`userspace-dp/src/nptv6.rs` `compute_adjustment`). Held out of #6420 because `compileNPTv6` carries three PRs' worth of live reject-vs-warn disposition logic (#4960 / #5818 / #6894 r9 / #7077) whose error returns are load-bearing, and because two existing guards observe the write:
   - `TestEachValidationPhaseRowRunsItsOwnCompiler_4960` binds the `nptv6` row NAME→BODY via `failOneDP{fail: "SetNPTv6Rule"}` — it would need rebinding onto the config-shaped hard error #6894 r9 added (which `TestHelperRefusedNPTv6PrefixStillHardErrors_7077` already exercises).
   - `TestHelperAcceptedNPTv6PrefixIsSkippedNotRejected_7077`'s `countingNPTv6DP.nptv6Writes != 0` assertion goes vacuous.
   Both are tractable, but they are NPTv6 review surface, not NAT-record review surface.

2. **`maps_nat.go`'s `(*Manager)` writers** and the corresponding `DataPlane` interface methods (`dataplane.go`). This changes an exported interface, so it drags the armed-gate matrices (`armed_gate_legs_test.go`, `armed_gate_matrix_test.go` class1/class2 tables) and every fake that implements the interface without embedding it.

3. **The now-defensive shim overrides.** With no caller, `userspaceShimCompileDataplane`'s and `discardingDataPlane`'s NAT overrides are dead — but they must be removed *together with* the interface methods, never before: a shim that stops overriding a method the interface still declares promotes a future caller to the retired eBPF writer (that promotion hazard is exactly what `TestPrePassShimFidelity` / `prePassShimDivergence` in `compiler_prepass_fidelity_4960_test.go` guards). Note `compiler_prepass_fidelity_4960_test.go`'s `len(shimDecl) < 40 || len(fakeDecl) < 30` vacuity floors will need lowering, since the population legitimately shrinks.

4. **Map helpers left with no production caller** by #6420: `ipToUint32BE`, `ipTo16Bytes` (`maps_helpers.go`), `protocolNumber`, `appPortsFromSpec` (`compiler.go`). Go does not flag unused package-level functions, so nothing reds today.

## Acceptance

- No production `.go` under `pkg/` references a NAT map writer on the `DataPlane` interface.
- The #4960 pre-pass shim and the production compile shim declare the same method set (the fidelity test still passes with its floors adjusted to the new population, not deleted).
- The #7077 / #6894 NPTv6 reject-vs-warn dispositions are unchanged and still bound — a rebinding of the `nptv6` row, not a weakening.
- `go test -count=1 ./...` green.

Behaviour-preserving by the same argument as #6420: the writes already land nowhere on the deployed path.

## #7273 — config: a malformed `policy-options prefix-list` entry is not validated at commit, so the userspace filter matcher still narrows per-token (residual of #6463) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-10-19)

## Problem

`#6463` closed the partial-list narrowing on the userspace filter wire by marking
a term `AddressUnrepresentable` when it carries a malformed address token. That
marker is derived from `term.UnknownAddresses`, which `recordFilterAddrTokens`
populates from **literal** `from source-address` / `destination-address` tokens
only.

A malformed entry inside a referenced `policy-options prefix-list` is a different
provenance and is covered by neither half:

1. **No strict commit gate.** `validateFilterAddressLiteralsStrict` (#3433) walks
   `term.SourceAddresses` / `term.DestAddresses` — literals. Prefix-list
   *references* are validated by `validateFirewallPrefixListReferencesStrict`,
   which checks that the name **resolves**, not that its entries parse. Nothing
   validates `PrefixList.Prefixes`.
2. **No marker.** The term's `UnknownAddresses` stays empty, so
   `snap.AddressUnrepresentable` stays false
   (`pkg/dataplane/userspace/filters.go`), and the Rust `parse_term` accepts the
   snapshot.

So the Rust `parse_address` drops the bad entry per-token and the matcher is
built over the surviving subset — the exact `#6463` narrowing, on the **ordinary
commit path** rather than only the lenient / peer-sync one. A `then discard` /
`then reject` term silently enforces a smaller address set than the operator
wrote and a host in the dropped range falls through to the implicit accept
(fail-OPEN).

## Evidence (firsthand, at `origin/master` 9e593d37c)

A throwaway test in `pkg/config` compiling this via `ParseSetCommand` +
`tree.SetPath` and `CompileConfig` (the STRICT path):

```
set policy-options prefix-list mgmt 10.0.0.0/8
set policy-options prefix-list mgmt 10.0.0.0/99
set firewall family inet filter protect-re term t1 from source-prefix-list mgmt
set firewall family inet filter protect-re term t1 then discard
set interfaces lo0 unit 0 family inet filter input protect-re
```

## #7280 — daemon/cluster: 13 cluster wiring assignments in startClusterComms are bound by nothing — cluster.Manager has no observation seam [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-30)

Split from **#6428**, which decomposed `Daemon.startClusterComms` and, in doing so, measured how much of its wiring is bound by nothing.

## The measurement

`go tool cover -func` over `./pkg/daemon/`: **0.0% statement coverage for all ten builders that run inside the constructor goroutine** (`startClusterComms` itself sits at 13.2%).

**Nilling all 30 wiring assignments at once left `pkg/daemon` and `pkg/cluster` fully green.**

The cause is structural rather than accidental: the tests that call `startClusterComms` deliberately configure it to early-return *before* the goroutine, so nothing downstream of that point is exercised at all.

#6428 bound the **17 observable sites** (15 `ss.*` handles plus `d.syncPeerAddr`/`1`, with both single- and dual-fabric arms), mutation-proven 17/17 with each red naming the dropped field. **This issue is the other 13.**

## The 13 unbound sites

- the ten `d.cluster.Set*()` hooks
- `ss.SetAuthProvider`
- `d.cluster.SetSyncTransport`

They could not be bound in #6428 because **`cluster.Manager` exposes no getter for any of them**. Binding them needs an observation seam in `pkg/cluster` — which is a production-surface change, and correctly out of scope for a pure-code-motion refactor.

## Why this is worth doing rather than filing and forgetting

This is the same class as **#7261**, where #6031's *already-merged* fix turned out to be fully revertible with a green suite: deleting one wiring assignment (`ss.BulkSnapshotSource = ...`) broke nothing, because its five tests called the producer directly rather than through the wiring.

The pattern across all of these is one thing: **a test binds a function where the property is the wiring.** Unbound wiring is invisible in exactly the way that matters — a reviewer reading a clean, focused builder assumes its contents are covered, and after a decomposition that assumption is *more* tempting, not less.

These particular hooks are cluster failover, fencing and sync-transport selection. A silently-dropped assignment there is not a cosmetic defect.

## What is wanted

1. An observation seam on `cluster.Manager` sufficient to assert that each hook was installed — a getter, an exported test accessor, or an installed-set the manager records. Prefer the smallest thing that makes installation observable; this does **not** need to assert behaviour.
2. A binding test for each of the 13, in the shape #6428 used: assert **installation**, one mutation per line, each red naming its field.

## One trap, already paid for once

#6428's first draft of the equivalent test was **vacuous**: it collected the func fields into a table of `any`, and **boxing a typed nil into an interface produces a non-nil interface**, so 14 of 17 mutations stayed green. It was caught only because the mutation matrix was actually run.

Write the checks as direct per-field `== nil` comparisons on the concrete types. If a table is used, it must hold something that preserves nil-ness — and the mutation matrix must be run per line rather than assumed, because this specific test shape fails silently in the safe-looking direction.

the fence strips it. These two topologies have **no accept at all**.

## #7291 — configstore: commit-confirmed on a NEVER-COMMITTED store arms firstCommit=false, so its timeout persists committed=1 over the never-committed DB [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-30)

## Problem

`commitConfirmedLocked` decides whether a pending window's rollback target is the empty bootstrap tree from **`s.compiled == nil` at arm time**. That is the wrong authority: the durable never-committed marker is `everCommitted`, and the two disagree in a reachable state.

After a #1922 Item 1b first-commit rollback the DB on disk is `committed=0` with the **empty** tree. The empty tree **compiles**, so the next `Store.Load` leaves the store at `everCommitted=false` **with `compiled != nil`**. The operator's next `commit confirmed` therefore arms with a non-nil `confirmPrevCfg`, records `FirstCommit=false`, and on timeout takes the non-first branch: `writeActive(emptyTree)` with `persistMarkerCommitted = true`.

That persists **committed=1 over a never-committed DB with an empty tree** — the "operator-committed-empty" state, which `computeBootClass` resolves to **NORMAL**. The restart after it runs the positional claim-all interface rename on an empty config: exactly the #1922 Item 2 case-5 hazard the Item 1b marker exists to prevent.

## Reproduced at `origin/master` (`4170db253`)

Driving the real entry points — `CommitConfirmed`, the rollback timer, `Store.Load` — with the persistence seams capturing which write happens:

```
after Item-1b rollback + restart: everCommitted=false compiled!=nil=true
armed record FirstCommit=false   (the rollback target IS the empty never-committed tree)
rollback: markerWrites(committed)=[] plainWrites=1 everCommitted=true
```

`markerWrites=[]` + `plainWrites=1` is the defect: no `writeActiveMarker(_, false)` at all, so `committed=1` is persisted and `everCommitted` flips to true.

Verified identical on `fix/6538-confirm-first-commit-sentinel` (PR #7290) — that PR deliberately preserves the arm-site derivation and only fixes the RECOVERY-path overload, so this is separate and pre-existing, not a regression from it.

## Why it is the same family as #6538

#6538 removed the overload on the recovery path by recording `Store.confirmPrevFirst` explicitly. This is the remaining half at the ARM site: `s.compiled == nil` is itself an incidental proxy for "first commit", and it is wrong in both directions —

- `everCommitted=false` with `compiled != nil` (this issue): the rollback should write `committed=0` and does not;
- `everCommitted=true` with `compiled == nil` (the #1960 broken-config load: the operator fixes the config and does `commit confirmed`): the rollback would write `committed=0` over a box that HAS a committed config.

## Fix sketch

Set `s.confirmPrevFirst` from the durable marker rather than the compiled pointer — the value of `s.everCommitted` captured **before** `commitConfirmedLocked` sets it true (both the post-rename-converge branch and the success branch set it before the arm site, so the capture has to happen earlier in the function).

Not done in PR #7290 to keep that change scoped to the recovery-path overload the issue described, and because flipping the arm-site predicate changes behaviour on paths #7290 does not otherwise touch.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A `commit confirmed` armed on a never-committed store (`everCommitted=false`) rolls back with the never-committed marker (`committed=0`) and leaves `everCommitted` false.
- [ ] A `commit confirmed` armed on a store that HAS committed but whose config failed to compile (`everCommitted=true`, `compiled==nil`) does NOT write `committed=0` on rollback.
- [ ] Fail-on-revert tests for both directions; the existing `TestFirstCommitRollbackWritesNeverCommittedMarker` must stay green.

*(truncated — 43 lines total)*

than no guard, so the registry needs to key on something sharper than "calls a

## #7296 — selftest: run-selftests.sh does not discover deploy-lib-selftest.sh — a hermetic gate the harness cannot see [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-30)

## Problem

`test/incus/deploy-lib-selftest.sh` is fully hermetic — its own header says "Runs WITHOUT incus or a live VM by mocking `incus exec` / `incus file push` against a local fake-VM rootfs … No cluster, no lock, no network" — but `scripts/run-selftests.sh` does not run it. It is reachable only by hand, via `make test-deploy-lib`.

That is the same shape as the defects this gate exists to catch: **the check is present and the harness that runs checks cannot see it.** `run-selftests.sh` describes itself as the single entry point that "DISCOVERS and runs every hermetic self-test with one command", and its own rationale is that the pre-existing self-tests "all pass but were wired into NOTHING … each self-test could only be run by hand". `deploy-lib-selftest.sh` is still in exactly that state.

## Mechanism — why it is not discovered

Discovery is two hardcoded lists, and `test/incus/` is in neither:

- `scripts/run-selftests.sh:139` — the Python glob is scoped to four directories:
  ```sh
  for t in scripts/image/test_*.py scripts/dist/test_*.py scripts/deploy/test_*.py scripts/test_*.py; do
  ```
- `scripts/run-selftests.sh:146-160` — the shell legs are enumerated by hand (`scripts/image/test-grow-root.sh`, `scripts/dist/selftest.sh`, and three `test/xsk-repro/` legs). There is no `test/incus/` entry.

So a `.py` self-test dropped into `scripts/image/` is picked up automatically (both #6494 and #6497 added one and it ran with no runner change), while a **shell** self-test must be added to the list by hand — and `deploy-lib-selftest.sh`, which predates the runner, never was.

## Why it matters

`deploy-lib.sh` is the shared implementation behind BOTH raw deploy paths (`setup.sh deploy` and `cluster-setup.sh deploy`). It carries the #2162/#2176 stale-pin, dangling-symlink and running-binary verifications, the #4009 rolling-deploy node ordering, and — as of #6493/#7256 — the #1864 `verify-dataplane` pre-flight and the ordering assertions that keep it ahead of `systemctl stop xpfd`.

A regression in any of those makes a deploy report success while the node runs stale code or no dataplane. The suite that catches it is 27 assertions that run in under a second with no root, no incus and no network — and `make selftest` does not run them.

## Suggested fix

Add `run_shell test/incus/deploy-lib-selftest.sh` to the shell self-test section. It needs `bash` (the script uses arrays and `[[ ]]`), which `run_shell` already handles — the `SH_SCRIPTS` lint section selects the interpreter from the shebang, and `deploy-lib-selftest.sh` has `#!/usr/bin/env bash`.

Worth deciding at the same time whether the shell-leg list should keep being hand-maintained. The Python side is glob-discovered and the shell side is not, which is precisely why this one was missed for as long as it was; a `test/incus/*-selftest.sh` glob would close the class rather than this instance. That is a judgement call about how much the runner should assume, so I am not prescribing it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `scripts/run-selftests.sh` runs `test/incus/deploy-lib-selftest.sh` and its pass count rises accordingly.
- [ ] A deliberately-broken `deploy-lib.sh` assertion fails `make selftest`, not just `make test-deploy-lib`.
- [ ] Either the shell-leg list is glob-discovered like the Python one, or the decision to keep it hand-maintained is recorded with its reason.

## Provenance

Found while implementing #6493 (PR #7256, merged), which added nine cases to `deploy-lib-selftest.sh` including the verify-dataplane pre-flight gate and its call-site ordering assertions. Those cases are green and, today, `make selftest` does not run them.

## #7297 — test: nothing pins that `commit check` cannot reach the host-mutating dataplane compiler (#4960 validate-only half) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-30)

Spun out of #4960. The apply-side redesign is #7289; this is the **validate-only** half, and the answer is that it is currently SAFE — but nothing holds it that way.

## The question, and the answer

#4960 is about `pkg/dataplane`'s `CompileConfig` mutating the host mid-compile: `compileZones` creates VLANs and reconciles addresses before later phases can still fail. The natural follow-on worry is whether a **validate-only** path reaches that compiler. A `commit check` that mutates the host would be a defect independent of the apply-side work.

It does not. Traced:

```
Store.CommitCheck -> compileTree -> compileTreeStrict
                  -> config.CompileConfig / CompileConfigForNode
```

That is **pkg/config's** compiler (AST → typed structs), a different function in a different package from **pkg/dataplane's** `CompileConfig(dp, cfg, ...)`. The two share a name — which is precisely why "commit check compiles the config" is easy to misread as "commit check runs the dataplane compiler". Only the dataplane one touches netlink.

The day-0 gate is the same: `CheckText` (`check.go`, `xpfd check-config`) routes through the same `compileTreeStrict`, which `store.go` documents as the shared pipeline so the two callers "can never drift apart".

Stronger than a call-site audit: `pkg/dataplane` is **not in `pkg/configstore`'s in-repo import closure at all**.

```
$ go list -deps ./pkg/configstore | grep -c psaab/xpf/pkg/dataplane
0
$ go list -deps ./pkg/config | grep -c psaab/xpf/pkg/dataplane
0
```

So today it is impossible at link level, not merely absent by inspection.

## Why it still needs a guard

Nothing enforces it. Every `Compile` call site in the tree is on an APPLY path (`applyConfig`, `ApplyConfig`), but that is a property of the current call sites, and a call-site test would pass again the moment someone added a different one. The realistic regression is someone adding a "dataplane pre-check" to `CommitCheck` for better error messages — which reads like an improvement and would silently make `commit check` mutate the host.

Partial enforcement exists by accident: `pkg/config` importing `pkg/dataplane` is an import CYCLE (dataplane imports config), so Go itself refuses that one edge. But `pkg/configstore` → `pkg/dataplane` compiles fine, and so does `pkg/configstore/journal` → `pkg/dataplane`. Those edges are unguarded.

## Acceptance

- A test pins the property at the IMPORT boundary — the level at which it is actually guaranteed — rather than at any one call site.
- Adding the import directly to `pkg/configstore`, or transitively via a package it reaches, makes it RED and names the chain.
- The walk has a non-vacuity control: a test that visited only the starting package (wrong root, silent parse failure) must fail rather than pass.

## #7315 — grpcapi: thread an admission-lease context through pkg/natshow so the four ShowText NAT walks honour cancellation (#6553 residual) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-31)

Successor to #6553 (PR pending), which gated all six gRPC NAT full-table conntrack walks on the shared `diagcmd.SessionWalkLimiter`.

## What #6553 shipped

- `GetNATPoolStats` / `GetNATDestination`: `AcquireCtx` **plus** lease-context sampling inside `countNATSessions`' v4 and v6 callbacks. Both halves.
- `ShowText{persistent-nat, persistent-nat-detail, nat-source-rule-detail, nat-dest-rule-detail}`: **admission only** (plain `Acquire`, matching the existing ShowText precedent in `server_show_flow.go` / `server_show_system.go`).

## The residual

The four `ShowText` topics reach their walks through `pkg/natshow`:

- `natshow.RenderPersistent` / `RenderPersistentDetail` — `pkg/natshow/persistent.go:85`, `:102`
- `natshow.RenderSourceRuleDetail` — `pkg/natshow/source.go:40`, `:48`
- `natshow.RenderDestRuleDetail` — `pkg/natshow/dest.go:43`, `:51`

None of those `Render*` helpers takes a `context.Context`, and `pkg/natshow` is **shared with `pkg/cli`** — it exists precisely so the gRPC `ShowText` path and the local CLI path single-source these renderers (#1687). Adding a `ctx` parameter is therefore a cross-surface signature change touching `pkg/natshow`, `pkg/grpcapi/server_show_nat.go` and every `pkg/cli` caller. #6553 declined to smuggle that into a bug fix.

## Why it matters

These four topics are on the **fabric** listener (`ShowText` is in `fabricAllowedUnaryMethods`), unlike the loopback-only NAT RPCs. A walk that holds its slot after the client is gone keeps that slot away from the REST surfaces that *do* honour cancellation — REST and gRPC alias one 4-slot `diagcmd.SessionWalkLimiter`.

The admission gate bounds *concurrency*, which is the larger half. This is about *duration* under a disconnected client.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `pkg/natshow`'s four walking `Render*` helpers accept a `context.Context` and sample it inside their session-iteration callbacks.
- [ ] `server_show_nat.go` switches from `sessionWalkLimiter.Acquire()` to `AcquireCtx(ctx)` and passes the lease down; `ShowText` already has `ctx` in scope.
- [ ] `pkg/cli` callers pass an appropriate context (the CLI's own, or `context.Background()` where none exists).
- [ ] A probe in the shape of `TestNATWalkStopsOnCancelledLease6553` — count visited rows, assert an early stop, and include the live-context control so the assertion cannot go vacuous.

## #7318 — dhcp: Kea Dhcp4 runs on an AF_PACKET raw socket, so host-inbound cannot gate DHCPv4 at all — decide the dhcp-socket-type posture [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-30)

Successor to #6460 (the enforcement half). #6460 shipped the commit-time advisory; this issue carries the behaviour choice it deliberately did not make.

## The residual

xpf renders Kea's `Dhcp4` with **no** `dhcp-socket-type` key — `interfaces-config` carries only the `interfaces` list (`pkg/dhcpserver/dhcpserver.go`, the `dhcp4` object). Kea's default is therefore `raw`, and the server receives on an **AF_PACKET** socket.

AF_PACKET delivery happens **before** the netfilter input hook. So this is not a matched-the-wrong-rule case that a better nft rule could fix: the packet never reaches the `xpf_hostinbound` chain. **No netfilter change can ever gate DHCPv4 here.** A zone whose `host-inbound-traffic system-services` omits `dhcp` does not stop the server answering on an interface its `dhcp-local-server` group binds.

Verified at `origin/master`: no code path EMITS `dhcp-socket-type`. (Cite corrected 2026-08-30 — the original wording said a repo-wide grep returns zero hits; it now returns 4, all of them prose describing the absence (`docs/host-inbound-multicast.md`, `pkg/dhcpserver/README.md`, `pkg/config/compiler_validate_warn_dhcp_hostinbound.go`). The substantive claim was unaffected.)

## Why #6460 shipped only the advisory

The advisory (`validateDHCPServerHostInboundBypassWarnings`, PR referenced below) makes the exposure loud and names the mechanism per family. It deliberately does **not** tell the operator to add the token as a *fix*, because on the v4 path adding the token enforces nothing — that would restate the same false signal in a new place.

## The choice this issue owes

Moving Dhcp4 to `dhcp-socket-type: udp` would put the server on a normal UDP socket that traverses netfilter INPUT. But:

1. **It is a behaviour change, not a bug fix.** Kea on UDP sockets cannot properly serve clients that have no address yet — the direct DHCPDISCOVER/DHCPOFFER exchange to a client with no IP needs raw broadcast reach. Flipping it unconditionally would break address-less clients, which is the normal DHCP case.
2. **It would not, by itself, close the exposure.** A DHCPDISCOVER is addressed to `255.255.255.255`, and every per-zone host-inbound rule — the accepts and the #3361 catch-all deny — is scoped `<fam> daddr <zone unicast addrs>`, with the base chain at `policy accept` (`pkg/nftables/netlink_installer.go`). A broadcast destination still matches no rule and still falls through. Closing it needs the **per-zone broadcast/multicast class gate**, which is #4455 Component A — PLAN-KILLed (`iifname` at INPUT is the post-VRF, post-collapse, post-rename identity, not the logical unit), and re-killed independently across #6460's 65-round research arc.

So the honest framing is: **the v4 leg needs BOTH a socket-type migration AND the killed class gate.** Neither alone is sufficient, and the socket-type half carries its own client-compat regression.

## The DHCPv6 sibling

`Dhcp6` has no raw mode — it already receives on UDP. Its leg is purely the multicast fall-through: a client addresses the server at `ff02::1:2`, which matches no per-zone unicast `daddr` rule. That half is exactly #4455 Component A and needs nothing new from this issue.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A decision, recorded either way: ship an opt-in `dhcp-socket-type` knob, or document the raw-socket posture as permanent and close.
- [ ] If a knob ships: address-less-client behaviour is validated, not assumed.
- [ ] Any enforcement claim is gated on #4455 Component A actually existing — a socket-type flip alone must not be described as closing the exposure.

## See also

- #6460 — the advisory that made this visible (closed by the referenced PR).

## #7323 — config-epoch guard: tagged-ConfigEpoch variant reopens the active/active reverse direction without a wire field (#6419 successor) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-03)

Successor to #6419, which was closed on the finding that the "reuse the RG0
authority's config-generation namespace" shortcut cannot work. A post-merge
hostile review of #7304 (the PR that recorded that close) constructed a variant
that answers all three of the objections, **without a new wire field and without
a `ProtocolVersion` bump** — both of which #6419's close had asserted were
required. That close was therefore too categorical, and this issue carries the
surviving design.

Background and the corrected analysis are in `docs/session-sync-architecture.md`
(item-1 residual section), updated in #7322.

## The problem, unchanged

In active/active the reverse (non-authority → authority) direction of the #5274
`configEpochStale` guard is inert / fail-OPEN: a non-authority stamps a
generation its `configGenCounter` has not advanced since it last held the
authority, and the authority's `lastAppliedConfigGen` never advances because it
applies no peer config. No false reject, but no stale-permit protection either.
Regression-pinned by `pkg/cluster/sync_config_epoch_active_active_6284_test.go`.

## The proposal: a stamp-source tag inside the existing field

Reserve the top bit of `ConfigEpoch` as a **stamp-source tag**.

| Sender state | Wire value | Receiver expectation |
|---|---|---|
| RG0 authority | raw `configGenCounter` (tag clear) | a non-authority receiver compares against `lastAppliedConfigGen` — exactly today's behaviour |
| Converged non-authority | `tag \| lastAppliedConfigGen` | an authority receiver strips the tag and compares against `configGenCounter` |
| Not converged (pinned/reset applied mark) | `0` | existing fail-OPEN (`epoch == 0` disables the check) |

A receiver accepts only the encoding its **own** role expects. Any tag/role
mismatch means the sender's role assumption disagrees with the receiver's, so
the epoch is treated as 0 and the guard disables.

### Why that answers #6419's three objections

1. **Role-branching requirement** — conceded, not defeated. Each counter is live
   in exactly one role, so both the stamp site and the threshold site branch on
   `IsLocalPrimary(0)`. The tag makes that branch *observable to the receiver*,
   which is the part the untagged shortcut lacked.

## #7328 — config-sync: #5863's (epoch × generation) dedupe marker defeats #4151's re-push convergence — a rejected/failed apply is never re-pushed [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

**Severity: Medium — HA convergence.** Repro included and confirmed at `origin/master` `d3aa9afdb`.
Found while reviewing the #6419 disposition (#7304/#7322); it is orthogonal to that issue.

## The contradiction

Two features state opposite contracts about the same event, and the later one wins.

**#4151 (M-2) deliberately pins the high-water so the SAME generation can be re-pushed.**
`configApplyLoop` advances `lastAppliedConfigGen` only on a nil `OnConfigReceived`
return; on failure it explicitly does not, and says why
(`pkg/cluster/sync_conn_config.go`):

> The apply did not take effect (compile/promote failure or a transient
> RG0-primary rejection). Do NOT advance the high-water: leaving it at the
> last-applied generation **keeps the standby eligible for the primary's
> re-push so it re-converges** instead of being silently stranded (M-2/#4151).

`errConfigSyncRejectedPrimary`'s own doc (`pkg/daemon/daemon_ha_sync.go`) is even
more explicit:

> the transient dual-active window **must heal via the peer's re-push** once
> this node settles into secondary (M-2/#4151).

**#5863 guarantees that re-push never happens.** `reconcileConfigSyncToPeer`
claims its `(epoch × generation)` dedupe marker **before** sending:

```go
d.configSyncMu.Lock()
if d.configSyncHasPushed && d.configSyncPushedEpoch == epoch && d.configSyncPushedGen == gen {
        d.configSyncMu.Unlock()
        return                    // <-- every later trigger no-ops here
}
d.configSyncHasPushed = true      // <-- claimed BEFORE the push
d.configSyncPushedEpoch = epoch
d.configSyncPushedGen = gen
d.configSyncMu.Unlock()
...
ss.QueueConfig(configText)
```

## #7331 — flaky: pkg/ddns is non-deterministic at rest — reproduced on an untouched base commit [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

## What was measured

`pkg/ddns` fails intermittently on a tree with **no local changes**. Reproduced on the untouched base commit `73b2ce98d`: **5 runs -> 1 red, 4 green.**

The failing test is **not stable between runs**, which is the part that makes this worth filing rather than retrying:

| where | test that failed |
|---|---|
| untouched base `73b2ce98d` | `TestPartialDualStackTeardownKeepsSharedDHCID` |
| a worktree with unrelated changes | `TestRFC2136UnsignedUpdateWarnsOncePerProvider` + `TestManagerPTRNotAuthCountedNotFailed` |

A flake that moves between tests points at shared state or a port/listener collision across the package, not at one bad test. A previously-observed instance in this package was `surface_a_rfc2136_test.go:259: bind: address already in use` (a hardcoded-port listener race, #7009) — so this may be the same root cause reaching more tests than #7009 records, or a second mechanism.

## Why it matters more than an ordinary flake

It is **actively costing verdicts**. During this campaign a PR body cited `go test ./...` rc=1 and attributed it to master; establishing whether the branch owned it required a separate 5-run bisect against base. Every lane that runs the full Go suite pays that tax, and the failure mode is one where a lane can reasonably conclude *its own change* broke something.

## Not yet established

- whether it is the #7009 port-bind race widened, or independent
- whether it is order-dependent (`-shuffle`) or time-dependent
- whether `-count=1` vs a warm cache changes the rate

## Suggested first step

Run `go test ./pkg/ddns/ -count=1 -race -shuffle=on` in a loop (20+ iterations) and record which test fails each time. If the failures cluster on tests that bind a listener, it is #7009's mechanism; if they spread across unrelated tests, look for package-level shared state.

Filed from a campaign observation rather than a dedicated investigation — the measurement above is firsthand, the diagnosis is not.

## #7334 — vrrp: the self-frame check compares against ONE selected address, not the interface's address set [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-30)

Split out of #6560, which fixed the two DELIVERY paths (the AF_PACKET `ETH_P_ALL` TX tap and IP multicast loopback). This is the residual in the COMPARISON itself, deliberately not folded in.

## The residual

`resolveLocalIPv4` (`pkg/vrrp/instance_addr.go`) selects **one** address — the lowest non-VIP IPv4 — and stores it as the snapshot. `resolveIPv6LinkLocal` does the same for the lowest non-VIP link-local. The receive-path self-checks then compare a frame's source against that single value.

So the self-check also fails with a **non-nil** snapshot: a self-advert sent from address A bypasses the comparison once the selected source has become B. `resolveEqualPriorityMaster` then compares `peerCmp` (our own old source A) against `localCmp` (our own new source B) and steps down whenever `A > B` — a coin flip.

Plausible triggers: flush-and-restore reordering across the #2528 RETH-MAC cycle, secondary-address churn, or a new link-local after the MAC change on the v6 side.

## Why it was not folded into #6560

#6560 suppressed both mechanisms by which a self-frame reaches the receiver at all — `PACKET_IGNORE_OUTGOING` plus an `sll_pkttype` drop on the AF_PACKET path, and `IP_MULTICAST_LOOP`/`IPV6_MULTICAST_LOOP` on the fallback raw sockets. With those in place a self-frame should not be delivered, which makes this residual much narrower than it was.

It is still worth closing, because the comparison is the last line of defence if a delivery path is ever re-opened (a new socket, a kernel without `PACKET_IGNORE_OUTGOING` **and** a path that bypasses the pkttype check), and because the current shape is a silent coin flip rather than a fail-safe.

## Candidate fixes

- Compare against the interface's address **set** rather than one selected address.
- Or compare the frame's **source MAC** against `vi.iface.HardwareAddr` on the AF_PACKET path, where the full Ethernet header is already in hand. Note `grep HardwareAddr pkg/vrrp/*.go` (non-test) currently returns zero hits, so the L2 identity is available and entirely unused.

Whichever is chosen must **fail open** on an unresolvable comparison, matching the posture #6560 established: dropping a frame that cannot be classified is a self-inflicted master-down, strictly worse than the bug.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A self-advert from a *previously selected* source address is dropped even though the current snapshot names a different one.
- [ ] A genuine peer advert is never dropped, including when the local snapshot is unresolvable.
- [ ] Fail-on-revert test.
- [ ] `make test-failover` (VRRP code).

## See also

- #6560 and its PR — the delivery-path fixes and the `pkg/vrrp/README.md` section "Self-frame filtering does not depend on the address snapshot", whose "Not addressed here" paragraph names this residual.
- #2528 — the RETH-MAC flush window.

## #7337 — userspace-dp/cos: unresolvable interface scheduler-map/classifier/rewrite-rule refs are silently unenforced — needs a Go strict gate BEFORE a Rust backstop [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-31)

## Problem

The four CoS interface reference fields resolve Rust-side with a bare `.get(...)` yielding `None`, with no `Missing*Ref` and no error:

- `cos_scheduler_map`, `cos_dscp_classifier`, `cos_ieee8021_classifier`, `cos_dscp_rewrite_rule`
- resolved in `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/forwarding_build/cos.rs` (`build_cos_iface_config` at ~`:642`, classifier arms at ~`:813`/`:822`)

An unresolvable reference silently degrades QoS to best-effort: the interface materializes no scheduler queues, or the classifier arm contributes nothing, while the committed config still says the interface is shaped/classified.

## Why this was split out of #6540

#6540 asked for these "in the same change" as `MissingPolicerRef`. Implementing it as written would introduce a **brick**, and that is worth recording rather than rediscovering.

The policer fix is safe because it has a **Go strict commit gate in front of it** (#2217 Finding A, `pkg/config/compiler_validate_strict_filter.go`). A freshly committed config can never carry a dangling policer reference, so the Rust rejection only ever fires on version/snapshot drift over the lenient boot / HA-peer-sync path. That is the shape of the whole `MissingFilterRef` / `ScreenMissingProfileRef` family.

The CoS interface references have **no strict gate**. All four are validated only as warnings, in `pkg/config/compiler_validate_warn.go`:

- scheduler-map — `:1668`
- dscp classifier — `:1686`
- ieee-802.1 classifier — `:1693`
- dscp rewrite-rule — `:1700`

(`validateClassOfServiceSchedulerMapRefsStrict` exists but gates a *scheduler-map entry → scheduler* reference, a different edge. There is no strict gate on *interface → scheduler-map/classifier/rewrite-rule*.)

So adding a Rust hard-reject today produces: operator runs `commit`, commit **succeeds** with a warning, and the helper then **refuses the entire snapshot** — taking down all forwarding config, not just CoS, on a config the commit gate accepted. That is strictly worse than the current degradation, and it inverts the #1960 no-brick rationale.

## Required sequencing

1. Add `validateClassOfServiceInterfaceRefsStrict` in `pkg/config` covering all four fields, hard-rejecting at strict commit and downgrading to a warning on the tolerant path (reuse the existing `lenient*` opt, as the sibling NAT/filter gates do).
2. Only then add the Rust backstop (`SnapshotIntegrityError::MissingCoSRef` or per-field variants) in `forwarding_build/cos.rs`.
3. Fail-on-revert test driving the lenient/HA-sync path, mirroring `missing_policer_ref_6540_*` in `userspace-dp/src/filter/tests.rs`.

Step 1 is a **behavior change at commit**: operators with a typo'd scheduler-map who commit successfully today would begin failing commit. That needs to be a deliberate, reviewed decision, which is the other reason it does not belong bolted onto #6540.

## Severity

Lower than #6540. An unresolvable scheduler-map degrades QoS to best-effort; it does not admit traffic a policy would deny, and it does not over-permit bandwidth the way a missing policer does.

## Acceptance criteria

## #7338 — cluster: 'No IP monitoring failures' is printed for an RG that ip-monitoring has DEMOTED — the status renderer's `ip:` prefix filter cannot see global-threshold mode's aggregate debt [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-30)

## Problem

`show chassis cluster ip-monitoring status` reports **"No IP monitoring failures"** for a redundancy group that ip-monitoring has actively demoted — and, in the same output, shows nothing about the individual unreachable targets either. The screen is blank in **both** dimensions on the primary HA failover diagnostic.

The renderer filters failures by string prefix (`pkg/cluster/status.go:698`):

```go
		for _, f := range rg.MonitorFails {
			if strings.HasPrefix(f, "ip:") {
				ipFails = append(ipFails, f)
			}
		}
```

But in **global-threshold mode** the engine installs a single aggregate debt under a fixed name that deliberately does not carry that prefix (`pkg/cluster/monitor.go:720`):

```go
const ipAggregateMonitorName = "ip-monitoring"
```

whose own doc-comment says it is *"deliberately distinct from the per-target `ip:<addr>` debts"*. It is installed at `monitor.go:769-777` once the cumulative weight crosses the threshold:

```go
		if cumulative >= rg.IPMonitoring.GlobalThreshold {
			w, _ := config.ClampInterfaceMonitorWeight(rg.IPMonitoring.GlobalWeight)
			desired[ipAggregateMonitorName] = w
		}
		return desired
```

That name lands verbatim in `rg.MonitorFails` (`pkg/cluster/election.go`), the prefix filter never matches it, and the renderer falls through to `status.go:713`:

```go
				fmt.Fprintln(&b, "  No IP monitoring failures")
```

And because global-threshold mode installs **no per-target debts by design** (`desiredRGIPDebts` returns early — see the doc at `monitor.go:740-748`: *"A SINGLE debt equal to global-weight … No per-target debts"*), the individual unreachable targets are invisible too.

Reaches both operator surfaces: CLI (`pkg/cli/cli_show_cluster.go:401`) and gRPC (`pkg/grpcapi/server_show_cluster_text.go:202`).
