## #7342 — flow: enforce security flow tcp-session initial/closing/time-wait timeouts — needs a CLOSING vs TIME_WAIT close-state split first [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-31)

Follow-up to #6539, which stopped the three leaves being **rendered** as enforced. This issue is the other honest outcome: actually enforcing them.

## Why this is not a small additive wire field

`initial-timeout` alone would be. It maps 1:1 onto `SessionTimeouts.tcp_opening_ns` (`userspace-dp/src/session/mod.rs:269`), whose own comment says *"Not operator-configurable yet … A future config knob would set it here without touching the state machine"*, and #3527 already built the per-zone override for that same window.

The other two cannot be done that way. `session_timeout_ns` (`userspace-dp/src/session/mod.rs:2232`) splits a TCP close only two ways:

```rust
if is_closing(tcp_flags) {
    if has_rst(tcp_flags) { TCP_RST_TIMEOUT_NS }   // 2s
    else { TCP_CLOSING_TIMEOUT_NS }                // 30s, described in-source
}                                                  // as "the full 30s TIME_WAIT-style window"
```

Junos distinguishes CLOSING (after the first FIN) from TIME_WAIT (after the close completes). The dataplane has **one** post-FIN window. Mapping `closing-timeout` onto it is a semantic guess; mapping `time-wait-timeout` onto it is an equally arguable guess; mapping both is impossible. So enforcement needs a close-state split in the Rust session machine before the wire work is even well-defined.

## Scope

1. Split the post-FIN state in `userspace-dp/src/session/` into CLOSING and TIME_WAIT, with the FIN-handshake completion that separates them.
2. Carry all three leaves in one additive wire bump — Go `omitempty` + Rust `#[serde(default)]`, the repo's skew-tolerant pattern — into `SessionTimeouts`.
3. Flip the three entries in `config.TCPSessionTimeoutLeaves` (`pkg/config/flow_tcp_timeouts_6539.go`). That is the single authority added by #6539: flipping `Enforced` retires the render annotation from REST, CLI and gRPC **and** the commit advisory at once. `pkg/dataplane/userspace/flow_tcp_timeout_carrier_6539_test.go` fails until the table agrees with the wire, so the two cannot drift.
4. Decide the upgrade posture. Today a configured value is inert; making it live activates whatever an operator already committed. A large `initial-timeout` becomes a half-open pin, so this wants a bound or at least a release note — the schema validator allows `0..MaxDurationSeconds`, and narrowing it would reject configs that commit cleanly today.

Doing all three behind one wire bump is deliberately cheaper than doing `initial-timeout` now: one protocol change, **one cluster smoke**, one release note.

## Owed

Reaches the Rust helper binary and bumps the snapshot wire, so this **owes a cluster smoke** on the loss userspace cluster (v4 + v6, push + reverse) — see `docs/engineering-style.md`.

## #7343 — converge: make the applied-marker invariant a compile-time guard — typed marker whose advance takes the error, plus a driver registry [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-30)

Follow-up to #6533, which PLAN-KILLED the proposed `analysistest` rule on measured evidence (`docs/applied-marker-invariant.md`). This is the mechanism that *would* work, costed honestly.

## Why a lint cannot do this

Measured at `f4a5297be` and written up in full in the doc: the rule missed 3 of 3 sampled historical defects, because the applied/published/converged vocabulary is the **remedy** each fix introduced rather than the defect's signature; and it flagged the mechanisms held up as correct, because they are correct via a caller contract (`rg_state.go`'s `MarkApplied` contains no error at all) or a status readback (`process_status.go`) — neither of which is a lexically-dominating nil-error check.

The property is semantic. Making it checkable means changing the API so the unsafe form cannot be written, not adding a rule that inspects the safe one.

## Proposed mechanism

A small `converge` package:

1. **A typed marker whose advance takes the error.** `m.Advance(gen, err)` is a no-op on non-nil, so a marker cannot be stamped without the caller holding the outcome. Signatures encode contracts — this is the `docs/engineering-style.md` preference applied to the thing that keeps regressing.
2. **A driver registry.** Each marker registers the periodic converger that re-drives it, and a test walks the registry asserting every marker has one whose predicate is `desired != applied`. That is the issue's **I2**, and it is the half that actually made the twelve prior fixes work — storage without a driver is the bug.
3. **A deliberate escape hatch, spelled out.** `pkg/dhcpserver` advances its marker on failure *on purpose* (#6535: a retry allocates a fresh gen so the superseded guard never blocks it, with convergence carried by `ClaimApplyRetry`). Any design that cannot express "advances on failure, converged elsewhere" will be `//nolint`-ed at that site — which is the failure mode #6533 was killed for. The escape must be a first-class, registry-visible declaration naming the driver, not a suppression.

## Cost

**43 non-test assignment sites**, concentrated in `pkg/dataplane/userspace`'s publish paths (`manager_compile.go`, `process_status.go`, `manager_overlay.go`, `manager_worker_arm_5134.go`, `manager_fabric_sync.go`, `manager_neighbor.go`), plus `pkg/feeds`, `pkg/configstore`, `pkg/routing`, `pkg/ddns`, `pkg/daemon`, `pkg/dhcpserver`, `pkg/ipmon`.

Not all 43 want migrating — copies, zero-resets, `append` accumulators and view read-outs are not markers at all (see the doc's Measurement 1). Triaging that set is the first task, and it is also the honest test of whether the abstraction fits: if a third of the real markers need the escape hatch, the guard is not buying much.

**This is not the ~30 lines the parent issue estimated.** It touches dataplane publish paths, so it wants its own research pass before implementation, and any change to those paths owes a cluster smoke.

## Meanwhile

The invariant stays review-enforced, with the two reviewer questions recorded at the end of `docs/applied-marker-invariant.md`.

## Problem

        for k in keys:
            getattr(h, SCENARIO_METHODS[k])()

```

and `bake.py:695-698` treats exit 0 as a pass:

**A scenario that `return`s is indistinguishable from one that asserted.** On a bake host without `qemu-utils`, scenario Q is skipped *entirely* — including the structural probe — the gate exits 0, and `finalize_artifacts` proceeds to `sign_step`, stamping `validated: true` into the **minisigned** manifest with zero libvirt/plain-QEMU evidence behind it.

`validate.py:29` (module docstring) sells the structural leg as unconditional:

## #7350 — test: TestStartClusterCommsWiresBulkSnapshotSource7259 races the publish-then-wire window — polls for the object, asserts a field wired later [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-30)

**Severity: Low — test soundness, not a production defect.** Found while landing #7349 (#7328); disclosed there rather than folded in, since this is #7259's test and a separate concern.

## The race

`startClusterComms` (`pkg/daemon/daemon_ha_sync.go`) publishes the SessionSync **before** it wires it:

```
:910  publishSessionSyncIfCurrent(commsGen, ss)   <- getSessionSync() becomes non-nil HERE
:915  wireSessionSyncTransportRefs(...)
:922  wireSessionSyncConfigCallbacks(ss)
:924  wireSessionSyncPeerCallbacks(ss)            <- sets ss.BulkSnapshotSource
:926  wireSessionSyncFailoverCallbacks(ss)
```

`ss.BulkSnapshotSource` is assigned at `pkg/daemon/daemon_ha_comms_wiring.go:289`, inside `wireSessionSyncPeerCallbacks`.

`TestStartClusterCommsWiresBulkSnapshotSource7259` (`pkg/daemon/bulk_snapshot_wiring_7259_test.go`, ~:129-145) polls for the OBJECT and then immediately asserts a FIELD that is set two wiring calls later:

```go
for deadline := time.Now().Add(5 * time.Second); time.Now().Before(deadline); {
        if ss = d.getSessionSync(); ss != nil {
                break
        }
        time.Sleep(10 * time.Millisecond)
}
...
if ss.BulkSnapshotSource == nil {
        t.Fatal("#7259: startClusterComms published a SessionSync with NO BulkSnapshotSource ...")
}
```

The poll's exit condition is satisfied at `:910`. The assertion's subject is written at `:924`. Nothing orders them.

## Not a production bug

`BulkSnapshotSource` has exactly one reader — `pkg/cluster/sync_bulk.go:60`, inside `doBulkSync` — which runs from goroutines spawned by `ss.Start()`, after all wiring. That ordering is the documented contract at `pkg/daemon/daemon_ha_sync.go:789`:

> `publishSessionSyncIfCurrent` -> ALL wiring -> `ss.Start`. Every `ss.On*` callback MUST be installed before `ss.Start`, which spawns the accept/connect goroutines that invoke them.

So no production consumer can observe the partially-wired object. Only a test reaching in via `getSessionSync()` can.

## #7353 — cos: ieee-802.1 rewrite-rules are rendered as fully modeled and NEVER published — no builder site, no wire carrier [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-30)

Found while fixing the CoS family of #6534 (PR #7348), and deliberately **not** annotated there — see below.

## The gap

`FormatCoSRewriteRules` renders `ieee-802.1` rewrite-rules **from config**, including their entries:

```
pkg/dataplane/userspace/format/cos_show.go:477   for _, name := range sortedMapKeys(cos.IEEE8021RewriteRules) {
pkg/dataplane/userspace/format/cos_show.go:482       for _, e := range cos.IEEE8021RewriteRules[name].Entries {
```

Nothing publishes them. Verified end to end at current master:

```
# builder — every non-test, non-format reference in pkg/dataplane/userspace/
grep -rn 'IEEE8021RewriteRules' --include='*.go' pkg/dataplane/userspace/ \
    | grep -v '/format/' | grep -v _test
  → NONE

# Rust snapshot — the only rewrite carrier
userspace-dp/src/protocol/cos.rs:25   #[serde(rename = "dscp_rewrite_rules", default)]
userspace-dp/src/protocol/cos.rs:26   pub dscp_rewrite_rules: Vec<CoSDSCPRewriteRuleSnapshot>,
  → no ieee8021 rewrite carrier at all
```

So an operator configures 802.1p CoS marking, `show` reports it as fully modeled with its entries, and **no packet is ever marked**. There is no builder site to fix and no field on the wire to carry it.

**This is NOT the #6534 shape.** #6534 is a per-object skip that a renderer reports as installed — the object is correctly excluded and the surface lies about that one object. This is **wholesale silent unenforcement of an entire feature**: no site skips anything, because nothing was ever built.

Note the contrast with the classifier half, which works: `IEEE8021Classifiers` **are** published (`pkg/dataplane/userspace/cos.go:80`) and **are** carried (`protocol/cos.rs:16` `ieee8021_classifiers`). Only the rewrite direction is missing, which is likely why it went unnoticed — 802.1p appears supported because ingress classification is.

## Why #7348 deliberately did not annotate it

Annotating those entries as "skipped" would have **misreported a bigger gap as a smaller one** — it would tell the operator "this entry was excluded" when the truth is "this feature is not implemented". #7348 instead pinned the *non*-annotation with its own test:

`pkg/dataplane/userspace/format/cos_exclusion_6534_test.go:133`
`TestCoSIEEE8021RewriteRuleIsNotFalselyAnnotated_6534`

That test exists to **prevent the wrong fix** — a future well-meaning change that extends the #6534 annotation to these entries would red it. That is unusual enough to state plainly: the guard is not protecting a behaviour, it is protecting a distinction.

## #7356 — class-of-service: ieee-802.1 rewrite-rules are configured, validated and RENDERED but never published to the dataplane [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

## Problem

`class-of-service rewrite-rules ieee-802.1 <name>` is parsed, compiled into `ClassOfServiceConfig.IEEE8021RewriteRules`, strict-validated, and rendered by `show class-of-service rewrite-rules` as a **fully modeled** rule with its per-code-point entries — and is **never published to the dataplane at all**.

`buildClassOfServiceSnapshot` (`pkg/dataplane/userspace/cos.go`) publishes `DSCPClassifiers`, `IEEE8021Classifiers`, `INetPrecedenceClassifiers`, `DSCPRewriteRules` and `SchedulerMaps`. There is no `IEEE8021RewriteRules` branch, and no `snap.IEEE8021RewriteRules` field.

So an operator configures 802.1p rewriting, sees it listed with all its code points, and no PCP bits are ever rewritten.

## How this was found

While fixing the CoS family of #6534. The per-entry annotation added there deliberately does **not** cover ieee-802.1 rewrite-rules, because annotating their entries as "skipped" would misreport a wholesale gap as an entry-level one. That non-annotation is pinned by `TestCoSIEEE8021RewriteRuleIsNotFalselyAnnotated_6534` so a later change cannot quietly widen the annotation into this and make the bigger problem look like the smaller one.

Note the shape difference from #6534: this is not a fail-closed exclusion. Nothing decided this rule was unrepresentable and dropped it. The publish path was simply never written, while every layer above it — parser, compiler, strict validator, renderer — behaves as though it had been. That is why no drop-warning exists for it and why a log-based audit could not have found it.

## Contrast with the DSCP sibling

`DSCPRewriteRules` IS published and IS enforced, which makes the asymmetry easy to miss: the renderer treats both families as `modeled: true` and prints their entries the same way.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Decide: implement 802.1p rewrite in the dataplane, or reject/warn at commit that the stanza is unenforced.
- [ ] If implemented: publish the collection, and extend the #6534 per-entry annotation to it (retiring the guard test above, deliberately, rather than by accident).
- [ ] If not implemented: `show class-of-service rewrite-rules` must say so for the ieee-802.1 family, and `docs/feature-coverage.md` must record it.
- [ ] Either way, the guard test's comment must stop being true silently.

## #7357 — #6534 remainder: flow-export + the two ifindex-dependent port-mirroring drops (the one place an applied-set readback IS the right mechanism) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-02)

## Scope

What is left of #6534 after the NAT (#7330, merged), CoS (#7348) and port-mirroring (#7354) families. Filed so the remainder is explicit rather than implied by #6534 staying open.

## 1. Flow-export server with an out-of-range port

`pkg/dataplane/userspace/flow.go:238` skips a flow-server whose port is negative or above 65535, so no collector entry is published, while the surfaces render the server from config.

Not done in #7354 because this one has **three** separate renderers:

- `pkg/cli/cli_show_routing.go:1109`
- `pkg/cli/cli_show_flow.go:1228`
- `pkg/grpcapi/server_show_forwarding.go:139`

Hand-copying an annotation into three places is how the duplication got here. This wants the renderer single-sourced into `pkg/dataplane/userspace/format` first — the same move `pkg/natshow` (#1687) and `dpformat` already made — and then one annotation.

## 2. The two runtime-dependent port-mirroring drops

`buildMirrorConfigSnapshots` also drops an instance when:

- the output interface does not resolve to an ifindex, or
- the ingress interface is already claimed by a lower-sorted instance (one output per ingress ifindex).

Both depend on the runtime **interface table**, not on config, so the shared-predicate mechanism used for every other family does not reach them: a renderer holding only a `*config.Config` cannot evaluate either.

**This is the one place in the whole #6534 audit where the issue's original "give the renderers the applied set" prescription is the right mechanism.** For the NAT and CoS families it was not — those drops are deterministic functions of the committed config, and the readback would have been plumbing. Here it is not plumbing: the surface genuinely needs an input it does not have. Whoever picks this up should thread the resolved ifindex map (or a small resolved-instance view) to the port-mirroring surfaces rather than trying to extend the config predicate.

## 3. Two adjacent defects in the port-mirroring renderers

Found while annotating them; neither is an unenforcement bug, both are real:

- **Duplication.** `cli.showPortMirroring` and `Server.showForwardingOptionsPortMirroring` are byte-identical copies with no shared formatter. #7354 had to annotate both and test both for that reason. They should be single-sourced like `natshow`/`dpformat`.
- **Nondeterministic output order.** Both iterate `for name, inst := range pm.Instances` over a map with no sort, so `show forwarding-options port-mirroring` lists instances in a different order on successive runs. Every sibling renderer in `format/cos_show.go` sorts via `sortedMapKeys`.

## Sites deliberately NOT counted as #6534 instances

Recorded so a future audit does not re-litigate them:

- **inet-precedence classifier** (`cos.go:139`) — excluded by the builder, but rendered by **no** show surface at all (`INetPrecedenceClassifierDefs` has zero hits in the format package). An exclusion with no lying renderer is not an instance of this issue.
- **Tunnel endpoint-id collision** (`tunnels.go:115`) — no surface renders tunnel endpoint IDs, and the path is a stable-hash collision. (Separately worth a look: the drop is a bare `return`, which exits the enclosing routine rather than skipping one tunnel.)

## #7359 — userspace-dp: the flowless embedded-ICMP NAT reversal forwards to the client BEFORE the interface input filter and PBR are evaluated [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-31)

Split out of the #6568 Rust-dataplane cohort (member 2), which is being closed with the provable subset fixed.

## Problem

The flowless embedded-ICMP NAT reversal reverse-translates an ICMP error and forwards it to the internal client from `poll_descriptor/mod.rs:3103-3143`, which `continue`s **before** the interface input filter at `:3170`. A configured `filter input` discard / reject / count / policer therefore never sees the packet, and PBR is not evaluated for it either.

## Severity

An operator who applies an input filter to an interface reasonably expects it to see every packet arriving there. This path is a hole in that expectation: the filter's counters do not advance, a discard term does not drop, and a policer does not meter. It is bounded to reverse-translated ICMP errors with no matching flow.

## Fix shape

Evaluate the input filter (and PBR) before the reversal's forward decision, or route the reversal through the same ordering the ordinary path uses. This is an ORDERING change in the hot path and deserves its own review and its own cluster gate — which is why it was not folded into the cohort's provable subset.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A `filter input` discard term drops a reverse-translated embedded-ICMP error.
- [ ] A `filter input` count term advances for one.
- [ ] Fail-on-revert test.

Verified against `origin/master` `679da542e7eb900b05a82f805f99280fc01c3e30`.

## #7360 — userspace-dp/HA: persistent-NAT lease state is not reconstructed on the standby — and a persistent client's 2nd..Nth sessions are DROPPED from sync entirely [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-31)

Split out of the #6568 Rust-dataplane cohort (member 5), which is being closed with the provable subset fixed.

## Problem

Persistent-NAT lease state (`PersistentLease` / `PersistentSourceKey` in `userspace-dp/src/nat/allocator.rs`) is not reconstructed on the HA standby. After a failover the new primary has no persistence bindings, so a client that held a stable translated address/port under `address-persistent` / persistent-NAT gets a DIFFERENT one.

## Severity

Persistence is the property the feature exists to provide, and it is exactly the property a failover is supposed to preserve. Any peer that pinned the client's translated identity — an application server with an IP allowlist, a session-affinity load balancer, a SIP registrar — sees the client move. It is not a fail-open, but it is a silent functional regression at the moment of failover, which is when it is hardest to diagnose.

## Fix shape

Extend the existing session-sync channel to carry lease state, or rebuild leases on the standby from the synced sessions that hold them. Sizing, ordering against the bulk-sync hold, and the reservation-refusal interaction all need design — this is a feature, not a residual.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A persistent-NAT binding survives a failover: the client keeps its translated address/port.
- [ ] `make test-failover` covers the persistence assertion.

Verified against `origin/master` `679da542e7eb900b05a82f805f99280fc01c3e30`. Owes a cluster gate.

## #7361 — natpoolalarm: the pool-utilization alarm structurally cannot fire for an address-only (`port no-translation`) source pool [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-30)

Split out of the #6568 Rust-dataplane cohort (member 8), which is being closed with the provable subset fixed.

## Problem

`pkg/natpoolalarm/natpoolalarm.go:278` computes capacity purely from the PORT range:

```go
capacity := uint64(s.AddressCount) * (uint64(s.PortHigh) - uint64(s.PortLow) + 1)
...
pct := s.UsedPorts * 100 / capacity
```

An address-only pool (`port no-translation`, the #5269 branch) allocates ADDRESSES, not ports, so `UsedPorts` never advances. `pct` is therefore permanently 0 and the raise-threshold can never be crossed — the alarm is structurally unable to fire for that pool class, no matter how exhausted it is.

## Severity

The alarm exists to warn before a pool exhausts. For this pool class the warning cannot arrive, and the operator's first signal is allocation failure — i.e. dropped traffic. It reads as configured-and-working: `show` renders the alarm config, and a 0% utilization is indistinguishable from a healthy pool.

## Fix shape

Compute utilization over the ADDRESS space when the pool is address-only: capacity = `AddressCount`, used = distinct addresses currently allocated. That needs a used-address count plumbed from the allocator, which the port-based sampler does not carry today — hence a successor rather than a cohort row.

Be careful not to regress the port-based path: the two denominators must not be mixed, and the #5269 address-only branch is the discriminator.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] An address-only pool crossing raise-threshold RAISES.
- [ ] A port-bearing pool's utilization is unchanged.
- [ ] Fail-on-revert test covering BOTH pool classes.

Verified against `origin/master` `679da542e7eb900b05a82f805f99280fc01c3e30`.

## #7363 — natshow: DNAT rule detail renders a name-scoped rule as 0.0.0.0/0 and shows only the first address of a bracket list [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-30)

## Problem

`natshow.RenderDestRuleDetail` computes the displayed destination match as:

```go
dstMatch := "0.0.0.0/0"
if rule.Match.DestinationAddress != "" {
    dstMatch = rule.Match.DestinationAddress
}
```

It reads **only** the singular `DestinationAddress`. It ignores both `DestinationAddresses` (the bracket-list form) and `DestinationAddressName` / `DestinationAddressNames` (the address-book reference form). Two consequences, both in the fail-open-looking direction:

1. **A rule scoped only by `match destination-address-name` renders as `0.0.0.0/0`** — i.e. as matching every destination — when it is in fact scoped to a named address-book entry. Verified against a live render:

```
destination NAT rule: d1
  Rule-set: drs                        ID: 1
    From zone: untrust    To zone:
    Match:
      Destination addresses: 0.0.0.0/0        <-- rule is `match destination-address-name NOPE`
    Action:                  pool dp1
```

2. **A rule with a bracket list `match destination-address [ A B C ]` renders only `A`.** `DestinationAddress` holds the first element for back-compat; `DestinationAddresses` holds all. The operator is shown a narrower scope than is configured.

## Why this is not #6534

#6534 is about objects the dataplane does not install being rendered as if it did. This is different: the rule may be installed perfectly, and the surface still misdescribes **which traffic it matches**. Both directions are wrong (over-broad for case 1, under-broad for case 2), so it is not a variant of the exclusion-annotation work and does not share its fix.

The source-NAT renderer has the same shape for `Source addresses` / `Destination addresses` (`RenderSourceRuleDetail` also reads only the singular fields) and should be checked in the same change.

## How it was found

While doing the renderer-visibility census for #6534. Case 1 surfaced because a rule scoped by an undefined address-book name publishes no dataplane rows at all — so the operator sees `0.0.0.0/0` for a rule that matches nothing. The display bug and the unenforcement are independent; fixing one does not fix the other.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Render the full destination match: bracket list and address-book names, not just the singular field.
- [ ] Same for the source side and for `RenderSourceRuleDetail`.

## #7367 — cluster: 'show chassis cluster status' cannot express an RG-ownership divergence — it reads rg.State and nothing else (#6656 successor) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-31)

Successor to #6656 (PR pending), which fixed one mechanism that produces an RG-ownership divergence. This is the **observability** half: the operator command that should surface such a divergence structurally cannot.

## The gap

`show chassis cluster status` → `Manager.FormatStatus` (`pkg/cluster/status.go`) renders, per RG:

- local row: `rg.LocalPriority`, `rg.State`, preempt, manual, monitor-fails
- peer row: `pg.Priority`, `pg.State` from `m.peerGroups`

**There is no VRRP term, no VIP term, and no `rg_active` term anywhere in it.** It reports the cluster state machine's view and only that. So the #6656 incident — node0 showing `primary` for RG0/RG1/RG2 with 1 session and 4,728 rx packets, while node1 carried 33 sessions and 4,675,178 — renders as a *completely healthy cluster*.

Two things make it worse than a missing column:

1. **The peer row is rendered from the post-override map.** `applyTransferCommitOverridesOnPeerStateLocked` rewrites `m.peerGroups` before it is stored, so an armed `peerTransferOutOverride` corrupts the election input *and* the operator's view of the peer with one write. node0 prints node1 as `secondary-hold` while node1 prints itself `primary`, and neither node shows anything anomalous.
2. **`rg_active` is an OR.** `rgStateMachine.reconcileLocked` computes `desired = s.clusterPri || s.allMasterLocked()` (non-strict mode), so a node whose state machine says primary forwards regardless of whether it owns the VIP. "Primary and forwarding-enabled but receiving nothing" is a representable, unflagged state.

## No consistency check exists

`rgStateMachine.CheckVRRPPosture` (`pkg/daemon/rg_state.go`) is the only thing comparing RG ownership against VRRP mastership. It is gated off entirely under `private-rg-election` (the compiler default), it emits a `slog.Warn` and a corrective call, and **it is not surfaced in any operator command**. Nothing anywhere compares RG ownership against actual VIP presence on the wire — `checkVIPReadiness` reads carrier, not addresses, and `directVIPOwned` is the daemon's own intent bookkeeping, never reconciled against `netlink.AddrList`.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `show chassis cluster status` (or `information`) surfaces enough to distinguish "primary and carrying traffic" from "primary and carrying nothing" — candidates: `rg_active`, VIP presence on the reth members, or the local session count per RG.
- [ ] The peer row makes an *overridden* peer state distinguishable from a peer-reported one, rather than silently substituting.
- [ ] A test asserting the render changes when ownership and forwarding disagree.

Needs cluster access to validate the operator-facing half.

## #7368 — test: test-failover.sh asserts 'the primary' with the same field it should be checking — no independent oracle (#6656 successor) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

Successor to #6656 (PR pending).

## The gap

`test/incus/test-failover.sh` picks "the primary" by grepping the very field the #6656 incident showed to be unreliable:

```bash
fw0_status=$(incus exec "$FW0" -- cli -c 'show chassis cluster status' 2>/dev/null)
if echo "$fw0_status" | grep -q "node0.*primary"; then
	pass "fw0 is primary"
```

and again per-RG after the manual failover phase. It then asserts a session count on that node:

```bash
[[ "$fw0_sessions" -ge "$MIN_SESSIONS" ]]
```

So the smoke's notion of "the primary" comes from `rg.State`, and its session assertion is the only thing that can contradict it — which is exactly the pair the incident split apart. **A 14/14 pass is fully compatible with the divergence**, and when the divergence does occur the failure surfaces as a session-count failure attributed to whatever change was under test, which is how #6656 was found in the first place.

Two smaller issues in the same file:

- `grep -q "node0.*primary"` also matches a line containing `secondary` (it is a substring), so the primary assertion is looser than it reads.
- The manual-failover phase uses the **no-`node`** form (`ManualFailover`), not the `node 0` transfer form (`RequestPeerFailover`) that arms `peerTransferOutOverride` — so the smoke never exercises the path `reassert_primary_node0` uses on every deploy.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The smoke establishes "which node is forwarding" from an oracle independent of `rg.State` — interface counters, `rg_active`, or the LAN host's ARP/neigh view.
- [ ] It FAILS with a distinct message when ownership and forwarding disagree, rather than reporting a session-count shortfall.
- [ ] The primary grep is anchored so `secondary` cannot satisfy it.
- [ ] Consider covering the `node <N>` transfer form, since that is what deploys actually issue.

Needs cluster access.

## Problem

A `to-zone junos-host` **permit** narrowed by `match application` is stricter
than the coarse kernel host-inbound gate, is not enforced on the direct
host-bound path, and emits **no** commit-time warning.

```
set security policies from-zone untrust to-zone junos-host policy app-only match source-address any
set security policies from-zone untrust to-zone junos-host policy app-only match destination-address any
set security policies from-zone untrust to-zone junos-host policy app-only match application junos-ssh
set security policies from-zone untrust to-zone junos-host policy app-only then permit
```

Measured on `5989ea046` (real `ParseSetCommand` + `SetPath` + `CompileConfig` +
`ValidateConfig`, no oracle):

```
app-scoped permit : programs=0  rules=0  junos-host-warnings=0
```

Zero kernel rules, zero warnings. The commit is clean and nothing enforces.

## Why it happens

`junosHostPolicyStricterThanCoarseGate`
(`pkg/config/compiler_validate_warn_host_inbound.go`) treats a permit as
stricter than the coarse gate only via `junosHostPolicySourceScoped`, which
inspects the SOURCE dimension alone. An application-narrowed permit never
reaches the test.

It genuinely is stricter: the nft `xpf_hostinbound` chain admits every
configured `system-services`/`protocols` token to the zone's local addresses,
so a policy that permits only `junos-ssh` leaves the zone's other admitted
services (https, ping, snmp, …) admitted by the kernel while Junos would drop
them to the junos-host default. The projection is DROP-only, so the permit's
implied "deny non-permitted" half is never synthesised either.

## #7377 — userspace-dp/HA: a refused synced import still reports ok to the peer, and its counter has no Prometheus metric [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-30)

Successor to #6600, which moved the peer-synced import's NAT reservation ahead of the shared-entry publish and made a refusal drop the import. Two half-measures were deliberately left out of that change; this issue carries them.

## 1. The refusal does not reach `ControlResponse.ok`

`sync_session`'s handler calls `guard.afxdp.upsert_synced_session(entry)`, whose return type is `()`, and sets `response.ok = false` only on a WIRE-PARSE failure. So a session dropped because this node could not reserve its translated port is reported to the peer as a **success**.

This was architecturally impossible to fix before #6600 — the reservation ran on a worker thread long after the RPC had answered — and #6600 is what makes it possible: the reservation now happens inside `upsert_synced_session`, on the control thread, before the publish.

The Go side is already wired to consume it: `process_control.go` turns `!resp.OK` into an error, and `manager_sessionsync_transmit.go` documents that an application-level rejection of one request does not stop the sync loop. So the plumbing exists; only the Rust return value is missing.

**Work:** give `upsert_synced_session` an outcome type, thread it through the handler, and set `ok`/`error` accordingly. Callers to update: the handler and `Coordinator::replay_synced_sessions`.

## 2. `synced_import_reserve_refused` has no Prometheus metric

#6600 added the counter and the `Coordinator::synced_import_reserve_refused_total()` accessor, but not the Go-side descriptor. A nonzero value is currently visible only through the control-socket status surface.

**Work:** mirror the `#5674` `xpf_userspace_synced_import_cap_drops_total` plumbing — `pkg/api/metrics_descriptors_userspace_session.go`, `pkg/api/metrics_userspace.go`, and the helper status field in `userspace-dp/src/server/helpers/status.rs`.

## Why this matters more than a usual observability gap

The refusal is a **dropped failover session**. That is the correct direction — a session naming a port this node does not own is worse than no session — but it means a real HA failover can silently lose flows, and on a healthy standby (owning RG passive) it should not happen at all. A nonzero value points at overlapping pools, an active-active RG pair sharing one SNAT pool, or NAT config drift between the nodes. Without a metric, an operator finds out from a user complaint.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A reservation refusal sets `ControlResponse.ok = false` with a distinguishable error, and the Go sync loop logs it without stopping.
- [ ] `xpf_userspace_synced_import_reserve_refused_total` is exported and covered by the metrics-descriptor tests.
- [ ] Fail-on-revert tests for both.

## See also

- #6600 and its PR — the reserve-before-publish change, and `docs/sync-protocol.md` "NAT-Port Reservation on Import (#6600)", whose closing note names both of these.

## #7389 — cli: streaming command output (tcpdump, ping, traceroute) cannot be termsafe-guarded without a shape change — plus the low-taint remainder (#6584 successor) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-31)

Successor to #6584 (PR pending), which sanitized the two cited sites plus their gRPC mirrors and the structurally-identical `journalctl --boot` the issue missed.

## The population is much larger than either issue states

#6584 named **two** sites. Sweeping the predicate — *external-command output that reaches an operator terminal, on either renderer, without `termsafe`* — found at least **9 raw-block, 4 parsed-row and 5 error-string sites** across `pkg/cli`, `pkg/grpcapi` and `pkg/ipsec`.

That is the enumeration-is-a-floor pattern: a cited count understating the real population.

## The two outliers — worse than either cited site

**`tcpdump`** — `pkg/cli/monitor_traffic.go`, `handleMonitorTraffic`. tcpdump renders packet bytes as ASCII, so this is **the most directly attacker-controlled surface in the whole class**: the payload is chosen by whoever sends the packet, and it goes straight to the operator's terminal.

**`traceroute`** — `pkg/cli/cli_request_ping.go`, `handleTraceroute`, and its gRPC twin `streamDiagCmd`. **Traceroute resolves PTR records by default**, so the displayed hostnames come from DNS an attacker may control.

## Why they were not fixed in #6584 — this is a design step, not a missing call

Both wire `cmd.Stdout = os.Stdout` **directly**. There is no string to sanitize. Guarding them requires a shape change to either:

- **buffered capture** — unacceptable for `tcpdump` (unbounded, interactive; breaks Ctrl-C and the streaming UX that is the point of `monitor traffic`), or
- **a line-wise sanitizing `io.Writer`** interposed between the command and stdout.

The second is the right answer and is a real piece of design: it must preserve line boundaries, not buffer unboundedly, and pass through cleanly on the common path. The gRPC ping/traceroute path (`streamDiagCmd`) already sends per line, so it is the easier half.

**A partial guard here would be worse than none** — it invites the reader to assume the class is handled.

## Also outstanding (low taint, same predicate)

Local CLI only; each writes `cmd.Stdout = os.Stdout` or prints parsed rows. Their gRPC mirrors **are** guarded as of #6584.

| site | command | taint |
|---|---|---|
| `cli_show_system.go` `showSystemProcesses` | `ps aux` | argv of root-controlled processes |
| `cli_show_system.go` `showSystemConnections` | `ss -tnp` | numeric; process column root-controlled |
| `cli_show_system.go` `showSystemNTP` | `chronyc -n` / `ntpq -pn` / `timedatectl` | refids/server strings from config |
| `cli_show_system.go` (~:786) | `ps -eo …` parsed row | `comm` process name |
| `chrony.go` `printChronyTracking` | parsed `chronyc tracking` rows | as above |

**Error-string sites** (external-command bytes folded into an error that reaches a terminal via `pkg/cli/cli.go`'s `fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "error: %v\n", err)` or the gRPC status): `pkg/cli/cli_clear.go` `handleClearArp` / `handleClearIPv6` and their `server_diag_system_action.go` twins; `server_diag_zeroize.go` (`userdel`, `passwd -l root`) — **undetermined** whether those reach an operator terminal; I did not trace the callers.

## #7395 — config: the LENIENT control-char sanitizer still logs a secret leaf's value — on every boot and every HA peer-sync [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

Follow-up to #6625, which fixed the STRICT commit-path validator (PR #7387). Its **lenient twin still leaks the same secret**, and it is the worse of the two surfaces.

## The leak

`sanitizeNodesControlChars` (`pkg/config/freetext.go`) returns one human-readable path per modified node, and the caller logs each one:

```go
ctrlCharWarnings = append(ctrlCharWarnings, fmt.Sprintf(
    "sanitized control characters in configuration value at %q (#1798)", p))
```

That path is built with `joinNodePath(prefix, n.Keys)` — **unredacted** — and for a secret leaf `n.Keys` *includes the secret*, because `authentication-key <PSK>` carries the value as a path component. Sanitizing the control characters makes it printable, not safe.

The strict validator was fixed to build its path through `redactSecretKeys`; the lenient one was not.

## Reproduced at `origin/master` `8b8245f53`

```
LENIENT (boot / HA peer-sync) warnings = ["chassis cluster authentication-key  MY-CLUSTER-PSK "]
STRICT  err = chassis cluster authentication-key <redacted>: value contains a control character (0x09) at byte offset 0 ...
```

Same AST, same secret. One surface redacts, the other prints it.

## Why this one is worse than the strict half

The strict validator fires **once**, on the operator's commit. The lenient path runs on:

- `Store.Load` — **every boot**, and
- `Store.SyncApply` — **every HA peer-sync**.

So an already-persisted key with a stray tab or CR — exactly the value the #1798 migration helper exists to clean up — is re-published to the daemon log on every single boot, indefinitely, with no operator action involved.

## Severity — Medium

Same class as #6625 and #5195 F10: a cleartext credential reaching journald. Narrow trigger (the value must contain a control character), but the repeat-on-every-boot behaviour makes the exposure window unbounded rather than momentary, and it needs no operator action to recur.

## Fix

Mirror what the strict side now does: build the returned path through the same secret-masking resolution rather than `joinNodePath(prefix, n.Keys)`. Both walkers should reach that decision through **one** shared resolution — `secretIndices` (`ast_redact.go`) is the existing SSOT the raw-AST display paths already use, so neither validator needs its own list.

## #7398 — userspace-dp: three Coordinator counters are computed and never shown to an operator [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-30)

Found while fixing #6641 (PR #7397), by the family-wide gate that fix introduced.

Three `Coordinator` `*_total()` accessors are computed, unit-tested, and **never assigned into `ProcessStatus`** — so they never reach the operator through status, gRPC, or Prometheus:

- `session_delete_stale_ignored_total`
- `session_install_stale_ignored_total`
- `synced_import_reserve_refused_total`

They are allowlisted in the new gate with **dead-entry rejection**, so the list reads as a work queue rather than a permission slip: an entry that stops matching a real accessor fails the gate.

## Why this happened, which matters more than the three counters

#6641's own wiring cell came back **green**: deleting the `ProcessStatus` assignment left the entire Rust suite passing, because every test builds a `ProcessStatus` **literal**. Nothing observed whether the helper ever copies the live counter into the status it actually sends.

The lane then deleted the **#1807 precedent's own populate line** — also silent. **The gap is in the pattern, not in one instance of it.** Mirroring the precedent faithfully, as #6641 was written to do, would have reproduced it and shipped a metric wired to nothing with a green matrix.

That is why the fix is a family-wide gate rather than one assignment, and why these three surfaced immediately once the gate existed.

## Scope

Wiring the three is mechanical — one assignment each, plus the Prometheus descriptor and the metric-count guard bump that already exists in `metrics_test.go`.

Two cautions from #7397, both learned the hard way there:
- a nil `*prometheus.Desc` field **compiles fine** and only surfaces as a segfault in `pkg/api`, so a green build proves nothing about the descriptor;
- the gate's own doc comment must not quote the assignment form it greps for — that satisfied the check on the code's behalf until comments were stripped.

Each counter needs a cell that deletes its assignment and reds. Moves the `userspace-dp` binary, so it owes a cluster smoke.

## #7405 — ddns: backendFingerprint FNV-64a-hashes fields that can carry userinfo, and the digest is persisted and logged [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-30)

Flagged by another lane while measuring #6703; filing because it is a judgement call about threat model rather than an obvious defect, and it should not be lost in a message.

`backendFingerprint` (`pkg/ddns/surface_a.go:1792`) FNV-64a-hashes `p.Server` and `p.URLTemplate`. Both can carry **userinfo** (`https://user:SECRET@host/...`), and the resulting digest is **persisted durably and logged**.

## What is already right

It deliberately **excludes every `Secret`-typed field**, which is the correct instinct and why this is not a cleartext leak. The concern is narrower.

## The concern

**FNV-64a is not a cryptographic hash.** It is fast, unsalted, and 64-bit. A short credential embedded in a hashed authority is therefore brute-forceable offline by anyone who obtains the persisted fingerprint or a log line containing it — the search space is the credential, not the hash.

That matters more than usual here because the digest is **durable**: it survives in state and in aggregated logs long after the credential itself might have been rotated out of the config.

## What this is not

- Not a cleartext disclosure.
- Not reachable through the #6703 surfaces (those are a separate, measured defect: JSON marshal and AST text render, where no redactor is called at all).
- Not necessarily worth changing — a fingerprint's job is change-detection, and if the threat model does not include an attacker holding the persisted state, the current form is adequate.

## Options if it is worth changing

1. Feed the fingerprint a **redacted** form of both fields (`RedactURL` already handles userinfo correctly) — keeps change-detection for everything except the credential, which is the one part that should force a re-handshake anyway.
2. Salt the hash with a per-install value, so a digest is not portable to an offline attack.
3. Accept and document, recording that the digest is credential-derived and should be treated as sensitive wherever it is persisted or shipped.

Option 1 looks cheapest and loses the least, but it changes fingerprint values for existing installs — so it needs the usual no-brick consideration: a changed fingerprint must trigger a benign re-detect, not a failure.

**Not yet measured:** whether any log sink or state export ships this digest off-box.

## #7406 — security: a secret embedded in a URL's HOST or PATH is unredactable by any string rule — #6703's criteria are jointly unsatisfiable for that row [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-30)

Split out of #6703 as the residual that **no redactor can close**, so it does not get lost inside that issue's fix. #6703 remains valid and is separately actionable; this is the part of it that is not.

## Measured behaviour

`config.RedactURL` (`pkg/config/secret.go`), measured firsthand at `4299a2e83`:

```
"https://user:SECRET@example.com/nic/update"   -> "https://<redacted>@example.com/nic/update"   OK  userinfo
"https://example.com/nic/update?token=SECRET"  -> "https://example.com/nic/update?<redacted>"   OK  query
"https://api.example.com/update#tok=SECRET"    -> "https://api.example.com/update#<redacted>"   OK  fragment
"https://host:SECRETPORT/nic/update"           -> "https://<redacted>/nic/update"               OK  #6609/#7345
"https://[SECRET]/nic/update"                  -> VERBATIM      <-- residual (bracketed authority)
"https://SECRET.dyn.example.com/nic/update"    -> VERBATIM      <-- residual (secret in HOST)
"https://example.com/nic/SECRET/update"        -> VERBATIM      <-- residual (secret in PATH)
"//SECRET.example.com/nic/update"              -> VERBATIM      <-- residual (scheme-relative host)
```

The path row was not listed in the original #6703 discussion. It is the same class and is included here.

Some dyndns providers legitimately issue a token as a hostname label, and some put the token in the path, so these are real configurations rather than hypotheticals.

## Why this is not a gap in an implementation

`https://SECRET.dyn.example.com/upd` and `https://api.example.com/upd` are **indistinguishable strings**. There is no property of the first that the second lacks. Any rule that redacts the first redacts the second.

`RedactURL`'s own doc already declines to guess here, and the reasoning is right: *"a redactor that guesses would be guessing about a secret."*

## The requirement contradicts itself for this row

#6703's acceptance criteria include both:

- *"Test asserts a URL WITH embedded credentials is redacted AND that one without is rendered unchanged"*
- *"Scheme, host and path remain visible so the field stays diagnosable"*

For a secret that **is** the host, these cannot both hold. Redacting it means redacting every host, which makes credential-free URLs render redacted and removes the host from view. This is a contradiction in the requirement, not a defect in `RedactURL` — worth stating explicitly so this is not re-filed as a bug against that function.

## Per-leaf narrowing relocates the choice without dissolving it

The natural narrowing — redact the whole authority only for the leaves known to carry credentials (`DDNSProvider.Server` / `URLTemplate` / `CheckIPURL`, `FeedServer.URL`) — does not escape it. Applied there, a clean `https://feeds.example/list.txt` gets its host redacted too. It confines the damage; it does not remove the trade.

## #7409 — userspace-dp: the helper FIB carries no FRR/DHCP-learned routes, so every learned destination is reinjected to the kernel unadjudicated [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

Split out of #6664 as the ROOT CAUSE of its `NoRoute` leg. Filed separately because closing it is a different fix from anything #6664 describes, and because it is the larger finding.

## The divergence

`buildRouteSnapshots` derives the helper's FIB from exactly three sources — **config statics, connected prefixes, and ip-rule leak rules** — then applies the ip-monitoring overlay (`pkg/dataplane/userspace/routes.go:20-22`). Every `SetRouteOverlay` caller was checked; the overlay is ip-monitoring-only.

The repo states it itself, `docs/multi-wan.md:666-668`:

> **DHCP uplink as PRIMARY fast-path uplink still needs a static default.** The dataplane FIB baseline is **config-derived and carries no DHCP-learned routes**.

But xpf ships BGP, OSPF, IS-IS and RIP via FRR, and `deriveUserspaceCapabilities` (`pkg/dataplane/userspace/capabilities.go:43-113`) does **not** disarm the helper when any of them is configured.

## The consequence

On any dynamically-routed box, a transit packet toward a BGP/OSPF/RIP/DHCP-learned prefix misses the userspace FIB, resolves `NoRoute`, and is reinjected to `xpf-usp0` — where the kernel forwards it via the learned route with **no zone policy, no session, no NAT and no screen**.

Nothing downstream catches it, and each of these was verified rather than assumed:

- **No nft forward chain exists.** Only `ChainHookInput` (`pkg/nftables/netlink_installer.go:161`) and `ChainHookOutput`. `pkg/daemon/daemon_transit_gate.go:20-22` says it plainly: *"no nftables `hook forward` chain at all … so the kernel routed transit under no policy whatsoever."*
- **`ip_forward` is force-enabled while armed** — `daemon_transit_gate.go:56-58`: *"the gate NEVER lowers the knob while armed."*
- **`rp_filter` is deliberately 0 on the reinject TUN** — `pkg/networkd/networkd.go:537-561` re-writes it after every networkd reload.
- **The rate limit is not a mitigation** — `userspace-dp/src/slowpath.rs:16-17`: 1,000,000 pps / 4 GiB/s.
- **No `ip rule` scopes `xpf-usp0`**, so reinjected packets take the main table. FBF rules are `iif`-scoped to real NICs (`pkg/routing/rules.go:625-635`), so they never match.

Attacker model: **any host on any zone, including untrust, chooses the destination.** No credentials, no tunnel, no timing.

## The second vector: PBR/FBF terms silently deferred to a path that cannot enforce them

`pkg/routing/rules.go:843-849` drops `is-fragment`, `tcp-flags`, `icmp-type`, and port/address-`except` terms from the kernel ip-rule mirror because they are unrepresentable there — on the stated theory that *"the userspace filter path still enforces the term exactly."*

It does not, when the steered table is empty: the userspace lookup yields `NoRoute` → reinject → kernel **main** table → the packet is forwarded down the very path the operator steered it away from.

`tests_fragment.rs:635` (`flowless_non_first_fragment_steered_by_pbr_routing_instance_3291`) asserts only `dbg.forward == 0` and `dbg.no_route == 1` while its comment claims "→ NoRoute → **drop**". It never asserts the packet stayed out of the slow path — expected-value-equals-failure-default.

## Why fixing this is the right order

#6664's remaining `NoRoute` leg cannot be fixed well while this stands. Its prescribed adjudication collapses to an unconditional drop (both `NoRoute` and `NextTableUnsupported` always carry `egress_ifindex: 0`, so `to_id` is always 0 and #3110 falls through to `default_action`), and an unconditional drop **black-holes every learned destination** — a total outage.

Close the divergence and `NoRoute` becomes rare and truthful; dropping it then becomes safe, and the reinject returns to being the small residual the #1913 doc always described.

## #7411 — security: license autoupdate url and RPM probe target url still render cleartext on GET /api/v1/config [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-30)

Found while measuring #6703. Two URL-bearing config leaves outside that issue's field table leak on the typed JSON config-read route.

## Measured

Probe staging one sentinel per leaf, driving the live handlers:

| leaf | `GET /api/v1/config` | `/config/export`, `/config/show` |
|---|---|---|
| `system license autoupdate url` | **leaks verbatim** | fixed by #7410 |
| `services rpm probe <p> test <t> target url` | **leaks verbatim** | fixed by #7410 |

Both were verbatim on all routes before #7410.

## Why #7410 fixed one surface and not the other

#7410 keys the **AST** redaction on the leaf NAME, so `url` matches in every context — these two leaves inherited redaction on `export`/`show` with no extra step, which is the property #6703 asked for.

The **typed JSON** route has no equivalent hook. `configHandler` json-encodes the compiled `*Config`, so redaction there needs a `MarshalJSON` per containing struct. #7410 added them to `DDNSProvider` and `FeedServer` — the two structs #6703 named. `LicenseAutoUpdate` is a field of `SystemConfig`, and the RPM target URL lives on the RPM probe types, so neither is reached.

## Fix

The same alias-copy marshaller pattern #7410 uses:

```go
func (c *SystemConfig) MarshalJSON() ([]byte, error) {
	type alias SystemConfig
	v := alias(*c)
	v.LicenseAutoUpdate = RedactURL(v.LicenseAutoUpdate)
	return json.Marshal(v)
}
```

The alias sheds the method to avoid recursion while keeping every field, so a field added later is still marshalled rather than silently dropped.

Same treatment for whichever struct holds the RPM probe target URL.

## Severity

Lower than #6703. A license autoupdate URL and an RPM HTTP probe target are less likely to carry a credential than a dyndns endpoint or a threat-feed subscription URL — but both accept an arbitrary URL, so both can, and the query string is exactly where a token would sit.

## #7415 — daemon/reth: the ARI slot/function encoding is unverified — no ARI non-VF netdev at a non-zero slot exists on available hardware [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-31)

Split out of #6677 as the one divergence that **could not be observed** on available hardware, so it is recorded rather than guessed at. #6677's PR fixes the divergences that *are* observable, by consulting udev; this issue records the residual and names the test article needed to settle it.

## The mechanism is real

systemd's `net_id` builtin reinterprets the PCI slot and function fields as a single 8-bit function number when ARI is enabled:

```c
if (ari_enabled)
        func += slot * 8;
```

Provenance, so a future reader does not conclude this was imagined:

- `ari_enabled` is referenced by the installed `udevadm` binary (`strings /usr/bin/udevadm | grep -c '^ari_enabled$'` → 1), systemd 261.
- The arithmetic above is from systemd's `net_id` source. systemd source is **not** installed on this host, so that line is cited, not compiled and stepped through. The behavioural consequence is what could not be reproduced — see below.

So a device at `0000:03:01.2` with `ari_enabled=1` would have combined function `1<<3 | 2` = 10, and `pciAddrToEnp` — which treats slot and function as separate — would derive `enp3s1f2`, a name udev never assigns.

## What could not be observed, and precisely why

This host has **38 ARI-enabled network devices**. Every single one falls into a category where the ARI arithmetic **cannot change the result**:

| category | count | why ARI is invisible |
|---|---|---|
| slot `00`, non-VF | 8 | `slot << 3 == 0`, so `func += 0` — ARI is a no-op |
| SR-IOV VF (slots `02`, `06`, `0a`, `0e`) | 30 | net_id's **VF path takes precedence**: the VF is named from its *physical function's* address plus the VF index, so the VF's own slot/func never reaches the arithmetic |

Measured (`udevadm test-builtin net_id`, systemd 261):

```
eno5v0  0000:b7:02.0  ari=1  VF   -> ID_NET_NAME_PATH=enp183s0f0v0
eno5v7  0000:b7:02.7  ari=1  VF   -> ID_NET_NAME_PATH=enp183s0f0v7
ix0     0000:b7:00.0  ari=1  PF   -> ID_NET_NAME_PATH=enp183s0f0np0
eno2    0000:67:00.1  ari=1  slot0-> ID_NET_NAME_PATH=enp103s0f1
```

`0000:b7:02.0`'s `physfn` is `0000:b7:00.0` — slot 0, func 0 — and the VF name `enp183s0f0v0` is built from *that* address plus `v0`. An ARI-combined name (`f16` for slot 2) appears nowhere.

**Note this also refutes the shape the original report implied.** The ARI-enabled devices #6677 listed as evidence are all at slot 0, where ARI provably changes nothing. The report named the divergence it could not observe and missed the two it could (VF naming and the `npN` port suffix).

## #7424 — harness: validate.py negative assertions read a transport error as 'absent'; rolling.go waitPredicate overshoots its deadline by one poll interval [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-31)

Successor to the #6567 harness cohort, which is being closed with per-row dispositions. Row 3 (the signed-manifest hole) is already split to **#7347**. These are the remaining rows that reproduce. Verified against `origin/master` `8dd3c9a53a2dba1bd32652a797eeb9ee29e3f3d2` (pinned at both ends of the sweep; `git diff --stat` over all five cohort files between the start and end SHAs was empty, so every line number holds at both).

## Row 1 — step3 returns a definitive OUT from a capture in which nothing was measured

`test/incus/step3-tx-kick-classify.py:151-156`:

```python
def t1_out_block(retry_delta, count_delta, sum_ns_delta) -> bool:
    if retry_delta >= RETRY_OUT:
        return False
    if count_delta == 0:
        return True          # zero measurement == passes OUT
```

All 12 all-zero blocks satisfy OUT → `verdict = "OUT"` → `main()` returns 0 unconditionally (`:447`). The report prints **"the TX-kick hypothesis is ruled out"** — a definitive negative about the dataplane — from a file in which nothing was measured. `grep -c INSUFFICIENT` over step3 = **0**; over its sibling step2 = **6**.

Reachability is real: step1 emits `shape = np.zeros(16)` on an empty capture (`step1-histogram-classify.py:311-312`) and its K2 no-evidence guard is traffic-gated (`if c == 0 and txp > 10_000`), so it stays silent when `txp == 0`.

**The sibling already settled this by name.** `step2-sched-switch-classify.py:314-332` carries the C175-HC-070 comment — *"Classifying that as a definitive OUT … rules the scheduler out from a measurement that never happened"* — sets `verdict = "INSUFFICIENT"`, and returns 2 (`:409`). Step3 has neither the state nor the exit code.

### ⚠️ The fix shape must be CHOSEN, not discovered

The cohort claims step3's own test pins the wrong behaviour. That is **PARTIAL**. `step3-tx-kick-classify_test.py:129-143` does assert `OUT`, but its fixture is a **valid normalised capture with zero kicks** (`make_block` builds `shape[3..6] = 0.2475`, summing to 1.0), not an all-zero capture (which sums to 0). So:

- **Narrow / step2-faithful fix** (INSUFFICIENT iff every block's `sum(shape) == 0` AND every kick delta is 0): test 3 **stays green**, no test churn.
- **Broad fix** (INSUFFICIENT whenever all 12 `count_delta == 0`): test 3 **goes RED at line 143** and the cohort's claim holds literally.

Test 3's fixture is close to unreachable from the real pipeline (step1's K2 raises on that shape once `tx_packets > 10_000`), so the broad fix is arguably right and the red test the correct casualty — but decide deliberately.

## Row 2 — validate.py negative assertions read a transport error as "absent"

`scripts/image/validate.py:1095`, `:1097` (scenario A), `:1341`, `:1343` (scenario C). The issue's `:357/:359/:421/:423` are stale line numbers.

`incus exec` returns 1 both when the in-guest `test -e` finds nothing **and** when incus itself fails (instance not running, agent down, connection refused). The code only tests `== 0`, so the two are indistinguishable. The unearned greens are the central negative claims of scenarios A and C: *"the factory boot installed no config"* and *"the REJECT wrote nothing"*.

Asymmetric and matching the filing: the sibling POSITIVE assertions (`:1299`, `:1301`, `:1372-1373`) use `!= 0 → fail(...)` and so fail closed. Only the negatives fail open.

**The file already contains the correct pattern three times** and says why: `:384` (*"a probe that silently produced nothing cannot be mistaken for a clean run"*), `:704-706` (*"a gate that could not observe the property it exists to assert has not asserted it"*), and `:911-916`. Fix shape: a `guest_absent(inst, path)` helper emitting an explicit `PRESENT`/`ABSENT` token and failing on anything else.

## #7426 — daemon/dataplane: two live implementations of systemd interface naming, wrong in opposite ways — single-source them [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

Residual from #6677 (PR #7420, merged). #7420 fixed the **daemon** copy by asking the kernel instead of re-deriving. It did **not** touch the second implementation, which is still live and still wrong — in a *different* way.

## Two live implementations of one contract

Both produce the `.link` `OriginalName=` for a RETH member, whose MAC alternates between physical at boot and virtual once the daemon programs the RETH virtual MAC — so `OriginalName=` is the only stable match and a wrong one is not self-correcting at boot.

| | `deriveKernelName` (`pkg/daemon/daemon_reth.go`, post-#7420) | `getOriginalKernelName` (`pkg/dataplane/compiler.go:1914`) |
|---|---|---|
| altname selection | **NamePolicy order** — `eno`, `ens`, `enp`, then `eth` last | **first match wins**, prefix set `enp\|eno\|ens\|eth`, whatever order the kernel listed |
| PCI fallback | **no `f0` handling** — `if fn > 0 { name += "f%d" }`, so `f0` is never emitted | **has the #4795 multifunction fix** — `pciFunctionSuffix(isPCIMultifunctionDevice(addr), fn)` |

**Each has exactly what the other lacks.** That is the shape that makes this single-source material rather than agreement-test material: two wrongnesses that differ cannot be reconciled by an agreement test, because the agreement would pin one wrongness to the other.

### The git history proves it rather than arguing it

**#4795** — *"getOriginalKernelName appends f0 for single-function PCI (wrong .link OriginalName)"* — landed in the **dataplane** copy and never reached the daemon copy. And the two are wrong in **opposite directions**: #4795 fixed *over*-emission (appending `f0` where systemd does not), while the daemon copy *under*-emits (never appending `f0` even where systemd does, on a genuine multifunction device).

Measured on real hardware: `0000:b7:00.0` is a multifunction NIC whose real `ID_NET_NAME_PATH` is `enp183s0f0np0`. The daemon's derivation yields `enp183s0`.

A fix that landed in one copy and never reached the other is what "a divergence here is always a bug" looks like in practice.

### The altname ordering is a real coin flip, not a nitpick

A device commonly carries several candidate altnames at once. Measured: `ix0` carries `eno5np0`, `enp183s0f0np0` **and** `enx3cecef6aa8bc` simultaneously. First-match-wins returns whichever the kernel happened to list first; the name udev actually assigns is the first its **NamePolicy** resolves (onboard before slot before path). The dataplane copy has no such ordering.

## It is LIVE — and the retired-eBPF flag does not cover it

`pkg/dataplane/compiler.go` is flagged in project notes as retired eBPF, which is why this is easy to dismiss. **That flag does not cover this file's interface path.** The call site is reached from `buildInterfaceNetworkdModels` → `compiler_iface.go:1051`, which is the networkd `.link`/`.network` generation path and very much live.

Verified at `origin/master`. Worth stating explicitly, because the next reader will otherwise dismiss it the same way.

## The import direction is the design's actual shape

`pkg/daemon` imports `pkg/dataplane`; the reverse does not and cannot. **So the shared resolver cannot live in `pkg/daemon`** — which is where both `udevPredictableName` (`device_map.go:824`) and the new altname resolver (`daemon_reth.go`) are today. A resolver placed there compiles fine until `pkg/dataplane` needs it.

It needs a leaf both can import:

- `pkg/devicemap` imports only `pkg/config` — but `pkg/dataplane` does not import it today, so this adds an edge.
- A **zero-xpf-import leaf** (e.g. `pkg/netname`) has no cycle risk in either direction.

## #7430 — frr: an unparseable IS-IS adjacency row is dropped silently rather than reported [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-30)

Follow-up from #6590. The parse defect is fixed (#7418, right-anchored off the header); this is the **display** residual it did not cover.

## What happens now

`GetISISAdjacency` `continue`s on a row it cannot parse — no header seen (`trailing <= 0`), or a row shorter than the trailing width. The row is **dropped**, so the adjacency simply does not appear.

## Why that is worth changing

An operator debugging a missing neighbour sees **nothing**, which is indistinguishable from "the adjacency does not exist". A row saying *this line could not be parsed* points at the real problem; an absent row points at the wrong one.

The alternative considered and rejected in the superseded #7427 is worth recording: **rendering the row with empty derived fields** would report a neighbour in state `""` — quieter than the original column-forgery, but still false. So the shape is *report as unparseable*, not *render partially*.

Proposed: `Malformed` set, derived fields left empty, `Raw` carrying the line, and both display sites branching on it.

## Scope — deliberately narrow

This only bites when the header is absent or a row is short, **both of which already mean something is wrong** (an FRR version change, a truncated `vtysh` response). It is not a live-traffic defect and should not be prioritised as one.

## One constraint any fix inherits

**#6590 and #6468 must stay orthogonal.** An escape-bearing but space-*free* hostname must remain a **well-formed** row. If it were marked `Malformed`, the #6468/#6579 escape fixtures would stop exercising the display guard they exist for — they would be testing this parser's rejection instead, and **the display guard could rot undetected**. Pin that with a test, as #7427 did.

## #7433 — snmp: findNextV1OIDSnap's termination depends on an unbound strictly-advancing invariant [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-30)

Found while gating #6597's fix (measured on the superseded #7432, which reached the same fix by a different route).

## The invariant

`findNextV1OIDSnap` contains the one unbounded loop over the successor lookup. It terminates **only** because the successor **strictly advances** past the cursor. Nothing asserts that.

Demonstrated by mutation: changing the search predicate from `>0` to `>=0` makes an OID its own successor, and the walk **never terminates** — the mutation cell **hung** rather than failing, which is how it was found. The matrix had to be re-run under `-timeout` afterwards.

## Why it is not a live defect today

Two independent bounds hold at HEAD, and both are incidental rather than asserted:

- **GETNEXT** performs one lookup per request OID — no loop over the successor.
- **GETBULK** is bounded by max-repetitions plus the byte budget (#6551).

So a spin is not currently reachable from the wire. The concern is that the loop's termination rests on a property of a *different* function, and neither the property nor the dependency is written down or tested.

## What is worth adding

1. **Assert strict advance** — for every OID in the view, the successor sorts strictly after it. That is the property the loop depends on, stated where it can red.
2. **A `-timeout` on the relevant suite**, so a future regression fails rather than hangs. A hang is worse than a failure: it reads as an infrastructure problem, and in a mutation matrix it silently costs the whole run.

## Note for whoever takes it

The mutation that must red is the one that breaks **strict advance** — not one that breaks the search's correctness generally. An equivalence test against a reference oracle passes under a linear revert **by construction** (under the revert the implementation *is* the oracle), so equivalence is not the guard for this property.

## #7437 — userspace-dp: the helper FIB has no kernel route-event trigger, so #7409's learned-route import leaves a bounded staleness window [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-03)

Follow-up to #7409, filed as its explicitly-deferred residual rather than discovered later. #7409 **narrows** the learned-route divergence; this is what would close it.

## The residual

`pkg/routing` `ImportLearnedRoutes` (added in #7409) reads the kernel FIB and feeds learned routes into `buildRouteSnapshots`, so the helper FIB now agrees with the kernel FIB the slow path reinjects into. But the snapshot is only republished on:

- an operator commit (`applyConfigLocked` → full `ApplyConfig`), and
- an ip-monitoring actuation (`pkg/ipmon` run loop, debounce 1s / throttle 3s).

**There is no kernel route-event trigger.** `RouteSubscribe` / `RouteSubscribeWithOptions` / `unix.RTM_*` / `RTNLGRP_ROUTE` return **zero hits repo-wide** — verified at `30c99fa70`.

So a route the kernel learns between two pushes is still absent from the helper FIB until the next one, and traffic for it still resolves `NoRoute` and takes the unadjudicated reinject that #7409 exists to stop. The window is bounded by "time to the next commit or ipmon actuation", which on a quiet box with a flapping BGP peer is unbounded in practice.

Two sub-cases, with different severities:

- **Stale-absent** (kernel learned a route the helper lacks) — `NoRoute` → reinject → forwarded by the kernel with no zone policy, session, NAT or screen. This is the #7409 exposure, just narrower.
- **Stale-present** (helper holds a route the kernel withdrew) — the helper forwards toward a next-hop that may be gone, gets `MissingNeighbor`, and reinjects; the kernel then decides. Self-healing, and the flowless `MissingNeighbor` arm enforces zone policy (#4024). Materially lower severity.

## Why `NoRoute` must stay slow-path eligible until this lands

#6664 proposes dropping `NoRoute` instead of reinjecting it. That is only safe once this window is closed. While it is open, dropping `NoRoute` black-holes every learned destination for the width of the window — and for the width of the *first* push after a fresh boot. The current posture is recorded in the `NoRoute` note in `poll_descriptor/mod.rs` and in `pkg/routing/README.md`; **both should be updated by whoever closes this**, not left asserting a limitation that no longer exists.

## Shape of the fix

The pattern already exists in-tree: `pkg/daemon/daemon_neighbor_listener.go:137` subscribes to `RTM_NEWNEIGH`/`RTM_DELNEIGH` via `NeighSubscribeWithOptions` and drives a helper push. A `RouteSubscribeWithOptions` sibling is the direct analogue.

## The constraint that a naive implementation will get wrong

**It must not push per netlink event.**

Every publish is a **full snapshot replace** — the Rust side rebuilds from `ForwardingState::default()` (`forwarding_build/mod.rs:407`) — over a control socket whose deadline scales at 3s + 1s/MiB (`pkg/dataplane/userspace/process_control.go:34-56`). `CLAUDE.md`'s control-socket rule is explicit that a new caller above 1/s starves session installs during bulk sync. Under BGP churn a per-event push would do exactly that, and the failure mode is a control-plane brownout rather than a visible error.

The listener must reuse the ipmon debounce/throttle discipline (1s / 3s is the in-tree precedent) and coalesce bursts.

## Also unresolved: the snapshot-size ceiling

Related and worth deciding in the same work: a box holding a full BGP table would push hundreds of thousands of `RouteSnapshot` entries as JSON on every publish. The #7409 import is **not** viable for a full-table BGP speaker. A bounded import (a configurable cap with a loud degraded-state diagnostic, mirroring the `maxPBRRules` / `config.NextTableRuleWindow` precedent) is the right shape, but choosing the cap needs a measurement nobody has taken.

## #7441 — cluster: a hostile session-sync stream admitted before the key commit is still never evicted (#6628 residual) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-31)

Split from #6628, which closed the two properties about the LEGITIMATE peer
(PR referenced there). This is the third, and it is the security one.

## The residual

A hostile session-sync stream admitted BEFORE the control-link key was
committed keeps injecting frames afterwards. The #6628 in-place upgrade does
not evict it: the upgrade only ever PROMOTES a connection whose peer answers,
and **a hostile peer declines by staying silent**.

**The problem is the indistinguishability, not a missing timer.** A peer that
does not answer an `AuthUpgradeHello` is indistinguishable from a legitimate
peer that is not keyed yet — which is exactly the rolling-upgrade case that
must keep working. Any fix has to separate those two, or accept dropping both.

Restarting `xpfd` remains the only thing that evicts such a stream, and
`pkg/cluster/README.md` says so.

## Inherited constraints — #5078 shipped a bounded window and REMOVED it

Quoted from `pkg/cluster/sync_auth.go`, because these are what killed the
mechanism last time and any attempt has to answer all three:

> A bounded dual-accept window was shipped and then removed. It had to bound a
> connection's LIFETIME rather than just its admission (an admitted
> pass-through stream outlived the deadline), it had to stop an admitted peer
> re-arming it through config-sync, and it could not survive a crash loop
> without persisting its deadline. A relaxation that needs three guards of its
> own does not belong in the fix that closes the hole.

The third is the hard one and it is why a naive grace timer keeps coming back:
a deadline held only in memory is reset by every restart, so a peer that can
induce a crash loop holds the window open indefinitely. Persisting it puts a
security deadline in the config DB, with its own rollback and clock questions.

## What has changed since #5078 that might make this tractable

- **#6629 landed.** The config payload is encrypted, so the established
  connection is no longer the thing protecting a secret in flight. A design
  that drops an un-upgraded connection no longer has to preserve cleartext

## #7446 — test/userspace: ~45 sites discard the buildSnapshot error and dereference the result [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

Split out of #6675 (PR #7445) rather than folded in.

## What is left

`pkg/dataplane/userspace` has roughly 45 test call sites of the form:

```go
snap, _ := buildSnapshot(cfg, config.UserspaceConfig{}, 1, 0)
// ... snap.Field
```

`buildSnapshot` returns `(*ConfigSnapshot, error)`. On any failure it returns a **nil** pointer, so every one of these dereferences nil and SIGSEGVs — which aborts the whole test binary, not just the one test.

Enumerate with:

```
grep -rn ", _ := buildSnapshot\|, _ = buildSnapshot\|, _ := buildSnapshotWithSchedulerState" \
  --include=*_test.go pkg/dataplane/userspace/
```

## Why this is lower severity than #6675, and why it is still worth doing

#6675 made the package hermetic with respect to the kernel ip-rule table, so these sites can no longer fail for an **environmental** reason — which was the whole phantom-regression cost. What remains is ordinary test-authoring breakage: a config that fails validation makes the test SIGSEGV instead of reporting which build step rejected it, and it takes the rest of the package with it.

So this is a diagnosability defect, not a correctness or coverage one. It is filed because the failure mode is disproportionate to the cause — a bad fixture should fail one test with a message, not crash the binary.

## Fix

Mechanical: capture the error and `t.Fatalf` with it. Roughly 18 files.

Worth considering instead of 45 individual edits: a `mustBuildSnapshot(t, ...)` helper in the package that does the check once and returns a non-nil snapshot, so the call sites get shorter rather than longer and new tests fall into the safe form by default.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] No test call site in `pkg/dataplane/userspace` dereferences a `buildSnapshot` result without checking the error.
- [ ] A guard that fails if the discarding form reappears — the population is large enough that a reviewer will not catch a re-introduction by eye. The `#6675` code-pointer guard is a precedent for binding this structurally rather than by convention; an AST scan for the discard shape would work here (`pkg/daemon/fabric_neigh_single_source_6598_test.go` is a worked example of scanning the AST rather than the text, so a comment showing the bad form cannot trip it).
- [ ] Deliberately induce a `buildSnapshot` failure and confirm the suite reports which test and which cause, rather than aborting.

## #7448 — config: fabric1-interface and fabric1-peer-address are compiled but not declared in the chassis schema [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-28)

## Summary

`compileChassis` compiles `chassis cluster fabric1-interface` and
`chassis cluster fabric1-peer-address`, but **neither is declared in
`schemaChassis`**. They are the only two cluster statements on that side of
the line.

Measured at `origin/master` (`769dde1e1`):

- compiled: `pkg/config/compiler_system.go` — `clusterNode.FindChild("fabric1-interface")`
  and `clusterNode.FindChild("fabric1-peer-address")`, landing in
  `ClusterConfig.Fabric1Interface` / `ClusterConfig.Fabric1PeerAddress`.
- declared: `pkg/config/schema_chassis.go` — `grep -n fabric1 schema_chassis.go`
  returns nothing. Its `fabric-interface` / `fabric-peer-address` siblings are
  declared with `args: 1` and a `placeholder`.

## Consequences

This is the two-SSOT class (#6663), and it costs two distinct things:

1. **No completion.** `set chassis cluster ?` never offers `fabric1-interface`,
   so an operator cannot discover from the CLI a knob the compiler implements.
   Identical in shape to the #6663 `strict-vip-ownership` gap.
2. **No value slot and no validator.** The sibling `fabric-peer-address` is a
   declared `args: 1` leaf; `fabric1-peer-address` is not, so the schema walker
   consumes it as an unmodeled keyword. The `chassis` subtree is open-world, so
   it commits and takes effect — this is a completion and validation gap, not a
   commit rejection.

## Why it is being filed now

#6672 added a packed-line splitter for the `chassis cluster` body whose
statement set must include every statement the compiler honours: a statement the
splitter does not know does not merely fail to compile, it **folds onto whichever
statement precedes it on a packed line**, so it silently does nothing *and*
corrupts its neighbour. The splitter therefore registers `fabric1-interface` and
`fabric1-peer-address` from a documented `clusterCompilerOnlyStatements`
exception set rather than deriving them from the schema.

That exception set is checked as an **equality**, not a containment
