## Problem

`reserve_synced_source_nat_allocation_*` (the #6600 pre-publish reservation)
cannot distinguish **"no pool owns this translated address, so there is nothing
to reserve"** from **"a pool-owning candidate REFUSED the reservation"**. Both
fall out of `reserve_synced_on_first_pool_owner` as `false`.

`upsert_synced_session` treats `false` as a refusal and `return`s **before
publishing**. So for any source-NAT mode with no pool — notably
**interface-mode SNAT** — every peer-synced import is silently dropped by the
helper on the standby.

## Measured, on the loss userspace cluster

Deployed a build that reports the refusal reason on the Go side and drove
iperf3 across the cluster:

```
fw1: 17 x "helper refused a synced session import ... err=...: reserve"
fw0: 0
xpf_userspace_synced_import_cap_drops_total 0     (not the #5674 cap)
```

The cluster's WAN SNAT is interface-mode — a session on fw0 renders as
`In: 172.16.80.8/42650 --> 172.16.80.200/5201` (172.16.80.8 is reth0.80's OWN
address, not a pool member).

## Root cause

`reserve_synced_on_first_pool_owner` (`userspace-dp/src/nat/source.rs`) loops
candidate rules and `continue`s on:

- `!rule.pool_mode` — an interface-mode rule is skipped entirely, and
- `addr_index == None` / `!in_pool` — no pool member matches `rewrite_src`.

If **no** candidate ever reaches `reserve_flow` / `reserve_address_only`, the
loop falls out and returns `false`, which is byte-identical to "every candidate
refused". `reserve_synced_source_nat_allocation_with_holder` already has the
correct shape one line earlier — `let Some(rewrite_src) = nat.rewrite_src else
{ return true; }` — "nothing to reserve" is not a refusal. The no-pool case is

## #7588 — userspace_bindings: bootstrap clear is a no-op on a fresh manager; stale pinned rows are safe only by shim ordering [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-31)

## Problem

`programBootstrapMapsLocked` zeroes stale `userspace_bindings` rows by calling
`clearAllBindingRowsLocked`, which iterates `m.lastBindingIndices` — an
in-process `Manager` field that is **nil on a freshly constructed Manager**. The
`userspace_bindings` Array is `PinByName`-pinned under `/sys/fs/bpf/xpf`, so its
rows outlive xpfd. On the first apply after a daemon restart the bootstrap clear
therefore zeroes **nothing**, and rows written by the previous process survive.

This is the same defect class as #6784 (fixed for `userspace_ingress_ifaces` by
`adoptIngressInventoryLocked`), one map over.

## Why it was deliberately NOT fixed in #6784

Two measurements, both taken at `c54d4b918`, that made it the wrong thing to fix
in that PR — and that are also the reason this is worth its own issue:

1. **Unreachable today, because a *different* gate covers it.** The XDP shim
   consults `userspace_ingress_ifaces` BEFORE the binding array
   (`userspace-xdp/src/lib.rs`: the `USERSPACE_INGRESS_IFACES.get(&ingress_ifindex)`
   test returns `cpumap_or_pass` before any `binding_slot` lookup). So once
   #6784 repairs the ingress gate, a stale binding row for a de-configured
   interface is never reached; and for an interface still in the config,
   `applyHelperStatusLocked` rewrites its rows from live helper status on every
   ~1/s poll.

2. **A blanket sweep is not viable at this size.**
   `BindingArrayMaxEntries = MaxInterfaces * BindingQueuesPerIface = 65536 * 16
   = 1,048,576` rows, against the `userspace_heartbeat` Array's 4096. The #6702
   "zero the Array's own capacity" precedent does not port: it would put a
   million map syscalls on every non-same-plan apply.

## Why it should still be tracked

"Unreachable today because another gate covers it" is a **dependency between two
structures that nothing asserts**. Nothing in the tree states that the ingress
gate must precede the binding lookup, and nothing fails if someone reorders the
shim or adds a path that reaches `USERSPACE_BINDINGS` without passing the
ingress test first. The safety of leaving stale binding rows in a pinned map is
currently an emergent property of shim ordering, not an invariant.

exits unexpectedly, the endpoint is gone for the life of the process — logged,

`pkg/daemon/daemon_run_servers.go`:

```go
go func() {

        slog.Error("gRPC server error", "err", err)
    }
}()
```

`pkg/grpcapi/server.go`, `Server.Run`:

```go
runErr := s.serveUntilDone(ctx, srv, lis)

return runErr
```

So a serve fault marks the state Failed (observable — `show system services`
reports it), returns, gets logged once, and the goroutine ends. There is no
retry: `Run` is called exactly once from `startGRPCServer`.

The **fabric** gRPC listener, in the same file, has had a bounded-backoff

## Problem

`applyErrSkipsPeerSync` (`pkg/daemon/daemon_apply_commit.go`) decides whether a
just-applied config is pushed to the cluster peer, and — in `syncAndApply`
(#5564) — whether a **peer-promoted config is DISCARDED**. It classifies two
error classes as fatal:

```go
func applyErrSkipsPeerSync(err error) bool {
	if err == nil {
		return false
	}
	if compileErrorMustAbortApply(err) {
		return true
	}
	return errors.Is(err, context.Canceled) || errors.Is(err, context.DeadlineExceeded)
}
```

The second is meant to catch the **#2926 daemon-stop abort** — the apply was
abandoned mid-pipeline because the daemon is shutting down. But it cannot
distinguish that from a **per-command timeout**, and every apply-path command
runner builds its own short context:

| runner | timeout | error it feeds into the tail join | joined since |
|---|---|---|---|
| `nftApplyPayload` (`daemon_nft.go:36`) | 5s | `lo0Err`, `hostInboundErr` | #3392 / #3333 |
| `daemon_dns.go:341-354` `systemctl is-enabled/disable/mask` | ctx-scoped | `dnsErr` | #6792 |
| `runCommandTimeout` (`exec_timeout.go:29`) | 15s | `loginErr`, `sudoersErr`, `absentUsersErr`, `sshConfigErr`, `rootAuthErr` | #6790 |

`exec.CommandContext` has **two** error shapes at a deadline:

1. the process **started** and was killed → `*exec.ExitError` ("signal:
   killed"), which is NOT a context error → correctly classified non-fatal;
2. the context expired **before fork/exec completed** → `Start` returns
   `ctx.Err()` and `CombinedOutput` hands back a **bare
   `context.DeadlineExceeded`** → classified FATAL.

## #7619 — daemon: the RSS indirection table is never restored on daemon stop (#6801's sibling trigger) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-30)

## Problem

`restoreStep0TunablesOnShutdown` (`pkg/daemon/host_tunables_daemon.go`) reverts
coalescence, the host-scope knobs and neigh `retrans_time_ms` on daemon stop —
but it does **not** restore the RSS indirection table recorded in
`priorHostTunables.rssOwned`.

So a NIC whose RSS table xpf concentrated onto the userspace-dp queue set keeps
that table after xpfd stops. The kernel network stack then runs on a table shaped
for a dataplane that is no longer there, until the next boot re-applies or an
operator runs `ethtool -X <if> default` by hand.

## Relationship to #6801

Same ownership hole, different trigger. #6801 (PR #7607) fixed the **allowlist
shrink** case — a NIC that leaves the userspace-dp binding set while the daemon
runs now gets its default RSS table and pre-xpf coalescence back on the same
commit. The **daemon-stop** case was deliberately left out of that PR:

- it adds a second bounded `ethtool` round-trip per owned NIC to a path already
  capped by the unit's `TimeoutStopSec=20`;
- it changes the restart profile — default table on stop, re-concentrated on next
  boot — which is a behaviour change worth its own review rather than a rider on
  a shrink fix.

The #6801 PR records the omission in code, `pkg/daemon/README.md` and `_Log.md`
so it is not silently dropped; this issue is the tracking number that deferral
owes.

## Fix direction

Extend `restoreStep0TunablesOnShutdown` to walk `priorHostTunables.rssOwned` and
restore each NIC's default indirection table, reusing the same restore path the
#6801 teardown uses so there is one implementation rather than two that can
drift. Points to settle rather than assume:

- **The stop budget.** `TimeoutStopSec=20` is the ceiling for the whole stop
  path, and this adds work proportional to the owned-NIC count. Bound it
  explicitly the way `hostAuthCloseoutBudget` (#5874) does, and report a
  timed-out restore rather than hanging the stop.

## Problem

The `#2473` / `#2490` / `#2539` guards drop a BGP import/export reference whose
target is not a defined policy-statement, rather than emitting
`neighbor <ip> route-map <name> in|out`. Their stated reason, repeated in
`filterDefinedPolicies`, two `protocols_render.go` comments, three tests and the
package README, is that a dangling route-map reference "resolves to PERMIT-ALL
in FRR".

**That is backwards, and it inverts the guards' effect.** FRR `stable/10.6`
`bgpd/bgp_route.c` — the deployed line (`vtysh -c 'show version'` on
`loss:xpf-userspace-fw0` reports FRRouting 10.6.0):

```c
bgp_input_modifier:   rmap = route_map_lookup_by_name(rmap_name);
                      if (!rmap) return RMAP_DENY;

bgp_output_modifier:  if (!rmap_name) return RMAP_PERMIT;
                      rmap = route_map_lookup_by_name(rmap_name);
                      if (rmap == NULL) return RMAP_DENY;
```

| state | FRR result |
|---|---|
| **no** attachment on the neighbor/AF | **permit** |
| attachment **names** a map that does not exist | **deny** |

So emitting the dangling reference would **deny** all affected routes, while
dropping it — what these guards do — removes the filter instead.

> `filterDefinedPolicies` returns the *surviving subset*, not all-or-nothing. So
> there are two distinct outcomes, and the original text described only one:
>
> | authored chain | after the drop | outcome |

## Problem

The repo-wide `go test -count=1 ./...` gate flakes at roughly **1 failure per 3
runs**, in two unrelated packages:

- `pkg/cli` — `TestDialPeerKeyedAttachesCredentialAcceptedByArmedFabric`

## Why this is worth its own issue rather than a re-run

A flaky repo-wide gate does not merely cost time — it **destroys the
interpretability of every future gate result**. The campaign discipline is that a
PR names the HEAD it gated at and reports `rc`, and reviewers act on that number.
With a ~33% false-red rate:

- the next person to see a genuine red has no way to distinguish it from noise;
- the cheapest wrong response — re-run until green, report the green — becomes the
  *rational* one, and it silently launders real regressions;
- "the gate was green" stops being evidence, which is the thing the whole
  discipline rests on.

The lane that hit it ran it down rather than re-running until green, which is the
behaviour we want; but the fact that doing the right thing costs three full-suite
runs is itself the argument for fixing the flake.

fail under the full parallel suite):

## #7632 — A slow SSE reader can pin a handler goroutine on the same unbounded-write mechanism as #6809 [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-27)

## Problem

`writeSSEEvent` (`pkg/api/sse.go`) writes each event straight to the
`ResponseWriter` and flushes, with no write deadline:

```go
func writeSSEEvent(w http.ResponseWriter, id string, event string, data string) {
	fmt.Fprintf(w, "id: %s\n", id)
	...
	if f, ok := w.(http.Flusher); ok {
		f.Flush()
	}
}
```

The server runs with `WriteTimeout` unset (0) process-wide — deliberately, so
these long-lived streams are not severed. So a subscriber that stays
**connected** and stops reading fills the socket buffers and parks the handler
goroutine in `Write` indefinitely, exactly as the BGP route stream did before
#6809.

As #6809 established (and as the corrected note in `server.go` now says): a
per-handler **context** deadline does not help here. It bounds the handler's
work, not a write already blocked in the kernel. Only
`http.ResponseController.SetWriteDeadline` ends that.

## Why this is a sibling, not a duplicate of #6809

Deliberately filed separately rather than folded into #6809, because the
profile differs in both directions:

- **Milder:** an SSE stream forks no child process. #6809's severity came
  largely from a pinned `vtysh` child plus its pipe and an in-flight RIB dump;
  here the cost is a goroutine, a socket and a subscription.
- **Already partly bounded:** `eventStreamHandler` calls
  `s.eventBuf.TrySubscribe(128)` and returns 503 over cap (#4484 L-2), so the
  number of concurrent subscribers is capped in a way the BGP endpoint's was

## #7635 — configstore: ExitConfigure clears exclusiveHolder but not configHolder — safe today only by an accident of check ordering [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-31)

## Problem

`ExitConfigure()` (`pkg/configstore/store_lock.go`) clears `exclusiveHolder` but
**not** `configHolder`, leaving a stale holder string behind with
`configDir == false`.

The store is then in a state that describes nothing real: a named holder who is
not in configure mode.

## Why it is not exploitable today — and why that is the problem

`ensureHolderLocked` short-circuits on `!s.configDir`, so the stale
`configHolder` is never consulted. Every holder check happens to ask about
`configDir` first, and the inconsistent field is never reached.

That is a **load-bearing accident**, not a design. Nothing states the invariant,
no test pins it, and the safety of the whole holder-check surface currently rests
on the ordering of two conditions in one function. A later change that:

- reorders `ensureHolderLocked`'s conditions,
- adds a new check that reads `configHolder` without first testing `configDir`,
  or
- "simplifies" the short-circuit as redundant,

re-arms it silently, with no test failing.

## Concrete near-miss

#6808 (holder-turnover binding) had to design around exactly this. The natural
implementation of a holder epoch keys off `configHolder` alone — and would have
inherited the inconsistency directly, because a stale non-empty `configHolder`
after `ExitConfigure()` reads as "still held" to anything that does not
independently check `configDir`.

That PR bumps the epoch on the `ExitConfigure` path so its own correctness does
**not** depend on the short-circuit, and documents the dependency. The next
feature to touch holder state may not notice.

`pkg/eventengine/engine.go` crossed the 1500 LOC `[WATCH]` floor in #6810

as a deliberate deferral, not a dismissal — this issue is the deferral's owner.

## Why it was deferred rather than done inline

#6810 is a lost-remediation fix, and its entire diff lives in `enqueue` and
`HandleEvent` — exactly the code a queue split would move. A verbatim move
carrying the fix inside it makes "is this line new, or moved?" unanswerable in
review, on a change whose whole point is a subtle ordering property between
latch-arming and queue admission. The project's own rule is that a bug fix and
a refactor do not ride together.

The other thresholds also argued for deferral rather than urgency: the addition
was 63 LOC (mostly the admission-verdict and latch-rollback rationale), well
under the ~200 LOC "the PR splits the module first" cue in
`docs/engineering-style.md`, and 1500 is the soft `[WATCH]` floor rather than the
hard 2000.

None of the three documented "When NOT to refactor" cases applies, which is why
this is an issue and not a permanent acceptance: `engine.go` is not a cohesive
generated schema, is not awaiting replacement, and the review-friction argument
is an argument for splitting it in a dedicated PR, not for never splitting it.

## Proposed split

Two cohesive units, both currently interleaved with engine lifecycle:

- **Queue admission** — `enqueue`, `supersede`, `actionQueueDepth`, the
  `enqueueMu` discipline and the queue counters. This is a self-contained
  bounded-channel admission policy with its own concurrency contract (#5062
  producer serialization, #5853 early dedup, #2869 FIFO, #6810 admission
  verdict). It has the clearest seam.
- **Evaluation** — `evaluateEvent`, `withinMatches`, `pruneWindow`,
  `attributesMatch`, `classifyPlan`. The `within`-clause semantics
  (#3751/#3756/#7223/#4423) are a body of rules that reads as one subject and

## Problem

A NAT rule whose `then` carries no translation action is rejected at strict
commit (`validateNATTerminalActionCardinalityStrict`, `case n == 0`). On the
tolerant load / peer-sync / rollback path that reject is downgraded to a
`cfg.Warnings` entry (`compiler_uniformgates_firewall_nat2.go:269-275`,
`lenientNATTerminalAction`, #1960 no-brick) — correctly, since the alternative
is a brick.

**But the warning has nowhere to go on exactly those paths.** `cfg.Warnings`
reaches an operator through:

- the commit **response** — `pkg/api/config.go:625`,
  `pkg/grpcapi/server_config.go:359`; and
- an apply-time log line — `pkg/daemon/daemon_apply.go:374`.

A tolerant **load** has no commit response. Boot, peer-sync and rollback are
precisely the paths where a malformed rule survives, and on all three the only
trace is one log line at startup — nothing alerts on it, and it scrolls away.
After that the node runs indefinitely with a rule the strict gate would reject
and nothing anywhere says so.

This is not specific to the actionless case: `lenientNATTerminalAction` also
carries the contradictory-action (2+ action) rules, whose resolution is a
fixed precedence the operator did not write (#5717, #7034/#7035).

## Why it matters beyond tidiness

#6823 is a live migration-contract decision — whether an actionless rule should
be terminal — and its crux is a question nobody can currently answer:

> How many real configurations actually reach this state?

That is a fleet question, and today there is no way to measure it, so the
decision has to be made on estimation. A count would convert it into a
measurement. If the count is zero across a fleet, the migration cost of the
terminal option is zero and the decision becomes easy; if it is not, the
affected configs can be found and fixed at authorship instead of being migrated
silently.

## #7655 — api/SSE: headers are not flushed at connect, so a client on an idle feed cannot tell 'connected and quiet' from 'not connected' [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-30)

## Defect

`net/http` sends no response headers until the first `Write` or `Flush`.
`setSSEHeaders` only sets header *values* — it does not flush them — so a client
connecting to an SSE feed with **no traffic** blocks waiting for headers that
were never sent.

A browser `EventSource` on a quiet firewall therefore hangs rather than
establishing the stream.

## Why it is not cosmetic

An SSE consumer cannot distinguish **"connected and quiet"** from **"not
connected"** until the first event arrives — which on a quiet box could be
hours. Every reconnect/backoff decision a client makes is built on that
distinction, so the client either sits on a connection it cannot confirm, or
tears down and retries a connection that was fine.

It also inverts the normal debugging order: the operator sees a hung client and
looks for a network or auth problem, when the stream is established and simply
silent.

## Reproduction context

Surfaced while building the #7632 slow-reader harness, which had to work around
it: the establishing event is published from a goroutine, because the `GET`
cannot return until one lands. That workaround is the evidence — a test harness
that must generate traffic to observe a connection is describing this defect.

## Fix shape

Flush after `setSSEHeaders`, so the header block reaches the client at connect
time rather than riding on the first event. The usual form is an explicit
`http.Flusher` flush immediately after the headers are set, with the
`Flusher` type assertion handled rather than assumed.

Worth a cell that asserts headers arrive **before** any event is published —
which is exactly the assertion the #7632 harness could not make, and the reason
that harness needed the goroutine.

## #7656 — userspace-dp/NAT64: a flowless fragment is filtered by the INGRESS family's output filter, so a v4 filter on the v4 egress does not see it [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-03)

## Defect

A NAT64 **non-first fragment** forwards through a **logging output filter** and is not logged.

That is the exact bypass the #5467 flowless branch exists to prevent. Its own comment says so:

> a flowless packet (non-first fragment / non-query ICMP) has NO `tx_selection_flow`, yet an interface output `then log` term may have matched its L3 tuple … Rebuild the L3-only flow (ports 0) SOLELY to attribute that filter-log event **so egress logging is not silently bypassed**.

## Measured

Same fixture, same interface, same filter term, two consecutive packets of one datagram:

```
first fragment  (has a flow)   tx=1   filter_log.sent = 1
non-first frag  (FLOWLESS)     tx=1   filter_log.sent = 0
```

The first half is the positive control: the filter demonstrably logs, on this interface, through this term. So the zero is not "nothing is wired" — it is the flowless packet specifically going unlogged.

Both fragments forward. This is purely a logging gap, not a forwarding one.

## Why nobody saw it

Two independent conditions gate the same `if let` at `forward_request.rs`:

```rust
let flowless_log_flow = if tx_selection_flow.is_none() && cos.filter_log.is_some() { ... }
```

and no NAT64 test could satisfy either:

1. The NAT64 meta fixtures left `flow_src_addr`/`flow_dst_addr` at their all-zero default, and `l3_session_flow_from_meta` returns `None` for an unspecified address (#6836).
2. **No NAT64 fixture has ever set an output filter** — `grep -c filter_log` over `tests_nat64_tunnel.rs` returns 0 — so `cos.filter_log` was always `None`.

#6836 identified (1). Fixing it alone changes nothing observable, which is worth stating because it is the trap: the fixture fix lands green and looks like progress while the block stays dark.

## Operator consequence

Audit and compliance. An operator with `then log` on an egress filter reasonably believes every forwarded packet on that interface is accounted for. Fragments of a NAT64-translated datagram are not — and fragments are exactly what a large transfer through a translator produces, so the loss is not a rare corner.

## #7667 — TestRetiredLegNeverGainsARotatedCredential_5561 is flaky under ./... — the flake direction is 'revocation did not land' [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-31)

## Observed

`TestRetiredLegNeverGainsARotatedCredential_5561` failed once during a full-repo `go test -count=1 ./...`:

```
--- FAIL: TestRetiredLegNeverGainsARotatedCredential_5561 (0.00s)
    listener_retiredauth_5561_test.go:124: secret-a still authenticates on the retired
    listener — a retiring leg must still honour a revocation immediately (#5561 round 7)
```

Seen on a branch (#7636) that touches **zero** `pkg/api` files, so it is not caused by that change.

**Reproduction rate so far: 1 in ~19.** Since the failure: **12/12 passes** running the test in isolation, **6/6 passes** running the whole `pkg/api` package, at the same head. The single failure occurred under `./...`, which runs packages in parallel — i.e. under markedly higher CPU contention than any of the passing runs.

## A mechanism — stated as an ARGUMENT, not a measurement

`ReplaceAuth` (`pkg/api/server.go:955`) does:

```go
s.auth.Store(a)
s.retireMu.Lock()
defer s.retireMu.Unlock()
for _, leg := range s.pruneRetiredLocked() {
    leg.slot.tighten(a)
}
```

and `pruneRetiredLocked` (`pkg/api/listener.go:400`) keeps only legs whose drain has **not** finished:

```go
for _, leg := range s.retiring {
    if !leg.drained.Load() {
        live = append(live, leg)
    }
}
```

So a retired leg that finishes draining *before* `ReplaceAuth` runs is pruned from `s.retiring` and therefore **never tightened** — its `authSlot` keeps `secret-a`, which is precisely the assertion that fired. The test holds its own `retired` handle, so it can still probe a leg the server has already forgotten. With no live connections, `Shutdown` returns almost immediately, so that drain is racing the very next statement in the test.

**This has not been demonstrated.** A scratch probe that forced `retired.drained.Store(true)` before `ReplaceAuth` panicked on incomplete leg setup, proved nothing, and was deleted rather than written up as a confirmation. Someone taking this should start by making that probe actually run — if it reproduces the exact message, the diagnosis is settled; if it does not, the mechanism above is wrong and worth saying so.

## #7673 — cluster smoke: make test-failover throughput is ~92 Mbits/s against a 1 Gbps floor, reproducing on master [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-31)

## The measurement

`make test-failover` on the loss userspace cluster completes **13 passed, 1 failed**, and the failure is aggregate throughput roughly **100x below the gate's floor**:

| tree | throughput | retransmits | failover assertions |
|---|---|---|---|
| `fix/6826-stop-flock-invariant` @ `1ba39fadc` | **0.0939 Gbps** (93.9 Mbits/s) | 1893 | 13/13 PASS |
| **`origin/master` @ `06e38ef48`** | **0.0924 Gbps** (92.4 Mbits/s) | 1563 | 13/13 PASS |

Both runs: `iperf3 -P8 -t120` to `172.16.80.200` (the correct reth0.80 AF_XDP target, **not** the 172.16.100.x uplink that was the misdiagnosed ceiling in #1578), each preceded by a fresh `make cluster-deploy` and `./test/incus/apply-cos-config.sh` (rc=0, atomic commit + verification OK).

The second row is the point: **this reproduces on master**, so it is not attributable to the PR that surfaced it.

## What is NOT broken

Every failover behaviour passes on both trees, which is what makes this specific rather than "the cluster is sick":

```
PASS  fw0 is primary for every redundancy group
PASS  fw0 has 10 established sessions
PASS  fw1 has 10 synced sessions
PASS  iperf3 survived fw0 reboot (failover to fw1)
PASS  fw0 rejoined as secondary (no auto-preempt)
PASS  fw1 remains primary after fw0 rejoin
PASS  iperf3 survived fw0 rejoin
PASS  fw0 became primary for all RGs after manual failover
PASS  iperf3 survived manual failover
PASS  iperf3 completed successfully
```

So sessions sync, the flow survives reboot / rejoin / manual failover, and the connection stays alive for the full 120s. Forwarding works; it is **slow**, with heavy retransmission (1500-1900 retransmits over the run).

## Why this needs an issue rather than a re-run

The gate is doing its job — this is exactly the sub-Gbit case #6897 was written for, and before that fix the run would have emitted **no cell at all** while still summarising "0 failed". So the shortfall may have been present for some time and invisible.

That is the part worth deciding: whether ~92 Mbits/s is
1. a genuine dataplane or CoS regression on master,
2. cluster/NIC/host environmental degradation (the retransmit count points at loss on the path), or
3. an expected consequence of the CoS config the smoke applies, in which case the **1 Gbps floor is wrong** and should be re-derived rather than left to fail every run.

## #7675 — commit-confirmed recovery integrity G+H+H2: tracker for the re-anchor + hazard table (split dissolved, v68 folds verified; 1 of 8 hazards residual) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-04)

Split out of #6739 so that issue can close on its provable half instead of standing as an unbounded blocker.

## Scope

Work items **G + H + H2 together**, per Codex r28's ordering constraint. They cannot be separated:

- **G** — startup-readiness gate: the recovered commit-confirmed rollback timer must not dispatch before startup completes. G releases recovery at **end-of-phase-5**, post-manager construction.
- **H** — the permanent recovery invariant: at `Store.Load`, any `FirstCommit` record whose recovered active config declares a cluster is reverted **at Load**, before manager construction.
- **H2** — confirm-record durability machinery: resolution tombstone, ArmID-keyed removal debt, shutdown-admission fence, scheduler latch, debt ledger, apply-health snapshot, authority/provider pinning.

**Landing G alone is worse than master.** H's revert-at-`Load` is only safe *before* `d.cluster` exists, while G's gate releases *after* manager construction — so G without H converts master's short pre-manager timer window into a post-manager bootstrap-with-live-cluster hybrid. H cannot land alone either: its correctness depends on H2's durability machinery.

## Why this is NOT ready to implement

The seed at `docs/research/2114-nat-pool-alarm-dp-race/followup-seed.md` (branch `research/2114-nat-pool-alarm-dp-race`, ~5.4k lines) is **explicitly not converged**:

- **Codex returned NEEDS-REVISION on eight consecutive rounds, r60 through r67.** Every MAJOR across those rounds was in this unit's machinery — shutdown-admission fence, callback join/debt ledger, scheduler abandonment, tombstone/debt durability, apply-health snapshot.
- **AGY and Claude SMR returned PLAN-READY / PLAN-READY-WITH-NITS at r66/r67.** The 2-of-3 split is recorded as *"genuine and unresolved."*
- **r68+ verification of the v68 folds was never run** — the unit was extracted from the #2114 verdict surface at v69 before that happened. Whoever takes this starts by verifying the v68 fold state.

A convergence round driven to a deadline does not settle a genuine technical disagreement about durability machinery whose failure mode is invisible until a recovery actually needs it.

## Re-anchored evidence (snapshot at master `c019b10db`)

The r67 findings' **substance survives; almost none of their line cites do.** Full table in #6739 (comment `5434895310`). Summary:

| finding | status | note |
|---|---|---|
| MAJOR 1 — ledger becomes an unbounded netlink-call lock | open, premise confirmed | fabric calls still non-contextual (`ensureFabricIPVLAN`, `reconcileIPVLANAddrs`, `CleanupFabricIPVLANs`) |
| MAJOR 2 — three-term fence check/call race | open, confirmed | `daemon_scheduler.go:192-218`; `SetPolicySchedulerActiveState` (`manager_compile.go:225-229`) releases `m.mu` before `UpdatePolicyScheduleState` (`:726-730`) reacquires it |
| MAJOR 3 — abandoned-stop latch | **limb 1 open, limb 2 RETIRED** | limb 2 shipped in #5308: the latch is the first term of `startPolicySchedulerLoopLocked`'s guard, bound by `daemon_goroutine_shutdown_5308_test.go:175`. Its cite pointed at a **blank line** |
| MAJOR 4 — `m.mu` wait vs `TimeoutStopSec=20` | open, **and worse** | the cited "~67 s" still computes for 64 MiB, but `controlMaxDeadline` is now **120 s** — a **6× overrun**, not 3.35× |

**Two things in that table matter more than the coordinates.**

MAJOR 4 **moved in the strengthening direction while the plan sat unconverged.** A round quoting "~67 s" as the bound would understate the hazard it is adjudicating.

MAJOR 3 is **half retired**, and its cite points at a blank line — so a reviewer re-checking it finds nothing and must choose between "stale, close it" and "open, re-specify it", when the truth is that half shipped 140 lines away in a different file. The likely move, re-specifying the whole finding, would have had the plan mandate machinery that already exists. **Stale cites do not fail loudly; they make a partially-fixed finding indistinguishable from an unfixed one.**

The surviving surface is **three-and-a-half MAJORs, not four.**

## #7678 — userspace-dp: stage_flow_cache_hit has no test fixture, so everything the flow-cache replay path consumes is unverifiable [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-31)

## The gap

`stage_flow_cache_hit` (`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/poll_descriptor/flow_cache_hit.rs`) has **no test fixture anywhere in the crate**. `grep -rn 'flow_cache_hit::' src/ | grep -i test` returns nothing, and the module contains no `mod tests`.

That surfaced concretely while closing a review finding on #6854. Four hops carry a filter term's `then reject <message-type>` from the filter result to the ICMP builder, and hostile review showed all four survived being hardcoded to the default — the wires were present, the assertions were not. Three are now mutation-bound:

| hop | site | bound by |
|---|---|---|
| output/CoS reject | `forward_request.rs` | `output_filter_reject_carries_the_configured_icmp_code_6854` |
| precomputed (flow-cache fallback) carry | `forward_request.rs` | same cell, precomputed arm |
| cached-descriptor fill (flowless + flow-keyed) | `cos_classify.rs` | `cached_cos_tx_selection_carries_the_reject_message_type_6854` |
| **flow-cache REPLAY consumption** | `flow_cache_hit.rs` | **nothing** |

Hardcoding `cached_descriptor.tx_selection.reject_message` to `RejectMessage::ADMIN_PROHIBITED` leaves the **entire suite green**. An operator's `then reject host-unreachable` would silently revert to administratively-prohibited on flow-cache-replayed traffic and nothing would notice.

## Why this is filed rather than fixed in #6854

The missing assertion is not the real problem — the missing *harness* is. Every other hop had somewhere to stand: an existing `build_live_forward_request_from_frame` fixture, or an existing `resolve_cached_cos_tx_selection` call site. The replay consumer has neither, so binding it means constructing a `BindingWorker`, a populated flow cache, a session table and a cached descriptor from scratch. That is its own piece of work, and doing it inside a message-type PR would bury it.

## Scope

The reject message-type is the instance that exposed this; it is not the interesting part. **Anything the replay path consumes is in the same position** — every value carried on `CachedTxSelectionDescriptor` reaches production through a consumer no test drives. The deliverable is a fixture for `stage_flow_cache_hit`, with the message-type assertion as its first user.

## Acceptance

- A fixture that drives `stage_flow_cache_hit` with a cached reject descriptor.
- A cell asserting the ICMP code byte on the replayed reply, which **reds** when `flow_cache_hit.rs`'s `reject_message` read is hardcoded to the default. That mutation is the acceptance test for the fixture itself — if it does not red, the fixture is not reaching the consumer.
- Ideally a second user, to show the fixture generalises past one field.

Refs #6854 (where this was found), #3608 (which added the replay reject path).

## #7686 — WireGuard: a malformed-but-authenticated inner packet does not roam its peer on a multi-peer interface (same discard as #7230) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-03)

Split out of #7230, which fixed the same discard on the keepalive path only.

## Defect

A **malformed-but-authenticated** inner packet does not roam its peer's endpoint on a multi-peer interface, for exactly the reason #7230 fixed for keepalives: the peer identity is discarded with the error.

`try_decap` returns `Err(DecapError::MalformedInner)` from two post-AEAD sites in `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/wg/engine.rs` — the inner-source-IP parse and the inner-length parse. Both are inside the scope where `session.peer_pubkey` is available, because `try_decap` demuxes the session from `hdr.receiver_index` **before** any AEAD work.

The caller (`coordinator/wg_control/dispatch.rs`) then recovers the identity with `engine.single_peer_pubkey()`, which returns `None` on any interface with more than one peer, so the datagram is reported `Unauthenticated` and no endpoint learning happens.

## Why it counts for endpoint learning at all

The record is **post-AEAD**. The sender provably holds the session keys, which is the whole basis on which #1865 made these datagrams count for endpoint learning in the first place. The dispatch comment has always said so: *"a malformed-but-authenticated inner also proves the peer holds the session keys. Both count for endpoint learning."* Only the attribution was missing.

## Why it was scoped out of #7230

Measured, not assumed: widening `DecapError::MalformedInner` to carry a pubkey touches **13 assertion sites** across the crate. #7230's acceptance criterion named the keepalive path specifically, and a keepalive is *continuous* traffic — a roaming peer sending nothing else is blackholed for 120–180s — whereas a malformed inner packet from an authenticated peer is anomalous rather than steady-state.

So the impact here is materially smaller than #7230's, and it was left rather than bundled into a change whose contract inversion was already the thing needing deliberate ownership. Scoped out, not overlooked — #7230's dispatch comment says so at the site.

## Suggested shape

Carry the identity the same way #7230 did: a variant that names the peer, plus the `count_decap_err` arm (that match is exhaustive with no `_`, so a new variant cannot silently become uncounted). The 13 assertion sites become `MalformedInner(_)` mechanically; none of them invert.

## Acceptance

A malformed-but-authenticated inner packet roams the correct peer's endpoint on a **multi-peer** interface, with a fail-on-revert test using at least two peers — a single-peer test passes today via `single_peer_pubkey()` and would be vacuous, which is the trap #7230's own test had to be built around.

Provenance: found while implementing #7230, by checking whether the identity was in scope at every `MalformedInner` site rather than only the one the issue named.

## #7689 — userspace-dp tests: CoSSchedulerSnapshot is 72/74 exhaustive literals, so every additive wire field is a 72-site compile break [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-31)

## The tax, measured

Adding an **additive** wire field — one with `#[serde(default)]`, designed to be invisible to older peers — is a compile break at every **exhaustive** struct literal in tests, i.e. every literal without a `..Default::default()` tail. Those literals do not care about the new field; they break only because they enumerate.

Three instances in one session:

- **#6853** added `syslog` to `FirewallTermSnapshot` — 28 literals to touch.
- **#6854** added `reject_message_type` to the same struct — 28 more, plus `CachedTxSelectionDescriptor` and `CoSTxSelection` sites.
- **#6846** added two fields to `CoSSchedulerSnapshot` — **71 literals across five test files**, all fixed mechanically with `..Default::default()`.

## But it is NOT a uniform tax — it is one outlier

Measured across `userspace-dp/src` at `abe25d5de`, counting literals with no `..` tail:

| struct | literals | **exhaustive** | share | files |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **`CoSSchedulerSnapshot`** | 74 | **72** | **97%** | 6 |
| `FirewallFilterSnapshot` | 264 | 29 | 11% | 6 |
| `FirewallTermSnapshot` | 330 | 12 | 4% | 2 |
| `InterfaceSnapshot` | 402 | 1 | 0.2% | 1 |

**Most wire structs are already well defended.** `InterfaceSnapshot` has 402 literal sites and exactly one enumerates; `FirewallTermSnapshot` is 12 of 330. The convention is in place and working nearly everywhere.

`CoSSchedulerSnapshot` is the outlier at **97% exhaustive**, which is why #6846 hit 71 and the others hit ~28. The next additive CoS scheduler field pays the same 72-literal toll, and the one after that pays it again.

## Proposed fix

Convert the 72 exhaustive `CoSSchedulerSnapshot` literals to carry `..Default::default()`, keeping only the fields each test actually asserts on. Mechanical, test-only, no production change.

Worth doing for the two mid-sized ones too (`FirewallFilterSnapshot` 29, `FirewallTermSnapshot` 12) if it is cheap once the pattern is established, but the 72 is where the cost is.

## What NOT to do

Do not reach for `#[non_exhaustive]` on the wire structs. It would force the `..Default::default()` at compile time, but it also blocks exhaustive construction *outside the defining crate* and changes the type's public contract to solve a test-hygiene problem. The convention plus this one cleanup is proportionate.

## Acceptance

- `CoSSchedulerSnapshot` exhaustive-literal count drops from 72 to ~0.
- A cell asserting the count stays low, so the pattern cannot silently return — same shape as the `#6874` sentinel guard, and the reason to have one is identical: the habit is what regrows it.
- `cargo test -- --test-threads=1` green (this crate deadlocks under parallel test threads).

## #7699 — userspace-dp: PPTP (RFC 2637) call-ID pairing needs a TCP 1723 control-channel ALG — the blocked half of #6842 [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-04)

Successor to #6842, carrying the part that needs a **TCP 1723 control-channel ALG**.

> **Rescoped.** This issue's original body said it was blocked on #7188 and gave three checks to prove it. **All three are now false** — #7188 is CLOSED and its substrate landed. The blocking text has been replaced rather than annotated, because a stale premise in a body outlives any comment correcting it. The substrate work #7188 left uncut is split to #8382; the documentation defect found while verifying this is #8380. What remains here is the ALG itself.

## State at master `5d10487a1`, verified

| the old body claimed | actually |
|---|---|
| `TunnelDiscriminator` returns **0 hits** | **219 hits**; `SessionKey.discriminator` exists at `session/key.rs:25` |
| #7188 is OPEN | **CLOSED** |
| no `pptp` `alg_type` member | still true — `{0=none, 1=FTP, 2=SIP, 3=DNS}` |

**Criterion 1 is already MET, and met better than the old body assumed.** It worried that #6842's decap guard was "not transitive" to the session path. It is present there independently: `gre_discriminator.rs:76` returns `Unparseable` on `GRE_VERSION_MASK != 0` **before** the Key read at :84, so a version-1 packet can never be `Keyed`. #7188 built that correctly and the transitivity worry was unfounded.

**Criterion 4 is NOT met, and the reason is documented in #8380.** A version-1 packet returns `Unparseable`, which is fail-closed *across* classes but equal to itself *within* one. Two simultaneous PPTP calls between one endpoint pair therefore share a `SessionKey` and alias. The enum's comment said "never merges with anything", which pointed the opposite way; corrected and pinned in #8380.

## Why header parsing still cannot do it

RFC 2637 §4.1: the Call ID field carries the call ID **of the peer the packet is being sent to**. Each side allocates its own during the control-connection exchange, so the two directions of one call carry *different* values. No symmetric reverse-key transform — of the kind `reverse_wire_key` / `reverse_canonical_key` apply for TCP/UDP ports — can pair them. Pairing requires learning the `(peer A call-id, peer B call-id)` tuple from the control channel on **TCP 1723** (Outgoing-Call-Request / Outgoing-Call-Reply) and installing that association for the GRE data channel.

## The real cost, stated so this is not estimated at a day

**This would build the first control-channel-learned association in the dataplane.** There is nothing to extend. `alg_type` today is a **label** derived from the well-known service port (`alg_type_for_session`, `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/bpf_map/publish_conntrack.rs`), not a parser — the project says so itself at `pkg/grpcapi/server_show_security_text.go`: *"nothing in the dataplane pinholes a data channel"*, guarded by #7423's test.

So FTP, SIP and DNS being present is not a precedent for "add one more ALG". None of them parses a control channel or opens a pinhole.

## Stage 1 COMPLETE — the identity substrate

Landed, so the remaining work starts from a working identity model rather than
inventing one:

| stage | what | PR |
|---|---|---|
| 1a | `TunnelDiscriminator::Pptp(handle)`, the derived call handle, the association table, fail-closed collisions | #8390 |
| 1b | cross-worker publication (`WorkerCommand::InstallPptpCall` / `ForgetPptpCall`), partial-broadcast reporting | #8392 |
| 1c | the call-id pair on the HA sync wire, with **withhold-not-downgrade** | #8394 |

**The decision that shaped all three:** the discriminator carries a locally
derived **call handle**, not the call id off the packet. RFC 2637 §4.1's call
ids are per-direction, so a packet-derived discriminator makes a reply match

## #7700 — pkg/api: split metrics_userspace.go — it crossed the 2000 LOC modularity floor [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-31)

`pkg/api/metrics_userspace.go` crossed the `[REFACTOR]` 2000 LOC floor at
**2010 LOC** in the #6842 PR (one 11-line counter emission). The crossing is
recorded in `docs/refactoring-audit-accepted.txt` as a deliberate decision, not
a silent pass; this issue is the owed follow-up that entry names.

## Why it was not split there

Splitting it is a mechanical repo-wide change that must carry
`pkg/api/metrics_test.go`'s per-function count assertion
(`TestEmitUserspaceDynamicBufferMetrics` asserts `len(got) != 45`) and the
descriptor-coverage sentinels with it, or the split silently decommissions
them. Doing that inside a one-counter dataplane fix would bury the change under
code motion.

## Why it should be split

None of the three documented "When NOT to refactor" cases
(`docs/refactoring-audit.md`) actually fits. The file is not a cohesive schema
and is not awaiting replacement — it is ~45 independent `emit*` methods over
the helper's `ProcessStatus`, which is the textbook case FOR splitting. It is
also a high-touch aggregation point: every new dataplane counter appends here,
so it is an O(n²)-ish conflict surface across concurrent PRs, the same shape
that closed `_Log.md` in #6874.

There is already a precedent for the split shape: `metrics_userspace_slowpath.go`
is a topical sibling, and the descriptor half is already split ~25 ways
(`metrics_descriptors_*.go`).

## Scope

- Move whole `emit*` methods into topical siblings (`_cos.go`, `_neighbor.go`,
  `_fairness.go`, `_worker.go`, `_wireguard.go`, ... following the existing
  `metrics_descriptors_*` topic split).
- **Move the tests with the code.** A per-function metric count assertion that
  stays behind while its function moves passes while guarding a different
  function — a split is exactly where a regression test stops guarding what it
  names.
- Prune the `docs/refactoring-audit-accepted.txt` entry once the file is under
  the floor. Per that file's own header it is a decision record, not state, so
  the entry is prunable as soon as it stops describing a live decision.

`pkg/config/compiler_nat_iface_egress.go:34-38` (PR 3a, merged in #7645):

> // snapshot-builder half of §5.7 and **needs the DRAIN discipline behind it**,
> // because marking a pool unusable with nothing draining would strand live
> // sessions.

So the config-time gate forecloses *configured* overlaps only, and the runtime
half was deliberately not shipped because it depends on a drain that does not
exist. That is a stated dependency, not an oversight.

Pool mode and interface mode maintain **independent** allocators keyed

| mode | structure | key |
|---|---|---|
| pool | `rule.pool_allocator` | `SourceNatPoolAllocatorKey` |
| interface | `InterfaceNatAllocators` | `IpAddr` |

Neither consults the other. An address that enters interface-SNAT service at
runtime (DHCP lease, netlink) while a NAT pool also covers it therefore has two
allocators minting `(E, port)` with no shared occupancy — the collision class
#6751 was filed about, reached by a route its fix does not cover.

`pool_failure.is_some()`, and `pool_failure` is set to `OverBudget` at apply
(`:717`, `:789`) — which is the retirement path the drain would have to quarantine.

no design rationale to adjudicate.

## 1. `PrefixSet::default()` is `MatchAny` — a defaulted prefix set matches EVERY address

`userspace-dp/src/prefix_set.rs:198-208`:

```rust
impl Default for PrefixSetV4 {
    fn default() -> Self { Self::MatchAny }
}
impl Default for PrefixSetV6 {
    fn default() -> Self { Self::MatchAny }
}
```

A prefix set that is defaulted rather than populated **matches every address**.
That is the permissive direction: a construction path that forgets to set the
field gets a universal match instead of an empty one, and nothing distinguishes
"deliberately match-any" from "never populated".

**What this needs first is a reachability measurement, not a fix.** Enumerate the
construction sites that can reach `default()` without an explicit assignment. If
none can, this is a latent hazard worth a comment rather than a change; if any
can, the fix direction and its blast radius follow from which. Do not flip the
default before that measurement — `MatchAny` may be load-bearing for a caller
that relies on it.

Two rows from the #6907 re-verification of the 004/005 finding set. Both **verified present at master `ac1f4d134`** by re-locating the symbol (the original citations had drifted; see #6907 and `docs/log/6907.md`), and independently re-checked against `git show origin/master:<path>` before filing.

These two are grouped because they share a shape: an `unsafe` boundary whose invariant is held by a comment rather than by the type system or a check.

## Row 05 — `MpscInbox` single-consumer invariant is not type-enforced

`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/mpsc_inbox.rs`:

```
59: unsafe impl<T: Send> Send for MpscInbox<T> {}
60: unsafe impl<T: Send> Sync for MpscInbox<T> {}
109:    let slot = unsafe { self.slots.get_unchecked(pos & self.mask) };
152:    let slot = unsafe { self.slots.get_unchecked(pos & self.mask) };
```

The `Sync` impl makes the queue shareable across threads, and the pop path indexes with `get_unchecked`. The single-consumer requirement that makes that sound is stated only in a doc comment at `:13` (*"correctness needs only the weaker single-consumer invariant"*). Nothing prevents a second consumer being introduced, and the failure mode is UB rather than a panic.

**Not claimed:** that a second consumer exists today. The finding is that the invariant is unenforced, so a future caller can violate it silently.

## Row 07 — `slice_mut_unchecked` on a shared `&MmapArea`

**Four** sites, at `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/cos/queue_service/drain.rs:97`, `:315`, `:384`, `:574`.

Neither is a live incorrect-behaviour report; both are hardening of an `unsafe` contract. A reviewer should decide whether the single-consumer invariant can be made a type (a non-`Sync` consumer handle, or a `!Send` token) and whether the drain sites can carry a bounds-checked variant on the non-hot paths.

## #7752 — userspace-dp: ShardedNeighborMap shard index derives from an UNKEYED hash — accidental clustering mitigated, adversarial targeting not (#6907 row 04) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-03)

Row 04 from the #6907 re-verification of the 004/005 finding set. **Verified present at master `ac1f4d134`**, in a narrowed form, and independently re-checked against `git show origin/master:userspace-dp/src/afxdp/sharded_neighbor.rs`.

Filed separately from the other #6907 survivors (#7750, #7751) because it is the only one with an adversarial-input shape rather than a robustness shape.

## The finding, and what survives of it

`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/sharded_neighbor.rs:162` (the original cite was `:176`, which has no such call):

```rust
let mut hasher = FxHasher::default();
```

The shard index is derived from an **unkeyed** hash. `FxHash` is not collision-resistant and carries no per-process secret, so an attacker who can choose neighbour addresses can concentrate entries onto one shard and defeat the sharding.

## What the code already answers, and what it does not

`shard_idx` post-multiplies by the Knuth constant and takes the **high** bits, documented in-tree as producing *"a uniform distribution for adversarial input patterns like `/24` LANs"*.

That is a real mitigation and it closes the **structural** clustering case — the accidental one, where a `/24` of neighbours lands in one bucket because the low bits are correlated.

**It does not add a secret.** A chosen-input adversary who can compute `FxHash` (it is a fixed, public function) can still search for addresses that collide in the high bits after the multiply, and target a shard deliberately. So the finding survives **only in its strong form**: adversarial, not accidental.

## Why that distinction matters for triage

The mitigation makes the *likely* case fine, which is why this reads as fixed on a quick look. Whether the strong form is worth closing depends on the threat model for who can inject arbitrary neighbour entries — a question this issue records rather than answers.

If it is worth closing, the shape is a per-process random key mixed into the hasher (`FxHasher::with_seed`-style or a keyed hash), seeded once at startup, which costs nothing on the hot path.

## Provenance

Filed from the #6907 sweep so the row is not lost when it closes. The citation resolves at `ac1f4d134`.

### Summary

`recordingDP` — the fixture most `pkg/dataplane` compiler tests pass to
`CompileConfig` — is classified by `isValidationPass(dp)` as **the validation
pre-pass**, not the real pass. Every test using it that touches
validation-pass-gated behaviour is therefore measuring a different pass than its
author intended, and nothing surfaces the discrepancy.

### Mechanism

```go
type recordingDP struct {
	discardingDataPlane
	...
}
```

`discardingDataPlane` is the pre-pass's own shim, and it carries the duck-typed
marker:

```go
func (discardingDataPlane) xpfValidationPass() bool { return true }
```

`recordingDP` embeds it and does not override that method, so it inherits
`true`. `isValidationPass` is a duck-typed check —

```go
func isValidationPass(dp DataPlane) bool {
	v, ok := dp.(interface{ xpfValidationPass() bool })
	return ok && v.xpfValidationPass()
}
```

— so every `CompileConfig(&recordingDP{}, ...)` in the package runs the REAL
pass against a DataPlane the compiler believes is the discarded validation pass.

**Harmless today.** The existing `recordingDP` tests assert on host mutation

## #7755 — dataplane: publishShimRegistryLocked overwrites m.maps/m.programs without closing the displaced handles — one map-set leaked per bootstrap cycle [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-02)

### Summary

On the Teardown-retain → re-`Start` recurrence path, `publishShimRegistryLocked`
overwrites `m.maps[name]` and `m.programs[userspaceShimEntryProg]` **without
closing the handles it displaces**. Nothing else closes them either. Each
bootstrap-enter/exit cycle therefore leaks one full shim map-set worth of FDs,
and — because an open FD keeps the kernel object alive after its pin is
removed — the obsolete generation's **locked kernel memory** as well.

This is the residual of #6741 AC2. It is filed separately because it is the
**opposite** defect from the one #6741 describes: AC2 says Teardown closes
without draining; the code never closes at all.

### Verified at `origin/master`

- **No close site exists for the registry.** `git grep` for a close over
  `m.maps` / `m.programs` returns nothing outside tests. The only two
  `userspaceCollection.Close()` calls (`loader_userspace_shim.go:198`, `:209`)
  are **error-return paths** — program-not-found and pin-failure — reached only
  when the registry was never published. On the success path the collection's
  maps are handed to `publishShimRegistryLocked` and retained.
- **The publish overwrites in place.** `armed_gate.go:262-267`:
  `m.programs[userspaceShimEntryProg] = prog`, then `m.maps[name] = umap` /
  `= smap` in two loops. A prior generation's handle at the same key is dropped
  on the floor.
- **`Cleanup` does not close them.** `loader.go:1439` unpins and closes *links*,
  then `os.RemoveAll(bpfPinPath)`. Removing a pin file does not close a held FD,
  so the map survives its own unpinning for as long as the leaked handle lives.
- **The re-`Start` creates fresh objects.** After `Cleanup` has removed the pin
  tree, `loadOrCreatePinnedShimMap` (`loader_userspace_shim.go:633`) takes its
  create arm. So the old kernel maps are not reused — they are stranded.

### Reachability

`Teardown()` has two callers in `pkg/daemon`:

- `daemon_run_shutdown.go:300` — process exits. **No leak of consequence.**
- `bootstrap.go:646` — `enterBootstrapMode`, where the **process continues** and
  can later re-`Start`. This is the leaking path.

## #7758 — userspace-dp/WireGuard: no RFC 6040 §4.1 ingress — inner DSCP/ECN is not propagated to the outer header on encap (GRE does) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-03)

Split out of the #6898 audit cohort (item `A1-b2-F3`), because it is **a product decision about an unimplemented feature, not a defect to fold into a cleanup**. Filed so it is not carried forward as a live defect and not "fixed" reflexively.

## The asymmetry

GRE propagates the inner DSCP/ECN onto the outer header at **encap** — the RFC 6040 §4.1 ingress direction — shipped in #2303 (DSCP, uniform model) and #2315 (ECN, normal mode), with the complementary §4.2 decap combine on the receive side.

**WireGuard implements only the decap half.** Every RFC 6040 reference under `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/coordinator/wg_control/` is §4.2:

- `mod.rs:159` — "the RFC 6040 §4.2 decap ECN combine has the outer ECN to fold into"
- `dispatch.rs:165` — "#2317: RFC 6040 §4.2 decap-side ECN combine"
- `dispatch.rs:194` — "Illegal RFC 6040 §4.2 combination — drop"
- `sock.rs:4` — module doc, "the RFC 6040 §4.2 decap ECN combine"

The send path (`sock.rs`, `wg_send_to`) ends at a bare `socket.send_to(buf, wire_target)` with no per-datagram control message, so no outer TOS/TCLASS is set.

## Why this is not filed as a defect

The original audit item reads as "the control socket sends with no per-datagram cmsg", which invites "add the cmsg" as the fix. That framing is misleading in two ways:

1. **The missing cmsg is a symptom, not the finding.** The finding is that §4.1 ingress is unimplemented for WG. A cmsg with nothing deciding what to put in it is not a fix.
2. **Adding it changes wire behaviour for every WG peer.** Outer DSCP/ECN becomes non-zero where it is currently zero, which is visible to every intermediate device doing DSCP-based QoS or ECN marking. That is a behaviour change requiring a decision, not a bug fix.

There is also a **decoy worth recording**, because it caught a reviewer already: the §4.2 receive-path handling sits in the same files and reads as if TOS handling is present. `IP_RECVTOS` / `IPV6_RECVTCLASS` are the **receive** direction. Reading them as the fix is the trap.

## Harm reachability: UNMEASURED, deliberately

Whether this causes harm depends on whether any deployment relies on WG outer DSCP for QoS — for example a WAN path that classifies on outer DSCP and would currently see WG traffic as best-effort regardless of the inner marking.

**That cannot be determined from the tree.** It is a question about deployments, not code, and is stated here as unmeasured rather than guessed. Anyone picking this up should establish it before implementing, because it decides whether this is worth the wire-behaviour change at all.

## If it is implemented

The GRE precedent is the model: uniform DSCP (RFC 2983 §3) and RFC 6040 normal-mode ECN copy at encap, so the outer carries the inner's marking and the existing §4.2 decap combine folds a path-applied CE back. The mechanism on this socket is `sendmsg` with `IP_TOS` / `IPV6_TCLASS` ancillary data per datagram, since the value varies per packet.

## Provenance

#6898 item `A1-b2-F3`, from audit cohort #5328 via PR #6384's "out of Go scope — deferred to the dataplane owner". Shape confirmed at master `7b8bd5aa4`; disposition changed from defect to feature question after tracing both directions.

## #7762 — cluster: the EMPTY-alternate-slot peer reboot needs the heartbeat epoch plumbed through clusterRuntime — #5084's incarnation cannot reach it [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-03)

Split from #6910, which closed the half that is closable with the signals currently wired. This carries the half that is not, with the measurement that shows why.

## What #6910's fix does and does not reach

#6910 landed the reboot-that-**primes** case: `notePeerBootIncarnation` reports a boot-id change, and `applyPeerIncarnationSwitchLocked` now advances the incarnation, drops the previous incarnation's ack capability and evicts the corpse.

**It cannot reach a replacement that never primes**, and that is structural rather than an oversight.

## The measurement

The original issue says this is *"blocked on #6669"*. **#6669 merged (2026-08-12)** — but two distinct peer-boot signals now exist and they are **not interchangeable**:

| signal | semantics | arrives | reachable in `installConn`? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `bootIncarnation` (**#5084**) | opaque `/proc` boot_id, **equality-only** — its own doc: *"Never order two boot ids"* | `syncMsgBulkStart` **payload** | **No** — strictly after the install |
| heartbeat boot epoch (**#6669**) | **ordered** `uint64` floor | independent UDP heartbeat, latched on `Manager.hbAuth` | **No** — see below |

**The root fact is one line.** `SessionSync`'s entire view of the outside world is:

```go
type clusterRuntime interface {
	Sessions() dataplane.SessionStore
	Telemetry() dataplane.Telemetry
}
```

There is **no Manager handle**, so the heartbeat epoch cannot be consulted from the classifier at all.

## Why "just re-classify when the boot id arrives" does not work either

`connBootIncarnation`'s own doc:

> *"or the zero value for a connection that never received an incarnated prime — **including the second fabric, which may carry config without having primed**. Zero puts the payload in the never-dropped class … the correct fail-open answer."*

The scenario is a replacement connecting *"first or exclusively on fabric 1"*. If it never primes, its incarnation is **zero forever**, and zero is deliberately fail-open. So #5084's incarnation is structurally unable to classify exactly the connection this case is about.

`TestUnknownIncarnationPrimeChangesNothing6910` asserts that limit in-tree, so it is a recorded property rather than a gap someone must rediscover.

## #7766 — test(shim-parity): the #4555 acceptance harness is wired into no gate, and has been unable to complete a run since the toolchain began printing thread ids [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-02)

Split out of #6920. The harness rot found there is fixed in that PR; **this is the reason nobody noticed it**, and it is the stronger defect.

## The harness runs in nothing

`test/mutation/shim-ext-parity-acceptance.sh` is referenced by:

- its own usage line;
- three source comments in `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/frame/tests_shim_ext_parity.rs` (`:464`, `:1260`, `:1664`) that cite it as evidence — the first reads **"PROVING THESE GUARDS FIRE"**;
- `_Log.md` (frozen, closed by #6874).

It is **not** in `scripts/run-selftests.sh`. It is **not** in any `Makefile` target. There is no `.github/workflows/` directory. So it runs only when a human types the path.

## Why that matters more than any single row

The harness aborts at row 7 with `HARNESS-RC=3` and a loud `fail()`. Its self-check works — that is good design, and it is why the rot was findable at all. **But a loud failure only helps if something is listening.** Row 7's mutation makes the walker index out of bounds, so the guards panic rather than assert; the panic fallback stopped matching once the toolchain began printing a thread id (`thread 'NAME' (338169) panicked at ...`). Since then the run has aborted before rows 8-21, every time, unnoticed.

So three source comments have cited this harness as proof the guards fire, while it has been unable to score two thirds of its own matrix. **An acceptance matrix nobody runs is invisible to review by construction**: nothing in a diff shows it, and its own alarm goes to a terminal nobody is at.

## What would fix it

Wire it into something. It is expensive — the header budgets ~1.5 h because every row is a full release rebuild — so `make test` is the wrong home. Candidates:

1. **`scripts/run-selftests.sh` with a SKIP gate**, matching the convention already used there (`rc=77` for tool-unavailable). It would still be too slow for the normal path, so it would need an opt-in env var — which reintroduces "runs only when asked".
2. **A scheduled/periodic job**, which suits a 1.5 h mutation matrix better than a per-change gate.
3. **A cheap liveness leg in `run-selftests.sh`** that does not run the matrix but proves the harness still *works*: run its preflights (P1/P2) and one row, and assert the run completes and scores what it attempted. That catches extractor rot, `fail()` regressions and toolchain drift for a few minutes rather than 90.

Option 3 is the one that matches the actual failure. The rot was not in the mutations — those still fire — it was in the harness's ability to *report*, and a single-row liveness leg would have caught it the week the toolchain changed.

## Also worth doing regardless: make the harness report its own completion

Currently an extraction failure calls `fail()`, which exits the whole run. A rot in a diagnostic path therefore destroys the entire matrix rather than one row's reason column. The rot-resistant shape is for the harness to score every row it attempted and assert **"N rows declared, N rows scored"** at the end — so a future break reports *"ran 7 of 21, 1 row unscored"* instead of aborting in a way that has to be interpreted.

That is being addressed in #6920's PR; noted here because it is the same root as the wiring gap — a check that cannot be observed is not a check.

## Provenance

Found while adding the missing `MAX_EXT_HDRS` / `eh_class` rows for #6920: the rows could not be validated because the harness would not run to completion. Confirmed independently by the reviewer with a three-line panicking Rust program against both regex forms on rustc 1.96.0.

## #7770 — cluster: fabric-redirected RETURN traffic has no policy basis on the LAN node — first packet of every new flow denied during an RG split [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-04)

## Measured symptom

A **LAN/WAN redundancy-group split** — RG0+RG1 primary on one node while RG2 stays on the other — costs the **first packet of every new flow**, in both address families, and does **not** self-heal.

Measured on `loss:xpf-userspace-fw0/fw1`, transit from the LAN host to the WAN-side target (`172.16.80.200` / `2001:559:8585:80::200`), `ping -c8`:

| placement | v4 transit | v6 transit |
|---|---|---|
| baseline — all RGs on node0 | 0% loss | 0% loss |
| **split** — RG0+RG1 node1, RG2 node0 | **12.5%** | **12.5%** |
| **split, +45s later (fresh probe)** | **12.5%** | **12.5%** |
| full failover — all three RGs on node1 | 0% loss | 0% loss |
| restored — all RGs node0 | 0% loss | 0% loss |

12.5% of 8 packets is exactly one packet, and it is the same one packet on a fresh probe 45 seconds later. This is **not a convergence transient**: it persists for as long as the split does, and it recurs for every new flow.

RTT is also consistently higher during the split (min ~1.0ms vs ~0.6ms baseline), which is consistent with the fabric crossing the split forces.

## Why it matters

The split is **operator-reachable and easy to reach by accident**. It is exactly what the #6934 reporter did: `request chassis cluster failover redundancy-group 0 node N` followed by the same for RG1, on a cluster where a third RG owns the LAN interface. Nothing warns that the RGs are now split across nodes.

A dropped first packet per flow is mild for long-lived TCP (one retransmit) but is not mild for:
- short request/response flows, where it is a large fraction of the exchange;
- UDP request/response (DNS especially), where there is no retransmit below the application;
- anything measuring connection-establishment latency.

## Not the same as #6934

#6934 reports v6 at **100%** loss for ~60s with v4 at 10%. This defect is **symmetric** — v4 and v6 equally affected at one packet — so it explains that report's v4 loss and explicitly does not explain its v6 blackhole. Filed separately for that reason.

## Note for whoever reproduces it

Measure **transit to the WAN-side target**, not reachability to the LAN VIP. The VIP is directly connected on the same segment, so pinging it never crosses the fabric: it reports **0% loss in every placement above**, including the split. A VIP probe stays green through this defect. (Measured — my first attempt at this repro did exactly that and produced a confident false negative.)

```
# from all-RGs-on-node0
request chassis cluster failover redundancy-group 0 node 1

```
ERROR: post-deploy primary reassert FAILED: node0 is not primary for every
redundancy group after 15 verification attempts. The cluster is left in whatever
state the transfer produced; do NOT run an HA smoke against it and read the
failure as an HA regression.
```

State at that point — node0 has the higher priority (200) everywhere, yet holds only RG0:

```
RG0  node0 200 primary    node1 100 secondary
RG1  node0 200 secondary  node1 100 primary
RG2  node0 200 secondary  node1 100 primary
```

`Preempt: no` and `Manual: no` on every row, failover counts 0. So the daemon restarts re-elected RG1/RG2 to node1 and node0's higher priority will not reclaim them — correct behaviour for a non-preempting cluster, but not the state the deploy requires.

Running the **same commands by hand, with a wait between them**, fixed it on the first attempt:

```
request chassis cluster failover redundancy-group 1 node 0   ; sleep 6
request chassis cluster failover redundancy-group 2 node 0   ; sleep 6
request chassis cluster failover reset redundancy-group {0,1,2}
-> node0 primary for all three RGs
```

`deploy_reassert_primary_node0` (`test/incus/deploy-lib.sh:~355`) drives each RG as:

```

2  reset pin on the reassert node

lan       wan     allow-all   permit 0       0
lan       sfmix   allow-all   permit 0       0
-         -       default-policy deny 0      0
--------------------------------------------------------
Total                                0       0
```

Snapshotted before and after a probe that was **provably** matched by policy — the same probe incremented `Policy deny` in `show security flow statistics` and emitted a `POLICY_DENY` journal line — and **no hit-count row changed**.

So the counters are not merely stale or lazily flushed; they appear never to be populated on this path.

## Why it matters

This is a **dead observability surface that looks live**. It renders a well-formed table with a plausible zero rather than an error or an "unavailable" marker, so an operator or an investigator reads "this policy has not matched" when the truth is "this view cannot tell you".

That failure mode is expensive in exactly the situation the surface exists for. During #7770 I reached for it to identify *which* policy was denying a packet; it reported nothing had matched, on a node that was demonstrably denying packets. The answer had to come from the `POLICY_DENY` journal line instead, which carries `src` / `dst` / `ingress_zone` / `egress_zone` / `policy_id`. Had I trusted the hit-count, I would have concluded no policy was involved.

It is the same class as the AF_XDP capture blindness documented in `docs/testing.md` (#7770): **an instrument that answers "nothing" when it means "I cannot see"**.

## Scope not established

I have not looked at whether this is a plumbing gap between the userspace dataplane's per-policy counters and the CLI renderer, a per-policy counter id that is never assigned, or a renderer reading the wrong source. It may also be specific to the userspace dataplane and fine elsewhere. Filed as an observation with a reproduction rather than with a diagnosis.

## Reproduce

```
# with traffic flowing lan -> wan through the node
cli -c "show security policies hit-count"          # all rows 0/0
cli -c "show security flow statistics"             # shows real, moving counters
journalctl -u xpfd | grep POLICY_DENY              # shows real per-event records
```

## #7780 — test(shim-parity): the corpus guard cannot report the divergences it exists to detect — it allocates unboundedly and fails hardest on the worst mutations [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-02)

Surfaced by #6920 (PR #7778). **Not an environment problem, and the OOM is the symptom rather than the finding.**

## The severity inversion

`shim_walk_and_userspace_walk_agree_over_a_corpus` accumulates every divergence it finds:

```rust
let mut drift: Vec<String> = Vec::new();
...
drift.push(format!("[l3={l3}] {name}: shim={s:?} userspace={u:?}"));
```

Unbounded, one `format!` per diverging pair, across the whole corpus at three L3 offsets. Sibling guards accumulate the same way.

A mutation that causes a **handful** of divergences reports them and the guard reds normally. A mutation that causes **thousands** makes the guard allocate instead of failing — and the mutations that cause thousands are the severe ones, the ones that change classification for a whole family of next-header values at once.

**So the guard is least able to report exactly the breakage it matters most for.** A narrow arithmetic slip is reported precisely; a wholesale semantic change is not reported at all.

## Measured, on the acceptance matrix's own row 18

Row 18 (`eh_class` generic arm narrowed to `{0,43,60}`, the pre-#4517 view) was killed:

```
Out of memory: Killed process (userspace.test) total-vm:60741660kB anon-rss:54567164kB
Out of memory: Killed process (userspace.test) anon-rss:56951500kB
Out of memory: Killed process (userspace.test) anon-rss:58046256kB
```

Three kills, at 54 / 56 / 58 GB RSS.

The row scored `FAIL (build) rc=137` — 128+9, SIGKILL. **The harness behaved correctly**: its build gate distinguished a killed build from an assertion red and printed *"this row proves nothing about the guards"* rather than counting it. That is the gate working; it is also why the problem is invisible unless someone reads the dmesg.

**The row itself is fine.** Re-run standalone, with memory available, it reds cleanly:

rc=101  binaries=1
  RED: over_limit_chain_never_becomes_a_session_flow

## #7786 — wireguard: per-unit peers are compiled and validated but never reach the dataplane [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-28)

## Summary

Per-unit WireGuard peers are compiled, deep-copied and validated, and then **never reach the dataplane**. Only the interface-level peer set is emitted, so a peer configured under a unit can never handshake. It fails silently: the tunnel comes up and carries the interface-level peers.

Found while re-deriving #6941. Same root, different symptom — filed separately because the repair is a design decision about per-unit WireGuard semantics, not an agreement patch.

## Measured at master `630957613`

Config is the shape the in-tree test `pkg/config/tunnel_perunit_deepcopy_test.go:123` establishes as supported — interface-level WG peers plus per-unit peers, each unit inheriting mode/listen-port/private-key and adding its own:

```
set interfaces gr-0/0/0 tunnel mode wireguard
set interfaces gr-0/0/0 tunnel wireguard listen-port 51820
set interfaces gr-0/0/0 tunnel wireguard private-key <priv>
set interfaces gr-0/0/0 tunnel wireguard peer <X> allowed-ips 10.100.0.0/24
set interfaces gr-0/0/0 unit 1 tunnel wireguard peer <A> allowed-ips 10.200.1.0/24
set interfaces gr-0/0/0 unit 2 tunnel wireguard peer <B> allowed-ips 10.200.2.0/24
```

Compiled config, then the emitted endpoint:

```
iface.Tunnel  name="gr-0-0-0"   peers=1 [X]
unit 1 tunnel name="gr-0-0-0u1" peers=2 [X A]
unit 2 tunnel name="gr-0-0-0u2" peers=2 [X B]
TunnelNameMap: map[gr-0/0/0.1:gr-0-0-0u1 gr-0/0/0.2:gr-0-0-0u2]
ENDPOINT ref="gr-0/0/0.1" tunnel.Name="gr-0-0-0" peers=1 [X]
```

Peers **A** and **B** are absent from the only endpoint emitted.

## Mechanism

1. `pkg/config/tunnelemit.go:100-104` — for an interface-level `tunnel mode wireguard` with units, the emitter emits **exactly one** endpoint, keyed by the lowest configured unit ref, carrying `iface.Tunnel` (#1910: "interface-level WireGuard is ONE persistent TUN"). Every per-unit `TunnelConfig` is discarded at this point.
2. `pkg/dataplane/userspace/tunnels.go:142` — `snap.WgPeers` is built from `tunnel.WgPeers`, i.e. from the endpoint's `TunnelConfig`. This is the **only** path from config to the dataplane for WG peers (checked repo-wide: no other non-test consumer of `WgPeers` outside `pkg/config`).

So the endpoint's key comes from the unit and its payload comes from the interface, and the unit's own payload has nowhere to go.

## #7792 — wg-interop.sh commits config through the piped CLI with no #6440 marker gate (4 sessions) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-31)

Found while fixing the same defect in `test-fbf-steering.sh` for #6936. Filing
rather than folding in: `wg-interop.sh` is a different venue (WireGuard
interop) and retrofitting it is not #6936's subject.

## The defect

`wg-interop.sh` drives **4** config-mode CLI sessions (`configure` ... `commit`)
by piping a heredoc into `/usr/local/sbin/cli`, and gates none of them on the
CLI's success markers.

Per #6440 — documented in `test/incus/cos-apply-lib.sh` and pinned by
`cmd/cli/cos_apply_markers_6440_test.go` — the piped-stdin CLI is a REPL, not a
batch runner. Verified again at HEAD in `cmd/cli/main.go`:

```go
err = c.dispatch(line)
if err != nil {
    if err == errExit { break }
    if err == context.Canceled { continue }
    fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "error: %v\n", err)   // print and CONTINUE
}
```

A failed `load merge` / `commit` prints one `error:` line, the loop advances,
and the process exits **0**. So any gate keyed on the session's exit status
cannot fire.

## Measured census

Predicate: a `test/incus/*.sh` that contains a config-mode `commit` and does
not reference the marker helpers.

## #7795 — config: an interface authored <base>.<vlan-id> resolves to the same kernel device as <base> unit N vlan-id <vlan-id> — no gate fires [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-31)

## What

Sibling of #6964, reached by a *different* derivation. #6964 covers the
per-unit **tunnel** device name (`<base>` + `u<unit>`). This is the
**VLAN sub-interface** name (`<base>` + `.` + `<vlan-id>`).

Measured on `origin/master` @ `dec5c6aa9`, via `ParseSetCommand` +
`tree.SetPath` (never `NewParser`):

```
set interfaces ge-0/0/0 unit 100 vlan-id 100
set interfaces ge-0/0/0 unit 100 family inet address 10.0.1.1/24
set interfaces ge-0/0/0.100 unit 0 family inet address 10.0.2.1/24

STRICT CompileConfig err = <nil>
  ResolveKernelIfName("ge-0/0/0.100")   = "ge-0-0-0.100"   <- the VLAN unit's device
  LinuxIfName("ge-0/0/0.100")           = "ge-0-0-0.100"   <- the authored interface
```

Two distinct authored config objects, one kernel device name, no
commit-time signal.

## Why no gate catches it

Same mechanism as #6964: `validateInterfaceNameCollisionStrict`
(`pkg/config/compiler_validate_strict_ifname_collision.go`) compares the
**authored** interface-name set. The two authored keys here are
`ge-0/0/0.100` and `ge-0/0/0`, which canonicalize to `ge-0-0-0.100` and
`ge-0-0-0` — different, so the gate does not fire. `.` and digits are
ordinary allowed characters in an authored name (`ValidateInterfaceName`,
#6834), so `ge-0/0/0.100` is authorable.

The derivation lives in `(*Config).ResolveKernelIfName`
(`pkg/config/types.go:269-276`): a unit with `VlanID > 0` resolves to
`fmt.Sprintf("%s.%d", kernelBase, unit.VlanID)`.

Note the collision is on the **vlan-id**, not the unit number — `unit 7
vlan-id 100` produces `ge-0-0-0.100` too, so the colliding authored name
need not resemble any unit number in the config.
