## #8103 — userspace-dp: the five SessionKey transforms drop the #7188 tunnel discriminator, so a keyed-GRE session's reverse companion is shared [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-03)

## The five `SessionKey` transforms drop the #7188 tunnel discriminator

`userspace-dp/src/session/key.rs` defines five key transforms. Every one of
them builds its output `SessionKey` with `discriminator: Default::default()`
while explicitly preserving its sibling `routing_domain`:

| transform | `routing_domain` | `discriminator` |
|---|---|---|
| `forward_wire_key` | `forward_key.routing_domain` | `Default::default()` |
| `translated_session_key` | `key.routing_domain` | `Default::default()` |
| `reverse_wire_key` | `forward_key.routing_domain` | `Default::default()` |
| `reverse_canonical_key` | `forward_key.routing_domain` | `Default::default()` |
| `reverse_session_key` | `key.routing_domain` | `Default::default()` |

`Default` for `TunnelDiscriminator` is `None` — the "no discriminator concept
for this protocol" class.

### Why it matters

`gre_keyed_session_flow` (`afxdp/gre_discriminator.rs`) sets
`flow.forward_key.discriminator` and nothing else. Every derived key — the
reverse companion published by `publish_shared_session`, the NAT-translated
key, the forward-wire alias — therefore lands in the `None` class.

Two consequences, both on the LOCAL packet path with
`gre-performance-acceleration` on, independent of HA:

1. **Two same-endpoint keyed tunnels share ONE reverse companion.** Protocol 47
   has no L4 ports, so their reverse keys differ only in the discriminator; with
   both `None` the second publish evicts the first.
2. **A reply may not match its own session at all.** A reply packet is parsed by
   the same `gre_keyed_session_flow`, so its `flow.forward_key` carries
   `Keyed(k)`, and `resolve_flow_session_decision` looks that key up
   (`lookup_session_across_scopes(..., &flow.forward_key, ...)`). The stored
   companion is keyed on `None`, so the lookup misses.

That is the issue's own acceptance bullet — *"reverse traffic for each resolves
only its own"* — not delivered by the landed half.

## #8104 — config: the AST redaction surface has no census, which is how the feed path leaked for years [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-31)

Found while measuring #7406 (fixed in #8096). Filing the **class** gap rather than leaving it implicit in that fix.

## The asymmetry

`pkg/config/url_field_redaction_census_6733_test.go` censuses the **JSON** surface: reflection over typed `*Config` fields, asserting a planted secret does not survive `json.Marshal`. Its own rationale is that *"the NEXT URL-shaped field will leak the same way"*.

There is **no equivalent for the AST surface.** `urlLeafIndices` (`pkg/config/ast_redact.go`) is a hand-maintained switch, and the only AST tests are per-instance (`url_redaction_6703_test.go`, `ast_redact_feed_path_7406_test.go`).

## And the predicted thing then happened, on the uncovered surface

`feed-name <f> path` is a URL-bearing leaf — `resolveBaseURL` joins it onto the feed-server URL, and `FeedEntry.MarshalJSON` has redacted it since #6703, whose doc comment says *"a `?token=SECRET` query is the common shape"*. The AST route did not:

```
feed-server et url                         https://feeds.example.com/base?<redacted>
feed-server et feed-name bad path          /sub/list.txt?token=SECRETPATHQ      <- VERBATIM
```

Same leaf, same value: REST redacted it, `show configuration` printed it. `RedactedClone` backs the on-box CLI, the gRPC config RPCs and the REST config reads, so the leak hit all three. Covered on JSON, uncovered on AST, for years — and nothing could see it, because the instrument that would have seen it only exists on one surface.

## What to build

A census asserting that every schema leaf whose value is URL-shaped is either covered by `urlLeafIndices` or on an explicit accepted-list. `hostname` and NTP `server` are the known accepted entries — both carry host-shaped values where the host itself is the secret-bearing part, which is the unsatisfiable class #7406 correctly identifies and this census must not pretend to solve.

Two properties it needs, learned from the JSON census and from #7406:

- **Dead-entry rejection on the accepted-list**, so it reads as a queue rather than a permission slip. An entry that stops matching a real leaf must fail the gate.
- It must assert the **agreement** between the AST and JSON renders for a shared leaf, not pin either to a literal. A literal encodes which surface is trusted, and in #7406 the AST side was the wrong one — a test pinning the AST output would have certified the leak.

## Why this is worth the build

Every URL leaf added from here needs someone to remember `urlLeafIndices`. That is the same discipline that failed three times before #6733 built the JSON census, and once more after it, on the surface the census does not cover. The fix for a class that recurs under a maintained switch is a census, not another instance test.

## #8108 — userspace-dp: authoritative HA resync for a static-filter revocation burst (the #7212 item-5 remainder) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-04)

Successor to #7212, which landed items 1-4 and 6 of that issue's "what a correct
implementation must engage" list. This is item 5, the only acceptance bullet
#7212's PR does not deliver.

## What #7212 shipped

Lazy per-tuple revalidation. An established session carries the config
generation its static input-filter verdict was computed under; on a hit whose
stamp is stale the verdict is re-derived once, side-effect free, and the session
is revoked only if the verdict is now DENY. Revocation goes through the #5622
pair teardown, which already `remove_shared_session`s, queues the cross-worker
`DeleteSynced`, and emits the FORWARD close delta.

## What is left

The close delta reaches the peer through the per-worker Close ring, and that
ring is bounded (4096 entries per worker) against up to 131072 sessions. #5858's
research raised this against the FAMILY PURGE, which revokes a whole address
family in one sweep and can therefore overflow the ring outright.

Lazy revalidation makes that far less likely without making it impossible. The
denied set now reaches the ring at the rate denied flows send packets rather
than as one burst, so a realistic revocation trickles. But a config change that
denies a large, uniformly-busy population — a `then discard` on a whole
`/16` at the head of a WAN interface's input filter — still hands the ring a
burst bounded only by how many of those flows have a packet in flight.

Two things are missing, and they are the same two #5858 named:

1. **A real ring-occupancy overflow predicate.** Today a delta that does not fit
   is dropped and latched (`SessionTable::delta_loss_pending`, #2442), which the
   worker turns into a full owner-RG export. That latch is the right shape, but
   nothing measures how close the ring runs to full during a revocation burst,
   so there is no evidence about whether the existing resync is reached in
   practice or whether deltas are being lost quietly first.
2. **A `SessionSync.BulkSync` fallback scoped to the denied set.** The existing
   recovery is a full owner-RG export, which is correct but expensive; a
   revocation burst knows exactly which keys it dropped.

## #8114 — userspace-dp: the cases #7212's static input-filter revalidation declines (PBR filters, sessionless decisions, cache-eviction windows) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-04)

Follow-up to #7212, which landed the lazy per-tuple static input-filter
revalidation. These are the cases that PR declines to handle, each stated in its
PR body and in the code rather than silently left. They are grouped because they
share one shape: the revalidation has a verdict but no place to apply it, or no
authority to derive one.

Found by hostile review of #8109. None is a regression — each is a case #7212's
mechanism does not reach, and each leaves behaviour exactly where it was before
#7212 (no revocation) rather than inventing a wrong one.

## 1. A route-lookup-affecting filter is not revalidated at all

`evaluate_input_filter_on_session_hit` declines when `filter.affects_route_lookup`.

The static verdict runs the NON-ROUTING walk, which DEFERS on a matched
`routing-instance` term: it returns the default `Accept` before the term's own
action is examined. #4392 established that
`then { routing-instance blue; discard; }` is a DROP — the session-MISS path
reaches that verdict through `ingress_route_table_override`, which returns
`RouteOverride::Drop`. Reading the deferral as an Accept would PRESERVE and
STAMP a session the routing-aware evaluation drops, and the stamp would keep it
from re-deriving until the next generation. The walk cannot distinguish "Accept
because nothing matched" from "Accept because it deferred", so declining is the
only honest answer available at that seam.

The cost is that a filter containing ANY `routing-instance` term gets no static
revalidation, including for flows its plain static deny terms match.

Wanted: one side-effect-free action core that preserves a matched PBR term's
terminal action, plus the counted/logged routing-aware replay for the DENY arm
so the revoking packet is accounted exactly once — the same two-phase shape the
non-PBR path already uses.

`canonical_session_key(...)` returns `None` and the revalidation declines. Two
populations reach it:

* the TRANSIENT peer-synced hit — `should_keep_synced_hit_transient` keeps the

#8111 makes a LOCAL, port-translating (PAT) source-NAT mint refuse a
`(pool address, port)` that another pool's occupancy bitmap already holds. Two
pools whose addresses overlap are two independent occupancy domains — the
allocator key carries the pool NAME — and each is blind to the other. That is
one route. Three others reach the identical duplicate and are untouched.

All four are reachable only from the same population: the Go #5144 strict gate
(`validateNATPoolExternalTupleOverlapStrict`) rejects overlapping pools at
commit on address overlap alone, so these arrive from a tolerated lenient load,
a peer sync, an older control plane, or a handcrafted snapshot — the population
#6812's aggregate-budget gate exists for.

## R1 — the address-only path claims no occupancy bit

`port no-translation` and port-less protocols mint an `address_only_owners`
reverse-identity token (`allocator.rs`), not an occupancy bit. The peer query
added in #8111 reads occupancy bits, so the two are invisible to each other in
BOTH directions: an address-only flow in pool A preserving `X:P` does not stop a
PAT mint of `X:P` in pool B, and two address-only flows in different pools
collide whenever protocol and remote tuple match.

Closing it needs a second query against `address_only_owners`, keyed by
`(protocol, translated ip, translated port, dst ip, dst port)` rather than by
`(address index, port)`.

## R2 — the HA synced reserve never reaches the check

`reserve_synced_on_first_pool_owner` (`nat/source/synced.rs`) calls
`reserve_flow` on one allocator directly. `reserve_flow` checks and sets only
that allocator's bitmap, so an imported flow narrowed to pool B succeeds while a
LOCAL flow already owns the same tuple in pool A. The coordinator then publishes
the imported session and the reverse-map insert can displace A's owner.

No concurrency and no weak-memory execution is needed — it is sequential.

## #8119 — compiler: an interface with both an interface-level and a unit-level MTU ALTERNATES its MTU on every apply [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-31)

Found by a hostile plan review on #7289 and independently verified at `origin/master` `f32aacbac`. It is not an #7289 abort-path defect — it is a **steady-state** defect on every apply, which is why it is filed separately.

## The defect

`mapZoneInterface` writes the interface-level MTU and then the unit-level MTU against the **same cached `netlink.Link` object**, and `netlink.LinkSetMTU` does not update that object's cached attributes. So the second comparison is made against a stale value, and the two writes take turns.

**Site 1 — interface-level** (`pkg/dataplane/compiler_iface.go:875-887`):

```go
nl, nlErr := result.cachedLinkByIndex(physIface.Index)
...
if nl.Attrs().MTU != ifCfg.MTU {
        if err := netlink.LinkSetMTU(nl, ifCfg.MTU); err != nil {
```

**Site 2 — unit-level, "overrides interface-level"** (`compiler_iface.go:992-1004`):

```go
if unitMTU > 0 {
        if nl, err := result.cachedLinkByName(physName); err == nil {
                if nl.Attrs().MTU != unitMTU {
                        if err := netlink.LinkSetMTU(nl, unitMTU); err != nil {
```

**The two lookups return the same object.** `cachedLinkByName` populates both caches from one `LinkByName` (`compiler.go:147-176`): it stores `r.linkCache[name] = link` **and** `r.linkIdxMap[link.Attrs().Index] = link`.

**And the write does not refresh it.** In the pinned `vishvananda/netlink v1.3.1` (`go.mod:14`), `LinkSetMTU` sends `RTM_SETLINK` and returns the error; it never assigns `link.Attrs().MTU`.

## The trace

Interface MTU `X`, unit MTU `Y`, `X != Y`, untagged interface (`vlanID == 0`, so both leaves address the same physical netdev). Live MTU starts at `Y`:

| apply | cached attr | site 1 (`!= X`) | site 2 (`!= Y`) | live MTU after |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `Y` | `Y != X` → **set X** | `Y != Y` false → skip | `X` |
| 2 | `X` | `X != X` false → skip | `X != Y` → **set Y** | `Y` |
| 3 | `Y` | → **set X** | skip | `X` |

It alternates forever. Every commit — including a no-op re-commit of the identical config — changes the interface MTU, and an operator watching `ip link` sees it flap between the two configured values.

## #8120 — compiler: an apply's FINAL host state depends on Go map iteration order when two units of one interface sit in different zones [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-31)

Found by a hostile plan review on #7289, at `origin/master` `f32aacbac`. Filed separately because it is a **steady-state** defect, not an abort-path one — the #7289 research round hit it while trying to establish that Phase 2 converges.

## The defect

Strict validation deliberately accepts **two units of one physical interface in different security zones** (`pkg/config/compiler_validate_strict_zones.go:187-193,250-253`), and the committed test does exactly that without giving either unit a VLAN ID (`pkg/config/zone_interface_membership_test.go:97-111`).

With no VLAN ID and no tunnel, both unit references resolve to the **same physical netdev** with `vlanID == 0` (`pkg/dataplane/compiler_iface.go:123-138`).

`programZoneMaps` then ranges the zone map (`compiler_iface.go:614-658`) — a Go map, so **iteration order is randomised per run**. Each unit independently:

- writes the same `{physIfindex, 0}` zone key (`compiler_iface.go:839-843`), so the last writer wins the zone attribution; and
- reconciles that one physical link to **its own** exact address set and unit MTU (`compiler_iface.go:964-1004`, address delete/add loop around `:341-364`).

Because `planAddressReconcile` computes `del`/`add` against *that unit's* desired set, the second unit processed deletes the addresses the first one just added.

## Consequence

The **final** host state after a successful apply — which zone the netdev is attributed to, which addresses it carries, which MTU it has — depends on Go's map iteration order. Two applies of the identical config on the identical box can land in different states, and the apply reports success either way.

This is distinct from, and worse than, the nondeterministic *abort prefix* discussed on #7289: that one says you cannot know how far a failed apply got. This one says a **successful** apply has no single defined outcome.

## Interaction with #8119

#8119 (MTU alternation via stale cached link attrs) is a different mechanism on the same code path, and the two compound: #8119 makes the MTU flap between two configured values on consecutive applies, and this makes *which* value is even a candidate depend on map order.

## Suggested direction (not prescriptive)

The root is that a per-zone loop performs per-*interface* actuation, so an interface reachable from two zones is actuated twice with different intent. Options: hoist the per-netdev actuation out of the zone loop and drive it once from a merged desired-state per netdev; or reject the config shape at strict-validate time (but the strict validator accepts it deliberately, and a committed test pins that, so changing it is a behaviour decision rather than a bug fix).

Deciding once per netdev is the option that also removes the ordering dependency rather than hiding it behind a sort.

## Notes for whoever takes it

- A sort over the zone map would make the outcome *stable* but still arbitrary; stability is not the same as correctness here.
- The existing test at `zone_interface_membership_test.go:97-111` passes today and documents the accepted config shape — it is the fixture to build from, not an obstacle.
- Any test needs two applies and an assertion on final host state, not just on the compile result.

## #8121 — userspace-dp/HA: an IDLE persistent-NAT lease cannot be rebuilt from synced sessions — the population #7360 cannot reach [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-04)

Split from #7360 (persistent-NAT lease reconstruction on the standby), which
lands the rebuild-from-synced-sessions half. This is the population that half
provably cannot reach.

## The gap

#7360 reconstructs a persistent-NAT lease on the standby by deriving it from the
synced sessions that hold it. That works for every lease with live flows, which
is every lease session sync can observe — a lease is learned from a session, so
`active_flows >= 1` holds by construction.

An **idle** lease has no session to be learned from:

- `PersistentLease.active_flows == 0` — every flow that held the binding has
  closed;
- `expires_at_ns > now_ns` — it is still inside its persistence timeout, so on
  the active node the binding is **still live** and the client would reuse it.

Between those two facts the lease exists, is reusable, and is invisible to
session sync. #7360 cannot rebuild it, and no session-derived mechanism can.

## Who this costs

A client whose flows all closed shortly **before** the failover, but within
`persistent-nat` `timeout` (`SourceNatRule.persistent_nat_timeout_ns`, from the
rule's configured `timeout_secs`).

Concretely: a client that goes quiet for 30 seconds under a 300-second
persistence timeout is, on the active node, still guaranteed its previous
translated port for another 270 seconds. Fail over inside that window and it
gets a new one. The window is exactly the configured timeout, so the exposure
scales with how generous the persistence setting is — a long timeout, which an
operator chooses precisely because they want long-lived stickiness, is also the
setting that widens this.

It is not a fail-open and not a forwarding outage: the client gets a working
translation, just not its previous one. It is the same *class* of silent
functional regression #7360 describes, on the subset #7360 does not fix.

## #8122 — compiler: a VLAN child's LinkSetUp failure is returned on the create path and only logged on the adopt path, so a re-apply reports success with the interface down [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-04)

Found during the #7289 research round and verified at `origin/master` `f32aacbac`. Filed separately because it is a concrete bug with a clear failure mode, independent of #7289's design question.

## The asymmetry

`ensureVLANSubInterface` (`pkg/dataplane/compiler_iface.go:197-275`) handles the same failure two different ways depending on which branch it takes.

**Create path** — the error is **returned**, so the apply fails:

```go
if err := netlink.LinkSetUp(link); err != nil {
        return 0, true, fmt.Errorf("set VLAN sub-interface %s up: %w", subName, err)
}
```
`compiler_iface.go:263-265`

**Adopt path** — the error is **logged and swallowed**, and the function returns success:

```go
if existing.Attrs().OperState != netlink.OperUp {
        if err := netlink.LinkSetUp(existing); err != nil {
                slog.Warn("could not bring existing VLAN sub-interface up",
                        "name", subName, "parent", parentName, "vlan_id", vlanID,
                        "err", err)
        }
}
...
return existing.Attrs().Index, false, nil
```
`compiler_iface.go:227-238`

## The failure

An apply creates the child (`LinkAdd` succeeds) and then fails — either at `LinkSetUp` itself, or anywhere later in the apply. The host now carries a **down** VLAN child.

The next apply takes the **adopt** branch, because the device exists. It nudges `LinkSetUp`, that fails again for whatever persistent reason, the failure is swallowed, and `ensureVLANSubInterface` returns `(index, false, nil)`. The apply **reports success** with the interface still down and nothing forwarding through it.

So the second apply neither converges nor fails. It reports a state it did not reach.

## #8129 — config: delete the #7342 tcp-session enforcement advisory — DEFERRED until a tag past v0.9.3 has shipped and deployed (do not close on a sweep) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-10-15)

Delete the #7342 enforcement advisory. That is the whole content of this issue.

## What to delete

`tcpSessionTimeoutAdvisory` in `pkg/config/flow_tcp_timeouts_6539.go`, its call
site in `compiler_validate_warn.go`, and the cells that pin it.

## Why it exists

#7342 made `security flow tcp-session initial/closing/time-wait-timeout` live.
Before it they were accepted-only, and #6539 had been telling operators so at
commit — so the population carrying a configured value is exactly the operators
who set one AFTER being told it did nothing. For them the upgrade activates a
value they had no reason to keep realistic, and `initial-timeout` is the sharp
one: a large value turns the half-open window from a fixed 20s bound into a
session-table pin.

The advisory says, at commit, that the value is now in force. It fires for
exactly that population and it is not keyed to any magnitude, because a
threshold would need a derivation nobody has.

## Why it is not self-retiring

Automatic retirement needs a release-version predicate, which is a mechanism
with its own failure modes for a message that costs one commit-time line. The
alternative — "keep until someone deletes it" — rots into permanent noise unless
the deletion is tracked, so it gets an object instead. Same shape as the
UNSURFACED queue and the dead-entry-rejecting accepted list: a thing that is
supposed to be removed has something tracking its removal.

The advisory's own doc comment names this issue, so the temporariness is visible
from the code rather than only from a changelog.

## When

Once operators upgrading across the #7342 boundary are no longer the population
committing configs — one release is the intent. There is no automated signal for
that; it is a judgement call, which is why this is an issue and not a timer.

## #8136 — harness: 20 of the 21 test/incus *_test.py files are run by no target — pytest-style, and pytest is not a dependency [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-31)

Found while fixing #7424 row 1, and it explains how that defect survived in a file that **has** a test suite.

## The gap

`test/incus` holds **21** `*_test.py` files. The Makefile runs exactly **one**:

```
test-host-inbound-lib:
	python3 -m unittest discover -s test/incus -p 'host_inbound_probe_test.py'
```

The other 20 are never executed by any target. They are also **pytest-style** — `import pytest`, bare `assert`, module-level `test_*` functions — so `unittest discover` would not collect them even if the pattern were widened, and `python3 -c "import pytest"` fails on this box: pytest is not a declared dependency of the repo.

So these files are read as coverage and provide none.

## Why it matters concretely

#7424 row 1: `step3-tx-kick-classify.py` returned a definitive `OUT` — *"the TX-kick hypothesis is ruled out"* — from an all-zero capture in which nothing was measured. `step3-tx-kick-classify_test.py` exists and is 260 lines. It did not catch the defect, and could not have failed if it had, because nothing runs it.

The sibling `step2-sched-switch-classify.py` had already solved the same problem (its C175-HC-070 guard), which is exactly the kind of divergence a running suite surfaces.

## What this is not

Not an argument that these tests are bad — several are careful, and #7424's own analysis leaned on reading one of them to decide between two fix shapes. The problem is only that their result is never observed.

## Options, roughly in increasing order of cost

1. **Add pytest to the toolchain and a `make test-harness` target** running all 21. Truthful and cheap to write; adds a dependency the repo has so far avoided.
2. **Convert them to `unittest`** and widen the existing discover pattern to `*_test.py`. No new dependency, and the existing target already proves the mechanism works. Mechanical but touches 20 files.
3. **Run them in whichever CI does have pytest**, if one does, and say so in the files — the smallest change, but it leaves a local `make` run silent about them.

I have no view on which; the decision is about whether pytest becomes a repo dependency.

## Worth checking as part of it

Whether any of the 20 currently **fail**. They have not been run as a suite, so some may have rotted against the code they test — and a target that lands red is worse than no target unless the rot is fixed in the same change. That should be measured before wiring, not after.

the first failing binary it takes the whole gate with it — 2 of 10 binaries run,
`RUST_RC=2`. It cost one merge cycle today and will cost more.

## Evidence that it is non-deterministic, not a regression

Same commit, same command, opposite outcomes:

```
run 1  make test-rust  RUST_RC=2  1 named failure  binaries=2 (aborted)
run 2  make test-rust  RUST_RC=0  0 failures       binaries=10  collected=5127
```

Control at pure `origin/master` (9b208bd91), full `make test-rust`:
`RUST_RC=0`, 10 binaries, 0 failures.

The failure:

```
thread '...snapshot_under_concurrent_writer_never_tears' panicked at
src/afxdp/cold_path_hist_tests.rs:996:5:
reader observed only zero samples across 1000 coherent and 0 retry-exhausted snapshots
```

## Why it flakes

The assertion is that a reader racing a concurrent writer observes at least one
non-zero sample across 1000 snapshots. It does not assert a *property* of the
seqlock — tearing, or retry exhaustion — it asserts that the WRITER made
progress within the reader's window. Those are different claims, and only the
first is about the code under test.

On a loaded box the writer thread can be starved for the whole reader loop, so
the reader legitimately sees 1000 coherent all-zero snapshots. `0
retry-exhausted` in the message is the tell: the seqlock behaved perfectly. The
test failed because the scheduler did not run the writer, which is not a
property of the histogram.

both describe the topic as one of four that "drive full v4+v6 conntrack walks".

It does not walk. `natshow.RenderPersistent`'s only dataplane read is
`PersistentNATTable.All()` — an O(bindings) snapshot copy of an in-process Go
map, taken under that table's own `RWMutex` (#4811). It touches no conntrack
bucket, holds no session-store lock, and contends with nothing on the shared
control socket. (#7315's premise inherited the same error: the two
`pkg/natshow/persistent.go` line numbers it cites for `RenderPersistent`, `:85`
and `:102`, are both inside `RenderPersistentDetail`.)

Pinned at HEAD by `TestRenderPersistentDrivesNoWalk7315` and
`TestShowTextPersistentNATDrivesNoWalk7315` (PR #8149), which count conntrack
rows visited and require zero.

## Why it matters

`MaxConcurrentSessionWalks` is 4, and REST and gRPC alias ONE
`diagcmd.SessionWalkLimiter`. `ShowText` is on `fabricAllowedUnaryMethods`, so
`persistent-nat` is reachable from the cluster peer, unlike the loopback-only
NAT RPCs.

A peer (or an automation loop) polling `show security nat persistent-nat` can
therefore hold all four slots for work that is not a session scan, and the
surfaces that genuinely are session scans — `GET /api/v1/sessions`, the session
summary and zone-pair endpoints, `GetSessions`, `GetStatus`'s `SessionCount` —
start returning **HTTP 429 / `codes.ResourceExhausted`**. That is the exact
starvation the limiter exists to prevent, sourced from a surface that does not
consume the resource being rationed.

## #8153 — selftest: mutate-selftest.sh is registered with run_shell, so it fails under dash on every `make selftest` [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-31)

`make selftest` is **red at `origin/master`** and has been since
`scripts/mutate-selftest.sh` was added.

```
FAIL: scripts/mutate-selftest.sh
    scripts/mutate-selftest.sh: 11: Bad substitution
    scripts/mutate-selftest.sh: 12: .: cannot open <root>/mutate-lib.sh: No such file
...
passed=96  skipped=0  failed=1
```

## Cause

`scripts/run-selftests.sh:192` registers it with `run_shell`, and `run_shell`
**forces `sh` regardless of the script's shebang**. The script declares
`#!/usr/bin/env bash` and resolves its library with `${BASH_SOURCE[0]}`, which
dash cannot parse — so line 11 is a syntax error, line 12 then sources the wrong
path, and nothing the self-test actually tests ever runs.

Verified on a pristine `origin/master` worktree: `sh scripts/mutate-selftest.sh`
reproduces both errors; `bash scripts/mutate-selftest.sh` prints
`mutate-selftest: all checks passed`.

## The contract was already written down

`run_bash` exists for exactly this, and the runner's own doc comment at
`scripts/run-selftests.sh:43-48` describes this failure by name:

> run_shell forces `sh` regardless of the script's shebang, which is correct for
> the POSIX self-tests it was written for. A self-test that legitimately needs
> bash (arrays, `[[ ]]`, `<<<` herestrings, `${var//pat/}`) fails under dash
> with **"Bad substitution" — a syntax error, not a real result**.

So this is not a missing contract, it is a registration that did not follow one.

## Why nothing caught it

The #7296 self-test census asks "is every self-test **invoked**". It globs

separately.

## The window

`upsert_synced_session` publishes a peer-synced row to the kernel session map at
three sites in `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/ha/session_import.rs` (`:403`, `:438`,
`:519`). All three are `if let Some(session_map_fd) = ..` with **no `else`**. When
the fd is absent the publish is skipped and the import still returns
`SyncedImportOutcome::Applied` — whose own doc comment says *"The entry was
published"* — so `refusal_reason()` is `None`, `response.ok` stays true, and Go
records a successful install and keeps its BPF mirror row.

`bpf_maps.session_map_fd` is set to `None` by `Coordinator::stop_inner`
(`coordinator/mod.rs:733`) and re-set by `reconcile::bringup`
(`bringup.rs:394`), so it is absent for the whole span of a reconcile.

## Why it is closed today

Two mechanisms, and both must be understood before changing either.

1. **Every reconcile replays the shared map.** `reconcile` opens with
   `teardown::tear_down` (`reconcile/mod.rs:337`), which calls
   `snapshot_shared_session_entries()` (`coordinator/mod.rs:837`). That **clones**
   the whole shared `synced` map — it does not drain it — and
   `replay_preserved_sessions` (`bringup.rs:157`) republishes it once the new map
   is up. So an import recorded while the fd was absent is published by the next
   reconcile. The pre-first-reconcile case, and the standby taking bulk sync
   before its first apply, both self-heal.

2. **The `ServerState` mutex closes the remainder.** The only genuinely lossy
   interval is an entry arriving **between** that capture and the replay.
   `handlers/mod.rs` dispatches `apply_snapshot` and `sync_session` under one
   `state.lock()`, so they cannot interleave and nothing can arrive in it.

## #8163 — flowexport: one undialable flow-server disables NetFlow/IPFIX export for EVERY collector [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-31)

Found while measuring #7422 row 11 (PR #8161). That PR fixes the SHOW surface —
`show security flow monitoring` / `show forwarding-options` now annotate a
collector the dataplane does not install. This issue is the availability half,
which is a forwarding-behaviour change and deliberately out of that PR's scope.

## The defect

A `flow-server` with no `port` (or a port outside 1-65535) produces a
`CollectorConfig.Address` that cannot be parsed as a UDP destination.
`dialCollectors` treats that as fatal, and the failure propagates all the way up
to abort the ENTIRE exporter rebuild — not just the bad collector, and not just
its group.

The chain, at `ae4802343`:

1. `collectInstanceVersionCollectors` (`pkg/flowexport/manager.go:200`) appends
   every flow-server to `collectors`. When `fs.Port <= 0` it skips the
   `net.JoinHostPort` and leaves `Address` as the bare host
   (`manager.go:246`). There is no exclusion filter here.
2. `dialCollectors` (`pkg/flowexport/transport.go:129`) loops the collectors and
   calls `net.Dial("udp", c.Address)`. On error it calls
   `fail(err)` — which closes every socket opened so far and returns
   `nil, err` for the WHOLE group. Measured:
   `net.Dial("udp", "10.0.0.1")` -> `address 10.0.0.1: missing port in address`;
   a >u16 port -> `address 70000: invalid port`.
3. `NewExporter` / `NewIPFIXExporter` (`netflow.go:595`, `ipfix.go:812`) return
   that error from the constructor, so the exporter object is never built.
4. `Daemon.reconcileFlowExporter` (`pkg/daemon/daemon_flowexport.go:211-235`)
   builds the full replacement set in a loop and, on the FIRST constructor
   error, cancels the context, closes the partially-built set and `return`s.

Step 4 is what makes this worse than "the bad collector's siblings". The loop is
over `ecs` — one `ExportConfig` per template/family group — so a single
unparseable collector in one group prevents EVERY group's exporter from being
constructed. All NetFlow v9 (and, via the IPFIX twin at `daemon_flowexport.go:370`,
all IPFIX) export stops.

## #8183 — show interfaces: the gRPC surface prints the ZONE host-inbound set for an interface whose override REPLACED it [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-04)

## The divergence

`pkg/grpcapi/server_show_interfaces.go:301-309` (`ShowInterfacesDetail`) renders
`li.zone.HostInboundTraffic.SystemServices` **verbatim** for the interface being
shown.

Its local-CLI twin, `pkg/cli/cli_show_interfaces.go:359`, routes the same render
through `zone.InterfaceHostInboundEffective(ref)`.

Since #6515 a per-interface `host-inbound-traffic` stanza **REPLACES** the zone
stanza on that interface. So for any interface that declares one, the two
`show interfaces` surfaces print **different admission sets for the same
interface**, and the gRPC one prints a set that is not what is enforced.

This predates and is independent of #7490 — found while censusing the
zone↔interface resolution sites for it. Not folded into that PR because it is a
separate surface with its own golden, and a display fix hidden inside an
enforcement change is exactly the shape that does not get reviewed.

## Why it is not cosmetic

`show interfaces <if> detail` is what an operator reaches for to answer "what
does this interface admit to the host". On the remote `cli` — the surface most
operators actually use — the answer is the zone's set, which the interface may
have narrowed to nothing. An operator who tightened an interface, confirmed it
with `show interfaces`, and read back the *zone's* tokens has been told
something specific and untrue about their posture: the #5619 doctrine.

The inverse is worse: a zone admitting `ssh` with an interface stanza of
`{ ping; }` renders as admitting `ssh` on that interface. That reads as an
exposure the box does not have — and the operator's remedy (removing `ssh` from
the zone) changes nothing on that interface.

## Fix shape

Route the gRPC path through `InterfaceHostInboundEffective` like the local CLI
does. `cfg`, `li.zone` and the interface ref are all in scope at the call site
(a `ref` is already built at `:316` for the lifeline check), so this is a
routing change, not a plumbing one.

## #8185 — showaudit: the #6534 surface gate counts SURFACES, not samples — a partly-fixed renderer reads as fixed [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-03)

The #6534 surface gate (`pkg/showaudit/surface_gate_6534_test.go`) marks a
render function **annotated** if it consults the family's drop predicate
*anywhere* in its body. A function that applies the verdict to one output and
not to another is therefore annotated, drops out of the `Unannotated` census,
and is never re-examined.

**A partly-fixed surface reads as fixed.**

## Mechanism

`reachesPredicate` walks the function's calls into `pkg/config` (plus
same-package callees, to a depth budget) and returns `true` on the first match:

```go
for _, sym := range configCallsIn(p.fset, rec.fd) {
    for _, pred := range preds {
        if sym == pred { return true }
    }
}
```

There is no association between the predicate's result and the output
statements it is supposed to gate. One consultation clears the whole function,
however many samples or lines it emits.

The failure is silent and permanent: the entry vanishes from the census, so
neither the gate nor a reader auditing the census sees it again.

## Reachable, not theoretical — three instances found

All three emit live source-NAT port usage for a pool the snapshot builder
refused, because `cr.PoolIDs` contains disarmed pools (`compiler_nat.go`
assigns IDs without consulting any disarm predicate), so every
`ReadNATPortCounter` lookup succeeds and returns a `0` the surface treats as
measured.

| surface | in the census? | why the gate cannot see it |
|---|---|---|
| `pkg/api/metrics_nat.go:collectNATPoolMetrics` | yes — **by accident** | It reaches `SourceNATPoolDisarmedReason` *transitively* through `SourceNATPoolReportablePorts`, and `reachesPredicate` does not follow calls into `pkg/config`. So it stayed listed for an unrelated reachability reason. Registering the helper as a `SurfacePredicate` — which the field's own doc invites — would have dropped it and taken the defect with it. |
| `pkg/cli/cli_show_nat.go:showNATSourcePool` | **no** | Prints `Unusable: <reason>`, which annotates it, then prints `Ports allocated` / `Ports available` ungated. `Utilization` is suppressed only incidentally, being gated on `totalPorts > 0`. |

## #8189 — system login: warn at COMMIT when a deny-commands pattern cannot be enforced on the gRPC surface [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-04)

## The gap this closes

#7172 cut 5b enforces `deny-commands` on the gRPC listener, and its
`unenforceableDenyPatterns` check answers a question the operator needs: does
this pattern match **any** command the gRPC surface can produce? A pattern that
matches none can never fire there — it restricts the on-box CLI only.

Today that answer is **logged once per class from the authorization path**
(`warnUnenforceableDenyPatternsOnce`, `pkg/grpcapi/authz_command_gate_7172.go`).
That is the wrong moment and the wrong surface for it:

- it fires when someone first makes a restricted call, not when the operator
  **authors** the restriction — so the feedback arrives detached from the edit
  that caused it, possibly days later, possibly on the other node;
- it lands in the journal rather than in the `commit` output, which is where
  every other #7172 advisory speaks (`validateHostInboundZoneLevelDHCPWarnings`
  and the #6515 replace advisory are the models);
- an operator who never exercises the class never learns.

The right shape is a commit-time advisory, alongside the other login-class
warnings.

## Why it was not done in cut 5b

Import direction. The advisory belongs with the other commit warnings in
`pkg/config`, and the three tables it must consult
(`methodCanonicalCommand`, `showTextTopicCommand`, `systemActionVerbCommand`)
live in `pkg/grpcapi`, which imports `pkg/config` and not the reverse.

Doing it needs the tables reachable from `pkg/config`. They are plain
`map[string]string` with nothing gRPC-shaped about them, so moving them is
mechanical — **but their guards are not**, and the guards are what keep the
tables honest:

- `TestEveryPricedMethodIsMappedOrNamedAbsent7172` walks `methodPermissions`;
- `TestEveryShowTextTopicHasACanonicalCommand7172` parses `server_show.go` with
  `go/ast`;
- `TestEverySystemActionVerbHasACanonicalCommand7172` parses the handler's
  `switch req.Action`.

## #8194 — harness: 19 of 21 test/incus python test files are invoked by no runner at all; 2 also depend on an uninstalled pytest [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-31)

Found while closing #7424. Verified at `origin/master` `583aa9748`.

## The defect

`test/incus/step3-tx-kick-classify_test.py` and `test/incus/step1-histogram-classify_test.py` `import pytest`. Nothing else in the repository does:

```
$ python3 -c "import pytest"
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'pytest'
$ grep -rn "pytest" Makefile scripts/run-selftests.sh
(no output)
```

So both files fail at **import**, before a single assertion is reached. They are not skipped — they are dead.

## Why this is a real gap and not a style nit

The 19 sibling files establish the working convention by weight of numbers:

| | count | runnable |
|---|---|---|
| `import unittest` + `__main__` self-runner | **19** | yes |
| `import pytest` | **2** | **no** |

`python3 -m unittest discover -s test/incus -p '<file>'` is the invocation the Makefile already uses (`Makefile:521`). The two pytest files cannot be run that way, and there is no other runner.

The concrete cost: **#7424's Row 1 fix is guarded by a test that never executes.** That fix — refusing a definitive TX-kick `OUT` verdict from a capture in which nothing was measured — is correct code with a correct test beside it (`:304` positive, `:355` negative control), and the pair is inert. The same applies to step1-histogram's 13 `pytest.raises` cells covering the K1/K2 invariant and every monotonicity check on the snapshot parser. Those are the guards that stop a corrupt capture producing a confident verdict, which is the entire point of the C175 harness family.

## What the port requires

Not mechanical, but small and bounded. The pytest surface actually used is narrow:

- `pytest.raises(ValueError, match="...")` → `self.assertRaisesRegex(ValueError, "...")` — 3 sites in step3, 13 in step1-histogram
- `pytest.approx(3000.0)` → `assertAlmostEqual` — 1 site in step3
- `sys.exit(pytest.main([__file__, "-v"]))` → `unittest.main()` — 1 site each
- bare module-level `def test_*` + `assert` → methods on a `unittest.TestCase`

Note `match=` is a **regex search** and `assertRaisesRegex` is also a search, so those port directly — but the existing patterns contain regex metacharacters (`"tx_kick_retry_count.*pre-#826"`, `"K2 violation"`) and at least one `#`, so each should be checked rather than bulk-substituted.

## #8195 — daemon: management listener state is invisible to every remote and automated observer [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-04)

Split out of #7611, which needs it but must not widen to it.

## The gap

A management listener's bind/serve state is exposed through exactly one path:

```
grpcapi.Server.setListenState
  -> Server.EffectiveListener()
  -> Daemon.effectiveListeners()  (pkg/daemon/daemon_run_servers.go)
  -> sysservices.Listeners
```

and that snapshot is consumed by exactly two surfaces:

1. the **local console CLI** (`pkg/cli/cli.go` wires `listenersFn` to
   `Daemon.effectiveListeners` in-process), and
2. **`show system services` over gRPC**.

It is on **neither REST nor Prometheus**. Measured at `583aa9748`:

```
$ grep -rn sysservices --include=*.go pkg/api/ | grep -v _test     # empty
$ grep -rn 'grpc.*listen|listener.*state' pkg/api/metrics*.go      # empty
```

## Why that combination is the problem

The two consumers fail together with the thing they report on.

- If the **primary gRPC listener** is down, consumer 2 is down *by definition* —
  `show system services` is served over it. The observability is circular.
- Consumer 1 works, because it is in-process. But it requires an operator
  **sitting on the console**.

So a primary-listener bind or serve failure is **invisible to every remote and
automated observer**. No scrape sees it, no REST client sees it, and the remote
CLI that would report it is the surface that is gone. The daemon keeps
forwarding — correctly — so nothing else degrades to signal it either.

## #8206 — test/incus: deploy-lib-selftest asserts the cluster-status parsers against hand-written fixtures, not real FormatStatus output [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-31)

Found independently twice today — by me while adding the #7367 `Forwarding:` sub-line, and by another agent reviewing that change. Verified at `origin/master`.

## The gap

`make test-deploy-lib` runs 48 assertions over `deploy_rolling_secondary_node`, `deploy_reassert_node0_primary_ok` and friends. Those functions parse `show chassis cluster status` **positionally**:

```awk
/^Redundancy group:[[:space:]]/ { rg = $3; next }
(rg == "0") && ($1 == "node0")  { st = tolower($3); ... }
```

so `$1` must be the node token and `$3` must be the status. `test-failover.sh` additionally does `grep -A1 "Redundancy group: $rg" | grep -q "node0.*primary"`, which requires the node row to be the **first line after the header**, and whole-output greps like `grep -q "node1.*primary"`.

**Every one of those 48 cells runs against string literals defined inside `deploy-lib-selftest.sh`** (e.g. `:615`, `:633`, `:722`, `:739`), not against output produced by `Manager.FormatStatus`. So the self-test proves the parsers still work **on the fixtures**, and says nothing about whether the fixtures still resemble what the daemon prints.

## Why this matters concretely

`FormatStatus` has grown indented sub-lines over time — `Takeover ready:`, `Transfer ready:`, and now `Forwarding:` (#7367) — all emitted **between** the local node row and the peer node row. The `-A1` window and the positional reads survive that, but only because each addition happened to respect the constraints. Nothing checks that.

The failure mode is specific and bad: `deploy_rolling_secondary_node` defaulting to the wrong node makes a rolling cluster deploy **restart the PRIMARY first**, which is the #4009 regression the function was written to fix. A drifted fixture would let that ship with `make test-deploy-lib` green, and only the cluster would notice.

I hit the near-miss directly: `make test-deploy-lib` passed 48/0 on my #7367 change, and that told me nothing, because the fixtures contain no `Forwarding:` line. I had to generate real `FormatStatus` output and pipe it through the functions by hand to learn the answer (all four parsers correct — but by inspection, not by any gate).

## Suggested fix

Generate the fixture rather than hand-writing it. A small Go helper (or `go test -run` with an env guard) that constructs a `cluster.Manager`, drives it to a known state, and prints `FormatStatus()` gives the self-test a real sample. Then either:

1. feed that output straight into the shell functions in the self-test, or
2. commit it as a golden the self-test parses, with the generator wired so a `FormatStatus` change that alters the shape reds the golden.

(1) is stronger — it cannot go stale — but needs the Go toolchain available where `deploy-lib-selftest.sh` runs. (2) is weaker but hermetic, and the golden's diff is exactly the review signal you want when someone adds a sub-line.

Either way the property to pin is the one the parsers actually depend on, which is **shape, not content**: the node row's `$1` is the node token, its `$3` is the status, it is the first line after the `Redundancy group:` header, and no other line in the block can be read as a node row.

## Adjacent observation, not chased

`test-failover.sh:397`'s `grep -q "node0.*secondary"` is a **whole-output** grep, unscoped to an RG — the same shape #7368 fixed at `:178` for the primary precondition. It may be deliberate at that point in the sequence; nobody has checked. Worth a look by whoever picks this up, since it is the same class of positional/scoping fragility.

## #8207 — test(cluster): the #7257 heartbeat-race probe's degeneracy guard reds under CPU load, so a busy gate fails on an unrelated change [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-04)

Hit while gating two PRs that cannot reach `pkg/cluster` at all. Verified at `origin/master` `4562ab691`.

## What happened

A combined gate over #8204 (Rust, `userspace-dp`) and #8205 (Go, `pkg/dataplane` **test files only**) came back `GO_RC=2` with one failure:

```
--- FAIL: TestStartHeartbeatDoesNotRaceStopHeartbeat7257 (0.04s)
    heartbeat_start_stop_race_7257_test.go:350: #7257 probe is degenerate: 240 of 240 starts
    were SUPERSEDED before publishing and none reached the window (310 stops). `StartHeartbeat`
    returns nil only after it publishes m.hbSender/m.hbReceiver, so zero published starts means
    the race this probe exists to detect was never executed — a green here would be vacuous,
    not evidence (#7663)
```

Neither PR touches `pkg/cluster`; the whole diff is two `pkg/dataplane` `_test.go` files and one `.rs` file, so the change is **structurally incapable** of affecting this package. Measured rather than assumed:

| where | result |
|---|---|
| `origin/master` alone, 3 runs, box idle | **3/3 green** |
| the gated tree, 3 runs, box idle | **3/3 green** |
| the gated tree, full `pkg/cluster`, box idle | **green, 48.8s** |
| the gated tree, inside a full `make test-go` + concurrent build | **FAIL** |

The discriminating variable is **CPU load**, not the diff.

## Why the guard is right and the failure mode is still wrong

The guard itself is good work and should not be deleted. `240 of 240` starts superseded means the probe genuinely did not execute the interleaving it exists to detect, and a green there **would** be vacuous — refusing to report it is exactly the #7663 discipline.

The problem is what it does with that information: it calls `t.Fatalf`, so **"I could not run the experiment" is reported as "the code is broken."** Those are different facts with different remedies, and under load the first one is common — every `StartHeartbeat` loses its scheduling window to a teardown before it can publish.

The practical cost is that any sufficiently busy gate reds on this test **regardless of the change under review**, and the failure text names `StartHeartbeat` and a race, so the natural response is to go looking for a heartbeat regression in a diff that contains none. I spent a full diagnostic cycle on it; the next person will too, and the one after that may "fix" `pkg/cluster` to make it stop.

This is the same class as a `-race` failure having no `--- FAIL` line: the harness reports something true, in a category that sends the reader to the wrong place.

## #8211 — pkg/snmp: TestGetBulkCostDoesNotScaleWithMaxRepetitions_6551 is a wall-clock ratio assertion and flakes under full-suite load [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-31)

## Symptom

Red once during a full `make test-go`, green on every isolated re-run:

```
getbulk_work_bound_6551_test.go:252: 580 repeaters: max-repetitions=1 1.795956ms,
    max-repetitions=100 20.892061ms (ratio 11.6x)
getbulk_work_bound_6551_test.go:255: GETBULK cost scales with max-repetitions ...
    the grid is still expanding past the response ceiling
```

`go test ./pkg/snmp/ -run TestGetBulkCostDoesNotScaleWithMaxRepetitions_6551
-count=3` passes; the subsequent full-suite run passes. Seen while gating an
unrelated change (#7172 cut 6, login-class regex enforcement) — `pkg/snmp` has
no dependency on anything that change touches.

## Why it flakes

The assertion is a **ratio of two wall-clock measurements** taken in the same
process. Under a full-suite run the machine is saturated, and the two timings
are not sampled under comparable conditions: a scheduler delay landing in the
`M=100` measurement inflates the ratio without the work having changed.

The property under test — GETBULK cost must not scale with `max-repetitions`
once the response ceiling is reached — is a **work** property, not a **time**
property. Time is a proxy for it, and it is the proxy that is flaky.

## Suggested fix

Count the work instead of timing it. The subject is whether the grid keeps
expanding past the response ceiling, so the direct observable is the number of
OID lookups / rows walked, which is deterministic and load-independent. A
counter incremented in the walk, compared between `M=1` and `M=100`, asserts the
same property with no timing dependence at all.

If a timing bound is genuinely wanted as well, it belongs behind a `-short`
skip or a benchmark, where a noisy sample does not red a correctness gate.

## #8213 — test-tooling: an anchored ^--- FAIL grep scores a genuine mutation red as an ESCAPE when parallel -v output splices the line [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-04)

Scoring a Go mutation matrix with `grep -c '^--- FAIL'` is **unsound**, and it
fails in the dangerous direction: a correct red is scored as an escape, which
reads as "the fix is not bound" and invites weakening a good test.

## What happened

Running the #8000 matrix (PR #8212), cell M4 scored `rc=1`, `built=yes`,
`collected=2260`, `namedFAIL=0`. That triple — a nonzero exit with zero named
failures — is a void shape, so I looked instead of scoring it. The test had in
fact failed exactly as intended. The `--- FAIL:` line had been spliced into the
middle of another line by parallel `-v` output:

```
failover_batch_barrier_disarm_8000_test.go:171: waitFailoverActuated(RG0) took 300.273042ms: the singular path left the barrier armed --- FAIL: TestR--- FAIL: TestRemoteFailoverDisarmsSupersededBarrier8000 (0.60s)
```

Note the doubled, truncated `--- FAIL: TestR` fragment: two goroutines writing
concurrently. Because the surviving `--- FAIL:` does not start at column 0, the
anchored grep matched nothing.

The same run shows `--- PASS` lines mangled the same way:

```
--- PASS: TestRaceGateCoversTheConcurrencyB--- PASS: TestD--- PASS: TestDaemonDataplaneCellAccessorBoundary (0.67s)
```

so this is not specific to failures — any anchored census over `go test -v`
output is exposed.

## Why this matters beyond one matrix

This is the same family as the already-documented "`-race` failure has no
`--- FAIL` line" hazard: the instrument reports the healthy value for an
unhealthy run. It is worse here in one respect — the `-race` case at least has
no `--- FAIL` anywhere, whereas this one *does* have the text, just not at
column 0, so a reviewer eyeballing the log sees the failure and the harness does
not.

An escape is the expensive direction to get wrong. It says the mutation was not
caught, which points at the test as the thing to change.

## #8218 — test policy: a correctness gate must assert on WORK, not on wall-clock time — two load-sensitive flakes in one day share one cause [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-31)

Filed to hold the general rule that **#8207** and **#8211** are both instances of, so it is not split across two symptom reports and re-derived a third time.

## The two instances

| issue | test | the assertion |
|---|---|---|
| **#8207** | `pkg/cluster` `TestStartHeartbeatDoesNotRaceStopHeartbeat7257` | a degeneracy guard that fails when the race under test never executed |
| **#8211** | `pkg/snmp` `TestGetBulkCostDoesNotScaleWithMaxRepetitions_6551` | a wall-clock **ratio** between two runs |

Both red under full-suite load, in packages the changes under review could not reach, and both were first read as real regressions by the person gating. #8207 cost me a full diagnostic cycle; its failure text names `StartHeartbeat` and a race, so the natural response is to go looking for a heartbeat regression in a diff that has none.

## Measured, not asserted

During the window both fired, this box was at:

```
load average: 84.64, 51.28, 35.21
```

That is several agents gating concurrently. At that load a goroutine needing to win a scheduling window essentially never gets one, and a ratio between two timed runs is dominated by scheduler noise rather than by the property being measured.

## The rule

> **A correctness gate must assert on WORK. Time may only be a proxy in a benchmark, or behind a `-short` skip.**

And the reason this is a rule rather than a preference — the sharpest statement of it, from one of the agents that hit it:

> **A proxy that reds under load reds hardest exactly when everyone is busiest.**

The failure is *correlated with the moment the signal is least affordable*. A flaky test that fires at random is an annoyance; one that fires preferentially during heavy CI is a tax on every concurrent change, and it trains people to re-run rather than read.

## What "assert on work" means concretely

Both instances already count the right thing and then do the wrong thing with it:

- **#8207** already measures *published starts* — a work quantity. Its defect is only what it does with a zero: it reports **"I could not run the experiment"** as **"the code is broken."** Those are different facts with different remedies, and under load the first is the *expected* outcome.
- **#8211** is measuring cost scaling. The property is "does the work grow with `MaxRepetitions`", so **count the work** — operations, allocations, iterations — rather than timing it. A counted assertion is load-independent by construction.

So the minimal fix in both cases is smaller than a rewrite: keep the counting, keep the refusal to report a vacuous green, and change what the degenerate/noisy case *resolves to*.

## #8225 — A correctness gate must assert on WORK, not on elapsed TIME — the proxy reds hardest when the signal is least affordable [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-31)

Generalising #8207 (`pkg/cluster` heartbeat probe) and #8211 (`pkg/snmp`
GETBULK cost ratio). Both are the same defect, both surfaced under full-suite
load within two days, and filing the rule separately so the next one is
recognised rather than re-diagnosed.

## The rule

**A test that gates correctness must assert on work performed — operations,
allocations, rows walked, calls made. Elapsed time may be a proxy only in a
benchmark, or behind a `-short` skip, never in a gate that reds a merge.**

## Why this is a rule and not a preference

The failure is **correlated with the moment the signal is least affordable**.

A wall-clock assertion does not fail randomly. It fails when the machine is
saturated — which is precisely when the most lanes are gating, when the most
people are waiting, and when a red is most expensive to investigate. The
measured example: load average **84.6** on this box during the window both
flakes fired (recorded on #8207).

So the noise is not spread evenly across runs; it concentrates in exactly the
runs where a false red does the most damage. That is the property that makes it
worth a general rule rather than a per-test judgement.

## The second cost, which is worse than the flake

Both failure texts asserted a **specific regression that had not happened**:

- #8211: *"the grid is still expanding past the response ceiling"*
- #8207: (the heartbeat equivalent)

So the natural response is to go looking for a change to that package — and in
both cases the change under gate could not reach it. A flaky assertion that
merely said "too slow" would waste a re-run. One that names a mechanism wastes
an investigation, and trains readers to distrust the next true report from the
same test.

## What to write instead

Follow-up to #8213 / PR #8226, recording a decision so the obvious "fix" is not
attempted.

## The tension

#8226 made the mutation harness's FAIL counting splice-tolerant, and added
name-based attribution (`mutation_go_failed_names_json`,
`mutation_verdict_for_target`) for callers that can produce `go test -json`.

**`scripts/mutate.sh` cannot use them**, because it gates through `make test-go`
/ `make test-rust`, which emit human-readable output. Its `KILLED` verdicts are
therefore count-based: they say *something* failed, not that the cell's target
failed. The driver now prints that limitation on every `KILLED` line rather than
hiding it.

## Do NOT close this by converting the driver to `go test -json`

That is the obvious repair and it is wrong: **it would narrow the gate.** The
make targets carry legs a bare `go test` does not —

- `go vet`,
- the targeted `-race` runs with `-count=2`,
- on the Rust side, `--release` and `--test-threads=1`.

A per-package `go test -json` driver would buy better attribution and pay for it
in **coverage**, and a narrower gate that agrees with the old one is
indistinguishable from a sufficient one right up until the day it isn't. Trading
gate strength for verdict precision is the wrong direction for a harness whose
whole job is to say whether a guard is real.

## The actual fix

Make the **gate targets** emit machine-readable results alongside their normal
output, so the driver can attribute without bypassing them. Sketch, not a
prescription:

- `make test-go` writes `go test -json` to a side file (`GOTESTJSON=<path>`)
  while keeping stdout as-is, so nothing that reads the current output breaks;

## #8233 — xpfd has no single-instance enforcement: SO_REUSEPORT lets a second daemon start silently [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-02)

Split out of #7501 rather than folded into it, because it is a *precondition*
that issue tolerates rather than the mis-ordering that issue fixes — and because
#7501's own acceptance criteria forbid the obvious form of the fix.

## The gap

Nothing enforces a single `xpfd` instance:

- there is no pidfile;
- the gRPC listener sets `SO_REUSEPORT` (`pkg/grpcapi/server.go`), so a second
  `xpfd` does **not** fail on a port collision.

So two daemons can run concurrently, each driving the dataplane, the config
store, FRR, and the cluster state machine. #7501 handles one consequence — the
boot-epoch mis-ordering — by making a refiner recognise a live sibling. That is
the right fix for that defect and it deliberately **accepts the precondition**.

## Why #7501 could not close this

#7501 lists single-instance enforcement as its option 3 and calls it "the only
one of the three that removes the precondition rather than tolerating it". Its
own **criterion 2** rules it out as written:

> a node that cannot take/observe it still emits heartbeats (the existing "a
> storage fault must not take a healthy node off the air" rule)

That criterion is met **structurally** by anything on the boot-epoch refine
worker: `heartbeat_epoch.go` publishes the wall-clock seed synchronously with no
file access, and every frame carries it from the first send. Single-instance
enforcement is different in kind, because it runs at **daemon startup —
upstream of publication**. A node that cannot take the lock has not emitted
anything yet, so:

- **refuse to start** on lock failure → a storage fault (read-only `/run`,
  ENOSPC, an unreadable lock file) takes a healthy node off the air;
- **start anyway** → it is not single-instance enforcement; the precondition
  survives exactly in the fault case.

Splitting on errno (`EWOULDBLOCK` = held, refuse; anything else = storage,
proceed) technically complies, but buys compliance by reintroducing the overlap

## #8244 — mouse-latency harness: MOUSE_PORT defaults to the one unprovisioned listener, and a preflight abort is indistinguishable from a gate failure [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-03)

Two harness defects that together made a one-port gap look like an unprovisioned lab, and cost #7100 two attempts.

## 1. The default selects the one listener that is down

`test/incus/test-mouse-latency-matrix.sh:93`

```sh
MOUSE_PORT="${MOUSE_PORT:-6200}"
```

Probed from `loss:cluster-userspace-host` toward `172.16.80.200`:

```
6200:closed  6201:OPEN  6202:OPEN  6203:OPEN  6204:OPEN  6205:OPEN
6206:OPEN    6207:OPEN  6208:OPEN  6209:OPEN  6210:OPEN  6211:OPEN
```

**Eleven of twelve echo listeners are up. The default names the twelfth.** The per-class iperf3 servers on 5200-5211 are up as well. So every default invocation aborts in preflight while a fully usable fixture sits idle.

This is not new. `docs/pr/1829-p2/evidence.md`, recording the 2026-06-10 run, already says:

> the operator-provisioned 6200 echo listener on 172.16.80.200 is currently down (connection refused); the probe used port **7** (the original #905 echo service, verified echo-correct), which like 6200 matches no `bandwidth-output` filter term and classifies to the same best-effort queue 0. All other 620x listeners are up

So 6200 has been down for roughly seven weeks, the substitution is documented **with its equivalence argument**, and the default has been pointing at it the whole time. I re-verified port 7 today: sent `xpf7159`, received `xpf7159`.

### Why this is worth fixing rather than working around
Two attempts on #7100 hit the abort and recorded it as *"neither the 6200-6211 echo daemons nor the 5200-5211 per-class iperf3 servers are running"* — which became that issue's blocking premise and stood until it was probed. **A default that selects the unprovisioned member of a set makes the entire set look unprovisioned.**

### Suggested fix
Prefer **a preflight that probes the listener matching `ELEPHANT_PORT`'s class** over retargeting the default. `620x` mirrors `520x` into the same forwarding class (`bandwidth-output` term N lists both), so the correct mouse port is derivable from the shape already being requested; the cross-class case is the deliberate exception and can stay an explicit override. Changing `6200` to `6205` would only move the default onto a port that happens to be up today.

## 2. A preflight abort exits like a failing gate

`test-mouse-latency.sh:265` aborts with `rc=1`, the same code a genuine latency-gate failure produces. #7100's own first comment flags this:

> the harness exits `rc=1` on this abort, which is indistinguishable from a failing gate if you only read the exit code. Check that per-rep JSON exists before reading any verdict — an empty `preflight/` directory means the run never happened.

That workaround is correct and should not be necessary. **A missing listener and a real latency regression are not the same event and should not produce the same exit code.** This is what made defect 1 durable: the abort reads as "the measurement ran and something is wrong", so the natural next step is to investigate the environment rather than the invocation.

A reserved exit code for preflight refusal (distinct from both pass and gate-failure) makes the two separable by any caller, including CI and the matrix wrapper. This is a distinct fix from defect 1 — either alone leaves the other.

- a fix for one cannot land with a fail-on-revert cell;
- diagnosis has to go through a live box and a shared cluster lock, which is

incus leaves the command running inside the instance when a non-interactive
client disconnects. Measured on `loss:cluster-userspace-host` during #7159: a
backgrounded `incus exec ... -- sh -c "sleep 137"` was still running 8 s after
its local client was killed.

## The remaining sites, `test/incus/test-mouse-latency.sh`

| var | backgrounded from | killed at | remote-stopped? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `IPERF_PID` :381 | `incus_exec "$SOURCE"` :377-380 | :248 | **yes** — #8268 pidfile + `mouse_elephant_kill_cmd` |
| `SETTLE_MPSTAT_PID` :385 | `incus_exec "$SOURCE"` :382-384 | :254 | **no** |
| `MPSTAT_PID` :437 | `incus_exec "$SOURCE"` :434-436 | :255 | **no** |
| `RG_POLL_PID` :343 | local subshell `) &` :342 | :253 | n/a — local, correctly unaffected |

`RG_POLL_PID` is the discriminator that makes this a real finding rather than a
pattern match: it has the same `kill "$VAR"` spelling and is NOT affected,
because its `$!` comes from a local subshell rather than an `incus_exec`.

## Why it matters here specifically, and why it is NOT #7159 severity

An orphaned `mpstat` is a monitor, not a load generator, so it does **not**
corrupt the throughput column the way an orphaned `iperf3` does — the #7159
determinations and the in-flight re-measurement stand, and nothing here
retroactively affects them.

But this harness measures **mouse LATENCY on the source container**, and an
orphaned mpstat is unaccounted CPU on exactly that container, accumulating one
per early-exit rep. A harness whose purpose is p99.9 tail measurement should not
leave uncounted samplers running through subsequent reps. There is also a
narrower correctness leg: both write `/tmp/mpstat-${REP_TAG}.txt`, so an orphan
outliving its rep can still be writing the file a later reuse of the same tag
reads.

is `docs/research/7167-tunnel-ingress/adjudication.md` (PR #8269).

**Read that document before proposing a design.** It refutes three alternative
mechanisms on measurement, and this issue does not re-litigate them:

- **Option B1** — an ingress-only AF_XDP binding on the tunnel netdev: refuted
  on four independent grounds (§2, Option B).
- **Option C** — a policy gate inside the WireGuard control thread: refuted on
  mechanism (§2, Option C). It has no `ForwardingState`, so to-zone is always
  0, #3110 makes zone 0 ineligible for every rule tier, and every packet falls
  to the DEFAULT action. It is a global switch, not a gate.
- **Option E** — a bounded packet-bearing `WorkerCommand` + an owned-frame
  adjudication entry point: feasible and priced (§2, Option E), but **not
  needed here**, and it belongs to the IPsec half.

Do not reopen those. If new evidence contradicts one, amend the adjudication
document in the same PR rather than arguing it in a comment.

## The defect

WireGuard's two directions are **asymmetric**, and only inbound is broken.

`coordinator/wg_control/dispatch.rs` writes authenticated plaintext straight to
the `wgN` TUN via `slowpath::write_packet_nonblocking`. There is no zone
lookup, session create, route/PBR/filter/NAT evaluation, zone counter,
policy-deny event or worker submission between `try_decap` and that write. The
kernel then routes and forwards it: xpf installs only `hook input` nftables
chains and holds `ip_forward` at 1 for as long as the dataplane is armed.

A peer's `allowed-ips` is a cryptographic check on the inner SOURCE address. It
has no destination, no zone-pair, no application and no direction. It is not a
security policy.

Encapsulation **already runs inside the AF_XDP worker, post-adjudication** —
`frame/mod.rs` dispatches `TunnelKind::WireGuard` to `wg::wg_encap_frame` from

## #8276 — userspace-dp: price the bounded kernel->userspace capture bridge for XFRM-decrypted IPsec plaintext (B2) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-04)

Successor to #7167 (IPsec half). The adjudication that produced this split is
`docs/research/7167-tunnel-ingress/adjudication.md` (PR #8269).

**This issue is a PRICING task first and an implementation second.** The
mechanism is chosen by elimination, not by preference, and its cost is
genuinely unknown. A PR that starts implementing before the pricing question
below is answered is doing the thing this split exists to prevent.

## The defect

Route-based IPsec plaintext, decrypted by the kernel XFRM stack, surfaces on an
`xfrmi` (`stN[.unit]`) and is routed by the Linux FIB. The `xfrmi` ifindex is
never in `USERSPACE_INGRESS_IFACES` — the Go builder excludes every
`InterfaceSnapshot` matching the `SecureTunnel` class and the Rust planner
independently excludes it in `include_userspace_binding_interface` — so the
shim misses and `XDP_PASS`es it. `evaluate_policy` never runs on it: no zone
policy, no session, no NAT, no screen.

A valid SA authenticates a peer and a traffic selector. It does not authorize
an inner from-zone -> to-zone flow.

## Why the obvious fix is refuted — do not re-propose it

**Option B1, an ingress-only AF_XDP / generic-XDP binding on the `xfrmi`, is
refuted** on four independent, each-sufficient grounds (adjudication §2, Option
B). Summarised so nobody re-derives them:

1. **Framing.** The shim's `parse_l2` is Ethernet-only (its sole branch is
   VLAN) and `frame_l3_offset` returns only 14 or 18. Worse, **the L2 parse
   runs BEFORE the ingress-set lookup**, so a raw-L3 frame is
   `pass_non_ip_l2_direct`ed without the set ever being consulted — and for an
   inner source of the form `8.0.x.x`, bytes `[12..14]` read as `0x0800` and
   the shim parses an IPv4 header 14 bytes into the real one.
2. **Queue collapse.** The binding planner takes a **global minimum** RX-queue
   count over all candidates and builds a uniform `queue_count x interfaces`
   grid. There is no per-interface queue count, so admitting a 1-queue `xfrmi`
   collapses **every physical NIC to one queue and one worker**.
3. **Bind fragility.** A generic-XDP non-virtio interface gets a **one**-element
   `COPY_ONLY_BIND_FLAGS` list and `alternate_bind_strategy` returns `None`, so
   exactly ONE attempt is made with no fallback; the shared-UMEM path is

## #8277 — mouse-latency gate cannot return FAIL on a CONCENTRATED tail — the degenerate-coroutine rule invalidates the phenomenon it exists to detect [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-04)

Filed from #7159. Independent of how that issue's comparison resolves — this is
a defect in the measurement apparatus, and it is why "#1359 item 3 cannot be
decided" has been true for **instrument** reasons rather than data reasons.

## The rule

`test/incus/mouse_latency_probe.py:445-451`:

```python
if concurrency >= 2:
    median_a = statistics.median(attempts_per_coroutine) ...
    min_a = min(attempts_per_coroutine) ...
    if median_a > 0 and min_a < 0.5 * median_a:
        reasons.append(f"degenerate-coroutine: min={min_a} < 0.5 * median={median_a}")
```

Any rep in which one probe coroutine completed fewer than half the median
number of transactions is INVALID. Present since the harness's first commit,
`840d5545d` (2026-04-25) — the same commit that carried the orphan defect fixed
in #8268.

## Why it cannot see the phenomenon

The rule is a **fairness** predicate being used as a **validity** predicate. A
mouse-latency gate under elephant load exists to detect a tail. When the tail
is *concentrated* — a minority of flows starved while the rest are fine — the
starved flows necessarily complete far fewer transactions, so the rule fires
and the rep is discarded. Enough such reps and the cell has zero valid reps,
and the reducer emits `INSUFFICIENT-DATA`.

Precisely: a **uniform** slowdown still FAILs correctly (every coroutine slows,
the median moves with the min, `min/median` stays ~1). It is specifically the
**concentrated** tail that is unreachable — and that is exactly the shape the
surplus-sharing fixture produces.

So on this fixture the gate can emit PASS and INSUFFICIENT-DATA, and cannot
emit FAIL.

## #8280 — Cluster smoke owed for the #7174 M13 NAT change ran and PASSED — but no cluster smoke exercises pool-mode NAT at all [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-03)

## What is owed

`1530738cf` ("nat: bound the recycle FIFO's length and per-claim cost", PR #8273) merged **without its cluster smoke**. It is a `userspace-dp` change, so the helper binary moves, and `docs/engineering-style.md` step 8 owes:

- `make cluster-deploy` on the loss userspace cluster + re-apply CoS (`./test/incus/apply-cos-config.sh loss:xpf-userspace-fw0` — deploy wipes CoS)
- `iperf3 -P 16 -t 30 -p 5211` → `172.16.80.200`, ≥ 23 Gbit/s
- `make test-failover` **and** `make test-ha-crash` — the change is in the NAT port allocator on the path an HA-synced `reserve_flow` drives, which is the HA row of that table, not merely the "any change" row.

## Why it did not run

It was not skipped and it did not fail — **it did not happen**, which is a third state. The lock cell queued correctly on `/tmp/xpf-cluster.lock` for ~13 minutes behind another agent's holder (`7159 CoS p99.9 surplus/exact re-measure`, held from 09:59) and was then stood down rather than left to fire unattended: a `cluster-deploy` landing the instant that holder released would have wiped the CoS configuration it was measuring, and an unread destructive HA smoke is not evidence of anything. The holder was never touched.

## What was validated

`make test-rust` green on the merged head (5052 passed, 0 failed, 5 ignored), with four fail-on-revert cells in `nat/tests_pool.rs`, each mutation-checked — including the false-exhaustion direction, which reds three cells. That is unit-level evidence only. It says nothing about the helper running on real traffic through a failover, which is exactly what the smoke is for.

## Specific risk to look for

The change makes `claim` return `None` immediately when `occupied == range`, and moves `free_recycle`'s occupancy-bit clear inside the per-address recycle mutex. The failure mode a smoke would catch and a unit test would not is a **spurious NAT exhaustion under real concurrency** — allocation failures (`nat_alloc_fail`) or dropped translations appearing during or after a failover, on a pool that still has free ports. Watch that counter across `test-failover`, not just the pass/fail line.
