## #8285 — Abort evidence needs a carrier that exists on the abort path (#7289 R2 — the ApplyResult route does not work) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-02)

Split out of #7289, whose R2 item asked for this. Filing rather than silently deferring, because **R2's stated mechanism does not work and the want behind it still does.**

## The want

An apply that ABORTS after `CompileConfig`'s Phase-2 host mutation leaves the host moved and the dataplane on its previous snapshot. PR #7288 made that visible, but only by **wrapping the error string** (`annotateHostMutationOnAbort`, `pkg/dataplane/compiler_hostmutation_4960.go:95`). The operator gets prose in a commit failure; nothing structured reaches a `show` surface, and nothing distinguishes a pre-publication failure from an ambiguous or post-publication one.

## Why R2's stated mechanism is wrong

R2 was scoped as *"most of it is threading `hostMutations`, which already exists but is dropped by `ApplyResultFromCompileResult`."* Verified at `origin/master` `9baa81bf5`:

- `hostMutations` **does** exist (`pkg/dataplane/compiler.go:61-66`), with three write sites, all `markHostMutated` calls in `compiler_iface.go` (`:728`, `:791`, `:1026`).
- `ApplyResultFromCompileResult` (`pkg/dataplane/apply.go:210-230`) **does** drop it — it copies ten fields and `ApplyResult` has no field of that shape (positive control: `PoolIDs` is present at `:114`).

But that is not where abort visibility is lost. **On the abort path `ApplyResultFromCompileResult` is never called at all.** `loader.go` returns before `recordApplyResult(ApplyResultFromCompileResult(result))`, and the same shape holds at `compiler.go:616` and `userspace/manager_compile.go:400,514`. Every consumer of an ApplyResult — gRPC (`pkg/grpcapi/apply_result.go:5`), REST (`pkg/api/api.go:117`), the CLI (`pkg/cli/cli.go:232`) — reads `LastApplyResult`, i.e. only the **successful** apply.

So threading `hostMutations` into `ApplyResult` would surface it on exactly the applies where it is always empty, and never on the one that needs it. Implementing R2 as written produces a field that is structurally unreachable for its own purpose.

## What is actually owed

A carrier for abort evidence that exists **on the abort path**. That is a design decision, not a plumbing job, and it is the reason this is an issue rather than a PR:

- the failure classes are not one bit — pre-publication, ambiguous publication, post-publication are three different operator instructions;
- an `ApplyResult` is the wrong carrier by construction (see above), so either the abort path must construct one, or the evidence needs a different home;
- and whatever carries it has to survive the error already being wrapped, or the operator reads the same fact twice in two formats.

## Not in scope

The convergence/undo redesign. #7289's r1 established that converge-forward cannot terminate for the class that produces the reachable abort — the trigger is a driver refusing an XDP attach, which is persistent, while #5679's self-heal is scoped to *transient* errors in its own sentence. The unadjudicated-surface half is closed separately (#7289 R1).

Refs #7289, #7288, #4960

## #8291 — userspace-dp: cargo suite is intermittently red on a clean master (~1 in 3 full runs), with the failing test moving between runs [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-02)

> **SEVERITY DOWNGRADED, and the reason matters more than the label.** The
> original body (kept below) implied this weakens every gate. It does not:
> **`make test-rust` runs `--test-threads=1`**, so no merge gate can exhibit
> this. Do not re-inflate it on the strength of a red you saw locally — check
> which command produced it first. Details and measurements in
> [this comment](https://github.com/psaab/xpf/issues/8291#issuecomment-5515658858).

## What this actually is

**An iteration-cost and habit problem, not a gate-integrity problem.**

A bare `cargo test` is the natural command while iterating, it reds roughly **1 run in 3**, and the failing test differs each time. The cost is not a wrong merge — it is that this **trains people to re-run reds reflexively**, and that habit is how a genuine intermittent regression eventually gets waved through. No amount of gate hardening fixes a habit.

**Second-order, and the real payoff:** `--test-threads=1` is itself a workaround that *hides* the defect, and it serialises ~5200 tests on every gate run. Fixing the underlying isolation would let the gate go parallel again.

## Root cause: an UNENFORCED requirement, not an unknown defect

Single-threaded execution is deliberate and documented twice:

- **Makefile** — *"some dataplane socket tests can wedge in `__skb_wait_for_more_packets` when run concurrently; single-threaded execution avoids the intermittent hang"*.
- **`afxdp/checksum.rs`, the #6872 canary** — the process-global DNAT counters are bumped by `publish_dnat_table_entry` / `delete_dnat_table_entry`, **production functions on the DNAT path that must not take a lock**, and dozens of tests call them unguarded. Its comment states the consequence outright: *"the reason the unguarded writers do not corrupt a sample today is that this crate's suite runs `--test-threads=1`"*.

The requirement lived only in the Makefile recipe, so the gate was always sound while a bare `cargo test` silently violated it.

## "The failing test differs each time" is wrong — it is three self-colliding families

Each family run **alone**, 20 runs, pristine `origin/master` worktree:

| family | tests | default threads | `--test-threads=1` |
|---|---|---|---|
| `tests_gre_version_6842` | 4 | **19/20 fail** | 0/20 |
| `tests_decap_dnat_table` | 21 | **14/20 fail** | 0/20 |
| `io_uring_write` | 29 | **8/20 fail** | 0/20 |
| `afxdp::wg::engine` | 28 | 0/20 | 0/20 |

They collide with their own **siblings**, not across modules — which is why the rate is *higher* in isolation than the 2-in-6 the full suite shows. Three separate root causes, not one wandering flake.

`afxdp::wg::engine` is **excluded from the population rather than folded in**: it is clean in both modes because it already carries a `wg_engine_test_serial()` guard (#6157). It is the in-tree **precedent for the fix**, not a member of the set.

```

and every signal said it was fine:

- `configstore.CheckText` returned **no error**;
- `make cluster-deploy` applied it to both nodes with no warning;
- `cli -c "show configuration security proxy-arp"` rendered the stanza back **verbatim**.

It was completely inert. `reconcileProxyARP` reads `cfg.Security.NAT.ProxyARP` (`pkg/daemon/daemon_proxyarp.go:159`), which stayed empty, so no `NTF_PROXY` entry was installed — `ip neigh show proxy` on fw0 was empty — and pool-mode source-NAT return traffic blackholed. The symptom on the wire was `iperf3: error - unable to connect to server ... Connection timed out`, with **no error anywhere on the firewall**.

## It is general, not proxy-arp-specific

Measured with a control rather than inferred from one instance — the baseline config validates first, so a silent pass is not an artifact of the harness:

| stanza inserted under `security { }` | `CheckText` result |
|---|---|
| `proxy-arp { interface reth0.80 { address 172.16.80.7/32; } }` | **nil** (accepted) |
| `not-a-real-stanza { interface reth0.80 { address ... } }` | **nil** (accepted) |
| `flooby { wibble 42; }` | **nil** (accepted) |

The schema has exactly one `proxy-arp` node, at `pkg/config/schema_security.go:672`, inside the NAT block. There is no `security`-level definition — the path is simply unknown, and unknown is accepted.

## Why this is worth an issue

The dangerous property is not the acceptance on its own — it is acceptance **plus** faithful read-back. `show configuration` re-renders the stanza, so an operator verifying their work sees exactly what they typed and concludes it is in force. On a firewall the classes where that matters are obvious: a misplaced `policies`, `zones`, or screen sub-stanza reads as enforced and enforces nothing, and there is no warning, no log line, and no counter to contradict it.

I hit this on a config whose *purpose* was to make an untested path testable, which is how it got caught at all; a misplacement in a security-policy stanza would have looked identical and had no test downstream to fail.

## #8297 — Both cluster nodes answer proxy-ARP for a NAT pool address regardless of RG ownership; pool-mode TCP never completes [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-03)

## Both cluster nodes answer ARP for a NAT pool address, so pool-mode TCP never completes a handshake

Found while closing #8280 (no cluster smoke exercises pool-mode NAT). Adding a pool-mode source-NAT rule + the `proxy-arp` stanza it requires reproduces this immediately on `loss:xpf-userspace-fw0/fw1`.

## Direct observation, not inference

```
fw0  node0  200  primary          ->  ip neigh show proxy: 172.16.80.7 dev ge-0-0-2.80 proxy
fw1  node1  100  secondary-hold   ->  ip neigh show proxy: 172.16.80.7 dev ge-7-0-2.80 proxy
```

Both nodes install the `NTF_PROXY` entry for the pool address regardless of redundancy-group ownership. On the wire, both answer:

```
ARP, Request who-has 172.16.80.7 tell 172.16.80.7
ARP, Reply   172.16.80.7 is-at 02:bf:72:16:01:00      <- node 0 RETH virtual MAC
ARP, Request who-has 172.16.80.7 tell 172.16.80.7
ARP, Reply   172.16.80.7 is-at 02:bf:72:16:01:01      <- node 1 RETH virtual MAC
```

Per-node RETH virtual MACs are `02:bf:72:CC:RR:NN`, so `…:01:00` and `…:01:01` are node 0 and node 1. The upstream sees one IP at two MACs.

## The discriminating control

Same host, same second, same target, same port, same secondary-address mechanism — **only the NAT rule that matches differs**:

| source | rule that matches | result |
|---|---|---|
| `10.0.61.230` (outside the pool match) | `snat` — **interface** mode | **5.95 Gbits/sec, iperf Done** |
| `10.0.61.240` (inside `10.0.61.240/28`) | `pool-snat` — **pool** mode | **connect times out** |

So it is not the secondary address, not the port, not the server, and not the lab. ICMP from `.240` through the same pool **does** work (3/3, 0% loss), which places address translation, routing and the reverse path in the clear and isolates the failure to the TCP handshake.

## What the firewall shows

The allocator ran correctly — the pool handed out ports from the configured range:

```
In:  10.0.61.240/37717 --> 172.16.80.200/5210;tcp,  Pkts: 0, Bytes: 0
Out: 172.16.80.200/5210 --> 172.16.80.7/30003;tcp,  Pkts: 0, Bytes: 0

## #8298 — screen: extract_screen_info admits IHL<5, and check_teardrop's payload math then under-counts the header [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-02)

Read at `origin/master` `f260e1d02`. Surfaced as finding 09 of
`/tmp/gemini-review-048.md`; the mechanism reproduces, the **reachability does
not** and is the open question.

## PROVEN — nothing in `extract_screen_info` rejects IHL < 5

`userspace-dp/src/screen/extract.rs` has two deliberate fail-closed checks and
neither catches it:

```rust
if l3_offset + 20 > frame.len() { return Err(TruncatedIpv4Header); }   // capture too short
...
let ihl_bytes = (info.ip_ihl as usize) * 4;
if l3_offset + ihl_bytes > frame.len() { return Err(TruncatedIpv4Header); }  // IHL overshoots
```

Both guard the header being **longer** than what was captured. `IHL = 0..4`
makes `ihl_bytes` 0..16, which is *smaller* than the 20 bytes already asserted
present, so both checks pass. RFC 791 makes IHL >= 5 mandatory, and nothing here
enforces it.

## PROVEN — the teardrop math then under-counts the header

`userspace-dp/src/screen/stateless.rs:195`, `check_teardrop`:

```rust
let hdr_len = (pkt.ip_ihl as u16) * 4;
if pkt.ip_total_len <= hdr_len { return Some("teardrop"); }
let payload = pkt.ip_total_len - hdr_len;
if payload < 8 { return Some("teardrop"); }
```

With `IHL = 0`, `hdr_len = 0` and `payload = ip_total_len` **unreduced**. A
non-first fragment with `total_len = 20` — whose real payload is 20 - 20 = **0**,
the canonical teardrop case the `< 8` test exists to catch — computes as 20 and
is **not flagged**. The attacker controls IHL, `total_len` and `frag_off`
independently, so the under-count is selectable.

`extract.rs:160`'s `if info.ip_ihl > 5` source-route scan is correctly unaffected
(no options to scan), so teardrop is the specific consumer at risk.

## #8308 — proto: GetSessionsResponse carries no peer_status, and PeerFetchStatus has no BUSY — a refusal reads as a partition to gRPC clients [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-04)

Residual from PR #8306 (#7294). Filed separately so it does not live only in a
merged PR body.

#8306 made a failed peer fetch visible on the REST session-list surface and
stopped reporting an admission refusal as a partition. Two halves could not be
fixed there, because both are wire changes with their own rolling-upgrade
question.

## 1. `GetSessionsResponse` has no `peer_status` field

`GetSessionSummaryResponse` and `GetZonePairSummaryResponse` both carry
`peer_status` / `peer_error`, and the REST bridge renders them.
`GetSessionsResponse` carries neither.

That is *why* the list surface never reported a peer outcome — the handler's
discarded error was downstream of a gap in the message, not the cause of it.
#8306 works around it: on success the REST layer sets `peer_status: "ok"`
locally, meaning only "the fetch succeeded".

**What is still not expressible on this surface:** a peer that returned an
empty table versus a standalone node. The summary surfaces distinguish these
through `PEER_FETCH_STATUS_NOT_APPLICABLE` vs `_OK`
(`peerAbsentStatus()` in `pkg/grpcapi/peer_only_5968.go`); the list surface
cannot, because there is no field to put it in. A gRPC client of `GetSessions`
sees nothing at all.

## 2. `PeerFetchStatus` has no `BUSY` member

`pkg/grpcapi/peer_only_5968.go` returns `codes.ResourceExhausted` when the peer
fetch is refused on admission. `attachPeerSessionSummary` /
`attachPeerZonePairSummary` classify any error as
`PEER_FETCH_STATUS_UNREACHABLE`.

An admission refusal means the peer **is** reachable and this node declined to
ask. Reporting it as a partition sends an operator debugging a fabric problem
after a network fault that does not exist. #8306 fixed the wording on the REST
surface (`busy` vs `unreachable`), so **REST and gRPC now disagree** about the
same event — which is a smaller wrong than both being wrong, but is still a
divergence with a shelf life.

## #8312 — CoS/admission: weighted cost for the session-scan limiter — measure it in-process, not through HTTP (the #7294 item 2 remainder) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-04)

Split out of #7294, whose items 1 and 3 are done (PRs #8292, #8301, #8306,
#8310). This carries item 2 alone.

## What is being asked

`diagcmd.SessionWalkLimiter` charges **1 slot per operation regardless of
work**. A full list, a `local + peer` request, a cursor page, a full-table
clear and a count-only `SessionCount` differ materially. #7294's acceptance
criterion is specific: *"The chosen cost model is stated with a measurement,
not asserted."*

Weighted acquisition also needs a decision about what a fractional/multi-slot
acquire does to the fail-fast semantics — today over-cap returns immediately
rather than queueing.

## The first attempt failed, and how it failed is the useful part

A cluster sweep timed six REST surfaces, 5 reps each, at three table sizes
(achieved `session_count` **1 / 55 / 969**) on the loss userspace cluster at
master. **No refused samples**, so nothing was excluded.

**Five of six fitted slopes came out negative.** A negative per-session cost is
not a small effect, it is an impossible one — the fit reporting that the
table-size term is below its noise floor. The spreads confirm it:

| op | within-N spread (noise) | between-N change (signal) |
|---|---|---|
| `list` | 19.7 – 36.3 ms | ~13 ms |
| `page` | 25.9 – 44.9 ms | ~8 ms |
| `status` | 13.6 – 38.5 ms | ~9 ms |

All 90 samples sat in one band of roughly 70–124 ms. Even `list`'s
+8.3 µs/session — the one slope with a plausible sign — is **not claimed**,
because its signal is smaller than its noise.

**The cause is the instrument, not the statistics.** ~80 ms of fixed cost —
HTTP through the API listener, request handling, JSON encoding — sits one to
two orders of magnitude above the walk at any table size reachable that way.
More reps would not fix it.

`/tmp/gemini-review-048.md`; the arithmetic reproduces, and the mechanism is
narrower and more interesting than the review states — **one of two spellings is
bounded and the other is not.**

## The encoding

`pkg/vrrp/instance_send.go` converts ms to centiseconds:

```go
maxAdvert := uint16(vi.cfg.AdvertiseInterval / 10) // milliseconds → centiseconds
```

`pkg/vrrp/packet.go:75` masks to the RFC 5798 12-bit field:

```go
binary.BigEndian.PutUint16(buf[4:6], p.MaxAdvertInt&0x0FFF)
```

`4500 & 0x0FFF` = 404 cs = **4.04 s** on the wire, and a peer computes
`masterDownInterval` from the truncated value — backups time out and flap on a
~12 s cycle against an interval the operator set to 45 s. An interval of 0 emits
0 cs, which RFC 5798 §5.1.1.4 peers discard.

**Bounded**, `pkg/config/compiler_chassis_cluster_packed.go:29`:

## #8325 — test: is_fixture missed the tests_<topic>.rs prefix for ~50 files — audited, zero realized impact, predicate fixed in #8324 [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-04)

> **Verdict up front, because it is not the alarming one: the predicate was wrong, and measured, NOTHING was affected.** Both plausible consequences were checked and both are absent. This is filed so the audit is not re-done, and so the method is on record for the next predicate change — not because something is broken.

## The defect (fixed in #8324)

`crate::afxdp::worker_queue::tests::is_fixture` classified a file as a test fixture by:

```rust
rel == "tests.rs"
    || rel.ends_with("/tests.rs")
    || rel.ends_with("_tests.rs")
    || rel.contains("/tests/")
```

No arm for the **`tests_<topic>.rs` prefix**, which is this tree's dominant per-subject suite convention — `tests_gre_version_6842.rs`, `tests_decap_dnat_table.rs`, `tests_fragment.rs`, … **50 files** under `userspace-dp/src/`.

So every canary built on it was evaluating 50 **test** files as production source. Fixed in #8324's second commit by adding `rel.starts_with("tests_") || rel.contains("/tests_")`.

**Sound by construction:** every `tests_*` module is declared `#[cfg(test)]` (`afxdp/mod.rs:528+`), so the compiler guarantees no production path reaches them. Excluding them from a scan named `afxdp_production_sources` is correct, not merely convenient.

## How it surfaced

Adding a test that assigns `coordinator.forwarding` tripped `forwarding_publish_population_is_pinned_7015`, whose failure message asks whether a new **apply path** appeared. It had not — a test file was being read as production.

That canary offers an allowlist for non-apply sites. Taking it would have written a misclassification into a list the next reader trusts, which is why the predicate was refined instead.

## The audit — consumers, and whether each one's result changes

Consumers enumerated by grep **with a positive control** (the definition itself must appear in the results, or the pattern is wrong):

| # | canary | what it scans for | `tests_*` files matching it | result changed? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | `worker_queue_6929_every_production_producer_routes_through_push_bounded` | `push_back(` on a command queue | **0** | no |
| B | `forwarding_publish_population_is_pinned_7015` | `.forwarding = ` | **1**, and it is `tests_gre_version_6842.rs` — the cell **added in #8324**, i.e. the one that surfaced this. Historically 0. | no |
| C | `every_commit_counter_prune_is_called_from_both_apply_commit_points_7015` | `commit_*_prune` call sites | **0** | no |
| D | `production_sources_7053` (`src/filter`) | — | **0** `tests_*` files exist under `src/filter` at all | no |

(A and D reach `is_fixture` directly; B and C consume it through `afxdp_production_sources()`.)

## #8336 — test/cluster: crafted-frame screen probes need an ARRIVAL witness, and the aggregate drop counter — not the per-reason one [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-04)

Filed from two VOID measurement attempts while validating #8298. Both failed for reusable reasons: anyone crafting frames at the cluster to exercise a screen will hit the same two traps, and will pick the same wrong counter I did.

## Trap 1 — the standard smoke exercises NO screen code

`stage_screen_check` is gated on `has_screen_state()` (`afxdp/poll_stages.rs`), and the loss userspace cluster carries **no `security screen` configuration**:

```
$ ... | cli
show configuration security screen
configuration path not found: security screen
```

So `extract_screen_info` is never reached and the whole screen stage short-circuits. A `make cluster-deploy` + `make test-failover` run against a screen change is **green for reasons that have nothing to do with the change** — the #8280 shape.

**Anyone validating a screen change must arm a profile first**, e.g.:

```
set security screen ids-option <name> ip tear-drop
set security zones security-zone lan screen <name>
```

and remove it afterwards — the cluster is shared, so leaving a screen bound to a zone changes the environment for every other lane. Verify removal on **both** nodes (config syncs to the peer); `show configuration | display set | grep -c <name>` returning 0 on each is the check.

## Trap 2 — the per-reason counter cannot see a parse-error drop

This is the one that cost the second attempt. The obvious instrument is:

```
xpf_screen_drops_by_reason_total{reason="teardrop"}
```

It is the wrong one for any drop that comes from a **parse failure**. `extract_screen_info` failing closed yields reason `ip-malformed`, and `afxdp/mod.rs` states that those reasons "are surfaced only through" the aggregate — `ip-malformed`, `syn-cookie` and `icmp-fragment` bump `xpf_screen_drops_total` and do **not** appear in the per-reason series at all. There is no `ip-malformed` label in that metric to sample.

So a fail-closed screen drop is invisible in the per-reason counter by construction, and the zero reads exactly like "nothing happened".

**Sample `xpf_screen_drops_total` for anything that may drop on a malformed header.** The per-reason series is correct only for drops attributed to a named screen check that ran to completion.

## #8337 — cluster: buildHeartbeat truncates GroupID to uint8 unsaturated, and peerGroups/election key on different values — lenient path elects a second primary [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-03)

Validated at `origin/master` `2f7157cd4` with executed probes. Surfaced as
A5b1-F1 in `/tmp/muse-spark-review-004.md`.

**#8322 did NOT fix this.** That PR tightened the *strict* commit gate (RG id
bounded by `MaxRedundancyGroups`); the wire cast and the runtime are unchanged,
and the lenient path still admits the value.

## The cast, and the asymmetry beside it

`pkg/cluster/heartbeat_manager.go:413`:

```go
GroupID: uint8(rg.GroupID),          // unsaturated
Weight:  clampWireWeight(rg.Weight), // :415, saturating helper at :443
```

Two adjacent wire fields, one saturated and one not. Whoever wrote
`clampWireWeight` knew the hazard.

## The consequence is a key disagreement, not just a wrong number

- `heartbeat_manager.go:468-476` — `peerGroups` is rebuilt keyed by
  `int(g.GroupID)`, i.e. the **truncated** byte.
- `election.go:318` — looked up by `m.peerGroups[rg.GroupID]`, the **raw** config
  id.

For any id whose low byte differs from the id, those two keys never match. Then
`election.go:133-135`:

```go
peerAlive && peerGroup == nil  ->  electLocalPrimary, "Peer has no RG info"
```

So a node that can see its peer, and whose peer is advertising the group,
concludes the peer has no RG info and **elects itself primary**. On a cluster
where the peer has done the same, that is a second primary — arrived at through
a heartbeat that was received and parsed successfully.

`group_state.go:20-38` `UpdateConfig` stores `rg.ID` raw, and there is **no
runtime bound anywhere** between compile and marshal.

edge-triggered. A commit that happens while the dataplane is *already* unarmed
produces no transition, so nothing reinstalls the debt — the node is left
penalty-free while still unable to forward.

## Measured, not impressions

## #8341 — Pool-mode source-NAT TCP never reaches the wire (ICMP through the same pool works) — independent of #8297 [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-03)

## Pool-mode source-NAT TCP does not reach the wire, independently of the proxy-ARP defect

Split from #8297 rather than folded into it: this is a **second defect wearing the first one's symptom**. #8297 (both nodes answering proxy-ARP for the pool address) is real and independently worth fixing, but it is **not** why pool-mode TCP fails.

## The measurement that separates them

With the proxy-ARP entry installed on the **RG owner only** — `fw0=1 fw1=0`, exactly the state a correct #8297 fix produces — pool-mode TCP still times out, while an interface-mode control from the same host in the same run reaches line rate:

```
BEFORE                  fw0=0 fw1=0
OWNER-ONLY INSTALLED    fw0=1 fw1=0

--- pool-mode TCP (source 10.0.61.240, matches `rule pool-snat`) ---
iperf3: error - unable to connect to server ...: Connection timed out

--- control: interface-mode (source 10.0.61.230, matches `rule snat`) ---
[  5]  0.00-3.00 sec  2.20 GBytes  6.29 Gbits/sec   receiver
iperf Done.

RESTORED                fw0=0 fw1=0
```

Same host, same target, same port, same seconds. The only difference is which source-NAT rule matches. State was restored.

## What else is known

- **The allocator runs correctly.** `show security flow session source-prefix 10.0.61.240` shows sessions translated to `172.16.80.7/30002`, `/30003` — ports from the configured pool range — and the `pool-snat` rule counts translation hits.
- **The sessions forward nothing**: `Pkts: 0, Bytes: 0` on **both** directions, while the rule counter records hits.
- **ICMP through the same pool WORKS** — 3/3, 0% loss — which clears address translation, routing, ARP and the reverse path for the pool address.
- **A WAN-side capture during a pool TCP attempt showed no TCP for `172.16.80.7` at all.** Only ARP. So the packet does not reach the wire; this is not a lost reply.

Taken together: a pool-mode **TCP** packet is dropped before egress, while a pool-mode **ICMP** packet is not, and an interface-mode TCP packet is not.

## What I have NOT established

The drop site. I stopped at the boundary rather than guessing which stage discards it — session install, admission, the TX path, or a checksum/rewrite step — because "pool TCP is broken" has several plausible causes and I would rather hand over a bounded fact than a confident hypothesis. The capture and the `Pkts: 0` both point at pre-egress, and that is as far as the evidence goes.

## Why this was invisible until now

No cluster config had a pool-mode source-NAT rule at all until #8280/#8300 added one, so no smoke exercised the pool data path. The `test-failover.sh` pool phase (on master) asserts the allocation; its data-path assertion is on branch `test/8297-acceptance` and currently fails **here**, not on #8297.

## #8346 — test/results/ledger.jsonl is a tracked single-writer file that every concurrent gate run appends to [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-03)

Raised by a lane mid-campaign, and it is a team-wide hazard rather than one
lane's problem.

## The shape

`test/incus/harness-result.sh` appends exactly one JSON row to
`test/results/ledger.jsonl`, which is **tracked**. With several lanes running
gates concurrently — which is the normal state of this repo — two lanes append
to the same file on different branches and conflict on merge.

Every row is a real record, so the conflicts are always **union-resolvable**. But
that makes it a recurring manual step on a file whose whole point is to be
written automatically, and a union resolve is exactly where a row gets dropped
by accident.

Already observed: a lane's `test-failover` row rode into an unrelated commit
(`b3f5b0680`) because the gate run wrote it there.

## The design anticipates conflicts but does not prevent them

`ledger_compare.py:58` already treats *"a committed conflict"* as ledger damage
and refuses to compare — which is the right failure mode, and it means a
botched resolve is loud rather than silent. Good detection. Still detection.

## Decision: one file per run, not one file

Move to `test/results/ledger.d/<run_id>.json`, one row per file, and have
`ledger_compare.py` glob the directory instead of reading one path.

**Conflict-free by construction**: two writers never touch the same path, because
`run_id` is already unique per run and already in the row. That removes the
decision rather than adding a rule people must remember under merge pressure —
which is the same reason the census exists rather than a convention about
registering harnesses.

Costs, stated honestly:
- more files in `git status`. Real, and the price of not hand-resolving a data
  file on every rebase.
- the comparator globs instead of opening one path. Small, and it already reads
  the whole ledger as a set of rows rather than caring about their order.

## #8348 — git: .git/config shadowed built-in merge=union with a no-op driver, silently dropping rows for months [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-03)

`.git/config` in the main checkout contained:

```
merge.union.driver = true
```

That defines a **custom merge driver named `union` whose command is the shell no-op
`true`**. A custom driver **shadows git's built-in `union`**, so every path marked
`merge=union` in `.gitattributes` resolved to *ours* and silently discarded the other
side's content. Exit 0, no conflict, no warning, nothing in the merge summary.
`git check-attr merge` reported `merge: union` throughout, so it looked healthy — the
attribute was honoured; the driver behind it was inert.

Worktrees share the main repo's `.git/config`, so this was in effect in **every lane's
worktree**, not just the main checkout.

## Control (real path, real repo)

Synthetic 3-way merge on `/test/results/ledger.jsonl` in a worktree sharing `.git/config`:

| driver | rows | theirs | ours |
|---|---|---|---|
| `true` | 7 -> **8** | **absent** | present |
| unset  | 7 -> **9** | present | present |

Independently reproduced by two lanes before this, each with its own control.

## Provenance

`docs/issues/pr-history.md:26283` — the verification checklist of **PR #1582**
(`_Log.md merge=union`, **closed/rejected** 2026-05-26 on structural-corruption grounds):

```
- [x] `git config --get-all merge.union.driver` returns `cat %A %B > %A` (built-in)
```

That item rests on a false premise: git's *built-in* union has no `.driver` config key,
so the command returns nothing in a healthy repo. The key appears to have been set to
make the check produce output, and set to `true`. The PR was rejected; the config
residue stayed and has been disarming union merges since.

## #8352 — test: an #[ignore]d fail-until-fixed cell has no wake-up — nothing censuses ignored cells [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-03)

## An `#[ignore]`d fail-until-fixed cell has no wake-up mechanism

`#8351` (merged) added a contention cell for #7209 marked:

```rust
#[ignore = "#7209: reds until the sync_session VERB, not merely its dispatch, is off the snapshot-wide ServerState mutex"]
```

That is the honest way to land a cell that documents a live defect — it states the
condition and it cannot red master. **But nothing will ever tell anyone to un-ignore
it.** `#[ignore]` is invisible to `make test-rust`, so when #7209's refactor lands the
cell stays ignored, stays green, and guards nothing — permanently.

This is a done-signal arranged in advance at a **layer the completing change never
reaches**. The cell is correct; its trigger does not exist.

## Census at `c72b844e7`

6 `#[ignore]` cells in the Rust tree:

| file | reason |
|---|---|
| `userspace-dp/src/server/tests.rs` | `#7209: reds until sync_session is taken off the ... mutex` |
| `userspace-dp/src/server/tests.rs` | `#7209: reds until the sync_session VERB ... is off the ... mutex` |
| `userspace-dp/src/io_uring_write_tests.rs` | `measurement, not an assertion; run with --ignored --nocapture` |
| `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/neighbor_dispatch_mirror_tests.rs` | `measurement, not an assertion; ...` |
| `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/cos/queue_ops/tests/bench.rs` | **(bare `#[ignore]`, no reason)** |
| `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/cos/queue_ops/tests/bench.rs` | **(bare `#[ignore]`, no reason)** |

So there are two distinct legitimate kinds — **fail-until-fixed** (should reactivate
when an issue closes) and **measurement, not an assertion** (should stay ignored
forever) — and they are indistinguishable to any tool, because the distinction lives
only in free-text prose. Two cells carry no reason at all.

**No gate tracks any of this.** Verified with a positive control: grepping
`scripts/`, `test/` and the `Makefile` for a census over ignored cells returns only
false positives (test *names* containing the word "ignored"), while the same sweep
confirms censuses genuinely exist in this repo (`scripts/harness-census.sh`,
`run-selftests.sh`'s interpreter and self-test censuses). The absence is real, not a
bad pattern.

## #8354 — ipmon: adopt pkg/coalesce so one debounce/throttle discipline exists, not two [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-04)

Filed **with** #7437's route listener rather than after it, because untracked
duplication is how a time-boxed second copy becomes a permanent one.

## What exists now

#7437 needed the debounce/throttle discipline `pkg/ipmon` already implements: a
dirty bit, a bounded settle, a minimum inter-actuation gap, and — the part that
is easy to miss — a generation counter so a change landing *during* an
actuation is not swallowed by the actuation that did not see it.

That discipline was **not** extracted from `ipmon` in #7437, deliberately.
`ipmon.Engine` entangles it with policy state, next-hop resolution and
`publishEnabled`, the HA-standby publication gate. Refactoring an HA-gated
engine inside a feature PR would put any regression on the cluster rather than
in review, and attribute it to the route listener.

So `pkg/coalesce` was written **as the type ipmon would adopt**, and used by
the route listener only. Two implementations of one discipline now exist.

## Why that is worth closing

A discipline whose entire purpose is to be obeyed identically, implemented
twice, is a divergence with a delay fuse. Whichever copy is edited first is
right, and nothing tells the other.

Concretely, `pkg/coalesce` carries these and a future edit to either copy alone
would break the pairing:

- `dirtyGen` incremented on **every** mark, so a mark during actuation keeps
  the state dirty rather than being cleared by the actuation that missed it;
- `lastActuation` advanced when the attempt **starts**, which is what paces a
  failing actuation's retry to one per throttle window instead of a hot loop;
- the dirty bit cleared only when the actuator **converged** AND the generation
  is unchanged.

Each is pinned by a mutation-verified cell in `pkg/coalesce`.

- `ipmon.Engine` uses `pkg/coalesce` for its coalescing loop; the policy

## #8355 — routing: decide the learned-route snapshot-size ceiling, with a measurement behind it [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-04)

Split out of #7437, which lists it as an acceptance item but does not depend on
it. Filed separately so the route listener is not gated on a measurement it
does not need.

## The question

#7409's `ImportLearnedRoutes` feeds kernel-learned routes into
`buildRouteSnapshots`, and every publish is a **full snapshot replace** carried
as JSON over the control socket. A box holding a full BGP table would push
hundreds of thousands of `RouteSnapshot` entries **on every publish**.

#7437 makes publishes *more frequent* (kernel route events now drive one,
coalesced at debounce 1 s / throttle 3 s), which does not change the per-publish
size but does change how often the size is paid.

**The import is not viable for a full-table BGP speaker**, and nothing today
says so to the operator or bounds it.

A bounded import — a configurable cap with a loud degraded-state diagnostic —
is the right shape, mirroring the `maxPBRRules` / `config.NextTableRuleWindow`
precedent. But choosing the cap needs a measurement nobody has taken:

- the control socket's deadline scales at **3 s + 1 s/MiB**

  question about serialized payload size, not route count;
- the relationship between route count and serialized bytes has not been

There is also a fixture problem: synthesising a table large enough to measure
against is its own piece of work, and doing it badly (a table of near-identical
routes that compresses or serializes unrepresentatively) produces a confident
wrong number.

## #8356 — Re-derive ZONE POLICY on the established-hit path for peer-synced imports (#7323 option C — the cost is the routing evaluation, not the policy walk) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-04)

Split from #7323, which closed on **B** (accept the zone-policy residual). This carries option C so it is not re-proposed under a description that understates it.

## The cost is NOT the policy walk

If you take one thing from this issue: **do not re-derive the policy-evaluation cost, find it affordable, and conclude C is cheap.** The policy walk was never the expensive part.

## What C actually requires

"Extend the established-hit revalidation to cover zone policy" sounds like adding a call. Measured at `c72b844e7`:

| input `evaluate_policy_result_with_icmp` needs | available at the hit arm? |
|---|---|
| `&PolicyState` | **YES** — `forwarding.policy`, and `forwarding: &ForwardingState` is already a parameter |
| `from_id` (ingress zone) | **YES** — `ingress_zone_override`, else an `ifindex_to_zone` lookup |
| 5-tuple, icmp, packet_len | YES — from `flow` / `meta` |
| **`to_id` (egress zone)** | **NO** |

`to_id` comes from `zone_pair_ids_for_flow_with_override(forwarding, ingress_ifindex, ingress_zone_override, egress_ifindex)` — it needs an **egress ifindex**. The hit arm's entry point has none:

```rust
pub(super) fn evaluate_input_filter_on_session_hit(
    forwarding, sessions, session_key, frame, flow, meta, ingress_zone_override)
```

Only ingress, resolved from `meta.ingress_ifindex`. Producing an egress ifindex for the flow means resolving the forwarding decision.

## The first-class constraint: #2620

That path **deliberately does not resolve forwarding**, and its counter semantics depend on that. Stated at the site (`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/poll_descriptor/filter.rs`):

> `#2620`: the session-HIT re-eval is the SOLE counter for this packet — it never calls `ingress_route_table_override`/the routing evaluator.

So C is not "add a policy call to an existing revalidation". It is **add a routing evaluation to the established-session hit path, and re-open the #2620 invariant that makes that path the sole counter for its packet.** Any proposal here must say what happens to that invariant — not as a footnote, as the design's first question.

## What C would buy

The residual #7323 accepted: a peer-synced imported session carries the **peer's** zone-policy verdict, and the receiver never re-asks its own. Input **filters** are already re-derived on that path (`filter_revalidated` vs `SessionTable::filter_revalidation_gen`, generation-gated, once per session per commit, revoking on DENY), so the exposure is precisely:

> a flow the receiver's newer **zone policy** would deny, **whose input filters permit it**, surviving as an imported session until it ends.

## #8357 — config: warn at commit when a chassis cluster is configured with no system ntp server — fabric RPC dies silently without it [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-03)

Split out of #7487, which closed as operationally closed. This is the **prevention** half; #6708 closed the diagnosis half at runtime.

## The gap

Cross-node fabric RPC authenticates with `HMAC(PSK, unix_time / 30)` and the verifier accepts the current window ±1. Beyond roughly a minute of clock skew **every** inbound fabric RPC rejects — permanently, because skew does not self-correct without NTP.

#6708 measured exactly that on the loss userspace cluster (`pkg/grpcapi/fabric_auth_skew_6708.go:19-20`):

> *141s of skew, **NTPSynchronized=no on both nodes**, every cross-node RPC dead. The symptom the operator saw named SESSIONS ("fw0 has only 1 established sessions"); the cause was the clock, and finding that cost an investigation.*

**The cluster simply had `system ntp` unset**, and nothing said so until cross-node RPC died.

## Why this is a product gap and not an operator error

Time synchronisation is a first-class, xpf-managed subsystem — the operator is *expected* to configure it here, and the platform is deliberately shipped with no default sources:

| piece | where |
|---|---|
| chrony installed and enabled on the appliance | `scripts/image/bake.py:78`, `:542` |
| every default pool/server **commented out**, `sources.d` created | `scripts/image/bake.py:543-544` |
| `set system ntp server …` is a config leaf | `pkg/config/schema_system.go:159` |
| xpfd renders the sources itself | `pkg/daemon/daemon_system.go:569` → `/etc/chrony/sources.d/xpf.sources` |
| compiled form | `cfg.System.NTPServers` (`pkg/config/types_system.go:20`) |

So a cluster with no `system ntp server` has **no time source at all** by construction, and the first thing that tells the operator is a dead control plane.

## Proposed

A **commit-time warning** when `chassis cluster` is configured and `System.NTPServers` is empty, naming **fabric RPC** as what breaks.

### Constraints, because two of these are easy to get wrong

- **Warning, never an error.** An operator legitimately configures a cluster before NTP is reachable; a hard reject would be worse than the fault it prevents.
- **Strict path only.** Not `CompileConfigLenient` / `CompileConfigForNodeLenient`, which back `Store.Load` (persisted-config boot) and `Store.SyncApply` (HA peer sync). A warning on those fires on **every boot and every peer sync of an already-committed config**, which trains operators to ignore it. `compileOpts` has no single "is lenient" predicate — it is a bag of named per-feature flags — so this needs its own flag set in `lenientCompileOpts()`, matching the file's convention.
- **Name the consequence, not the condition.** #6708's entire finding was that the symptom named sessions and the cause was the clock. A warning that says only "no NTP configured" recreates that gap at commit time; it must say that cross-node fabric RPC will fail.

Mechanism: `cfg.Warnings = append(cfg.Warnings, …)` (`pkg/config/compiler.go:370+`); `pkg/config/garp_clamp_5695_test.go` is the worked example for testing one.

## #8363 — frr: measure whether a synthesized deny is safe in a NARROWED BGP policy chain (the #7625 remainder) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-03)

Split out of #7625, which fixed the **emptied** half (PR #8362, merged): a BGP policy
chain whose every authored member is undefined now renders a bounded explicit deny under a
reserved name instead of dropping the attachment and leaving the direction permit-all.

The **narrowed** half was deliberately left at today's behaviour, pending a measurement
nobody has taken.

## The shape

`filterDefinedPolicies` returns the surviving subset. For `import [REAL GHOST]` the chain
resolves to `[REAL]` — the direction is still filtered, just less strictly than authored.
`narrowedPolicyChains7625` (#8221) detects and reports this; nothing changes behaviour.

## Why the emptied fix was not extended to it

Extending the synthesized deny to the narrowed case was argued to be wrong on the grounds
that a deny emitted for the undefined member becomes an **ordered member of the chain**, so
routes passing `REAL` reach it and are dropped — taking a works-but-narrowed config to
**deny-all** rather than to "filtered by REAL plus a correct deny".

That is plausible and it may be right. **It has not been measured**, and the whole decision
turns on it:

- if an **accepting** earlier member **terminates** chain evaluation, the synthesized deny
  catches only the fall-through — which is the *correct* behaviour, and the objection
  dissolves;
- if evaluation **continues** past an accepting member into the deny, the objection stands
  and the narrowed case must keep the surviving subset.

## The measurement

Render a `[REAL, GHOST]` chain with the deny synthesized, and establish what actually
happens to a route `REAL` accepts. This is a fact about FRR route-map chain semantics as
xpf renders them — not something to settle by reading the Junos-side intent or by argument.

State the expected result first; the answer is not obvious in either direction, which is
exactly why it should not be inferred.

## #8367 — userspace-dp: a flowless packet's output filter and filter-log use the PRE-NAT tuple under plain SNAT/DNAT (the non-NAT64 half of #7656) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-04)

## Defect

On the **flowless** TX-CoS path (non-first fragment / non-query ICMP — no `tx_selection_flow`), the egress output filter is matched, and the filter-log event attributed, against the **pre-NAT** addresses read from the ingress `meta`.

`#7656` fixed this for **NAT64**, where the staleness is a *family* change (the packet arrives IPv6 and leaves IPv4) and therefore highly visible: the wrong-family filter was selected outright. The same staleness exists for plain **SNAT/DNAT**, where the family is unchanged but the addresses are not.

## What this looks like

A v4 flowless fragment leaving through source NAT:

- the egress output filter is evaluated against the **pre-translation source**, so a `from source-address <post-NAT pool>` term does not match a packet whose on-wire source *is* that pool address — and a `from source-address <private range>` term matches a packet that no longer carries it;
- the filter-log event records the **pre-translation** tuple for a packet that left with a different one.

Junos applies an interface `filter output` on the egress interface AFTER NAT (this is the #3642 contract, stated in `resolve_cos_tx_selection_internal`'s own comment: *"both the filter FAMILY and the matched tuple must be the POST-NAT (on-wire) ones"*). The flow-bearing path honours it. The flowless path did not, and #7656 closed only the family-changing half.

## Why it was split out of #7656

Deliberately, so it does not ride along in a NAT64 PR and get lost. #7656's scope is bounded by `forward_wire_key`, which leaves family and protocol alone when `nat.nat64` is false — so the NAT64 fix does not reach the address-only case, and extending it there is a separate behaviour change on a separate population.

## Where

Two arms, and the second is the one #7656 did **not** touch:

1. `tx/cos_classify.rs` — the fresh flowless arm. #7656 routes this through a synthesized post-NAT wire key when `decision.nat` is available, so **this arm is already fixed for any NAT** as a side effect: `l3_wire_session_flow_from_meta` applies `forward_wire_key`, which rewrites `rewrite_src`/`rewrite_dst` regardless of `nat64`. Worth confirming by measurement rather than assumed from this sentence.
2. `tx/cos_classify.rs` — the **cached** flowless arm in `resolve_cached_cos_tx_selection_impl` (its own independent `is_v6` / `l3_addrs()` / `meta.protocol` reads). This one is **not** reachable for NAT64 — `flow_cache::should_cache` excludes it (`&& !decision.nat.nat64`, verified) — which is exactly why it is unaffected by #7656 and why plain SNAT/DNAT is the case that reaches it. A cached descriptor replayed for a flowless packet evaluates the pre-NAT tuple.

## Suggested shape

The same one #7656 used, for the same reason: thread the synthesized post-NAT L3 key rather than patching the individual pre-NAT reads, so family, addresses and protocol move together by construction. The cached arm needs the key threaded from `flow_cache.rs`'s seed, which already computes `forward_wire_key(&flow.forward_key, decision.nat)` for the flow-bearing selection.

## Fixture warning, carried over from #7656

**Do not validate this with address-less filter terms.** A term with no address match fires whichever tuple the evaluator was handed, so it cannot distinguish "matched the post-NAT tuple" from "matched the pre-NAT one". On #7656 a family-only half-fix passed the address-less cell and was caught only by a cell carrying a `destination-address` term. Any fixture here needs an address-bearing term whose expected value **differs** between the pre-NAT and post-NAT tuple, plus a flow-bearing positive control proving the term is well-formed and reachable on that path.

## #8369 — frr: synthesize a bounded deny for a SUFFIX-narrowed BGP policy chain (the #8363 remainder — changes live routing at load time) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-04)

## Read this first: it changes live routing at LOAD time

This is not a fail-open being closed. A ghost-last narrowed chain is **currently working and carrying traffic**, with fall-through **permitted** (`route-map <policy> permit <n>`, the #2998 Junos BGP default-accept). Synthesizing a deny changes that to **denied**.

And because strict commit already rejects an undefined policy reference in both directions (`config.TestBGPNeighborImportTypoRejected`), the entire affected population arrives via the **lenient** path — `Store.Load` / `SyncApply`. So the change lands on a **reboot, peer sync or rollback**: the operator experiences a routing change triggered by an unrelated event, on a config they did not just edit, with no commit to warn them at.

That is the reason this was split out of #8363 rather than folded in, and it is the first thing to weigh — not the last.

Contrast with #7625/#8362, which is *not* precedent for shipping this quickly: that only ever replaced **no filter at all**. The config was already failing open, so a deny could not take away anything an operator was relying on. This can.

## What is already established

#8363 measured the two facts this depends on (`pkg/frr/policy_chain_narrowed_eval_8363_test.go`, merged):

**1. The original objection is refuted.** It held that a synthesized deny becomes an ordered chain member, so routes passing the surviving member reach it and are dropped. They do not. xpf emits `on-match next` only for NON-terminating terms, so a `then accept` term is a bare `permit` and FRR stops there:

```
route-map C-xpf-chain permit 10
 match ip address prefix-list PL      <- no on-match next: STOPS here
exit
route-map C-xpf-chain deny 20         <- fall-through only
exit
```

**2. Position is the real constraint, and it is worse.** A synthesized deny is a chain member with a terminating **default** action, and `renderComposedRouteMap` does `terminated = true; if terminated { break }`. So a deny at a non-final ghost position does not shadow the rest of the chain — it **deletes** it. Composed `[SYNTH-DENY, ACCEPTER]` renders in full as:

```
route-map C3-xpf-chain deny 10
exit
```

Deny-all, and invisible in the rendered output because nothing is left that looks wrong.

**The safety condition that follows:** a synthesized deny is safe **iff the undefined members form a SUFFIX** of the authored chain. Ghost-last is safe. Ghost-first or ghost-middle is a routing outage.

## Sizing input — measure before deciding

`xpf_frr_policy_chains_narrowed_deny_safe` (#8363, merged) publishes exactly the population this would affect: narrowed attachments whose ghosts form a suffix. Its complement — `xpf_frr_policy_chains_narrowed` minus that — is the set a deny would break.

**Do not decide this from argument.** #8363's whole content was a measurement overturning a plausible mechanism that had been reasoned to twice. Collect the split from real deployments first, then decide. If the safe shape turns out to be rare, the change buys little and risks the rest; if it dominates, the case is much stronger.

## #8371 — 42 guard tests skip without memlock privileges and the package still reports ok [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-04)

## What

42 test sites across 22 files call `rlimit.RemoveMemlock()` and `t.Skipf` when it fails. In any environment without the privileges to raise the memlock rlimit, those tests **skip**, the package still reports `ok`, and the guards they encode provide no protection.

```
files with a RemoveMemlock skip:  22
skip sites:                       42
  pkg/dataplane/userspace          20 files
  pkg/dataplane                     2 files
```

This is not a hypothetical. It cost me a full round on #7497 (PR #8370): I wrote four guard tests copying the harness of the sibling `#4894` guard (`maps_sync_queue_id_bound_4894_test.go`), ran them, and got:

```
ok  github.com/psaab/xpf/pkg/dataplane/userspace  0.006s
```

Every one had skipped on `RemoveMemlock: operation not permitted`. Worse, one reported

```
--- PASS: TestApplyRejectsBindingSlotBeyondSlotMapCapacity7497 (0.00s)
```

because only its **subtests** skipped — so a top-level `PASS` covered a test that never executed. The only thing that gave it away was a 0.006s runtime that did not fit the work the test claimed to do.

## Why it matters beyond the inconvenience

A skipped guard is indistinguishable from a passing one at the package level. That is the failure shape this codebase keeps finding elsewhere — a check that fails to a value indistinguishable from healthy — except here it applies to the checks themselves. A reviewer greps, finds `TestApplyHelperStatusRejectsQueueIDBeyondStride`, and reasonably concludes the `#4894` aliasing defect is guarded. Whether it is depends entirely on where the suite ran.

## What is NOT claimed

I have not established where these do and do not run. If CI executes the suite with `CAP_SYS_RESOURCE` (or as root), they are live there and inert only for developers running `make test-go` locally — still worth knowing, because local runs are where most changes are first validated, but a much smaller problem. **Someone should measure which environments actually execute these 42 sites before deciding what to do.** That measurement is the first task here, not the fix.

## Possible directions, in rough order of preference

1. **Move the assertion below the privilege boundary where the logic allows it.** Several of these tests do not need a real BPF map at all. #8370 rewrote its four to drive `applyPrimaryBindingRowsLocked` / `applyAliasBindingRowsLocked` directly through the existing `ctrlMapUpdater` fake (`fakeCtrlMap`, added by #5486 for this same reason — its comment already says "the real-map link-cycle tests skip when memlock is unavailable"). Those now execute unprivileged and still assert the row was never written. This is not always possible: tests that verify kernel-side behaviour genuinely need the map.
2. **Make the skip loud at the suite level.** A package-level check that fails, rather than skips, when a named set of guard tests did not execute — so "the guards did not run" is a red, not an `ok`.
3. **At minimum, mark them.** If a guard is known to be environment-dependent, say so in its doc comment, so a reviewer reading the test knows its protection is conditional.

  made this loop "the persistent recovery owner", but it owns only the create half.

## #8373 — daemon: the deferred OnXSKBound fabric-IPVLAN callback recreates overlays from a stale captured list, undoing a later config apply [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-03)

## Defect

The deferred fabric-IPVLAN `OnXSKBound` callback recreates overlays from a **closure-captured** list, with **no re-derivation from the active config and no shutdown fence**, in an **unjoined goroutine**. A config apply that removes a fabric overlay can therefore be undone by a callback registered by an earlier apply.

Provable on `origin/master` `8edbf0913`.

## Mechanism

`pkg/daemon/daemon_apply_interfaces.go:118-127` — the callback captures `deferredOverlays` and iterates it unconditionally:

```go
bindingCtrl.SetOnXSKBound(func() {
    for _, ov := range deferredOverlays {
        if err := fabricEnsureFn(ov.parent, ov.name, ov.addrs); err != nil { ... }
    }
})
```

No `stopping` check, no `runCtx.Err()`, no re-read of the active config.

`pkg/dataplane/userspace/helper_status_apply.go:88-93` — it is dispatched **asynchronously and fire-once**:

```go
// Fire OnXSKBound callback once when all bindings are bound.
if allBindingsBound && !m.xskBoundNotified && m.OnXSKBound != nil {
    m.xskBoundNotified = true
    go m.OnXSKBound()
}
```

The goroutine is not joined and not gated on shutdown, so it can also run during or after teardown.

Immediately below the registration, the same function deletes overlays that are **not** in the active config (`daemon_apply_interfaces.go:129-140`) — so the deleter and the stale creator are twenty lines apart and disagree about which config is authoritative.

## Sequence

1. Apply A runs before XSK binding completes → registers the callback capturing `[fab0 on parent P]`.
2. Apply B lands, dropping `fab0` from the config → the stale-overlay loop `LinkDel`s it. Apply B has no deferred overlays, so it never calls `SetOnXSKBound` and **the callback from apply A stays registered**.
3. All bindings bind → `go OnXSKBound()` → `fabricEnsureFn(P, fab0, ...)` recreates `fab0`.

## #8377 — NAPI bootstrap sends a fixed 30 probes; coverage collapses to 10% at 16 queues [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-04)

## What

`pkg/dataplane/userspace/process_napi.go:96-102` sends a **hard-coded 30** UDP probes to trigger a first NAPI event on every RX queue, so each zero-copy queue posts its XSK fill-ring WQEs. The comment four lines above states the rule it is supposed to implement:

> Sending **~2× the queue count** with varying IDs makes it very likely that every queue sees at least one hardware RX event, which posts XSK fill ring WQEs for zero-copy packet reception.

```go
// Send 30 probes across port range 40000-40029.
for i := 0; i < 30; i++ {
    sendUDPProbeForNAPI(linuxName, targetIP, uint16(40000+i))
```

Two separate problems, and the second is the one that bites.

## 1. The stated rule is wrong

Queue selection is by RSS hash, so this is a coupon-collector problem, not a linear one. Covering `n` queues with high probability needs roughly `n·ln(n)` draws, not `2n`. Measured against the actual model, `2×` is far too few at every queue count that matters:

```
probes needed for P(all queues covered) ~= 0.99:
  n=6   ->  36 probes  (6.0x queue count)
  n=16  -> 115 probes  (7.2x queue count)
  n=32  -> 255 probes  (8.0x queue count)
```

The code has never followed the `2×` rule anyway — 30 probes on a 6-queue NIC is `5×` — which is why this has not bitten: the constant was generous relative to its own stated rule at the queue counts that existed.

## 2. The fixed 30 does not scale, and #7497 moved the ceiling

With the per-interface queue planning landed in #8374, an interface now binds up to `BindingQueuesPerIface` (16) queues instead of the global minimum across all interfaces. So 16-queue interfaces are now routinely bound where previously the count collapsed to the smallest interface on the box.

`P(all queues get a first NAPI event)` with 30 probes:

| queues | probes | ratio | E[uncovered] | P(all covered) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 6 | 30 | 5.00× | 0.03 | **0.975** |
| 8 | 30 | 3.75× | 0.15 | 0.864 |
| 16 | 30 | 1.88× | 2.31 | **0.099** |
| 32 | 30 | 0.94× | 12.35 | 0.000 |

## #8378 — Bound-but-idle AF_XDP queues hold UMEM when workers < bound queues [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-04)

## What

When `workers < bound_queues`, the RSS indirection table is reshaped to feed only `[0, workers)`, so the remaining bound queues are **registered, bound, ready and heartbeating while receiving nothing** — each holding its own UMEM.

Measured against `computeWeightVector` after the #7497 blocker-7 fix:

| workers | hw queues | bound | RSS feeds | bound-but-idle |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | 6 | 6 | 2 | **4** |
| 8 | 32 | 16 | 8 | **8** |
| 4 | 6 | 6 | 4 | 2 |

Per `docs/userspace-dataplane-architecture.md:2471`, an mlx5 zero-copy binding is `reserved_tx (min(ring/2, 8192)) + 2 × ring_entries` = `8192 + 32768 = 40960 frames × 4 KB` = **~160 MB per binding** at `--ring-entries 16384`, which is what the loss cluster runs. So `workers=2, hwq=6` pins roughly 640 MB of resident UMEM for queues that by construction receive no traffic.

## This is deliberate today, which is why it is a question and not a bug

The concentration is the point of #785: feeding only `[0, workers)` gives a 1:1 worker-to-queue mapping, so a worker owns one queue rather than round-robining several. The idle bindings are the price of that choice, and the file header states the intent plainly — hash outputs should land only on queues a userspace worker consumes.

What has changed is the price. Before #7497 the planner bound `min(rx_queues)` across **all** candidates, so the bound set was small and usually close to the worker count. After #8374 each interface binds its own `min(rx, 16)`, so the gap between "bound" and "fed" is now as wide as `bound - workers` on every interface independently, and the memory scales with it.

## The options are not obviously ranked

1. **Do not plan bindings that RSS will not feed** — plan `min(rx, 16, workers)` per interface. Reclaims the memory, but re-couples the binding plan to the worker knob, which #7497 deliberately decoupled, and means changing `workers` re-plans bindings.
2. **Spread RSS across all bound queues** — abandons the 1:1 concentration #785 chose. Needs a measurement showing multi-queue workers do not cost more than the memory saves.
3. **Leave it and document it** — the current behaviour, with the cost written down so an operator sizing a box knows that `workers` below the queue count buys idle UMEM.

**Option 2 in particular should not be taken on reasoning.** #785 chose concentration for a stated reason, and reversing it needs a throughput measurement on a topology where the two configurations actually differ — the same discrimination problem #7497 hit with its symmetric cluster.

## Not urgent

No correctness consequence: an idle bound queue drops nothing and misroutes nothing, it just holds memory. The correctness half of this area — RSS feeding queues with **no** binding, which the shim drops as `BINDING_MISSING` — is fixed separately as #7497 blocker 7.

Filed from #7497 blocker 7, where it was deliberately left out of scope to keep a correctness fix reviewable.

## #8380 — userspace-dp: TunnelDiscriminator::Unparseable is documented as "never merges with anything", which is false within its own class [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-03)

## Defect

`TunnelDiscriminator::Unparseable` (#7188, `userspace-dp/src/session/discriminator.rs`) is documented:

> `/// The header could not be read. Fails closed: never merges with anything.`

**"Never merges with anything" is true ACROSS classes and false WITHIN one.** The enum derives `PartialEq`/`Eq`/`Hash`, so:

- `Unparseable != Unkeyed`, `!= None`, `!= Keyed(_)` — correct, and this is the property the variant exists for: an unreadable header must not be taken for a legitimate unkeyed tunnel.
- `Unparseable == Unparseable`, and hashes equal — so two sessions sharing an outer 5-tuple whose GRE headers **both** fail to parse resolve to the **same** `SessionKey` and merge into one session.

The variant's surrounding paragraph is actually about the first case, which is why the sentence reads as reasonable. But as written it describes a guarantee the type does not have, for **every** caller of the enum — not only GRE.

## Why the wording matters beyond pedantry

Found while verifying #7699 (PPTP), whose acceptance criterion 4 is *"a version-1 packet with no learned control-channel association fails closed rather than aliasing onto another call."*

A version-1 (PPTP) GRE packet returns `Unparseable` (`gre_discriminator.rs:76`, before the Key read). So **two simultaneous PPTP calls between one endpoint pair** produce the same outer 5-tuple and the same `Unparseable` discriminator — identical keys, one shared session. That is exactly the aliasing criterion 4 forbids, and a reader consulting this comment would conclude it was already handled.

So the comment does not merely overstate: it points the opposite way from the behaviour, on the specific question a sibling issue is scoped around.

## Fix

Correct the comment to state the real guarantee — fail-closed **across** classes, non-splitting **within** — **and pin it with a cell**, because a corrected comment with no test is one edit from regressing to the comfortable version. The cell must assert both halves:

- `Unparseable` is distinct from every other class (the guarantee that holds);
- `Unparseable == Unparseable` **and their hashes agree** (the non-guarantee), since a session map keys on `Hash`, so equality alone would not pin what callers depend on.

## Not in scope

Changing the behaviour. Whether unparseable headers *should* split is a design question that belongs to the callers that need it (#7699 for PPTP). This issue makes the documented contract match the implemented one.

## #8382 — userspace-dp: add the PPTP call-ID class to TunnelDiscriminator and its HA wire tag (#7188's uncut third class) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-03)

Split out of #7699 (PPTP ALG), which is now rescoped to the control-channel work. This is the substrate piece, and it is separable.

## What

Add a PPTP call-ID class to `TunnelDiscriminator` (`userspace-dp/src/session/discriminator.rs`) and its HA session-sync wire tag.

#7188's sixth decision **named** three disjoint classes — unkeyed, keyed-with-value, and **PPTP call-ID** — and shipped only the first two. The landed enum is `None | Unkeyed | Keyed(u32) | Unparseable`. The third class was decided and never cut.

## Why it is its own issue, not part of the ALG

**It is a wire change.** The HA session-sync codec is tag-based, and `discriminator.rs`'s own doc block is about exactly this hazard: reserved tag `0` must keep meaning "the peer could not express it" and must not collapse into a real class. In a rolling upgrade the two nodes run different binaries on one wire, which is the #7487 lesson — **add a field, never redefine one** — and it deserves its own review surface rather than arriving inside a greenfield ALG.

The precedent is already in the file: `every_class_encodes_to_a_distinct_nonzero_tag_7188` asserts the disjointness as a **set property over every class**, specifically so a future class cannot be added with a colliding tag and still pass. A new class must extend that cell, not sit beside it.

## The open question — deliberately not assumed

**Whether the call ID from the packet alone is enough to separate calls has NOT been verified.** It is plausible that carrying the version-1 call-ID as a discriminator satisfies #7699's criteria 2 and 4 without any control-channel parsing, since it would stop two calls between one endpoint pair from sharing a key.

But RFC 2637 §4.1 says the Call ID field carries the call ID **of the peer the packet is being sent to**, so the two directions of one call carry *different* values. A discriminator built from the on-packet value would then split one call into two half-sessions rather than merging them — which may be better than aliasing two calls together, or may be worse, and that is the thing to measure before claiming this closes anything.

**Do not let "slice 2 probably closes criterion 4" harden into a premise.** That is how #7699 acquired the stale premise this split came from.

## Related state, verified at master `5d10487a1`

- A version-1 packet already returns `Unparseable` (`gre_discriminator.rs:76`) **before** the Key read, so it can never be parsed as RFC 2890 keyed GRE. #7699's criterion 1 is met on the session path.
- `Unparseable` does **not** separate two version-1 calls between one endpoint pair: it is equal to itself and hashes equal, so they share a `SessionKey`. Documented and pinned in #8380.

## Acceptance

- The new class round-trips through the wire codec and is distinct from every existing class, asserted by extending the existing set-property cell rather than adding a parallel one.
- Reserved tag `0` still decodes to "absent", not to the new class.
- A node that predates the class is not misread by one that has it, and vice versa — the skew case, asserted rather than argued.
- Whether this satisfies #7699's criteria 2 and 4 is **stated with evidence**, either way, rather than assumed.

## #8384 — Binding Ready is defined over socket setup only; a queue that cannot receive reports Ready=true [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-04)

## The asymmetry

**The counters can see a queue that cannot receive, once it costs something. The readiness predicates cannot see it at all.**

An operator reading `show system buffers` has a signal. Every automated consumer of binding readiness does not. A human can see the failure; the machine cannot.

## The gap

`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/coordinator/refresh_bindings.rs:262` is the sole definition of binding readiness:

```rust
binding.ready =
    binding.registered && binding.bound && binding.xsk_registered && snap.heartbeat_fresh;
```

Four terms, all of which describe **socket setup**, none of which describes **whether the queue can actually deliver a packet**. In particular there is no fill-ring term, so a binding whose fill ring was never populated — see #8377, where the NAPI bootstrap's fixed 30 probes cover every queue only ~9.9% of the time at 16 queues — reports:

- `registered` ✓ (the planner registered the slot)
- `bound` ✓ (the XSK bound to the queue)
- `xsk_registered` ✓ (the socket is in the XSKMAP)
- `heartbeat_fresh` ✓ (the worker thread is alive and polling)

…and therefore **`Ready = true`, permanently, while unable to receive a packet.**

The worker is healthy. The socket is healthy. The queue is dead.

## Who consumes this, and why that makes it a shared-surface change

The blast radius is the reason this is filed separately rather than folded into #8377: that issue's fix is a probe count, and this predicate is not its to change.

| consumer | site | what it decides |
|---|---|---|
| forwarding admission | `pkg/dataplane/userspace/maps_sync.go:99` — `b.Registered && b.Armed && b.Ready && !deadWorkers[...]` | whether the shim may steer transit to the binding |
| wedge detector | `maps_sync.go:1333` (`hasBusyBindingsWedgeLocked`) | whether auto-rebind recovery fires |
| HA standby readiness | `manager_ha.go:365,370` (`standbyBindingsReadyLocked`) | whether this node is fit to take over |
| link-cycle reconcile | `process_linkcycle.go:922` | post-cycle rebind decisions |
| CoS lease assignment | `userspace-dp/.../cos_leases.rs:43` | which ifindexes get worker leases |
| plan/status derivation | `planning.rs:110`, `:991`, `:1060` | per-worker group readiness, replan gating |
| operator surfaces | `format/status_sections.go:164`, `format/status.go:334` | `show` output |

## #8385 — test: the harness doc guard pins test/results/ledger.jsonl, a path that no longer exists [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-03)

`pkg/api/firewall_validation_harness_doc_guard_test.go:144` pins the harness design doc to
the string `test/results/ledger.jsonl`.

**That path does not exist.** At `origin/master`:

```
$ git ls-tree origin/master test/results/
040000 tree ...    test/results/ledger.d
```

#8346/#8359 migrated the ledger to per-run shards (`ledger.d/<run_id>.json`) and did not
update this guard. `harness-result.sh:10` documents the new layout; `:91` prints it.

## Why it stayed green, which is the interesting part

**A pin between two spellings only fires when they disagree.** The migration changed the
underlying artifact and updated *neither* the guard nor the doc, so the pair stayed
self-consistent while both were wrong. The guard asserts a claim about a file that is not
there, and reports success.

**Worse, it actively resists the correction.** PR #8379 rewrites the doc to `ledger.d/` —
which is right — and gets a **red** `go test ./pkg/api/` for it. Without a careful proof
chain the obvious reading is "this PR breaks the build", so a stale guard makes the correct
change look like the defect.

## Fix

Anchor at least one side to something that cannot drift silently. Each path the guard names
is now checked against the **filesystem** before the doc is checked for it:

```go
for _, p := range []string{"test/results/ledger.d", "test/incus/harness-result.sh"} {
        if _, err := os.Stat(filepath.Join(root, p)); err != nil {
                t.Errorf("path %q named by this guard does not exist ... update the
                          guard AND the doc together", p, err)
                continue
        }
        if !strings.Contains(doc, p) { t.Errorf("doc does not cite %q", p) }
}
```

## #8388 — Auto-rebind recovery is global: one wedged binding tears down all of them [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-04)

## The disproportion

**Only a targeted rebind removes the disproportion; hysteresis and attempt caps only narrow *when* the disproportionate response fires.**

Auto-rebind recovery for a stuck XSK binding issues `ControlRequest{Type: "rebind"}`, and rebind is **global**. `userspace-dp/src/server/handlers/rebind.rs` clears `bound`, `xsk_registered`, `xsk_bind_mode`, `zero_copy`, `socket_fd`, `ready` and `last_error` on **every** binding and reconciles the whole set. There is no way to rebind one slot.

So recovering **one** wedged binding currently means tearing down **all** of them — on a 16-queue interface, fifteen healthy sockets destroyed and recreated to fix one — plus resetting XSK liveness state and re-running the NAPI bootstrap.

## Why this matters more after #7497

Before the per-interface queue planning landed (#8374), the binding set was small and a bind failure plausibly hit all of it at once, so a global response was roughly proportionate to a global fault.

With `Σ min(rx, 16)` bindings the realistic failure is **partial** — fifteen bind, one returns EBUSY. #7497 blocker 5 makes recovery fire on that partial case, because previously it did not fire at all (the predicate required `bound == 0`, so one dead queue meant permanently no recovery and, per #8384, no readiness signal either).

That fix is right — a momentary global rebind beats permanent silent loss on one queue — but it makes the disproportion routine rather than rare. Every single-binding EBUSY now costs a full dataplane rebind.

## Why a cap is not the fix

Blocker 5's change adds `maxConsecutiveAutoRebinds` to bound the EBUSY/rebind loop that `handlers/rebind.rs` warns about (*"an infinite EBUSY/rebind loop (the live virtio multi-queue forwarding outage)"*). That is necessary, and it is not this.

A cap limits **how many times** the oversized response fires. It does not make the response the right size. After the cap is reached, recovery stops entirely and logs — which is the honest outcome, but it means a fault a targeted rebind could have fixed in isolation instead ends with recovery abandoned.

## What is wanted

A control verb that rebinds a **single slot**: tear down and recreate one AF_XDP socket, leaving the other bindings and their traffic untouched.

Consequences worth stating, since they are the argument for doing it:

1. **Recovery becomes proportionate.** One wedged queue costs one socket recreation, not sixteen.
2. **The loop pressure largely disappears.** The EBUSY/rebind loop is dangerous because each iteration tears down everything. A targeted retry that fails is cheap, so the attempt cap could be far more generous — or the fault could be left retrying in the background without risking forwarding.
3. **The 500ms zero-copy teardown quiesce shrinks in scope.** Today it gates the whole set; per-slot teardown only needs to quiesce that slot's pool.

## Not proposed here

- The **wire shape**. The existing `rebind` verb takes no arguments; whether this is a new verb or an optional slot field on the current one is a protocol-compatibility question, and during a rolling HA upgrade the two nodes run different binaries — an older helper must reject or ignore a targeted request safely rather than silently doing a global rebind.
- **Whether per-slot teardown is safe against the `xsk_pool` race.** The quiesce reasoning in `handlers/rebind.rs` is written for the whole-set case and would need re-deriving per slot. That is the main technical risk and should be settled before the wire shape.

Filed from #7497 blocker 5, which took the bounded-global-rebind approach deliberately as the shippable fix, with this recorded as the correct one.
