## #8397 — No helper crash history survives recovery: the episode record is wiped and nothing else retains it [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-04)

## What

Nothing retains helper crash history across a recovery. Once the helper restarts successfully, `restartHelperAfterCrash` wipes the whole record:

```go
m.helperCrash = HelperCrashRecord{}
```

so `Restarts`, `At`, `ExitCode`, `Signal`, `Detail`, `NextRestart`, `LastExitWasCrash` and `LastRestartAttempt` all go to zero together. A helper that crashed four times in the last hour and is now healthy presents a **completely clean crash surface**.

**And nothing else keeps it either.** There is no crash or restart metric — `pkg/api` exposes none — so after recovery the only trace is journald (`userspace dataplane helper restarted after unexpected exit`, with the attempt count). Correlating that requires the operator to already suspect a problem, which is the opposite of what a status surface is for.

## Why this is not the #5838 bullet, and must not be shipped as it

#5838 asked for "exit code/signal, restart count, last exit/**restart** timestamps, backoff deadline, and crash-loop reason". Every item on that list is a **current-episode** fact, and all of them are now rendered (the last-restart timestamp by #7967).

**History is a different requirement.** It answers a different question — *"is this recurring?"* rather than *"what is happening now?"* — and it is the question a crash surface exists for once the immediate crisis is over. Shipping history instead of the bullet would have left the bullet unmet while looking done; shipping the bullet does not make history unnecessary.

## Why the episode record cannot be extended to cover it

The wipe is not incidental. The record's contract is "the current crash episode", and that is what makes `LastExitWasCrash`, `RestartPending` and `CrashLooping()` mean what they mean. Keeping some fields across the clear would put two lifetimes in one struct, and every reader would then have to know which fields survive a recovery and which do not — the exact ambiguity the current all-or-nothing wipe avoids.

So this needs a **separate** store, not another field.

## Shape, not a prescription

A bounded ring of the last N episodes, each carrying: exit disposition (code/signal), PID, when it was observed, restart attempts made, and whether it ended in recovery or in a crash loop. Bounded so a flapping helper cannot grow it without limit.

Two things worth deciding rather than assuming:

- **Where it lives.** On the Manager it is lost on daemon restart, which may be acceptable (journald outlives the process) or may not.
- **Whether it is rendered or only queryable.** The `show chassis forwarding` block is already dense, and "4 crashes in the last hour" may belong behind a separate verb rather than in the same table.

## Not claimed

- **No measured incidence.** I have not established how often helpers crash in practice; the loss cluster journals show **zero** `resource busy` and zero auto-rebind events across the retained window, so crash-loop pressure there is low. This is a diagnostic gap, not a reported outage.
- **Not blocking anything.** #5838's bullet is closed by #7967. This is the follow-on requirement that the bullet's phrasing does not cover.

Filed from #7967, where the distinction between the bullet and history was the substance of the decision.

## #8426 — config: duplicate same-family `filter F` blocks silently overwrite (last-write-wins) — the same-family remainder outside #3884 [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-03)

Verified at master `570745967`. Split out of the muse-spark-005 review (L003 / A3-b2 F2);
independently re-derived here rather than taken from the review.

## The gap

`validateFirewallFilterFamilyCollisionsAST` (`pkg/config/compiler_firewall.go:355`) rejects a
filter name defined under **multiple non-inet6 families** — the #3884 cross-family case — and
is structurally blind to two blocks under the **same** family.

The reason is one dedupe, and it is deliberate for the case it was written for:

```go
record := func(name, fam string) {
    for _, f := range filterFamilies[name] {
        if f == fam {
            return // same family already recorded — not a cross-family reuse
        }
    }
```

`filterFamilies[name]` is documented as *"the ordered set of **DISTINCT** non-inet6
families"*. So two `family inet filter F { ... }` blocks record `fams = ["inet"]`, the guard's
`if len(fams) < 2 { continue }` skips them, and compilation reaches
`dest[filter.Name] = filter` (`:304`) which is unconditional last-write-wins.

## Why it matters

The consequence is the one the existing guard's own message describes for the cross-family
case: *"a discard filter can become accept-all — fail-open"*. A second `filter blockX` under
the same family silently replaces the first **whole**, including its `then discard` terms.
Downstream consumers resolve filters by NAME within the inet/inet6 buckets
(`compiler_validate_warn.go`, `routing/rules.go`, `dataplane/userspace/filters.go`), so
nothing downstream can disambiguate or notice.

Strict commit accepts it. There is no warning.

## Scope — what is already covered, so nobody rebuilds it

- **#3884 / `1ee4fb34b`** covers the CROSS-family case and is closed. This is the remainder
  outside its scope, not a regression of it.

## #8429 — CoS: single-rate policers enforce 1/8th of the configured bandwidth — bytes shipped in a bps-named wire field, then divided again [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-03)

Split out of muse-spark-005 (L009 / A6-b2 F1), verified at master `570745967`. **This is a
residual of #4514's own fix, not a regression of it.**

## The unit chain divides twice

- `parseBandwidthLimit` returns **bytes/sec** — the struct comment says so.
- Go assigns it straight across: `BandwidthBps: pol.BandwidthLimit`. The wire field is
  *named* bits-per-second and *carries* bytes-per-second.
- The Rust consumer then does `snap.bandwidth_bps / 8`.

So a configured `bandwidth-limit 8m` is enforced at **1 Mbit/s — 12.5% of the configured
rate**.

`git log -S` dates the Rust `/8` to `99e82a42b`, the #4514 fix: the consumer added a
bits→bytes conversion without checking that the emitter was already shipping bytes.

## Why it went unnoticed — the contrast control

**Three-color policers parse through the SAME function and are correct**, because they emit
`CommittedRateBytes` into `committed_rate_bytes_per_sec` — a byte-named field — and the Rust
side does not re-divide. The eBPF leg is consistent too.

**The single-rate userspace leg is the sole crosser**, and each side is internally coherent:
Go is consistent in bytes, Rust is consistent in "divide a bps field by 8". Only the
end-to-end chain is wrong, which is exactly the class no single-side test can see.

## Impact

Every single-rate policer enforces one eighth of its configured bandwidth. With `then
discard`, **conforming customer traffic is dropped and the policer counters attribute it to
the customer** — the surface an operator would check confirms the wrong story.

## What a guard must bind — the END-TO-END unit chain

**Never a pin on one side.** Both sides are individually self-consistent today, so a Go-side
cell and a Rust-side cell both pass while the product is wrong.

Assert the chain: `bandwidth-limit 8m` ⇒ wire `bandwidth_bps == 8000000`.

## #8433 — ipsec: duplicate hierarchical `proposal P` blocks wipe encryption, authentication AND dh-group — the empty fields then default to a weaker proposal [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-03)

From muse-spark-005 L024 (A3-b2 F17), **probe-verified at master `53cd289e8`** and found to be
worse than the review argued.

## The defect

Two hierarchical `proposal P { ... }` blocks under one IKE proposal name compile to a proposal
with **every negotiated attribute wiped**:

```
P{ encryption-algorithm="", authentication-algorithm="", dh-group=0 }
```

Strict commit is clean, `warnings = 0`, and it still commits **while actively referenced by an
ike-policy and a gateway**. The review claimed only `dh-group`; encryption and authentication
are lost too.

## Why it is a crypto downgrade, not a config-loss bug

`pkg/ipsec/ike.go:436` treats each empty field as "unset" and fills a default:

- empty `EncryptionAlg` → silently defaults to **aes256**
- empty `AuthAlg` → appends **no integrity algorithm**
- `DHGroup == 0` → appends **no DH group**

So an authored `aes-256-cbc` / `sha-256` / `group14` proposal renders to the bare string
**`aes256`** — losing the authored integrity algorithm and PFS group entirely, with no error
and no warning at any layer. The operator's `show configuration` still shows what they wrote.

## What a guard must bind

## #8434 — config: the typed-leaf validator echoes `encrypted-password` values in commit errors — a leaf the secret registry already claims [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-03)

From muse-spark-005 L032, **probe-verified at master `53cd289e8`**, and the escalation below is
what makes it unambiguous.

## The leak

A commit error from the typed-leaf validator **echoes the credential value back**, twice in one
message, for both:

- `system login user <u> authentication encrypted-password`
- `system root-authentication encrypted-password`

A canary planted as the password appears verbatim in the error text an operator sees, logs, and
pastes into a bug report.

## Why this is not a judgement call — the project already decided

`config.IsSecretLeafKeyword("encrypted-password")` returns **true** (negative control:
`"host-name"` → false). The leaf is already registered in `secretLeafKeywords`
(`secret.go:353`) as a credential whose value must never be rendered. **The typed-leaf
validator renders it anyway.**

And the redaction machinery is live in this build, not missing: the same canary placed in
`security ike policy pre-shared-key` renders `<redacted> <redacted>` with an echo count of
**zero**. So this is one path not consulting a registry the project maintains and other paths
honour.

## What a guard must bind

**A cross-check between the secret registry and the error renderers** — that no error text
reachable from the commit path contains the value of any leaf the registry claims.

**Not a per-validator assertion.** A cell pinning `encrypted-password` specifically leaves the
next typed secret leaf to reintroduce it, which is exactly how this one arrived while the
pre-shared-key path was already correct. The registry is the enumeration; bind against it.

Include the `pre-shared-key` path as a **positive control** in the same cell — it proves the
redaction is reachable, so a failure means "this path does not use it" rather than "redaction
is broken".

## #8435 — cluster: peerTransferOutOverride survives RG removal — a same-id re-add inside the 20s ack window self-promotes to primary (4th map-lifecycle gap in this loop) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-04)

From muse-spark-005 L033, **dual-primary reproduced at master `53cd289e8`** with a control that
makes it decisive.

## The defect

`UpdateConfig`'s RG-removal loop (`group_state.go:41-73`) purges `holdTimer`, `degradedTimer`,
`monitorWeights`, `garpCounts` and `groups` — **but not `peerTransferOutOverride`**. A stale
override survives an RG being removed and re-added under the same id, and the subject then
**self-promotes to primary**.

**Reproduced**: remove + re-add with the override armed → subject becomes primary.
**Control**: identical remove + re-add with no override → correctly stays secondary. That
control is what makes this a defect rather than an observation.

## Reachability — narrower than the prose suggests, and stated so

The override is armed only between `commitRequestedPeerFailover` succeeding and
`notePeerTransferCommitted`, bounded by `failoverAckTimeout = 20s`.

So this is **a ~20s window per operator `request chassis cluster failover`**, requiring a
config commit that removes and re-adds that RG inside it. A race, not a steady state. Filed
with that scope rather than as an always-on dual-primary.

## This class is established here

The loop's own comment calls `garpCounts` *"the third same-id-re-add map-lifecycle gap in this
loop after #5990"* — so #5990 and #6027 are the first two, and this is the fourth.

## What a guard must bind

**That an RG's incarnation boundary purges every per-RG authority map, enumerated from the
struct** — not a test naming the maps someone remembered.

A cell naming three maps cannot see the fourth. That is precisely how this one survived #5990
and #6027, both of which added a map to the loop and a test for that map.

## #8436 — config: duplicate hierarchical named blocks have SIX different reduction rules chosen per call site — bind the conservation property, not another registry row [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-04)

Umbrella for a class established by measurement, not by inspection. Verified at master
`b854f39a3`. Two independent agents reached this recommendation separately.

## The root

**The compiler has no single rule for duplicate named/kind blocks in the hierarchical AST.**
Each call site picks its own reduction, independently, and **six different dispositions have
now been measured**:

| disposition | site |
|---|---|
| append both | duplicate OSPF `area X` (two areas, same ID) |
| first-wins, drop the rest | two `ospf {}` blocks in one `protocols` root |
| last-wins, drop whole | two `protocols {}` roots — the first root's router-id is discarded too |
| last-write-wins **per field** | duplicate `filter F` (fixed in #8426) |
| find-or-create **merge** | dhcp-**relay** — the correct behaviour |
| last-wins with **per-field wipe** | duplicate IKE `proposal P` (#8433) — encryption, auth and dh-group all cleared |

Plus duplicate `dhcp-local-server group` (first silently dropped) and duplicate `unit N`
(#8427), which is *simultaneously* last-wins for filters and append-only for tunnel addresses.

**A `security log stream` duplicate is correctly rejected** — proving the `namedDupRules`
registry exists and has power. It simply has no row for most containers.

## Why per-container rows are the wrong fix

Every instance so far has been closed by adding a registry row or a bespoke gate: #3884,
#4287, #5180, #5631/#5878, #5649, #8426. **That is an opt-in pattern, and the opt-ins are
being discovered one review at a time.** A registry-row test proves the row exists; it cannot
see the next uncovered container — and the list of uncovered containers is not enumerated
anywhere.

## The reachability story, which is now sharper than any individual issue states

**Flat-set `set` spelling merges correctly in EVERY measured case.** So this class is
reachable only through a hierarchical config file, a `load merge`, or a `load override` — not
through `set` commands. That is a real narrowing and it should be stated on each instance
rather than rediscovered.

## #8437 — config: a missing semicolon fuses two hierarchical statements — the second is silently dropped from the compiled policy while `show configuration` still displays it [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-03)

From muse-spark-005 L028, **probe-verified at master `b854f39a3`**.

## The defect

A missing semicolon **fuses two statements into one**, and the second silently vanishes from
the compiled policy while `show configuration` still displays it.

```
route-filter 10.0.0.0/8 orlonger protocol static
```

(the `;` after `orlonger` omitted) → **parse errors `[]`**, **strict commit OK**, and the
compiled term has `FromProtocols = []`. The protocol dimension is gone from a `then accept`
term.

**Control**: with the semicolon present, `FromProtocols = [static]`. **One character apart,
both green.**

Reproduced a second time in a different stanza: `no-redirects` fused with
`domain-name example.com` → `DomainName = ""` entirely.

## Why it is worse than a parse bug

`FormatSet` renders the fused line back, so **`show configuration` displays a constraint that
is not in the compiled policy**. The operator's verification step confirms the config they
intended, while the dataplane enforces a wider one.

The reverse direction fails **closed** — an extra semicolon errors — so the asymmetry is
entirely in the dangerous direction.

**Hierarchical-only**: flat-set does not fuse.

## What a guard must bind — the widening, not the parse

**A cell asserting "the route-filter prefix and type survived" stays green** — both *are*
intact in the defective case. The loss is the `protocol` dimension.

Assert that **the compiled term's match-dimension set equals the set of statements authored**.
That is the only form that fails on this input, and it generalises to the `no-redirects` /
`domain-name` instance rather than needing a second bespoke cell.

## #8438 — config: `interface-range` `member` lists are uncapped and expand O(N²) — 32k members takes 142s with zero diagnostic, while `member-range` caps at 4096 [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-03)

From muse-spark-005 L017, **measured at master `b854f39a3`**. Filed as a CPU / wall-clock DoS;
the review's memory-exhaustion claim is **refuted** below.

## Measured

`interface-range` **`member`** lists are uncapped, and expansion is superlinear:

| members | wall clock |
|---|---|
| 8,000 | 6.0 s |
| 16,000 | 19.5 s |
| 32,000 | **142 s** |

All **strict-OK with zero diagnostic**, at 8× past the 4096 cap that the sibling spelling
enforces.

**Control fired on that sibling**: `member-range ... to ge-0/0/5000` is **ignored with a
warning**; `to ge-0/0/4095` expands 4096 interfaces in 1.17 s. So the cap exists, works, and
**only the `member` list escapes it** — same command shape, same expansion.

**Root cause**: `Node.FindChild` is a linear scan, making the Nth `SetPath` O(N) and the whole
expansion O(N²). 4× the input costs 14–19× the time, which matches.

## What is supported and what is not

**Supported — wall clock.** 142 s at 32k extrapolates to tens of hours: a commit that never
returns. It hits the **strict path AND the lenient peer-sync / boot path**, so a config that
reached the store this way stalls the peer and the next boot too.

**NOT supported — memory.** The review says "hours/OOM at 16 MB". Measured: **62 MB resident
at 32k members**, extrapolating to ~1.2 GB. Large, not an OOM. Filed accordingly — the harm is
availability through CPU, not exhaustion.

## What a guard must bind

**One total-expanded-member budget that BOTH spellings debit**, tested by driving each past
4096 and requiring the same disposition.

**A `member-range`-only test stays green if the fix is reverted on the `member`-list side** —
which is exactly the state today: the cap is present, tested, and applied to one of the two

From muse-spark-005 L084, verified at `b854f39a3`. The review describes "a degraded bond that
reads as fully populated". **Measured on the cluster path it is worse than that.**

## A one-character typo yields a cluster with no fabric link, and a clean commit

```
SUBJECT  member 'faster'  -> CheckText OK, warn=0, fabricMembers=[ge-0/0/1 faster]
CONTROL  zone member typo -> CheckText ERR "security zone \"trust\" references interface
                             \"faster\", which is not defined under `interfaces`"
```

That contrast is both the positive control and the asymmetry, produced in one run: **the same
typo in a security zone is rejected; in `fabric member-interfaces` it is not.**

`compiler_validate_warn.go:518-553` checks fabric-**interface** definedness and fab0/fab1
non-overlap. It never checks **member existence**.

## Why it takes the fabric down entirely

`compiler_derivations.go:130-160` auto-populates `cc.FabricInterface` **only when a local
member resolves**:

```
CONTROL members=[ge-0/0/0 ge-7/0/0] -> localMember="ge-0/0/0"  fabricIf="fab0"
SUBJECT members=[fabster ge-7/0/0]  -> localMember=""          fabricIf=""     CheckText OK
```

Every fabric bring-up in `daemon_run_bringup.go:229/234/260` is gated on
`cc.FabricInterface != ""`, so with it empty they are **all silently skipped** — no sync-hold,
no fabric.

**The RESOLUTION, not the token.** Every name in `FabricMembers` must resolve to a configured
interface, **AND** a clustered fab0/fab1 must resolve a non-empty `LocalFabricMember`.

**Binding "the member list is non-empty" stays green through BOTH failures** — the list is
populated in every one of them. That is the assertion the current shape invites and it has no

## #8445 — firewall: a policer `then` with both `discard` and a marking action keeps only the last — `discard` becomes a complete no-op and the rate limit is unenforced [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-03)

From muse-spark-005 L069/F24, verified at `b854f39a3`. The review states the surviving action
replaces the lost one. **The downstream read makes it worse: the policer becomes a complete
no-op.**

## The rate limit is not degraded — it is absent

```
then { discard; loss-priority high; }   ->  ThenAction = "loss-priority high"
```

Last-wins; source order decides which action survives.

Downstream: `filters.go:758` sets `DiscardExcess` **only** for `"discard"`. With
`loss-priority` surviving, `compiler.rs:493` picks `ThreeColorTreatments::default()` — no drop
— and the module doc at `compiler.rs:481` says a non-discard policer is *"METERED but not
acted upon — the marking action is not wired here."*

**So `discard` does not degrade to mark-and-forward. It becomes a complete no-op, and the rate
limit is entirely unenforced** while the config says otherwise.

## What a guard must bind

**The set of AUTHORED `then` actions, not the survivor.**

Reject a policer `then` carrying both a terminal action (`discard`) and a non-terminal one
(`loss-priority`, `forwarding-class`) — those are contradictory intents, and silently keeping
whichever was written last is the failure.

A cell asserting "the compiled ThenAction is what was authored" **passes today**: it *is* what
was authored, for one of the two statements. The property is that both were authored and only
one survived.

## Related, and deliberately not folded in

The sibling finding on duplicate `if-exceeding` blocks (L071) is a different defect with the
**opposite** disposition — it fails CLOSED, dropping 100% of matched traffic — and belongs
with the duplicate-block family (#8436) rather than here.

## Summary

`protocols isis` accepts **any** string for `level` / `is-type` at commit, and the FRR
renderer's `switch` on that string has **no `default` case**. A value outside the three it
handles emits **no `is-type` line at all**, so FRR falls back to its own default —
`level-1-2` — and the router forms Level-1 adjacencies it was configured not to form.

The sharpest instance is self-inflicted: **`is-type level-2-only` is the exact string xpf
itself writes into `frr.conf`**, and feeding it back in silently widens the router.

## Measured at `origin/master` `000a24a4c`

Through `Manager.generateProtocols` (`pkg/frr/protocols_render.go:625-637`):

| `ISISConfig.Level` | rendered into frr.conf | effective IS-IS level |
|---|---|---|
| `level-1` | `is-type level-1` | L1 |
| `level-2` | `is-type level-2-only` | L2 only |
| `level-1-2` | `is-type level-1-2` | L1+L2 |
| **`""` (nothing authored)** | `is-type level-2-only` | **L2 only** |
| **`level-2-only`** | **nothing** | **L1+L2** ← wider than the default |
| `2` | nothing | L1+L2 |
| `1` | nothing | L1+L2 |
| `LEVEL-2` | nothing | L1+L2 |
| `garbage` | nothing | L1+L2 |

**Configuring the level explicitly can be less restrictive than not configuring it.** An
operator who writes `is-type level-2-only` — because that is what `show configuration`-adjacent
FRR state and every FRR/IS-IS reference calls it — gets L1 adjacencies enabled, silently.

## The finding

Adding `persistent-nat` to a source-NAT pool stops sessions installing at all.

Controlled A/B on `loss:xpf-userspace-fw0/fw1` — same rule, same pool NAME, same
port RANGE, same pool address, same client, target, port and query. The only
difference between the arms is the two `persistent-nat` lines:

| pool | ICMP | TCP connect | **pool-translated sessions** |
|---|---|---|---|
| plain (`address` + `port range`) | LOSS | FAILED | **2 and 4** |
| **+ `persistent-nat permit any-remote-host` + `inactivity-timeout 300`** | LOSS | FAILED | **0 and 0** |

Reproduce with `test/incus/pnat-catchall-outage-check-8341.sh`:

```
PERSISTENT=0 POOL_NAME=p1 POOL_LOW=51400 POOL_HIGH=51499 ./test/incus/pnat-catchall-outage-check-8341.sh
PERSISTENT=1 POOL_NAME=p1 POOL_LOW=51400 POOL_HIGH=51499 ./test/incus/pnat-catchall-outage-check-8341.sh
```

## Why this is NOT #8341

In **both** arms ICMP is lost and both TCP connects fail. Pool-mode traffic not
transiting is therefore a separate, pre-existing problem that persists even when
sessions install correctly — that is #8341, and it is untouched by this.

What is new here is that with `persistent-nat` on the pool, no session is
created in the first place. Those are different layers: one is a forwarding
problem with correct session state, the other is missing session state.

## What it explains

#8440 measured "no session at all" under a catch-all pool and concluded the flow
never reaches the allocator. That probe used a **persistent-NAT** pool, so what
it actually measured was this defect. Its observation was right; its attribution
was not. With a plain pool the sessions install and are pool-translated.

A `policy-options community` member containing a regex metacharacter is rendered into an FRR
**expanded** community-list, where FRR runs it through `regcomp`. A member that is not a
valid POSIX ERE commits clean, renders into `frr.conf`, and fails the reload — and a single

both a strict commit gate **and** a render-side belt; the community side got neither.

Commit gate (`configstore.CheckText`) then renderer (`Manager.generatePolicyOptions`):

| member | list kind | POSIX `regcomp` | commit | rendered into frr.conf |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `65000:100` | standard | OK | ACCEPTED | `bgp community-list standard c1 permit 65000:100` |
| `65000:.*` | expanded | OK | ACCEPTED | `bgp community-list expanded c1 permit 65000:.*` |
| **`65000:[`** | expanded | **FAILS** | **ACCEPTED** | **`bgp community-list expanded c1 permit 65000:[`** |
| **`*65000`** | expanded | **FAILS** | **ACCEPTED** | **`bgp community-list expanded c1 permit *65000`** |

Both bad members reach `frr.conf` verbatim. There is no belt: `policy_render.go:290` formats
every member through `sanitizeFRRValue` only, which strips control characters (#4097) and
says nothing about regex validity.

Three other malformed members (`65000:(`, `65000:a{3,1}`, `65000:\`) *are* rejected — but by
the **lexer**, as `parse error: unexpected character`. That is an accident of tokenization,
not a gate, and it is why the hole is easy to miss: a spot-check of malformed members mostly
returns "rejected".

`policy_render.go:307-322` on the as-path side, in its own words:

An **unquoted** regex-valued leaf containing `[` … `]` has its brackets stripped and replaced
with spaces by the bracketed-list lexer, before any validator sees it. The result is a
**different regular expression that still compiles**, so every gate downstream reports success
and the policy silently matches a different set than the operator wrote.

```
set policy-options as-path ap1 .*65000[0-9]*     ->  stored: ".*65000 0-9 *"
set policy-options as-path ap1 [0-9]+            ->  stored: "0-9 +"
```

Both stored forms are valid POSIX EREs. #6686's `ValidASPathRegex` — the gate that exists
precisely to keep an unrenderable as-path out of `frr.conf` — compiles them happily, because
what it checks is *compilability*, and the mangled value is compilable. It matches literal
text `65000 0-9` followed by spaces, which no real AS path contains, so the policy term never
fires.

## Measured at `origin/master` `33711ee25`

Every row has its quoted twin as the control, which is what makes the diagnosis unambiguous —
the quoted spelling is preserved byte-for-byte through the same path:

| authored | stored | compiles? | |
|---|---|---|---|
| `.*65000[0-9]*` | `.*65000 0-9 *` | yes | **SILENTLY CHANGED** |
| `".*65000[0-9]*"` | `.*65000[0-9]*` | yes | control — exact |
| `[0-9]+` | `0-9 +` | yes | **SILENTLY CHANGED** |
| `"[0-9]+"` | `[0-9]+` | yes | control — exact |
| `^65000[0-9]+$` | — | — | rejected: `unexpected character: ^` |
| `"^65000[0-9]+$"` | `^65000[0-9]+$` | yes | control — exact |

## It splits values, not just mangles them

On a `multi: true` leaf the same lexing turns **one** member into **several**, each of which
is then a distinct value the policy matches on:

| authored `community c1 { members … }` | compiled `Members` |
|---|---|
| `65000:100` | `["65000:100"]` |

## #8482 — cli: the flow-trace directory is never Lstat-checked before MkdirAll — O_NOFOLLOW protects the file but not its parent [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-04)

Surfaced by `/tmp/muse-spark-review-006.md` (L013) and **verified against `origin/master`**. The mechanism is real and genuinely new — six prior archived reviews marked this confinement "VERIFIED SAFE" and each checked the file, not the directory. **The privilege escalation the review claims is NOT real**, and that correction is part of this issue so it is not filed at the wrong severity.

## The gap

`openTraceFile` hardens the *file* against symlink redirection and leaves the *directory* unchecked:

```
$ git grep -nE "MkdirAll|O_NOFOLLOW|Lstat" origin/master -- pkg/cli/monitor.go
72:	if err := os.MkdirAll(traceLogDir, 0o700); err != nil {
76:	f, err := os.OpenFile(path, os.O_CREATE|os.O_WRONLY|os.O_APPEND|unix.O_NOFOLLOW, 0o600)
```

`MkdirAll` stats *through* a symlink, so if `/var/log/xpf-flow-trace` is a pre-existing symlink to a directory, it succeeds and returns nil. The subsequent `O_NOFOLLOW` open then applies to `<target>/<name>` — a real file at the redirected location, not a symlink — so it passes, and the daemon appends root-written flow traces into the attacker-chosen directory.

Positive control — `Lstat` is absent from the production path, not from the package:

```
$ git grep -c "Lstat" origin/master -- pkg/cli/
pkg/cli/monitor_security_test.go:1
pkg/cli/userclass_entrypoint_canary_test.go:2
```

Both hits are tests. `monitor.go` has none.

A *dangling* symlink fails (`MkdirAll: file exists`), so the target must already exist as a directory — worth knowing when writing the test.

## What is NOT true — corrected severity

The review files this as a PermControl privilege escalation. It is not. Exploitation requires the ability to create an entry in `/var/log`, which is `0755` and root-owned. The CLI user supplies the *trigger*; someone else must already have the *write*. Those are two different capabilities and the finding conflates them.

This is therefore **defence-in-depth hardening**, not a live escape: it converts "root already had write access to /var/log" from a full trace-redirection primitive into a failed open.

## Suggested shape

`Lstat` the directory before `MkdirAll` and refuse a non-directory or a symlink, with the same fail-closed shape the basename sanitiser at `:31-34` already uses. `openat2` with `RESOLVE_NO_SYMLINKS` would be the stronger form if the kernel floor allows it.

[FLAT set packed                           ] SchemaValidate=REJECT Compile=ok groups=1 AdvertiseInterval=256

Property order does not matter (interval-first also slips).

**NOT reachable via `set`.** `SetPath` normalizes packed tokens into schema-structured children, so every flat-set spelling is gated (last row above). Reachable via:

## #8484 — config/cli: commit-time advisories never reach the remote CLI — #8402's and #7509's are both produced and both invisible [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-04)

Split out of #7509 rather than fixed there: it is not caused by #7509's change, and the already-merged #8402 advisory has the same behaviour.

## Measured

On `loss:xpf-userspace-fw0`, running the branch build of `xpfd` + `cli`, in one session:

| candidate | advisory it should raise | rendered by remote `cli`? |
|---|---|---|
| `gr-0/0/0` unit 1 added, in no zone, unit 0 in `sfmix` | #7509 shared-device-unzoned-unit | **no** — `commit` printed only `commit complete: 1 statement(s) changed` |
| same, plus `security-zone control interfaces gr-0/0/0.1` (units span `sfmix` + `control`) | #8402 contested-trunk (MERGED) | **no** |
| `gr-0/0/0` unit 1 added, in no zone | either | **no** on `commit check` either — `configuration check succeeds` |

The #8402 row is the control: the gap is **not** introduced by the #7509 advisory, and it is not a wiring mistake in either one.

## The advisories ARE produced

`TestBothZoneAdvisoriesReachTheRealCompiler7509` (`pkg/config/contested_trunk_zone_advisory_7509_test.go`, added on the #7509 branch) drives the real `CompileConfig` from real `set` lines and asserts both warnings land in `cfg.Warnings`. It is the only cell binding that wiring — removing BOTH call sites in `compiler.go` reds it and nothing else, which is also how this was found.

## Where the trail stops

The render path looks wired end to end and was not traced to a root cause:

- `pkg/cli/cli_config.go:315` — local CLI calls `printConfigWarnings(compiled.Warnings)` before printing `commit complete`.
- `pkg/grpcapi/server_config.go:291` — the `Commit` RPC returns `Warnings: configWarnings(compiled)`.
- `cmd/cli/main.go:427` — the remote CLI calls `printRemoteConfigWarnings(resp.Warnings)`.
- `compiled` comes from `d.commitAndApplyOperator` → `commitAndApply` → `commitWithGenBinding` → the store's commit, which compiles with strict `CompileConfig` (`pkg/configstore/store.go:449`), i.e. NOT the tolerant path that sets `suppressContestedTrunkZoneAdvisory`.

So one of those hops drops or replaces the `*config.Config` whose `Warnings` were populated. `commit check` failing the same way suggests the check path shares the defect rather than that it is specific to the commit response.

## Why it matters

Both advisories exist for legibility, and #8402's stated rationale is the #8296 shape — a config that commits clean, renders back verbatim, reaches no consumer, and leaves traffic dying with nothing on the box saying why. An advisory an operator cannot see does not close that.

## Suggested acceptance

- A test that binds the RENDERED output of a remote-CLI `commit` (and `commit check`) for a candidate that raises a warning — not just `cfg.Warnings`. Every existing advisory cell asserts the slice, which is exactly why this survived.
- A positive control in that test: a candidate that raises NO warning must render none, so the assertion cannot pass by printing unconditionally.

## #8486 — userspace-dp: peer-supplied owner_rg_id is filed into the owner-RG indexes unbounded [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-04)

## Summary

`metadata.owner_rg_id` arrives from the peer as a raw `i32` and is filed into
the shared owner-RG indexes without any bound. A peer sending N distinct
positive ids creates N buckets in `OwnerRgSessionIndex`, and nothing shrinks
that allocation afterwards.

## Where

* Wire decode: `userspace-dp/src/protocol/control.rs` — `owner_rg_id` is a raw
  `i32` field.
* Copied into the entry without validation:
  `userspace-dp/src/server/helpers/session_sync.rs` (`build_synced_session_entry`).
* Filed for every positive value:
  `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/shared_ops.rs` — `reverse_prewarm_owner_rg_candidates`
  inserts `entry.metadata.owner_rg_id` whenever it is `> 0`; the three sibling
  indexes file it through `update_owner_rg_index`.

The Go side does bound it, but only on the strict path:
`pkg/config/compiler_validate_strict_chassis.go` limits redundancy-group ids to
`0..15`, and `pkg/config/compiler_uniformgates_cluster_zone.go` downgrades the
violation to a WARNING on the tolerant load / peer-sync path. So the helper is
the last line and it does not hold one.

## Why it matters

Two effects, both mild on their own:

1. **Unbounded index width.** `OwnerRgSessionIndex` is an `FxHashMap<i32, ...>`.
   Its capacity grows with the number of distinct ids seen and never shrinks.
2. **The authoritative un-file walks that capacity.**
   `remove_owner_rg_index_key_from_every_bucket_locked` uses `HashMap::retain`,
   which is documented O(capacity) — it visits empty slots too. Removing N keys
   filed under N distinct ids is therefore Θ(N²) of outer-capacity work, on the
   session-control thread.

Neither is a packet-path cost and the un-file runs once per authoritative
removal rather than per refresh, so this is hardening rather than a live
regression. It is filed because the alternative — asserting "single digits on a
real chassis cluster" in a comment — is a claim the code does not enforce, and

*(truncated — 64 lines total)*

## `git stash push` in a worktree can exit 0 and leave no entry

Three incidents on this box now, and this one is a different shape from the
other two: the earlier ones were bad **pops** (a lane popping another lane's
entry); this is a silent loss on the **write** side.

### What happened

In `.claude/wt-7699`, to set an edit aside for the duration of a mutation run:

```

The command **exited 0**. The file was reverted in the working tree, so the
first half of the operation plainly happened. But:

```
git stash list --format='%gd %H %gs' | grep lane7699-overreach   ->   no match
```

The entry was never findable. The stack held 31 entries at the time, and its top
two were **both rescue markers from previous stash accidents** — one from earlier
the same night (`RESTORED-by-lane-7174 … dropped in error`) and one from
2026-08-21.

No work was lost in this instance only because the edit was generated by a
script that still existed on disk.

`git stash` operates on the **repository**, not the worktree. Every
`.claude/wt-*` worktree in this tree shares one stack, and several agents run
concurrently in different worktrees. So a `push` races every other lane's
`pop` / `drop`, and neither side gets any signal: the pusher sees exit 0, the
popper sees a plausible-looking entry.

`CLAUDE.md` already warns about the **pop** direction ("you could pop another
session's changes") and prescribes `stash push -m <tag>` + `apply <sha>`. That
mitigation does not cover this case: the tagged push itself left nothing to

## #8564 — configstore: an invalid-UTF-8 byte in a free-text leaf stale-drops the LIVE commit-confirmed record on restart (#4577 violation) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-04)

Found by the #7675 item-4 hazard census over the G+H+H2 seed's §4-mirror bodies. Measured at `origin/master fd3f2e76b`; the seed asserted it as a *"master #4577 violation TODAY for every record class"* and the assertion holds.

## Defect

`confirm.json`'s `GuardedHash` (#5835) is `sha256(activeTree.Format())` computed at ARM time over the **in-memory** tree (`store_commit.go:632`) and re-computed at BOOT over the tree **decoded from disk** (`store_persist.go:176`). Anything that normalizes a value between those two points makes the hashes differ, and recovery then classifies a **LIVE** record as stale, drops it, and leaves the UNCONFIRMED config standing with no rollback timer — the exact failure #4577 exists to prevent.

One such normalization is reachable from ordinary config today:

- `hasControlChars` rejects only C0/DEL (`pkg/config/freetext.go:71-78`), so a raw `0xff` byte in a free-text leaf commits cleanly;
- the DB persistence format is `json.MarshalIndent` (`pkg/configstore/db.go:449`), and Go's `encoding/json` coerces invalid UTF-8 to U+FFFD.

## Measured

Hermetic, in `pkg/configstore`:

```
commit `interfaces eth0 description "lan\xffside"`, then `commit confirmed 10`
  in-memory active contains raw 0xff: true
restart (fresh Store.Load on the same directory)
  after reload contains raw 0xff: false   (U+FFFD: true)
  WARN ignoring a stale pending commit-confirmed record on boot: it guards a config
       that is no longer active (a later commit/confirm superseded it)
  IsConfirmPending after restart = false
  record still on disk: false
```

Nothing superseded it. The log line is not merely unhelpful, it asserts something false — which is how this stays invisible: the operator sees a message describing a normal, benign situation.

## Consequence

The operator armed `commit confirmed`, the daemon restarted inside the window, and the safety net is gone. The unconfirmed config is now permanent, silently. On a config that stranded management, that is the management-stranding trap the whole mechanism exists to close.

## Scope note

The invalid-UTF-8 byte is ONE instance, not the root. The root is that the hash basis is not canonical: `Format()` over an in-memory tree vs `Format()` over a JSON-round-tripped tree. The seed names a second instance (`system dataplane-type ebpf` committing under the compiler's prune-before-validation and being deleted by a reboot-time rewrite) which is DEAD at master — `ErrEBPFDataplaneRetired` hard-rejects that leaf at commit (`pkg/config/compiler_validate_strict.go:34`) — but its mechanism is the same one. A fix that only rejects `0xff` at commit time leaves the class open.

The seed's proposed fix is the canonical basis at BOTH ends: `canonicalConfigHash(tree) = sha256(Format(jsonRoundTrip(tree)))`, computed at the sole arm site (`writeConfirmState`) and at the recovery capture. That makes the two bases equal by construction rather than by the absence of any normalizing value.

## #8565 — configstore: a confirm resolution with no error channel reverts an already-CONFIRMED config on boot when confirm.json removal fails [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-04)

Found by the #7675 item-4 hazard census. Measured at `origin/master fd3f2e76b`.

## Defect

`pkg/configstore/README.md` records a residual for #5835 and calls it safe:

> A residual case remains by design: an explicit confirm with NO later commit + an immediate crash before the retry heals fails SAFE (reverts on boot) — consistent with `ConfirmCommit` having returned an error.

That rationale is sound **for `ConfirmCommit`**, which returns the removal error to the operator. It does not cover the other resolution paths that reach the identical state and tell nobody:

- `ConfirmPendingOnDemotion` (`store_commit.go:865`) returns a **bool**. Its own comment says the failure "converges autonomously" — but a restart before it converges does not converge, it reverts.
- the plain-commit / HA-sync resolutions ignore `clearPendingConfirmLocked`'s returned error.

For all of these the active config is **unchanged by the confirmation**, so `GuardedHash` still matches the active tree at boot and #5835's staleness guard is structurally blind: it exists to catch a record whose active config has ADVANCED, and a confirmation advances nothing. `store_commit.go:775-776` states the premise directly — *"ConfirmCommit/ConfirmPendingOnDemotion do not replace the active config at all"*.

## Measured

Hermetic, in `pkg/configstore`, injected unlink failure (the existing `installConfirmDeleteSeams` seam):

```
arm `commit confirmed` (window B), then resolve it via ConfirmPendingOnDemotion
  ConfirmPendingOnDemotion returned true          <- no error channel at all
  record lingers = true ; GuardedHash matches active = true
restart with the deadline past
  WARN commit-confirmed window expired while the daemon was down;
       configuration rolled back to the pre-confirm state on boot
  => a config CONFIRMED on RG0 demotion was rolled back on boot
```

And with the deadline still in the future the same setup gives:

```
  INFO restored pending commit-confirmed window after restart;
       auto-rollback re-armed remaining=59.99s
```

i.e. the timer is re-armed over an already-confirmed config and will fire.

## #8566 — configstore: a boot ReadConfirm error silently discards the commit-confirmed rollback window (Load succeeds, no timer, no debt, no degraded health) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-04)

Found by the #7675 item-4 hazard census. Measured at `origin/master fd3f2e76b`. The seed calls this *"a pre-existing #4577 violation (an unconfirmed config stands with no timer, no debt, no retry)"* and the assertion holds.

## Defect

`recoverPendingConfirmLocked` (`pkg/configstore/store_persist.go:157-162`):

```go
rec, err := s.db.ReadConfirm()
if err != nil {
    slog.Warn("failed to read persisted commit-confirmed state; cannot restore the "+
        "pending auto-rollback window", "err", err, "issue", "#4577")
    return nil
}
```

A read failure logs and returns `nil`, so `Load` SUCCEEDS. The commit-confirmed rollback window is discarded for the lifetime of the process: no timer, no retry debt, no degraded health. The unconfirmed config stands permanently.

`ReadConfirm` errors on a transient IO failure, on a decode failure, AND on the #5637 degenerate-record rejection — so a single unreadable `confirm.json` at boot silently removes the safety net.

## Measured

Hermetic, in `pkg/configstore`:

```
arm `commit confirmed`, corrupt confirm.json, restart
  WARN failed to read persisted commit-confirmed state; cannot restore the pending
       auto-rollback window err="parse confirm state: invalid character 'n' ..."
  Load with unreadable confirm.json: err=<nil>
  IsConfirmPending after boot = false
  ConfigPersistDegraded          = false
  => the UNCONFIRMED config stands with no timer, no debt
```

`ConfigPersistDegraded() == false` is the part worth singling out. Every other way the store can end a boot in an unsafe state raises degraded health and /health returns 503. This one does not, so no operator surface reports it and no alert fires — the only evidence is one WARN line.

## Consequence

This is the failure mode `commit confirmed` exists to prevent, reached by a single unreadable file. If the unconfirmed config stranded management, the operator's rollback is gone and nothing says so.

## #8573 — cluster: the #1449 forwarding gate's stated reason no longer describes the tree — persistent-NAT leases ARE HA-synchronized now [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-04)

Split out of #8121 deliberately: **removing a gate's premise and removing the gate are different changes**, and the second is a user-facing availability change that should not arrive as a side effect of the work that removed its premise.

## The gate

`pkg/dataplane/userspace/capabilities.go` disarms userspace forwarding whenever a chassis cluster has any source-NAT rule referencing a `persistent-nat` pool (`config.UsesPersistentSourceNATPool`). The reason it reports, at three surfaces, is:

```
userspace persistent-nat source pool leases are not HA-synchronized
```

The consequence is not subtle. #8447 spent five rounds of cluster measurement rediscovering it: the config commits cleanly, the interfaces stay up, and **transit stops**. It presents as a link failure. That is why #8447 added a commit advisory, a WARN at disarm, and a Prometheus series.

## The premise is no longer true

Every persistent lease an active node holds now reaches a standby, by one of three routes:

| lease | route | landed |
|---|---|---|
| live flows, port-translating | rebuilt from the synced sessions | #7360 |
| live flows, address-only (`port no-translation`, port-less protocols) | rebuilt from the synced sessions | #8132 |
| idle, inside its persistence timeout | exported and imported over the cluster sync | #8121 |

**That exhaustiveness is bound, not asserted.** `every_persistent_lease_creation_site_has_a_sync_route_8121` (landed in #8572) pins the five production sites that insert into `persistent_by_source`, by enclosing function, each annotated with the route that carries it — two that create a lease on the ACTIVE and three that create one on a STANDBY. A sixth site reds it until somebody classifies it, and if the new site creates a lease on a standby it is a new ROUTE and the argument has to be re-made rather than inherited. It carries a positive control so it cannot rot into comparing empty to empty.

The #8121 chain is wired end to end — allocator verbs, control handler, Go manager, `pkg/cluster` sync payload, daemon hook — and its Go/Rust wire is pinned by a populated specimen (#8555), so a field renamed on one side reds rather than decoding to a zero.

## What this issue is, and is not

**It is a decision, not an implementation.** The mechanism exists. What has to happen is: verify the three routes hold together under a real failover, then decide whether the gate narrows, lifts, or stays.

**It is NOT a request to just delete the predicate.** Two things argue for care:

1. **The gate is currently the only thing that makes this configuration's limitations visible.** Lifting it removes the advisory, the WARN and the metric along with the disarm. If any residual gap remains, the operator loses the signal at the same moment the gap starts mattering.
2. **A residual IS known.** A lease imported mid-reconcile, or one whose pool address the standby's config does not have, is refused by design — those refusals are correct, but they mean "every lease reaches the standby" is a statement about the mechanism, not a guarantee about every deployment. The refusals are counted; whether the counters are the right operator surface for a post-lift world is part of the decision.

## Suggested shape

- Run `make test-failover` on the loss userspace cluster with a `persistent-nat` pool configured, which is exactly the run #8121 could never do **because this gate disarmed the forwarding it needed** — the circularity recorded on that issue. Lifting the gate is what unblocks its own verification, which is why this cannot be answered from the lock graph alone and needs a measured run.
- Decide between: lift entirely; narrow to the configurations that still have a gap (if the measurement finds one); or keep it and rewrite the reason, since "leases are not HA-synchronized" is now the wrong sentence whatever else is decided.
- Whatever is decided, `docs/ha-failover-status.md`'s "Persistent SNAT Lease Boundary" section and the three #8447 surfaces have to move together — they read one predicate today precisely so they cannot disagree.

## #8580 — nat: the CLI default view and the REST stats handler hand-roll rendering and drift behind pkg/natshow (not-installed, then-off, address-book names) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-04)

Validated against `origin/master` as part of the #8321 gemini-review-048 tail. This is gemini-048 findings **11, 12 and 13**, filed as ONE issue because they share a root: filing three would get three patches and leave the root in place.

## Root

**A NAT surface that hand-rolls its rendering instead of going through the shared `pkg/natshow` renderer is behind that renderer, and each gap is invisible from its own output.** The shared renderer is correct in every case below; the hand-rolled paths are the ones that drift.

## Instance A (finding 11) — the CLI default view, plus one the review did not name

`showNATSource`'s sub-command paths dispatch to dedicated renderers; its **default zero-argument path** hand-rolls with `fmt.Printf` and never consults `sourceNATPoolNotInstalled` / `sourceNATRuleNotInstalled`. Not-installed references per function, measured:

| path | refs |
|---|---|
| `showNATSourceSummary` | 2 |
| `showNATSourceRuleAll` | 1 |
| **`showNATSource` default path** | **0** |
| **`showNATSourcePool`** | **0** |

`showNATSourcePool` is a **second affected path and is not in the finding** — `show security nat source pool <name>` also renders a disarmed pool as active. Found by counting across the population rather than checking only the site named.

Consequence is what the finding says and no more: a disarmed pool or rule renders identically to an armed one on the two most-used views. Observability, not forwarding — the dataplane behaviour is unchanged and the reason predicates themselves are correct (#8329 / #7473).

## Instance B (finding 12) — `Then.Off` parity gap

`pkg/config/types_security.go` — `Off bool // source-nat / destination-nat off (no-NAT exemption, #3844)`.

- `pkg/natshow/source.go` — `case rule.Then.Off:` ✔
- `pkg/api/nat.go` — `action := "interface"`, overridden only for `PoolName`; **never reads `Then.Off`** ✘

A `then source-nat off` bypass rule reports `action: "interface"` over REST. The shared renderer already gets this right, which is what makes it a parity gap rather than a missing feature.

## Instance C (finding 13) — plural address-book fields

`SourceAddressNames` / `DestinationAddressNames` exist on the rule type.

- `pkg/natshow/source.go` — 2 uses ✔
- `pkg/api/nat.go` — 0 uses ✘

The handler reads only the singular `Match.SourceAddress` / `DestinationAddress` and defaults empty to `0.0.0.0/0`, so an address-book-scoped rule is reported over REST as matching **everything**.

## #8581 — userspace-dp: pkt_len means the L2 frame length at four meta-construction sites and the L3 packet length at a fifth, with no documented convention [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-04)

Found while validating the #8321 gemini-review-048 grouped cohort (item 4). The finding as stated — *"logical ingress metadata sets `pkt_len` to the inner packet length rather than the synthetic Ethernet frame length"* — is **mechanically true and is not a defect**. What it exposes is an undocumented convention split, which is worth closing on purpose rather than by patching one site.

## The measurement

`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/logical_ingress.rs` builds a synthetic frame as `vec![0u8; 14 + inner_packet.len()]` and sets `l3_offset: 14`, but `pkt_len` from `inner_packet.len()` — so `pkt_len == frame.len() - 14`.

Every other meta-construction site holds the invariant *`pkt_len` == the length of the buffer the meta describes, measured from offset 0*:

| site | buffer | `l3_offset` | `pkt_len` |
|---|---|---|---|
| `userspace-xdp/src/lib.rs` | Ethernet frame | 14/18 | full frame ✓ |
| `afxdp/coordinator/inject.rs` (frame) | Ethernet frame | 14/18 | `frame_len` ✓ |
| `afxdp/coordinator/inject.rs` (raw) | raw packet | 0 | `packet_length` ✓ |
| `afxdp/tunnel.rs` `local_origin_packet_meta` | raw IP packet | 0 | `packet.len()` ✓ |
| **`afxdp/logical_ingress.rs`** | 14 + inner | **14** | **inner only** ✗ |

4-to-1. Not a regression from the #7167 extraction — the removed inline GRE code was byte-identical.

## Why it is not a defect today

Every consumer was enumerated. **No consumer wants the L2 length.**

- The only slicing consumer is `frame/mod.rs`'s `trim_l3_payload`, and it is correct under BOTH conventions: it is a fallback reached only on a malformed L3 header, and it tries `pkt_len` as an L3 length first (bounded) and then as a frame length minus `l3_offset`. The downstream already defends itself.
- Everything else is byte accounting that never indexes: session volume (`account_packet`, whose own doc says **"of on-wire length"** — and the synthetic Ethernet header was never on any wire), per-zone volume, filter/policy term counters, three-colour policers, flow-cache `observed_bytes`, screen event payloads.
- Screen carries `pkt_len` but **no live predicate reads it**; the ping-of-death check that once did is recorded in-tree as structurally unsatisfiable dead code.

Visible effect: a GRE-decapped inner packet is billed 14 bytes lighter than an equivalent native packet in filter/policy/policer/session/zone counters. A consistency wart — and arguably the *more* correct number, since the 14 bytes are fabricated.

## What is actually open

**Which convention xpf intends for byte counters, L2 or L3.** The tree currently does L2 on the native path and L3 on the GRE-decap path, and neither is written down anywhere in `docs/`. That is a product decision, not a code fact, and it is the reason this is filed rather than fixed: patching `logical_ingress.rs` alone would pick a convention silently, in the direction that makes GRE-decapped traffic count MORE than the on-wire bytes the packet actually consumed.

Closing this means picking one, writing it down, and making all five construction sites agree — ideally with an invariant tying `pkt_len` to the described buffer's length at each site, so the next one cannot drift.

## #8586 — userspace-dp: a refused DeleteSynced still leaves the sibling worker's session entry and flow-cache slots (the #8114 item-4 remainder) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-04)

## The half of #8114 item 4 that #8576 could not repair

`replicate_session_delete` fans a `DeleteSynced` out to every sibling
worker's queue, and `push_bounded` REFUSES at
`MAX_PENDING_WORKER_COMMANDS` (4096). #8576 established what a refused
delete costs by reading what the command actually does
(`handle_delete_synced`), and repaired the part that had no other owner:

| the refused worker never... | repaired? |
|---|---|
| drops its source-NAT / NAT64 holder bits | **yes** — #8576, on the worker's behalf, by `Arc`-identity-resolved worker id |
| deletes its LOCAL session-table entry | **no** |
| invalidates its FLOW-CACHE slots for the key | **no** |

The second and third are the stale-forwarding window #8114 item 4 named
first, and they are not reachable from the deleting thread: both live
behind that worker's `&mut SessionTable` and its own per-binding caches.

## Why the obvious signal does not work

The signal that would have to reach the refused worker cannot travel
through the queue that is full — that is the whole condition. So it needs
an out-of-band per-worker latch (an epoch the worker reads on its own loop
pass), which is the shape #8114's "Wanted" proposed and which the #2442
`delta_loss_pending` latch is the precedent for.

## Why it was not built as a rider on #8576

Flushing the caches on the epoch is not sufficient on its own. After the
flush the refused worker still holds its LOCAL session-table entry for the
revoked key, and the next packet resolves against that entry and forwards.
So the epoch has to drive a RECONCILE, not just an invalidation.

And the naive reconcile is dangerous. "Drop local entries that are absent
from the shared map" is correct only if every live local session is
published to the shared map; a locally-owned session that is not would be
deleted by its own recovery. That premise needs to be established (or the
sweep scoped to peer-synced entries by origin) before anything is built —
it is a design decision with a worse failure mode than the bug.

Under sustained session ESTABLISHMENT — no revocation involved — the

## #8597 — [tracking] muse-spark-review-004 residual — all High and Medium dispositioned; Low tier remaining; successor to #8340 [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-04)

Successor to #8340, which is closed. That issue's High tier is fully dispositioned (3 real and fixed, 2 invalid) and four of its five tracked families are settled. **This carries the balance.**

---

# READ THIS FIRST — the standing instruction

**Establish the population yourself before acting on any finding, and record the count you found beside the count claimed.** Every finding worked so far has had a different population than the document assigned it — in both directions:

| finding | claimed | actual | consequence had it been taken as filed |
|---|---|---|---|
| K105 | one inline MAC | a two-copy search key | a fix that left the search key drifting |
| K29 | 1 site | **3** (2 are the LISTENER, not the dial) | IPv6 fabric listener still never binds |
| K93 | "two remaining sites" | **8**, and none is the described defect | a remedy applied where there is no defect |
| K90 / K91 | a nil-guard gap | **0** — the compiler cannot emit the nil | two more dead guards, the thing #6780 exists to stop |
| K94 | 1 handler | **41** | one typed error among 40 untyped, worse than uniform |
| K21 | 1 path | **2 layers, disagreeing** | half the defect fixed, the layers still inconsistent |
| K32 | 2 sites | **2 — accurate** | none; the count held, and saying so is part of the practice |
| K34+K35 | 3 sites | 3 as named, but the FAMILY has **18 more lines** in 9 knob families | four private copies of one clamp, and a fifth site missed |
| K17 | 1 site | **3 wire casts** in two protocols | the VRRP half left open, its reachability still "unestablished" |
| K20 | 2 sites + 1 "inspection-only" | **4 unlocked statements** — `sendAdvert` has two | one advert arm still racing |
| K05 | 2 append sites | **2 — accurate** | none; the other CLI session views stream |
| K70 | 2 sites | **6** — the rescue text, the rollback slots and BOTH master-key reads were also unbounded | four sites left unbounded by a fix that took the finding's count |
| K19 | one bump loop | **correct as filed** | none — and the census's negative result matters: `WithdrawInterfaces` has the SAME shape and is not defective |
| K23 | 1 unbounded shutdown acquire | **correct as filed** | none — 7 acquires use `context.Background()`, only one is shutdown-reachable |
| K15 | the `interface` modifier + a qualified `preference`/`metric` | `preference` was ALREADY rejected; the real population is **every valueless `args > 0` leaf**, at a different site | a per-leaf fix for a walker-wide hole |
| K16 | "every instance compiler" | **2 of the 4 named spellings drop; 3 are READ**, one of them by the shipped HA config | a blanket gate that refuses the configuration this repo ships |
| K24 | 1 renderer, 2 predicates | 1 renderer (**accurate**), **3 predicates** | the family-mismatch route still poisons every reload |

The cheap form is a census **with a positive control**, so "I found only the sites the document named" is distinguishable from "my search was wrong".

## Three traps this document produces, all confirmed in practice

1. **"The symbol is in the file" is not "the symbol guards this path."** The document cites per-file. A grep *count* saying a gate exists answers a different question, confidently. Check reachability **from the named function** — does the guard dominate the path the finding describes?
2. **A rationale is scoped to the axis it was written against.** When a finding cites a deliberate comment as justification, ask *"true against what?"*. K21's comments reason correctly about a v4-mapped literal's FAMILY and are silent about its KEY FORM; the code reads as handled because on one axis it is.
3. **Two tests can cover both axes and still miss their intersection.** K21 had a first-pass test and an idempotency test, and no cell where they crossed — which is exactly where it lived.
4. **A guard in front of a decoder must answer the decoder's question, in the decoder's terms.** K69 was the FOURTH fix to the same empty-config boot: #4888 tested four of five fields, #7454 tested the wrong error class, #8288 tested a hand-maintained subset — and all three matched keys case-sensitively against `encoding/json`, which matches case-insensitively. When a finding is the Nth in a family, look for what every previous fix assumed rather than what each one missed.
5. **A kernel that ACCEPTS your encoding has not agreed with it.** K06's broken interval set loads fine — `Flush` succeeds — so a package whose kernel-gated tests assert "every construct LOADS" could not see it. Read the state back. The same shape applies to any downstream that validates on ingest.
6. **A function that contradicts its own docstring is a free finding.** K07's swallow sat three lines below "an unprobeable file is not evidence of safety", and its sibling in the same file handled the identical error LOUDLY. When a finding cites a file, read what that file already says about itself — the disagreement is cheaper to spot than the defect.
7. **A refutation is worth building the fix to get.** K16's prescribed gate took twenty minutes to write and the suite answered in two — 16 cells red, including the shipped HA config and four existing over-reach controls. If a change makes an over-reach control red, that is the control working, not a fixture to update. Measure the population BEFORE building, and if you did not, let the corpus tell you.
8. **Assert the CONSEQUENCE you care about, not the mechanism you chose.** "The heap is bounded" and "memory does not scale with the table" look like the same claim and are not — K05's first fix bounded the heap and still allocated a closure per session, measuring 125x growth over a 200x table. If a finding is about a resource, measure the resource, and give the probe a positive control that proves it can see the growth.

## #8615 — natshow: the persistent-NAT table cannot show a binding with live flows — the idle-only export is the #8607 remainder [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-04)

`show security nat source persistent-nat-table` cannot show a binding that still has LIVE flows, and the reason is a deliberate constraint on the record it would have to travel on.

Split from #8607, which fixed the half that was entirely missing.

## What #8607 landed, and where it stops

#8607 fills the SHOW table from the helper's `export_idle_leases` (#8121). That export is filtered:

```rust
.filter(|(_, lease)| lease.active_flows == 0 && lease.expires_at_ns > now_ns)
```

So a binding is observable once its sessions are gone, and NOT while they are open. An operator running the command during traffic still sees `No persistent NAT bindings`, which is one of the three states the #8607 report measured.

## Why it was not just widened

The obvious move — add `active_flows` to `IdleLeaseWire` and drop the filter — is forbidden by that module's own first design rule (`userspace-dp/src/nat/idle_lease_sync_8121.rs`):

> **Never carry `active_flows`.** The standby installs a strict SUBSET of what the active sends … A carried count credits the lease for sessions this node does not hold, so it never reaches zero, never enters `lease_expirations`, and no GC path can reclaim it.

That is a rule about the HA **sync** record, and it is right. A display read has no such constraint — but it must not reach for the sync record to get around one.

## What this needs

A separate, display-only export:

- **Rust allocator** — an export over `persistent_by_source` without the `active_flows == 0` filter (`nat/idle_lease_sync_8121.rs:104` is the template).
- **Rust coordinator** — fan-out over `forwarding.source_nat_rules`, deduped by pool (`afxdp/coordinator/idle_lease_sync_8121.rs:68`).
- **A NEW wire struct**, not a widened `IdleLeaseWire`, carrying `active_flows` and the same address/remaining fields. Keeping it distinct is the point: the import path must remain unable to receive a count.
- **A new control verb** + `ControlResponse` field + `match` arm (`server/handlers/idle_leases.rs`, `server/handlers/mod.rs:310`).
- **Go**: a `Manager` method wrapping `requestDetailedLocked` with `SuppressStatus: true`, and the #8607 refresher preferring it, falling back to `export_idle_leases` when the helper rejects the verb (an unknown verb answers `ok=false` with `unknown request type <verb>`, so the degrade is loud and distinguishable).
- **A wire-agreement cell**, per the #8121 precedent (`idle_lease_wire_agreement_8121_test.go` + `userspace-dp/tests/fixtures/protocol_wire_v1.json`).

Roughly seven hand-written pieces; there is no generic verb mechanism, but #8121 is a complete, recent blueprint.

## Cadence caveat, already documented

`manager_idle_leases_8121.go` and CLAUDE.md are explicit that the control socket is shared with the 1 Hz status poll and that a caller above 1/s starves session installs during bulk sync. #8607's refresher runs at 30s for that reason; a display verb must stay on that cadence or be demand-driven, not polled.

## #8618 — userspace-dp: the #7323 zone-policy residual survives for ICMP alone after #8356, and now has no tracking item [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-04)

Narrow, self-limiting, and filed only because it is now **homeless**: both issues that disclaim it are closed.

#8356 (merged as #8616) re-derives zone policy on the established-session hit path, closing #7323's residual — a peer-synced session carrying the PEER's zone-policy verdict that the receiver's newer policy would deny. It deliberately **declines ICMP**, and the decline is correct:

```rust
// GATE 1b: DECLINE for ICMP. A zone policy can match on ICMP type/code via
// an application term, so an ICMP verdict is a property of the PACKET, not
// of the flow — and this derivation is deliberately frame-independent, so it
// has no type to offer. Evaluating with no type would fail to match a
// type-specific term and manufacture a DENY for a flow the policy permits;
// stamping a single packet's type as the flow's verdict would be just as
// wrong in the other direction.
if matches!(meta.protocol, PROTO_ICMP | PROTO_ICMPV6) { return None; }
```

`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/poll_descriptor/policy_revalidation.rs:93-105`.

**Nothing here is a defect in what landed.** Declining is the honest answer for a
frame-independent derivation facing a packet-dependent verdict, and it is the
same reasoning the static input-filter walk uses to decline a
route-lookup-affecting filter.

## The residual

For **ICMP and ICMPv6 only**: a peer-synced imported session whose flow the
receiver's newer zone policy would deny — and whose input filters permit it —
survives as an imported session until it ends. That is exactly #7323's residual,
now scoped down from "all protocols" to "ICMP".

#7323 is CLOSED (it closed on option B, accepting the residual). #8356 is CLOSED
(it closed the residual for everything else). So the ICMP remainder is described
only in a source comment, which is durable but is not a work item and will not be
revisited on its own.

## Severity: low, and self-limiting — do not prioritise this over anything

* ICMP session timeouts are short, so the exposure window is a flow lifetime,
  not "until the box reboots".
* It requires a policy narrowing to land DURING an established peer-synced ICMP
  flow.

## #8629 — grpcapi: 41 handler error returns are bare errors (gRPC codes.Unknown) rather than typed status codes [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-04)

Found while working the muse-spark-review-004 residual (#8597), as finding K94. The finding named **one** handler; the class is **41**.

## The finding, and the correction

K94: *"`ClearDHCPClientIdentifier` returns bare errors (gRPC `Unknown`) instead of status codes"*. That is true — `pkg/grpcapi/server_dhcp.go` returns `fmt.Errorf("clear DUID: %w", err)`, which gRPC surfaces as `codes.Unknown`, so a caller cannot distinguish "no such interface" from "the DHCP client is not running" from a genuine internal fault.

**Measured at `origin/master`:**

| pattern | count |
|---|---|
| `return nil, err` / `return nil, fmt.Errorf(...)` in non-test `pkg/grpcapi/*.go` | **41** |
| `status.Error(...)` in the same files (positive control) | 56 |

The control matters: 56 hits means the search finds real code, so 41 is a real population and not a bad pattern.

## Why this is filed rather than fixed

**Fixing the one named handler would be worse than leaving it.** Today the behaviour is uniform — every one of these 41 sites yields `codes.Unknown`, and a client can at least rely on that. Converting one produces a surface where some errors carry a meaningful code and most do not, with nothing telling a caller which is which.

Converting all 41 is not mechanical either. Each site needs a decision about which code its error actually is:

- `NotFound` vs `InvalidArgument` for an unknown interface or identifier — these are different contracts for a caller retrying;
- `FailedPrecondition` vs `Unavailable` for "the subsystem is not running" — the first says do not retry, the second says retry later;
- `Internal` for a genuine fault, which is the only one that is currently correct by accident.

Getting that wrong is not cosmetic: gRPC clients and the CLI's own retry logic branch on the code. A wrong `Unavailable` produces a retry storm against a permanent failure; a wrong `FailedPrecondition` makes a transient failure look permanent.

## What a fix would owe

- The 41 sites enumerated with a code assigned to each and a one-line reason.
- A census guard, with a positive control, so site 42 cannot land bare — the same shape as `TestNoSprintfBuiltEndpoints_8597`.
- A check of what the CLI and any in-process caller currently do with `codes.Unknown` from these RPCs, because that is the behaviour the change alters.

Severity is Low and the current behaviour is uniform, so this is a coherence improvement rather than a defect repair. Recording it with the real count so nobody sizes it from the finding's "one handler".

## #8631 — config: expandProxyARPPrefix classifies a ::ffff: block as v6 while the install path classifies it as v4 [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-04)

Found while fixing #8597 finding K21 (merged as #8630). K21 named the reconcile path; this is the same root one layer up, reaching a *different* wrong answer, and it is filed rather than fixed because the fix is not the same one-liner.

## The root

`::ffff:a.b.c.d` parses to a **4-in-6** `netip.Addr`. Nothing unmaps it at parse in either layer, and the two layers then classify the identical literal differently:

| layer | predicate | verdict for `::ffff:10.0.0.0/126` |
|---|---|---|
| `ReconcileProxyARP` (`pkg/dataplane/proxyarp.go`) | `addr.Is6() && !addr.Is4In6()` | **v4** — installs as `AF_INET` |
| `expandProxyARPPrefix` (`pkg/config/compiler_nat_proxyarp_prefix.go`) | `addr.Is4()` | **v6** — expands under v6 rules |

`Is4()` is **false** for a 4-in-6 address, so the expansion:

- does **not** skip the network address (the v4 rule for a block wider than /31), and
- emits a `/128` suffix rather than `/32`.

So a v4-mapped block expands into host entries the install path then treats as v4. The two layers disagree about what one literal is.

## Why it is not `Unmap()` and done

The prefix **length** is in v6 bit-space. `::ffff:10.0.0.0/126` describes four addresses — the v4-equivalent mask is `126 - 96 = 30`. Unmapping the address while keeping `Bits()` at 126 constructs an invalid prefix (a v4 address with a /126 mask), and everything downstream of it is then wrong in a new way.

I tried exactly that first, and a control caught it: a plain-v4 control arm asserting `10.0.0.0/126` expands to 3 hosts returned **1** — because that prefix does not parse at all, which is the same class of nonsense the naive unmap produces for the mapped form. Recording the near-miss because the fix looks like a one-liner and is not.

## What a fix owes

- Convert the mask when unmapping: for a 4-in-6 prefix with `Bits() >= 96`, the v4 prefix is `Bits() - 96`. Decide what a `Bits() < 96` mapped prefix means — most likely reject it at commit, since it does not denote a v4 block.
- A cell that distinguishes the two rule sets **by count as well as by spelling**: a v4 `/30` yields 3 hosts (network address skipped), a v6 `/126` yields 4. Asserting only the `/32` vs `/128` suffix would pass on a half-fix.
- A control on a genuine v6 block, since `Unmap` must remain a no-op there.
- A check of whether `::ffff:` blocks are reachable at commit at all — if the schema or a strict gate already rejects them, this is documentation rather than a change, and that is worth establishing **before** writing the conversion.

Severity is Low: the entries still install, and the observable effect is an extra host entry (the network address) and a mis-shaped literal in the expanded set rather than a forwarding fault.

if key.routing_domain == 0 {

A delete whose routing domain resolves to 0 is retried once per configured
routing domain. Routing instances exist to carry **overlapping address
space**, so two tenants holding the identical 5-tuple is the normal case,

Not an oversight at the call site. `pkg/dataplane.SessionKey` is a bare

Enumerating the two cases a proxy-ARP entry can be in, against

| target's route | today | with `proxy_arp=0` |
|---|---|---|
| egresses a **different** device | pneigh arm answers (`rt->dst.dev != dev && pneigh_lookup(...)` — **no sysctl term**); `arp_fwd_proxy` also answers, for *any* address | pneigh arm still answers, for the **listed addresses only** |
| **same** device (the #2160 / #8621 case) | neither kernel arm answers; the userspace responder does (#8621) | unchanged — the responder is not sysctl-gated |

So the sysctl's only distinct contribution is the over-answer itself: it fires
for addresses that are **not** in the entry list. Removing it removes exactly
that and nothing else, which is the Junos parity item 3 asked for.

Surfaced by #8621, which removed this deferral's stated blocker. Filing because the reason it could not be done is gone and the mechanism to do it now exists.

## The over-answer

With the default `medium_id=0`, `net.ipv4.conf.<if>.proxy_arp=1` makes the kernel
answer ARP on that interface for **any** target routed out a different interface
— not merely the addresses the operator listed. Junos `proxy-arp` proxies only
the configured addresses.

So the box makes ARP claims on the wire for addresses nobody configured, whenever
they happen to route out another interface. That is an over-claim with real
consequences on a shared segment, and it has been known and documented since

`docs/feature-gaps.md` records it as **#2197 item 3 (PLAN-DEFER, lab
characterization pending)**, with the stated blocker:

of the interface the request arrives on, `arp_fwd_proxy` returns 0 on its **first
line** (`if (rt->dst.dev == dev) return 0;`) — before it ever reads
`IN_DEV_PROXY_ARP`. The sysctl was never serving the same-L2 case it was recorded
as load-bearing for. Confirmed by intervention on the loss userspace cluster: the

gated per request on redundancy-group ownership.

**different** interface — that is precisely what `arp_fwd_proxy` exists for. So
