## #8642 — sweep: config seconds/milliseconds knobs still reaching time.Duration multiplies unbounded (the #6769 family, 9 knob families / 18 sites) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-04)

Filed from #8597 (muse-spark-review-004 residual) while fixing K34 (feeds) and K35 (event-options). Both are instances of a family the project has now fixed **four times, one package at a time**, and the census below says how many are left.

## The family

A config `seconds`/`milliseconds` knob is stored by the compiler as a plain `int` from `strconv.Atoi` with **no range check**. A consumer computes `time.Duration(n) * time.Second`. Past `math.MaxInt64 / 1e9` ≈ 9.2e9 seconds the multiply overflows int64 nanoseconds and **wraps**, and — this is the part that defeats the guards actually present — **the residue can be small and POSITIVE**. `gcd(1e9, 2^64) = 512`, so the residues are 512ns multiples and the smallest is exactly 512ns: `20211507185753197` yields a 512ns interval.

Every site below already has a guard. Every one of those guards is `<= 0` or `> 0`, which is blind to the positive residue by construction.

Reachability is the tolerant ingress, and it is stated in the tree rather than inferred — `Store.compileTreeLenient` (pkg/configstore/store.go):

> the typed-leaf SchemaValidate gate is STRICT only on the operator-driven commit / commit-check path (compileTree). Here — the tolerant Store.Load / Store.SyncApply ingress for configs the operator did NOT just author — a violation downgrades to a warning.

So a schema ceiling stops an operator's `commit`; it does not stop a persisted config from an older binary, or one pushed by an un-upgraded cluster primary.

## Already fixed, one package at a time

| # | package | helper |
|---|---|---|
| #5705 | `pkg/routing` tunnel keepalive | inline bound |
| #5723 | `pkg/rpm` | `clampRPMIntervalSeconds` |
| #6769 | `pkg/flowexport` | `secondsToDuration` |
| #8597 | `pkg/feeds`, `pkg/eventengine` | `feedIntervalSeconds`, `withinWindow` |

#8258 named this sweep in general and is closed. Each of the four fixes carries its own copy of the same clamp.

## Census — the sites still unswept

**9 knob families, 18 source lines.** The two numbers differ (pkg/ra alone carries 7 lines, ipmon 3), and the table is by family; the "site" column names every line so a reader can check the arithmetic rather than inherit it.

Established by grepping `time.Duration(<ident>) * time.<Unit>` across `pkg/` and `cmd/` (62 matches, including comments and the four hardened helpers, which is the positive control: the fixed packages no longer show a raw site) and then reading each one's guard.

| site | knob | strict ceiling | runtime guard | what a 512ns value does |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `pkg/lldp/lldp.go:325` | `protocols lldp transmit-interval` | `ValidateInteger(5, 32768)` | `interval <= 0` | `time.NewTicker(512ns)` in `txLoop` — an LLDP frame every 512ns on **every** configured interface. A sustained TX storm, the closest sibling of #6769. |
| `pkg/cluster/group_state.go:130` | `chassis cluster heartbeat-interval` | `ValidateInteger(1, MaxDurationMillis)` | `> 0` | 512ns heartbeat ticker on the HA control channel. CLAUDE.md's own warning — "adding a new control socket request at >1/s will starve session installs" — with the rate set to ~2e6/s. |
| `pkg/cluster/group_state.go:168` | `chassis cluster takeover-hold-time` | `ValidateInteger(0, MaxDurationMillis)` | `> 0` | hold collapses to ~0: takeover becomes immediate where the operator asked it not to be. |
| `pkg/ipmon/ipmon.go:483,484,847` | `services ip-monitoring policy hold-down` | `ValidateInteger(0, MaxDurationSeconds)` | `hold > 0` | recovery damping collapses to ~0, so the WAN-failover route flap the hold-down exists to damp is undamped. 3 sites, one semantic. |
| `pkg/vrrp/instance_preempt.go:157` | `vrrp preempt hold-time` | `ValidateInteger(1, 3600)` | `<= 0` | preempt hold collapses to ~0 — immediate preemption of a live master, the behaviour #2082 exists to gate. |

## #8657 — config: flat-set SetPath NESTS successive modifiers, so only the first survives — same config compiles differently in the two AST shapes [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-04)

Found by lane-8526 while censusing #8597 K15. **K15's own site cannot exhibit this** — `routing-options static route next-hop` declares a single modifier — so it was invisible to the finding that led here. `system ntp server` declares four, and that is what exposes it.

## The defect

The same configuration, written in the two spellings the parser accepts, compiles to two different results:

```
FLAT-SET       set system ntp server 1.2.3.4 prefer version 4
               -> {Prefer:true  Version:0}      <- "version 4" LOST

HIERARCHICAL   server 1.2.3.4 { prefer; version 4; }
               -> {Prefer:true  Version:4}      <- both kept
```

**Exactly one modifier survives, whichever was written first.** Order decides which:

- `... 1.2.3.4 prefer version 4` keeps `Prefer`, loses `Version`
- `... 1.2.3.4 version 4 prefer` keeps `Version`, loses `Prefer`

## Root cause: the AST shape, not the compiler's read

`SetPath` **nests** each successive modifier under the previous one rather than making them siblings:

```
[server 1.2.3.4]
  [prefer]
    [version 4]        <- a CHILD of prefer, not a sibling of it
```

The compiler scans siblings, so it sees only the first modifier and everything after it is unreachable. The compiler's read is correct for the shape it is given; the shape is wrong.

## Why this is its own row and not part of #8597 K15

- **Different root cause.** K15 is a missing validation diagnostic (a trailing modifier with no value is accepted and dropped). This is an AST construction defect.
- **Different severity.** K15 silently drops a modifier the operator typed incompletely. This silently drops a **completely and correctly specified** modifier, on the `set` path — which is also the config-sync path between cluster nodes.
- **Different change.** Fixing K15 (arity-aware rejection) does not fix this, and fixing this does not fix K15.

## Class

This is the dual-shape divergence class `CLAUDE.md` warns about under "Parser Dual AST Shape" and that #8436 spent six batches on. This leaf was explicitly set aside during #8436 as "NOT that shape and needs its own reading" — that call was right, for a reason not yet known at the time.

## #8660 — policy-scheduler shutdown join can still block on a wedged apply: the tick acquires applySem with the production-uncancelled daemonCtx [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-04)

Split out of #8597 (muse-004 K23) under that issue's splitting criterion (3): this needs a decision about ownership, not a bound.

## What the K23 fix did and did not do

`stopPolicySchedulerLoop` acquired `applySem` with `context.Background()`. On the shutdown path, with an apply wedged, it never returned: the scheduler was never cancelled, shutdown never reached HA relinquish, and systemd's `TimeoutStopSec` SIGKILLed the process — no `rg_active` clear, no priority-0 advert, no RA goodbye.

That acquire is now bounded by `applyCloseoutDrainTimeout`, matching the rule `daemon_run_shutdown.go` already states at its own drain.

**It is a partial fix, and the code and `pkg/daemon/README.md` both say so.**

## The residual

`stopPolicySchedulerLoop` ends in `d.schedulerWg.Wait()`. The goroutine it joins is the scheduler's `Run`, whose tick calls `publishPolicyScheduleState`, which acquires `applySem` with **`d.daemonCtx`**.

`d.daemonCtx` is the RAW parent. `daemon_run.go` says so twice — *"d.daemonCtx is the RAW parent (production: context.Background)"* and *"d.daemonCtx stays the (production-uncancelled, ...)"*. So in production it is never cancelled, and `d.schedulerCancel()` — which cancels a CHILD of it created in `startPolicySchedulerLoopLocked` — does not release a tick parked on that acquire.

Net: if a tick is already mid-publish when an apply wedges, the join still blocks behind the same wedged apply. The bound moves the stall from one line to the next in that specific interleaving.

**The finding's own prescribed fix asserted otherwise** — *"the join is already safe: the tick blocks on applySem acquire with the daemon ctx, which is cancelled"*. That sentence is false for production; it would be true if the acquire used the scheduler's own ctx.

## Why this is a decision and not a patch

The obvious repair is for `publishPolicyScheduleState` to acquire with the scheduler's ctx, so `schedulerCancel()` releases the parked tick. Getting there is an ownership change, not a bound:

- `scheduler.NewPrimed` takes `updateFn func(map[string]bool) error` — no ctx.
- The closure is built in `reconcile` (`daemon_scheduler.go`), BEFORE `startPolicySchedulerLoopLocked` creates the ctx it would need to capture.
- Stashing the ctx on the `Daemon` and reading it from the tick introduces a read that is not covered by the lock discipline the surrounding fields use — `schedulerCancel` is guarded by `applySem`, which is exactly the thing the parked tick is waiting on.

So there are at least three shapes, and they differ in what they cost:

1. **Thread a ctx through `scheduler`'s updateFn signature.** Cleanest; touches `pkg/scheduler`'s public shape and every other updateFn.
2. **Give the daemon a separately-guarded scheduler-ctx holder** (its own mutex or an atomic), read by the tick. Local; adds a second synchronisation domain beside `applySem` for related state.
3. **Bound the tick's acquire too**, so it gives up and retries next tick. Smallest; makes a publish droppable, which interacts with the #3780 retry latch and the #5669 fail-closed semantics.

Whoever takes this should pick one deliberately. Please do not "fix" it by widening the timeout.

## What is already covered

`pkg/daemon/scheduler_stop_bounded_8597_test.go` pins the bounded acquire, that a timed-out stop does NOT release a permit it never took (releasing on a weight-1 semaphore admits a second holder alongside the wedged apply), and that the call still reaches the cancel after a timeout. None of those cells covers the residual above — they cannot, because reproducing it needs a tick parked inside the real scheduler goroutine.

## #8662 — brace-elided hierarchical text is silently dropped for some named instances (zone interfaces, CoS transmit-rate) — and the blanket gate rejects the shipped HA config [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-04)

Split out of #8597 (muse-004 K16). The finding's **mechanism is real for two of the spellings it names and false for the others**, and its prescribed fix — reject any named-instance node carrying Keys past its identity — was implemented, measured, and **rejects the project's own shipped HA cluster config**. Filing the measurement rather than the patch.

## The real half

Junos accepts brace-elided hierarchical text. `walkInstanceChildren` documents what happens to it:

> Any extra tokens packed into the instance node's Keys beyond the name are ignored (the compiler does not compile them...)

For two containers that is exactly true, and the consequence is a silent drop on a commit that reports success. Measured at HEAD by compiling both spellings and comparing the compiled config:

| spelling | elided result | braced result |
|---|---|---|
| `security-zone trust interfaces ge-0/0/0.0;` | **commits clean, zone has 0 interfaces, no warning** | strict commit REJECTS ("references interface ... which is not defined") |
| `class-of-service { schedulers be transmit-rate 1g; }` | **transmit-rate = 0** | transmit-rate = 125000000 |

The zone case is the worse of the two, and not only because zone membership is security-relevant: **the elided form walks past the strict gate that exists to catch exactly its content.** The braced form is rejected at commit; the elided form is accepted, and the zone boots with no members.

## The false half — and why the obvious fix cannot ship

The finding generalises to "every instance compiler reads only Children". Measured, that is not so:

| spelling | elided | braced | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| `firewall ... filter F term T from protocol tcp;` | 1 term | 1 term | **read** |
| `policy-options ... term t1 then accept;` | `accept` | `accept` | **read** |
| `chassis cluster redundancy-group 0 node 0 priority 200;` | read (see below) | read | **read** |

The last one is decisive. That packed one-liner is what the **shipped HA cluster config uses**, and `compiler_validate_strict_chassis.go` says so in its own words: *"`node 0 priority <v>;` carries the value inside the node instance's own key tail, which the schema walker consumes as identity and never validates — compileChassis still reads it into NodePriorities."*

I implemented the prescribed gate (reject a non-compound named instance carrying Keys past its identity, restricted to tails whose first token names a child of that container) and ran the suites. **16 cells fail**, including:

- `TestShippedHAClusterConfigPassesCommitCheck8280` — the config this repo ships no longer commits.
- `TestSchemaValidate_ChassisCluster_DeployedConfigShapeAccepted`
- `TestFusedStatementGateDoesNotCondemnValidTrailingTokens_8437`, `TestLoginPathPackedCommitCheckOverReach_6706`, `TestNATScopeOnlyRuleStillCommits_8430`, `TestCommunityValidMembersStillCommit_8449` — four existing **over-reach controls**, doing exactly the job they were written for.

## #8664 — flaky: pkg/ipmon/TestNotifyNextHopChangeGate fails intermittently under full-suite load (2 sightings) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-04)

Reported by a lane after a second sighting. Filing so it has an owner before the re-run-and-move-on reflex sets in — an intermittent gate failure gets cheaper to dismiss every time it happens, and this one has now cost two lanes a diversion each.

## Observed

`pkg/ipmon/TestNotifyNextHopChangeGate` fails intermittently, twice so far (once during #8629 work, once during #8663). Both times:

- failed inside a full `go test ./...`
- **passed on an immediate re-run** of the same full suite
- **passed 5x in isolation**
- the lane's tree had **no Go changes** either time

The first sighting was attributed to a polluted working tree (a foreign stash). **That attribution was wrong** — it recurred with a clean tree, so the earlier explanation should not be reused.

Counter-data: three full-suite runs from the orchestrator at `56ae35712`, `90fbebaab` and `7d7446fd3` were clean (77 packages, 0 FAIL each). So it is genuinely intermittent, not head-specific.

## Likely mechanism — the test mixes two idioms, and only one is load-fragile

`pkg/ipmon/nexthop_test.go:185`. The timings are `debounce = 5ms`, `throttle = 5ms`, and the test uses **two different waiting styles**:

**Robust — polls to a deadline:**

```go
deadline := time.Now().Add(2 * time.Second)
for actuations.Load() == base && time.Now().Before(deadline) {
    time.Sleep(5 * time.Millisecond)
}
```

**Fragile — fixed sleep, then assert something HAS happened:**

```go
failWAN(e)
time.Sleep(40 * time.Millisecond)
base := actuations.Load()
if base == 0 {
    t.Fatal("probe failure did not actuate")
}
```

Under full-suite parallelism a 40 ms budget covering debounce + throttle + goroutine scheduling is not generous, and the assertion fires immediately at the end of it. The poll-to-deadline form above cannot fail this way; the fixed-sleep form can. That asymmetry matches the reported signature exactly — fails only under `./...` load, never in isolation.

## #8667 — nat64: prefix gate describes a failure mode #3888 removed; /+96 rejected at commit but installed by the dataplane [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-04)

## Summary

A NAT64 rule-set prefix carrying a leading `+` in its mask (`64:ff9b::/+96`) is **rejected at commit, warned about on the tolerant load path, and then installed and actively translating in the dataplane**. The control plane tells the operator the rule is inert; the dataplane is running it.

Found while resolving #8597 K62. The grammar divergence itself was known; what was wrong was my conclusion that it was unreachable — that was a commit-path argument, and the commit path does not bound what reaches the dataplane.

## Measured end to end

| stage | result |
|---|---|
| strict commit | **REJECTED** — `must be an IPv6 prefix of length /96` |
| `Store.Load` / `Store.SyncApply` (lenient) | prefix retained **verbatim**; one warning emitted |
| Rust `Nat64State::from_snapshots` | **rule INSTALLED**, `prefix_bytes = 00:64:ff:9b:00…` (`64:ff9b::`), active |
| same loader, `/64` (control) | `is_active=false`, `0` prefixes — the loader *does* reject bad lengths |

The control matters: acceptance is specific to the `+`, not a broken probe.

## Root cause

Two independent parsers for the same token, disagreeing on exactly one character class:

- **Go** (`pkg/config/compiler_validate_strict_nat.go`) validates with `strconv.ParseUint(parts[1], 10, 8)` — **permits no sign**.
- **Rust** (`userspace-dp/src/nat64.rs`) validates with `parts[1].parse::<u8>()` — **permits a leading `+`**.

Swept exhaustively over all 7,240 strings of length ≤3 from `[0-9 + - _ space x X . e E]`: **110** tokens are accepted by Rust and rejected by Go — every one a leading `+`; **0** the other way; **0** value disagreements.

The Go comment directly above that check says it must *"Mirror the Rust loader `Nat64State::from_snapshots` **EXACTLY**"*. It does not.

## Why it is not caught

`validateNAT64PrefixStrict(cfg, lenient)` takes a lenient flag. On the tolerant path `emit()` appends a warning and returns nil, and the loop `continue`s — **the rule is not dropped and not zeroed**, so `NAT64RuleSnapshot.prefix` carries `/+96` through to the helper.

## The false claim

The warning emitted on that path reads:

> …on a userspace-dataplane apply/preflight the helper's `Nat64State::try_from_snapshots` rejects the whole forwarding snapshot and the previous live state is kept, so this rule — and every later config change — **will not reach the dataplane until it is corrected**

For this input every clause of that is false. This is the part I would fix first regardless of the direction chosen for the behaviour: a warning that asserts non-delivery while the rule is live is worse than no warning, because it actively redirects the operator away from the running config.

## #8699 — config: a re-opened named block is REJECTED at strict commit but silently split on the lenient load path, discarding the second block's contents [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-04)

Found while lane-8526 was building #8662's fixture sweep, and **verified independently at `e53100d7e`** with a control, because the original report did not distinguish the two compile paths and the distinction turns out to be the finding.

## Measured

Source:

```
protocols {
    bgp {
        group g1 { type external; neighbor 10.0.0.1 { peer-as 65001; } }
        group g1 { description d1; }
    }
}
```

| path | result |
|---|---|
| `CompileConfig` (strict commit) | **REJECTED** — `duplicate bgp group "g1": each block is compiled independently with its own state … the config is silently split, not merged — author it once (#5180)` |
| `CompileConfigLenient` (`Store.Load` / `SyncApply`) | **`err = nil`**, and the neighbour compiles with `description=""` |

Control, same tree authored as one block: `neighbor=10.0.0.1 group="g1" description="d1"`.

So the strict path is **correctly protective and its error message is excellent** — it names the mechanism and prescribes the fix. The defect is that the tolerant ingress does not share it.

## Why this is a defect and not the #1319 doctrine working

`compileTreeLenient` deliberately downgrades rather than blackout-booting a node on a stale persisted config, and that doctrine is right. But here the outcome is not "accept a value an older binary allowed" — it is **accept a structure the commit gate has never allowed, and silently discard part of it.**

The population that reaches this path is named in the code itself: a leniently-loaded persisted config, or an **HA peer-synced** one. So a node can boot, or a standby can accept a sync, with a group's `description` — or anything else authored in a re-opened block — silently absent, while the config it was compiled from is one no operator could have committed.

This is the same shape as #8667 (`/+96` rejected at commit, installed and translating on the lenient path), and it is the third instance today of the strict/lenient pair diverging in a way that loses data.

## Relationship to #8436

#8436 ("duplicate hierarchical named blocks have SIX different reduction rules") is **closed**, by #8609. Its closing comment records that its census reported `SILENT = 0` over **29 CHECKED of 49 named containers, with 20 SKIPPED** — and that hand-checking five of the skips found a real defect at `services rpm probe <p> test <t>`.

This is not a claim that #8436 was closed wrongly: its conservation property was bound on the strict path, which is where it was scoped. It is that **the tolerant path was not in that scope**, and a guard bound on one of a pair says nothing about the other.

## #8725 — config: re-opened named blocks are not merged — deferred by decision, but the cost is now measured three times [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-05)

Filing a **deferred decision** whose cost has now been measured three times by three lanes, so it stops living in issue comments and becomes something that can be decided on the merits.

## The behaviour

A re-opened named block is **not merged**. Junos merges it; this compiler compiles each block independently:

```
group g1 { neighbor N; }
group g1 { description d1; }
  ->  neighbour present, description EMPTY
```

Strict commit **rejects** this with a good message (#5180, naming the mechanism and the fix). The tolerant path **warns** — verified across seven containers: where data is lost both paths report it, and where they are silent nothing is lost. **So this is not a silent-data-loss bug.** #8699 was filed on that premise and closed as refuted.

## Why it is still open as a decision

Because **not merging blocks measurement**, and three independent investigations have now hit it:

| # | lane | what it blocked |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | #8697 fixture sweep | ~150 "thin fixture" sites in #8690's census cannot be probed: supplying a required sibling *inside* a stanza needs the instance re-opened, and the second block's contents are discarded. The mechanism was **built, measured at zero effect, and removed** rather than landed |
| 2 | #8690 `PreservesCompiledResult` audit | **18 sites the normalizer pass rewrites that its guard cannot examine** — each needs a required sibling the compact spelling cannot carry. Production is normalizing those today with no guard coverage |
| 3 | #8690 unruled-population work | same dependency, reached from the other direction |

**The compounding effect is the point.** #8690's "186 remaining sites" is a **floor, not a count** — the drop-shape markers only answer for sites that registered at all, and ~255 never registered. Every per-family number quoted during that sweep rests on a census that cannot see a third of its own population, for this reason.

## Why it was deferred, and why that still holds

Merging on the lenient path would, **on the next reload, add content that has never been in effect on that box.**

The configs carrying re-opened blocks predate #5180's check or were hand-edited — so those nodes have been running *with the split* for as long as they have loaded that file. Merging trades a silent loss for a **silent gain**, which is the worse direction on a reload, and the population reaching that path includes **HA peer-synced** configs. A box that was forwarding one way before an upgrade and another way after is precisely what the #1319/#1960 tolerant-load doctrine exists to prevent.

That argument has not weakened. What has changed is that the **cost of not deciding** is now measured rather than hypothesised.

## What a decision needs

1. **Scope**: strict path, tolerant path, or a merge used only by test fixtures. The third is the cheapest way to unblock measurement without changing any running box, and it should be considered before the other two.
2. **Blast radius**: which containers change compiled output under merging, measured rather than reasoned — the #8436 census already enumerates 49 named containers and records 20 it could not check.
3. **A cluster smoke** if either production path changes; this reaches the forwarding snapshot.
4. **An agreement cell** binding whichever paths are supposed to behave alike, failing on divergence in **either** direction.

## #8752 — config: a repeated `policy <p>` statement duplicates rather than merging, and the duplicate wins on the tolerant load path [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-05)

A second `policy <p> …` statement inside the same from-zone block does not merge
into the first — it creates a **second policy with the same name**, and on the
tolerant load path that second policy wins.

Measured on the LENIENT path, which is what `Store.Load` (boot-time load of the
persisted active config) and `Store.SyncApply` (HA peer sync) use
(`configstore/store.go`):

```
policy p1 { match { source-address any; destination-address any; application any; }
            then { permit; } }
policy p1 scheduler-name S;

-> pol#1  sched=""   src=[any]  PERMIT    the operator's policy, schedule LOST
-> pol#2  sched=""   src=[]     DENY      spurious match-less duplicate
```

The braced reference spelling compiles to a single policy with `sched="S"` and
its match intact, so the duplicate statement is the entire difference.

## Why this is not a brace-elision defect

It was found underneath #8690 and deliberately excluded there. #8690's normalizer
folds a packed tail back into its stanza; admitting this pair moves the tail into
the **duplicate's** body:

```
with the pair admitted:  pol#1 sched=""   src=[any] PERMIT   <- still scheduleless
                         pol#2 sched="S"  src=[]    DENY     <- schedule lands here

## #8763 — config: the brace-elision pass never traverses into a braced multi-key container, so `family inet { filter input f4; }` is unreachable to any scope entry [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-05)

The brace-elision normalizer **never traverses into a braced multi-key
container**, so an elided statement inside `family inet { … }` is unreachable to
it. Not "declines to fold" — never asks.

Verified at master with **every pair admitted** (`compactNormalizeInScope`
patched to return true unconditionally and record what it was asked):

```
family inet { filter input f4; }       folds=0  filterInV4=""    asked=[]
family inet filter input f4;           folds=3  filterInV4="f4"  asked=[(family,inet) (inet,filter) (filter,input)]
family inet { filter { input f4; } }   folds=0  filterInV4="f4"  asked=[]     <- reference
```

The middle row is the one-liner the #8690 scope work operates on. The top row is
the same drop in a different spelling, and **admit-all does not fix it**, so no
scope entry ever can.

## Mechanism

For a braced node with `Keys=[family inet]`, `normalizeCompactNodes` takes
`kw = Keys[0]` = `"family"` and recurses with `schema.children["family"]`. But
the node's children belong to `family inet`, whose schema is
`family.children["inet"]`. **The recursion advances the schema one level where
the node advanced two**, so every lookup beneath a braced multi-key container
misses and the subtree is never visited.

It does not bite `unit 0`, where the second token is an instance **arg** consumed
by `identity`. It bites exactly where the second token is a **child keyword** —
`family inet` and `family inet6`.

## Why it matters beyond a missed optimisation

Two spellings of the same intent are both natural in a hand-written config, a
`load override` payload, or a peer config-sync push:

```
family inet filter input f4;        one-liner                        -> reachable by a scope entry
family inet { filter input f4; }    braced family, elided statement  -> unreachable, permanently
```

## #8768 — config: the brace-elision fold recovers only the FIRST statement of a multi-statement packed tail, and swallows the rest [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-05)

### The brace-elision fold recovers only the FIRST statement of a multi-statement packed tail

Found while measuring the blast radius of a fix for #8763. **This is live on
master today**, independent of that fix.

`normalizeCompactNodes` folds a packed tail by moving **the whole remaining key
run** into one child node:

```go
tail := append([]string(nil), node.Keys[identity:]...)
node.Keys = append([]string(nil), node.Keys[:identity]...)
node.Children = append(node.Children, &Node{Keys: tail, IsLeaf: true})
```

That is correct when the tail is one statement. A packed run may hold several,
and then every statement after the first is swallowed into the first one's Keys.

**Measured on master, `security ike policy <p>`:**

```
BRACED reference                              psk="<redacted>"  mode="main"
PACKED `policy p1 pre-shared-key ascii-text SEKRIT mode main;`
    pass ON                                   psk="<redacted>"  mode=""
    pass OFF                                  psk=""            mode=""
```

Resulting tree with the pass on:

```
policy p1
  [pre-shared-key ascii-text SEKRIT mode main]      <- one node, `mode main` inside it
```

**The pass is a net improvement here and is not the defect** — it recovers the
PSK that was previously lost entirely. But `mode main` is silently dropped in
both spellings, so the site is only half-fixed, and the inventory reports it as
resolved because the compiled result now differs from the empty stanza.

Same shape under `snmp trap-group <t> targets 10.0.0.1 version v2;` — `version
v2` is swallowed into the `targets` node.

A firewall filter's `from traffic-class` match criterion is **silently lost** in
the brace-elided spelling, while its sibling criteria in the identical position
read correctly.

Verified at master `a0295cef4`:

```
firewall { family inet { filter f1 { term t1 { <BODY> then accept; } } } }

BODY                          folds   protocols   dscps
from traffic-class 0;           0        []        []      <- VALUE LOST
from { traffic-class 0; }       0        []        [0]     <- kept
from protocol tcp;              0      [tcp]       []      <- control: elided WORKS
from { protocol tcp; }          0      [tcp]       []
```

**The control is the finding.** `from protocol tcp;` and `from traffic-class 0;`
are the same shape in the same container — a packed criterion inside a filter
term. The compiler reads the packed form of `protocol` natively and does not read
the packed form of `traffic-class`. So this is not a fold or traversal issue:
`folds=0` for both, the brace-elision pass is not involved, and the difference is
in how the compiler consumes the term body.

`traffic-class` is a **match criterion on a firewall filter term**. Losing it does
not fail the commit and emits no warning — the term simply matches on one fewer
dimension than the operator wrote, which by the #3044 reasoning already recorded
in this codebase means the term is **wider than intended**: a permit matches
traffic it should not, a discard drops traffic it should not.

the pass does not need to reach, so:

- the traversal defect (#8763) does not cause it and fixing that will not fix it;

## #8781 — config: a firewall filter's `from next-header` protocol match is silently dropped in the packed spelling, so an IPv6 term matches every protocol [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-05)

`from next-header` is the CORRECT Junos spelling of the protocol match in a `family inet6` firewall filter. `compileFilterFrom` handles it (`case "protocol", "next-header":`), but the schema does not declare it under `from` in either family.

The packed reader resolves its tail through the schema (`packedBodyChildren` -> `resolveSchemaChild`) and returns the node's children unchanged when the lookup fails, so the criterion is dropped — silently, and only in the packed spelling. Measured, with `from protocol` as a control that works in both spellings:

```
inet6  from { next-header tcp; }   protos=[tcp]     <- braced: applied
inet6  from next-header tcp;       protos=[]        <- packed: SILENTLY DROPPED
inet   from { next-header tcp; }   protos=[tcp]
inet   from next-header tcp;       protos=[]
CONTROL inet from { protocol tcp; } / from protocol tcp;   protos=[tcp] / [tcp]
```

Both spellings COMMIT CLEANLY on the strict path.

## Why this is worse than #8773

#8773 was the same mechanism, but the dropped criterion was a CROSS-FAMILY spelling — a configuration Junos would reject anyway. Here `next-header` in `family inet6` is what Junos tells operators to write. A correctly-authored IPv6 filter term, written in the packed spelling, loses its protocol match entirely and therefore matches EVERY protocol.

That is the failure direction `docs/config-schema.md` already names for this class: *"a filter term whose `from` was dropped matches EVERYTHING (#7457)"*. A term intended to accept TCP accepts everything; a term intended to discard TCP discards everything.

## Reachability

The packed spelling is not what the CLI produces — `ParseSetCommand` + `SetPath` builds a real child node, so a `set` session is unaffected. It reaches a running system the way this whole class does: a hand-edited configuration file, one written by an older build, or an HA peer push — the population `Store.Load` and `Store.SyncApply` exist to accept.

## How it was found

Census of the #8773 class rather than a fresh observation: enumerate every keyword a compiler switch arm handles, and check whether the schema declares it at that path. Any keyword the compiler names but the schema does not is a leaf whose packed spelling is inert. `from next-header` is the only surviving member for the firewall `from`/`then` arms; `then next` was a candidate that measured clean (both spellings agree, both leave Action empty).

## Suggested fix

The #8773 shape: declare `next-header` under `from` in both families so the packed reader can resolve it, with a commit advisory for the cross-family case (`next-header` under `family inet` is the IPv6 spelling, as `traffic-class` there is). Both halves — declaring alone would make the spellings agree silently, and the advisory alone would not stop the drop.

## #8785 — security ike policy|proposal description commits clean and is stored nowhere — modelling the leaf does not fix it [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-05)

## `security ike policy|proposal description` commits clean and is stored nowhere — and modelling the leaf does NOT fix it

Split out of a sizing question on #4313. **The broad half of that question is already answered and closed** — see "Not a duplicate of #4313" below.

### Measured

```
set security ike proposal pr1 description hello   SchemaValidate=OK  commit=OK  IKEProposal compiled (n=1)
set security ike policy   p1  description hello   SchemaValidate=OK  commit=OK  IKEPolicy   compiled (n=1)
```

Both commit clean. Neither stores the text:

- `security ike proposal` **DOES** model `description` in `setSchema` (`schema_security.go`), and `IKEProposal` has **no `Description` field**.
- `security ike policy` does **not** model it, and `IKEPolicy` has **no `Description` field**.

**The two cases are indistinguishable in outcome.** An operator's `description` is accepted at commit and silently inert in both.

### Why this is worth its own issue: the obvious remedy is refuted by the tree

The natural fix for the unmodelled case is "declare the leaf in `setSchema`". **`ike proposal` already has that fix and it changes nothing** — the value still has nowhere to go. So the remedy is three parts, not one:

1. declare the leaf in `setSchema`,
2. add the field to the typed struct,
3. read it in the compiler.

`ike proposal` has (1) and lacks (2) and (3). A PR doing only (1) for `ike policy` would look correct, pass a schema test, and leave the defect exactly where it is — with a green cell certifying it.

### What NOT to do

**Do not flip `closedWorld` on these containers.** `description` is valid Junos here (it is modelled on the sibling `proposal` containers, which is our own evidence that it was believed valid). Closing the subtree would hard-reject working config — the #4191 class that `docs/config-schema.md` records as the reason blanket closure was rejected. **Model-then-close is the supported order; close-first breaks configs.**

Note also that `ike proposal` is `closedWorld: true` **and** models `description` — so the flip there was done correctly, and the gap that remains is (2)+(3), not the world flag.

### Not a duplicate of #4313

#4313 — *"config schema is opt-in — unmodeled Junos leaves commit clean and are silently inert"* — is **CLOSED as COMPLETED**: the `closedWorld` mechanism shipped and the high-risk security/reachability subtrees were flipped. Open-world for un-flipped subtrees is the shipped doctrine, not an oversight, and re-filing it would duplicate a closed root cause.

Production `closedWorld: true` declarations are now **18** (excluding comments and tests), up from the **10** its closing comment recorded at `dd23119aa`, so the per-subtree flips have continued as intended.

## #8787 — Census: compiler-named leaves setSchema never declares — 22 keywords, 4 confirmed silent drops (generator of the #8781 class) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-05)

## Census: leaves the COMPILER names that `setSchema` never declares — 22 keywords, 4 confirmed silent drops

The generator of the #8781 class. A compiler `switch` matching a keyword the schema does not declare is a leaf that resolves to nothing in the **packed** spelling, so its value is dropped silently. #8781 (`next-header`) is one instance; this is the class.

### Method

- **Declared set:** walked the LIVE `setSchema` at runtime, not the source, so it cannot drift from it. **760** distinct keywords.
- **Compiler set:** `go/ast` over every non-test, non-`schema*` file in `pkg/config`, collecting string case-literals from the **144** switches whose tag is a call to `.Name()` — i.e. dispatching on a config node's keyword rather than on a value.
- **Report:** compiler keywords absent from the declared set.

### Positive control

`next-header` **must** appear: `compiler_firewall.go:994` matches `case "protocol", "next-header":` and `setSchema` declares it nowhere. The cell `t.Fatal`s if it is missing — a census that finds nothing is indistinguishable from one that never ran.

### An instrument bug that halved the count, recorded because the wrong number was ready to publish

The first run reported **50** undeclared keywords. Spot-checking flagged entries against schema source found `lease-time` and `keepalive` **are** declared — false positives.

Cause: `schemaNode` carries both `children` and a **`wildcard`** child, and named-instance subtrees (`interfaces <name> …`) hang off `wildcard`. A `children`-only walk reports `interfaces` as having **zero** children and every keyword beneath it as undeclared. Walking both gives 760 declared (was 691) and **22** hits (was 50). The surviving 22 were re-spot-checked against schema source.

### Confirmed by compiling BOTH spellings

"Not declared" and "dropped" are separate claims; these are the ones where both were measured. Three outcomes, not two — a loud rejection is **not** a silent drop:

| keyword | braced | packed | verdict | reachable from flat `set`? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `next-header` (firewall inet6 `from`) | `[tcp]` | `[]` | **SILENT DROP** | — (#8781, already filed) |
| `routing-instances instance-type` | `vrf` / `forwarding` | *no instance at all* | **SILENT DROP** | **No** — flat `set` compiles correctly |
| `snmp location` | `rack 4` | `` | **SILENT DROP** | not measured |
| `snmp contact` | `ops` | `` | **SILENT DROP** | not measured |
| `tcp-mss all-tcp` | `1350` | rejected | **REJECTED LOUDLY** (fail-closed, safe) | — |
| `tcp-mss gre-in` | `1350` | rejected | **REJECTED LOUDLY** (fail-closed, safe) | — |

### Ranked by consequence

1. **`next-header`** — widens an inet6 filter term to every protocol. Firewall fail-open. Already #8781.
2. **`routing-instances instance-type`** — the whole instance vanishes in the brace-elided spelling. The harmful direction is `forwarding`: `InstanceType == "forwarding"` is what makes the daemon SKIP VRF creation (`daemon_apply_interfaces.go`), so a dropped value creates a VRF the operator asked not to have and moves interfaces into it. **Reachable from a loaded config file, NOT from `set`** — so a CLI-authored config is unaffected and a hand-written or peer-synced one is not.
3. **`snmp location` / `snmp contact`** — documentation-only. Cosmetic.

## #8792 — cluster-sync: persistent-NAT lease decoder allocates from an unvalidated wire count (4-byte frame requests 448 GiB) before any bounds check [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-05)

A **4-byte frame from any host reachable on an unkeyed HA control segment kills
xpfd unrecoverably**, repeatably across reconnects, on both nodes. Verified
end-to-end at master `b0f3aba21`.

Split out of the #8791 triage because it should not wait on that plan converging —
the fix is a two-line clamp on a cold path.

## The defect

`pkg/cluster/sync_persistent_nat_lease_8121.go:112`

```go
func decodePersistentNatLeasePayload(buf []byte) ([]userspace.IdleLeaseWire, bool) {
	if len(buf) < 4 {
		return nil, false
	}
	count := int(binary.LittleEndian.Uint32(buf))
	off := 4
	out := make([]userspace.IdleLeaseWire, 0, count)   // <-- allocation BEFORE any bounds check
	for i := 0; i < count; i++ {
		if off+4 > len(buf) {                          // <-- the check, one line too late
			return out, false
```

`count` comes straight off the wire. Every truncation check happens *after* the
`make`.

## Why it is fatal, and why `len=0` does not save it

The obvious refutation is that `make` with a huge **capacity** but zero **length**
touches no pages, so Linux overcommit hands out the mapping harmlessly. **That is
wrong.** `sizeof(IdleLeaseWire)` measured at **112 bytes**, so `ff ff ff ff` asks
for `112 × 4294967295 = 481,036,337,040 bytes = 448.0 GiB`. Measured on a host
with `overcommit_memory=0` and 131 GB RAM:

```
attempting make([]wire, 0, 4294967295) = 481036337040 bytes
fatal error: runtime: out of memory
runtime.sysMapOS(0x370643800000, 0x7000000000, ...)
```

## #8796 — config: an IKE gateway's packed body silently drops `local-identity`, so the tunnel negotiates under the wrong peer identity [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-05)

A member of the #8787 census (compiler-named leaves the schema mis-declares), and the security instance of it.

An IKE gateway whose body is written as a PACKED TAIL silently loses `local-identity` — and, depending on statement order, everything else too. Measured against the braced spelling as reference:

```
braced   gateway gw1 { ... local-identity hostname foo; }        local=hostname/foo  ext=ge-0/0/0
packed   gateway gw1 local-identity hostname foo;                local=""/""         ext=""
packed   gateway gw1 local-identity hostname foo
                     external-interface ge-0/0/0;                local=""/""         ext=""
packed   gateway gw1 external-interface ge-0/0/0
                     local-identity hostname foo;                local=""/""         ext=ge-0/0/0
```

All of them COMMIT CLEANLY on the strict path. `remote-identity` has the identical shape and the identical defect.

## Consequence

An IKE gateway compiled with no local identity does not fail closed. strongSwan falls back to the local address, so the tunnel negotiates under a **different peer identity than the operator configured** — it authenticates as the wrong party or not at all. Where the whole tail is lost the gateway also loses its address, policy and external interface.

## The symptom is ORDER-DEPENDENT, which is the useful clue

`external-interface` before `local-identity` compiles the external interface and drops the identity; the reverse order drops both. The first leaf in the tail decides whether the normalising pass fires at all, because the pass is admitted per (container, leaf) PAIR — `inScope(gateway, external-interface)` is true and `inScope(gateway, local-identity)` is false.

## Three decisions, not one

Measured, each shown load-bearing by mutation:

| decision | controls | state before |
|---|---|---|
| pair admitted to `compactNormalizeInScope` | **whether** the tail folds | `gateway local-identity` / `gateway remote-identity` absent, while every other value-bearing gateway leaf is present |
| `packedStatements: true` on the container | **how** the folded tail splits | not set on either `gateway` container |
| `args: 2` on the identity leaves | where the statement **ends** | absent, while the compiler reads `Keys[1]` and `Keys[2]` and the description says "type and value" |

**Declaring the arity alone is INERT** — measured byte-identical output — because nothing folds without the admission. A fix that changes only the arity would measure as correct on a harness that forces the other two and would change nothing shipped.

And the arity hypothesis is refuted outright by a control: two `args`-declared siblings in one packed tail (`external-interface ge-0/0/0 ike-policy pol1`) also lost the second statement, so the missing arity cannot be the whole cause — the tail was building a CHAIN, each statement nested under the previous.

## #8797 — config: `forwarding-options family inet6 mode` commits clean and is read by nothing — identical to the statement being absent [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-05)

`set forwarding-options ... family inet6 mode <value>` commits successfully and
**compiles identically to the statement being absent, in every spelling.**
Nothing reads it.

Found while measuring the 30 newly-activated pairs for #8763, by an instrument
that compiles a **baseline with the statement removed** alongside the braced and
elided forms. Two-way `packed == braced` checks call this a clean pass, because
both spellings deliver the same nothing.

```
braced          == baseline(statement removed)     -> the braced spelling delivers NOTHING
packet-based    == flow-based                       -> the VALUE is not read either
```

So this is not a brace-elision defect and the #8763 traversal neither caused nor
cures it. It is a leaf that is declared and accepted and has no reader — the
"declared-but-inert" class also seen in #8785 (`security ike proposal
description`, declared in the schema with no struct field to hold it).

## Why it is worth an issue rather than a note

The operator gets every signal that it worked: completion offers the leaf, `?`
help describes it, commit returns success, and `show configuration` renders it
back. Nothing anywhere says the value has no effect.

**Severity is not established here.** `mode` on an IPv6 forwarding-options
family is plausibly a forwarding-behaviour selector, in which case an operator
choosing `packet-based` and silently getting whatever the default path does is a
real behaviour difference — but that consequence has **not** been measured, only
the compile-time inertness. Whoever picks this up should establish the
consequence before assigning severity, rather than inheriting it from the shape.

## Fix direction

Either read the value in the compiler (and add the field if it is missing — note
that declaring a leaf alone changes nothing, per #8785), or reject it at commit
so the operator learns the option is unimplemented, or document it as accepted
and inert the way `access-profile` / `service-profile` already are
("parsed, not implemented" in their schema descriptions).

## #8800 — config: a packed `nat source pool` compiles with ZERO addresses while the braced spelling carries them [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-05)

A source NAT pool written in the packed spelling **compiles with zero addresses**.
Verified at master `29d9cb196`:

```
braced  security { nat { source { pool p1 { address 10.0.0.1/32; } } } }   addresses=1
packed  security { nat { source { pool p1 address 10.0.0.1/32; } } }        addresses=0
```

The commit succeeds in both cases. The packed spelling produces a named pool that
exists and contains nothing.

## What is NOT established here

**The consequence is unmeasured and should not be inferred from the shape.** A
source NAT pool with no addresses could plausibly:

* fail **closed** — a rule referencing the pool finds nothing to translate to and
  the flow is dropped; or
* fail **open** — translation is skipped and traffic egresses with its original
  (private) source address, which would be a leak rather than an outage.

**Whoever takes this must measure which**, end to end, before assigning severity.
The distinction has decided severity twice in this family already: #8778's empty
`clients` list meant allow-all (fail-open), while the manual-key IPsec SA path
turned out to warn loudly and was not a defect at all.

Also unmeasured: **flat-`set` reachability**. `set security nat source pool p1
address 10.0.0.1/32` may build a different AST shape and be unaffected — that is
the column that made `routing-instances instance-type` (#8795) a config-file-only
drop rather than an operator-facing one, and it is cheap to check.

## Context

Found while measuring the arity predicate of the #8787 census (now closed). It is
the same family as #8781 (`next-header`), #8795 (`instance-type`) and #8796
(`local-identity`): a statement that survives the braced spelling and is lost in
the packed one.

**Do not assume the remedy from the family.** Those three needed three different
fixes — a schema declaration, a compiler change, and a scope admission

## #8807 — config: build the POSITIONAL predicate #8787 deferred — predicate B is position-blind too, and #8800 is the proof [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-05)

**This is the positional predicate that #8787 deferred, not a new census.** Its closing comment states the deferral directly:

> **Not done, stated rather than implied.** The positional predicate — *"declared at position P and unread at P"* — was not built. It needs the schema position and the compiler's call path, not a keyword set. The gap is recorded here with its failing control, so the next person inherits the diagnosis instead of rediscovering that keyword-anywhere does not work. **The trigger to build it is a C hit landing on a committable security leaf; none does today.**

#8800 is the first empirical instance. It changes two things about that paragraph.

## 1. The positional blindness is not confined to predicate C

#8787 attributes keyword-anywhere failure to predicate **C** (inert leaves), which failed its own control. But predicate **B** — existence, *"the compiler names it and the schema never declares it"* — was built the same way, against a flat declared set of 760 keywords drawn from the whole live schema. It therefore has the identical blind spot, and #8800 is the proof:

`security nat source pool <p> address <a>;` compiled to a **zero-address pool**. `address` is read by the compiler at that path (since #4521) and declared nowhere under `pool`. But `address` **is** declared in several other containers — `proxy-arp interface address`, `port deterministic host address`, and others — so it is in B's declared set, and B could not report it.

**So B's "22 keywords" is complete only with respect to keywords absent from the schema *everywhere*.** Keywords declared somewhere but missing at the path the compiler reads them are invisible to it, and that set is unbounded. That scoping caveat is not currently on #8787, and the count reads as a complete existence census without it.

## 2. The stated trigger cannot fire for this shape

The trigger is *"a C hit landing on a committable security leaf."* A B-side positional miss is not a C hit, so it never arms that trigger no matter how consequential it is. #8800 itself does **not** clear the severity bar — it fails closed (strict commit rejects the empty pool, the dataplane drops rather than leaking) and flat `set` is unaffected — so this is not an argument that #8800 was urgent. It is an argument that **the trigger is keyed to the wrong predicate** and would stay unarmed through a B-side positional miss that *was* fail-open.

## 3. An extra consequence specific to the brace-elision route

#8800 arrived through the normalizer rather than through `packedBodyChildren`, and that route has a property worth building into the predicate. The pass asks `compactNormalizeInScope(container, head)` only for a head that is already a declared schema child — `isBody` is false otherwise. An undeclared head is not refused, it is **never asked about**. So:

- it appears in no pass-derived inventory, by construction, no matter how thorough that inventory is;
- **a scope entry alone can never fix it** — the remedy is two parts, declare so the pass asks and admit so it says yes, and declaring alone was measured to still compile to zero addresses.

This sits alongside #8787's two existing remedy-shape notes (the three-part declare/field/read case from #8785, and the instance-name bound that forced #8795 compiler-side) as a **fourth** distinct remedy shape in this family.

## What to build

The predicate #8787 specified: **declared at position P and unread at P**, and its converse, **read at position P and undeclared at P** — keyed on the schema position and the compiler's call path, not on a keyword set.

Two extraction hazards, both already solved on #8787 and recorded here so they are not re-hit:

1. **Walk the LIVE schema, not the source.** `schemaNode` carries both `children` and a `wildcard`, and named-instance subtrees hang off `wildcard`; a children-only walk called everything under `interfaces` undeclared and produced 56% noise. A source-regex walk is worse still — schema entries written as variable references (`"chassis": schemaChassis,`) are missed entirely by literal extraction, which I confirmed independently.
2. **Filter to true leaves, then re-run the control.** Predicate A's container false positives (`family`, `flood`, `from`, where `args: 0` is correct) took 21 to 17, and the control was re-run *after* the filter — a filter that kills the control invalidates everything downstream.

## Acceptance

A positive control that the instrument re-finds, at the commit before each fix:

```
chassis { device-map { interface [ ge-0/0/1 ge-0/0/2 ] { pci 0000:01:00.0; } } }

**The severity is set by a DIFFERENT stanza than the one carrying the defect**, and the default is the benign half:

```
unmapped-interface-policy = leave-alone   (DEFAULT)  the lost NIC is silently UNMANAGED —

                                                     name. A misconfiguration.
unmapped-interface-policy = manage-down              the lost NIC is brought DOWN and marked
                                                     ActivationPolicy=always-down. An OUTAGE.

Measuring only the default reports the mild answer. A finding whose consequence is selected by a policy elsewhere has to report the **range** and the setting that picks it.

### Why the corpus zero does not cover it

The #8794 census found **0** bracketed name-groups in 8 `.conf` + 5 `.set` shipped configs. **Those are test and doc configs.** `device-map` is the **bare-metal** deployment mode (#1956), it is opt-in, and no test config uses it — so its absence there carries almost no information about a customer config that does.

CLAUDE.md is explicit that in device-map mode **the console is the lifeline** — §9.6, no auto-`fxp0`, no bootstrap DHCP. A lost mapped NIC therefore has no in-band fallback.

## #8814 — config: the NAT pool address-range 256 cap is enforced in the compiler, so a persisted config with a large range FAILS TO LOAD [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-05)

## The defect

The 256-address cap on a NAT pool `address <low> to <high>` range is enforced **in the compiler**, so it fires on the LENIENT path as well as the strict one. That defeats the guarantee `CompileConfigLenient` exists to provide. Its own doc comment states it:

> ... so an upgraded node boots through. MUST NOT be used on the candidate-commit path: commit / commit-check use the strict `CompileConfig` so new operator edits hard-reject.

Measured on master at `5184c40fe`:

```
braced, 257 IPs   CompileConfigLenient -> FAILS TO LOAD:
                    security: nat: source: pool "p1" address range:
                    address range too large: 257 IPs (max 256)
braced, 256 IPs   CompileConfigLenient -> loads          (boundary correct)
```

Fixture: `security { nat { source { pool p1 { address 10.0.0.1/32 to 10.0.1.1/32; } } } }`

A persisted config carrying such a range does not load. The lenient path is supposed to accept it and let the strict path be the thing that rejects operator edits.

## Where it comes from

`expandAddressRange` (`pkg/config/compiler_nat_helpers.go:339`) returns an error, and `appendPoolAddresses` propagates it out of `compileNATSource`. That is a COMPILER error, not a validator one — so no `compileOpts` can downgrade it.

That is the structural half of this issue. The lenient/strict knobs in this package are consumed by validators (`compiler_uniformgates_*`, `compiler_validate_strict_*`), which receive `opts`. The security compiler chain does not: `compileSecurity(node, sec)` -> `compileNATSource(node, sec)` carries no opts at all. So there is currently **no seam** at which this cap could be made lenient-tolerant, and the same is true of every other hard error raised inside the security compiler.

## Why it surfaced now

#8800 declared `address` under the source and destination NAT pools so the brace-elided spelling stops compiling to a zero-address pool. That makes the address actually get read, which extends this pre-existing failure to a spelling that previously escaped it:

```
packed, 257 IPs   before #8800: loads (the address was DROPPED -- the #8800 defect)
                  after  #8800: FAILS TO LOAD (same cap, now reached)
```

So #8800 does not introduce this bug — it removes the accident that was hiding it for one spelling. But it does mean #8800 changes a config from loading to not loading, which is why that PR is held pending this.

## Remedy shape

Move the cap out of the compiler and into a strict NAT validator, so that:

## #8823 — security { alg ftp disable; } leaves the FTP ALG enabled — doubly-elided spelling drops disable [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-05)

## `security { alg ftp disable; }` leaves the FTP ALG ENABLED — the doubly-elided spelling drops `disable`

Found by the #8800 remedy-class sweep of `schema_security.go`. **It is NOT the #8800 class** — the distinction is the useful part.

### Measured

```
security { alg { ftp { disable; } } }   FTPDisable = true    (braced)
security { alg { ftp disable; } }       FTPDisable = true    (singly elided)
security { alg ftp disable; }           FTPDisable = FALSE   <-- the drop
set security alg ftp disable            FTPDisable = true    (flat set)
```

An operator who writes the doubly-elided form gets a commit reporting success and **an FTP ALG that is still enabled** — the opposite of what the stanza says.

### Why it is not the #8800 class

#8800's signature is an **undeclared head**: the pass never *asks* about it, because `isBody` is false. Here the pass asks and is refused:

```
security { alg ftp disable; }     pass asks ("alg","ftp")   inScope = FALSE   touched = 0
security { alg { ftp disable; } } pass asks nothing         (already nested)  touched = 0
```

`ftp` **is** a declared child of `alg`, so the head is asked about. The pair is simply not admitted to the normalizer's scope. **That makes this the ordinary #8690 unadmitted-pair class, not the declare-and-admit class.**

### The remedy is ONE half, and that was measured rather than assumed

`alg/ftp` declares **zero** children, so `disable` is undeclared one level down — which looked like a stacked two-level problem needing both declare and admit. It is not:

```
real predicate today          touched=0  FTPDisable=false
admit ("alg","ftp") ONLY      touched=1  FTPDisable=TRUE
```

Admitting the pair alone fixes it. After the fold, `ftp` gains a `disable` child node and the compiler reads it directly rather than through the schema, so the undeclared child never blocks it. **I predicted two halves and the measurement said one.**

### Reachability and severity

**Config-file-only.** Flat `set` compiles correctly, so the CLI path is unaffected; this reaches a loaded or peer-synced config file — the boot and HA-sync paths.

## #8824 — config: `set security flow tcp-mss <kind> mss <n>` is REJECTED while the braced form works — the sub-blocks are undeclared [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-05)

> **RESOLVED — and the body below has been rewritten, because what shipped is not what this issue originally described.** The original text named only the flat-`set` rejection. Measuring found a second, worse defect the text did not name, a third the text was wrong about, and a population wider than the one it scoped. Three PRs: #8834, #8835, #8837.

## What was actually wrong — three defects, not one

**1. A silent fail-open (not in the original text, and the most severe).**

`security { flow tcp-mss all-tcp 1350; }` committed clean with MSS clamping **OFF**. The operator configured a clamp, the commit succeeded, and forwarded TCP went unclamped — a PMTU blackhole on tunnels with no diagnostic.

The same stanza failed **loudly** at one elision depth and **silently** at the next. Depth alone flipped it from fail-closed to fail-open, which is why the loud symptom was reported and this one was not.

**And it was not specific to the disputed `mss` spelling.** It hit `all-tcp 1350`, `gre-in 1360` and `gre-out 1370` — the short form this project itself ships in `docs/ha-cluster.conf:140` and `test/incus/xpf-test.conf`. The affected population is "operators who write the shipped form and elide two levels", not "operators who write a contested spelling".

Cause: `inScope("flow","tcp-mss")` was false, so `[flow tcp-mss all-tcp 1350]` never folded, `compileFlow` walked an empty child list, and nothing refused it. Fixed in #8835 by one scope entry.

**2. An unparseable value silently zeroed (also not in the original text).**

`all-tcp { mss notanint; }` committed clean, clamped nothing, warned nobody — while `all-tcp notanint;` (same bad token, flat) and `all-tcp { mss 70000; }` (same braced shape, out of range) were both refused. `selectMSSToken` fell through to the flat token when the child did not parse; with no flat token to fall through to, "no value selected" was reported as "nothing configured". Fixed in #8834.

**3. The reported rejection — real, but the issue's reasoning about it was incomplete.**

`set security flow tcp-mss all-tcp mss 1350` was refused. That refusal was *deliberate*, pinned by `TestCompactLeafTCPMSSKeywordStillRejected6564` on the premise that inline `mss` is a typo. The premise is wrong, and **the disconfirming evidence was in the same instrument all along**:

```
all-tcp { mss 1350; }           ACCEPTED, compiles to 1350   <- never checked by #6564
tcp-mss { all-tcp mss 1350; }   was REJECTED
tcp-mss all-tcp mss 1350;       was REJECTED
set … all-tcp mss 1350          was REJECTED
```

If `mss` were a typo the braced form would refuse it too. It does not, so `mss` is real grammar — and CLAUDE.md's contract is that a hierarchical form and its flat-set flattening compile the same. Fixed in #8837, which replaces the #6564 cell rather than deleting it.

## Why #6564 got it wrong, which is the reusable part

Its acceptance criterion was *"compile identically in both AST shapes **OR** be rejected at commit"*. It found the half-packed form rejecting and satisfied the criterion through the **OR** branch — propagating the rejection so the two shapes would agree — without checking the third shape, which already accepted.

**Consistency achieved by levelling down: two forms made to agree by matching the broken one, with a working form a single spelling away.** An "identical or rejected" criterion is satisfiable by making everything wrong.

## Provenance of the blind spot

`compact_leaf_cohort_6564_test.go` builds every member with the container braced, so double elision is outside its model by construction — the cohort certified this stanza green throughout. Filed as #8832.

## #8825 — config: a packed `applications application-set` compiles with ZERO members while the braced spelling carries them [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-05)

## The defect

`applications application-set <name> application <member>;` — the brace-elided spelling — compiles to an application-set with **zero members**, while `application-set <name> { application <member>; }` compiles correctly.

```
BRACED   set="as1" members=[a1] unknown=[]   lenient=nil  strict=nil
PACKED   set="as1" members=[]   unknown=[]   lenient=nil  strict=REJECTS
```

Note `unknown=[]` in the packed row: the member is not even recorded in `ApplicationSet.UnknownMembers`, the field that exists to catch unrecognised member statements. It is lost before that.

## Cause — same class as #8800, found by the positional predicate

`application-set` is declared as an opaque `args: 1` leaf with `children: nil` (`schema_security.go:1416`), while `compileApplications` reads three heads under it — `application`, `application-set` and `description`. The `ApplicationSet` struct comment already states the condition:

> The schema declares `application-set` as an opaque args:1 leaf (children:nil), so the SchemaValidate walk never reaches its [members]

So the head is not a schema child, the brace-elision pass is never *asked* about the pair, and no scope entry could name it — the #8800 shape exactly.

## Severity: loud at commit, exposed only on the load path

The strict path rejects it, and the message is explicit about the consequence (#3146):

```
security policies policy "p1" match application "as1" is a defined but EMPTY
application-set (it expands to zero applications) — the policy commits but the
userspace dataplane then REFUSES to arm security policies (commit/apply split,
fail-open) — add at least one member or remove the reference
```

So an operator committing this gets a clear error. **The exposure is the lenient path**: `CompileConfigLenient` accepts it (`lenient=nil`), and that is what `Store.Load` uses so an upgraded node boots through. A config arriving by a route other than commit — a config file loaded directly, or a peer sync — would load with an empty application-set and reach the #3146 condition, where the dataplane refuses to arm security policies.

That makes it **config-file-only, like #8800**, and the existing #3146 gate is what keeps the commit path safe.

The original text treated `application`, `application-set` and `description` as one gap because they sit under one undeclared node. Measured one at a time, they are not:

## #8829 — config: InterfaceSlot cannot parse the dash-form FPC name, so node 1 resolves a RETH to node 0's member [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-05)

`InterfaceSlot` requires a `/` and returns `-1` for the dash spelling, which is
the spelling the runtime itself presents. Measured at `d79b71351`:

```
InterfaceSlot("ge-7/0/3") = 7
InterfaceSlot("ge-7-0-3") = -1     <- the runtime spelling
InterfaceSlot("ge-0/0/0") = 0
InterfaceSlot("ge-0-0-0") = -1
```

## Consequence: node 1 selects node 0's physical member

An ordinary two-member flat cluster (one fpc-0 member, one fpc-7 member),
compiled **as node 1**:

```
SLASH form   node 1 RethToPhysical = map[reth0:ge-7/0/0]    correct
DASH  form   node 1 RethToPhysical = map[reth0:ge-0-0-0]    node 0's member
```

`RethToPhysical` scores local versus peer members with the same helper. With both
members scoring the neutral `-1`, the lexical tie-break picks the first name, so
node 1 binds the RETH to the member that belongs to node 0. On the loss cluster
that name is the **fabric IPVLAN parent**, not a data-plane member.

The config is accepted with no error or warning on either path.

## Why the dash spelling reaches a config

It is not an exotic form — it is what the box calls its own interfaces.
`pkg/daemon/linksetup.go:251` names them `fmt.Sprintf("ge-%d-0-%d", fpc, idx-2)`,
so `show interfaces` and every operational surface present `ge-7-0-0`. An operator
copying a name out of operational output into configuration writes exactly the
spelling that misresolves. `validate_interface_name.go` and
`ValidateDeviceMapLogicalName` both accept it.

## Reachability, stated rather than assumed

**Every shipped cluster config uses the slash form** — `docs/ha-cluster.conf`,
`docs/ha-cluster-loss.conf`, `docs/ha-cluster-userspace.conf`,

## #8830 — config: the #8807 converse predicate has a FALSE NEGATIVE shaped like its own class — a clause that reads a value into nothing is scored as 'read' [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-05)

The #8807 converse predicate (*declared at P and unread at P*) answers "unread"
by asking whether **any `.Name()` clause at that container names the head**. It
never checks that the clause *does anything with the value*. That admits a false
negative shaped exactly like the class the predicate exists to find.

### The three cases

```
no clause at P                       -> REPORTED       (this is #8785, and why its control passes)
clause at P, value reaches a field   -> not reported   (correct)
clause at P, value reaches NOTHING   -> NOT REPORTED   (FALSE NEGATIVE -- a real defect, missed)
```

The third row is **#8785's own defect with a clause in front of it**.
`description` under `security ike proposal` is caught only because no clause
exists at all. Add a `case "description":` that assigns to a local and drops it,
and the predicate goes quiet while the value is still lost.

### Why this is worse than a documented blind spot

**The #8785 control passing is partly luck about which form #8785 took.** Had the
motivating case been the clause-that-drops variant, the control would have
failed, and the gap would have been found during the build. Had it been that
variant *and* not been used as a control, #8807 would have shipped a predicate
that cannot see its own motivating case.

So the honest statement is stronger than "the control proves sensitivity, not
soundness": **the control's success is contingent on an incidental property of the
example**, and a different example from the same class would have inverted the
result.

It is also the same failure one level up as the one that made #8787 call
`then next` clean: **checking for the existence of a read rather than for where
the value lands.** #8787 checked `Action` while `next term` sets `NextTerm`. This
predicate checks that a clause exists while the value may reach nothing. Same
error, applied to the instrument instead of the config.

## #8832 — compact_leaf_cohort_6564 models one elision level, so double elision is outside its model — it missed its own member (#8823) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-05)

## The brace-elision cohort models ONE level of elision, so it cannot see double elision — and missed its own member

`compact_leaf_cohort_6564_test.go` is the cohort built to catch brace-elision drops. **#8823 was one of its members and it stayed green through the whole defect.** This is why.

### The cohort's model, from its own header

```go
//	security { alg { dns { disable; } } }   -> child "dns" with child "disable"
//	security { alg { dns disable; } }       -> ONE leaf, Keys=["dns","disable"]
```

Every member is built from exactly three spellings:

```go
block   := compileHier6564(t, "security { alg { <proto> { disable; } } }")   // fully braced
compact := compileHier6564(t, "security { alg { <proto> disable; } }")       // SINGLY elided
flat    := compileSet6564(t, "set security alg <proto> disable")             // flat set
```

**The container is braced in all three.** The cohort's "compact leaf" is elision of the *innermost* level only, producing `Keys=["dns","disable"]`.

**Double elision — the container itself brace-elided — produces `Keys=["alg","dns","disable"]`, which is not a shape this cohort can construct.** It is not excluded and not overlooked: it is outside the model by construction. That is why #8823 was live with a green cohort cell sitting on the same stanza.

### It is not only `alg` — measured across the members

```
                          braced          singly          doubly
M1 alg dns disable        true            true            true      (ok — #8823 fixed it)
M3 prefix-list            prefixes=1      prefixes=1      prefixes=1  ok
M7 flow tcp-mss all-tcp   allTCP=1350     REJECTED        allTCP=0   *** DIFFERS ***
```

**M7 is a live silent drop.** `security { flow tcp-mss all-tcp mss 1350; }` compiles clean with **MSS clamping off**, while the braced form sets 1350. Note the asymmetry: the *singly*-elided form is loudly REJECTED and the *doubly*-elided one is silently wrong — **the same stanza fails loudly at one elision depth and silently at the next**, and only the silent one is a fail-open.

### Root cause of M7, and its relationship to #8824

```
security/flow/tcp-mss declares: []      all-tcp/gre-in/gre-out/ipsec-vpn all undeclared
doubly-elided: admit-all touched=1, asked=[flow|tcp-mss]
```

Two `security flow tcp-mss` spellings still commit clean with **MSS clamping
off**. Both are pre-existing — measured identical at `6d2b0a7c4` (before #8837)
and `0b25be04c` (after), so **not a regression from #8824's fix**, which is
verified complete on its own axes.

### Measured at `0b25be04c`

```
braced  all-tcp { msss 1350; }      ACCEPTED  allTCP=0  no warning   <- SILENT
braced  all-tcp { mss; }            ACCEPTED  allTCP=0  no warning   <- SILENT
packed  tcp-mss all-tcp msss 1350;  REJECTED  "not an integer: \"msss\""
flatset ... all-tcp msss 1350       REJECTED  "not an integer: \"msss\""
braced  all-tcp { mss 70000; }      REJECTED  "integer out of range [0..65535]"
braced  all-tcp { mss notanint; }   REJECTED  (fixed by #8835)
```

### The asymmetry is the argument

**The same typo is loud in the packed and flat spellings and silent in the braced
one.** That is the identical shape #8824 just fixed for the *value* — a stanza
failing loudly at one elision depth and silently at another — running in the
opposite direction. A config that refuses `msss` when written one way and
accepts-and-discards it when written another cannot be doing both correctly.

And `all-tcp { mss; }` is the residue of #8835's own defect class. That fix
addressed *"no value selected reported as nothing configured"* for an
**unparseable token** (`mss notanint`, now correctly refused). The **absent
token** case reaches the same end state — `allTCP=0`, clean commit, no advisory —
through the same path, and was not covered. The remedy family was enumerated by
token *content* and not by token *presence*.

### Why it matters

MSS clamping exists to stop PMTU blackholes on tunnels. A clamp that silently
does not happen is indistinguishable from one never configured, and the operator
who typed it has every reason to believe it is active. `msss` is a plausible
typo; `mss;` is a plausible truncation.

## #8839 — config: `args: 1` identity slots carry no keyValidator — 121 untyped, and a non-numeric vrrp-group id commits silently [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-05)

## The defect, measured

`vrrp-group` is declared `args: 1, placeholder: "<group-id>"` with **no `keyValidator`**. A VRRP group id must be numeric, and nothing enforces that — so an operator typing `set … vrrp-group foo` is not rejected, and the compiler silently discards the group.

Isolated, on the #7484 gate fixtures:

```
synthetic names + virtual-address    priority moves output = FALSE
real names      + virtual-address    priority moves output = TRUE
real iface + SYNTHETIC vrrp id       priority moves output = FALSE
```

The third row isolates the cause to the **group id**, not the interface name. `xa60` is type-invalid, the compiler drops the group, and every leaf under it reads as inert regardless of what prerequisite is supplied.

**This stands on its own as an operator-facing defect**, independent of any instrument: a non-numeric VRRP group id is accepted at commit and silently does nothing.

## The class, censused

The issue is not `vrrp-group`. It is **`args: 1` identity slots with no `keyValidator`** — a container whose next token names an instance, where nothing constrains what that token may be.

Measured by walking the live schema (a node is an identity slot if `args == 1` and it has children, so the arg is a name the children hang under), excluding the `groups/` mirror:

```
args:1 identity slots WITH    keyValidator:  40
args:1 identity slots WITHOUT keyValidator: 121
```

Not all 121 need one — a free-form `<name>` legitimately has no constraint. The subset whose placeholder names a **constrained type** is the actionable core:

| placeholder | count |
|---|---|
| `<interface-name>` | 11 |
| `<level>` | 7 |
| `<address>` | 5 |
| `<group-id>` | 3 |
| `<prefix>` | 2 |
| `<interface>` | 2 |
| *(empty placeholder)* | 4 |

The rest are name-shaped (`<name>` 9, `<policy-name>` 6, `<rule-set-name>` 4, …) and are plausibly fine as they are. **Deciding which of the 121 genuinely want a validator is part of this issue's scope, not a precondition for it** — censusing the remedy rather than the defect is the point, because fixing `vrrp-group` alone leaves the same gap everywhere else and nothing would report it.
