## #8844 — security: packed `perfect-forward-secrecy keys <group>` silently DISABLES PFS [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-05)

## The defect

`security ipsec policy <p> perfect-forward-secrecy keys <group>;` — the brace-elided spelling — silently disables PFS.

```
braced   perfect-forward-secrecy { keys group14; }   PFSGroup=14
packed   perfect-forward-secrecy keys group14;       PFSGroup=0   <- identical to ABSENT
absent   (no statement)                              PFSGroup=0
```

`PFSGroup == 0` means **PFS disabled**. So an operator who authors perfect forward secrecy in the packed spelling gets an IPsec policy with **no forward secrecy**, and the compiled result is indistinguishable from never having written the statement.

## Cause — the #8800 shape

`schema_security.go:1197` declares:

```go
"perfect-forward-secrecy": {desc: "Perfect forward secrecy (keys group<N>)", children: nil},
```

`children: nil`, while `compileIPsec` reads a `keys` **child** of it (`compiler_ipsec.go:355`). So `keys` is not a schema child, `isBody` is false, the brace-elision pass is never *asked* about the `("perfect-forward-secrecy","keys")` pair, and no scope entry could name it.

Note the `desc` already documents the intended grammar — *"Perfect forward secrecy (keys group<N>)"* — so the schema describes a child it does not declare.

## Severity

**Higher than the other members of this class**, and it should not be triaged alongside them by shape alone. #8800 and #8825 fail closed or loud — a zero-address NAT pool is rejected at strict commit, an empty application-set is caught by the #3146 gate. This one **fails silently in the insecure direction**: the tunnel comes up, traffic flows, and forward secrecy is off. Nothing rejects it and nothing warns.

I have not yet measured whether any strict validator catches it downstream; the lenient path certainly does not, and the compiled `PFSGroup=0` is a legitimate value meaning "disabled", so there is nothing for a gate to detect.

## Remedy

The two-part #8800 shape: declare `keys` as a child of `perfect-forward-secrecy`, and admit the pair in `compactNormalizeInScope`. Declaring alone was measured insufficient on #8800.

**Check before landing** whether `keys` should also carry a validator — `parseDHGroup` accepts `group<N>` forms, and an unparseable value currently leaves `PFSGroup` at 0, which is the same silent-disable outcome by a different route.

## Provenance

Found by the #8807 behavioural predicate (#8830) after correcting a defect in the probe itself: it had been comparing only the FIRST value pair, so a leaf needing a type-specific value looked inert. #7484's `wordInert` already tried every pair, with a comment saying exactly why. With that corrected the SILENT bucket went 32 → 3, and this is one of the three survivors.

```

  severe: `0` is a legitimate "disabled" value, so no downstream gate can tell

identified why before I did: `keys` is now reachable on the **tolerant** path,
so validating it would newly REJECT a value `Store.Load` and `SyncApply` accept
today. That is a new rejection on the load path — the failure mode this campaign
has treated as the most dangerous class of change, because it bricks a node that
boots an existing config.

## #8858 — security: packed `system root-authentication encrypted-password` compiles to NO stanza — clean commit, no warning, and the daemon then REVOKES and locks root [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-05)

`system root-authentication encrypted-password "<hash>";` — with the top-level
`system` brace elided — compiles to **no root-authentication stanza at all**, on
a **clean strict commit with no warning**. The daemon then **revokes and locks
root**.

### Measured at `c6c5a8b3c`

```
BRACED   system { root-authentication { encrypted-password "$1$abc"; } }   root=$1$abc   strictErr=false
d1       system { root-authentication encrypted-password "$1$abc"; }       root=$1$abc   strictErr=false   works
d2       system root-authentication encrypted-password "$1$abc";           root=<NIL>    strictErr=false   LOST
```

No warning on any path. The only warning that mentions this material
(`compiler_validate_warn.go:117`) is gated on
`userspaceSynCookieProtectionActive(cfg)`, so an ordinary config gets **nothing**.

### The consequence is a LOCKOUT, not a breach — and that is worth stating precisely

`pkg/daemon/daemon_hostauth_apply.go:895` `applyRootAuth`:

> A **nil** stanza means "root-authentication not configured": the desired
> password AND key list are empty, so the reconcile **REVOKES whatever xpf
> previously provisioned** (gated by the marker) instead of early-returning and
> orphaning a live root credential (#5276).

So the sequence is: operator authors a root password → it silently does not
compile → `RootAuthentication == nil` → `reconcileUserPassword` D2-locks root.

**This fails closed, which is the right direction**, and it is why this is an
availability hazard rather than a security one. It is still severe: the operator
has positive evidence the credential is set — the stanza is in the file, the
commit succeeded, `show configuration` displays it — and root is locked.

### Reachability: latent, absorbing, replicating (unchanged from #8850)

`Format()` never *creates* the elided shape and no shipped config contains one, so
no deployment reaches this by using xpf normally. But `Format()` **preserves** it
verbatim and HA sync **transports** it, so a config that ever acquires this shape
keeps it through every commit and rollback and propagates it to the standby.

being *bypassed* rather than every packed statement being waved through, which

## #8876 — config: 93 admitted brace-elision pairs sit under a container that is itself UNREACHABLE — 4 of 6 adjudicated lose data silently, incl. all of IPsec, IKE and BGP [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-05)

## The mechanism, generalised from #8858 and #8875

Folding a fully-elided stanza needs **two** admissions, and both #8858 and #8875 turned out to be the same shape: the **inner** pair admitted, the **outer** one absent.

```
#8858   system -> root-authentication         ABSENT      4 inner pairs INERT
        root-authentication -> <credential>   admitted

#8875   security -> policies                  ABSENT      4 inner pairs INERT
        policies -> from-zone / global        admitted
```

The pass cannot reach a container it has not yet created, so **an admitted pair whose container half is missing never fires.** Critically, **it is indistinguishable from a working pair by inspection** — `("policies","from-zone")` is right there in `compactNormalizeInScope`, so anyone auditing the table concludes `policies` is handled.

Two lanes found this independently within hours in unrelated stanzas. That is the signature the wire-count class had, and the response there was to enumerate.

## The census

Predicate over the 500 pair literals in `compactNormalizeInScope` at master `f36be93c5`: **a container `C` is a candidate if `C` is never the `head` of any admitted pair, and `C` is not one of the 19 top-level `setSchema` roots** (top-level stanzas are the container themselves and need no parent admission).

```
admitted pairs                                    500
distinct container keywords                       168
top-level roots (excluded)                         19
CANDIDATES (container half never admitted)         93
admitted pairs sitting beneath a candidate        232 of 500
```

**Positive control — the predicate re-finds all three known cases:** `root-authentication` (4 pairs), `policies` (4), `zones` (1). It was not built from them.

A candidate is not a defect. Compiled braced vs fully-elided through `CompileConfigLenient`, with a gate column:

## #8879 — config: the #8859 elision population is not benign — at least 37 of 38 silent drops lose a value something reads [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-05)

Adjudication of the #8859 sweep population. **#8859 is the population; this is
its verdict.** Nothing there should be closed by this.

## The finding is a ratio, not a hit list

Of the SILENT candidate-drop rows, **at least 37 of 38 drop a value that
something downstream actually reads.** One reaches nothing.

Thirty-eight issues each saying "this field is dropped" would bury their own
signal. The single actionable claim is that **nearly every member of this class
drops something consumed** — the exceptions are the exception.

## Why "at least", and why that is a bound rather than a count

The reader predicate counts selector references to the dropped `Config` field
outside `pkg/config`. **Its error is one-way: it UNDERCOUNTS readers.** A
consumer reaching the value by some other route is invisible to it.

So a field reported as *reaching a reader* cannot be a false positive, and only
a **zero** can be wrong. **Every zero was individually checked.** If the number
is wrong at all it is wrong toward **38 of 38**, never toward fewer.

## The method, and evidence it is not selector noise

For each row the dropped field is taken from the sweep's own diff fragment, then
counted as `\.<Field>\b` outside `pkg/config`. The four fields most likely to
inflate on a common word were checked by hand and all four resolve to genuine
config reads:

```
.Screen    -> cfg.Security.Screen        (pkg/daemon/daemon_apply_dataplane.go)

.Gateways  -> ipsecCfg.Gateways          (pkg/ipsec/policy.go)

## #8880 — security: a second from-zone/to-zone block is SILENTLY DISCARDED when the `policies` brace is elided — clean commit, zero warnings, on both paths [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-05)

## Measured at master `85bbbbabe`

Both arms carry **the same two zone-pair blocks**. Only the brace around `policies` differs.

```
BRACED   security { policies { from-zone a to-zone b {…} from-zone c to-zone d {…} } }
         zonePairs=2  [a->b(1) c->d(1)]  warn=0  strictRejects=false

PACKED   security { policies   from-zone a to-zone b {…} from-zone c to-zone d {…}   }
         zonePairs=1  [a->b(1)]          warn=0  strictRejects=false     <- c->d GONE
```

**The second zone-pair policy set is discarded entirely.** Silent on the strict commit path *and* on the tolerant `Store.Load` / `SyncApply` ingress — no error, no warning, nothing in `show`. The operator writes two policy sets, commits clean, and enforces one.

## This is the truncation half of a two-mode class

It is **not** the same defect as #8875 (now fixed), which was the fully-elided `security policies …` spelling losing everything. **Here `security`'s brace is present and only `policies`' brace is elided**, so the pair `("security","policies")` — admitted by #8874 — is not the issue. The issue is that **`policies` does not declare `packedStatements`**, so a multi-statement run after it folds into one child and the later statements are dropped.

The class splits on the predicate's own disjunction, and the two halves behave **oppositely**:

| leaf shape | failure mode | example |
|---|---|---|
| `multi` | **INJECTION** — the repeated keyword is absorbed as a list *value* | `application-set AS application a1 application a2` → members `[a1, application, a2]` |
| `args >= 2` | **TRUNCATION** — later instances are lost | this issue: `[a->b, c->d]` → `[a->b]` |

**A reader told "injection" will not expect truncation from the same list**, and the injection half produces *more* members while this half produces fewer. A cell comparing **counts** scores injection as increased coverage and truncation as a plain loss; only comparing **contents** distinguishes them.

## Severity is not a property of the mode — it must be measured per pair

Adjudicated members of this population:

```
pool / address          INJECTION    SILENT           accept, 0 warns
system / name-server    INJECTION    SILENT           accept, 0 warns
policies / from-zone    TRUNCATION   SILENT           accept, 0 warns   <- this issue
peer / allowed-ips      INJECTION    STRICT-REJECTS
application-set / …     INJECTION    STRICT-REJECTS + tolerant WARNS
address-set / address   INJECTION    commits + WARNS naming the phantom
```

`walkSchemaNode` already has the rejection, gated on opt-in:

```go
childSchema := resolveSchemaChild(parent, keyword)
if childSchema == nil {
    // Only a subtree that opted in (schemaNode.closedWorld, inherited via closed)
    if closed {
        return typedLeafErrorf(path, "unknown configuration keyword %q under closed-world subtree", keyword)
    }
    return nil
}
```

**Every armed subtree is deep. None is a top-level stanza, and none of the big containers (`security`, `system`, `interfaces`, `protocols`) is armed.** So the mechanism works exactly where it was pointed and has never been pointed at the level where a typo costs the most.

## Why the load path is not a reason to leave it open

The obvious objection is forward compatibility: a config written by a newer binary must still load on an older one, which is why #1319 exists. **That objection does not apply, because the tolerant path never reaches this code.**

Established by measurement twice today: **`compileTreeLenient` — which `Store.Load` and `Store.SyncApply` use — does not schema-validate at all.** `schema_validators.go:443` states it, and a braced bad `name-server` gives `SchemaValidate=REJECT` with `CompileConfigLenient=accept` and **zero warnings**.

## #8883 — config: a packed multi-leaf run INJECTS the repeated keyword as a value — `system name-server` gets a resolver literally named "name-server", silently [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-05)

## Measured at master `85bbbbabe`

```
BRACED       system { name-server { 1.1.1.1; 8.8.8.8; } }              nameServers=[1.1.1.1 8.8.8.8]
PACKED       system { name-server 1.1.1.1 name-server 8.8.8.8; }       nameServers=[1.1.1.1 name-server 8.8.8.8]
BRACED flat  system { name-server 1.1.1.1; name-server 8.8.8.8; }      nameServers=[1.1.1.1 8.8.8.8]

all rows: warn=0, strictRejects=false
```

**Two independent controls give the correct result, so the packed spelling is uniquely broken.** The box ends up with a DNS resolver whose address is the literal string `name-server`, silent on the strict commit path and on the tolerant `Store.Load` ingress.

## Mechanism, and why it is the opposite of #8880

A `multi` leaf absorbs trailing non-sibling tokens (#2419). When the container does **not** declare `packedStatements`, the run is never split, so the first leaf swallows the **next statement's keyword** as one of its values.

This is the **injection** half of a two-mode class; **#8880 is the truncation half**:

| leaf shape | mode | direction | example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `multi` | **INJECTION** | packed produces **more** members | this issue: `[1.1.1.1, name-server, 8.8.8.8]` |
| `args >= 2` | **TRUNCATION** | packed produces **fewer** | #8880: `[a->b, c->d]` → `[a->b]` |

**A cell comparing counts scores injection as increased coverage.** Only comparing contents distinguishes them — which is how this was found, by printing members rather than lengths.

## Injection is worse than truncation here, and the reason is worth stating

A dropped entry breaks whatever referenced it and somebody notices. **A garbage entry sits in the resolver list and is used** — every lookup that reaches it fails, intermittently and without an obvious cause, and `show configuration` renders what the operator wrote.

## `packedStatements` does NOT fix this — measured, not assumed

The obvious remedy is to opt the container into `packedStatements` so the run splits. **Giving `system` the opt-in does not fix `name-server`**: the multi leaf absorbs the rest of the run inside `consumeNodeKeys` and the split still yields one statement.

**This was established by mutation-testing the proposed advice**, and it partitions the population being tracked in PR #8881:

```
462 members at args >= 1
  368 non-multi   opt-in is a candidate remedy
   86 multi       opt-in is MEASURED INSUFFICIENT     <- this issue's class
```

## #8889 — config: nested application-set expansion is quartic and re-runs per policy, under the store read lock [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-05)

`expandAppSet` re-expands every nested `application-set` from scratch on each
visit, with no memoization. Depth is capped at 3, so the exponent is **fixed at
four** — the cost is B⁴ in the *branching* factor, and `CommitCheck` holds the
store read lock across the whole of it.

## Measured at `c2e0a9ecb`

A maximally-nested legal config — `TOP → L1 → L2 → L3 → application`, each level
with B members — compiled through strict `CompileConfig`:

| branching B | application-sets | compile |
|---|---|---|
| 16 | 49 | 128 ms |
| 20 | 61 | 390 ms |
| 24 | 73 | 876 ms |
| 28 | 85 | 1557 ms |
| 32 | 97 | **2942 ms** |

Doubling B from 16 to 32 costs **23×**, consistent with ~B⁴·⁵. Extrapolating,
B=64 (~193 sets) is roughly 68 s.

**And each referencing policy re-expands** — there is no sharing across policies:

```
policies referencing TOP=1   357 ms
policies referencing TOP=2   404 ms
policies referencing TOP=4   836 ms
policies referencing TOP=8  1125 ms
```

So the real cost is *N policies × B⁴*.

## It runs under the store read lock

```go
func (s *Store) CommitCheck() (*config.Config, error) {
	s.mu.RLock()
	defer s.mu.RUnlock()
	compiled, err := s.compileTree(s.candidate)
```

## #8890 — userspace-dp: NAT64 egress skips GRE/WireGuard encapsulation — the copy path chooses the NAT64 builder exclusively [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-05)

The TX copy path selects its frame builder on `is_nat64` **exclusively**, and only
the branch it skips performs tunnel encapsulation. A NAT64-translated packet whose
route resolves through a GRE or WireGuard endpoint is emitted on the physical NIC
**unencapsulated**.

## Structural chain, read at `c2e0a9ecb`

```rust
// afxdp/tx/dispatch/mod.rs:409  (inside enqueue_copy_fallback_frame)
match if is_nat64 {
    build_nat64_forwarded_frame(...)      // no tunnel awareness at all
} else {
    build_forwarded_frame_from_frame(...) // the ONLY encapsulating builder
}
```

```rust
// afxdp/frame/mod.rs:404, inside build_forwarded_frame_from_frame
if decision.resolution.tunnel_endpoint_id != 0 {
    ...
    Some(TunnelKind::WireGuard) => wg::wg_encap_frame(&out, meta, decision, forwarding),
```

`build_nat64_forwarded_frame` (`frame/mod.rs:253`) contains **no** `encap`,
`tunnel`, `wg_` or `gre` reference — grepped, not assumed. It receives
`&request.decision`, which carries `resolution.tunnel_endpoint_id`, and ignores it.

## The combination is routed *into* this path, not away from it

```rust
// dispatch/mod.rs:931
let uses_native_tunnel = request.decision.resolution.tunnel_endpoint_id != 0;
// dispatch/mod.rs:1073
let direct_built = if is_nat64 || uses_native_tunnel {
    // ... direct TX disallowed, fall back to the copy path
```

Direct TX is refused when **either** holds, so `is_nat64 && uses_native_tunnel`

mechanism that would refuse a mismatched helper. It does not fire here because

## #8896 — userspace-dp: NAT64 cannot egress through a native GRE/WireGuard tunnel — #8890 made it fail closed, the capability is still missing [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-05)

#8890 / PR #8895 stopped a NAT64-translated packet routed through a native GRE or WireGuard endpoint from being emitted **unencapsulated** on the physical NIC. It now drops, with a `nat64_tunnel_encap_unsupported` counter.

**That was the minimum correct behaviour, not the desired one.** An operator who configures NAT64 with a tunnel route today gets a black hole plus a counter. This issue tracks making the two transforms compose.

## Why it is not a small change

The tunnel post-pass in `build_forwarded_frame_from_frame` is a wrapper over a **finished inner frame**:

```rust
// frame/mod.rs — after the inner frame is built
if decision.resolution.tunnel_endpoint_id != 0 {
    return match kind {
        Some(TunnelKind::WireGuard) => wg::wg_encap_frame(&out, meta, decision, forwarding),
        Some(TunnelKind::Gre) => encapsulate_native_gre_frame(&out, meta, decision, forwarding),
        Some(TunnelKind::Unknown) | None => None,   // #2327 fail-closed
    };
}
```

So it *looks* like the NAT64 builder's output can be fed to the same post-pass. **It cannot, as written.** `wg_encap_frame` parses the inner frame using `inner_meta.addr_family` in three places:

| site | what it reads | what happens with a NAT64 output + ingress meta |
|---|---|---|
| `packet_trimmed_len(inner_packet, addr_family)` | IPv6 payload-length @4 | reads the IPv4 fragment-offset/flags word — garbage length |
| `inner_dst_ip(inner_packet, addr_family)` | 16 bytes @24 | reads past a 20-byte IPv4 header into the TCP payload — wrong AllowedIPs peer, or none |
| `inner_tos_byte(inner_packet, addr_family)` | IPv6 traffic class | wrong DSCP/ECN copied to the outer header (#2303) |

After NAT64 the frame is **IPv4** while `meta` still describes the **IPv6 ingress**. `frame_l3_offset(inner_frame)` is consulted first and is likely self-correcting for the offset; `addr_family` is the field that is wrong.

That is only the inner half. The outer half is the harder one: `#2680/#3992/#5292` resolve the PHYSICAL underlay egress once per packet and derive the outer MTU, outer IP source and outer L2 (dst MAC / src MAC / VLAN) from that single snapshot, deliberately NOT from `decision.resolution` (which describes the tunnel logical ifindex). Whether that chain is correct for a **family-translated** inner packet has not been established.

## What a fix owes

1. A corrected `ForwardPacketMeta` for the post-NAT64 frame (family at minimum), constructed rather than inherited — and a statement of which other `meta` fields the two encapsulators read.
2. Evidence that the outer-identity derivation (#2680/#3992/#5292) holds when the inner family changed mid-pipeline.
3. The inner-MTU clamp re-checked: `post_transform_inner_mtu` already takes `is_nat64` AND the tunnel state (`dispatch/mod.rs`, the `is_nat64 || uses_native_tunnel` arm), so the MTU side may already anticipate this combination — worth reading before assuming it does not.
4. A cell asserting the emitted frame's OUTER header is the tunnel's, with the plaintext case kept as the negative control. `nat64_8890_tunnel_marked_decision_is_not_emitted_plaintext` (added in PR #8895) becomes that control directly.
5. The `nat64_tunnel_encap_unsupported` counter narrows to the genuinely unsupported residue (unknown mode / missing endpoint row) rather than the whole combination, and `docs/userspace-dataplane-gaps.md` loses its mixed-boundary row.

## Do not regress the gate while doing this

## #8898 — config: master-password pseudorandom-function selector is silently dropped when the `system` brace is elided — the config DB is encrypted with a KDF the operator did not choose [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-05)

Found by lane-8015 working the #8876 tail. Filed separately because it has a **different consumer path from every other row in that census** and a security consequence the census row does not convey.

## The defect

With the `system` brace elided, the `master-password pseudorandom-function` selector is lost. `crypto.go:153` then falls back to `defaultMasterPasswordPRF`.

**So the configuration database is encrypted with a key-derivation function the operator did not choose — while `show configuration` renders the one they did.** The displayed config and the enforced behaviour disagree, and nothing warns.

```
system -> master-password    pseudorandom-function selector lost    crypto.go:153    SILENT
```

Measured lost for both `hmac-sha2-256` and `juniper-prf1`.

## Why the census instrument could not see this

Every other row in #8876 is adjudicated by comparing **compiled structs**. This row's consumer never touches the compiled config: `effectiveMasterPasswordPRF` scans the **raw AST**. A compiled-field predicate says nothing about it.

This is the same false negative #8859's closing record already flagged from the other direction — `MasterPassword` came back with *zero readers* under the reader predicate, precisely because it is consumed from the AST rather than from `Config`. **Two independent instruments both blind to this field, for the same structural reason.** It was caught only because the row was measured against its real consumer instead of inheriting the classifier's answer.

## Two fixture faults on this row, and the second is the transferable one

lane-8015 caught both before filing.

1. The first fixture used `prf`; the leaf is `pseudorandom-function`. All four arms returned `""` **including braced** — a dead reference arm, so two empty results agreed and the row read clean.

2. **The first value tried was `sha256` — which is the fallback.** Losing the selector produces the same effective PRF as keeping it, so the comparison was real, the arms were live, and **the row still measured clean while being broken.**

That second one is a distinct trap from the empty-arm kind and worth stating on its own: **choosing the default value as the fixture value hides exactly the defect the fixture exists to find.** A fixture value must be one the fallback cannot produce.

## What a fix owes

1. The selector surviving the elided spelling, like any other #8876 row.
2. A cell whose fixture value is **not** `defaultMasterPasswordPRF` — with the reason written down, because the next person to touch it will reach for the default.
3. A check on the display/enforcement divergence itself: if the selector is ever unresolvable, `show configuration` must not render a PRF that is not in force. Silent disagreement between the two is the part that makes this a security defect rather than a config-loss defect.

Refs #8876, #8859.

## #8899 — dataplane: a process-config change during XSK startup is acked without restarting the helper — the plan key is blind to process identity [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-05)

`snapshotBindingPlanKey` does not include the helper's process identity, so a
config changing only `binary`, `control-socket`, `state-file` or `poll-mode`
leaves the key unchanged. During the pending-XSK-startup window that means the
restart trigger cannot fire, and the pending branch returns apply-success after
writing the *desired* config over the *running* one — while the child keeps its
original argv and socket.

## Measured, with controls

`snapshotBindingPlanKey` over snapshots differing in exactly one field:

```
base plan key: "workers=4;ring=2048;"

Binary A->B                  plan key unchanged = true
ControlSocket A->B           plan key unchanged = true
StateFile A->B               plan key unchanged = true
PollMode busy->interrupt     plan key unchanged = true

CONTROL Workers 4->8         plan key unchanged = false
CONTROL RingEntries          plan key unchanged = false
```

The two controls are what make the four negatives mean something: the key *does*
discriminate the fields it covers, so the blindness above is real rather than a
function that returns a constant.

## The control flow it feeds, line-verified

```
manager_compile.go:369  publishedPlanChangedDuringStartup :=
                            pendingXSKStartup && m.publishedPlanKey != "" &&
                            m.publishedPlanKey != newPlanKey     <- cannot fire
manager_compile.go:385  if pendingXSKStartup {
manager_compile.go:424      m.cfg = ucfg                          <- desired recorded as running
manager_compile.go:432      return result, nil                    <- apply reported successful
manager_compile.go:443  if err := m.ensureProcessLocked(ucfg)     <- the ONLY restart call, unreachable from above
```

So a commit that renames the control socket during the startup window is accepted

## #8901 — dataplane: Rust hashes SharedUMEM into its binding plan but the Go plan key omits it — a SharedUMEM change passes the same-plan startup exception while the helper rebuilds bindings [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-05)

Found by review during #8899. **Pre-existing and independent of that change** — filing separately rather than folding it in, because the two have different mechanisms and different fixes.

## The skew

```
userspace-dp/src/server/helpers/planning.rs:137   Rust HASHES SharedUMEM into the binding plan
pkg/dataplane/userspace/maps_sync.go:1513         Go's snapshotBindingPlanKey OMITS it
```

`snapshotBindingPlanKey` covers workers, ring entries and interface/fabric topology. It is the Go side's answer to *"did the AF_XDP binding plan change?"*, and it gates two things:

1. the **restart** trigger during the pending-XSK-startup window, and
2. the **same-plan refresh exception** — the rule that lets a FIB-only update publish during that window, because blocking it deadlocks (XSK liveness needs RX traffic, transit traffic needs FIB data).

**A config changing only `SharedUMEM` leaves the Go key unchanged, so it is classified as a same-plan refresh and published straight through — while the Rust side, whose plan hash *does* include it, rebuilds its AF_XDP bindings.** The two planes disagree about whether the binding plan moved, and the Go side is the one deciding whether it is safe to publish mid-startup.

## Why this is not #8899

#8899 is about **process identity** — the helper's argv, binary and sockets — and its fix consults `configEqual`, which correctly does *not* cover `SharedUMEM`: a SharedUMEM change reaches the helper inside the snapshot, not on the command line, so it needs no process restart. That classification is right.

This is the adjacent question: not *does the process need restarting*, but **does the Go plan key agree with the Rust plan hash about what constitutes a plan change**. The #8899 classification guard asserts every `config.UserspaceConfig` field is either process-identity or exempt; it says nothing about binding-plan correctness, and should not be read as if it did.

## What a fix owes

1. **Decide which side is authoritative.** If Rust rebuilding bindings on a SharedUMEM change is correct, the Go key must include it so the same-plan exception stops firing. If it is not, the Rust hash should drop it. One of the two is wrong and it is not obvious from here which.
2. **A cross-plane guard**, not a Go-side one. The failure is a disagreement between two independently-maintained hashes, and a cell on either side alone re-derives that side's opinion. Nearest existing model is the shape-digest guard from #8892, which forces a decision when a wire struct's shape moves.
3. Check the rest of the key the same way. `SharedUMEM` was found by inspection; **whether it is the only field where the two hashes disagree has not been established** — the population is a diff of two hash inputs, and nobody has run it.

## Severity

Not a leak and not a crash: the observable is a binding rebuild the Go side did not expect during XSK startup, in a window whose whole purpose is to avoid back-to-back AF_XDP reconciles that self-collide. Worth fixing before it is discovered as a startup flake with no obvious cause.

Refs #8899.

## #8903 — config: the compact fold is a property of the COMPILE path — every raw-AST reader outside it silently sees the un-normalized tree [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-06)

Generalised by lane-8015 while fixing #8898, and it is a **population nobody has censused**. Filing it before the shape gets attributed to the two issues that are instances of it.

## The mechanism

`compactNormalizeInScope` / `normalizeCompactStanzas` run **inside the compiler**. Anything that walks the raw `ConfigTree` never sees them, so an admitted compact stanza is folded for the compiled config and **not** for that reader.

Two instances are known, and they failed in two different ways:

| site | walks the raw tree and… | consequence |
|---|---|---|
| `SchemaValidate` (#8867) | **validated** nothing | a typed-leaf violation passed the gate |
| `effectiveMasterPasswordPRF` (#8898) | **resolved** nothing | the config DB encrypted with a KDF the operator did not choose, while `show configuration` rendered the one they did |

**#8898 is the sharp demonstration that this is a separate axis.** Admitting `system master-password` to the scope — the ordinary #8876-class remedy — repaired the *compiled* config and **changed nothing observable**, because the consumer does not read the compiled config. The scan site had to fold too. lane-8015's own note: *"my load-bearing census would have scored this row correctly for the wrong reason."*

## Why neither existing instrument can see it

- The **scope list** (`compactNormalizeInScope`) answers *is this pair admitted*, not *who reads it*.
- The **compiled-config classifier** used across #8876/#8879 compares compiled structs, so a consumer that never touches `Config` is invisible to it by construction.

Both instruments are correct and both are blind here, for the same structural reason. This is not a gap in either census — it is a third question.

## The population, unmeasured

16 files outside `pkg/config` reference `ConfigTree` (excluding tests):

```
pkg/configstore/  crypto.go store.go store_commit.go store_command.go store_format.go
                  store_persist.go history.go envelope.go db.go dataplane_retire.go
                  test_seams.go
pkg/daemon/       daemon_apply_commit.go daemon_ha_sync.go daemon_ha_node_local_7441.go
pkg/cluster/      sync_config_crypto.go
pkg/dataplane/userspace/  screens.go
```

**That is a file list, not a finding.** Most of these almost certainly pass the tree through without interpreting stanza structure — persistence, envelopes, history. The ones that matter are those that **make a decision by scanning for a stanza**, which is what `effectiveMasterPasswordPRF` does. `pkg/cluster/sync_config_crypto.go` and `pkg/dataplane/userspace/screens.go` look like the next candidates by name alone, and by name alone is not evidence.

## What a census owes

1. Separate **structural readers** (decide something from stanza shape) from **pass-through carriers**. Only the first class can have this defect.

`TestSweepFull` dedupes by `(stanza, child)` pair and keeps the **first site it reaches**, so the published verdict is a property of whichever leaf `collectCompactSites()` happened to enumerate first — an order a reader of the table cannot see.

The gate column then claims *"this PAIR's elided spelling is refused / warned / silent"* while the measurement supports only *"the elided spelling OF THAT ONE LEAF was"*. ## #8915 — daemon: a netlink overflow drops the ONLY helper-FIB refresh edge, and nothing periodic recovers it [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-05)

The route listener's netlink channel is bounded at 256. On overflow the kernel
drops updates, the `ErrorCallback` that receives the resulting `ENOBUFS` only
`slog.Debug`s it, and **nothing else can produce a FIB refresh** — so the helper
FIB stays stale until the next route event that is not dropped.

$ grep -rn '\.Mark()' pkg/daemon/     (non-test)
pkg/daemon/daemon_route_listener.go:125:   loop.Mark()
```

Inside the `case upd, ok := <-updates:` arm. The netlink channel is the sole
source of refresh edges.

**2. The bounded channel and the silent error callback.**

```go
updates := make(chan netlink.RouteUpdate, 256)
…
ErrorCallback: func(err error) {
    slog.Debug("route listener: netlink error", "err", err)
},
```

`ENOBUFS` — the overflow signal — arrives here and is logged at Debug. It does not
mark, resubscribe, or force a refresh.

**3. The coalescer's ticker is a sweep, not a periodic actuate — measured.**

`coalesce.go:324` runs a 100 ms ticker, which reads like a periodic refresh. It is
not: `Tick` fires only `if !l.dirtySince.IsZero()`.

```
actuations with NO mark, 50 sweeps: 0
actuations after ONE mark:          1     <- CONTROL

if ciphers := filterSSHAlgorithms(ssh.Ciphers); len(ciphers) > 0 {
    lines = append(lines, "Ciphers "+strings.Join(ciphers, ","))
}
if macs := filterSSHAlgorithms(ssh.MACs); len(macs) > 0 {
    lines = append(lines, "MACs "+strings.Join(macs, ","))
}
```

An empty list writes **no `Ciphers` line into the sshd drop-in at all**, so sshd falls back to its permissive compiled-in default. The narrowing the operator asked for is not applied, on a commit that reports success and a `show configuration` that renders what they wrote.

## The finding is the SIBLING ASYMMETRY, not the drop

`key-exchange`, `ciphers` and `macs` are **schema-identical** (`pkg/config/schema_system.go:526-548`):

| leaf | args | multi | validator | children | reader | sshd line |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `key-exchange` | 1 | true | `ValidateSSHAlgorithm` | nil | `firewallMatchValues` | `KexAlgorithms` |
| `ciphers` | 1 | true | `ValidateSSHAlgorithm` | nil | `firewallMatchValues` | `Ciphers` |
| `macs` | 1 | true | `ValidateSSHAlgorithm` | nil | `firewallMatchValues` | `MACs` |

Three leaves, one shape, one reader, one drop-in, one consequence. `compactNormalizeInScope` admits **`(ssh, key-exchange)` and neither of the other two**:

    inScope(ssh, key-exchange) = true
    inScope(ssh, ciphers)      = false
    inScope(ssh, macs)         = false

So a config hardening all three gets `KexAlgorithms` applied and `Ciphers`/`MACs` silently ignored. **Partial application reads as success** — it is worse than all three failing, because the drop-in visibly contains the operator's key-exchange line and looks like the change landed.

## #8924 — Lexer rejects unquoted @ so the SSH algorithm names the schema offers as completions fail to parse; validator regex explicitly permits @ [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-05)

## The contradiction

`ValidateSSHAlgorithm` is built to accept `@`-bearing OpenSSH names. `pkg/config/schema_validators_system.go:216-224`:

```go
// OpenSSH algorithm names are letters, digits, and the punctuation `- _ . @ +`
// (e.g. curve25519-sha256@libssh.org, diffie-hellman-group-exchange-sha256,
// hmac-sha2-256-etm@openssh.com, aes256-gcm@openssh.com).
var sshAlgorithmRE = regexp.MustCompile(`^[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9._@+-]*$`)
```

The schema then offers exactly those names as `valueExamples` (`schema_system.go:541-548`):

    ciphers   -> aes256-gcm@openssh.com, chacha20-poly1305@openssh.com
    macs      -> hmac-sha2-256-etm@openssh.com, hmac-sha2-512
    key-exchange -> curve25519-sha256, diffie-hellman-group-exchange-sha256

**The lexer refuses `@` before either can run**, so a value copied verbatim from the completion fails:

    set system services ssh ciphers aes256-gcm@openssh.com
      -> unexpected token error at line 1, column 43

    system { services { ssh { ciphers aes256-gcm@openssh.com; } } }
      -> line 1, column 45: unexpected character: @

Both surfaces, both spellings. Also affects `key-exchange curve25519-sha256@libssh.org`, the value the validator's own comment names first.

So the `@` branch of `sshAlgorithmRE` is unreachable for any unquoted input, and the completion suggests values the parser rejects. `set … ciphers ?` offers `aes256-gcm@openssh.com`; typing it errors.

## Severity: there IS a workaround, and it is undiscoverable

**Double quotes work**, on both paths:

    ciphers "aes256-gcm@openssh.com"                       -> Ciphers=[aes256-gcm@openssh.com]   OK
    set system services ssh ciphers "aes256-gcm@openssh.com" -> Ciphers=[aes256-gcm@openssh.com]  OK

Single quotes are not supported by the lexer at all.

So the modern AEAD ciphers and ETM MACs **are** configurable — but only by quoting, which nothing in the completion, the placeholder, or the error message suggests. The operator's evidence is a completion offering a value and the parser rejecting it; the natural conclusion is that the feature is broken rather than that the value needs quoting.

## #8928 — config: validation-suppressing elision is a CLASS — 2 instances fixed, elision census complete, other drop mechanisms un-enumerated [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-06)

## The shape

A container whose child carries a **cross-reference that strict commit
validates**. Elide the container and the child is dropped *before* the check
runs, so a dangling reference commits clean:

    braced, bad reference  ->  REJECTED at commit  (correct)
    elided, bad reference  ->  COMMITTED CLEAN     (fail-open)

The operator gets **no value and no complaint**. It is the worst shape the
`#8879` campaign produced, because a silent drop that also disarms its own
detector leaves no channel by which anyone learns — and it inverts the usual
intuition that the more explicit spelling is the risky one.

## Two confirmed instances, both fixed

| pair | what the elision cost |
|---|---|
| `routing-options forwarding-table` | typo'd export policy → ECMP / consistent-hash load-balancing silently disabled |
| `services ip-monitoring` | typo'd rpm-probe → **probe-driven WAN failover silently never arms** |

Both closed by admitting the pair to `compactNormalizeInScope`, both measured
two-sided (removing the admission restores the fail-open), and both guarded by
the two-row table in `TestElisionSuppressedAValidation8879`. It is a table
rather than two cells deliberately: a single case reads as an oddity, a table
reads as a class.

Neither was found by looking. The first turned up while adjudicating an
unrelated pair; the second only because a fixture happened to name an RPM probe
that did not exist.

## The elision census is COMPLETE and negative

The class needs **both** a validated cross-reference **and** an un-admitted
container above it. After the `#8879` admissions only 12 top-level containers
remained un-admitted (now 8, after `#8925`), so the surface is small and was
enumerated rather than sampled:

- 207 cross-reference validation strings exist in the compiler.
- Every un-admitted container that can hold a body was drop-tested.

This is the same shape lane-8526 found in #8879's population (issue 8925), arriving by a different route: that one was built by *running the pass*, this one from *reading the pass's table*. ## #8933 — routing: a brace-elided policy-statement then clause loses every attribute AND corrupts the terminal action — the term matches, sets nothing, and falls through [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-05)

The one live defect remaining from the brace-elision census (issue 8876). Measured at master `86d4db841`.

## The drop

    policy-options { policy-statement p1 { term t1 { from { protocol bgp; }
        then { metric 50; local-preference 200; accept; } } } }

      -> term t1  matches [bgp]  action="accept"  metric=50  localpref=200

    policy-options { policy-statement p1 { term t1 { from { protocol bgp; }
        then metric 50; } } }

      -> term t1  matches [bgp]  action="metric"  metric=0   localpref=0

All eight value-carrying routing actions are dropped in the elided spelling:

    as-path-prepend   community   load-balance   local-preference
    metric            metric-type   next-hop       origin

`accept` and `reject` survive — they are `args:0` flags with no value to lose. **The two that cannot show a loss are the two a minimal fixture reaches for**, which is how this row was originally filed NOT A DEFECT.

`strictErr=false`, `warnings=0`. Silent on the strict commit path and on the tolerant `Store.Load` / `SyncApply` ingress.

## It is not only a dropped value — the TERMINAL ACTION is corrupted

The compiler consumes the first packed token into the action slot, so `then metric 50;` yields **`Action="metric"`** — a value that is neither `accept` nor `reject`.

`pkg/frr/policy_render.go:462,492`:

```go
action := "permit"
if term.Action == "reject" { action = "deny" }
...
nonTerminating := term.Action != "accept" && term.Action != "reject"
```

`"metric"` fails both comparisons, so the term renders as **`permit` + `on-match next` with no `set` clauses at all**. Against the braced spelling, which renders `permit` + `set metric 50` + stop, the elided form changes routing behaviour twice over:

1. **No attributes are applied** — no metric, local-preference, next-hop, community, AS-path prepend, origin.
2. **The term stops terminating.** `on-match next` makes it fall through to the following terms and ultimately the policy default-action, per the #2451 fall-through semantics. A term written to `accept` now does not accept.

## #8936 — "partial" drop shape is not a permanent exclusion, and three controls were built on the assumption that it is [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-05)

Split out of the #8933 landing because it is a claim about the *method*, not about the eight sites #8933 fixed.

## The rule as written

`compact_block_permanent_exclusions_8690.txt` classes a site `partial` when the brace-elided spelling compiles to something non-empty, and documents the consequence as:

> something already consumes part of the tail. Truncating it removes a value that is READ, on a config that commits clean. Forbidden to every scope by `TestNormalizerScopeNeverCoversAPartialSite8690`.

## What is actually measured, and what is inferred

The measurement is **something consumed the tail**. The inference is **that something is entitled to it**. Those are different claims and only the first was measured.

For the eight `policy-options policy-statement <p> term <t> then <action>` sites, the consumer was the defect: the compiler packed the action name into `PolicyTerm.Action`, so the term lost its attribute *and* stopped terminating (`policy_render.go` treats anything that is neither `accept` nor `reject` as non-terminating). Removing the consumer is the fix; the fold then preserves everything, including the multi-token tails — `community add <v>`, `community delete [ a b ]`, `as-path-prepend "<asn> <asn>"`.

So `partial` is a live classification, revisable by the next fix. It is not a permanent property.

## Why this is worth an issue: three controls were built on the contrary

The `filedStillOpen` anchor in `compact_block_equivalence_2419_test.go` was **deliberately re-anchored to a partial site**, with the reasoning recorded in the file:

> This one is chosen to be DURABLE rather than convenient. It is a site whose drop shape is "partial" ... so `TestNormalizerScopeNeverCoversAPartialSite8690` FORBIDS any scope from covering it. It cannot be normalized by a family sweep.

That anchor was `then local-preference`. #8933 normalized it. It is the **third anchor in a row** consumed by the next family to land, and the only one chosen expressly to end that churn — the two before it were `empty` sites, and lane-8015 lost the same control twice before that.

The register's own entry recorded the premise as fact: `also the #2419 positive-control anchor, chosen BECAUSE a partial site is immune to the sweep`.

## The property that actually holds

The first anchor, `interfaces xpfname mtu`, is durable and nobody wrote down why: **its container slot is an arg placeholder**. The predicate is keyed on a (container keyword, head) pair and production calls it with `node.Keys[0]`, which for that site is an arbitrary instance name (`ge-0/0/0`). No static pair can name it — a permanent bound of a pair-keyed predicate (#8921), not a classification a fix can dissolve.

#8933 re-anchored to `bridge-domains xpfname routing-interface` on that basis (and a third compiler file, `compiler_services.go`).

## Proposed work

1. Audit every control and register entry whose durability argument is "this site is partial". Known: the `#2419` `filedStillOpen` anchor (fixed in #8933), the `partial` class doc (amended in #8933), and `TestNormalizerScopeNeverCoversAPartialSite8690`'s framing.
2. Decide whether the remaining 13 partial sites are partial-by-defect or partial-by-legitimate-reader. That distinction does not exist in the register today and it is the one that decides whether a site is ever admissible. Nine of the thirteen are `interfaces`, two `system login`, two `bridge-domains`.
3. Prefer instance-name-slot sites for any control that needs to survive the next widening.

Found while landing #8933; every claim above is measured at master `2338ae3b0`.

## #8939 — config: 76 containers whose compiler never learned to walk a packed chain — an accepted spelling with an incomplete reader (not malformed input) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-06)

## The shape

`ParseSetCommand` + `SetPath` accept a single `set` command carrying **several leaf/value pairs** and build them as a **nested chain** rather than as siblings:

    set interfaces gr-0/0/0 unit 0 tunnel source 10.0.0.1 destination 10.0.0.2

    [interfaces]
      [gr-0/0/0]
        [unit 0]
          [tunnel]
            [source 10.0.0.1]          <- destination becomes a CHILD of source
              [destination 10.0.0.2]

The compiler reads `tunnel > source` and never looks below it, so:

    two commands      set … tunnel source 10.0.0.1
                      set … tunnel destination 10.0.0.2     src=10.0.0.1 dst=10.0.0.2   correct
    one packed command                                      src=10.0.0.1 dst=""         SILENT

The command is **accepted**. No parse error, no compile error, no warning. **A command accepted and half-executed is worse than one rejected** — the operator has no signal at all, and `show configuration` renders what they typed.

## It is not one stanza

Every one of these is accepted and builds an over-deep chain:

    set interfaces gr-0/0/0 unit 0 tunnel source 10.0.0.1 destination 10.0.0.2      depth 6
    set firewall policer p1 if-exceeding bandwidth-limit 10m burst-size-limit 100k  depth 5
    set system services ssh ciphers aes256-ctr macs hmac-sha2-256                   depth 4
    set security policies from-zone a to-zone b policy p1 match source-address any destination-address any   depth 6

This is a property of the flat-set grammar, not of any one container.

## This is a DIFFERENT mechanism from the hierarchical packed run

Issue 8904 covers the hierarchical spelling — `tunnel source A destination B;` inside braces — where the tokens land as a **packed tail on one node's Keys** and the remedy is `packedStatements`, splitting the run. That fix is landing separately.

**It does not and should not reach this.** Here there is no packed tail to split: `SetPath` has already built the tokens as nested nodes, and `normalizeCompactStanzas` correctly folds nothing (measured: `folded=0`). Fixing this in the compact-normalize pass would mean changing the flat-set grammar under cover of an unrelated change.

## #8943 — config: 26 of 50 depth-2 elision pairs DROP their value — the corrected census has no tracker and the work is unowned [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-05)

The corrected depth-2 census (#8938, landed in PR 8940) measured **26 DROP / 20 SAME / 4 unanswerable** across a population of 50. #8929 and #8938 are both closed, so **the 26 adjudications currently have no tracking issue**. Filing one so the measurement does not evaporate — this is the failure mode where landing produces no artifact and the work falls off.

## What was measured

Corrected from an earlier report of "1 of 6". That earlier sample was not under-powered — it answered a different question. The elision under test is HEAD's brace under MID; five of its six fixtures compared the fully braced form against one that elided `(security, flow)` instead, an **admitted** pair that folds correctly. `nat source` was the only fixture built correctly, which is precisely why it was the only drop found.

## The rows

**`security nat` — five of six children drop:** `destination`, `nat64`, `natv6v4`, `proxy-arp`, `static`. (`source` landed as #8931.)

**`security flow` — five children drop:** `aging`, `tcp-session`, `udp-session`, `icmp-session`, `traceoptions`.

**`security log`/`syslog` — three drop:** `file`, `host`, `user`.

The remaining rows of the 26 are in the census output on the branch that landed with PR 8940.

## One row carries a security consequence the others do not

**`nat destination` is a third instance of the #8928 fail-open class.** Braced, a rule naming an undefined pool is REFUSED:

```
destination-nat rule-set rs1 rule r1 references undefined pool nope7717
```

The elided spelling **commits clean**. Destination NAT, so the same consequence shape as the ip-monitoring instance: a validation the operator is relying on silently stops running. This row should be taken first.

## The bound, and why the SAME column clears nothing

**26 is a LOWER bound.** The 20 SAME rows are not adjudicated clean, and the evidence for that is concrete rather than cautionary: **`policy-statement then` reads SAME under this instrument and was #8933** — a real drop that also corrupted the term's terminal action, found only by printing the compiled object rather than diffing a fingerprint.

The sweep synthesises one body statement per pair, so it carries the leaf-contingency defect: a pair whose drop only manifests for a particular leaf reads SAME when probed with a different one. **Three instruments now carry this defect**, and it is the reason a SAME verdict here means "this probe did not detect a difference", not "nothing is lost".

Operative rule for whoever takes these: a row whose lost field is one a compiler or renderer **branches on** has a hidden second half. #8933 is the worked example — the fingerprint saw the missing metric and could not see that the term had stopped terminating.

The 4 unanswerable rows are a statement about the fixture, not about the pairs.

## Shape of the work

Each row is an ordinary admit-or-decline adjudication, the same method as the #8879 batches. Siblings usually share a shape, so the `nat` and `flow` families should go as families rather than one row at a time. Every admission needs the #8921 collision check first — the scope predicate is keyed on (container, head) with no parent context, so an admission can be effective at schema sites it was never adjudicated at.

## #8945 — tooling: `cargo fmt` rewrites ~380 files and BREAKS the #6592 runtime-view canary — the repo is not rustfmt-clean under a current toolchain [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-05)

Hit while landing #8896. Recording it because the failure lands in a file the author never touched, which makes it expensive to attribute.

## What happens

Running `cargo fmt --manifest-path userspace-dp/Cargo.toml` on a clean checkout of master rewrites **~380 files**. The repo is not rustfmt-clean under the toolchain I have, so the command is not a no-op on untouched code — it is a whole-crate rewrite.

## Why it is worse than diff noise

It **fails the test suite**, in a file unrelated to any edit:

```
thread 'runtime_view_publish_and_read_sites_are_pinned' panicked at
tests/runtime_view_publish_canary.rs:750:5:
#6592 runtime-view canary: 1 violation(s)
  [rule 2 (no view built outside the choke point)]
  src/afxdp/worker/loop_body/mod.rs: 2 RuntimeView construction(s), expected 0
```

The #6592 canary detects constructions and publishes by scanning source lines. `cargo fmt` rewraps a construction across lines, and the canary's count changes. Reverting the formatting alone turns the suite green again — verified, not inferred: with only my six intended files present the same canary run is `31 passed; 0 failed`.

So the sequence an author sees is: make a small change in `frame/`, run `cargo fmt` out of habit, run the suite, and get a failure in `worker/loop_body/` about a rule you did not touch. The natural next move is to investigate the canary or your own change, and both are dead ends.

## Second-order cost, which is the reason to file

It silently inflates every diff. On my change the same six files went from **1349 insertions / 593 deletions to 669 / 114** once the formatting was reverted — and `tx/dispatch/mod.rs` alone went from **665 changed lines to 38** for what is a three-hunk edit. A 665-line diff on a 38-line change is not reviewable; the actual edit is buried, and a reviewer who skims it is not reviewing the change at all.

## Suggested resolutions, in preference order

1. **Pin rustfmt and make the tree clean under it**, then add a `cargo fmt --check` leg so drift is caught once rather than rediscovered per-author. `make generate` already pins a toolchain for the shim build (#1864), so the pattern exists in this repo.
2. **If the tree is deliberately not rustfmt-managed**, say so in `docs/engineering-style.md` and in `userspace-dp/README.md`, because "run the formatter" is the default habit and nothing currently contradicts it.
3. Make the #6592 canary robust to line wrapping. Lower value than the above — the canary is doing its job, and it already has self-tests for wrapped publishes (`detects_a_publish_wrapped_across_lines_by_rustfmt`), which suggests wrapping was anticipated for detection but not for the *count* assertion.

Option 1 or 2 is the real fix; either one turns this from a trap into a rule.

## Interim guidance for anyone working in `userspace-dp`

Do not run `cargo fmt` across the crate. Format only the files you edited (`rustfmt <path>`), and check `git status --porcelain` before running the suite — a modified-file count in the hundreds means the formatter ran wide, and the suite failure you are about to debug is probably not yours.

## #8946 — config: every census that synthesises ONE value per site inherits leaf-contingency — three instruments, one remedy [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-06)

## The defect is in the METHOD, not in any one census

A census walks sites, synthesises **one** body statement or value per site,
compares two spellings, and publishes a verdict **about the pair**. The
measurement supports only a claim about *that leaf*. The two come apart whenever
the behaviour under test is contingent on which child is present — and when they
do, the census publishes a confident verdict that is wrong.

The direction of the error is the dangerous one: a pair that drops via leaf B
but not via leaf A is published **SAME**, and **a SAME verdict is never
audited**. It costs nothing to be wrong about, so nobody re-opens it.

## Three instruments, all of them found the same way

1. **`TestSweepFull`** (#8907/#8908). `interfaces <name>` published
   STRICT-REJECTS from one synthesised leaf; with a hand-written leaf both arms
   accept. Fixed by evaluating every site and publishing `LEAF-CONTINGENT` with
   the disagreeing set instead of collapsing to whichever leaf was sampled.
   **Four of seven contingent rows mixed SAME with CANDIDATE-DROP** — i.e. they
   could have published "no defect" over a real one.

2. **My batch-5 hand re-check** (#8879). I re-checked the sweep's SAME rows *by
   hand* — and used a single `dscp` fixture, clearing `class-of-service
   classifiers` and `rewrite-rules` as "genuinely SAME". Both drop via
   `inet-precedence` and `exp`. I had reported the sweep's version of this
   defect **one batch earlier**.

3. **My depth-2 sweep** (#8938). Synthesises one body statement per pair.
   `policy-statement then` reads SAME under it and is the row filed as #8933,
   where the compiler consumes the packed token into the terminal-action slot so
   the term stops terminating. The 26 DROPS it found are a **lower bound**; its
   20 SAMEs clear nothing.

Naming the failure did not prevent instances 2 and 3 — a mechanism caught both
(lane-8388's `LEAF-CONTINGENT` verdict named my batch-5 rows the moment it
shipped).

`pkg/config/compact_normalize_8662.go` is **1992 LOC** against a 2000-LOC

came back under by moving eleven lines of prose into `docs/log/`. **The next
admission crosses it again**, and the lane that hits it will be mid-batch with a

## The file holds two things with different growth rates

A data table that grows monotonically living in the same file as the algorithm
that reads it is why the threshold was reached. Splitting it is not a cosmetic
tidy: it puts the file that changes hourly in a different place from the file
that encodes the pass's behaviour, so an admission diff stops touching the
algorithm at all.

No behaviour change, no test changes beyond package-internal references. The
scope predicate's godoc should carry the admission criteria (gate column first,

## #8963 — frr: DHCP-learned routes carry no virtual-router ownership and render only in the default context [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-05)

`DHCPRoute` has no VRF field and `renderDHCPDefaults` takes no VRF context, so a
DHCP-learned default or classless route is emitted once, in the default FRR
context — even when the interface that learned it belongs to a routing instance.

## The sibling asymmetry, in the same file

**Static routes are VRF-aware** (`pkg/frr/config_render.go:154-160`):

```go
// the static-route `vrf <name>` clause, so it covers every static route
vrfPart = " vrf " + sanitizeFRRValue(vrfName)
```

**DHCP routes are not.** The type carries no instance
(`pkg/frr/manager.go`):

```go
type DHCPRoute struct {
	Destination string // "" = default route; else a classless-route prefix
	Gateway     string // "10.0.2.1" or "fe80::1"
	Interface   string // needed for IPv6 link-local gateways
	IsIPv6      bool
}
```

and the renderer is called once with no context (`manager.go:596`):

```go
renderDHCPDefaults(&b, fc)
```

`renderDHCPDefaults(b *strings.Builder, fc *FullConfig)` emits no `vrf` clause,
and its default-suppression logic compares against `fc.StaticRoutes` /
`fc.Inet6StaticRoutes` — the **top-level** statics — so a static default inside a
routing instance neither suppresses nor is suppressed by the DHCP-learned one.

The comparison is what makes this a finding rather than an observation: the same
file, for the same kind of object, threads a VRF clause for statics and not for
DHCP-learned routes.

## #8964 — configstore: admitting `system dataplane-type` will blackout-boot any node using the packed spelling — the retired-value rewriter runs on the un-normalized tree [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-06)

## Admitting `system dataplane-type` will blackout-boot any node whose config uses the packed spelling

**This is inert today and becomes a boot failure the moment the admission campaign reaches this container.** Filing before that happens rather than after.

### The reader

`rewriteRetiredDataplaneType` (`pkg/configstore/dataplane_retire.go:91`) exists to rewrite a retired `system { dataplane-type ebpf; }` into the userspace default *before* the compiler sees it — because the compiler **hard-rejects** `ebpf` (`ErrEBPFDataplaneRetired`, #1373).

It runs on the **raw tree**, at `store_persist.go:66` (Load) and `store.go:538` (SyncApply), so it never sees the normalizer — which runs inside the compiler. Measured, with a live control:

```
braced          system { dataplane-type ebpf; }   rewrites=1   leaf removed
packed          system dataplane-type ebpf;       rewrites=0   survives verbatim
control         system { host-name fw1; }         rewrites=0   (so 0 is not universal)
```

### Why it is harmless right now

`system dataplane-type` is **not** an admitted compact pair, so the packed leaf is dropped by the compiler anyway:

```
braced ebpf       DataplaneType="" EffectiveType=userspace
packed ebpf       DataplaneType="" EffectiveType=userspace
control userspace DataplaneType="userspace"
```

Same outcome by a different route. Nothing is wrong today.

### Why it stops being harmless

The depth-2 campaign is admitting containers one at a time. Simulating the admission of `system dataplane-type` — one line added to `compactNormalizeInScope`, everything else untouched:

```
DR packed   rewrites=0        <- the rewriter STILL misses it
ET packed   COMPILE-ERR: "the legacy eBPF dataplane backend has been retired"
LC packed   Store.Load FAILS: "config DB present but does not compile"
            activeNil = TRUE
```

`ActiveConfig() == nil` with `everCommitted` true is the #1922 bootstrap/lifeline state: the node comes up with no configuration. **A persisted config that boots fine today stops booting**, and the rewriter that exists to prevent exactly that is blind to the spelling.

## #8965 — daemon: a live HA control-endpoint change restarts comms on the new endpoint BEFORE telling the peer, stranding both nodes [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-06)

A commit that moves the cluster control tuple restarts the local node's cluster
comms onto the **new** endpoint, and only then tries to push the config to the
peer — which is still on the **old** endpoint. The push has no connection, so the
peer never learns the new tuple and the two nodes are durably partitioned.

## Verified at master `53f7fa891`

**The edit is permitted.** `cluster_topology_preflight.go` refuses only *mode*
changes (standalone ↔ clustered, which require a reboot). Its own comment:

> *Desired mode already matches the running HA runtime: an intra-mode edit (both
> standalone, or both clustered) reconciles live.*

A clustered→clustered control-endpoint move is exactly such an intra-mode edit.

**The ordering is apply-then-push**, in `applyAndSyncCommitted`
(`pkg/daemon/daemon_apply_commit.go`):

```
:264   applyErr := d.applyConfigLocked(d.applyCancelCtx(), compiled)
        └─ step 20 → stopClusterComms(); start(d.daemonCtx)   on the NEW endpoint
:306   d.pushCommittedConfigToPeer()
```

Forty-two lines apart, and the transport the push needs was torn down and rebuilt
on a different address by the call above it.

## Why it does not self-heal

- The peer never received the candidate, so it stays on the old tuple. Both sides
  are durably configured, so **reconnect retry and reboot reproduce it** — retry
  knows only the new endpoint, the peer knows only the old.
- `QueueConfig` returns early on a nil/disconnected connection, so the push fails
  **silently** rather than erroring the commit.
- The #5863 reconciler is gated on `syncPeerConnected`, so it cannot bootstrap a
  mismatch in which nothing is connected.
- Heartbeats carry no config, so the surviving channel cannot deliver the fix.

second fabric stream — overwrites the in-progress epoch and discards the
accumulated receive set, after which the newer stream's `BulkEnd` is rejected as

}

accumulators:

s.resetRecvGen()
s.bulkMu.Lock()
s.bulkInProgress = true

s.bulkRecvV4 = make(map[dataplane.SessionKey]struct{})    // newer snapshot discarded
s.bulkRecvV6 = make(map[dataplane.SessionKeyV6]struct{})
s.bulkZoneSnapshot = zoneSnap

So a stale `BulkStart` is accepted, the newer bulk's accumulated state is thrown
away, and the newer `BulkEnd` then fails the guard at `:314` — the two handlers
disagree about which epoch is authoritative, and only one of them checks.

`startClusterSyncAuxLoops` launches four comms-scoped loops. Three of them handle

starts nothing, until an unrelated comms restart.

## The four loops, and the one that is different

```go

go d.configSyncReconcileLoop(commsCtx)      // unconditional, by design
d.ensureDHCPLeaseSyncLoop(cc.DHCPLeaseSync) // idempotent starter, by design
go d.runPersistentNatLeaseSyncLoop(commsCtx)// unconditional

The siblings state their reasoning in place:

> *`configSyncReconcileLoop` — Started unconditionally (**config-sync may be
> enabled by a later commit without a comms restart**)*

> *`ensureDHCPLeaseSyncLoop` — Routed through the idempotent starter (#4647) so a
> **later `dhcp-lease-synchronization` knob toggle from the apply path** shares
> this same launch/stop path*

to the third.**

## #8969 — deploy: a tilde prerelease sorts AFTER its base release, so it passes the image anti-rollback watermark [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-05)

`_ver_key` in `scripts/deploy/xpf-deploy.py` splits a version on the first `-`
only. A Debian-style tilde prerelease (`1.2.3~rc1`) therefore has no recognised
suffix, its release component parses as the non-numeric token `3~rc1`, and it
sorts **after** `1.2.3` — so it passes an anti-rollback watermark set at the
final release.

## Measured, with the sibling as its own control

Executing `_ver_key` directly:

```
watermark      candidate       newer?
1.2.3          1.2.3-rc1       no (blocked)                 <- correct
1.2.3          1.2.3~rc1       YES (passes anti-rollback)   <- the defect
1.2.3          1.2.4           YES (passes anti-rollback)   <- control: a real upgrade
1.2.3          1.2.3-5-gabc    YES (passes anti-rollback)   <- control: ahead of tag, by design
1.2.3~rc1      1.2.3-rc1       no (blocked)
```

**Rows 1 and 2 are the same semantic operation in two spellings and they
disagree.** The hyphen form is handled exactly as the docstring promises —
*"a pre-release sorts BEFORE its base release … 1.2.3-rc1 < 1.2.3"* — and the
tilde form gets the opposite ordering.

The other two rows are controls: the comparator is alive and discriminating, so
row 2 is a real mis-ordering rather than a dead function.

## Mechanism

```python
rel, _, suffix = s.partition("-")     # "1.2.3~rc1" -> rel="1.2.3~rc1", suffix=""
for tok in rel.split("."):
    rel_key.append((0, int(tok)) if tok.isdigit() else (1, tok))
if not suffix:
    pre_rank = (1,)                   # "base release" — but this is not one
```

`"3~rc1".isdigit()` is false, so the third component becomes `(1, "3~rc1")`, which
sorts **after** `(0, 3)`. The prerelease is ranked as a base release *and* its
release component outranks the real one.

## #8971 — config: the #7484 spelling-gate lost 14 sites of coverage when the filter-term then actions were registered as not-a-value-list [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-06)

Tracker for a coverage reduction taken deliberately in the `firewall <f> term <t> then` fix (issue 8939). Filed so the number is **owed rather than absorbed** — a floor that drops with a paragraph attached is absorbed; one that drops with an open issue naming the sites is not.

## The accounting, verbatim

    master      1098 enumerated   706 compared   392 blind
    after       1076 enumerated   692 compared   384 blind

**Net: 14 fewer sites compared.**

## What happened, in order

1. `packedStatements` on the two filter-term `then` nodes made a packed run split. Eight leaves left the `flag (read, but value-less)` blind bucket (209 → 201) and became **comparable to the spelling gate for the first time**.
2. Once comparable, 22 sites (11 actions × inet/inet6) immediately reported `#2419 class: shape-dependent drop`.
3. Following the gate's own instruction — *"if this leaf is not a value list at all, add it to notAValueList with the reason, having VERIFIED where the extra tokens land"* — all 22 were registered, which removed them from enumeration.

## The differential is PRE-EXISTING, not introduced

This was measured, because the first reading was wrong. The compiled objects for the two spellings the change actually touches are **identical, before and after**:

    then { count c1 c2; }   braced   count="c1"   before AND after
    then count c1 c2;       packed   count="c1"   before AND after

So the opt-in did not create a divergence between those arms. The gate compares six spellings (A–F) and reports the divergence among ones this change does not touch — it was there all along, invisible because the sites sat in a blind bucket. **The change exposed it; it did not cause it.**

## Why registration is still the right call, and what it costs

None of the eleven actions is a value list: `accept` / `discard` / `log` / `syslog` are `args:0`, and `count` / `dscp` / `forwarding-class` / `loss-priority` / `policer` / `routing-instance` / `traffic-class` are `args:1`. A two-element list is malformed input at every one of them, and the divergence is only in how six spellings mishandle a token that should not be there.

Verified before registering, as the map's contract requires:

    then { count c1 c2; }      count="c1"        c2 DISCARDED
    then { dscp af11 af21; }   dscp="af11"       af21 DISCARDED
    then { accept extra1; }    action="accept"   extra1 DISCARDED

`strictRejects=false`, `warnings=0` on all three.

## What is owed

1. **Whether the A–F divergence on malformed input matters at all.** If it does not, these sites are correctly out of the gate's population and the floor drop is permanent and fine — but that should be a decision someone took, not a side-effect nobody re-opened.
2. **The silent discard itself** is a separate defect: a trailing token on a `then` action is dropped with no rejection and no warning. Deliberately scoped out of the 8939 fix rather than folded in; recorded here so it is not lost.

def _virsh_domain_exists(name):

    except FileNotFoundError:
        return False
```

`virsh dominfo` exits non-zero for a missing domain **and** for a failed
connection to libvirtd, a permissions failure, or a timeout. All of them become
`False`, which the callers read as "nothing to tear down".

```

## Mechanism

`scripts/ignored-cell-census.sh:141`:

```sh
HITS=$(grep -rn --include='*.rs' '#\[ignore' $SCAN_LIST 2>/dev/null)
```

Unanchored, and with no exclusion of `//`/`///` comment lines. Any prose that *mentions* `#[ignore` — including a backtick-quoted mention inside a doc comment — is counted as a live ignored cell and then judged for whether its "reason" declares a kind. Note it also matches `#[ignore` as a prefix, so `#[ignored_...]` would count too.

## Why this one bites

The prose landed in `a7729e8da` ("server: serve sync_session without the ServerState mutex"), which **removed** two `#[ignore]` attributes and documented that it had done so. So the guard fires precisely on the correct behaviour: un-ignoring a cell and recording why. The cheapest way for a lane to get `make selftest` green is to delete the explanation — the guard's incentive points at erasing the record it exists to protect.

## #8987 — daemon: a live control-INTERFACE move has the same partition shape as #8965 and is not gated [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-06)

Split out of #8965, which fixed the peer-**address** half. Filed rather than left in a code comment because it is, in the words of the person who found it, *"exactly the kind of half nobody re-opens"* — and a landed partial fix removes the reason anyone looks again.

## The shape

#8965: changing the cluster control-link peer **address** on a running cluster restarted comms on the new endpoint and then pushed the config to the old one, stranding both nodes in a durable partition. That is now refused at all three apply paths by a commit preflight.

**A `control-interface` move has the same shape.** The local node moves its control link to a different interface, comms restart there, and the peer is still reachable only via the old one — with no path by which either learns. `reconcileConfigSyncToPeer` returns early on `!syncPeerConnected`, that flag is set true in exactly one place (the session-sync connect callback), and both delivery paths funnel through `QueueConfig`, which no-ops without a connection. The same "no healing" argument #8965 established applies unchanged.

## Why it was not fixed with the address half

The manager keeps no **running** value for `control-interface` to compare a candidate against. A gate written without that would compare **config to config**, which:

- cannot tell "the operator is changing it" from "this is the value it already had", and
- would fire on a **peer-synced text** at `syncAndApply`, refusing a legitimate sync.

The address gate is safe there for a measured reason: `PeerAddress` is per-node, a synced text compiles for the local node, so in steady state candidate equals running and the gate is a no-op. **That reasoning does not transfer**, so extending the gate needs the plumbing to expose the running interface first.

## What a fix owes

1. **A running value to compare against** — the manager exposing the interface the control link is actually bound to, not the one the candidate config names.
2. **The same peer-sync no-op property the address gate has**, demonstrated rather than assumed: refusing at `syncAndApply` without it would be a new defect, which is the trap the address half had to measure its way out of.
3. **The refusal must name the procedure**, as #8965's does — both endpoints, the both-nodes-then-restart path, and an explicit warning against committing on each node separately, which is the same partition by hand. A refusal without a path sends operators to the workaround that reproduces the defect.
4. **All three apply paths.** `commitAndApply`, `syncAndApply` and `commitConfirmedAndApply` all run the existing preflights; a gate wired at one is the partial-fix shape on a row where the remaining half is silent.

## Severity

Same as #8965: a durable partition on a commit whose purpose was to preserve HA, with both nodes reporting success. Lower likelihood only because moving the control link to a different interface is a rarer operation than re-addressing it — not because the consequence is smaller.

## #8990 — go test ./pkg/grpcapi/ is RED on master: the #8965 unmodeled-stanza gate rejects TestShowTextGolden's own `vlans` fixture [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-06)

`go test ./pkg/grpcapi/` fails on a clean `origin/master` (`d70616804`):

```
--- FAIL: TestShowTextGolden (0.00s)
    server_show_golden_test.go:242: Commit() error = commit check failed:
    unknown configuration stanza "vlans": it is not a recognised top-level
    keyword, so everything configured under it would be silently discarded
```

Reproduced against pristine master with no local edits.

## Cause

`1265b6498` ("config: reject an unmodeled top-level stanza at commit") added the gate at `pkg/config/schema_walk.go:1243`. `TestShowTextGolden`'s fixture commits a top-level `vlans` stanza:

```
server_show_golden_test.go:108:  "vlans",
server_show_golden_test.go:210:  "vlans v100 vlan-id 100",
```

**`vlans` has never been a modelled top-level keyword** — there is no `"vlans"` anywhere in non-test `pkg/config`, and `git log -S'"vlans"' -- pkg/config/` is empty. So the fixture was always configuring a stanza the compiler did not model; before the gate, the stanza was silently discarded and the test passed anyway.

That makes this a **correct gate finding a pre-existing latent defect in a test fixture**, not a bad gate. The fixture was asserting ShowText output for a config whose `vlans` half never reached the compiler — the exact "silently discarded" outcome the new gate exists to make loud.

## Why it needs a decision rather than a mechanical fix

Two remedies, and they differ in what they claim:

1. **Drop `vlans` from the fixture.** Correct if xpf models VLANs only through `interfaces <if> unit <n> vlan-id` (which is what the compiler supports today). The fixture then stops asserting anything about a stanza that does not exist.
2. **Model a top-level `vlans` stanza.** Junos has one, and `README`/`CLAUDE.md` advertise "VLANs: 802.1Q tagging, trunk ports" without saying through which grammar. If an operator can reasonably type `set vlans v100 vlan-id 100`, then the gate has just converted a silent discard into a hard commit rejection for a spelling the product implies it accepts — which is the right failure direction but is a user-visible behaviour change worth naming.

Choosing (1) without checking (2) would resolve the red while leaving the question of whether the documented VLAN support is reachable by the grammar operators would try.

## Scope note

Filed rather than fixed because `1265b6498` looks like live work and its author is better placed to say which remedy matches the gate's intent. Found while re-verifying an unrelated `pkg/grpcapi` comment for #8942; my change there is comment-only and this failure reproduces without it.
