## #8992 — configstore: a packed stanza cannot be deleted and the error claims the `system` container does not exist [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-06)

## A stanza written in the packed spelling cannot be deleted, and the error says the wrong thing

`delete` operates on the RAW candidate tree, so it cannot find a stanza written in the packed spelling — and the diagnostic it returns denies the existence of a container the operator can see in their own configuration.

### Measured

`applyEditLine` (`pkg/configstore/store_command.go:563`) → `tree.DeletePathGrouped`:

```
braced   system { master-password { pseudorandom-function juniper-prf1; } }
         delete system master-password
         -> err=nil, stanza removed

packed   system master-password pseudorandom-function juniper-prf1;
         delete system master-password
         -> err = path not found: container "system" does not exist
         -> stanza REMAINS

control  system { host-name fw1; }                 (master-password genuinely absent)
         delete system master-password
         -> err = path not found: no node matching "master-password"
```

The control matters: the truly-absent case produces a **different** message, so the packed failure is not the generic not-found path. The edit walker is looking for a `system` **container** and the packed spelling puts `system` on a leaf's own `Keys`, so the lookup fails one level up from where the operator is pointing.

### Why the message is the harm

`container "system" does not exist` is false on its face — `show configuration` renders `system master-password pseudorandom-function …`, and `system` is a top-level stanza of every real config. An operator reading that has no path from the diagnostic to the cause, and the natural next step (re-check the spelling of `master-password`) is looking in the wrong place.

### Class

This is the raw-AST reader class (#8903), in the **mutator** subclass #8964 established — a reader under-reads, a mutator changes the wrong thing or nothing. It differs from both known members in its failure direction:

```
#8867  SchemaValidate     silent    validated nothing
#8898  master-password    silent    resolved nothing
#8964  retired rewriter   silent    let a fatal token through (latent)
this   delete             LOUD      refuses, with a diagnostic that misdirects
```

## #8993 — security: policy-rematch `extensive` is accepted but only partially enforced — sessions of an unchanged policy survive an address-book change [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-06)

Split out of #8942, which found the residual documented in code and tracked nowhere: the comment at `pkg/config/compiler_validate_warn.go:675` says *"The `extensive` gap stays tracked in #4234"*, and **#4234 is CLOSED**.

## The residual, and it is live

`set security policies policy-rematch extensive` commits, and four lines below that comment live code emits an advisory saying so:

```
security policies policy-rematch extensive configured but only partially
enforced — xpf re-evaluates live sessions of a policy whose own match/action
changed, but does NOT re-evaluate sessions of an UNCHANGED policy when a
referenced address-book / application object changes (the `extensive` case);
those sessions keep forwarding until idle timeout (#4234)
```

## What actually shipped, and what did not

The **modified-policy** half of #4234 shipped: `changedPolicyRuntimeIDs` / `clearSessionsForModifiedPolicies` in `pkg/daemon/daemon_policy_invalidate.go`, gated on `policy-rematch`. `daemon_policy_invalidate.go:24-35` documents that an earlier comment calling it "deferred, intentionally out of scope" stopped being true when that half shipped.

The **`extensive`** half did not. `changedPolicyRuntimeIDs` compares policies via `PoliciesByStableKey` — the policy's own match/action text. A policy whose text is unchanged but which references an address-book entry or application whose *definition* changed is not detected, so its live sessions are never re-evaluated.

## Why it is worth its own issue

Junos `policy-rematch extensive` exists precisely to catch the object-definition case. An operator who tightens an address-set to remove a host reasonably expects existing sessions from that host to be re-evaluated. Today they keep forwarding until idle timeout, which for a long-lived TCP session is unbounded in practice.

The advisory means this is **named rather than silent**, which is the right posture and is why this is a gap rather than a defect. But the deferral pointed at a closed issue, so nothing tracked closing it.

## Closure condition

Either `extensive` re-evaluates sessions when a referenced address-book / application object changes, or the advisory is rewritten to state the limitation as permanent with the reason (the shape `TestRatifiedGatesDoNotPromiseAFollowUp_6674` guards). Both are closable; the current state — advisory promising a gap, tracker closed — is neither.

## #8994 — routing/dataplane: three interface-name resolvers are kept in step by a NOTE, and the migration that was to centralize them is closed [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-06)

Split out of #8942. Found by READING rather than by its sweep — the pattern had no arm for "tracked as a follow-up to #N".

## The residual

`pkg/config/types.go` carries:

> NOTE: Keep in sync with `snapshotLinuxName` in `pkg/dataplane/userspace/interfaces.go` and `resolveJunosIfName` in `pkg/daemon/daemon_dhcp.go`. Migration to centralize all callers is tracked as a follow-up to **#1565**.

**#1565 is CLOSED** and the centralization did not happen. Three resolvers still compute a Linux interface name from a Junos ref, and they are held in agreement by a comment.

## Why a NOTE is the wrong mechanism here

The three do not merely duplicate logic — they have *known structural differences* that the note does not capture:

- `ResolveKernelIfName` decides which arm to take by splitting on `"."`, so an interface whose AUTHORED name contains a dot (`ip-0/0/0.0` is legal in the config tree) takes the dotted arm and can consume an unrelated unit's `TunnelNameMap` entry.
- `snapshotLinuxName` has no such ambiguity because it branches on `unit != nil` — a structural fact rather than a string shape.

That divergence is documented in `types.go` itself as load-bearing. So the resolvers are not interchangeable, and "keep in sync" understates what a caller has to know.

## Observable consequence today

The routing-vs-dataplane instance is filed separately as a sibling issue: routing keys its desired tunnel set by `TunnelConfig.Name` while the dataplane binds via `snapshotLinuxName`, and an orphan device can result. That is one instance of this general condition rather than a separate cause.

## Closure condition

Either the callers route through one resolver (with the dotted/structural distinction expressed as an explicit argument rather than inferred from the string), or the NOTE is replaced by a guard that FAILS when the three disagree on a shared corpus of refs — including the dotted-authored-name case. A comment cannot detect drift; a table-driven equivalence test can.

Filed rather than left on #8942 because this is separately ownable and separately closable, and because a residual tracked only in a comment on a closed issue is the defect #8942 documents.

Split out of #8942. The comment at `pkg/config/compiler_validate_strict_tunnel_ipip.go:351` attributes an orphan-device case to *"the routing-vs-dataplane name divergence tracked in #6941"*. **#6941 is CLOSED and both halves still key differently.**

## The divergence, verified

- Routing: `pkg/routing/tunnel.go:215` — `desired[tc.Name] = true`, keyed by `TunnelConfig.Name`.
- Dataplane: `pkg/dataplane/userspace/interfaces.go:859` — `snapshotLinuxName(cfg, ifName, iface, unit)`.

These are two different functions producing the name a tunnel is known by, and nothing makes them agree.

## Consequence

The comment describes the observable: an orphan `reth0` device that an operator can see and that carries no traffic. It notes the same orphan appears with `mode gre`, where the #4785 IPIP gate is deliberately silent — so the IPIP gate is not its cause, and no advisory owns it. The device is real, no gate claims it, and the tracker that was to fix the cause is closed.

## Relationship to the sibling issue

This is one **instance** of the general condition filed alongside it: three interface-name resolvers kept in step by a "keep in sync" NOTE, whose centralizing migration (#1565) is also closed. Fixing the general case subsumes this one; fixing this one alone leaves the other two resolvers free to drift. They are filed separately because they are separately ownable and the general fix is much larger — but whoever takes either should read both.

## Closure condition

Either routing and the dataplane resolve the tunnel's Linux name through one function, or a guard asserts they agree across a corpus of tunnel configs including the cases that distinguish them (unit-0 collapse, `reth` resolution, an authored name containing a dot). Closing it by deleting the comment would leave the orphan device unexplained, which is worse than the current state.

## #8996 — routing: ClearTunnels does not flush WireGuard addresses, and whether it should is deferred to a closed issue [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-06)

Split out of #8942. `pkg/routing/tunnel.go:1283`:

> Whether ClearTunnels should also flush WG addresses is deferred to **#1434** (full teardown grammar).

**#1434 is CLOSED** and `ClearTunnels` still does not flush them.

## What the code does

`clearLocked` deliberately does NOT delete WireGuard links — they are persistent and are excluded from `tunnels`/`ownedNames` (#1432 S2a). It drops `t.wgConfigured` so a post-Clear `Apply` re-adopts cleanly. What it does not do is remove addresses previously configured on those persistent links.

## Why this is an open QUESTION rather than a known bug

The surrounding comments show the teardown semantics were reasoned about carefully: non-WG links are removed precisely because leaving them would strand "stale addresses and XFRM if_id state that xpf no longer tracks". WG links are exempt from removal by design. Whether the *addresses* on an exempt link should also be exempt was left open — and both answers are defensible:

- **Flush them**: a Clear should leave no xpf-configured state on any link, matching the reasoning applied to every other link type.
- **Keep them**: the link is persistent precisely because something outside xpf's teardown cycle may depend on it, and its address is part of that.

That is exactly the kind of question a tracking issue is for, and its tracker is closed — so nobody is going to answer it.

## Closure condition

Either `ClearTunnels` flushes WG addresses (with the re-adoption path checked, since `wgConfigured = nil` means the next `Apply` believes it is configuring fresh), or the comment states the retention as a decision with its reason and stops deferring. A one-line answer closes this; what cannot stand is a deferral pointing at a closed issue.

Smallest of the four split out of #8942, and the most likely to be settled by whoever last touched WG teardown.

## #8997 — cluster: an elided `chassis cluster strict-session-auth` is silently dropped on HA config sync — the node-local preserve hook cannot see it [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-06)

## `strict-session-auth` is silently lost on HA config sync when written in an elided spelling

`preserveNodeLocalChassis` exists to stop config-sync carrying node-local `chassis cluster` flags between peers (#7441). It decides using `chassisClusterFlagSet`, which walks the **raw tree** with `FindChild` — so it cannot see the flag in either elided spelling, concludes the local node does not have it, and lets the incoming config overwrite the posture.

### Measured, end to end

Local node has the flag; the incoming synced config does not. The hook should preserve the local posture:

```
local braced           chassis { cluster { strict-session-auth; } }   preserved: TRUE
local cluster-elided   chassis { cluster strict-session-auth; }       preserved: FALSE
local fully packed     chassis cluster strict-session-auth;           preserved: FALSE
```

The reader underneath, with a control that proves `false` is not universal:

```
braced                 chassisClusterFlagSet = true
cluster brace elided   chassisClusterFlagSet = false
fully packed           chassisClusterFlagSet = false
control (flag absent)  chassisClusterFlagSet = false
```

### Why it goes silent rather than loud

`preserveNodeLocalChassis` compares `localSet` against `incomingSet` and `continue`s when they agree. Misreading the local node as *not having* the flag makes both sides `false`, so they agree, so the hook does nothing — the branch that logs and the branch that fails closed are both downstream of a difference that is never detected. **The fail-closed handling in that function is correct and unreachable for this input.**

### Consequence

`strict-session-auth` is a session-authentication posture. A node that has it set in an elided spelling keeps it until its peer sends a config sync, and then loses it, with:

- no warning — the hook took no action, so nothing logged
- no visible config change the operator initiated
- `show configuration` on the local node still rendering the flag before the sync

The two nodes then run different session-auth postures, which is the asymmetry #7441 exists to prevent.

### Class

Raw-AST reader (#8903): the fold is a property of the compile path and this reader runs outside it. Fourth confirmed member, and the second whose consequence is a security posture rather than a lost value.

## #9006 — harness census: an UNTRACKED local file fails the gate with a diagnostic that points at master [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-06)

## What happened

`make selftest` reported `passed=155 skipped=0 failed=2` on my checkout, with `scripts/harness-census.sh` and its selftest both failing:

```
FAIL: UNREACHED and undeclared -- invoked by no Makefile recipe, and not
      declared in test/incus/HARNESSES.unreached:
        test/incus/per-stream-diag.sh
      Remedy, pick one:
        - add a Makefile recipe that runs it (then it is a gate someone can run), or
        - add a line to test/incus/HARNESSES.unreached: '<path>  <one-line reason>'
```

**`test/incus/per-stream-diag.sh` is not in the repository.** It is an untracked local file:

```
$ git ls-files --error-unmatch test/incus/per-stream-diag.sh
error: pathspec ... did not match any file(s) known to git
$ git log -- test/incus/per-stream-diag.sh      # (no output)
```

In a clean checkout of the same SHA the census is fine — `52 runnable harnesses`, `OK`, against `53` with the stray file present.

## Why this is worth a change rather than a shrug

The census scans the **filesystem**, which is correct — a harness you have added and not yet committed is exactly the thing it should catch. The defect is the **diagnostic**, and it is the shape this campaign has been cataloguing (compare #8992, where `delete` refuses with `container "system" does not exist` while `show configuration` renders the container).

The message asserts *"a harness was added or a recipe removed"* and offers two remedies, **both of which are wrong for this input**:

- *add a Makefile recipe* — for someone's local scratch diagnostic, no.
- *declare it in `HARNESSES.unreached`* — that would commit a declaration naming a file that does not exist in the repo, and the census has a separate check that FAILS exactly that (`a declaration for a path that no longer exists is a FAIL`). So following the printed remedy produces a different failure.

## #9018 — userspace-dp/wireguard: the worker discards the peer identity that Keepalive/MalformedInner carry, so an authenticated keepalive never roams a NAT-rebound endpoint — and it clears the T7 reinit arm on the way out [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-06)

`try_decap` returns `DecapError::Keepalive([u8;32])` and `DecapError::MalformedInner([u8;32])` —
both carrying the **proven peer public key**, added by #7686 and #7230 precisely so the identity
would stop dying with the error. The AF_XDP worker throws it away:

`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/wg/decap.rs:148`

```rust
let outcome = engine.try_decap(record, &mut decap_buf).ok()?;
```

`.ok()?` collapses every error arm. The socket path does it correctly —
`wg_control/dispatch.rs:230-261` maps both to `InboundOutcome::Authenticated(pk)` — but the socket
path is unreachable for these packets, because `wg_classify.rs:136-143`'s
`wg_worker_claims_record` is true for any type-4 record on the steered port to a local destination
and `lib.rs:757` then declines `cpumap_or_pass`. A keepalive **is** a type-4 transport record.

The file knows: `decap.rs:153-155` says *"It authenticated, so the control thread's endpoint
learning still wants it"* — and then does not do it. `note_worker_observed_endpoint`
(`decap.rs:210-217`) is reached only after a successful decap **and** a successful
`build_logical_ingress_packet`, so the declined arms never roam the endpoint.

`engine.rs:1630-1636` stamps `peer.note_authenticated_recv(now_ns)` **before** returning
`Err(Keepalive(..))` at `:1664-1666`. `peer.rs:358-361` shows what that stores: it sets
`last_recv_any_ns` and **clears `t7_armed_send_ns`** — the no-reply reinit arm. So the session is
refreshed as alive while its endpoint stays stale, and the mechanism that would otherwise force a
re-handshake is disarmed by the very packet that should have roamed the peer.

A keepalive from a **new** endpoint updates nothing. The declined frame then continues as ordinary
outer UDP to a local address (`poll_stages.rs:366-372` returns the original meta and no owned
frame), reaches the LocalDelivery arm, and `host_inbound_gated_lo0_action`
(`poll_descriptor/filter.rs:1160-1169`) calls `host_inbound_admits_iface`, which has **no
WireGuard exemption** (`forwarding/host_inbound.rs:817-833`) and no WG port injected into the
userspace zone views. Denied, silently dropped, counted only in the aggregate

## #9025 — logging/dataplane: syslog UDP writes and trace/local-log disk writes are synchronous and deadline-free on the EventStream reader goroutine — the one that also carries HA session sync and the ISSU drain signal [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-06)

Two synchronous, deadline-free I/O sites sit on the EventStream reader goroutine. That goroutine is
not a logging goroutine — the same `switch` loop (`pkg/dataplane/userspace/eventstream.go:541-611`)
also handles `EventTypeSessionOpen/Update/Close` (**HA session sync**), `EventTypeDrainComplete`
(**ISSU**) and `EventTypeFullResync`. Stalling it stalls those.

## Site 1 — syslog UDP writes have no deadline, and the comment exempting them is false

`pkg/logging/syslog.go:696-698` (`writeMsg`) and `:814-816` (`writeBinaryMsg`) do a bare
`s.conn.Write(...)` for UDP. TCP/TLS route through `streamWrite`, which arms `defaultWriteTimeout`
(4 s). **UDP is the default protocol** (`:235-236`).

The exemption rests on a comment — `syslog.go:22-23`, repeated at `:642`:

> UDP is connectionless and never blocks on Write, so these do not apply to it.

The project's own flowexport module refutes that verbatim, `pkg/flowexport/transport.go:174-179`
(#4423 H07):

> A connected-UDP Write is normally instantaneous, but it **can block indefinitely on a full socket
> send buffer** (ENOBUFS / a congested or down egress path parks the goroutine in the netpoller
> until the buffer drains).

Two modules in one tree hold opposite beliefs about the same syscall; one of them armed a deadline
and one did not.

## Site 2 — trace and local-log writers do synchronous disk I/O inline

`pkg/logging/trace.go:128` — `TraceWriter.HandleEvent` takes `tw.mu` and calls
`tw.file.WriteString(line)` on a raw `*os.File` (**no `bufio`**), then calls `tw.rotate()` inline
when the size cap trips. `pkg/logging/locallog.go:17,162` has the same shape.

Both run inside the synchronous callback loop `for _, cb := range cbs { cb(rec, data) }`
(`pkg/logging/ringbuf.go:725-727`) via `flowTraceCallback` (`pkg/daemon/daemon_flow.go:685-691`).
No queue, no async handoff — one `write(2)` per logged event on the shared reader goroutine.

The contract is already stated in-tree, and it names this collateral by name.
`pkg/flowexport/routemask.go:45-50` (#3743) moved FIB lookups off this exact path because they
*"stall the event reader and every other callback behind it (**including the trace writer**)"*.

## The defect

#7160 / PR #8106 made `routing_domain` part of session identity and stamped it
at what its own comment calls

> **THE single site that populates `SessionKey.routing_domain` for a received
> frame** — `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/poll_descriptor/mod.rs:326-338`

The local-origin GRE path does not go through that site. It reads packets off
the TUN device, outside the AF_XDP descriptor loop, so nothing ever stamps its
key and the session is published under **domain 0**.

```rust
// userspace-dp/src/afxdp/tunnel.rs — build_local_origin_tunnel_tx_request
let flow = parse_session_flow_from_bytes(&inner_frame, meta)  // routing_domain: 0
    .ok_or_else(|| "parse_local_origin_session_flow_failed".to_string())?;
...
let session_entry = SyncedSessionEntry {
    key: flow.forward_key,        // <- domain 0, never stamped
```

The domain **is** available at that point: the function has already resolved the
tunnel's own logical ifindex (`decision.resolution.egress_ifindex`) and uses it
one line earlier for `forwarding.egress_zone_id(...)`. Rust records the
per-ifindex domain in `afxdp/forwarding_build/interfaces.rs`; Go supplies it in
`pkg/dataplane/userspace/interfaces.go`.

## The prerequisite is in the shipped reference config

`docs/ha-cluster-userspace.conf`:

```
routing-instances {
    sfmix {
        instance-type virtual-router;
        interface gr-0/0/0.0;
```

## #9039 — vrrp: chassis cluster reth-advertise-interval has no compiled-Config gate (the seconds knob got one in #8483) and the sender never clamps the 12-bit wire field [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-06)

`chassis cluster reth-advertise-interval` is milliseconds, stored by a bare `strconv.Atoi`,
and reaches the VRRPv3 wire through a 12-bit centisecond field with **no clamp anywhere on the
send path**. The local timer is bounded; the wire is not. The two therefore disagree, and the
peer derives its master-down window from the value that wrapped.

This is the sibling site of #8483, which fixed the *seconds* knob (`vrrp-group <id>
advertise-interval`, gated by `validateVRRPGroupTimersStrict`). The *milliseconds* knob never got
the same treatment, and #8315 — which established the 12-bit encodable range — recorded
`reth-advertise-interval` as **bounded**. That is true at `commit` and false on every tolerant
ingress.

## The chain, verified at `9bb0e8f11`

**1. Admission is a bare `Atoi`** — `pkg/config/compiler_system.go:2486-2492`:

```go
if n := clusterNode.FindChild("reth-advertise-interval"); n != nil {
        if v := nodeVal(n); v != "" {
                if ms, err := strconv.Atoi(v); err == nil {
                        ch.Cluster.RethAdvertiseInterval = ms
                }
        }
}
```

**2. The only bound is a SCHEMA bound** — `pkg/config/schema_chassis.go:175-177`:

```go
valueDesc: "RETH VRRP advertisement interval in milliseconds (10..40959; default 30)",
validator: ValidateInteger(10, 40959),
```

**3. A schema bound does not bind on the tolerant path, and the tree says so in its own words.**
`pkg/config/duration_bound_8642.go`:

> **WHY A SCHEMA CEILING IS NOT THE FIX.** `Store.compileTreeLenient` downgrades a typed-leaf
> violation to a warning on the tolerant `Store.Load` / `Store.SyncApply` ingress — configs the
> operator did not just author. So a schema bound stops an operator's `commit` and does not stop
> a persisted config from an older binary, or one pushed by an un-upgraded cluster primary.
> **The bound has to be at the conversion.**

is a one-line change at a site the second also touches.

`pkg/grpcapi/server_sessions.go:1681` — the function **does not take a `ctx` parameter at all**, so
it structurally cannot propagate one:

```go

        ...
        ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 5*time.Second)   // :1691
        ... peer ClearSessions ...                                                 // :1694
```

Its five siblings all derive from the caller: `fetchPeerSessions` `:724`,
`proxyPeerSessionSummary` `:1047`, `proxyPeerZonePairSummary` `:1198`, `proxyMonitorInterface`
(`server_diag_monitor.go:594`, from `stream.Context()`), `proxyPeerSystemAction`
(`server_diag_system_action.go:26`).

*Positive control:* `grep "WithTimeout(context.Background()"` over non-test `pkg/grpcapi` returns
exactly **two** sites — this one and `dialPeer`'s probe — so the population is complete and the
outlier is real.

**Consequence:** an operator cancelling a slow clustered clear returns immediately; the peer clear
proceeds to completion — a **ghost clear** — and the local scan slot stays pinned for up to ~9 s
(4 s dial + 5 s RPC) after the caller is gone. The objection "a clear must complete once started"
is contradicted by the code itself: #5882/#2468 built the whole `clearErrors` / partial-success
apparatus precisely because partial clears are normal and must be **reported**. A ghost clear is
the one outcome that apparatus cannot represent.

**Fix:** `context.WithTimeout(ctx, 5*time.Second)`, making this site identical to its five
siblings. One line.

## 2. Four handlers hold the local session-walk slot across the peer RTT

`GetSessions` (`:77` acquire -> `:715` `dialPeer` -> `:724` peerCtx -> `:747` peer RPC),

per-connection; the **verdict and the log line are per-call**. No limiter, no dedup, no sampling,

`principalForPeer` returns `Unauthenticated` for any unattributable peer, and `PrincipalForUID`
returns an **empty-Class principal** for any resolvable UID that is not a configured

service account, any compromised unprivileged daemon) can drive the line, at one `Warn` per unary
call on an already-open connection.

  postures are full-volume or exactly zero.

  mechanism this project has already been bitten by (the HA watchdog at 15 req/s producing 35K+
  lines per session).

## #9043 — UNRESOLVED: two in-tree READMEs make mutually inconsistent claims about XDP_PASS consuming UMEM frames in zero-copy — and one of them is steering the shim's non-IP design. One flood test or one kernel read settles it [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-06)

**This is an unresolved validation task, not a confirmed defect.** It is filed because the thing
that cannot be resolved is a **documented claim that is steering design decisions**, and the tree
contains two statements about it that cannot both be right.

## The claim

`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/umem/README.md:60-69`:

> In zero-copy mode on mlx5, an `XDP_PASS` action **permanently consumes a fill-ring frame**: the
> kernel holds the UMEM buffer in an SKB and never returns it.

If true, the shim's non-IP arm is a frame sink. `userspace-xdp/src/lib.rs:485` sends every non-IP
ethertype to `pass_non_ip_l2_direct()` (`:1289-1293`, a bare `XDP_PASS`), **before** the
`USERSPACE_INGRESS_IFACES` gate at `:524`, and — unlike its sibling
`pass_non_ip_l2_control_direct` at `:1285-1288` — it increments **no** `incr_fallback_stat`. The
arm is uncounted and unrate-limited, and an adjacent-LAN sender can drive it at wire rate with
plain ARP or LLDP.

A frame census confirms there is no independent replenishment: every `pending_fill_frames` producer
is a recycle of a frame userspace already owns (`worker/lifecycle.rs:332-336`, `tx/rings.rs:128,136`,
`shared_recycle.rs:65,175`, `transmit/mod.rs:128`, `neighbor_dispatch.rs`) plus the pre-bind prime.

## Why it could not be resolved

The README sentence could not be corroborated from anything else in the tree, and it **conflicts
with the mlx5e XSK zero-copy path**, where `mlx5e_xsk_skb_from_cqe_linear` copies into a fresh SKB
and reuses the UMEM frame on `XDP_PASS`.

Worse, the tree carries a **second, differently-scoped and mutually inconsistent** statement —
`userspace-dp/README.md:141`: *"Generic-XDP fallback consumes UMEM frames permanently on mlx5"* —
but generic-XDP interfaces bind `COPY_ONLY` (`bind.rs:6,187-189`), where `XDP_PASS` never touches
UMEM at all. So one of the two documents is wrong as written, and possibly both.

An independent verifier in the same run reached the opposite conclusion by a different route while
checking a neighbouring finding (#F021's "leaks fill frames" claim): *"an `XDP_PASS` on a
zero-copy socket makes the driver build an skb by copying out of the UMEM and then recycle the
frame; there is no descriptor leak."*

`test/incus/ledger_compare.py`'s merge-completeness lint is HEAD-only by construction:

```python
parents = subprocess.run(["git","rev-parse","HEAD^@"], ...).stdout.split()
if len(parents) < 2:
    print("lint-merge: HEAD is not a merge commit — nothing to check")
    return 0
```

Exit **0**. `scripts/run-selftests.sh:508-515` maps `rc == 0` to
`passl "ledger-merge-completeness (...)"` — so on any non-merge commit, `make selftest` prints a
**PASS line whose own text says nothing was checked**.

## Why that is not a cosmetic distinction here

A merge `M` that drops a ledger shard is caught only if someone runs `make selftest` while `HEAD`
is exactly `M`. One commit later it is permanently invisible, because plain `ledger-lint`
**cannot** see a missing row — the docstring at `:472-479` and `run-selftests.sh:480-484` both say
so: a deleted shard leaves a lint-clean directory.

So silent row loss corrupting a baseline is structurally possible. No evidence was found that it
has occurred; this is about the gate, not a known loss.

## Coverage check, including a correction to my own first attempt

I initially grepped for other git-history walkers using BRE, where `^` in `HEAD^@` is an anchor —
which returned a **false absence**. Re-run with `grep -F`:

```
grep -rn -F 'HEAD^@'   ->  ledger_compare.py:846 only
```

plus `harness-result.sh:412` (`git rev-parse HEAD` for a build sha). No watermark, no `rev-list`,
no history walk anywhere.

## Fix direction

Walk the merges since a stored watermark rather than inspecting `HEAD` — record the last-linted
commit and check every merge between it and `HEAD`, advancing the watermark on success. Failing
that, at minimum the non-merge path must **not print a PASS line**: a gate that did not run should

## #9048 — cluster: the session-sync generation guards fall through unconditionally when the LOCAL stored generation is 0 — which it is for every locally-created session, so a second primary overwrites and deletes freely [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-06)

Both HA session-sync generation guards fall through unconditionally when the **local** stored
generation is 0 — and it is 0 for every session this node created itself.

`installGenGuardV4` refuses only on `ok && stored != 0 && incoming != 0 && incoming < stored`;
`deleteGenGuardV4` only on `stored != 0 && deleteGen != 0 && deleteGen < stored`. `recvGenV4` is
populated **only** by `recordInstalledGenV4` — prior *peer* installs. So for a locally-created
session `stored == 0` and both guards pass anything.

`installClusterSyncedV4` / `deleteClusterSyncedV4` contain no `IsLocalPrimary*`, no RG, no zone and
no peer-liveness predicate — generation and `configEpochStale`, and nothing else. A second writer
therefore overwrites and deletes freely.

## Promotion on peer loss is unconditional

`electSingleNode` skips the readiness gate entirely once `peerEverSeen && !peerAlive` — by design
("peer LOSS … Fail open") — and `handlePeerTimeout` empties `m.peerGroups`, which removes the
`electRG` dual-active resolution arm (`election.go:215-237`) from reach. So both nodes can be
primary, and neither guard notices.

## The premise the originating report asserted and did not establish

It claimed a partial partition (heartbeat down, sync up). By **default** those share the same L3
interface and peer address — `clusterSyncTransport` prefers `ControlInterface` — and differ only in
transport and port (UDP/4784 vs TCP/4785), so a link failure kills both.

The partial partition needs a **UDP-selective** failure: plausibly a 1-2 s loss or CPU-starvation
burst against the sub-second heartbeat threshold (200 ms x 5) while the TCP connection, whose own
silence timeout is 30 s, stays established; or an ACL on 4784 alone; or a heartbeat auth/epoch
rejection. **When `ControlInterface` is unset**, sync falls back to the fabric and the two are
genuinely independent links, making the premise straightforwardly reachable.

That is the honest statement of reachability, and it is narrower than the report's.

## A guard the report missed, and why the finding survives it

`chassis cluster peer-fencing` (`pkg/config/schema_chassis.go:192-200`) sends `syncMsgFence` **over
the session-sync link** on heartbeat timeout (`heartbeat_manager.go:743` for `disable-rg`; the
#7147 `disable-rg-confirmed` variant fences *before* the election and awaits an ack). The receiver
(`sync_conn_read.go:686-705`) logs *"fence received from peer — disabling all RGs"* and calls
`OnFenceReceived()`. That is precisely a single-writer restoration for exactly this scenario — it

*(truncated — 101 lines total)*

## #9049 — rpm: an http-get whose body drain times out returns err=nil and is scored a SUCCESS — the io.Copy error is discarded and the 10s is folded into AvgRTT [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-06)

`pkg/rpm/rpm.go:882` drains the HTTP response body and **discards the error**:

```go
io.Copy(io.Discard, resp.Body)          // error dropped:  _, _ =
rtt := time.Since(start)                // :884 — body-transfer time billed to RTT
```

So a probe whose body read hits `http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}` returns
**`rtt ~= 10s, err = nil`** — and `runSingleTest`'s caller scores it a **SUCCESS**. A partial or
timed-out response is recorded as healthy, and the 10 s is folded into `MinRTT`/`MaxRTT`/`AvgRTT`
and the jitter figure.

This is the half the originating report did not find; its own headline claim is weaker than it
stated, and both corrections are recorded here so the fix lands in the right place.

## Correction 1 — the drain is NOT unbounded

`http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}` bounds body reads, and `io.Discard`'s pooled buffer means
no memory growth. Measured against a drip-feeding server: headers returned in **704 us**, and the
drain aborted at exactly the configured test timeout with
`Client.Timeout ... while reading body`. So the bound is 10 s in production, not unbounded.

## Correction 2 — no RTT threshold exists, so this does not slow remediation

A survey of the `thresholds` schema leaves (`pkg/config/schema_system.go:690-698`) finds the only
RPM threshold is `successive-loss`. Nothing keys off RTT, so the inflated figure does **not** drive
`services ip-monitoring` actuation. The report's "slows remediation" is unsupported.

## What is real

1. **A false success.** A timed-out body read is indistinguishable from a fast, complete one in the
   probe's own verdict. That is the direction that matters: the probe reports the path healthy when
   it is not.
2. **Measurement distortion of ~2800x** in the case measured above — 704 us of true responsiveness
   reported as 2.0 s — folded into the averages and jitter an operator reads to judge a path.

Both are observability rather than enforcement, but this project's contract is explicit that an
observability defect is not downgraded by default, and a probe that scores a timeout as a success
is the sharper end of that.

## #9050 — frr: a whitespace-bearing routing auth secret renders as a splittable vtysh line on the tolerant/peer-sync path — sanitizeFRRValue turns a TAB into a splitter and defers token safety to the gate that path downgrades [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-06)

A routing authentication secret containing whitespace renders as a **splittable vtysh line** on the
tolerant load / HA peer-sync path. The strict commit gate rejects it; the lenient path downgrades
that gate to a warning; and the render-side belt explicitly defers token safety to the gate that
was just downgraded.

## The seam, and the code's own comments are the proof it is unclosed

`pkg/config/compiler_validate_strict_routing.go:464-472` — `frrTokenUnsafeIndex` rejects `' '`,
`'\t'`, bytes `< 0x20`, and `0x7f`.

`pkg/frr/render_validate.go:42` — `sanitizeFRRValue` rejects **only** `< 0x20` / `0x7f`, and maps
them **to `' '`**. Its own doc:

> A single SPACE (0x20) is preserved … (unlike a whitespace-split auth secret, which
> `frrTokenUnsafeIndex` **also rejects at commit**)

So the render belt defers auth-secret token safety to the commit gate — and
`pkg/config/compiler_uniformgates_log_feed_routing.go:380-384` downgrades that same gate to
`cfg.Warnings` on the lenient path.

Worse, the strict validator's stated rationale (`compiler_validate_strict_routing.go:496-499`) —
*"the render path strips control chars and the offending line stays inert / single-line"* — is
**false for a literal space**, and false in the worse direction for a **tab**, which `sanitize`
converts *into* a splitter.

All six auth-key emit sites (BGP `password`, OSPF md5 and simple, RIP string, IS-IS area and
domain) go through `sanitizeFRRValue` only. No render-side token check exists: `render_validate.go`
covers router-id, cluster-id, prefixes, next-hops, interface operands, neighbor addresses and
origin — a positive control that the search reaches the belt code — and none covers auth-value
tokenization.

`configstore.CheckText` (`pkg/configstore/check.go`) calls `compileTreeStrict` and hard-rejects, and
`Store.Commit` uses the same. So a **new commit cannot introduce this**, and the day-0 config-drive

## #9051 — grpcapi/api: long-lived authorized streams are never re-authorized, so a demoted principal keeps its feed — and readAuthz's stated rationale ('a GET has no window') is exactly what SSE contradicts [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-06)

A principal demoted or deleted mid-stream keeps receiving `PermView`-tier feeds until it
disconnects or xpfd restarts. Both streaming surfaces adjudicate **once**, at stream open.

- **gRPC:** `pkg/grpcapi/authz.go:313-318` — `principalStreamInterceptor` calls `authorizeRPC` once
  then `return handler(srv, ss)`. `MonitorInterface`'s loop
  (`server_diag_monitor.go:539-582`) and `MonitorPacketDrop`'s (`:188-282`) select only on
  ctx / event / ticker.
- **REST:** `readAuthz` (`pkg/api/authz.go:823-843`) adjudicates once, then
  `eventStreamHandler` / `logStreamHandler` loop forever.

Only four streaming RPCs exist; `Ping` and `Traceroute` are self-terminating and correctly
excluded.

**Unary RPCs on the same connection ARE re-adjudicated** — `authorizeRPC` re-reads
`s.activeConfig()` and `/etc/passwd` every call — so the window is stream-only, and a *new*
connection gets a fresh identity (`TestANewConnectionGetsAFreshIdentity_5278`).

## The rationale that this hollows

The originating report cited the wrong contract. The sharper evidence is `readAuthz`'s own doc:

> A GET has no body to withhold: the handler is entered immediately, so **there is no window
> between the verdict and the action for a revocation to fall into**.

SSE is a GET whose handler runs **indefinitely** — exactly the window that sentence says cannot
exist — and both SSE routes sit behind that gate. The one-pass design was justified by a property
server-sent events do not have.

The same package independently treats this class as a defect worth fixing: `pkg/api/authz.go`'s
#5561-round-7 note calls *"a super-user demoted to read-only … kept the authority its old class
carried for the duration of an in-flight request"* a defect, and shipped a two-pass fix for it.

## Consequence, bounded

A demoted or deleted principal keeps receiving `PermView`-tier feeds — `POLICY_DENY` /
`SCREEN_DROP` records, log lines, interface counters — until it disconnects or the daemon
restarts. **No config, no secrets, no mutation.** Exploiting it requires an **already-open** stream
at the moment of demotion, which bounds it to a revocation-response gap rather than an access
bypass. There is no written revocation SLA anywhere in the tree, so "how long is too long" is
currently undefined — which is itself part of the finding.

## #9052 — [cohort] assurance: four gates that report a clean board for subjects they never examined — test-shim-run in no aggregate, cold-path-flooder unreached, a merge criterion citing CI that does not exist, and 310 uncounted Go skips [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-06)

Four independently-verified gaps in the assurance surface, grouped because they share one
acceptance criterion — *a gate that did not examine its subject must not report a clean board* —
and because fixing them one at a time re-learns the same lesson four times. Each is stated with its
own evidence and its own fix; split them if that suits the work better.

All verified at `9bb0e8f11`.

---

### 1. `make test` never runs the only behavioural coverage of the XDP shim

`test-shim-run` is defined at `Makefile:88` and is **a prerequisite of nothing**. `make test` is
`test: test-go test-rust` (`:79`). Every other occurrence of the string in the tree is a
self-reference inside its own recipe (`:90,110,111`), a docs mention
(`engineering-style.md:1682`), or the test file's own skip text.

The cells skip unprivileged, and the skip message states the gap itself
(`pkg/dataplane/userspace/fragment_disposition_7494_test.go:76-82`):

> **SKIPPED, NOT PASSED**: loading a BPF program needs root. `make test-go` never runs this file;
> use `make test-shim-run`. **A green `make test-go` is NOT evidence that fragment handling is
> covered.**

Its file header (`:13-31`) adds that this is the **only** behavioural coverage of the shim's
control flow, and that the #1864 verifier gate is a headroom instrument that **passes two distinct
wrong fixes**. There is no `.github/workflows/` (only `.github/instructions/`), no ledger row, no
adapter, and no mention in `docs/testing.md` or `docs/harness-ledger.md` — so there is not even a
documented manual task.

**Fix:** wire it into an aggregate that a root-capable run reaches, or add a ledger row declaring it
manual with an owner and a cadence. Silence is the current state and it is the worst option.

## #9053 — [cohort] userspace-dp: eight per-new-flow cost bounds verified, none measured — the #4800 harness is the owed action, plus two doc defects found while checking (a comment naming the wrong thread, and a shipped signal described as missing) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-06)

An external review filed eight separate per-new-flow / per-reconcile cost findings. **All eight
structural facts verified at `9bb0e8f11`; none of the consequence claims did.** This issue records
what is real, corrects two scope errors, links the existing owner, and carries the two genuine
defects found *while* checking them — which are documentation, not cost.

## The structural facts, verified

| Site | Proven source bound |
|---|---|
| `replicate_session_upsert` (`session_glue/mod.rs:1051-1104`) | per call: `(W-1)` mutex acquisitions + `(W-1)` entry clones + 1 replica clone |
| `publish_shared_session` (`shared_ops.rs:1139-1214`) | up to 4 entry copies + up to 4 key copies + 1 more key copy per index insert + up to 2 index acquisitions |
| `publish_live_session_entry` (`bpf_map/mod.rs`) | up to **6** serial `bpf()` syscalls per forward install |
| `remove_shared_session` (`shared_ops.rs:1249-1292`) | 3 map mutexes held simultaneously, with the index mutex nested inside all of them |
| `snapshot_shared_session_entries` + `replay_synced_sessions` | O(S) clone under the global lock; S x (<=4) BPF syscalls; S x W queue pushes with no drain |
| source-NAT `matches` (`nat/source/match_rules.rs:330-360`) | O(R) cheap compares + O(R_zone-matching x P) prefix scans |
| bulk HA import (`ha/session_import.rs`) | the full install chain per session, plus one control-socket round trip per request |

Two absence claims survive a positive control: **no BPF batch API is used anywhere** in the crate
(the libbpf_sys symbol census is exactly `{update_elem, lookup_elem, delete_elem, get_next_key}`),
and there is **no source-NAT rule index** while `policy.rs:1493` has a `zone_pair_index` — so the
contrast the review drew is the right one.

**No deadlock.** Every ordering site was checked and none is inverted: `publish_shared_session`
takes the three maps in separate scopes, `demote_owner_rg_sessions` sequentially in scoped blocks,
and `owner_rg_session_keys_serialized` takes sessions then index — the same direction as the
removal path. The nesting in `remove_shared_session` is depth, not a cycle.

## Why none of them is filed as a defect

`docs/userspace-newflow-ceiling.md` **already documents `publish_shared_session` and
`replicate_session_upsert` as the two known contention sites**, and states the discipline the
review broke:

> **Status: the code ships; the measurement is OWED.** … No connection-rate number for this
> dataplane exists yet, and **nothing in this document should be cited as one**.
> … Anyone quoting a per-connection cost should measure it against
> `xpf_userspace_shared_session_publishes_total` and
> `xpf_userspace_session_replication_upserts_total` over a known number of connections, **and say
> that it is measured**.

pair **before** the slow-path chokepoint. Egress is unresolved, so `to_zone_id` is the #3110
unzoned sentinel `0`; per `forwarding/mod.rs:171-185` policy evaluation "refuses to match
any rule" against zone 0 and falls through to the default action; `noroute_policy_denial`
returns `Some(result)` for anything that is not `Permit` (`forwarding/mod.rs:152-156`) and
the frame is downgraded to `PolicyDenied` and dropped.

The Rust comment says so in as many words:

> "On a Junos-default deny box that means a NoRoute frame now drops. That is the intended fix
> and it is availability-visible on upgrade."

## #9055 — config: compileRoutingInstances implements 3 of the 8 keywords it admits — an elided routing-options DROPS the VRF static route and an elided protocols STEALS the OSPF interface into the VRF member list [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-06)

`compileRoutingInstances` hand-rolls a keyword switch that implements **three** of the
**eight** keywords its own admission helper names. Two of the missing five are
`routing-options` and `protocols`, and the brace-elided spelling of either commits clean.

## Measured at `9bb0e8f11`, through `configstore.CheckText` (the commit gate, not `CompileConfig`)

`isRoutingInstanceKeyword8787` (`pkg/config/compiler_routing.go:492-499`) names eight
keywords. The `child.Keys` switch at `:546-570` handles `instance-type`, `description`
and `interface`. Both spellings below are ACCEPTED with no error and no warning:

| keyword | braced result | brace-elided result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `instance-type` / `description` / `interface` | correct | correct |
| **`routing-options`** | `static=1` | **`static=0`** — the VRF's static route is silently gone |
| **`protocols`** | `ospf=true` | **`ospf=false` AND `ifs=[ge-0/0/1.0]`** |
| `vrf-target` / `route-distinguisher` / `vrf-table-label` | no compiled field | no compiled field (accepted-but-inert; no divergence) |

The `protocols` row is **not a plain drop — it is keyword theft.** The OSPF area's
interface token falls through to the `interface` case and is bound as a VRF member. So one
accepted statement produces two wrong outcomes: OSPF vanishes, *and* an interface silently
changes routing table. That is an isolation change, not only a routing one.

The compact normalizer cannot reach this, and the code says so: the pair it would need is
`(<instance-name>, routing-options)`, whose container slot is the **operator's instance
name** — the permanent bound of a pair-keyed scope predicate. Confirmed against both census
artifacts with a positive control on the grep: **zero** `routing-instances` rows in
`testdata/compact_block_divergences_2419.txt` and zero relevant rows in
`testdata/compact_block_permanent_exclusions_8690.txt`.

Dedup, checked individually rather than by title: **#8939** (OPEN) is the flat-set nested
chain and its own body says it "does not and should not reach" the hierarchical packed tail.
**#8904** (CLOSED) is `packedStatements` splitting, which this site is structurally outside.
**#8787** (CLOSED) is the change that *created* this hand-rolled loop and stopped at three

## #9057 — logging/configstore: rotate-a-generation-set has no persistence class and no durable primitive — 4 sites rename without a directory fsync, 2 of them in no review report, and the #1916 canary only scans os.WriteFile [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-06)

Rotating a generation set — `x` -> `x.1` -> `x.2` — is a **namespace** mutation, and none
of the four sites that do it fsync the containing directory. The reason they all get it
wrong is one level above the call sites: **append-then-rotate has no row in the #1894
persistence taxonomy, and the canary that enforces the taxonomy cannot see it.**

## The class-level defect, which is the part worth fixing

`docs/engineering-style.md` §"Persistence classes (#1894)" defines exactly three classes —
DurableState / AtomicGeneratedConfig / BestEffortKernelKnob — and every one of them is
defined over *replace-a-file* writes. Rotation is a different operation and has no row.

The enforcement has the same shape. `pkg/fsatomic/canary_test.go`'s
`TestNoDirectOsWriteFile` (#1916, a go/ast walk of every non-test `.go` under `pkg/`)
flags direct `os.WriteFile` selectors. It never looks at `os.Rename`:

```
$ grep -n 'Rename' pkg/fsatomic/canary_test.go      -> rc=1, no output
$ grep -c 'WriteFile' pkg/fsatomic/canary_test.go   -> 8      (positive control: the file IS being read)
```

And `pkg/fsatomic` exports no rotation primitive. The full exported surface at `9bb0e8f11`
is `WriteFileAtomic`, `WriteFileDurable`, `SyncDir`, `MkdirAllDurable`, three Options,
`PostRenameSyncError` and one test seam. There is no `RenameDurable`/`RotateDurable`.
That absence is deliberate — the fsatomic README documents `SyncDir` as "one directory
fsync covering **previously-completed** renames/unlinks", i.e. a caller doing its own
renames is expected to call `SyncDir` itself — but combined with a taxonomy that never
names the operation and a canary that never checks it, "expected to" is doing all the work.

## The four members

Swept with `grep -rn 'os.Rename(' --include=*.go pkg/ cmd/`, non-test, excluding
`pkg/fsatomic` itself:

| Site | imports fsatomic | syncs the dir | shape |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `pkg/configstore/journal/journal.go:492,496` | yes | **conditionally** | calls `fsatomic.SyncDir` at `:308`, but a `sync(f)` failure returns at `:305` **before** the `if created \|\| rotated` block — helper known, skipped on an error path |
| `pkg/logging/locallog.go:250,258` | **no** | **no** | no fsync of any kind; `rotate()` closes without `Sync()`, shifts generations, renames, returns |
| `pkg/logging/trace.go:529,537` | **no** | **no** | near-verbatim sibling of locallog.go — same #3478 counters, same shift loop |
| `pkg/cli/monitor.go:153,161` | **no** | **no** | same shape, different error handling |

## #9058 — configstore: a WriteConfirm failure is the ONE confirm-durability leg that sets no degraded flag, writes no journal entry and arms no retry — commit confirmed reports success and /health stays 200 [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-06)

Every neighbouring confirm-record durability failure in `pkg/configstore` carries health
state and self-heals. The confirm **write** failure is the sole exception: it warns to
journald and returns, and `commit confirmed` then reports success.

## The asymmetry, which is the decisive evidence

`ConfigPersistDegraded()` (`pkg/configstore/store_persist.go:499-502`) is exactly
`s.persistDegraded || s.confirmRemoveDegraded || s.confirmRecoveryReadFailed`.

| failure | flag set | journal entry | retry | health |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| confirm **read** at boot | `confirmRecoveryReadFailed` (#8566, `store_persist.go:181`) | yes | — | degraded |
| confirm **removal** | `confirmRemoveDegraded` (#5835/#7675) | yes | `persistRetryLoop` (`store_persist.go:562-620`) | degraded |
| **active-config** write | `persistDegraded` | `persist_error` | retry loop started | degraded |
| **confirm write** (`store_commit.go:634-638`) | **none** | **none** | **none** | **200 OK, gauge 0** |

```go
// store_commit.go:634-638
if err := s.db.WriteConfirm(rec); err != nil {
        slog.Warn(...)
        return
}
```

`CommitConfirmed` then returns `compiled, nil` and logs "commit confirmed started".

## What in the finding did NOT survive, kept explicit

The source finding's ENOSPC walkthrough is **wrong**. A pre-rename `writeActive` failure —
what a full disk actually produces — returns an error and **rejects the commit**
(`store_commit.go:491-493`); a post-rename durability failure takes
`noteActivePersistFailureLocked`, which **does** set `persistDegraded`. So in both
`writeActive` failure modes the claim "persistDegraded remains false" is false.

## The window that IS reachable, without a race

`writeActive` fully succeeds (clearing `persistDegraded` at `:508`) and `WriteConfirm`
then fails **independently**. Concretely: a commit that **removes** `system master-password`
means `writeActive` no longer encrypts and succeeds, while `WriteConfirm` still encrypts off
`rec.PrevTree`'s PRF and needs `readOrCreateMasterKey()` — an unreadable or corrupt

## #9059 — grpcapi: the fabric listener allowlists ShowText as a METHOD, admitting 126 of 127 topics — only chassis-forwarding is ever proxied, and the per-topic permission table already exists on the loopback chain [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-06)

The fabric listener's allowlist is a **method**-name allowlist. `ShowText` multiplexes
~127 topics behind one method, so allowlisting the method admits all of them — while the
only topic either peer-proxy call site ever sends is `"chassis-forwarding"`.

## The file already makes this exact argument, about a sibling method

`pkg/grpcapi/server.go` on `SystemAction`:

> SystemAction is deliberately absent: it multiplexes fabric-safe cross-node cluster-failover
> with destructive node actions (zeroize/reboot/halt/power-off) under ONE gRPC method, so a
> method-name allowlist that included it would still expose zeroize. It is gated separately,
> by request-action, in `isFabricSafeSystemAction`.

`ShowText` sits four lines below in the same map (`fabricAllowedUnaryMethods`,
`server.go:1079-1086`), with no equivalent per-topic gate.
`fabricAllowlistUnaryInterceptor` (`:1176-1185`) applies none.

## The per-topic gate already exists and is machine-checked — on the other chain

`pkg/grpcapi/authz_methods.go:124, 259-263, 300-312` prices `test-policy:` /
`test-routing:` / `test-zone:` at `PermControl`, with the comment calling them
"policy reconnaissance… exactly the tier confusion this file exists to prevent", and
`TestEveryShowTextTopicHasAPermission_5278` keeps the table exhaustive. It runs on the
**loopback principal** chain only. `pkg/grpcapi/authz.go:104-110` states the fabric listener
shares no interceptor with it, pinned by
`TestFabricListenerDoesNotInstallThePrincipalGate_5278`. So the pricing table needed to
close this is already written and already maintained; it is simply not on this chain.

## Only one topic is ever proxied

Both peer-proxy `ShowText` call sites send `Topic: "chassis-forwarding"`:
`pkg/grpcapi/server_show_forwarding.go:123` and `pkg/cli/cli_show_chassis.go:153`. The
allowlist's own comment says each entry is "a method the local node actually proxies" —
true at method granularity, false at topic granularity.

- **Bind:** `pkg/daemon/daemon_ha_comms_wiring.go:170-174` →

## #9060 — grpcapi: the legacy getSessions walk has none of the REST path's three guards and cannot be cancelled — both shipped clients use it, and it pins one of four session-walk slots shared with REST [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-06)

The REST session walk has three guards, each added for a named harm. The gRPC legacy walk
at `pkg/grpcapi/server_sessions.go:827-916` has none of them, and **both shipped clients
use the legacy path**.

## The three-way split, at `9bb0e8f11`

| guard | REST (`pkg/api/sessions.go`) | gRPC legacy (`server_sessions.go`) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| offset ceiling | `:209-214` (#8597 K25) | absent |
| count cap / `capped` flag | `:262-266` (#5318) | absent |
| request-cancel sampler | `:239` `newRequestCancelSampler` (#5237/#5233) | absent — both callbacks unconditionally `return true` (`:878`, `:903`) |

## What survives and what does not, split deliberately

**The missing offset ceiling is inert, and the report's headline trigger is wrong.**
`Total: int32(idx)` (`:909`) counts *every* matching row, so the v4+v6 walk runs to EOF on
**every** legacy call regardless of offset. An offset cap would change nothing.

**The missing cancellation is the live defect.** Once started the walk cannot be aborted. It
holds one of `MaxConcurrentSessionWalks = 4` slots (`pkg/diagcmd/limiter.go:230`), and that
limiter is **shared with REST**. Four abandoned legacy calls block every REST *and* gRPC
session scan until each walk finishes. A poller that times out keeps paying.

**The brief's own suggested refutation does NOT apply, and this is worth recording.** "eBPF
is retired, so there are no BPF map locks" is false here: `s.dp.IterateSessions` resolves to
`pkg/dataplane/maps_session.go:46` (`cilium/ebpf` `sm.Iterate()`) on the shared `sessions`
hash map, `MaxEntries = 10_000_000` (`loader_userspace_shim.go:719,740`), and the **Rust
helper writes that map on the packet path** — `publish_bpf_conntrack_entry` is called from
`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/poll_descriptor/mod.rs:670, 2335, 3072, 5911`. So contention with
new-session installs is real.

**But the fast-path half IS refuted.** "Elevates fast-path packet latency / drops transit
packets" does not hold — established flows are served from the Rust in-memory table; the BPF
map is touched on session **creation**, not per packet. The consequence is new-flow install
contention and diagnostic starvation, not transit loss.

`cmd/cli/show_flow.go:54` sends `Limit:100, IncludePeer:true` with **no** `PageSize`, and

## #9061 — cluster: decodeIPsecSAPayload turns a 16 MiB peer frame into ~675 MB transient and a 128 MB retained name set that the takeover path then iterates — a third uncovered site in the peer-frame-allocation family [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-06)

`decodeIPsecSAPayload` splits a peer-supplied frame with no element-count or name-length
bound. This is a **third, genuinely uncovered site** in the peer-frame-allocation family that
#8791 finding 03 and #8865's DHCP-lease clamp already cover at two other functions.

## The code, at `9bb0e8f11`

```go
// pkg/cluster/sync_protocol.go:801-814
func decodeIPsecSAPayload(payload []byte) []string {
        if len(payload) == 0 { return nil }
        parts := strings.Split(string(payload), "\n")
        var names []string
        for _, p := range parts { if p != "" { names = append(names, p) } }
        return names
}
```

**The only bound in the chain** is `pkg/cluster/sync_conn_read.go:60-66`:
`if hdr.Length > 16*1024*1024 { … return }` then `payload = make([]byte, hdr.Length)`.

## Measured, not asserted

Executed at `9bb0e8f11`:

| frame | split parts | transient heap | retained |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 16 MiB of `\n` | 16,777,217 | **272.1 MB** | 0 names |
| 16 MiB of `"a\n"` | 8,388,609 | **674.8 MB** | **128 MB** in `s.peerIPsecSAs`, plus the whole 16 MiB backing string (each 1-byte name shares it) |

**The retained set is the sharper end.** `pkg/daemon/daemon_ha.go:2296-2314`
(`reinitiateIPsecSAs`) iterates every retained name **on takeover** and calls
`d.ipsec.InitiateConnection(name)` — 8.4 M exec-shaped calls on the failover path, i.e. the
cost lands exactly when the cluster is least able to absorb it.

## Actor and reachability, stated precisely

The session-sync TCP listener binds to the fabric address (`sync_conn.go:821-836`), so an
attacker needs fabric-link reach. HMAC verification runs after the read but **before**
`handleMessage` (`sync_conn_read.go:75-88`), so the amplification is post-auth **when the
connection is keyed**. It is not always keyed: `pkg/cluster/sync_auth_strict_7441.go:1-52`

## #9062 — nat: SourceNatFlowKey and SourceNatPoolAllocatorKey both omit the routing domain, so two VRFs sharing one pool collide on an identical 5-tuple — the residual of #7160 one layer down [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-06)

`SourceNatFlowKey` omits the routing domain, and so does the allocator key that selects
which `PortAllocator` a rule-set uses. Two rule-sets scoped to **different** routing
instances that reference the **same** pool therefore share one allocator and one
flow-identity space.

## The two keys, at `9bb0e8f11`

```rust
// userspace-dp/src/nat/source/mod.rs:106-113
SourceNatFlowKey { protocol, src_ip, dst_ip, src_port, dst_port }      // no routing domain

// userspace-dp/src/nat/source/mod.rs:313-319
SourceNatPoolAllocatorKey { pool_name, addresses, port_low, port_high } // no routing instance
```

`grep -rn routing_domain userspace-dp/src/nat/` returns **zero** non-test hits — the whole
NAT module is domain-agnostic.

`allocate_translation_locked`'s `live.live_by_flow.get(&flow)` (`nat/allocator.rs:1878`)
then treats two distinct-VRF flows carrying an identical 5-tuple as one flow and hands the
second the first's translated tuple.

## Why #7160 does not recover it

#7160 restored per-domain demux at the `SessionKey` level. It cannot help here:
`nat_reverse_index` is inserted with `routing_domain: 0` (`session/key.rs:315-317`) and
probed zeroed (`reverse_match_key`, `key.rs:332-340`), and
`find_forward_nat_match`'s two-pass domain **preference** (`session/lookup.rs:254-320`) —
the mechanism #7160 uses — has nothing to prefer once both forward sessions carry the same
reverse identity. The reply arrives in the pool's WAN domain, which matches neither tenant, so
pass 2 returns an arbitrary validating candidate.

Second-order: the shared `live_by_flow` record means the first close frees an identity the
second session still has on the wire. The `holders` mask (`allocator.rs:400-418`) is
per-**worker**, and an identical 5-tuple RSS-hashes to the same worker, so it does not save
this.

## #9063 — routing: logicalUnitDeviceKey collapses unit 0 to the bare base, so a VRF-attached ge-0/0/0.0 excludes every ge-0-0-0.<vlan> prefix — an IPv6 link-local static next-hop then never installs [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-06)

A default-table IPv6 static route with a **link-local** next-hop silently fails to install
whenever its egress VLAN sub-unit shares a physical port with a VRF-attached unit 0 — a
routine dual-tenant trunk layout.

## The mechanism, which is not the one the source finding names

The finding calls it "indiscriminate VLAN stripping". It is not. `logicalUnitDeviceKey`
(`pkg/daemon/daemon_run_routehelpers.go:55-66`) collapses a unit with **no vlan-id and unit
number 0** to the **bare base**: `return base`. So an entirely routine

```
routing-instances blue { interface ge-0/0/0.0; }
```

puts the bare key `ge-0-0-0` into `claimedByVRF`. The base-strip at `:426-439` then discards
**every** `ge-0-0-0.<vlan>` prefix from `connectedByVRF[""]`.

It is also the dual of `collectPrefixesForInterface` (`:358-370`), which pulls all
`ge-0-0-0.*` prefixes **into** the VRF pool for the same bare key. One root cause, two sites.

## Measured at `9bb0e8f11`

```
global next-hop 2001:db8:bb::9 on ge-0-0-0.20 (default table)
  VRF blue member = ge-0/0/0.0   -> resolves to ""            (defect)
  VRF blue member = ge-0/0/1.0   -> resolves to "ge-0-0-0.20" (positive control)

link-local fe80::1, ports ge-0/0/0.0 + ge-0/0/0.20
  VRF blue member = ge-0/0/0.0   -> ""           (the only surviving default candidate lost)
  VRF blue member = ge-0/0/0.20  -> "ge-0-0-0"   (control)
```

## Consequence, narrowed on evidence

For a **global-unicast** next-hop the missing entry is harmless:
`generateStaticRouteInTable` (`pkg/frr/config_render.go:203-206`) renders a scopeless
`ipv6 route <p> <gw>` and FRR resolves it recursively.

The harm is real only for a **link-local** next-hop, where FRR rejects a scopeless

`pkg/cli/permissions_regex.go:139-146` accepts only `CanonicalOK`; the live call site is

Refused: `ping X count 5`, `ping X source Y`, `ping X size N`, `traceroute X source Y`,

`show configuration apply-groups`, `clear dhcp client-identifier interface ge-0/0/0`,

**One report claim is FALSE and is not carried here:** `ping X routing-instance vrf1` and

`Canonicalize(OperationalTree, words)`, so the remote `cli` binary does not hit this. Only

## #9066 — cos: the demote-failure path drops the saved flow-fair frontier, and the comment calling cos_queue_restore_front round-trip neutral is false for a multi-bucket queue — measured +4200/+2700/+3300 [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-06)

`demote_prepared_cos_queue_to_local` saves the flow-fair frontier and restores it only on
the success path. Both early returns drop it. The code comment justifying that omission is
**false for any multi-bucket queue**, and I measured the deviation.

## The code and its (incorrect) justification

`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/tx/cos_classify.rs:1616-1622` restores `saved_flow_fair_frontier`
on success; the early returns at `:1587` and `:1591` call `cos_queue_restore_front` and
drop it. The comment at `:1557-1559` says:

> "The failure-rollback path (`cos_queue_restore_front`) is round-trip neutral per
> #913 §3.7 and stays correct without snapshot/restore."

**That is true for a single bucket and false for several.** Executed at `9bb0e8f11` (three
flows x two packets, vtime 5000, forced down the `else` arm by a Local head):

```
bucket[0] pre(head=6500,tail=8000)  post(head=10700,tail=12200)  delta_head=+4200
bucket[1] pre(head=5900,tail=6800)  post(head= 8600,tail= 9500)  delta_head=+2700
bucket[2] pre(head=6200,tail=7400)  post(head= 9500,tail=10700)  delta_head=+3300
vtime 5000 -> 5000        newcomer anchor = 6500 -> jumps all three restored buckets
```

Each bucket's frontier is inflated by the bytes of *other* buckets drained ahead of its own
last item.

## What this is and is not

It is **not** the "bogus finish times / permanently lost state" the source finding describes:
relative order among the restored buckets is preserved and vtime round-trips exactly. What it
**is**: a new flow arriving right after a failed demote anchors at `vtime + bytes` and is
served ahead of the entire restored backlog. That is the temporal-inversion class **#926
(CLOSED)** fixed on the success path and left open on the failure path.

## Reachability is high and repeatable

`cos_queue_accepts_prepared` (`cos_classify.rs:1655-1666`) refuses Prepared once
`local_item_count != 0`, so a queue that has taken any Local item is Local-dominant — and the
first drained Local trips the `else` arm on **every** subsequent
`demote_prepared_cos_queue_to_local`, which itself runs on TX-frame exhaustion from

## #9067 — ddns: the Cloudflare backend early-returns on an IP-content match and never compares TTL, so a TTL-only change NEVER propagates — Route 53 compares both and converges at the 24h floor [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-06)

The Cloudflare DDNS backend short-circuits on an IP-content match and never compares TTL, so
a TTL-only configuration change is **never** propagated — not delayed, never.

## The two backends, side by side at `9bb0e8f11`

```go
// pkg/ddns/backend_cloudflare.go:325-330   -- content only
if r.Content == content { return nil }

// pkg/ddns/backend_route53.go:412          -- content AND ttl
if live.found && live.ttl == ttl && sameValueSet(...) { ... }
```

`cfRecord.TTL` **is** parsed (`backend_cloudflare.go:117`) — the datum is available and
simply unread.

## Why it is permanent rather than eventually-consistent

On Route 53 a TTL-only change converges at the next forced refresh
(`defaultForcedRefresh = 24h`, `pkg/ddns/surface_a.go:55`). On Cloudflare **every**
subsequent refresh — including the operator's explicit
`request system dynamic-dns update` force latch — re-enters the same early return. The
engine does re-invoke `UpsertLease` on a TTL-only change via the forced-refresh floor
(`surface_a.go:1138`), so the backend early return is the operative blocker, not the caller.

A second, backend-independent contributor: the reconcile's
`changed := addr != rt.lastAddr` (`surface_a.go:1119`) does not treat a TTL change as a
change, so nothing republishes *promptly* on any backend. That one is a delay; the Cloudflare
early return is the permanent blocker.

`pkg/ddns/backend_cloudflare_test.go` contains **no TTL assertion at all** — the omission is
untested in both directions.

## #9068 — ipsec: liveConnNames parses swanctl through CombinedOutput while GetSAStatus uses a stdout-only buffer for the same parser — a mid-line stderr splice LOSES a connection name (UNRESOLVED: reachability) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-06)

> **This is an explicitly UNRESOLVED validation task, not a confirmed defect.** The mechanism
> is pinned by execution; its reachability is not established. Filed at
> NEEDS_VALIDATION per the review contract rather than as a bug.

## What IS established

**Structural (EXECUTED, `9bb0e8f11`):** `pkg/ipsec/manager.go:377-381` iterates
`for name := range live`, so a removed connection **absent from `live`** is never terminated
**and** never entered into `pendingTerminate`. Because `prevConnNames` has already advanced
past the departed name, that name is gone forever — the #6542 fail-open through a different
door.

**One parser, two exec channels.** `GetSAStatus` (`pkg/ipsec/ike.go:669-700`) uses a
dedicated **stdout-only** buffer, with the explicit comment "the parser needs stdout alone".
`liveConnNames` routes through `m.sc` -> `runSwanctl` -> **`CombinedOutput()`**
(`manager.go:34-42`) — stderr folded in — on the security-critical teardown path. That
asymmetry is real, and its in-place justification (`manager.go:403-404`: "parseSAOutput
ignores any unrecognized stderr lines CombinedOutput may fold in") is **asserted, not tested**.

**Executed tolerance matrix on `parseSAOutput`:**

| injected | result |
| --- | --- |
| a whole stderr line before the IKE header | name preserved |
| a stderr line containing `": #"` | a SPURIOUS extra name (harmless — not in `removedSet`) |
| CRLF | tolerated |
| **a mid-line splice into the IKE header** | **the real name is LOST** (`vpn-corp` -> `vpn-cowarning`) |

So the code's justification is true for whole lines and **false in the one direction that
matters**.

## What is NOT established — the reason this is not filed as a bug

Whether a mid-line splice can actually occur. swanctl's stdout to a pipe is block-buffered
while stderr is unbuffered, so a splice needs an SA listing large enough to force a mid-stream
flush **plus** a concurrent stderr write — and whether `swanctl --list-sas` writes to stderr
at all on a *successful* listing is not established.

## #9069 — nat64: the ICMPv6 recompute arm can emit checksum 0x0000 while its sibling UDP arm and the declared SSOT adjust_zero_checksum_illegal both canonicalise it — producible payload found by brute force [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-06)

The NAT64 translator's ICMPv6 checksum arm can emit `0x0000` where its own sibling arm ten
lines above canonicalises to `0xFFFF`, and where the codebase's declared SSOT says V6 zero is
illegal for ICMPv6.

## Structural, and the arithmetic is EXECUTED not asserted

`userspace-dp/src/nat64.rs:3394-3402`, the `PROTO_ICMPV6` arm of
`recompute_l4_checksum_after_nat64_v4_to_v6`, writes `sum` raw. The `PROTO_UDP` arm at
`:3386-3392` has the `if sum == 0 { 0xFFFF }` fixup.

**The zero is producible, not theoretical.** I brute-forced two payload bytes of a real
IPv6+ICMPv6 Echo Reply until `checksum16_ipv6_pseudo` folded to 0 — found at payload
`(0xa1, 0x2a)` — then ran the real function. It wrote `0x0000` into `l4[2..4]`.

## The source finding's stated consequence is REFUTED; a different one survives

The report cites RFC 4443 §2.3 and RFC 8200 §8.1 for a mandatory all-ones substitution on
ICMPv6. **That rule is UDP-specific in RFC 8200 §8.1; RFC 4443 §2.3 contains no such
sentence.** A `0x0000` ICMPv6 checksum verifies correctly at a compliant receiver — there is
no "no checksum" sentinel for ICMPv6 — so "dropped by compliant IPv6 destination hosts" does
not follow, and this issue does not claim it.

**What survives is an internal inconsistency**, which is a real contract violation:
`adjust_zero_checksum_illegal` (`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/frame/checksum.rs:117-125`, #1839) is
this codebase's declared single source of truth and says V6 zero is illegal for **UDP and
ICMPv6**. The afxdp-side `recompute_l4_checksum_ipv6` canonicalises the ICMPv6 arm
(`checksum.rs:637-644`). The NAT64 translator diverges from the rule its sibling path
enforces.

## Severity: Low

Bounded: roughly 1 in 65,536 translated ICMPv6 messages, and no observable loss against a
standards-conformant receiver. It is filed as a one-line consistency fix against a declared
SSOT, not as a wire-correctness defect.

## Dedup

**GEMINI-049-013** (on **#8869**) is `frame/checksum.rs:391-418`, IPv4 **UDP** — different
file, function and protocol arm, so not a duplicate by the contract's rule. But it is the
**same class**, and both should ride on one fix that routes every recompute arm through

as an exact host.

`pkg/nat/deterministic.go:736-758` reconstructs only the 32-bit subscriber word and emits
the result as a bare address string in `ReverseResult.InternalHost`, rendered as

length appears anywhere on the surface.

The value **is** the deterministic unit's network base, and the type already documents that
(`deterministic.go:143`: "recovered subscriber (IPv4, or **IPv6 prefix**)"), as does
`docs/deterministic-nat-cgnat.md`. The live defect is that a bare address under
"Internal host" reads as an exact /128. No enforcement, isolation, or data-path consequence.

   is octets `[8..12]` and the deterministic unit for a `/64`-configured pool is a **/96**,
   not a /64. Annotating `/64` would replace an ambiguous answer with a confidently wrong one.

An operator-facing CGNAT attribution surface presents a network base as a host with no prefix
qualification. It is a contract/labelling defect. The lawful-intercept framing in the source
finding overstates it: the correct value is derivable and documented, it is simply not shown.

None. GEMINI-049-027 is the missing compile-time sizing gate — different mechanism.

## #9071 — userspace-dp: bulk_replace_neighbors and learn_pair_if_changed never bump insert_generation, and the neigh_schedule rationale claiming only the STATIC map is uncovered is now false [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-06)

`sharded_neighbor.rs`'s three per-key insert paths bump `insert_generation`; the two
**bulk** paths do not. The larger half of this is that a rationale comment is now false.

## Structural, EXECUTED at `9bb0e8f11`

`bulk_replace_neighbors` (`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/sharded_neighbor.rs:531-568`) and
`learn_pair_if_changed` (`:593-640`) install entries via `bulk.insert(...)` and bump only
`bump_shard_epoch` — never `insert_generation`. The three per-key paths do bump (`:368`,
`:423`, `:469`). Verified by a unit check with a positive control on
`insert_if_changed`/`insert`.

The consumer is #7156's poll-loop optimisation: a full resolution pass runs only when
`neigh_generation != binding.last_neigh_generation`.

## Consequence, split — the worst half is refuted

- **REFUTED:** "may time out and be dropped as `MissingNeighbor` despite the neighbor being
  present". `next_due_for_pending` (`neigh_schedule.rs:198`) arms **every** key at
  `min(next probe, timeout, now + RESOLUTION_RECHECK_INTERVAL_NS)` = <=50 ms, against a
  pending timeout of 800 ms-2 s. **No drop.**
- **REFUTED:** this is not the primary resolution path. The ARP-reply / NDP-NA learn that
  actually resolves a probed hop is `poll_stages.rs:207` / `:290` -> `insert_if_changed`,
  which **does** bump. Only the Go control-plane snapshot push
  (`coordinator/mod.rs:740`) and the #1787 RX source-MAC transit learn
  (`neighbor_dispatch.rs:892`) are uncovered.
- **HOLDS:** <=50 ms of added dispatch latency for the one buffered packet per hop resolved
  through those two paths.

## The more valuable half is a documentation defect

`neigh_schedule.rs:91-99` states the recheck "covers the one case that gate cannot see: the
STATIC `forwarding.neighbors` map." There are **two dynamic cases** it also cannot see, and
that rationale is now false. A future reader tuning `RESOLUTION_RECHECK_INTERVAL_NS` upward
on the strength of that sentence would convert a 50 ms latency into a real drop.

## Severity: Low

Bounded latency on a narrow path, with a correct backstop. Filed because the fix is trivial
and because the false rationale is the kind that gets acted on later.

## #9072 — nftables: an lo0 reject term with an explicit protocol emits a dead first rule carrying two contradictory meta l4proto compares — the goldens pin only the no-protocol case [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-06)

An `lo0` filter `reject` term with an **explicit** protocol emits a dead first rule: a
`meta l4proto` compare against the term's protocol AND a second, contradictory compare
against TCP. Enforcement is unaffected; the rule is simply unreachable.

## Measured at `9bb0e8f11` (`buildLo0TermNetlink` + `canonRules`)

| term | r00 | r01 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| no protocol | `l4proto==06` -> tcp-reset | (bare) -> icmpx | *(both live — the golden case)* |
| `protocol udp` | `l4proto==11 && l4proto==06` -> **dead** | `l4proto==11` -> icmpx |
| `protocol tcp` | `l4proto==06` -> tcp-reset | `l4proto==06` -> icmpx, **unreachable** |
| `protocol icmp` | `l4proto==01 && l4proto==06` -> **dead** | `l4proto==01` -> icmpx |
| `protocol [udp icmp]` | `set{01,11} && ==06` -> **dead** | `set{01,11}` -> icmpx |
| `protocol [tcp udp]` | `set{06,11} && ==06` -> **correct** | `set{06,11}` -> icmpx |

**Mechanism:** `l4protoSet` on a single protocol routes to `needL4proto` and latches
`l4Val` (`pkg/nftables/netlink_build.go:181-191`); `a1.needL4proto(protoTCP)` then sees
`l4Val != 6` and appends a second, contradictory `meta l4proto` compare (`:137-144`).

## Consequence — enforcement is NOT affected, and this issue does not claim otherwise

`r01` always carries the correct family-agnostic reject for the specified protocols in every
cell, **including** the mixed `[tcp udp]` cell, which renders correctly. The cost is <=1 dead
rule per explicit-protocol reject term, evaluated as a single failing `meta l4proto` compare.
No packet's verdict changes.

## The existing goldens are silent here, not contrary

I checked for contrary evidence rather than assuming its absence.
`TestGoldenRejectTermPair` (`pkg/nftables/netlink_golden_test.go:180-191`) pins
`Lo0FilterTerm{Name:"r", Action:"reject"}` with **no** `Protocols`, and the `reject-term`
case in `netlink_scenario_test.go:151-158` also sets none.
`netlink_lo0_proto_icmp_6806_test.go` never touches `reject`. So the goldens pin only the
no-protocol case; they are not evidence against this.

## Severity: Low

A theoretical inefficiency with no measured cost and no behavioural change. Filed because the
fix is trivial and the emitted ruleset is operator-visible in `nft list ruleset`, where a
self-contradictory rule invites misdiagnosis.
