## #9073 — daemon: the sshd -t validation-failure arm skips noteSSHDReloadResult, so the reload-failure counter stays FLAT while the retry owner is running and failing — the exact discriminator it exists for [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-06)

The service-reload-debt counters exist to tell an operator whether the retry owner is
**running and failing** (count climbing) or **wedged** (count flat). One leg does not
increment, so under a persistent `sshd -t` failure the count stays flat while the owner is
running and failing — the exact discriminator the counters were built for.

`pkg/daemon/daemon_service_reload_debt.go:322-332`: the `sshdValidateCmd()` failure arm logs
and falls through **without** `d.noteSSHDReloadResult(err)`, so `sshdFailures` never
increments. The counters' own contract is stated at `:85-92`.

The counters are exported: `ManagedServiceReloadFailures` -> `daemon_run_servers.go:463` ->
`pkg/api/server.go:325` (Prometheus).

The operator is **not** blind. `ManagedServiceReloadOwed()["sshd"]` stays true, and on every
pass **both** a WARN ("sshd reload still owed…retrying") and an ERROR ("sshd config validation
failed") fire. Only the **metric** channel is blind. Two channels already report the condition
every tick.

## The fix is safe, which is worth stating

`noteSSHDReloadResult(err)` sets `sshdReload = err != nil`, which re-latches an
already-latched debt — no behavioural side effect.

An assurance/observability gap on one of three channels, with a one-line fix.

None. Grepped 049 for `sshdValidate` / `noteSSHDReloadResult` / `reassertServiceReloadDebt`

Call `d.noteSSHDReloadResult(err)` on the validation-failure arm.

## #9074 — grpcapi: ClearCounters is not fanned out to the peer while ClearSessions is — the parity argument does not carry (counters are not replicated), so this is a grammar/scope decision to make explicit [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-06)

`ClearCounters` clears counters on the local node only, while its sibling `ClearSessions`
fans out to the peer. An operator must SSH to the other node to reset the peer's baseline.

## Structural

`pkg/grpcapi/server_cluster.go:896-911` calls `s.dp.ClearAllCounters()` with no
`peerForwardedFromContext` check and no peer dial. `ClearSessions` fans out at
`server_sessions.go:1268-1270`.

## The parity argument does NOT carry, and that is why this is Low

Sessions are **replicated** between nodes, so a local-only clear is undone by sync — that is
the stated reason for the session fanout (`pkg/cli/cli_clear.go:607-611`, #2468). Counters
are **not** replicated, so a node-local clear is self-consistent. The two are not analogous.

Two further facts that make this a design position rather than an oversight:

- The shipped grammar explicitly disclaims scope: `cmd/cli/clear.go:21-27`,
  `requireClearNoScope` — *"this command clears all counters and takes no scope (per-scope
  clear is not supported)"* — and `ClearCountersRequest` has no node field.
- `ClearCounters` is **absent from `fabricAllowedUnaryMethods`**, so a fix requires widening
  that allowlist. (See the companion issue on the fabric `ShowText` allowlist — widening it
  should be done deliberately, not as a side effect.)

I checked every `dialPeer()` site in `pkg/grpcapi` and `pkg/cli`: only sessions,
session/zone-pair summary, `chassis-forwarding` and `SystemAction` failover are proxied.
Nothing suggests a counter fanout was intended and lost.

## Severity: Low

An operator-contract gap against Junos node scoping. No loss of enforcement, integrity, or
availability; the workaround (SSH to the peer) is available and obvious.

## Fix direction

Either fan out under a `peerForwardedFromContext` guard (which requires adding
`ClearCounters` to the fabric allowlist — do that with a per-method rationale, not
wholesale), or add explicit `node <local|peer|both>` scoping to the grammar and document the
node-local default. **Regression acceptance:** whichever is chosen, a cell asserting the
documented scope, since today's behaviour and today's help text already agree with each other.

## #9088 — security/ipsec: a packed `vpn <V> gateway G ipsec-policy P bind-interface st0.1` COMMITS CLEAN and drops the policy and the binding — operator-reachable, unlike the rest of the #8939 class [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-06)

Filed separately from #8939 because **this one is reachable from the keyboard** and most of that class is not. That distinction was established by lane-8388 and is the reason this is a different severity story rather than another row.

## Measured through the OPERATOR path

`compileTreeStrict` — the pipeline behind every `commit` / `commit check` and behind `configstore.CheckText` — with a complete IPsec preamble so no rejection can be an undefined reference:

```
CONTROL  set security ipsec vpn v1 gateway G
         set security ipsec vpn v1 ipsec-policy P
         set security ipsec vpn v1 bind-interface st0.1
           -> STRICT ACCEPTED   gw="G"  ipsec-policy="P"  bind-interface="st0.1"

PACKED   set security ipsec vpn v1 gateway G ipsec-policy P bind-interface st0.1
           -> STRICT ACCEPTED   gw="G"  ipsec-policy=""   bind-interface=""
```

Same configuration, one command instead of three. **It commits, `show configuration` renders what the operator typed, and two values are gone.**

## Consequences, both silent

- **`ipsec-policy` dropped** — phase 2 negotiates the strongSwan default proposal set instead of the configured crypto. This is the same failure mode the phase-1 `ike-policy` gate exists to prevent, arriving on a path that gate does not watch.
- **`bind-interface` dropped** — `xfrmiIfID()` returns 0, so a route-based VPN commits with **no XFRM interface**. That is the silent-tunnel-down condition #5297 was written to prevent, reached by a route #5297 does not cover.

## Why this one is admissible when its siblings are not

The closed-world typed-leaf gate runs before the compiler and rejects a packed run wherever the container's leaves are declared — `security flow tcp-session` is refused with `closing-timeout: unknown modifier "established-timeout"`, so an operator simply cannot type it.

**`security ipsec vpn <V>`'s `gateway` and `ipsec-policy` are read by the compiler and absent from `setSchema`.** With nothing declared there is no closed-world check to fail, so the packed spelling passes admission and the compiler drops everything after the first token.

**The schema being behind the compiler is what makes a site operator-reachable.** That is the discriminator for this whole class, and it is a property of the (container, declaration) pair rather than of the container.

## Why the #8939 census never listed it

Two separate reasons, both instrument defects:

1. The census calls `config.CompileConfig`, not the strict pipeline — so it has been measuring the tolerant Load/SyncApply channel and reporting it as the operator channel.
2. This container's row leaves the population as **`unmeasured`**, because the generator hands `bind-interface` the placeholder `ge-0/0/0` (rejected by the #5297 gate) and `local-ip` the placeholder `xpfval` (rejected by the #4098 gate). Both arms fail, so the row is skipped rather than recorded.

## #9091 — config: the schema walk does not descend into instance-name containers — 102 containers accept an unknown keyword at commit [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-06)

Splits out a mechanism #8928 names as un-enumerated ("packed statements", "apply-groups inheritance"), found via a discriminator lane-8388 measured on #8939. Cross-referenced both ways; #8928 remains the class report.

## The defect

`schemaValidateExpandedTreeForNode` stops at a container's **instance-name slot**. For a container declared with `args>=1`, declared children, and no wildcard, an **unknown keyword** in its body is not rejected — it commits clean and is silently ignored.

**Scope, corrected — see the correction comment below.** This is NOT "nothing in the body is validated". A DECLARED leaf's VALUE is still checked. Measured:

```
system login class c1 { xpfbogus 5; }            -> ACCEPTED   (unknown keyword)
system login class c1 { idle-timeout notanum; }  -> REJECTED   (declared leaf, bad value)
system login class c1 { idle-timeout 30; }       -> ACCEPTED   (control)
```

So the operator-facing consequence is narrower than an unqualified reading: a mistyped KEYWORD is silent; a bad VALUE on a correctly-spelled leaf is still caught.

Measured end-to-end at `configstore.CheckText` (the real commit gate, not `CompileConfig`):

```
security flow tcp-session { bogus-token 5; }   -> REJECTED   (closed world, walk descends)
security ike gateway g1   { bogus-token 5; }   -> ACCEPTED   (walk stops at "g1")
security ipsec vpn v1     { bogus-token 5; }   -> ACCEPTED
class-of-service interfaces ge-0/0/0 { unit 0 { bogus 5; } } -> ACCEPTED
CONTROL: bogus TOP-LEVEL stanza                -> REJECTED   (the gate is live)
```

## #9105 — frr: an ABSENT isis/rip authentication-type is rendered as a deliberate PLAINTEXT choice — silent MD5→cleartext downgrade, and the diagnostic built for it cannot fire [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-06)

Filed separately from the flat-run fix in progress, because **this is reachable from any source of an empty `AuthType`, not only from a packed `set` line.** Fixing the flat run removes today's known route to it and leaves the render-site defect standing.

## The two predicates disagree about the empty string, and the defect lives in the gap

`pkg/frr/protocols_render.go:683-695`:

```go
if isis.AuthKey != "" {
    if config.AuthTypeUnrecognized(isis.AuthType) {
        slog.Warn("...rendering PLAINTEXT area/domain password", ...)   // #8443
    }
    if config.AuthTypeIsMD5(isis.AuthType) {
        " area-password md5 %s"
    } else {
        " area-password clear %s"          // <- the key, in cleartext
    }
}
```

Measured directly:

```
AuthType=""        Unrecognized=false  IsMD5=false  -> renders CLEAR  (SILENT)
AuthType="md5"     Unrecognized=false  IsMD5=true   -> renders md5    (SILENT)
AuthType="simple"  Unrecognized=false  IsMD5=false  -> renders CLEAR  (SILENT)
AuthType="bogus"   Unrecognized=true   IsMD5=false  -> renders CLEAR  (warned)

accepted spellings: [md5 simple text]
```

**An ABSENT type is not `unrecognized` — so #8443's warning stays silent — and it is not `md5` — so the renderer emits plaintext.** #8443 was written about a *wrong* value and never about a *missing* one.

## The sharper half: `""` is indistinguishable from a deliberate choice

Look at the `simple` row. It renders `clear`, silently, and **that is correct** — the operator asked for plaintext. The empty string takes the identical path.

So at the render site, *"the operator chose plaintext"* and *"the type was dropped somewhere upstream"* are **the same state**, and the code cannot tell them apart. That is why no amount of care at this site would have caught it: the information needed to distinguish them was destroyed before the renderer ran.

## #9110 — test: two timing-sensitive tests flake under parallel gating, and a flaky red is indistinguishable from a real one at the moment you must decide [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-06)

Two tests failed spuriously in repo-wide gates today, both under parallel load, both from changes that do not touch their packages:

| test | package | the change that "failed" it |
|---|---|---|
| `TestStartHeartbeatSingleStartRuns` | `pkg/cluster` | test-only changes in `pkg/config` |
| `TestRestartTimeoutNoGoodbyeNoReplacement` | `pkg/ra` | test-only changes in `pkg/config` |

Both pass **15/15 and 20/20 in isolation**, on the branch *and* on clean master, and neither branch touches a single file in the failing package.

## Why this is worth an issue rather than a shrug

**At the moment you have to decide whether to merge, a flaky red and a real red look identical.** The cost is not the rerun — it is that the correct response to a red gate (do not merge) and the correct response to a flake (merge) are opposites, and the output does not distinguish them. Today that produced two bad outcomes in one session:

- Once I **merged three PRs on a red gate**, because the merge was not conditioned on the result. The red was flaky, so the outcome was benign — but the process was wrong and would have shipped a real break.
- Once I **refused to merge on a red that was my own fault** — I had started a background gate and then checked out a different branch in the same worktree, so the gate measured a tree that changed underneath it. Re-running in an isolated worktree came back clean.

The second one is not this issue's subject but it is the same failure shape: **a gate whose result cannot be trusted is worse than a slow gate**, because it trains you to explain reds away.

## What would help, roughly in order of value

1. **Make them not flake.** Both are timing-sensitive (`SetClock`-style seams exist elsewhere in this tree — `docs/engineering-style.md` §"Time in tests (#8218)"). A test that depends on wall-clock progress under load is the defect; the parallel gate only exposes it.
2. **Failing that, mark them** so a repo-wide gate can distinguish "known timing-sensitive" from "signal". A red that names itself as suspect is far more useful than one that does not.
3. **Record the rule that already works**: gate in a dedicated worktree with nothing else running. That is what turned an unexplainable red into a clean pass twice today, and it is cheap.

## Not claimed

I have not established that these are the only two, or that the cause is the same in both. The population is "tests that failed a repo-wide gate today under load and passed in isolation", which is a set assembled by noticing rather than by measurement — so treat 2 as a floor. A sweep would be `go test -count=N ./...` under deliberate parallel load, which nobody has run.

Both instances are recorded with their full context in this session's PRs (#9095/#9096/#9101 and #9109).

## #9116 — userspace-dp: TCP segmentation refuses a FIN-bearing oversized segment, so an IPv4 DF-clear flow with no MSS clamp blackholes its own connection close — the sibling declination in #5159 was fixed, this one was not [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-06)


- Gate verdict: **MATERIAL**
- Claimed severity: High   Verified severity: **Medium** (claimed High → verified Medium)
- Confidence: Medium-High
- Verification: STATIC
- **Claim split: right about the mechanism, wrong about the reachability.** The report says
  this happens "during normal HTTP/database response completion". It cannot, on the normal
  path — see the DF analysis below.
- Prior-report column: **no prior**
- Evidence:
  - `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/frame/tcp_segmentation.rs:248` and its prepared twin
    `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/tx/tcp_segmentation.rs:95`:
    `if (tcp_flags & (TCP_FLAG_SYN | TCP_FLAG_FIN | TCP_FLAG_RST)) != 0 { return None; }`
    — no `#<issue>` rationale at either site, unlike every other gate in these files.
  - `tx/dispatch/mod.rs:934-980`: on a double `None` the miss is counted
    (`seg_needed_but_none`, exception `tcp_segmentation_miss`) and control falls to
    `compute_forwarded_egress_ptb`; when `!mtu_signalled` the oversized frame is
    built/rewritten and submitted.
  - `record_forwarded_tcp_segmentation_miss` (`dispatch/mod.rs:1457-1466`) states the
    consequence in its own doc: *"the dispatcher falls back to forwarding the original
    oversized frame, which the NIC/switch/peer then drops — black-holing the flow"* (#1282).
  - `icmp_ptb.rs:107-124` `forwarded_egress_mtu_decision`: **IPv4 with DF set → PTB;
    IPv6 → always PTB; IPv4 with DF clear → `Forward`.**
  - No IPv4 transit fragmentation engine exists in the dataplane (grepped; the only
    fragmentation code is NAT64's).
- Trace and the true reachability set: an over-egress-MTU TCP datagram carrying FIN
  declines both builders → `compute_forwarded_egress_ptb`. If **DF is set** (the default
  for Linux and every PMTUD-enabled stack) or the packet is **IPv6**, a Packet-Too-Big is
  emitted and the frame is not forwarded — correct RFC 1191/8201 behaviour, and the sender
  retransmits at a smaller size. The blackhole is therefore confined to **IPv4 with DF
  clear**, over an ingress-MTU > egress-MTU step, on a flow whose MSS was not clamped
  (`security flow tcp-mss` is operator-configured, not default). There the final
  data-bearing `FIN|ACK` — which Linux piggybacks onto the last full-MSS data segment — is
  forwarded oversize, dropped downstream, and retransmitted forever with no PMTUD signal:
  the connection's data transfers fine and then hangs at close. SYN-with-data (TFO) and
  RST-with-data share the arm but are far rarer.
- Refutation attempt: I looked for (a) an upstream gate that would have PTB'd before
  segmentation — no: `forwarded_tcp_may_need_segmentation` (`dispatch/mod.rs:1556`)
  deliberately does not test DF, and CLOSED **#6125** adjudicates that as intended
  ("re-segment all oversize forwarded TCP regardless of DF — delivery-guarantee posture");

## #9118 — logging: a failed rotation reopen wedges the local audit/trace writer permanently — #3478 made the wedge observable and never added the recovery leg [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-06)

One transient fd or disk error at a log-rotation boundary silences
`security log mode event` and `traceoptions` until the next config commit —
on the exact channel an operator relies on to reconstruct an incident.

## Evidence at `930767a40a610226af6e55970b3dd774d429b719`

`pkg/logging/locallog.go:240-278` — `rotate()` does
`lw.file.Close(); lw.file = nil`, and on an `openHardenedAuditLog` failure it
does `lw.failedRotations.Add(1); return …` with `lw.file` left **nil**.

`pkg/logging/locallog.go:152-160` and `:186-192` (`Send` / `SendBinary`), and
`pkg/logging/trace.go:374-381` (`WriteRecord`), all drop when `file == nil` and
**never attempt a reopen**.

`rotate()` is called only from `if lw.written >= lw.maxSize`, i.e. *after a
successful write*. Once wedged, `written` never advances, so rotation can never
re-fire and nothing else reopens the file.

## Trace

`Send` → `rotate` → `openHardenedAuditLog` fails (EMFILE / ENFILE / ENOSPC /
EROFS / EACCES) → `file = nil` → every subsequent `Send` / `SendBinary` /
`WriteRecord` drops, indefinitely.

## What bounds it — why this is Medium and not High

- **It is not silent.** `droppedWrites` and `failedRotations` are atomic
  counters with exported getters, and a ≤1/s WARN on separate per-failure-class
  clocks fires on every drop. `pkg/logging/README.md:661-673` names this exact
  state: *"a writer wedged by a prior failed reopen would otherwise drop every
  subsequent event after a single FailedRotations bump"*.
- **Historical data survives.** The primary `os.Rename(path, path+".1")` has
  already landed when the reopen fails, so everything written before the wedge
  is intact.
- **It self-heals on the next commit.** `pkg/daemon/daemon_system.go:75-90`
  constructs a fresh `LocalLogWriter` and calls `er.ReplaceLocalWriters` on
  every config apply in `event` mode — so the wedge lasts until the next commit
  or daemon restart, not "until daemon restart" as the source report claims.

What survives all of that: on an unattended appliance in steady state, "until

    leaves `IsDirty() == true`. The asymmetry is exactly as claimed.
- Trace / reach (where the report overstates): the two production callers are
  `pkg/cli/cli_dispatch.go:283` (local console `configure exclusive`, holder `"cli"`) and
  `pkg/grpcapi/server_config.go:82` (`EnterConfigure` RPC with `Exclusive`). **Neither
  shipped CLI can call it twice**: both route `configure` through the operational
  dispatcher, which is unreachable once the prompt has switched to config mode
  (`cmd/cli/shared.go:176-215`, `pkg/cli/cli_dispatch.go:277`). So the reachable actor is a
  third-party gRPC client (or an automation script) that re-asserts the lock on one
  connection — a legitimate use of a supported RPC, which succeeds in shared mode and
  fails in exclusive mode.
- Refutation of the severity: the wipe half is real but is **not new loss**. Past the
  10-minute idle lease, `reclaimStaleLockLocked` discards the candidate for *any* entrant
  by #4476's explicit design; the exclusive holder self-wiping is the same forfeit, reached
  by the holder itself. The genuinely novel part is the denial half plus the asymmetry with
  the shared-mode sibling. Also note `connSessionID` is connection-scoped (#5849), so a
  reconnecting client is a different session and would be refused regardless.
- Fix direction: the report's patch is right in substance but must use the **effective**
  holder, not `exclusiveHolder` alone, and must sit **before** `reclaimStaleLockLocked` (as
  the report says) or the stale branch still wipes:
  `if s.configDir && holder != "" && s.exclusiveHolder == holder { s.configLockAt = time.Now(); return nil }`.
  Regression criterion: the three-cell table above — fresh-lease self-reentry returns nil
  and preserves `IsDirty()`, stale-lease self-reentry preserves it too, and a *different*
  holder is still refused (that third cell is what stops the fix from becoming a lock
  bypass).
- Dedup: no prior finding in 049/050, no open issue on `EnterConfigureExclusive`.

## #9120 — cluster: FenceAckOK promises the peer relinquished every redundancy group, but the fence releases no VIPs and the RG disable is re-driven by the next reconcile within 2s — #3917's invariant and #6530's revert are in tension at head [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-06)


- **Gate verdict:** MATERIAL
- **Claimed severity:** Critical → **Verified severity: Medium.** The *structural* claim survives; the *consequence model* ("intractable traffic blackhole", "split-brain VIP collision created by fencing") is refuted by a mechanism the repo pins with its own test. Critical requires broad catastrophic loss; what is actually lost is the durability of a documented ordering guarantee.
- **Confidence:** High
- **Verification:** EXECUTED
- **Prior-report column:** **no prior** (049-060 is `SendFenceAwait` scheduler race — different).

**Evidence**
- `pkg/daemon/daemon_ha_sync.go:1139-1186` `fenceAllRedundancyGroups` — loops `rt.HA().SetRGActive(ctx, rg.ID, false)` + `d.getOrCreateRGState(rg.ID).InvalidateApplied()`. No `ResignRG`, no `resignRethRG`, no `reconcileDirectVIPOwnership`. **Confirmed at the pinned SHA.**
- `pkg/daemon/daemon_ha_comms_wiring.go:478-491` — `ss.OnFenceReceived` is wired to *only* `d.fenceAllRedundancyGroups(commsCtx)`. Nothing else on the receive path.
- `pkg/cluster/sync_conn_read.go:686-706` — `syncMsgFence` calls `OnFenceReceived` synchronously and encodes its `FenceResult` into the ack. No cluster-state transition is triggered on the fenced node.
- `pkg/daemon/rg_state.go:14-24` + `:367-372` (`reconcileLocked`) — **`desired = clusterPri || allVrrpMaster`**.

**Trace (the actual sequence the brief asked for)**
1. Peer B's heartbeat to A times out → `handlePeerTimeout` (`pkg/cluster/heartbeat_manager.go:611-761`) → under `disable-rg-confirmed`, `awaitPeerFenceLocked()`; under `disable-rg`, `electSingleNode()` then `peerFenceFn`.
2. A receives `syncMsgFence` → `OnFenceReceived` → `fenceAllRedundancyGroups` → `rg_active=false` for every live-config RG, `InvalidateApplied()`.
3. Ack `FenceAckOK` is written **after** step 2 returns.
4. **A's cluster state machine is never told.** A's own heartbeat also timed out on B, so A's `electSingleNode` keeps A Primary ⇒ `clusterPri` stays `true`.
5. A's VRRP is untouched ⇒ every RETH instance stays MASTER ⇒ `allVrrpMaster` stays `true`.
6. `reconcileRGStateLoop` (`pkg/daemon/daemon_ha.go:965-982`, **2 s ticker**, plus `reconcileNowCh`) runs `s.Reconcile(clusterPri, vrrp)`; `tr.Changed` is false but `s.NeedsApply()` is true (that is exactly what `InvalidateApplied` armed) ⇒ **`SetRGActive(rg, true)` is re-driven.**

So the honest bound: **VIP release = 0 ms (never attempted). Dataplane deactivation ≤ 2000 ms** (one reconcile tick; shorter if anything calls `triggerReconcile`). There is no permanent blackhole and no fencing-induced dual-active VIP state — VRRP is the arbiter of VIP ownership and is simply not involved.

**Refutation attempt (what killed the Critical)**
`pkg/daemon/rg_state_fence_rearm_6530_test.go:87-170` `TestFenceRearmsReconcileRetry` **pins the revert as required behaviour**: "The property: the very next reconcile pass must re-drive the apply … rg_active=true". Ran it:
```
WARN cluster: fence: disabling all RGs rg_count=1
INFO reconcile: retrying rg_active apply rg=1 active=true
--- PASS: TestFenceRearmsReconcileRetry (0.01s)
```
So the report's "the fenced node drops transit traffic, creating an intractable blackhole" is the *inverse* of the pinned behaviour.

**The surviving — and sharper — claim**
The repo contains two comments that cannot both be true at head:
- `daemon_ha_sync.go:1128-1131` (#3917): *"when a fence message arrives the local node **must relinquish ALL redundancy-groups** so the peer can own them without a dual-active split-brain."*
- `rg_state.go:220-247` (#6530): the relinquishment is deliberately un-done on the next reconcile pass.
- `pkg/cluster/sync_fence_ack_7147.go:29-36`: *"`fenceAckOK` therefore means **'the peer confirms it relinquished every RG it knows about'**, which is the property a takeover gate should be built on."*

`FenceAckOK` therefore asserts a relinquishment that (a) never included the VIPs and (b) expires in ≤2 s while the fenced node still believes it is Primary. `peer-fencing disable-rg-confirmed` gates the surviving node's takeover on that assertion. That is a real gap between a documented operator-facing guarantee and the mechanism, and it is *not* recorded anywhere in the fence path.

## #9121 — daemon: clusterControlEndpointCommitPreflight omits FabricPeerAddress while clusterTransportKey includes it — the third member of the #8965/#8987 partition family, and on a fabric-transport cluster the gate misses twice [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-06)


- **Gate verdict:** MATERIAL
- **Claimed severity:** High → **Verified severity: High**, with the reachability bound stated in numbers below.
- **Confidence:** High
- **Verification:** STATIC
- **Prior-report column:** **no prior review finding**; it is a third member of a *filed* family (#8965 closed, **#8987 open**).

**Evidence**
- `pkg/daemon/cluster_topology_preflight.go:222-230` — the preflight passes **only** `newCfg.Chassis.Cluster.PeerAddress` to `controlEndpointDecision8965(running.HeartbeatPeerAddr(), …)`. `controlEndpointDecision8965` (`:243-253`) returns `nil` when either side is empty.
- `pkg/daemon/daemon_ha_sync.go:1354-1361` — `clusterTransportKey` **includes `FabricPeerAddress` and `Fabric1PeerAddress`**.
- `pkg/daemon/daemon_apply_tail.go:347-368` — step 20 restarts cluster comms whenever `newTransport != active`, i.e. on a fabric-peer-address change.
- `pkg/daemon/daemon_ha_comms_wiring.go:104-120` `clusterSyncTransport` — when `ControlInterface == "" || PeerAddress == ""`, session/config sync runs on `FabricInterface` / **`FabricPeerAddress`**.
- `pkg/daemon/daemon_ha_sync.go:882-886` — the heartbeat only starts when *both* `ControlInterface` and `PeerAddress` are set. In fabric-only mode there is no heartbeat, so `running.HeartbeatPeerAddr()` is also empty — the gate misses twice.
- No config validation requires `control-interface` (`pkg/config/schema_chassis.go:144` declares it as an optional leaf; `compiler_validate_warn.go:531` only warns if the named interface is undefined).

**Trace:** commit changing `fabric-peer-address` on a fabric-transport cluster → `clusterControlEndpointCommitPreflight` returns `nil` (PeerAddress empty) → step 20 sees `clusterTransportKey` changed → `stopClusterComms` + restart dialing the **new** fabric address → peer still on the old one → `pushCommittedConfigToPeer` → `syncConfigToPeer` → `QueueConfig` no-ops on a nil connection → **silent** push failure → durable partition. Every "nothing heals it" argument in `cluster_topology_preflight.go:186-198` (`reconcileConfigSyncToPeer` early-returns on `!syncPeerConnected`, that flag is set only in the session-sync connect callback, heartbeats carry no config) applies unchanged.

**Refutation attempt:** I checked whether the fabric address is somehow re-keyed live, or whether a fabric change routes the push over a surviving control link. It does not, in fabric transport mode — that mode *is* "no control link". In control-link mode a fabric-address change still restarts comms, but sync re-dials the unchanged control address and reconnects, so no partition; that is the bound.

**Reachability bound (numbers):** applies to clusters where `ControlInterface == ""` **or** `PeerAddress == ""` — the legacy fabric-transport shape `clusterSyncTransport` documents as "(legacy compatibility)". Zero of the repo's shipped cluster fixtures use it (`docs/ha-cluster-userspace.conf` and `test/incus/loss-userspace-cluster.env` both configure a control link), so this is not exercised by any harness.

**Fix direction:** unlike #8987's `control-interface` (whose blocker is that no running value exists), the running fabric peer address **is** already available — `d.activeTransport()` returns the live `clusterTransportKey`. So the gate is straightforwardly buildable: extend the preflight to compare `active.FabricPeerAddress` / `active.Fabric1PeerAddress` against the candidate, reusing `controlEndpointDecision8965`'s empty-side and equality rules so a peer-synced text stays a no-op. **Acceptance criterion:** a cell at the decision level (not the message builder — `controlEndpointDecision8965`'s own doc records that mistake) that reds when the fabric arm is neutered to `return nil`, plus a cell proving a *peer-synced* fabric text is not refused. Must be wired for all three apply paths, as #8987 item 4 requires.

**Dedup:** #8965 (CLOSED, PeerAddress half), **#8987 (OPEN, control-interface half)**, #7073, #7448, #8997. Distinct third field; file as a sibling of #8987 or fold into it.

**Why it matters:** a commit whose purpose is to renumber the fabric leaves both nodes durably partitioned while reporting success, and reboot/retry reproduce it.

## #9122 — dhcpserver: a Kea DHCPv6 group narrowed by the RG member filter renders subnet6 with an EMPTY interface selector, contradicting the renderer's own #1835 invariant three lines above — and it is the steady state, not a failover transient [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-06)


- **Gate verdict: MATERIAL** (narrowed — the report's own stated scenario is impossible)
- Claimed severity: High → **Verified severity: Medium** (bounded service-availability loss on one config shape, not "any cluster failover breaks IPv6")
- Confidence: High
- Verification: **EXECUTED**
- Evidence:
  - `pkg/dhcpserver/dhcpserver.go:840-848` — `subnetInterface` returns `""` first on `group.MembersFiltered`.
  - `pkg/dhcpserver/dhcpserver.go:1296-1305` — the v6 renderer's own invariant: *"Kea v6 subnet selection cannot fall back to address matching the way v4 can ... so subnet6 REQUIRES the interface selector — silently omitting it for a multi-interface group would orphan the subnet (Codex review on PR #1835)"* — then immediately `sub.Interface = subnetInterface(group)`.
  - `pkg/daemon/daemon_ha.go:1906` — `cp.MembersFiltered = len(kept) != len(group.Interfaces)`, inside `if len(kept) > 0`.
  - Function is `generateKea6Config`, not `buildKea6Config` as the report names it.
- Trace: `desiredClusterDHCPConfig` (`daemon_ha.go:1785-1796`) → `filterDHCPConfigForMasterRGs` → `MembersFiltered` → `dhcpServer.ApplyAsync` → `Apply` (`dhcpserver.go:362-367`, v4/v6 independent) → `generateKea6Config` → `subnetInterface` → `subnet6` rendered with no `interface`.
- Refutation attempt (what I killed, and what survived):
  - **KILLED — the report's probe cannot happen.** Its scenario starts from a *single-interface* group (`group g1 interface ge-0/0/0.0`) and asserts failover sets `MembersFiltered=true`. It cannot: the flag is `len(kept) != len(group.Interfaces)` with `len(kept) > 0`, so `MembersFiltered=true` **requires the resolved group to have had ≥ 2 interfaces**. A singleton is either unchanged (flag false) or dropped entirely. `resolveDHCPRethInterfaces` (`daemon_ha.go:2319-2333`) is 1:1, so a one-`reth` group resolves to one interface.
  - **KILLED — "failover" is the wrong trigger word.** `filterDHCPConfigForMasterRGs` is driven by the 2 s periodic converger as well as RG edges, so for a group spanning two RGs in an active/active cluster this is the **steady state on both nodes**, not a post-failover transient. That makes it worse, not better, but the report's causal story is wrong.
  - **SURVIVED — the defect itself.** For a v6 group authored with ≥ 2 interfaces and narrowed to ≥ 1, `len(group.Interfaces) > 1` no longer trips (it sees the *filtered* list), so the loud rejection is bypassed and the subnet renders selector-less. #6520's remedy — "fall back to address-based selection" — is **valid for v4 and invalid for v6 by this file's own comment**. The #6520 consumer test covers only v4.
- Probe (EXECUTED, then removed; tree restored):
  - Added `pkg/dhcpserver/zzz_probe_L10_test.go` calling `generateKea6Config` three ways and reading the rendered JSON:
    - CONTROL, singleton unfiltered → `map[2001:db8:1::/64:ge-0-0-1]` (selector present)
    - SUBJECT, singleton + `MembersFiltered=true` → `map[2001:db8:1::/64:]` (**selector empty**)
    - CONTROL, two interfaces unfiltered → `err = DHCPv6 group spanning interfaces [ge-0-0-1 ge-0-0-2]: Kea subnet6 requires a single interface selector — split the group per interface`
  - The third cell is the control that matters: it proves the loud path exists and that filtering is what routes around it.
  - Existing guard checked: `pkg/dhcpserver/kea_filtered_group_selector_6520_test.go` exercises only `generateKea4Config`. No v6 cell exists, so no mutation was needed to show the gap.
- Fix direction: make the v6 renderer refuse a narrowed group the same way it refuses a multi-interface one — `if len(group.Interfaces) > 1 || group.MembersFiltered { return fmt.Errorf(...) }` — i.e. keep #6520's "do not cross-bind" property by failing LOUD on the family that has no address fallback. Regression acceptance: the two probe cells above, as v6 twins of the existing #6520 v4 pair, plus a cell pinning that the v4 suppression is unchanged.
  **The report's proposed fix is HARMFUL.** Its `subnet6Interface` returns `group.Interfaces[0]` for a narrowed singleton — which is precisely the cross-bind #6520 was filed to stop, re-opened for v6: the removed member's pool gets bound to the survivor's interface and Kea leases a foreign prefix on that link.
- Dedup: `gh issue list --state all --search` on "dhcpv6 subnet interface selector" / "MembersFiltered" / "kea subnet6" → no open or closed match. `#6520` is the introducing change (v4-scoped); `#7318` (closed) is unrelated Kea wiring. **Distinct.**
- Prior-report collision: **no prior** (049/050 A10 carry no DHCPv6 subnet finding).
- Index accuracy: **accurate** — Section 5 `pkg/dhcpserver/dhcpserver.go:840-848` matches the body.
- Why it matters: on a cluster where a DHCPv6 group spans two RGs, both nodes render a `subnet6` with no interface selector and Kea cannot select the subnet for a link-local SOLICIT — silent total DHCPv6 outage for that group, with no error anywhere. Bounded by requiring a ≥ 2-interface v6 group, a shape the renderer tells the operator to split whenever it is *not* narrowed. Attribution caution: "DHCPv6 stopped after failover" also has other causes on this box (Kea stop inside the 20 s budget, #9035) — this one is distinguishable by the rendered `kea-dhcp6.conf` carrying a `subnet6` with no `interface` key.

## #9123 — snmp: the SNMPv1 Trap-PDU hardcodes agent-addr to 0.0.0.0 and its justifying comment cites the wrong RFC 2576 section — the normative text mandates the opposite, and no source-address knob exists to carry the value [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-06)


- **Gate verdict: MATERIAL**
- Claimed severity: Medium → **Verified severity: Medium** (narrowed: interop/attribution loss for `version v1` groups; the report's "NMS drop the trap as invalid" arm is unsupported)
- Confidence: Medium-High
- Verification: STATIC
- Evidence: `pkg/snmp/traps.go:202` — `pduBody = append(pduBody, berEncodeTLV(tagIPAddress, []byte{0, 0, 0, 0})...)`. Wiring confirmed: `traps.go:227` and `:230` dispatch `buildLinkTrapV1` for `version v1` and `version all` respectively (#3948).
- Refutation attempt, and what it turned up instead:
  - I went looking for a discarded configured value — the coordinator's severity discriminator. **There is none**: `config.SNMPTrapGroup` (`pkg/config/types_system.go:818-840`) carries only `Name`, `Targets`, `Version`, `Categories`. No `source-address` / `trap-options` knob exists in the schema. So this is "never implemented", not "configured value ignored" — which caps severity below the alternative reading.
  - But the code's **justification comment is a miscitation**, and that is the load-bearing discovery. `traps.go:160-162` says *"agent-addr is 0.0.0.0, per the RFC 2576 §3.1 SNMPv2->SNMPv1 mapping for a standard generic trap."* RFC 3584 (which obsoletes 2576) puts the SNMPv2→SNMPv1 translation in **§3.2**, not §3.1 (§3.1 is the opposite direction), and its normative text is: *"If the translation occurs within a notification originator application, and the notification is to be sent over IP, the SNMPv1 agent-addr parameter SHALL be set to the IP address of the SNMP entity in which the notification originator resides. If the notification is to be sent over some other transport, the SNMPv1 agent-addr parameter SHALL be set to 0.0.0.0."* xpf is a notification originator sending over IP, so the cited authority mandates the **opposite** of what the code does; 0.0.0.0 is the non-IP-transport / indeterminate-proxy fallback.
  - I did **not** verify the report's stronger consequence. Many receivers (net-snmp `snmptrapd` among them) fall back to the UDP source address, so "the trap is dropped as malformed" is not established. The established consequence is attribution: a receiver that keys its inventory on `agent-addr` files link-up/down against node `0.0.0.0`.
- Probe: no execution evidence — this is a wire-format conformance question settled by reading the emitter, the RFC, and the config schema. No on-wire capture was taken (out of scope: no live cluster probes).
- Fix direction: populate `agent-addr` from the local address of the UDP association to the trap target (the socket already exists; `net.UDPConn.LocalAddr` or a route lookup toward the target), falling back to 0.0.0.0 only when no IPv4 address can be determined — which is then the RFC-sanctioned use of that value. Separately, add the Junos-parity `snmp trap-options source-address <addr>` leaf so an operator can pin it. **And fix the comment in the same change**: it currently cites a section number that is the wrong direction and a rule that says the opposite. Regression acceptance: a cell decoding `buildLinkTrapV1`'s output and asserting the `tagIPAddress` field equals the configured/derived source, plus a cell pinning 0.0.0.0 for the no-IPv4 case.
- Dedup: `#3948` (CLOSED) added the v1 PDU shape and is where this line was written; `#5049` (CLOSED) added v1 polling. Neither covers `agent-addr`. Distinct; a residual of #3948.
- Prior-report collision: **no prior**.
- Index accuracy: **accurate** (`pkg/snmp/traps.go:198-208`).
- Why it matters: for `version v1` / `version all` trap groups, link-state alarms arrive attributed to 0.0.0.0 on any NMS that trusts `agent-addr` over the UDP source. Bounded: v2c is the default and is unaffected; a receiver that uses the packet source is unaffected.

## #9126 — config: `show | display set` emits a bare `deactivate <path>` with no preceding `set` for an empty inactive container — three ordinary CLI commands produce it, and LoadSet being atomic aborts the WHOLE restore [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-06)

  lost object carries no configuration — but it aborts a whole `load set`/`load merge`
  transaction, which is a restore-path availability cost)
- Confidence: High
- Verification: **EXECUTED**
- Channel measured: `ConfigTree.FormatSet` (the `show | display set` renderer) and the real
  `configstore.Store` replay paths (`LoadMerge`, and `LoadSet` via `applyEditLine`).
- Evidence: `pkg/config/ast_format.go:251-263` — a non-leaf node emits no `set` line of its own,
  recurses into (empty) `Children`, then unconditionally emits `deactivate <path>`.
  `pkg/config/ast_edit.go:1012-1020` — `setInactiveAtPath` errors `path not found: container %q
  does not exist`.
- Probe, executed against a real `Store`, **with two controls that pass**:
  ```
  Store.LoadMerge("protocols { inactive: bgp { } }")
      -> merge: path not found: container "protocols" does not exist        <- FAILS
  Store.LoadMerge("protocols { inactive: bgp { group g1 { type external; } } }")
      -> nil                                                               <- control passes
  Store.LoadMerge("protocols { bgp { } }")
      -> nil                                                               <- control passes
  ```
  And the reachability is better than the report's: **three ordinary CLI commands** produce it,
  no config file required —
  ```

  deactivate protocols bgp
  delete protocols bgp group g1

  ```

  same (`inactive: bgp { group g1 { } }` → same single line, same replay error).
- Blast radius: `LoadSet` is atomic since #5187 (`store_command.go:604-652` replays into a clone
  and swaps only on complete success), so ONE unreplayable line **aborts the entire load** with a
  line-numbered error and leaves the candidate untouched. `LoadMerge`'s hierarchical branch
  renders the parsed file with `FormatSet` and replays it through the same `applyEditLine`
  (`store_command.go:490-510`), so a hierarchical restore hits it too.
- Refutation attempt: is an empty inactive container an illegitimate AST shape? No — it survives
  `configstore.CheckText` (measured ACCEPT), it is producible from the CLI as shown, and Junos
  accepts an empty stanza.

## #9128 — nat64: a quoted FIRST fragment loses its fragmentation fields in the ICMPv6-to-ICMPv4 embedded translation — the non-first case is gated shut, so this is the reachable half [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-06)


- Gate verdict: **MATERIAL (heavily narrowed)**
- Claimed severity: High   Verified severity: **Low** — the claimed consequence ("errors cannot be
  correlated to sockets") is refuted; what remains is an RFC 7915 §5.1/§5.2 conformance gap.
- Confidence: High
- Verification: STATIC
- Evidence: `nat64.rs:3178-3179` in `translate_embedded_v6_to_v4`:
  `out[4..6].copy_from_slice(&[0, 0]);` / `out[6..8].copy_from_slice(&0x4000u16.to_be_bytes());`
  — Identification 0, DF=1, MF=0, offset=0, unconditionally.
  RFC 7915 §5.1 (which §5.2 defers to for the embedded header) requires, when a Fragment Header
  is present: Identification from its low 16 bits, DF cleared, M flag and Fragment Offset copied.
- Trace: `write_v6_to_v4_translate` → `translate_icmpv6_message_to_icmpv4:2924` →
  `write_icmpv4_error_with_embedded` → `translate_embedded_v6_to_v4:3121`.
- Refutation attempt (what narrows it):
  - The report's own probe (`offset = 100, MF = 1`) is **refuted**: `nat64.rs:3147-3150`
    `if ipv6_is_non_first_fragment(quote_in) { return None; }` (#2290) drops it. Only a **FIRST**
    fragment quote (offset 0, MF=1) reaches the defective write.
  - The consequence claim is refuted: a first-fragment quote carries a real L4 header, the ports
    are preserved, and #6472 (`nat64.rs:3193-3200`) even restores the translated port — which is
    what Linux/BSD ICMP-error socket demux actually keys on. Nothing in a receiver's error path
    reads the quoted IPv4 ID/MF/offset.
  - The emitted header is well-formed (RFC 6864 §4.1 permits ID 0 on an atomic DF=1 datagram); it
    is unfaithful, not invalid.
  - The OUTER v6→v4 path does this correctly (`nat64.rs:2398-2405` copies MF/offset/ident from the
    IPv6 Fragment Header), so the defect is specific to the embedded twin.
- Probe: none executed — the write is unconditional and needs no runtime evidence; the guard that
  bounds it (`ipv6_is_non_first_fragment`) was read in full.
- Fix direction: in `translate_embedded_v6_to_v4`, carry the walked `Ipv6FragInfo` (already parsed
  by `walk_ipv6_ext_chain`) into `out[4..8]`: `ident & 0xFFFF`, DF=0, `M`→MF, offset copied. Pair
  it with the v4→v6 mirror (see -025) as ONE change. **Regression acceptance:** an ICMPv6 error
  whose quote is a first fragment produces an embedded IPv4 header with the original ID, MF=1,
  DF=0; an unfragmented quote stays byte-identical; a non-first-fragment quote still drops.
- Dedup: distinct from #6472, #2488, #2562, #2371, #5177 (all read). Same COHORT as -025.
- Why it matters: conformance/assurance only. Bounded by the non-first-fragment drop.
- **Prior-round column: no prior same-claim** (050-024 is the OTHER direction).

## #9130 — nat: allocate_deterministic_v4/v6 hold the allocator mutex across the whole linear CAS port probe, while the sibling PAT path was deliberately restructured the other way in #4676 — a residual at a site #2852/#4676 never reached [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-06)

  (and the identical shape in `allocate_deterministic_v6`, `:2617` / `:2630-2660`). The in-code
  comment concedes the shape: *"The block is small (typically a few thousand ports) and this is
  the cold path (first packet of a flow), so a linear CAS probe is fine."*
  `docs/deterministic-nat-cgnat.md:38` documents `block-size 2016`, so the report's 2016-4096
  figure is grounded in the repo's own example.

  claims the port lock-free (`occ.claim()`, `:1774`) and takes `lock_live()` only for the tiny
  reuse/cap/insert critical section (`:1793-1826`), with `#4676` explicitly moving GC off that
  section: *"run the amortized expiry GC OFF the insert critical section … so the insert CS stays
  genuinely tiny."* The deterministic arms kept the pre-restructure shape.

  the report's "packet processing serialized" framing overstates it; (b) it is the first packet of
  a flow only; (c) the probe is O(occupied prefix of the block), not O(block_size), because it
  restarts at `port_start` and freed ports leave holes — so the worst case needs a subscriber
  near its own block budget; (d) no `Rx ring drop` evidence is offered and none exists — the loss
  userspace cluster carries no deterministic-NAT config, so this has never been measured.
  None of these makes the lock scope correct.
- **The report's governing authority is phantom.** It cites "Core Mandate 4 in `GEMINI.md`" and
  `docs/engineering-standards-hpc.md`. Neither file exists at this SHA and neither was ever added
  (`git log --all --diff-filter=A` on both paths returns nothing). The real in-repo contract is
  `docs/engineering-style.md` ("If a mutex is unavoidable, isolate it to a slow path") plus the
  #4676 comment above, and both support the finding on their own.
- Probe: none executed. A meaningful probe needs a deterministic-NAT config on the loss cluster
  plus lock-wait instrumentation, which is outside this run's scope (no live-cluster probes).
- Fix direction: mirror `allocate_translation_inner` — probe/claim the block on
  `self.shared.occupancy[ip_idx]` WITHOUT the mutex, then take `lock_live()` for the
  idempotency + cap check + insert, and `free_translated_port(ip_idx, port, /* recycle */ false)`

  direction is the right shape but omits the `recycle = false` detail, which matters.

  For GRE(47)/ESP(50)/ICMP the key degenerates to `(proto, translated_ip, 0, dst_ip, 0)`, so two
  port-less flows from different sources to the SAME remote collide whenever they land on the same

    `address_index` is `sticky_pool_index(src_ip, …)` — a pure function of the source — and
    probing elsewhere would break the `address-persistent` contract; the roundrobin sibling
    likewise sets `address_attempts = 1` there. With an EXISTING lease the address is pinned by
    `persistent-nat` and must not move. Only the **fresh lease + `address-persistent` off** case
    (where `address_index` is just a round-robin counter, `allocator.rs:1631-1635`) can safely
    probe on.

    fallback that `address-persistent` forbids.

  pinned cases. **Do NOT** apply the report's blanket fallback — it would break both

## #9132 — dataplane/routing: a BARE routing-instance interface reference binds no addressed unit, so the VRF's connected prefix installs into inet.0 — buildInterfaceZoneMap fans bare refs down to units and the two routes.go builders do not [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-06)


- Gate verdict: **MATERIAL**
- Claimed severity: High   Verified severity: **High** (mechanism corrected — see below)
- Confidence: High
- Verification: **EXECUTED** (hermetic probe through the strict `CompileConfig` path, with a cross-subsystem control)
- Prior: no prior in 049/050. Related-but-distinct open issues #9063 and #8994 (both checked, see Dedup).

- **The report's mechanism is right; its framing is one step off, and the corrected form is stronger.** Both `buildInterfaceRouteTables` (`pkg/dataplane/userspace/routes.go:521-544`) and `buildInterfaceRoutingInstances` (`routes.go:554-…`) key on `config.CanonicalInterfaceUnitRef(ifname)`. The defect is not a canonicalization *mismatch* — both maps and the snapshot consumer agree on the canonical spelling. It is a **missing bare→units fan-down**: a bare `ge-0/0/0` reference produces only the key `ge-0/0/0`, while the addressed row is the per-unit snapshot `ge-0/0/0.0` (`interfaces.go:397`, `:432`).
- **The control that makes this a defect rather than an unsupported input:** the sibling binder in the same documented family DOES fan down. `config.InterfaceZoneMap` (`pkg/config/host_inbound_effective_view.go:57-72`) explicitly walks `cfg.Interfaces.Interfaces[iface].Units` and writes `<base>.<unit>` keys for a bare reference. `CanonicalInterfaceUnitRef`'s own doc (`pkg/config/schema_validators.go:241-245`) names `buildInterfaceZoneMap`, `buildInterfaceRoutingInstances`, `buildInterfaceRouteTables` as the family that must stay aligned. Two of the three do not.
- **Bare references are accepted and are treated by the repo as load-bearing VRF membership.** `validateInterfaceUnitReferencesStrict` skips a bare ref by design (`pkg/config/compiler_validate_strict_unitref.go:38-40`). And `TestRoutingInstanceInterfaceMultiValueFlat` / `…Hierarchical` / `…SingleValue` (`pkg/config/compiler_routing_instance_interface_3904_test.go`) use **bare** names throughout, under a header calling the failure to capture them "a VRF isolation break". #3904 fixed the bracket-list read so all three bare names reach `ri.Interfaces` — and then nothing binds them.
- Probe (EXECUTED, hermetic, strict `config.CompileConfig`; scratch tests written into the worktree, run, then removed; tree restored and re-verified clean):
  ```
  === BARE:  set routing-instances tenant-a interface ge-0/0/0 ===
  interfaceTablesV4 = map[ge-0/0/0:tenant-a.inet.0]
  iface name="ge-0/0/0"    RI="tenant-a"  addrs=[]
  iface name="ge-0/0/0.0"  RI=""          addrs=[{inet 192.168.10.1/24 0}]
  route  table="inet.0"          family="inet" dest="192.168.10.0/24"      <-- LEAK

  === CONTROL, UNIT: set routing-instances tenant-a interface ge-0/0/0.0 ===
  interfaceTablesV4 = map[ge-0/0/0.0:tenant-a.inet.0]
  iface name="ge-0/0/0.0"  RI="tenant-a"  addrs=[{inet 192.168.10.1/24 0}]
  route  table="tenant-a.inet.0" family="inet" dest="192.168.10.0/24"      <-- correct

  === CROSS-SUBSYSTEM CONTROL (same config, bare in BOTH subsystems) ===
  buildInterfaceZoneMap          = map[ge-0/0/0:trust ge-0/0/0.0:trust]    <-- fans down
  buildInterfaceRoutingInstances = map[ge-0/0/0:tenant-a]                  <-- does not
  ```
  The third block is what rules out "bare is simply unsupported everywhere": the zone binder resolves it, the routing binders do not.
- Trace, both planes: `ri.Interfaces=["ge-0/0/0"]` → `buildInterfaceRouteTables` keys `ge-0/0/0` → `buildRouteSnapshots`' per-interface loop (`routes.go:232-247`) misses on `ge-0/0/0.0` and falls back to `"inet.0"` → connected `RouteSnapshot` in the default table. Independently, `buildInterfaceRoutingInstances` misses, so `InterfaceSnapshot.RoutingInstance == ""` for the addressed unit → Rust `connected_route_tables(&iface.routing_instance)` yields `inet.0` and pushes `ConnectedRouteV4{ table: "inet.0", ifindex }` (`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/forwarding_build/interfaces.rs:524`, `:570`), and `local_tables_v4` records the interface host address as owned by `inet.0` (`:564-568`).
- Refutation attempt: (1) Is the addressed row's routing instance recovered anywhere downstream? No — Rust derives the connected table purely from `iface.routing_instance`. (2) Does the #2388 table-scoping fix cover it? It is the fix that is **hollowed**: #2388 (CLOSED) made `connected_v4` table-keyed off `iface.routing_instance`, which is exactly the field that is empty here. (3) Does the base row rescue it? Only partially and only on a real box: the base `InterfaceSnapshot`'s addresses come from `buildLinkSnapshot(linuxName)` (kernel), so in production the base netdev's unit-0 address would ALSO produce a `tenant-a.inet.0` entry — a duplicate publish rather than a pure misattribution. **State the reach precisely: hermetically, the addressed unit row binds to `inet.0` and the tenant table gets nothing; in production the prefix is expected in BOTH tables. In either reading `inet.0` gains a connected prefix, with a valid egress ifindex, for a VRF-attached interface.** I could not close the production half hermetically and say so rather than asserting it.
- Fix direction: give `buildInterfaceRouteTables` and `buildInterfaceRoutingInstances` the same fan-down `InterfaceZoneMap` already implements (bare ref → every configured unit of that interface), ideally by hoisting that loop into one shared `pkg/config` helper so the three cannot drift again. Regression acceptance: a table-driven cell over the SAME corpus of refs asserting all three binders agree on which snapshot rows a bare ref reaches, plus the two rows above as fixtures (bare → `tenant-a.inet.0`, unit → `tenant-a.inet.0`). The residual half (a base row inheriting kernel addresses that belong to a unit) deserves its own cell.
- Dedup: **distinct.** #9063 (OPEN) is `logicalUnitDeviceKey` in `pkg/daemon/daemon_run_routehelpers.go` collapsing unit 0 **to** the bare base for FRR link-local next-hop inference — the dual direction, a different site, a different consequence. #8994 (OPEN) is the three *Junos→Linux name* resolvers (`ResolveKernelIfName`/`snapshotLinuxName`/`resolveJunosIfName`), a different family. #2388 (CLOSED) is the Rust-side table scoping this defect renders inert. #5878 phase 2 canonicalized the suffix but never added the fan-down. Same *class* as #9063/#8994 (interface-reference key shape held together by a note); worth cross-referencing on filing.
- Why it matters: an operator writes a routine, accepted, strict-commit-clean `set routing-instances <ri> interface ge-0/0/0`, the box reports the interface as a VRF member on every show surface, and the dataplane installs its subnet in the default table with a working egress. Bounded by: the operator must use the bare spelling (the unit spelling is correct), and the interface must carry addresses on a unit.

## #9133 — snmp: BER OID sub-identifiers are platform-width signed int with no RFC 2578 bound — a crafted GET makes the agent emit a lone continuation octet its own decoder rejects, and inverts oidCompare ordering [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-06)


- **Gate verdict: MATERIAL**
- Claimed severity: High → **Verified severity: Medium** (no crash, no memory unsafety, no auth bypass, no cross-client effect; community + source-ACL gated)
- Confidence: High
- Verification: **EXECUTED**
- Evidence, three sites, one root cause:
  - `pkg/snmp/agent_ber.go:270-292` — `berDecodeOID` accumulates `val = (val << 7) | int(data[i]&0x7f)` into a signed `int` with no overflow check and no RFC 2578 `0..4294967295` bound.
  - `pkg/snmp/agent_ber.go:161-174` — `berEncodeSubID` tests `if val < 0x80 { return []byte{byte(val)} }`, which is **true for every negative value**.
  - `pkg/snmp/agent_ber.go:396-408` — `oidCompare` does signed `<` on components.
- Trace (fully established, not inferred): UDP → community + source-ACL check (`agent.go:960-990` v2c, `:1029-1048` v1 — **the gate precedes the PDU decode**) → `handleV1Get`/`handleV1GetNext`/`handleGetBulk` → `decodePDUFields` (`agent_ber.go:359`) → `berDecodeOID` → negative component in `oids` → on a miss, `echoVarbinds(oids)` (`agent.go:1108`, `:1137`) puts the *request* OIDs into the response → `berEncodeOID`/`berEncodeSubID` (`agent.go:1583`, `:1892`, `v3.go:1082`).
- Probe (EXECUTED; three throwaway test files added under `pkg/snmp/`, all removed, tree restored):
  - **Silent value corruption.** Input `2b 06 01 04 01 81 fd 59` + `81 80 80 80 80 80 80 80 80 01` (10 continuation octets, 70 bits) → `berDecodeOID` returns `[1 3 6 1 4 1 32473 -9223372036854775807]` with **no error**; `berEncodeOID` of that yields `2b 06 01 04 01 81 fd 59 01`, i.e. `.32473.1` — a *different, well-formed* OID than the one requested.
  - **Malformed BER on the wire.** Input `2b ff ff ff ff ff ff ff ff ff 7f` → `[1 3 -1]`; `berEncodeSubID(-1)` → `ff`, a lone continuation octet with no terminator; full re-encode `2b ff`; feeding that back through **the agent's own decoder** returns `ber: OID sub-identifier truncated`. So the agent emits a response it cannot itself parse.
  - **Ordering inversion.** `oidCompare([...32473 -1], [...32473 1])` → `-1` (a huge sub-id sorts *before* 1). `findNextOIDSnap([1 3 6 1 2 1 -9223372036854775807])` → `[1 3 6 1 2 1 1 1 0]`, i.e. a GETNEXT from a huge sub-identifier restarts at the top of the subtree — the walk-loop mechanism, though only a crafted client can enter it.
  - **Negative control on the panic hypothesis**: I looked for a crash and did not find one. `getOIDValueSnap` / `findNextOIDSnap` with negative components return cleanly, no panic. `berEncodeSubID` on a negative value returns from the first branch and never enters the `v > 0` loop. Reporting this because it is what bounds the severity — a "DoS" reading is not supported.
  - Sanity: `berEncodeSubID(4294967295)` → `8f ff ff ff 7f`, correct, so the encoder is right for the whole *legal* RFC 2578 range. The defect is purely the unbounded/unsigned modelling.
- Refutation attempt: the strongest counter is reachability — the community string and the optional client ACL both gate the decode. That is a genuine bound and it is why I am not carrying High. It is not a refutation: v1/v2c community strings are weak shared secrets, the ACL is optional, and the report's specific claim about `byte(val)` producing `0xFF` is *confirmed* for the `-1` input above. What I did refute is the report's framing "corrupting the SNMP response **stream**" — SNMP over UDP is one datagram per response, so a crafted request corrupts only the crafting client's own reply.
- Fix direction: model sub-identifiers as `uint32` per RFC 2578 §7.1.3. In `berDecodeOID`, reject before the shift (`if val > (math.MaxUint32 >> 7) { return error }`) and bound the continuation run; in `berEncodeSubID`, make the negative/out-of-range case unrepresentable rather than silently truncating. Regression acceptance: the two probe vectors above as table cells asserting a decode *error* (not a value), plus a round-trip property cell over the legal `0..4294967295` range.
- Dedup: `gh issue list --search "OID sub-identifier"` / `"berDecodeOID"` → nothing. Distinct.
- **Prior-report collision and the cross-lane question the coordinator asked**: `GEMINI-050-048` is `pkg/snmp/agent_ber.go:202-221`, `berDecodeLength` 32-bit overflow → negative slice bounds. That is a **different function** and a different symptom (panic vs. silent corruption), so at *finding* granularity it is same-site-different-claim. At **class** granularity it is the same defect: `agent_ber.go` models BER integers as platform-width signed `int` with no bound, and every one of these findings is a consequence. My independent judgement on `-041`/`-042` (held by another lane at the same file, which I have not read): **if either of them is about signed/unbounded integer arithmetic in `agent_ber.go`, it is the same root cause as -098 and the three should be one finding with three call sites.** The discriminator I would apply is the fix: any finding whose repair is "represent this quantity as an unsigned type with an explicit RFC bound" is the same defect. Only a finding about a *different* property — a missing length check, a wrong tag, a mis-parsed structure — is genuinely separate. Report 051 therefore very likely triple-counts one BER defect toward its 100.
- Index accuracy: **the report's Section 5 index is misleading** — it lists `agent_ber.go:398-408` (`oidCompare`), which is the *third* of the three sites the body names and the least load-bearing. The body's own citation (`161-174` + `278-294`) is right.

## This issue covers TWO source finding IDs — one root cause

Two lanes reached the same conclusion independently, from opposite ends of the
same pipeline:

- **`GEMINI-051-098`** (this body) cites the **encoder** side,
  `pkg/snmp/agent_ber.go:161-174`.
- **`GEMINI-051-042`** cites the **decode accumulator**,
  `pkg/snmp/agent_ber.go:278-294`, and was verified MATERIAL (narrow) with an
  executed end-to-end reproduction: a crafted GET makes the agent emit the
  varbind OID TLV `06 02 2b ff` — a dangling continuation octet that is
  unparseable BER. No hang, no walk inversion, no cross-session effect.

They are **one defect**: BER integers modelled as platform-width signed `int`
with no RFC 2578 bound, in a single sub-identifier pipeline. One fix closes
both. The discriminator applied: any finding whose repair is "unsigned type +
explicit RFC bound" is the same defect; only a *different property* (a missing
length check, a wrong tag, a mis-parsed structure) is genuinely separate.

## #9134 — api: HEAD is admitted as a safe method but restReadPermissions has 40 "GET " keys and 0 "HEAD " keys, so readAuthz fails OPEN and every guarded read route executes its handler with NO authorization decision [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-06)

`isSafeHTTPMethod` admits `HEAD`, `readAuthz` keys its permission lookup on
`r.Method + " " + r.URL.Path`, and `restReadPermissions` contains **40 `"GET "`
keys and zero `"HEAD "` keys**. An unknown key is the documented **fail-open**
arm, so a `HEAD` request to any of the 40 guarded read routes is handed straight
to the mux — which routes `HEAD` to the `GET` pattern **directly, with no
redirect**. No authorization decision runs at all.

## Measured on the production middleware chain

Driven through the real chain with `PeerLookupFn: fixedPeerUID(4244)` — a real
local account present in `/etc/passwd` with **no `system login user` entry**, so
its class is `""`:

```
GET  /api/v1/config            -> 403  "permission denied: uid 4244 (stranger, class \"\") is not a conf..."
HEAD /api/v1/config            -> 200  (handler executed)
GET  /api/v1/config/export     -> 403
HEAD /api/v1/config/export     -> 200  clen=168   (handler ran; exact body SIZE disclosed)
HEAD /api/v1/security/ipsec/sa -> 200  clen=57
HEAD /api/v1/security/sessions -> 503  straight out of sessionsHandler
HEAD /api/v1/routing/ospf      -> 200  clen=55    (FRR handler ran)
HEAD /api/v1/config/set        -> 405  (mutating routes correctly NOT aliased)
```

The same server refuses this caller on `GET` and serves it on `HEAD`.

## Evidence at `930767a40a610226af6e55970b3dd774d429b719`

Four links, each read at the pinned SHA:

1. `pkg/api/crosssite.go:53-60` — `isSafeHTTPMethod` includes `http.MethodHead`.
2. `pkg/api/authz.go:845-850` — `mutationAuthzGuard` routes any safe method to
   `readAuthz`.
3. `pkg/api/authz.go:823-828` — `route := r.Method + " " + r.URL.Path;
   required, known := restReadPermissions[route]; if !known { next.ServeHTTP(w, r); return }`.
   `grep -c` confirms both directions: **40** `"GET /api/v1…"` keys, **0**
   `"HEAD "` keys.
4. Go's `ServeMux` routes a `HEAD` request to a `GET`-registered pattern
   directly. All 61 mux registrations are literal — no wildcard or subtree
   pattern — so there is no redirect to re-enter the guard on.

## #9146 — UNRESOLVED: cluster — the HA session-sync DELETE wire carries no routing domain, so a standby's delete hits #8636's ambiguous-routing-domain refusal; #8636's "leaks for ONE PACKET" acceptance was written for a caller a standby never has [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-07)


- **Gate verdict:** NEEDS_VALIDATION
- **Claimed severity:** High → **Verified severity: Medium** (bounded standby-side stale-session leak; two of the four sub-claims refuted outright).
- **Confidence:** Medium
- **Verification:** STATIC
- **Prior-report column:** **same-family, different site.** 049-022 / OPEN #9033 is the NAT64 *reverse session key* inside `userspace-dp`; #9032 is the native-GRE TUN producer; #9062 is the NAT pool key. This claim is the **Go cluster-sync delete wire + gen maps** — a genuinely different site in the same #7160 family.

**What is established (STATIC, certain)**
- `pkg/cluster/sync_protocol.go:398-435` `encodeDeleteV4` — 16-byte bare 5-tuple + 8-byte gen. No routing domain, no discriminator. Install (`:240`, `:386`, decode `:612`, `:779`) *does* carry `val.RoutingDomain`.
- `pkg/dataplane/types.go:13-21` — `dataplane.SessionKey` is the bare 5-tuple; `RoutingDomain` lives on the **value** (`types.go:342-360`), carried as a length-gated trailing sync-only field.
- `pkg/dataplane/userspace/manager_sessions.go:298-314` `DeleteSession` → `m.syncSessionV4Locked("delete", key, **nil**)`; `manager_sessionsync_request.go:16-30` with `val == nil` leaves `RoutingDomain = 0` **and** `IngressIfindex = 0`.
- `userspace-dp/src/session/routing_domain_wire.rs:20-26` — wire `0` is `WIRE_ABSENT`, so the helper falls to `view.synced_routing_domain(0, 0)` → `None` → delete uses `unwrap_or(0)`.
- `userspace-dp/src/server/handlers/sync_session.rs:196-230` — with `key.routing_domain == 0` the helper probes `view.routing_domains()` (the deduped **non-zero** set) and **refuses** with `ambiguous-routing-domain` when ≥2 match.

**What is refuted (with mechanisms)**
1. *"Tenant B's later installs are dropped as stale by the tombstone."* **No.** `takeDeleteGenV4` (`sync_conn_gen.go:213-221`) returns `s.nextInstallGen()` — a **globally monotonic** counter, not a per-key echo. Every install stamped after the delete is strictly greater than the tombstone, so `installGenGuardV4`'s `incoming < stored` never fires for it. Only an install stamped *before* the delete and reordered after it is dropped, and the 1 s sweep re-stamps and re-sends. The report's step 5 does not happen.
2. *"Premature session purging."* The bare-keyed `genSentV4`/`recvGenV4` collision the report describes is real but is a *consequence* of `dataplane.SessionKey` having no domain axis at all — which #7160 (CLOSED, `plan-deferred-operator`) explicitly decided, and which the Go BPF `sessions` map enforces anyway (see 053).

**The genuinely NEW sub-claim, and it is the one worth keeping**
`sync_session.rs`'s #8636 acceptance argument for refusing an ambiguous delete is: *"A refused delete therefore leaks for ONE PACKET, not until idle timeout"* — because #8356 re-derives zone policy on the established-session hit path. **That argument does not transfer to the HA session-sync delete path**, which lands on a **standby**: a synced session there receives no packets, so nothing re-judges it. It leaks until its idle timeout, and is then *promoted* on failover. #8636's comment names only *"the `clear security flow session` / batch-revoke path"*; the arm it guards also serves the cluster-sync delete. That is an acceptance scope written for one caller and silently inherited by another with a different consequence.

**What is NOT established — the decisive check**
For the refusal to fire, the standby helper must hold **two synced sessions with the same 5-tuple in two different non-zero routing domains**. Both nodes' Go mirrors are bare-keyed BPF hashes, so the two tenants' sessions collide to one row there; the only route I can see is *alternation* — the mirror row flipping between the two tenants' values across sweeps, pushing first one domain then the other. I did not demonstrate that.
**Next decisive check (cheap, hermetic first):** (1) a Rust cell in `userspace-dp` that upserts two synced sessions with identical 5-tuple under two non-zero domains and issues a bare delete, asserting `SYNCED_DELETE_REFUSED…ambiguous-routing-domain` — this pins the helper half; (2) the Go half is the real question — instrument or reason out whether successive `syncSessionV4Locked("upsert", …)` for one bare key can carry two different `val.RoutingDomain` values, given the mirror holds one row. If (2) is no, this collapses to NEG.

**Fix direction:** the report's "extend the wire + composite Go key" is the #7160 Option B shape and is **not** free — read #7160's own correction comment first (an earlier contract there told an implementer to bump `CurrentHAProtocolVersion`, which the maintainer later struck as *"actively harmful"*). The cheap, in-scope repair is at `pkg/dataplane/userspace/manager_sessions.go:298-314` and `pkg/dataplane/session_store.go:412-432`: **the value is already in hand at the delete site** (`GetSessionV4` is called for `ReverseKey`) and is discarded — pass `val.RoutingDomain` into the delete request so the exact delete lands and the ambiguity probe never runs. Acceptance criterion: a helper-side cell proving a delete for a tenant session names its domain, plus a cell proving a delete for a *default-instance* session still resolves domain 0.

**Dedup:** #7160 (closed, posture decision), #8636 (closed, the refusal), #9031/#9032/#9033/#9062 (open siblings, different sites), #2170/#2221 (gen guards), #9048. Distinct site; belongs in the #7160 family.

- Evidence: `pkg/ddns/backend_route53.go:320-341` (`mergeUpsertValues`, `seen` keyed on the raw string), `:345-355` (`removeValue`, `v == owned`), `:359-375` (`sameValueSet`, raw-string sets), `:440-465` (`DeleteLease`, `if !removed { return nil }`). `listRRSet` (`:175-230`) appends `strings.TrimSpace(rr.Value)` with no `netip` normalization. The report's code reading is accurate.
- Trace: `UpsertLease`/`DeleteLease` → `listRRSet` (raw strings from AWS XML) → `mergeUpsertValues`/`removeValue`/`sameValueSet` (byte compare) → `buildChangeBatch`.
- Refutation attempt:
  - **The whole finding rests on one unverified external premise**: that Route 53 echoes an AAAA value in a form `netip.Addr.String()` never produces. The report asserts this with no citation.
  - **Evidence FOR the premise**: AWS's own *Supported DNS record types* page gives the AAAA example as `2001:0db8:85a3:0:0:8a2e:0370:7334` — leading zeros retained, zero groups uncompressed. That is not RFC 5952 and not what Go emits. An operator following AWS's documented format produces a string that can never byte-equal xpf's.
  - **Evidence AGAINST the harm**: the delete arm is largely self-defeating. `DeleteLease`'s doc comment already declares a non-matching value as *intended* no-op ("deleting a FOREIGN value would itself be the bug — the Surface A sole-delete-authority boundary"). And xpf only ever *writes* the canonical form, so if a publish ever succeeded, xpf's canonical value **is** in the live set and `removeValue` finds it. The "record leaked forever" story therefore requires that xpf never published — in which case the lingering record is the operator's own and must not be deleted.
  - The surviving credible arm is the **upsert duplicate**: an operator pre-seeds the FQDN with the *same* address in AWS's documented expanded form; `mergeUpsertValues` dedups on the raw string, so both representations go into one ChangeBatch. `mergeUpsertValues`'s own comment states "Route 53 rejects a duplicate value in one RRset" — so if Route 53 dedups semantically, that publish fails 400 and never converges.
  - Same byte-exact pattern exists in `backend_cloudflare.go:327,376` (`r.Content == content`), so this is a package-wide convention, not a Route-53 slip. `backend_rfc2136.go` is immune (miekg/dns parses to `net.IP`).
  - Note: `wireRRClaim` (`pkg/ddns/state.go:449-470`) **does** normalize rdata through `netip` precisely so "an IPv6 address written expanded vs compressed" compares equal across surfaces — the repo already owns the helper this path does not use.
- Probe: no execution evidence exists, and this is the reason: the discriminating fact is Route 53's echo behaviour for AAAA, which cannot be observed without a live `ChangeResourceRecordSets` + `ListResourceRecordSets` round trip. Two web searches and the AWS record-type doc did not settle it; the doc's *example* format is suggestive but not normative about storage.
- **Exact next decisive check**: in a scratch hosted zone, `aws route53 change-resource-record-sets` an AAAA with `2001:0DB8:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0001`, then `aws route53 list-resource-record-sets` and read the `Value` back. Echoed verbatim ⇒ the finding is MATERIAL at Medium and the fix below applies. Returned as `2001:db8::1` ⇒ **NEG**, premise false, all three arms unreachable.
- Fix direction (only if the check comes back "verbatim"): a `canonicalIP(s)` helper used as the *comparison key* in `mergeUpsertValues`/`removeValue`/`sameValueSet` — reuse `wireRRClaim`'s existing normalization rather than adding a fourth copy. Emit the ORIGINAL string for foreign members you preserve (normalizing a foreign member on write-back would rewrite someone else's record). The report's `canonicalIP` returns the normalized form for *output* too, which quietly rewrites foreign values — narrow it to key-only.
- Dedup: no open/closed issue on Route 53 value canonicalization. **Consistency with #9067 (OPEN)**: #9067's Route 53 baseline is that it "compares both [IP and TTL]" (`live.found && live.ttl == ttl && sameValueSet(...)`). That is a claim about *which fields* are compared, not *how*; -092 questions the comparison's semantics for one field. **The two are consistent**; -092 would not falsify #9067, only add that the value half is byte-exact. -092 is not a duplicate of #9067. Report-quality note: the report claims it suppressed #9067, i.e. it read that issue and still filed three Route 53 findings — none of which is the Cloudflare TTL defect that the prior review (GEMINI-050-095) found in the adjacent file and that verified MATERIAL.
- Prior-report collision: **same-site-different-claim** — `GEMINI-050-096` is `pkg/ddns/backend_route53.go:379-387`, a *pagination / `maxitems=1`* claim. Different function, different mechanism.
- Index accuracy: **accurate** (`backend_route53.go:320-375`).
- Why it matters (bounded): if the premise holds, a DDNS FQDN that an operator pre-seeded from AWS's documented example format never converges — the publish 400s on every tick. It does **not** produce the report's "stale AAAA leaked forever", because a leaked record implies a successful publish, which implies the canonical value is present.

## #9151 — config: `protocols rip group` is a CONTAINER to the compiler and a LEAF in the schema — a packed run there commits clean and loses both the group body and the sibling statement [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-06)

Found while attributing a census `vacuous` verdict rather than accepting it. **The verdict was wrong and the row is a defect, not correct behaviour.**

## The mismatch

```
schema     protocols rip group   args=1  children=0  wildcard=false   -> a LEAF
compiler   case "group": for _, gc := range child.Children            -> a CONTAINER
```

`compiler_protocols.go:827` iterates the group's children. The schema declares it a one-argument leaf with no children, so the closed-world walk has nothing to descend into and nothing to reject.

## Measured through `compileTreeStrict` (the operator commit path)

```
set protocols rip group g1 neighbor 10.0.0.1        ACCEPTED  ifaces=[10.0.0.1]   <- control, works
set protocols rip group g1                          ACCEPTED  ifaces=[]           <- nothing asked
set protocols rip group g1 authentication-key secret1
                                                    ACCEPTED  ifaces=[] authKey=""
```

**The third row is the finding.** It commits clean and loses *both* — the group content and the sibling `authentication-key`. `show configuration` renders what the operator typed.

This is the same schema-behind-compiler class as #9088 (`security ipsec vpn <V> gateway`/`ipsec-policy`): where the schema declares less than the compiler reads, there is no closed-world check to fail, so the packed spelling passes admission and everything after the first token is dropped. It is **operator-reachable** for exactly that reason.

The lost `authentication-key` is worth noting given #9105 — RIP authentication is the same subsystem where an absent `authentication-type` silently renders `mode text`.

## Why the census called it `vacuous`

The #8939 generator synthesizes a bare `group xpfval` with no body. Nothing observable lands, `split(3)` equals `split(2)`, and vacuity control 2 fires — filing the row as *"the last leaf is not observable in the typed config at all."*

That reads as a verdict about the compiler and is not one. The leaf is read perfectly well; the harness could not express what reading it requires, because the schema does not say it is a container.

## The category correction, stated so it conjoins rather than replaces

A peer proposed three causes wearing the single `vacuous` label:

1. **placeholder mislabel** — the leaf is read, the synthesized value is unusable. A defect. (Fixed for the name/type case in #9108 and the arity case in the PR alongside this.)
2. **genuinely unread** — no struct field, no compiler case. A real finding.
3. **legitimately empty** — a bare container instance contributes nothing. Correct behaviour.

## #9152 — configstore: two supported spellings of `system master-password` skip at-rest encryption entirely — active.json and confirm.json are written in cleartext with a clean commit [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-06)

## The defect

`system master-password` decides whether the config DB is encrypted at rest. Two supported
spellings of that stanza make the decision read "no master-password configured", so
`active.json` and `confirm.json` are written in **cleartext** — including IKE pre-shared keys —
while `show configuration` renders the stanza back to the operator and the commit succeeds
with no warning.

This is not "the wrong KDF is chosen". It is **no encryption at all**.

## The two questions, and only one of them was fixed

`pkg/configstore/crypto.go:88-105` asks two questions in order:

```go
// Question 1: is at-rest encryption required at all? Fail-closed broad
// scan (dormant/unapplied/wildcard included). Empty means plaintext.
if !masterPasswordConfigured(tree) {
    return ""
}

// Question 2: choose a SUPPORTED, DETERMINISTIC algorithm from the
// effective/applied scope.
if prf := effectiveMasterPasswordPRF(tree); prf != "" && prfSupported(prf) {
    return prf
}
```

Closed #8898 fixed **Question 2**. Its fix (`f9fdc477c`) routes `effectiveMasterPasswordPRF`
through the compact-stanza normalizer, and the comment it left says exactly why:

```go
// pkg/configstore/crypto.go:155-162
// issue 8898: fold admitted compact stanzas before scanning. This reader
// walks the RAW tree, so it never sees the normalizer that runs inside the
// compiler -- `system master-password pseudorandom-function <p>;` resolved
// to nothing here even after the pair was admitted to the scope ...
tree = config.NormalizeCompactForScan(tree)
```
