## #9153 — config: a firewall-filter `then` clause with 3+ actions silently drops the terminating action — `then count c1 log discard` commits clean and the term falls through [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-06)

## The defect

A firewall-filter term written on one `set` line loses its terminating action when the `then`
clause carries three or more items. The commit succeeds with **zero warnings**, and the term
falls through to whatever follows — a fail-open.

## Measured through the strict commit gate

`configstore.compileTreeStrict`, from plain CLI `set` lines. Case D is the positive control
(the same three actions written as three separate lines):

```
D control  `then count c1` + `then log` + `then discard`  -> action="discard" count="c1" log=true  warnings=[]
A          `then count c1 discard`                        -> action="discard" count="c1"           warnings=[]
B          `then count c1 log discard`                    -> action=""  terminals=[]  log=true count="c1"  warnings=[]
C          `then count c1 dscp af11 policer p1`           -> policer=""  (dscp survived)           warnings=[]
E          `then discard log count c1`                    -> count=""                              warnings=[]
```

**Case B is the fail-open.** An operator-authored `discard` compiles to *no terminating action*.
Both leaf orders were tested; the loss moves with the order but is always present at three or
more items.

## Mechanism

`flattenThenChain8939` (`pkg/config/compiler_firewall.go:1432-1490`) is descent-only. At `:1462`
a childless node is appended with its full `Keys` unsplit:

```go
if act == nil || len(act.children) > 0 || act.wildcard != nil || len(n.Children) == 0 {
    out = append(out, n)
    return
}
```

so a node whose `Keys` are `["log","discard"]` survives intact, and the reader at `:1354` takes
only `child.Name()` — the first token. Everything after it is dropped.

## #9159 — nat: a prefix-scoped `destination-nat off` is never withdrawn from the enclosing translate prefix, so the exempt hosts are registered firewall-local and blackholed (executed) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-10)

## The defect

A `destination-nat off` rule written on a **prefix** never withdraws those addresses from the
firewall-local registry of the broader translate prefix that contains it. The exempt hosts are
registered as firewall-local — i.e. blackholed — while the DNAT match itself correctly selects
the `off` rule. The two views disagree.

## Executed probe

A `/26 destination-nat off` inside a `/24` translate rule. Both controls passed; the claim
assertion failed:

```
test nat::tests_destination::v038_probe_prefix_off_shadowing_broad_translate_prefix_not_local
panicked at src/nat/tests_destination.rs:2555:
V038: exempt /26 host 203.0.113.65 IS registered firewall-local (blackhole); locals_len=255
```

`locals_len=255` is the whole `/24` expansion with **zero** of the 62 exempt hosts withdrawn.
(Temporary cell; removed, tree left clean.)

## Mechanism

`userspace-dp/src/nat/destination.rs:1145-1148` builds `exact_off` from `self.entries` — the
**exact-host** map — only. A prefix `off` lives in `prefix_entries` and is merely `continue`d at
`:1152`, which suppresses its own registration and withdraws nothing from the broader slot.
`match_prefix_slots:973` is strictly longest-wins, so the `/26 off` *does* win the DNAT match.

## Why it matters

`destination-nat off` is the operator's way of carving an exception out of a broad DNAT rule —
"translate this /24 except this /26". Today the /26 keeps matching `off` correctly and is
simultaneously treated as an address the firewall owns, so traffic to it is dropped instead of
forwarded. The exception silently becomes a blackhole, and the operator's own `show` of the NAT
rules looks correct.

Ordinary supported configuration; no attacker.

## #9160 — config: `then accept local-preference 100` on one line commits clean and the local-preference never reaches FRR — compiler_routing never received the #8939 flatten [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-06)

## The defect

A BGP route policy written on one `set` line loses its modifiers. This commits clean at the
strict gate and the modifier never reaches FRR:

```
set policy-options policy-statement p1 term t1 then accept local-preference 100
```

`local-preference` is silently dropped. The route is accepted with the router's default
preference.

## Measured through `compileTreeStrict`, both orders

```
POS-CONTROL then accept                     -> action="accept"
POS-CONTROL then local-preference 100       -> locpref=100  hasLP=true
BRACED then { local-preference 100; accept; } -> action=accept locpref=100

REPORTED ORDER then local-preference 100 accept  -> STRICT REJECT  unknown modifier "accept"
REVERSE  then accept local-preference 100        -> STRICT ACCEPT  action="accept" locpref=0 hasLP=FALSE
REVERSE  then accept metric 10                   -> STRICT ACCEPT  action="accept" hasMetric=FALSE
REVERSE  then accept next-hop 10.0.0.1           -> STRICT ACCEPT  action="accept" nexthop=""
REVERSE  then reject local-preference 100        -> STRICT ACCEPT  action="reject" hasLP=FALSE
REVERSE  then next-hop 10.0.0.1 accept           -> STRICT ACCEPT  nexthop="10.0.0.1" action="" (accept dropped)
```

The order matters and the report tested only the rejecting one. The accepting order is the one
an operator naturally writes.

## Mechanism

`pkg/config/compiler_routing.go:1138` walks `tc.Children` directly with no flat-run expansion.

## #9161 — dataplane: the hybrid-apply guard compares REDACTED JSON, so a WireGuard key rotation is invisible to it and a stale-key snapshot is marked applied [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-07)

## The defect

The hybrid-apply guard decides whether the helper's configuration changed by comparing
`json.Marshal` output — in which `config.Secret` fields render **redacted**. A rotation that
changes only secret material is therefore invisible to it, and the guard reports "no change" on
a config the helper genuinely needs.

Its own justification says the opposite of what the code does:

```go
// pkg/dataplane/userspace/manager_overlay.go:318-321
// the helper ALWAYS receives the redacted JSON encoding … it never sees raw secrets
```

That is false. The helper receives the revealed values:

```go
// pkg/dataplane/userspace/tunnels.go:137
snap.WgLocalPrivkeyHex = tunnel.WgLocalPrivkeyHex.Reveal()
// pkg/dataplane/userspace/tunnels.go:149
WgPresharedKeyHex: p.PresharedKeyHex.Reveal(),
```

## Measured, with the non-secret delta as control

```
SECRET-ONLY delta : configsContentEqual=true   routeOnlyPublishHybrid(refuse?)=false
NON-SECRET delta  : configsContentEqual=false  routeOnlyPublishHybrid(refuse?)=true
```

`manager_overlay.go:331` is the comparison; `:188 next := *m.lastSnapshot` inherits
`TunnelEndpoints` carrying the **old** keys, `:193 next.Config = cfg`, `:257
markAppliedSnapshotLocked()`.

## Why it matters, and why Medium rather than High

The #5680 fail-closed refusal exists so a route-only republish cannot silently ship a stale
config. A WireGuard key rotation defeats it: the guard sees equality, the refusal does not fire,
and the snapshot is marked applied with the previous keys — the tunnel stays up on the old
material while the operator is told the rotation applied.

## #9162 — userspace-dp: the NAT64 ICMP-error V6->V4 arm misses non-default routing domains, and the V4->V6 arm is correct ONLY because of open #9033 — fixing #9033 alone breaks it [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-06)

## The defect

The NAT64 ICMP-error match has two arms. One is **correct only because of an existing open bug**;
the other is genuinely broken for non-default routing domains. Filing them together because
fixing the open bug in isolation will break the working arm.

## The V6→V4 arm is broken (the real defect)

`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/icmp_embed/nat64_match.rs:210-220` resolves the **forward** session,
whose key *is* domain-stamped — `poll_descriptor/mod.rs:306-338` is, in its own words, *"THE
single site that populates `SessionKey.routing_domain`"*. All three fallbacks in
`lookup_session_across_scopes` (`shared_ops.rs:751`, `:763`, `:778`) key on domain-preserving
indexes (`key_to_handle`, `reverse_translated_index`/`translated_session_key`,
`forward_wire_index`/`forward_wire_key`). The domain-agnostic `nat_reverse_index` is reachable
only via `find_forward_nat_match`, which this path never calls (`session_match.rs:86` does).

So with `has_routing_domains == true`, an ICMPv6 error about the translated reply never matches
→ **PMTUD blackhole in the server→client direction** for every NAT64 flow in a VRF.

Positive control on the asymmetry: `grep -c ingress_routing_domain` →
`nat64_match.rs: 0`, `nat_match_v4.rs: 1`, `nat_match_v6.rs: 1`.

## The V4→V6 arm is currently correct, and that is the trap

`icmp_embed/parse.rs:241-246` hardcodes `routing_domain: 0` and its own comment argues that is
right:

```rust
// #7160 (#2387): a REVERSE-direction key, so domain 0 is the correct
// value and not an omission — the reverse-match transforms and index
// are domain-agnostic by construction (session/key.rs). The forward
// `embedded_key` its callers build alongside this one DOES carry the
// arriving interface's domain.
routing_domain: 0,
```

That probe resolves the NAT64 v4 reverse companion — and the companion is itself installed at
domain 0 (`poll_descriptor/mod.rs:3217-3226`, inside `if nat64_info.is_some()`). Probe and entry
agree. **This arm works because of the bug filed as #9033.**

## #9163 — userspace-dp: retained-pool index remap is a nested linear scan on the snapshot-apply critical section — 1.11s measured at 65k addresses, and the commit gate admits ~1M [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-09)

## The defect

The retained-pool index remap is a nested linear scan over source-NAT pool addresses, on the
snapshot-apply critical section. It is O(n·m) in a quantity the commit gate lets an operator set
to about a million.

```rust
// userspace-dp/src/nat/source/mod.rs:522-541
for (new_i, addr) in new_v4.iter().enumerate() {
    if let Some(prev_i) = prev.addresses_v4.iter().position(|a| a == addr) {
        map.insert(prev_i, new_i);
    }
}
```

## The cardinality, from real limits rather than guessed

`MAX_POOL_PREFIX_HOSTS = 65536` per prefix member (`expand.rs:21`); aggregate
`max_addresses: 16 * MAX_POOL_PREFIX_HOSTS` = 1,048,576 (`mod.rs:437`). That is a **sum**, so a
single pool may hold the whole budget, and the Go compiler admits it
(`MaxSourceNATAggregatePoolAddresses`, `pkg/config/compiler_validate_strict_nat.go:3528`).

## Measured (standalone `rustc -O`, same loop shape)

| n = m | time |
|---|---|
| 4096 | 4.6 ms |
| 16384 | 74 ms |
| **65536** | **1.11 s** |

Quadratic extrapolation to the committable maximum (1M × 1M) is roughly **4 minutes**.

This is a measured cost for the isolated loop, not an end-to-end apply benchmark — stated that
way deliberately.

## Where it runs, and why that is the harm

`reseed_retained_pool` (`mod.rs:902`) ← `resolve_pool_allocators` ←
`parse_source_nat_rules_with_previous` ← `forwarding_build/mod.rs:678` — i.e. **inside snapshot
apply, under the same `state` mutex** that serializes the control socket.

## #9165 — logging: UDP syslog write failures are neither counted nor warned, and UDP is the default — the drop counters also have zero production readers [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-07)

## The defect

UDP syslog write failures are neither counted nor warned, and UDP is the default transport. On a
box whose collector is down, `droppedWrites` stays 0 and the operator-facing warning never
fires — while the same box on TCP would report both.

## The asymmetry, at two sites

```go
// pkg/logging/syslog.go:643  (and verbatim again in SendBinary at :777)
if err := s.writeMsg(line); err != nil {
    // For stream protocols, attempt one cooldown-gated reconnect. UDP
    // never blocks or needs reconnect, so it just returns the error.
    if s.protocol != "udp" {
        ... pendingWarn = s.noteDrop(...) ...
    }
    return err          // <- UDP: no noteDrop, no pendingWarn
```

UDP is the documented default (`:202`, `:236`, `:306`). Consequence: `droppedWrites` stays 0
**and** the rate-limited
`slog.Warn("syslog message dropped", …, dropped_writes, dropped_dials, dropped_cooldown)`
(`:536-547`) never fires. On Linux a *connected* UDP socket does surface `ECONNREFUSED` from a
dead collector, so these are real, observable failures being discarded.

## Broader than filed: the counters have no production reader at all

`DroppedWrites()`, `DroppedDials()` and `DroppedCooldown()` have **zero** production consumers
anywhere in the tree. Positive control on that absence: the same grep finds real call sites in
`pkg/daemon/daemon_flowtrace_3932_test.go` and `pkg/logging/*_test.go` — and only in tests. So
even the counted TCP/TLS drops reach an operator solely through that one rate-limited Warn;
there is no metric and no `show`.

## The log-level half of the finding is NEG, and should not be fixed

`pkg/logging/ringbuf.go:839` `slog.Debug("syslog send failed", "err", err)` sits in the
per-event syslog fan-out loop. This repo's own rule mandates `slog.Debug` for high-frequency
paths and forbids `slog.Info` in per-packet/per-session loops. That line is correct. The defect
is the missing **counter**, not the level — recording this explicitly so a fix does not raise the
level and reintroduce the log flood the rule exists to prevent.

## #9166 — daemon: a failed flow-exporter build is indistinguishable from "not configured" on every surface, and nothing retries until the next commit [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-07)

## The defect

When a flow exporter fails to build, the resulting state is **indistinguishable from "flow
export is not configured"** on every surface, and nothing retries until the next commit. On a
box that is never re-committed, flow export is off forever with one `slog.Warn` at boot as the
only trace.

## The three surfaces, all silent

- `d.flowExportErr = err` → `FlowExportError()` has **zero** production readers (grep finds only
  `pkg/daemon/daemon_flowexport_reconcile_test.go:478`).
- The Prometheus family is *"omitted entirely when no `FlowCollectorHealthFn` is wired or when
  **no flow export is configured (empty slice)**"* (`pkg/api/metrics_system.go:128-129`). So
  build-failed and not-configured produce the identical observation: the series vanishes.
- `show` renders the configuration as present, because the config *is* present.

`reconcileFlowExporters` runs only from the apply tail (`pkg/daemon/daemon_apply_tail.go:259`)
and the boot block (`pkg/daemon/daemon_run.go:370`, `:384`) — so the retry cadence is "the next
commit", which on a stable box is never.

## One correction to the finding as filed

It narrates "the hash is withheld on failure" as the defect. That is the **fix**:
`d.flowHashSet = false` (`pkg/daemon/daemon_flowexport.go:231-233`) is what makes the next commit
retry rather than hash-gating into a dead family, and the existing exporters keep running
(`slog.Warn("failed to create flow exporter; keeping existing exporters running")`). What
survives is the observability claim, and it is the stronger half.

## Why it matters

The triggering fault is ordinary: a collector hostname unresolvable at boot, or a pinned
source-address bind attempted before the interface is up. Both resolve minutes later, and
nothing re-tries. NetFlow is frequently the only record of what traversed the box, and its
absence looks exactly like a deployment where it was never turned on — which is why nobody
investigates.

Give `flowExportErr` a reader, and make the Prometheus family distinguish *configured but

## #9170 — xpf-deploy: the printed install digest is re-hashed from the PUBLIC file after signature verification, and the test that guards this asserts a substring the defective code satisfies [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-07)

`xpf-deploy.py`'s K08 install path prints a SHA-256 for the operator to verify, and that digest
is **re-hashed from the public output file after signature verification has already finished**.
The printed digest therefore binds "the bytes in `--out` at print time", not "the bytes that
passed the signature". Worse, the signed digest was already in hand and was discarded.

The report that surfaced this rated it a minor "narrow (sub-ms window)". The window is not
sub-millisecond, the repo already implements the correct pattern three lines away, and the test
that is supposed to guard this property asserts something the defective code satisfies.

```python

# scripts/deploy/xpf-deploy.py:1750

# scripts/deploy/xpf-deploy.py:1757

```

`sign.py:254` `verify_manifest_map()` already returns the **signed** `{basename: hash}` map. The
value that should be printed was computed and thrown away.

## The window is not sub-millisecond

On `--no-import` the gap between the verification read and the digest read spans a complete
second `verify_manifest_map` → `verify_and_read` → `verify_signature` →
`subprocess.run(minisign)` (`sign.py:145`), plus two `mkdtemp`/`rmtree` cycles and the watermark
`os.replace`. Tens of milliseconds, and it contains a subprocess spawn.

## The repo already fixed this class, and skipped this path

`xpf-deploy.py:1545-1566` implements `_verified_private_artifacts` for #5817, whose own comment
says:

> The public `--out` dir may be writable by another local process.

Both importing paths use it. The `--no-import` path does not.

## What this is

Ten further defects established during validation of the `full-firewall-100r2` external review,
each verified at `9b1b3cdba` with the evidence below. They are grouped in one issue because each
is a small, independent, single-site fix and the board is already carrying ~120 open items —

split this issue if any of them is picked up.

### 1. `update_ha_state` queues behind the apply barrier and can expire the forwarding lease (V035)

`update_ha_state` is the **only** refresher of the helper's per-RG forwarding lease, which
`is_forwarding_active` consults **per packet**. The daemon sends it on a 3 s cadence
(`haWatchdogIPCBackstopSecs = 3`, `pkg/dataplane/userspace/manager_ha.go:855`) against a 10 s
stale window (`HA_WATCHDOG_STALE_AFTER_SECS`, `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/mod.rs:447`). But
`served_off_lock` covers `sync_session` only (`server/handlers/handlers/mod.rs:176-180`), so
`update_ha_state` takes the snapshot-wide `state` mutex — which `apply_snapshot` can hold across
a 10 s worker-readiness barrier (`WORKER_STARTUP_BARRIER_TIMEOUT_NS`,
`coordinator/reconcile/bringup.rs:41`).

The throttle's own justification says it leaves *"a >3× margin under the helper's ~10 s
stale-lease window"* — but that is a claim about **send** cadence, and `active_lease_until`
anchors on **receipt** (`ha/state.rs:11-13`). A lock hold beyond ~7 s expires the lease. The
repo's own comment calls the outcome "an OUTAGE". Residual of closed **#7209**, which fixed
exactly one verb. The common apply holds ~0.5–1 s; the >7 s case needs the readiness barrier to
actually time out — which is why this is Medium, and why the sibling finding on the O(n·m) pool
remap (filed separately) matters: it is a direct trigger.

## #9173 — research: the SYN-cookie master key is derived from the root password hash and never rotates; and bump_fib_generation is the only >1Hz control-socket caller that asks for an unread status [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-11)

## What this is

Two defects found by **this research run** while refuting claims in a supplied external review.
Neither is in that review; both were discovered by the validation itself, which is why the origin
label differs from the review-derived issues filed alongside it.

---

## 1. The SYN-cookie master key is derived from the root password hash and never rotates

`pkg/dataplane/userspace/screens.go:485-500` and `:502-509`:

```go
h.Write([]byte("root-auth-encrypted-password\x00"))
h.Write([]byte(secretMaterial))   // cfg.System.RootAuthentication.EncryptedPassword.Reveal()
```

The key is `SHA256(domain ‖ cluster-id ‖ root crypt hash ‖ zone list)[:16]`. That makes it:

- **a pure function of configuration** — identical on both HA nodes by design, which is the
  property the design wanted, but achieved by deriving from a credential rather than by
  distributing a random secret;
- **stable for the entire life of the configuration** — no rotation on boot, on failover, or on
  any timer. Linux seeds its own syncookie secret from `get_random_bytes()` per boot;
- **derived from a password verifier.** The crypt hash is the material an offline cracker
  targets. Using it as key material for a network-facing MAC couples two things that should not
  be coupled: anyone who learns the root hash can forge cookies, and the cookie MAC becomes an
  oracle-adjacent surface for the hash.

**What this is not.** The MAC width is 24 bits, which is forced by the 32-bit ISN and matches
Linux's own `COOKIEBITS = 24`; that is not a defect, and a validated cookie installs no session
(it sends AckRst and recycles), so a forged cookie buys one half-open-slot bypass, not a session.
The defect here is the **key derivation and the absence of rotation**, not the tag length.

**Open question, stated as such:** whether `EncryptedPassword` is reachable by a non-root
`read-only` login class via `show configuration`. The typed surface redacts it; the AST render is
the part I did not settle. If it is reachable, the severity rises sharply.

**Fix direction:** derive the cookie secret from a CSPRNG at boot and distribute it over the
existing cluster config-sync channel (or derive it from a dedicated synced secret), so both nodes

## #9174 — cluster: three bulk-session-sync gaps let a stale or mistimed peer frame complete, reset or gut a bulk — BulkEnd carries no incarnation, the #8966 guard misses the between-bulks window, and epochReboot never arms needColdPrime [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-07)

## The defect

Three separate gaps in the HA bulk-session-sync protocol let a stale or mistimed frame from the
peer complete, reset or gut a bulk transfer. They share a file and a review pass; they do **not**
share a fix, and the acceptance below keeps them apart deliberately.

### 1. BulkEnd carries no incarnation (V013)

`pkg/cluster/sync_conn_read.go:334-341,355-366` matches an inbound BulkEnd on **epoch alone**.
The BulkStart frame carries a boot incarnation (`sync_bulk.go:296`); the BulkEnd frame does not.
A BulkEnd buffered from the peer's previous boot therefore completes the bulk that is currently
in progress, and the standby marks itself synced with a partial table.

### 2. The #8966 guard does not cover the between-bulks window (V015)

The landed guard is `!switched && s.bulkInProgress && epoch <= s.bulkRecvEpoch`
(`sync_conn_read.go:263-271`). Between two bulks `bulkInProgress` is false, so a stale full
BulkStart/BulkEnd pair is accepted, resets the accumulators and drives a reconcile — a
mass-delete followed by resurrection. Two consecutive bulks *can* pin different fabrics
(`BulkSync` pins `getActiveConn` once, `sync_conn.go:1165`), which is the ordinary path to a
reordered pair.

### 3. `epochReboot` never arms `needColdPrime` on the empty-slot edge (V014)

`pkg/cluster/sync_conn.go:772-776` arms retirement on `epochReboot`, but `epochReboot` is
**absent** from the `needColdPrime` condition at `:807-809`, and no other site arms it on that
edge. Grepped for a peer-side prime-request frame: none exists. A rebooted peer that comes back
into an empty slot is therefore never refilled.

## Why it matters

Each of the three ends in the same place: a standby that believes it is synced and is not. That
is invisible until a failover, at which point every session absent from the standby's table is a
dropped flow. Closed #7762 and #8966 each fixed one arm of this family; these are the arms their
acceptances do not reach.

None of the three requires a compromised peer. #1 and #2 arise from an ordinary peer reboot or a
cross-fabric reorder; #3 is a plain reboot-into-empty-slot.

## #9175 — configstore: appliedDigest is never invalidated, so an A->B(fail)->A(fail) flap reports the config converged — the #4957 fail-open, re-entered through its own remedy [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-09)

## The defect

`appliedDigest` is stamped on a successful apply and is **never invalidated**, so a config that
is promoted, fails to apply, and is later re-promoted reads back as converged.

## Measured, with the middle row that makes it a defect

```
step1  active=A  ActiveApplied=true    (A applied)
step2  active=B  ActiveApplied=false   (B promoted, apply failed -- conservative, CORRECT)
step3  active=A  ActiveApplied=true    (A re-promoted, apply ALSO failed)   <- FALSELY CONVERGED
```

Step 2 is the row that shows the shortcut is normally right. Step 3 is the defect: the digest
left over from step 1 still matches the active text, so `ActiveApplied()` returns true for a
dataplane that never took the config.

`pkg/configstore/store.go:919-922` compares `appliedDigest == digest(active)`. The only writers
are success stamps — `MarkActiveApplied` (`:904-907`) and `MarkAppliedDigest` (`:961`). Nothing
clears it.

## The comment states the invariant the defect violates

```go
// pkg/configstore/store.go:373-374
// a stale value can only make the shortcut MORE conservative … never falsely converged
```

True for a forward sequence; false for re-promotion of a previously applied text.

## Why it matters

`pkg/daemon/daemon_ha_sync.go:662` uses the shortcut to skip an apply. On the false-converged
path it returns nil, the config high-water advances, and the standby reports the generation
applied while its dataplane holds an older one — the #4957 fail-open, re-entered through the
remedy #4957 itself prescribed. The failure is only observable at failover.

Reachable in ordinary HA operation. It needs an apply failure on a text previously applied in
the same process, which is why it is Medium rather than High.

## #9176 — daemon: the IPsec SA sync loop shutdown guard is a tautology — loopCtx.Err() is always non-nil there, so an old goroutine clears the NEW loop cancel [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-07)

## The defect

The IPsec SA sync loop's shutdown guard is a tautology. Its comment states the invariant it is
meant to enforce; its condition is unconditionally true, so it does the opposite.

```go
// pkg/daemon/daemon_ipsec_sa_sync_loop.go:98-104
go func() {
    d.syncIPsecSAPeriodic(loopCtx)
    d.ipsecSASync.loopMu.Lock()
    // Only clear if this loop is still the registered one: a stop
    // followed by a restart must not have the OLD goroutine's exit
    // clear the NEW loop's cancel.
    if d.ipsecSASync.loopCancel != nil && loopCtx.Err() != nil {
        d.ipsecSASync.loopCancel = nil
    }
```

`syncIPsecSAPeriodic` (`pkg/daemon/daemon_ha.go:2281-2293`) has exactly **one** return —
`case <-ctx.Done(): return`. So `loopCtx.Err() != nil` is always true when this line executes,
and the guard reduces to "always clear" — precisely the behaviour the comment forbids.

## Consequence

Reachable by knob-OFF then knob-ON (or a comms-wiring OFF at
`pkg/daemon/daemon_ha_comms_wiring.go:538` followed by the apply-path ON at
`daemon_apply_tail.go:398`) while goroutine A is still inside an in-flight
`advertiseIPsecSAOnce`. A's exit then clears B's cancel, so loop B runs **unregistered**:

- a later knob-OFF silently does nothing — the publisher keeps advertising after the operator
  disabled it;
- a later knob-ON starts a **second** publisher.

That second outcome is exactly the leak the file's own `launches atomic.Uint64` counter was
added to make observable.

`stopClusterComms` (`pkg/daemon/daemon_ha_sync.go:1295`) calls `d.resetDHCPLeaseSyncLoop()` and

## #9177 — cluster: the bulk stat reset runs above the #8966 accept, and BulkAck accepts a FUTURE epoch — two small independent defects in one reader [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-09)

## The defect

Two smaller defects in the same bulk-sync reader, both established with their headline claims
partly refuted — recorded here at the severity that survived rather than the one filed.

### 1. The bulk stat reset runs above the #8966 accept (V052 residual)

`pkg/cluster/sync_conn_read.go:231-233` zeroes `BulkSyncStartTime`, `BulkSyncEndTime` and
`BulkSyncSessions` **before** the `bulkMu` accept decision. So the reordered BulkStart that
#8966's own text calls *"the ordinary case"* leaves `show chassis cluster` reporting
`Bulk sync in progress since …` indefinitely and miscounts subsequent incremental installs as
bulk (`sync_conn_read.go:100-101,135-136`, `pkg/cluster/status.go:410-422`).

The #8966 author already moved `resetRecvGen` below the accept for exactly this reason; the three
stat stores were left above it. This is a statement-ordering defect, not an epoch-validation one
— no incarnation rule fixes it.

**The headline claim is refuted.** The `len(payload) >= 8` read at `:203` is the deliberate #5084
legacy-compat path (`sync_boot_incarnation.go:166` says so), and a short frame is accepted as
epoch 0 only when no bulk is in progress — a state in which *any* epoch is accepted, since the
`:262` guard requires `bulkInProgress`. A malformed short frame therefore grants nothing a
well-formed frame does not, and legitimate senders always write 8 or 24 bytes
(`sync_bulk.go:205`). Telemetry only; nothing that makes a forwarding decision reads these
fields.

### 2. BulkAck accepts a future epoch (V053)

`pkg/cluster/sync_conn_read.go:385` is `if pending == 0 || epoch < pending`. The authority here
is **local**: `pendingBulkAckEpoch` is set by our own send path under `bulkSendMu`
(`sync_bulk.go:171-172,290`) before the BulkEnd write, so it is by construction the largest epoch
we ever put on the wire. A correct peer cannot echo a larger one. `epoch != pending` is strictly
tighter, costs one operator, and needs no incarnation input.

Today a future-epoch ack clears `pending`, latches `bulkEverCompleted` / `outboundBulkAcked` and
fires `OnBulkSyncAckReceived` — releasing the #3912 failover gate on a bulk that never completed.

Reachability is honest: this needs a non-conforming or compromised peer past the #5303 pre-auth
admission, which is why it is Low rather than a High. It is filed because the fix is one
character and the current comparator has no reason to be loose.

## #9192 — compiler: one authored BGP neighbor split across set commands compiles to TWO BGPNeighbor entries and renders a redundant remote-as [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-07)

Found while fixing #9007; filed separately because it is broader than that issue and has a different remedy.

## The defect

`compileBGP` appends one `*BGPNeighbor` **per AST node**. A single authored neighbor can occupy more than one node, because a bare declaration and a later sub-leaf are separate nodes:

```
set protocols bgp group G type external
set protocols bgp group G peer-as 65001
set protocols bgp group G neighbor 10.0.2.2
set protocols bgp group G neighbor 10.0.2.2 import PS
```

That is ordinary flat-set authoring — and it is the shape `pkg/config`'s own slot-escape fixtures use (`slotEscBGP` in `schema_slot_escape_fixtures_test.go:118`).

Measured at `2f80dc085` via `CompileConfigLenient`:

```
neighbors=2
  [0] addr=10.0.2.2 group="G" peer-as=65001 import=[]
  [1] addr=10.0.2.2 group="G" peer-as=65001 import=[PS]
```

Two entries for one peer. `generateProtocols` then renders:

```
neighbor 10.0.2.2 remote-as 65001
neighbor 10.0.2.2 remote-as 65001
neighbor 10.0.2.2 activate
neighbor 10.0.2.2 route-map xpf-emptied-chain-xpf-chain in
```

## Severity: low, but it is a live trap

The rendered output is **redundant, not wrong** — FRR accepts a repeated `remote-as`, and the `activate`/route-map lines that only entry `[1]` carries are still emitted. Nothing is currently broken for the operator.

What makes it worth fixing is that the duplication is invisible in the typed config's contract and **anything that reasons over `BGP.Neighbors` as a set of peers is wrong by construction**. Two concrete consequences already observed:

1. A duplicate-address check keyed on `Address` alone reports a peer as "configured in more than one group (G and G)" — the same group twice — and false-rejects a legitimate config. This is exactly what happened in the first version of the #9007 fix; `TestSlotEscapeTable` caught it.
2. A first-wins dedup at the renderer's `validNeighbors` construction — the natural remedy for the #9007 symptom — **silently drops the policy-bearing entry**, deleting the `activate` and `route-map … in` lines. That fix was reverted for this reason.

## #9206 — config: a multi leaf DEFEATS its container's closed world — an undeclared statement behind it is injected as a bogus value, not refused [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-06)

A `multi` leaf absorbs every trailing token as a VALUE (the #2419 contract),
which happens BEFORE any closed-world keyword check could see them. So an
undeclared statement following a multi leaf is not discarded and not refused —
it is **injected as a bogus value**.

## Measured

```
set protocols rip group g1 neighbor ge-0/0/0 authentication-key secret1
  gate=ACCEPT  compile=nil
  ifaces=[ge-0/0/0 authentication-key secret1]
```

`authentication-key` and `secret1` become RIP interface names. `pkg/frr` renders
`RIP.Interfaces` into the managed section, so two non-existent interfaces are
named to FRR.

## Why closing the container did not fix it

#9151's second half armed `closedWorld: true` on `protocols rip group`, which
correctly refuses the statement when it stands alone:

```
set protocols rip group g1 authentication-key secret1        -> REJECT
set protocols rip group g1 neighbor ge-0/0/0 authentication-key secret1 -> ACCEPT
```

The difference is the multi leaf in front. Absorption wins the race: by the time
the walk could ask "is `authentication-key` a declared child here", the tokens
are no longer keywords, they are `neighbor`'s values.

This is a general property of `multi` leaves under a closed-world container, not
something specific to RIP. Any `multi: true` leaf whose container is closed has
the same shape — the closed world is defeated by standing behind the multi leaf.

## Attribution

**Pre-existing.** Not introduced by #9183's declaration. The identical input
produces the identical interface list on a tree where `protocols rip group` still
declared `children: nil`, verified in a worktree at that commit.

## #9236 — zeroize: factory reset never touches /var/lib/xpf/versions, so a self-decrypting copy of the prior tenant's config DB survives it — with a success receipt [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-06)

muse-spark-007 finding 21, adjudicated **GENUINE** at `48d0caab7`. Trace read
end-to-end; not executed on a box.

`PerformZeroizeWipe` erases the live config DB key-first, then the DB, TLS
material, login accounts, the archive, BPF pins and networkd files. It has **no
knowledge of `/var/lib/xpf/versions` at all** — 1210 lines, zero occurrences of
`versions`, `upgrade` or `dbsnap`. It knows `/var/lib/xpf/provisioned-users` and

the same comparison and opposite consequences.

## #9239 — daemon: withdrawing the LAST delegated prefix looks identical to never having had one, so a standalone box keeps advertising the withdrawn PD indefinitely [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-06)

muse-spark-007 finding 14, adjudicated **GENUINE** at `48d0caab7`. Read
end-to-end, not executed.

## A transition detector written as a state test

`pkg/daemon/daemon_dhcp.go:224`:

```go
func (d *Daemon) dhcpLeaseChangeRequiresRecompile(cfg *config.Config) bool {
	if cfg == nil {
		return false
	}
	// Prefix delegation can affect downstream addressing/RA and still needs
	// a full re-apply.
	if d.dhcp != nil && len(d.dhcp.DelegatedPrefixesForRA()) > 0 {
		return true
	}
```

The callback runs **after** `commitLease` has already deleted the withdrawn
prefix, so this predicate reads the post-state. When the final IA-PD is
withdrawn, `DelegatedPrefixesForRA()` is empty — the identical value a box that
never had PD produces. The one event that most needs a re-apply is the one the
predicate is blind to, because the comment's reasoning (*"prefix delegation can
affect downstream addressing/RA"*) is about **having** a prefix, and losing the
last one is when that is most true.

## Why nothing else catches it

- Every DHCP client on this composition is the management lifeline, so the
  management-only branch is selected. It refreshes routes, DNS and IPsec — **not
  RA**.
- The authoritative periodic RA reconcile is cluster-only. Its own doc comment:
  *"Standalone (non-cluster) mode is a no-op here; that path applies RA directly
  in applyServicesReconcile."* So in standalone the full-apply path is the sole
  RA applier, and the predicate above is what decides whether it runs.
- The mode-agnostic 30-second loop retries **dead** senders. This sender is
  alive; only its desired state is stale, which is exactly what that loop does
  not inspect.

1. `dmz` is dropped — the reported symptom.
2. **The surviving `trust->untrust` context has zero policies.** The authored

   config.

The controls are what make this readable: the identical policy body yields
`policies=1` when the zone is named on its own, so `policies=0` is produced by
the bracket, not by my fixture being wrong.

The zone pair falls through to the default policy. Which way that fails depends
on a **sibling stanza**, not on this defect:

- default deny (the usual posture) — a lost `permit` silently blackholes the
  traffic it was written to allow.
- `default-policy permit-all` — a lost `deny` is a **fail-open**: the traffic the
  operator wrote a rule to block is permitted, with a clean commit and a policy
  they can still see in their own config source.

In both directions the operator's evidence is a config file containing a rule
that is not in force anywhere.

> peer's `allowed-ips` … and then writes the plaintext inner IP packet straight
> to the wgN TUN.

**#8274 step 3 changed exactly that**, for transport-data records on the steered
port. Three statements at HEAD:

the steered port is the only port — is told at every commit that its decapsulated
plaintext is not zone-adjudicated. Post-#8274 that is false for its transport

## #9259 — cluster: NeverArmed and already-consumed fence verdicts are still indistinguishable from Actuated — two more routes into #9036's collapse [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-06)

Split out of issue #9036's acceptance list rather than left implicit. PR #9247 separated **Superseded** from **Actuated**; the acceptance also asked for a typed `Actuated / Superseded / NeverArmed / Failed` state, and the other two routes into "looks fenced" are still open.

## Measured at merged master

```
never armed        -> <nil>
first wait (real)  -> <nil>
second wait        -> <nil>
```

`waitFailoverActuated` returns `nil` in all three cases, and `sync_failover.go` sends `failoverAckApplied` **exactly when it returns nil**. So the peer promotes on:

1. **NeverArmed** — a `(rgID, reqID)` pair for which no barrier was ever armed. `waitFailoverActuated` takes its `b == nil` arm and returns nil.
2. **Verdict already consumed** — the first waiter deletes the entry after reading it (deliberately, so a later wait cannot re-read a stale verdict, #6177). A second wait for the same request then sees an empty slot and returns nil.

Both reach `failoverAckApplied` without any evidence that this node fenced.

## Why this is the same defect and not a variant

#9036's chain was: *the barrier is gone → the wait returns nil → nil means applied.* PR #9247 removed **one** way for the barrier to be gone. The final link — **absence of a barrier is read as proof of fencing** — is untouched, and these are two more ways to reach it.

`waitFailoverActuated`'s own doc comment already names both: *"A nil barrier means the request was never armed (or an earlier waiter already consumed the verdict) — return immediately."* The comment is accurate; what it describes is the collapse.

## Reachability

Requires a `WaitFailoverApplied` call for a `(rgID, reqID)` whose barrier was never armed or has already been consumed — a duplicate or stale failover-ack, or a retry across a fabric blip. This is #9036's own acceptance row **"stale request IDs"**, which PR #9247 did not implement.

## Remedy sketch

The typed state #9036's acceptance asked for: distinguish `Actuated` from `NeverArmed` and from `VerdictConsumed`, and make only `Actuated` produce `failoverAckApplied`. The safe default for the other two is `failed` — the peer holds, which costs a failover attempt, whereas the current default costs the one-owner-per-RG property.

Filed separately so the residue is visible rather than buried in a closed issue's acceptance list.

## #9298 — userspace-dp: PPTP-quoted ICMP errors are fail-closed but unresolved — #9031 left the call-ID association half undone [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-10)

#9031 threaded the quoted GRE discriminator into the embedded-ICMP lookup keys
and closed the RFC 2890 half (unkeyed / keyed / keyed-zero / multiple keys,
IPv4 and IPv6). **It did not do the PPTP half**, which that issue's acceptance
also named: *"Resolve PPTP call IDs through the worker association table rather
than wildcarding."*

This carries it, so the close of #9031 does not remove the reason to look again.

## Current behaviour, and why it is safe but incomplete

`gre_transit_discriminator` returns `Unparseable` for a version-1 (PPTP
enhanced GRE) header, because the 32 bits after the flags word are
`Payload Length | Call ID` and **not** an RFC 2890 Key — reading them with
RFC 2890 field order would promote a per-packet-varying length as a stable
tunnel identity.

`Unparseable` is a DISTINCT class from `Unkeyed` (#7188 decision 6) and equals
no live session's discriminator, so a PPTP-quoted ICMP error **misses**. That is
**fail-closed and correct as far as it goes** — #9031's requirement that "a
malformed or truncated quote must MISS rather than wildcard across tunnels" is
met. A cell pins it (`an_unreadable_quote_is_unparseable_not_unkeyed_9031`).

**But a miss is still a miss.** A live PPTP session carries
`TunnelDiscriminator::Pptp(handle)`, and no embedded lookup can produce that
today, so ICMP errors for PPTP data tunnels remain unresolved — the same
PMTUD/unreachable suppression #9031 fixed for keyed GRE, still present for PPTP.

## Why it is harder than the RFC 2890 case, and cannot be copied from it

`Pptp` is deliberately **not** built from the packet's own Call ID. Per
`session/discriminator.rs`: the PPTP GRE Call ID names *the peer the packet is
being sent to* (RFC 2637 §4.1), and each side allocates its own, so the two
directions of one call carry **different** values. A discriminator built from
the wire value would differ per direction and the reverse companion would never
equal the forward key.

So the handle is **locally derived** through a worker association table
(`pptp_call_id` / `pptp_data_session_flow` in `afxdp/gre_discriminator.rs`). An
embedded parser therefore cannot compute it from the quote alone — it has to
*resolve* the quoted Call ID through that table, which means the embedded path

## #9322 — dataplane/HA: a control response over 64 MiB is truncated and reported as "the helper rejected it before replying" — the in-source premise that the cap is unreachable is false for the unbounded owner-RG export [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-06)

## The defect

A helper control response larger than 64 MiB is truncated by `io.LimitReader` and reported to
the operator as *"the helper rejected it before replying"*. The in-source justification for
not discriminating those two cases states a premise that is false for the one verb that can
actually produce an over-cap response.

```go
// pkg/dataplane/userspace/socket_trust_9003.go:292-305
// A LimitReader ends in io.EOF at the cap, which json.Decoder reports as
// io.ErrUnexpectedEOF for a truncated body — indistinguishable from a helper
// that died mid-write. That is the right shape here: both are "no usable
// response", both fail closed at the caller, and neither is worth a distinct
// error path. The cap being reached at all is not a reachable state for the real
// helper (it is bounded by the same MaxControlRequestBytes ceiling on what it
// can be asked to produce), so the case this discriminates is a hostile peer.
func boundedResponseReader(r io.Reader) io.Reader {
	return io.LimitReader(r, MaxControlResponseBytes)
}
```

The chain is: (1) the cap is unreachable → (2) so it is not worth a distinct error path →
(3) so a truncation gets the sentence at `pkg/dataplane/userspace/process_control.go:199-202`:

```go
return ControlResponse{}, fmt.Errorf(
    "control socket closed with no response to %q request (EOF); the "+
        "helper rejected it before replying — check the helper log "+
        "for a decode/handler error: %w", req.Type, err)
```

## Premise (1) is false, and the counter-example is an ordinary HA path

`MaxControlRequestBytes = 64 MiB` (`pkg/dataplane/userspace/process_control.go:33`) bounds what
can be **asked**. The ask here is about 60 bytes:

- `pkg/daemon/daemon_ha_userspace_export.go:55` and `:106` call

## #9328 — userspace-dp: an oversized DF-CLEAR IPv4 datagram is submitted at full length and booked as a successful forward — no fragmenter, no PTB, no counter; #2301's acceptance narrowed to DF-set and its own Impact still names this half [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-07)

## The defect

There is no IPv4 egress fragmentation in the userspace dataplane, and an oversized
**DF-clear** IPv4 datagram is submitted to TX at full length and **booked as a successful
forward** — no PTB, no drop counter, no exception. This is the residual of closed **#2301**,
and #2301's own Impact paragraph still describes it.

## (a) Does the TX path ever fragment IPv4? No.

Positive-controlled grep for MF/offset **writers** (`grep -rn "0x2000\|0x1fff\|frag_off" src/`):
every hit outside `nat64.rs` is a reader (`screen/stateless.rs`, `icmp_embed/parse.rs`,
`fragment_assoc/key.rs`). The three writers — `nat64.rs:2477`, `:3276`, `:3853` — copy MF and
offset **verbatim from an existing IPv6 Fragment Header** (`nat64.rs:2474-2481`); none splits a
datagram. The grep's positive control is those NAT64 writers: it *can* find a writer, and finds
none elsewhere.

The tree says the same in its own words, in `38dee52ca` (#9116, merged hours before HEAD):
*"There is no IPv4 transit fragmentation engine to catch it; the only fragmentation code in the
dataplane is NAT64's."* — also at
`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/frame/tcp_segmentation.rs:258-262`.

## (b) What happens to a non-TCP oversized DF-clear frame? Forwarded oversize.

```rust
// userspace-dp/src/afxdp/icmp_ptb.rs:108-118
libc::AF_INET => {
    // A non-DF oversized datagram is the downstream's to fragment
    if ipv4_df_set(packet) { EmitPacketTooBig { next_hop_mtu } } else { Forward }
}
```

`Forward` ⇒ `mtu_signalled == false` (`tx/dispatch/mod.rs:966-979`) ⇒ the in-place/copy build
at `:1003-1108` runs. The **only** length guard on that path is `copy_frame_is_oversized`
(`tx/dispatch/mod.rs:78-84`), which compares `cp_len > tx_frame_capacity()` = `> UMEM_FRAME_SIZE`
(4096) — **the UMEM chunk, not the egress MTU**. Nothing in `tx/transmit/`, `tx/rings.rs` or
`tx/drain/` compares a frame against an MTU (grepped, zero hits).

> `pkg/dataplane/userspace/process_napi.go:95`

So on any box where **at least one** queue ever proved live — which is every
healthy box — busy-binding wedge detection is off for **every** queue. A queue
that binds and then goes RX-dead, or one of sixteen that never bound while the
other fifteen did, is not detected and not repaired.

The other signal is gone too. `binding_wedge_recovery.go:157-168` says it in its
own give-up message:

> the affected queues will not forward and **no readiness signal reports them**

That is #8384. So for a masked queue there is **no detection, no recovery, and
no readiness signal** — the box reports healthy and silently drops whatever RSS
hashes to that queue.

## #9333 — snmp: decodePDUFields SKIPS an undecodable varbind instead of failing the PDU, so a GET gets a noError response with FEWER varbinds than it asked for — an RFC 1157 §4.1.2 arity violation [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-07)

Found while fixing #9133; **pre-existing and not a #9133 regression** — see the measurement below.

## What

`decodePDUFields` (`pkg/snmp/agent_ber.go`) walks the varbind list and `continue`s past any varbind it cannot decode, in **five** places: short body, wrong tag, bad length, body overrun, and `berDecodeOID` failure. The PDU then reaches the handler with a SHORTER OID list than the client sent, and the handler answers `noError` with that shorter list.

RFC 1157 §4.1.2 requires the GetResponse's variable-bindings to name the same variables as the request. A manager that matches values to requests **by position** — the normal implementation — reads the wrong value for every varbind after the dropped one, or errors out.

## Measured

A two-varbind SNMPv1 GET, varbind 1 = `sysDescr` (valid), varbind 2 = an OID the decoder rejects, through `Agent.handlePacket`:

```
RESULT: response with 1 varbinds (request had 2), errStatus=0 errIndex=0
  vb[0] oid=[1 3 6 1 2 1 1 1 0] tag=0x04
```

## Reachable at master, independently of #9133

The vector `06 02 2b 80` — an OID value of `2b 80`, a dangling continuation octet with nothing after it — makes `berDecodeOID` return `ber: OID sub-identifier truncated` on **master** as well as on the post-#9133 tree, so it takes this same skip path in both. `pkg/snmp/ber_oid_subid_bound_9133_test.go`'s `TestAnUndecodableVarbindIsSkippedNotRejected9133` carries that vector alongside the #9133-specific one precisely so the "pre-existing" claim is measured rather than argued: under a mutation that removes the #9133 decoder bound, the `overflowing-subidentifier` sub-case goes red and the `truncated-continuation` one stays green.

What #9133 changes is only *which* inputs reach this path: an overflowing sub-identifier now takes it instead of being echoed back as malformed BER.

## Why it was pinned rather than fixed in #9133

The remedy is a decision about **all five** `continue` arms, not about OID bounds. Making one of the five behave differently from its four siblings would be the worse outcome: the arity violation would remain, but only for four of the five malformed shapes, and nothing would say which.

## Candidate remedies (not yet chosen)

1. **Fail the PDU** — return an error from `decodePDUFields` on any undecodable varbind, so `handleV1Get` / `handleGetBulk` / v3 drop the datagram, which is what they already do for a malformed request-id / error-status / varbind-list header. Simplest, consistent with the rest of the function, and arguably the right SNMP answer: a manager that sent a malformed PDU gets a timeout.
2. **Preserve arity with an exception value** — carry a placeholder so the response has the same varbind count with `noSuchObject` in the offending slot. Closer to RFC 1157's letter for v2c/v3 but wrong for v1, which has no per-varbind exception values (that is why #5049's v1 path uses `noSuchName` + an error-index).
3. **v1 `noSuchName` + error-index** for the offending position, v2c/v3 exception value. Most faithful, most code.

Whichever is chosen, the five arms must move together, and `TestAnUndecodableVarbindIsSkippedNotRejected9133` is written to be **updated deliberately** rather than deleted — it fails with a message saying so if the PDU starts being dropped.

## Severity

Low. It needs a malformed varbind to reach the agent, which is gated by the community string and the optional client ACL, and one datagram's response affects only its own client (SNMP over UDP is one datagram per response). But it is not purely adversarial: a corrupted packet that survives the UDP checksum reaches the same path, and the result is a silently wrong-arity answer rather than a retransmit.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

## #9335 — snmp: TestV2cTrapIsUnaffectedByTheTargetMove9123 is FLAKY at a measured 1.08% — it asserts packet-length identity across builds whose randomized request-id changes the length [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-06)

Hit while gating #9133 with `go test ./...`. **Not caused by that change** — the mechanism is `math/rand` and BER integer width, neither of which #9133 touches.

## The red

```
--- FAIL: TestV2cTrapIsUnaffectedByTheTargetMove9123 (0.00s)
    agent_addr_9123_test.go:191: the v2c packet length varies with the target ([132 132 131]);
        it does not depend on the target and must not start to
```

## Mechanism, established by reading rather than by re-running

`buildLinkTrapV2` draws `requestID := rand.Int31()` (`pkg/snmp/traps.go:139`) and encodes it with `berEncodeIntegerTLV`. `berEncodeIntegerValue` emits the minimum number of octets, so the request-id's **encoded width** varies with its value:

- `value >= 2^23` (probability 255/256) → 4 content octets
- `value <  2^23` (probability 1/256) → 3 or fewer

The test builds the trap three times, once per target, and asserts all three packet lengths are equal. The three draws are independent, so a short one in any of them makes the lengths disagree — with nothing about the target having changed.

## Measured rate

20,000 iterations of exactly what the test does, in-tree:

```
MISMATCH 216/20000 = 1.080%   lengths=map[129:2 131:215 132:59783]
```

**~1.1% of runs of `go test ./pkg/snmp/` red on this cell**, and the 129 bucket shows the two-octet case occurs too.

## Why it is worth fixing rather than tolerating

The cell's own comment records that byte-identity was the author's first attempt and was abandoned *for this exact reason*:

> Byte-identity was my first attempt and it was simply wrong: the v2c PDU carries a RANDOMIZED request-id, so two builds of the same trap differ at bytes 18-21 with no change to anything.

The replacement changed the *symptom* (differing bytes → differing length) without removing the *cause* (a randomized field of variable encoded width). It went from failing every run to failing 1 in 90, which is worse in the way that matters: a gate that reds occasionally teaches people to re-run it.

## Candidate remedies

1. **Compare the length of the packet with the request-id TLV excised** — the invariant the cell means is "nothing structural changes with the target", and the request-id is the one field that legitimately differs.

## #9340 — system-login: the unenforceable-deny advisory is per-PATTERN, so one enforceable alternation branch silences the warning for the argument-text branch beside it [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-11)

The #8189 advisory that tells an operator "this `deny-commands` pattern cannot
fire on the gRPC surface" asks an **existential** question per pattern: *does
this regex deny ANY command in the surface's registered set?* A pattern that
denies **some** commands there and silently misses **others** answers "yes", so
the advisory reports nothing — and the operator is told nothing about the half
of their posture that is console-only.

Combining restrictions into one alternation is the natural way an operator
writes a single rule for several things, and it is exactly the shape that
silences the warning.

## Measured

Same command, same surface, two spellings of the same intent:

```
deny = ^show route table secret-vrf$
  commit/runtime advisory: [the gRPC surface]          <- WARNED
  remote `show route table secret-vrf` -> cmd="show route table" allowed=true

deny = ^(show route table secret-vrf|request system reboot)$
  commit/runtime advisory: []                          <- SILENT
  remote `show route table secret-vrf` -> cmd="show route table" allowed=true
```

The silencing command, identified by walking `allCanonicalCommands()` with the
combined pattern:

```
pattern DOES deny registered command: "request system reboot"
```

So one enforceable branch buys silence for the whole pattern. The on-box CLI
denies `show route table secret-vrf` in both cases (`EvaluateForms` matches the
full canonical line, which carries the value), so the two surfaces diverge and
only the single-restriction spelling says so.

Probes were run in-tree against `master` at `1c79f5dbf`, driving
`config.UnenforceableDenySurfaces`, `grpcapi.rpcCanonicalCommand` and
`CompiledLoginRegexes.Evaluate` directly. They have been removed.

## #9344 — dataplane/HA: the owner-RG session export has no terminating bound — the 64 MiB response cap is crossed at ~7.8k sessions/worker, and paging is not expressible because the export DRAINS and discards the has-more bit it already computes [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-07)

Split out of #9322, which fixed the DIAGNOSTIC (a truncation was reported as *"the helper rejected it before replying"*) and corrected the false in-source premise that the cap is unreachable. This issue is #9322's acceptance criterion 4 — *"Decide the export's real bound"* — answered with a measurement, because the answer turned out not to be either of the two options as stated.

## What #9322 established

`export_owner_rg_sessions` is asked with a ~60-byte request and answered with the UNBOUNDED owner-RG session set. `MaxControlRequestBytes` bounds the ASK, not the answer. A response over `MaxControlResponseBytes` (64 MiB) is truncated. `doBulkSync` fails closed, so on a busy cluster the HA cold prime / full resync fails **every time, permanently**.

#9322 makes that failure *diagnosable*. It does not make it *not happen*.

## Measurement 1 — the per-delta size, derived rather than sampled

`SessionDeltaInfo` marshalled by reflection, every string field set to a full-width IPv6 text address and every numeric to its maximum:

```
ZERO-VALUE  delta JSON =   83 bytes
WORST-CASE  delta JSON = 1424 bytes   (43 fields: 14 string, 23 numeric)
```

#9322's issue body used 577 B, a typical IPv4 delta. The worst case is **2.5x that**, and the worst case is what a bound must use.

## Measurement 2 — the ceiling is a FUNCTION OF WORKER COUNT, so "raise the cap" has no fixed answer

`workers x DEFAULT_MAX_SESSIONS(131072) x 1424 B`, against the 64 MiB cap:

| workers | theoretical max response | vs. cap | cap crossed at |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 178 MiB | 2.8x | 47,127 sessions/worker |
| 4 | 712 MiB | 11x | 11,781 |
| **6** (the loss cluster's VF queue count) | **1068 MiB** | **16x** | **7,854** |
| 8 | 1424 MiB | 22x | 5,890 |
| 16 | 2848 MiB | 44x | 2,945 |

So #9322's criterion-4 option A — *"the response cap rises above `DEFAULT_MAX_SESSIONS * workers * bytes-per-delta`"* — is **not a number**. It is a number *per box*, scaling linearly with a runtime quantity, and the only source for that quantity is `ProcessStatus.Workers` / `.MaxSessions`, which the **helper itself reports**. Sizing a security allocation bound from a value the bounded party supplies is not a bound. Any fixed constant large enough for a 16-worker box (≥ 2.8 GiB) reopens exactly the unbounded-allocation case #9003 closed.

**Option A is refuted.** That leaves paging.

## Measurement 3 — paging is not expressible against today's helper, and the reason is not obvious

The protocol already carries `max`, so "just call it repeatedly with `max=N`" is the fix everybody will reach for first. It does not work, for two reasons found by reading `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/ha/export.rs` and `session_delta.rs`:

1. **The export DRAINS.** `drain_session_deltas_fair` calls `bindings[cursor].drain_session_deltas(take)`, which REMOVES the deltas from the per-binding buffers. A capped export therefore consumes the first N and leaves the remainder buffered — it does not re-read them.

passes** — Codex + AGY + Claude SMR — over every research conclusion. The AGY
pass has been failing deterministically, so results are being produced with
**two**, and the degradation is silent unless the run reports it.

Surfaced by a research run that attempted it **3/3 times through two entry
points** and got the same failure each time. That run did the right thing — it

export function buildAgyArgv(options = {}, supportsPrintTimeout = true) {
  const normalized = normalizeRunOptions(options);
  const argv = ["--print"];
  if (supportsPrintTimeout) {
    argv.push("--print-timeout", normalized.printTimeout);

  ...
```

**`--print` takes a value.** From `agy --help`:

```
  --print          Run a single prompt non-interactively and print the response
  --print-timeout  Timeout for print mode wait (default 5m0s)
  --prompt         Alias for --print
  -p               Short alias for --print
```

`--prompt` being documented as an alias for `--print` settles it: `--print` is
the prompt-bearing flag, not a boolean. So the emitted argv
`--print --print-timeout <ms> …` hands agy the **literal string
`--print-timeout`** as the prompt, and the real prompt never arrives.

## Measured

`compileRoutingInstances`' `case "protocols"` calls the SAME `compileProtocols` as the global tree and then copies **five** of the seven `ProtocolsConfig` fields into the instance:

```go
ri.OSPF   = proto.OSPF
ri.OSPFv3 = proto.OSPFv3
ri.BGP    = proto.BGP
ri.RIP    = proto.RIP
ri.ISIS   = proto.ISIS
```

`proto.RouterAdvertisement` and `proto.LLDP` are compiled and then dropped on the floor when `proto` goes out of scope. Measured, with the global spelling as the control in the same run:

```
routing-instances { V { instance-type vrf; protocols {
    router-advertisement { interface ge-0/0/0.0 { max-advertisement-interval 30; } } } } }
  -> ACCEPTED. cfg.Protocols.RouterAdvertisement has 0 interfaces.
     ri.OSPF/BGP/RIP/ISIS all nil. The stanza compiled to NOTHING, anywhere.

routing-instances { V { instance-type vrf; protocols { lldp { interface ge-0/0/0.0; } } } }
  -> ACCEPTED. cfg.Protocols.LLDP == nil. Same.

CONTROL  protocols { router-advertisement { interface ge-0/0/0.0 { ... } } }
  -> ACCEPTED, 1 RA interface.
CONTROL  protocols { lldp { interface ge-0/0/0.0; } }
  -> ACCEPTED, LLDP non-nil.
```

Clean commit, no error, no warning, and `show configuration` renders the stanza back. The operator gets no value and no complaint — the #8928 shape.

## Why it did not surface before

Until PR #9373 the per-instance `protocols` node did not declare `lldp` or `router-advertisement` at all, so in the FLAT-SET spelling the tokens packed onto a container key and never reached `compileProtocols` either. The braced spelling has always reached it and been discarded. Both spellings end in the same place — nothing configured — so the defect was reachable the whole time; the schema gap merely hid one of the two routes to it.

PR #9373 deliberately did NOT add these two to the shared per-instance node, precisely because declaring them would make completion offer a keyword whose value is discarded. `TestRoutingInstanceProtocolsShareTheGlobalGrammar9351` asserts that boundary in both directions and derives it from the `ri.X = proto.X` assignments in the source, so it will red if either side moves without the other. ## #9382 — userspace-dp: the #8356 re-derivation judges the PRE-translation destination, so an unrelated commit or route change revokes every live DNAT/NPTv6 session [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-09)

## Summary

Admission evaluates zone policy on the **post-translation** destination tuple
(#2345). The established-session re-derivation (#8356) evaluates the **wire
(pre-translation)** tuple. For any session with an inbound destination
translation (DNAT / static-DNAT / NPTv6, and NAT64 in one shape), the two sites
therefore ask different questions about the same session.

The dominant, ordinary-operations consequence is **fail-closed**: a published
service whose permit names the real server is **revoked and its packet dropped**
on the first flow-cache miss — with the policy completely unchanged. The
fail-open direction also exists (a deny narrowing against the real server is
missed because the VIP tuple still matches a permit).

## Evidence (base `444173473ce6568edbcde3e9dc1bcea0b1e782ec`)

Admission derives and passes the translated tuple:

- `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/poll_descriptor/mod.rs:1542-1546` — `policy_dst_ip = effective_resolution_target`, `policy_dst_port = pre_routing_dnat…rewrite_dst_port.unwrap_or(flow.forward_key.dst_port)`; the comment at `:1537-1541` states it "carries the correct post-translation tuple for all inbound destination translations (DNAT/static-DNAT/NPTv6/NAT64)".

## #9385 — [cohort] userspace-dp: the #8356 re-derivation records a phantom policy hit, and its 'side-effect freedom is STRUCTURAL' claim is false [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-10)

## Summary

Two tightly related accounting/contract defects in
`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/poll_descriptor/policy_revalidation.rs`, sharing one
corrective edit:

1. every zone-policy re-derivation records a **phantom packet hit** on whichever
   rule (or the implicit default) it matches;
2. the module header states side-effect freedom as a **structural** property, and
   that statement is false.

## Evidence (base `444173473ce6568edbcde3e9dc1bcea0b1e782ec`)

The header claim, `policy_revalidation.rs:62-67`:

> **3. Side-effect freedom is STRUCTURAL, not a flag.** … `evaluate_policy_result_with_icmp`
> takes `&PolicyState` and RETURNS a counter handle (`policy_counter_idx`) for the
> caller to bump; it cannot count, log or meter by itself. This module simply never
> bumps what it is handed.

True of the handle. False of the evaluation, which counts internally:

- `userspace-dp/src/policy.rs:652-657` — `fn add(&self, packet_len: u64) { self.packets.fetch_add(1, …); if packet_len != 0 { self.bytes.fetch_add(…) } }`. The zero-length gate covers **bytes only**; the packet increment is unconditional.
- `policy.rs:3700` — `try_match_rule` calls `rule.hit_counter.add(packet_len)` on every match.
- `policy.rs:3091-3097` — the implicit-default path calls `state.default_counter.add(packet_len)`.
- `policy_revalidation.rs:255` — the re-derivation passes `packet_len = 0`.

`&PolicyState` does not prevent this: the counters are atomics behind shared
references, so an immutable borrow is not the structural guarantee the header
claims it is.

## Impact

`show security policies hit-count` and the default-policy counter inflate by up
to one packet per live session per config generation, with bytes unchanged. No
forwarding effect. It is kept visible for two reasons: hit-count is exactly what
an operator watches to confirm a narrowing took effect, so the noise arrives at
the worst moment; and a stated structural guarantee that is not structural will
invite a future side effect into this path.

## #9391 — config: 26 of 99 measured containers LOSE a statement when its leaves are written on one line — incl. `system login user … class` and `security-zone … screen` [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-11)

Measured by the `(container, leaf-run)` differential gate landed for #9156 (`pkg/config/leaf_run_differential_gate_9156_test.go`). #9156 fixed the one operator-reachable instance it was filed for (`interfaces <if> tunnel`) and built the gate; this issue is the population that gate found.

## The measurement, with its denominator

For every container that holds an untyped **admission head** (a childless leaf declaring no `valueType` and no `validator`, so `validateModifierChild` has nothing to reject the following token with) alongside at least two childless leaves, the gate compiles two configs that say the same thing — the leaves on ONE line, and the leaves on SEPARATE lines — and compares the compiled `Config`. **The separate-lines form is the oracle.**

```
111 containers enumerated
 99 COMPARED      -> 73 agree, 26 DIFFER
 12 skipped       -> 3 no synthesizable value
                     0 one-line form did not compile
                     9 ORACLE did not compile
```

The comparison runs on the **lenient** path deliberately. A census that compiles strictly loses a row exactly where a validator rejects its synthesized value, so it goes blind at the gated sites — the ones a reader is most likely to have skipped. Per #1960 the lenient path is what `Load` and `SyncApply` take, so a strict rejection does not mean the loss cannot happen; it means it happens on boot and HA sync instead of at commit.

## The 26

```

forwarding-options sampling instance <i> family inet output flow-server <s>   [source-address -> port]

interfaces <if> tunnel wireguard                            [private-key -> listen-port]

## #9392 — userspace-dp: recycle_scan_pops is #[cfg(test)], so the non-amortizing recycled-phase state has no operator-visible signal [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-09)

Split out of #9327 (its third acceptance checkbox) so the measured half could land without a wire addition attached to it.

## What is known, measured

The recycled phase of `PortAllocator::claim` (`userspace-dp/src/nat/allocator.rs`) walks the per-address FIFO. #9327 corrected the in-code comment, which claimed the HA-churn spike "amortizes itself"; measured pops per claim in steady state:

```
K=15, F=1 -> [16, 16]                    <- never amortizes; every claim pays K+1
K=12, F=4 -> [13, 1, 1, 1, 13, 1, 1, 1]  <- (K+F)/F = 4, not K-once
```

where K is out-of-band-occupied tokens ahead in the FIFO and F is free tokens. Retained tokens go to the BACK, which buys exactly F cheap claims before the K are at the head again. The cost is O(K/F) amortized, degrading to O(K) per claim as F → 1 — **worst exactly as an address approaches exhaustion**, i.e. when the pool is busiest. K is bounded by the range, so the near-exhaustion worst case is O(range) pops per claim.

The `occupied >= range` short-circuit covers only FULL exhaustion. The cliff is the window just below it.

## What is NOT known, and why this issue exists

**Whether a production pool ever reaches K-large / F-small.** The fixture proves the mechanism, not the reachability. `recycle_scan_pops` — the counter that would answer it — is `#[cfg(test)]` (`allocator.rs`, `debug_recycle_scan_pops`), so there is no signal from a running firewall at all.

That is the cheapest way to settle it, and it is why #9327 corrected the comment rather than bounding the walk: bounding is the riskier change and the reachability question is unanswered.

## Why #9327 did not just promote the counter

Surfacing it is a Rust → `ProcessStatus` → Go → CLI chain. Promoting the field to a production build **without** the rest would put an atomic increment on the allocation path feeding a counter nothing reads — an unfalsifiable claim rather than a signal, and the kind of inert code that later reads as coverage. Doing it properly is this issue.

## Acceptance

- [ ] `recycle_scan_pops` (or an aggregate derived from it) leaves `#[cfg(test)]` and reaches `ProcessStatus`.
- [ ] It is readable from the Go side and surfaced somewhere an operator looks — `show security nat source pool` is the natural home, beside the existing pool utilisation.
- [ ] ADD a wire field, never redefine one: the helper and the daemon roll independently, so a redefined field is a rolling-upgrade break.
- [ ] A cell that the counter moves under the K-large/F-small shape and stays ~1/claim in the healthy case — a counter that always reads 0, or always reads large, answers nothing.

## Do not re-open the bounding question on this issue's evidence

The comment beside the amortization claim is sound and #9327 left it standing: a bare scan budget cannot distinguish "scanned enough" from "genuinely full", so `None` on budget exhaustion turns a slow allocation into a **spuriously dropped NAT translation**. If the counter shows the cliff is real in production, a bound needs a way to tell those two apart — `occupied == range` is the existing exact discriminator and a budget is not.

## #9395 — userspace-dp: decide the policy for an oversized DF-clear IPv4 datagram — fragment (RFC 791), drop-and-count, or keep forwarding [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-11)

The "real half" of #9328, split out because it is a policy decision on an unmeasured population and the cheap half should not wait behind it.

## What #9328 established and landed

There is no IPv4 transit fragmenter in this dataplane (positive-controlled grep: the only MF/offset writers are `nat64.rs`, which copy MF and offset verbatim from an existing IPv6 Fragment Header). Nothing in `tx/transmit/`, `tx/rings.rs` or `tx/drain/` compares a frame against an MTU; the only length guard on the forward path is `copy_frame_is_oversized`, which tests the UMEM chunk (4096), not the egress MTU.

So an oversized **DF-clear** IPv4 datagram is submitted to TX at full length and the NIC, switch or next hop drops it.

#9328 landed the observability only: `EgressMtuDecision::ForwardOversizeNoDf` and an `egress_mtu_exceeded_forwarded_no_df` exception. **Behaviour is unchanged.**

## What is NOT decided, and why it was left open

Three candidate policies:

1. **Fragment on egress.** RFC 791 permits a router to fragment a DF-clear datagram, and it is the only option that delivers the packet. It is also a real feature: splitting, header rewrite, ID assignment, per-fragment checksum, multiple TX descriptors, and interaction with NAT/CoS/session accounting on the AF_XDP path.
2. **Drop and count.** Honest, cheap, and arguably no worse than today given the frame is likely dropped downstream anyway.
3. **Keep forwarding** (today's behaviour), now that it is at least counted.

**A PTB is not a candidate.** ICMP Fragmentation-Needed is meaningful only to a sender that set DF; this one did not and will not act on it. #2301's `Forward` branch exists precisely to avoid PTB-storming these flows.

## The measurement that decides it

**The wire-level fate of the oversize submission was never measured.** Whether the driver rejects the TX descriptor, the NIC truncates, or the next hop drops it is unknown — and option 2 versus option 3 turns entirely on that, because dropping a path that currently *works* would be a regression introduced by a fix.

Decisive check: send a 1600-byte DF-clear UDP datagram through the box toward a 1400-MTU egress and capture the far side. On the loss userspace cluster that is a `reth0.80`-side egress with a reduced MTU and a capture on `cluster-userspace-host`.

The second input is now available and was not before: `egress_mtu_exceeded_forwarded_no_df` says how often this happens in production at all. If it never fires, option 3 is fine and this issue closes as "measured, not worth it". If it fires, the frequency argues between 1 and 2.

## Acceptance

- [ ] Capture the far side of an oversized DF-clear datagram and record what actually arrives (or does not).
- [ ] Read `egress_mtu_exceeded_forwarded_no_df` from a real deployment or the cluster smoke.
- [ ] Pick one of the three with the numbers attached, and document the deviation if it is not RFC 791 fragmentation.
- [ ] Update `oversized_v4_without_df_forwards` and `oversized_no_df_is_forwarded_and_counted_9328`, which currently pin "still forwarded" as the contract.
- [ ] Re-read #2301's Impact paragraph against the outcome — it names this population with no DF qualifier, and its acceptance test list omitted the DF-clear case.

## #9403 — userspace-dp: the twice-NAT source-NAT teardown frees nothing — release.rs rebuilds the allocation key with the PRE-DNAT destination port that #9034 moved [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-07)

## The defect

`#9034` moved the source-NAT **match/allocate** tuple onto the post-DNAT destination **port**. The
**teardown** reconstruction was left on the pre-DNAT port, so for a twice-NAT flow whose DNAT
rewrites the destination port (the ordinary VIP shape, 443 -> 8443) a session teardown looks up a key
the allocator never stored, frees nothing, and returns `false`.

`userspace-dp/src/nat/source/release.rs:211-218` (at `3c4d3bfa867d6b20bab0afcc6f98b44bf98a4033`):

```rust
let flow = SourceNatFlowKey {
    protocol: key.protocol,
    src_ip:   key.src_ip,
    dst_ip:   nat.rewrite_dst.unwrap_or(key.dst_ip),   // POST-DNAT address
    src_port: key.src_port,
    dst_port: key.dst_port,                            // PRE-DNAT port
    routing_scope: key.routing_domain,
};
```

The address line and the port line disagree about which side of DNAT they are on. That asymmetry was
CORRECT before `#9034` — the match then used the post-DNAT address with the pre-DNAT port, so
`release.rs` matched it exactly. `#9034` moved one half and not the other.

## The chain

| step | site | key |
| --- | --- | --- |
| post-DNAT port derived | `afxdp/poll_descriptor/mod.rs:1543-1546` | `policy_dst_port` |
| SNAT match/allocate tuple | `afxdp/poll_descriptor/mod.rs:2560-2561` | `flow.with_destination(effective_resolution_target, policy_dst_port)` |
| key inserted into `live_by_flow` | `nat/source/match_rules.rs:327-341` | **post-DNAT** dst_ip + dst_port |
| SESSION installed | `afxdp/poll_descriptor/mod.rs:2840` | `flow.forward_key.clone()` — **pre-DNAT** |
| teardown reconstruction | `nat/source/release.rs:211-218` | post-DNAT addr, **pre-DNAT port** |
| lookup | `nat/allocator.rs:2347-2360` | exact `live_by_flow.get(&flow)`; returns `false` on a miss |

Every post-install teardown caller passes the stored pre-DNAT key: `worker/loop_body/mod.rs:1761`
(GC reap), `session_glue/mod.rs:626`, `:1313`, `session_glue/promote.rs:198`,
`session_glue/commands/delete_synced.rs:94`, `commands/upsert_synced.rs:148`,
`ha/session_import.rs:260`, `:874`, `ha/tunnel_purge.rs:141`.

## #9404 — userspace-dp/HA: the standby source-NAT replay keys on the PRE-DNAT destination port — wrong rule, wrong lease identity, and an unguarded address-only identity collision [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-07)

## The defect

The HA standby's PASS-1 source-NAT rule replay reconstructs the active's SNAT-match tuple with the
post-DNAT destination **address** and the pre-DNAT destination **port**, so for a
destination-port-scoped source-NAT rule behind a port-rewriting DNAT it replays a tuple the active
never matched.

`userspace-dp/src/nat/source/synced.rs:228-234` (at `3c4d3bfa867d6b20bab0afcc6f98b44bf98a4033`):

```rust
let flow = SourceNatFlowKey {
    protocol: key.protocol,
    src_ip:   key.src_ip,
    dst_ip:   nat.rewrite_dst.unwrap_or(key.dst_ip),   // POST-DNAT address
    src_port: key.src_port,
    dst_port: key.dst_port,                            // PRE-DNAT port
    routing_scope: key.routing_domain,
};
```

That `dst_port` is fed to `rule.matches_ignoring_scope(...)` (`synced.rs:251-262`), which routes it
into `l4_matches` -> `match_dst_ports` (`nat/source/mod.rs:1067-1081`). Since `#9034` the ACTIVE
matches on the post-DNAT port, so the two nodes evaluate different rules.

**The file's own comment now asserts the opposite** — `synced.rs:242-245`:

> "`flow` is byte-identical to the active's SNAT-match tuple (`nat_match_flow.forward_key` in
> `poll_descriptor`: original source, POST-DNAT destination, **original ports**)"

"original ports" was accurate before `#9034` and is false after it. The comment should read
"original source, post-DNAT destination (address **and** port)".

## What the divergence actually causes — measured, because the intuitive answer is wrong

PASS 1 does not only filter on `matches_ignoring_scope`. Inside the loop each surviving candidate
must also OWN the active's translated address (`synced.rs:525-535` and `:729-739`:
`let Some(addr_index) = … else { continue; }`). If the wrongly-matched rule's pool does not contain
that address the loop ends with `saw_candidate == false` and returns `NothingToReserve`, which
`synced.rs:319-321` documents as explicitly **not** a refusal and which falls through to PASS 2 —
and PASS 2 finds the right rule.
