## #9669 — xpf-deploy: virsh and virt-install pass no connection URI while the disk paths are hard-wired to system-scope libvirt [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-11)

## What this is

A split-out from #9325, from its "three more" list. #9325's branch addresses the other defects in that cohort; this one needs a design decision, so it is not changed there.

`scripts/deploy/xpf-deploy.py` runs `virsh` and `virt-install` without `--connect`, and nothing in `scripts/` or `docs/` sets `LIBVIRT_DEFAULT_URI`. Meanwhile the golden and overlay paths are hard-wired to the system-scope `/var/lib/libvirt/images`. A root invocation therefore talks to `qemu:///system`, while a non-root invocation talks to libvirt's default for that user, normally `qemu:///session`. Both operate on the same system-scope disks.

## Why it matters once teardown needs an affirmative ABSENT

#9325 makes teardown unlink a disk only when a probe affirmatively reports the domain gone. A probe against the WRONG connection gives exactly that answer. libvirt keeps a separate domain namespace per URI (cited from libvirt's model, not measured here), so a domain defined in `qemu:///system` reads as not found from `qemu:///session`. A non-root `destroy` would then remove the system-scope overlay of a running VM. The #9325 change does not close this route.

## Why the obvious fix is not the fix

The obvious fix is to pass `--connect qemu:///system` everywhere, because the disks are system-scope. That is itself a wrong ABSENT for any operator who has been deploying non-root: their existing domains live in the session URI, a pinned system URI would report them absent, and their disks would be unlinked. The fix has to choose between options such as:

- refuse non-root libvirt invocations outright, because the disks are system-scope;
- probe both URIs, and treat a domain present in either as present;
- record the URI each domain was created with, and tear it down through that URI.

## Acceptance

- [ ] Teardown never reads a domain as absent from a URI other than the one it was defined in. Add one cell per arrangement, including a domain defined in the other URI.
- [ ] `deploy` and `destroy` agree on the URI for a given domain, and the operator docs name the URI the tool uses.

## #9678 — userspace-dp/HA: a peer-synced import reserves NAT before the ownership check, so a same-flow synced upsert evicts a live local allocation the worker then refuses to replace [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-11)

## What is wrong

`SessionDomain::upsert_synced_session` takes the coordinator's pre-publish NAT reservation for a
peer-synced session **before** anything asks whether this node owns the flow. When a same-flow local
session already holds a different translated tuple, the reservation retires that live local
allocation. The worker then correctly refuses to replace the locally owned session, so the
session keeps forwarding on a translated tuple whose allocator record is gone.

## Mechanism, at `a21c23ac70d02cc156ba898ff51855c1b8cd4bec`

1. `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/ha/session_import.rs:544-553` — for a peer-synced forward entry with at
   least one registered worker, `reserve_synced_translation(&entry)` runs with no ownership test.
   The only earlier refusals are a standalone reverse, a stale generation when **both** generations
   are non-zero (`:428-437`; a local entry carries generation 0), and capacity.
   The BPF publish later in the same function **is** gated on
   `synced_entry_allows_local_replace` (`:627-638`), so the guard exists but is not applied to the
   allocator.
2. The reservation builds the same `SourceNatFlowKey` the local allocation used
   (`userspace-dp/src/nat/source/synced.rs:228-247`) and reaches
   `reserve_flow_maybe_persistent` (`userspace-dp/src/nat/allocator.rs:~3263-3330`). When
   `live_by_flow[flow]` holds a different translated tuple, it calls
   `unlink_live_allocation_locked` and `complete_persistent_lease_locked` on the incumbent
   (`:~3293-3329`) before reserving the new tuple. For plain PAT the unlink returns the port to
   the recycle queue; for a persistent incumbent it drops a lease reference.
3. The worker command then refuses the replace: `upsert_synced_with_origin` returns false when the
   existing entry is local-origin and `!allow_replace_local`
   (`userspace-dp/src/session/install.rs:~358-364`), and `handle_upsert_synced` derives
   `allow_replace_local` from `synced_entry_allows_local_replace` — false exactly when the owner RG
   is locally forwarding-active (`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/session_glue/commands/upsert_synced.rs:~64-67,123`).
   The refusal is silent: there is no else branch and the dispatcher records nothing.
4. Every refusal inside `reserve_flow_maybe_persistent` (occupancy CAS, lease mismatch, the
   `peer_owns_wire_identity` rollback) happens **after** the incumbent was unlinked, so even an
   import answered `RejectedReserve` has already freed the local tuple.
5. A later local teardown cannot repair it: `release_flow` no-ops when the translated tuple does not
   match (`allocator.rs:~2483-2488`).

Identical ordering and eviction existed at the report base
(`session_import.rs:544@5fafce23f`, `allocator.rs:3238@5fafce23f`); post-base changes to these files
(#9514, #9412, #9536) do not reorder or guard the reservation.

## #9679 — userspace-dp: remove_shared_session deletes a colliding session's shared reverse-NAT and forward-wire alias without checking it belongs to the removed session [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-11)

## What is wrong

The shared (cross-worker) NAT reverse-alias and forward-wire maps are single-value maps.
`publish_shared_session` overwrites an alias another session already holds and only counts the
displacement. `remove_shared_session(A)` later derives A's alias keys and deletes whatever occupies
them, without checking that the stored entry is A. When two sessions collide on an alias, removing the
first also removes the survivor's shared alias. A worker that has no local copy of the survivor then
misses both lookups and sends the survivor's reply traffic to new-flow adjudication.

## Mechanism, at `a21c23ac70d02cc156ba898ff51855c1b8cd4bec`

1. `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/shared_ops.rs:~1194-1231` — `publish_shared_session` inserts into
   `shared_nat_sessions` at the reverse-wire and reverse-canonical keys (and into
   `shared_forward_wire_sessions`) unconditionally; `record_shared_nat_displacement` counts a displaced
   entry with a different forward key. The counter's doc (`:~159-185`, #1760) states "Two distinct
   forward NAT sessions mapping onto one reply tuple K is the #1758/#1760 latent 1:N collision".
2. `shared_ops.rs:1235-1307` — `remove_shared_session` removes `nat_sessions[reverse_wire]`,
   `nat_sessions[reverse_canonical]` and `forward_wire_sessions[wire_key]` derived from the removed
   entry with no `removed.key == key` check.
3. Worker-local NAT reverse lookup is 1:N and validated (`userspace-dp/src/session/lookup.rs:~269-341`),
   but a worker without local B falls back to the shared alias (`shared_ops.rs:~870-897`); after A's
   removal B's reply misses both.
4. The removal runs on ordinary paths: every Close-delta drain (`afxdp/session_delta.rs:~522-538`),
   terminal deletes (`afxdp/session_glue/mod.rs:~704-771`) and coordinator deletes
   (`afxdp/ha/session_import.rs:~787-808`).

Present at the report base (`shared_ops.rs:1174,1256@5fafce23f`); post-base #9517/#9412 changes to the
file do not touch this removal.

## Reachability

Collision classes that reach the shared alias at the pin:

- DNAT to a shared backend (documented as a reverse-key collision class).
- NAT64 flows from two routing instances sharing one translated binding (filed separately; see the
  NAT64 allocator-scope issue from the same review).
- Cross-routing-instance identical 5-tuples on `reverse_canonical_key`, which forces
  `routing_domain: 0` by design (`userspace-dp/src/session/key.rs:~240-319`).

## #9680 — nat64: the BIB allocation key pins routing scope 0, so identical IPv6 5-tuples in two routing instances share one translated binding [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-11)

## What is wrong

`SourceNatFlowKey` carries a `routing_scope` so that identical flows from different routing instances
do not share an allocator identity (#9062). NAT64 pins that scope to 0 at allocation, release and HA
synced reservation. Identical IPv6 5-tuples arriving in two routing instances that reach the global
NAT64 prefix therefore build byte-identical allocator keys, and the second flow reuses the first
flow's translated IPv4 binding.

## Mechanism, at `a21c23ac70d02cc156ba898ff51855c1b8cd4bec`

1. `userspace-dp/src/nat64.rs:265-279` — `NAT64_ROUTING_SCOPE_9062: u32 = 0`, with the rationale
   "NAT64 pools are per-PREFIX ... Zero preserves today's behaviour exactly".
2. `nat64.rs:~1366-1373` (allocate), `:1488` (release) and `:1765` (synced reserve) all build
   `SourceNatFlowKey { ..., routing_scope: NAT64_ROUTING_SCOPE_9062 }`; the NAT64 match itself takes no
   routing-domain input (`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/poll_descriptor/mod.rs:1513-1540`).
3. The packet's session key does carry a routing domain: it is stamped at
   `poll_descriptor/mod.rs:333` (`forwarding::ingress_routing_domain`) before the NAT64 match, so the two
   flows install as two sessions (#7160).
4. Allocation's `live_by_flow` hit returns the existing translation for the identical key
   (`userspace-dp/src/nat/allocator.rs:~1915-1938`; the deterministic path shares the reuse arm), which
   violates the per-flow uniqueness NAT64 documents (#4381).
5. The NAT64 reverse keys are domain-agnostic by convention (`userspace-dp/src/session/key.rs:~240-297`),
   so both sessions share one reverse identity; a reply arriving in a domain matching neither tenant
   takes the pass-2 candidate (`userspace-dp/src/session/lookup.rs:~269-341`).

Identical at the report base (`nat64.rs:265,1373@5fafce23f`, `allocator.rs:1897@5fafce23f`); no post-base
change to these sites.

## Reachability (configuration admission executed)

A strict `CompileConfig` probe at the pin accepts a global NAT64 rule-set and source pool alongside
two `instance-type vrf` routing instances in distinct zones with zero warnings; with both routing-instance
interfaces on the same /64 it still commits, emitting one advisory. #9323 refuses only NAT64 nested
**under** a routing instance, so global NAT64 with multiple routing instances is an accepted shape.
Issues #9033 and #9162 (both closed) already established that NAT64 flows from non-default routing
domains reach the translation arms.

## Consequence (bounded)

- Two tenants' flows share one translated `(pool v4, port)` binding.

## #9683 — test/incus: `incus exec` inside a `while read` loop swallows the loop's stdin — the post-deploy reassert transfers only RG0 and the build-identity guard probes only node0 [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-11)

## Summary

`incus exec` forwards its stdin to the remote command. Three `while read` loops under `test/incus` call it without `-n`. So the first iteration's `incus exec` consumes the rest of the loop's input, and the loop body runs **once**.

| site | loop | effect |
|---|---|---|
| `test/incus/deploy-lib.sh:450` | `deploy_reassert_primary_node0`: reset, then transfer, per RG | only RG0 is transferred to node0 |
| `test/incus/deploy-lib.sh:496` | same function: trailing pin clear per RG | only RG0's manual pin is cleared (the #7688 shape) |
| `test/incus/cluster-build-identity.sh:78` | `xpf_cluster_build_probe`: one sha per node | only FW0 is probed, so a binary swapped under a cell on FW1 is invisible to the "BUILD CHANGED" guard |

**Severity: High.**
- On the loss userspace cluster, `make cluster-deploy` dies in the post-deploy reassert whenever node1 still holds RG1/RG2 after node0 restarts.
- The error is "node0 is not primary for every redundancy group". It reads as an HA regression in whichever branch deployed.
- That blocks every `make test-failover` gate.
- The third site silently halves a guard that exists to catch a binary swapped mid-cell.

## Measurements

Taken 2026-09-11 on loss:xpf-userspace-fw0/fw1 at master 906705ca7.

- **Journals.** Three consecutive deploys (03:38Z, 03:50Z, 03:58Z on fw0's clock).
  - The reassert issued `failover reset` and `failover request sent to peer` for `rg=0` only, on both nodes.
  - No `rg=1` or `rg=2` command reached either daemon.
  - The final status still showed node1 primary for RG1 and RG2.
- **The transfer mechanism is healthy.** `request chassis cluster failover redundancy-group 1 node 0` by hand returned "transfer committed", and RG1 was on node0 within 10 s.
- **The RG parser is not the cause.** `deploy_rolling_rg_ids` on the captured status prints `0 1 2`.
- **Loop shape.** A read-only command against fw0, 3 trials each:
  - `while read -r rg; do incus exec fw0 -- cli -c "show version"; done <<<$'0\n1\n2'`: 1 iteration, in 3/3 trials.
  - The same loop with `</dev/null` on `incus exec`: 3 iterations, in 3/3 trials.
- **Build-identity probe.**
  - `xpf_cluster_build_probe` as shipped prints one line (fw0).
  - The same loop with `incus exec -n` prints both fw0 and fw1.
- **Client version.** incus client and server are 7.0.0, and `/usr/bin/incus` is dated 2026-06-25. There was no client change.

## Why nothing caught it

Both hermetic self-tests mock `incus exec` without reading stdin: the `incus()` function in `deploy-lib-selftest.sh` and the mock script in `cluster-build-identity-selftest.sh`. A mock that ignores stdin cannot see a loop that loses its input.

## #9684 — userspace: a lost update_neighbors/update_fabrics response is rolled back by the next scheduler, overlay or worker-arm republish of lastSnapshot [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-11)

**Severity: MEDIUM.** Pre-existing. Found by the Codex round-3 review of the #9173 SYN-cookie key rotation, which republishes the same way.

## Defect

`update_neighbors` and `update_fabrics` write their content back into `m.lastSnapshot` only after a successful round trip:
- `RegenerateNeighborSnapshot` and `BumpFIBGeneration` send `update_neighbors`.
- `SyncFabricState` sends `update_fabrics` (the #1197 / #5306 mutate-after-success).

A round-trip failure other than an in-band refusal can follow an update the helper applied: a deadline, EOF, or response-decode error. `process_control.go` records this for `apply_snapshot`: a fixed deadline "reported the apply FAILED while the dataplane had applied it live". After such a failure the helper holds the new neighbors or fabrics, and `lastSnapshot` still holds the old ones.

The partial-rebuild publish paths start from `next := *m.lastSnapshot` and republish `Neighbors` and `Fabrics` verbatim: `UpdatePolicyScheduleState`, `PublishRouteOverlaySnapshot` and the #5134 worker-arm re-apply. `manager_fabric_sync.go` names all three. The next of those to run rolls the helper back to the stale set. For fabrics that is the #5306 revert: cross-chassis fabric redirect uses the unresolved peer MAC.

Nothing records the uncertainty. Neither verb touches `applySnapshotOutcomeUnknown` (#9520), which tracks only `apply_snapshot`.

## Bound

The partial path's own re-send restores the content, because the failure left `lastSnapshot` differing from live state:
- neighbors: the 60 s safety tick, or the next neighbor event;
- fabrics: the 30 s fabric refresh, which runs `SyncFabricState` only after a successful `fabric_fwd` map update.

The exposure is a rollback that lasts up to that cadence. It needs a transport failure after an applied update, followed by one of the three republishes before the re-send.

## Fix direction

#9173 first tried to close this for its own hourly key rotation, which also republished `lastSnapshot`. The attempt is a map of what a fix here must handle:
- **A time-bounded hold is unsound.** When the partial path never re-sends (a `fabric_fwd` update that keeps failing stops `SyncFabricState`), elapsed time proves nothing, and the republish rolls back after the timeout.
- **Carrying the unresolved content forward** (republish the latest unresolved `update_neighbors` / `update_fabrics` content in place of `lastSnapshot`'s section) needs that content to stay the latest live sample. That collides with three things:
  - the neighbor path's equality shortcut, and the daemon neighbor listener's own change filter, which suppresses the event that would refresh it;
  - the control socket's 1/s budget, if the fix re-sends while unresolved;
  - #9696, the Go neighbor-replace ACK check cannot recognise a #6034 fence.

#9173 stopped republishing altogether: the helper now derives the rotating keys itself. The exposure left is only the three pre-existing paths above, and a fix for them has to address those interactions rather than repeat the attempt.

Acceptance:
- A lost-response `update_neighbors` or `update_fabrics`, followed by each of the three republishes, does not publish the stale section.
- An in-band refusal does not hold anything.
- No republish is delayed waiting for a re-send.

## #9685 — config: a flat 'set routing-instances apply-groups <g>' (or apply-groups-except) is silently lost — SetPath files the group name one level down, so nothing is inherited or excluded on a clean commit [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-11)

**Found while validating #9657; measured by execution at origin/master `ff4171851`.**

A flat `set` apply statement placed **under `routing-instances`** is silently lost. The group is defined, the commit is strict-clean, and the inheritance or exclusion simply does not happen. The same statements work at the top level, in hierarchical form, and under `system`.

| # | Config | Strict | Compiled instances |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | `set groups g1 routing-instances ri1 instance-type virtual-router` + `set routing-instances apply-groups g1` | accepts | **`[]`**: `ri1` is not inherited |
| B | same group + `set apply-groups g1` (top level) | accepts | `[ri1]` |
| C | hierarchical `routing-instances { apply-groups g1; }` | accepts | `[ri1]` |
| D | same group + `set apply-groups g1` + `set routing-instances apply-groups-except g1` | accepts | **`[apply-groups-except ri1]`**: the exclusion is not honoured, plus a phantom instance |
| E | hierarchical `routing-instances { apply-groups-except g1; }` with a top-level `apply-groups g1` | accepts | `[apply-groups-except]`: the exclusion is honoured, plus a phantom instance |
| F | `set groups g1 system host-name fromgroup` + `set system apply-groups g1` | accepts | `HostName="fromgroup"` (works) |

## Mechanism

Under `routing-instances`, `SetPath` stores `apply-groups g1` as a node `Keys=["apply-groups"]` with a child `Keys=["g1"]`. `apply-groups-except g1` is stored the same way. The routing-instances schema's wildcard instance-name slot takes the keyword as an instance name, so the group name lands one level down.

- Group expansion reads group names from the statement's own `Keys[1:]` (`expandGroupsRecursive`, `pkg/config/ast_groups.go`). It finds none, and then strips the node by name.
- The #9422 exclusion reads the statement's keys the same way, and so excludes nothing.
- Under `system` the schema declares the statement, so the name stays on its own keys (row F).

## Consequence

A configuration written as flat `set` commands that applies a group at the routing-instances level loses every routing instance that group supplies: no VRF, no routes. The commit reports success. An exclusion written the same way does not exclude.

## Not this issue

- The phantom `apply-groups-except` / `apply-macro` routing instances in rows D and E are addressed by #9657, which makes the compiler skip those statements.
- #9657's reachability helper reads the same keys as expansion, so it agrees with expansion on this shape and needs nothing more once the shape is fixed.

## Fix direction

Declare `apply-groups`, `apply-groups-except` and `apply-macro` in the routing-instances schema ahead of the wildcard instance slot, as they are declared elsewhere, so `SetPath` keeps the names on the statement's own keys. Then check every other stanza whose schema has a wildcard name slot (security zones, interfaces) for the same shape.

## Acceptance

- Rows A and D compile like their hierarchical controls C and E: `[ri1]`, and the exclusion is honoured.
- A cell per stanza with a wildcard name slot fails on today's code.
- `show configuration` renders the flat-set result as the statement.

## #9686 — daemon/HA: the default fail-closed HA shutdown detaches every XDP program but never closes kernel transit forwarding, so a stopped node routes transit with no policy [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-11)

## What is wrong

On a chassis-cluster node, stopping xpfd takes the fail-closed shutdown path by default. That path
detaches every XDP program and removes all pinned BPF state. It never lowers
`net.ipv4.ip_forward` / `net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding` and never installs the #7191 transit barrier.
After the stop the node has kernel forwarding enabled, no XDP adjudication and no forward-hook
barrier. Transit that still reaches a surviving address or route is routed by the kernel with no zone
policy, no session state and no NAT, for the whole downtime.

## Mechanism, at `a21c23ac70d02cc156ba898ff51855c1b8cd4bec`

1. Mode selection — `pkg/daemon/daemon_run_shutdown.go:183-188`: `hitless := !haMode` (a standalone
   node keeps its dataplane). For an HA node only an explicit `chassis cluster hitless-restart` selects
   the hitless branch; the leaf is opt-in ("HA default is fail-closed", `pkg/config/schema_chassis.go:180`,
   compiled at `pkg/config/compiler_system.go:2872-2873`).
2. The fail-closed branch clears `rg_active` (`daemon_run_shutdown.go:~190-211`), stops RA/VRRP/cluster and
   session sync, then calls `rt.Teardown()` (`:~385-393`, "HA shutdown: tearing down BPF state").
3. `rt.Teardown()` goes through `LegacyDataPlaneAdapter.Teardown`
   (`pkg/dataplane/userspace/legacy_dataplane.go:219-225`), then the userspace `Manager.Teardown`
   (`pkg/dataplane/userspace/manager.go:721-727`: stop the helper, `bpfShim.Teardown()`), then
   `dataplane.Manager.Teardown` (`pkg/dataplane/loader.go:1428+`), whose `Cleanup` unpins and closes every
   pinned link under the link pin path and removes the pin tree (`loader.go:~1476-1497`). No XDP program
   remains attached.
4. Nothing on that path closes forwarding. The only writers of the forwarding sysctls and the barrier are the
   #5275/#7191 gate helpers in `pkg/daemon/daemon_transit_gate.go`, and the shutdown path calls none of them.
   While armed the gate holds forwarding at 1 and keeps the barrier removed (`daemon_transit_gate.go:57-80,
   162-170`); the gate's own contract is that no nftables `hook forward` chain exists (`:10-24`).
5. No stop hook compensates: the shipped `debian/xpf.xpfd.service` is generated from
   `test/incus/xpfd.service`, injecting only `ExecStartPre=/usr/local/sbin/xpfd verify-dataplane`
   (`debian/rules:55-64`); the source unit has `ExecStart`, `Restart=on-failure`, `TimeoutStopSec=20` and no
   `ExecStop`/`ExecStopPost`.
6. FRR keeps its routes: the daemon's FRR manager `Stop` cancels only its own reload/retry machinery
   (`pkg/frr/manager.go`), not the FRR service.

Contrast: a standalone (hitless) stop keeps the pinned links attached with userspace control disabled, and a
crash keeps the pins with a stale helper heartbeat; in both cases the shim drops transit. The path named
"fail-closed" is the one that ends with kernel forwarding open.

Present at the report base; no post-base commit touches the shutdown file, the transit gate, the loader's
teardown or the unit.

## #9687 — ipsec: removed-VPN teardown debt lives only in memory, so an xpfd restart before the retry leaves their child SAs forwarding under an unloaded config [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-11)

## What is wrong

The IPsec manager's record of which swanctl connections were removed and still need their SAs terminated
exists only in process memory. xpfd constructs a fresh manager on every start and performs no swanctl
teardown at shutdown. If xpfd restarts before a pending teardown completes — a failed terminate (#6542
debt), a failed reload whose removal was deferred (#4898), or a stop while a teardown is still running —
the restarted daemon has no record of the departed connection and never terminates its live child SA.
strongSwan keeps that SA forwarding although its connection is no longer rendered or loaded, and the
first post-restart apply reports success.

## Mechanism, at `a21c23ac70d02cc156ba898ff51855c1b8cd4bec`

1. `pkg/ipsec/manager.go:108-132`: `prevConnNames` ("nil until the first Apply") and `pendingTerminate`
   (the #6542 teardown debt) are plain in-memory fields.
2. `pkg/daemon/daemon_run_bringup.go:76`: `d.ipsec = ipsec.New()`; `pkg/ipsec/manager.go:176-186`: `New()`
   returns a manager with neither set populated.
3. The removed set is derived only from those two fields (`promoteConnNames`, `manager.go:412+`), and
   `terminateRemovedConns` (`manager.go:472+`) terminates only that set.
4. Shutdown stops only the IPsec DHCP-rebind retry loop (`pkg/daemon/daemon_run_shutdown.go:280-285`);
   `Manager.Clear()` (`manager.go:305`) is not called on stop, and nothing reconciles charon's live SAs
   against the rendered connection set at start.
5. strongSwan is a separate service, so its SAs survive the xpfd restart. Unloading a connection's config
   (the boot `swanctl --load-all`) does not terminate an established child SA, which is why #3941 added
   explicit termination of removed connections.

Present at the report base. The post-base #9511 commits (`0fb50d348`, `20e18fb09`) change re-initiation
attribution and the loaded-generation record; they neither persist the teardown debt nor reconcile SAs at
start.

## Executed evidence

A hermetic Go probe at the pin (one of the three reviewers; `pkg/ipsec`, 7 test executions, all compiled)
models charon reporting live SAs {vpnA, vpnB} while the new configuration renders {vpnA}:

- the same Manager terminates vpnB in every arm: plain removal, #6542 debt retried, #4898 failed-reload
  retry;
- a fresh Manager, modelling a restart, issues zero terminate calls in every arm.

## #9689 — feeds: a hold-interval drop cannot choose its fail direction — an allowlist feed keeps permitting removed addresses, and later commits are not enforced until the feed recovers [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-11)

## What happens

When a dynamic-address feed's `hold-interval` elapses, `recordFailure` drops the feed to empty. Measured by reading the chain at `ff4171851`:

1. `SnapshotForBindings` omits every binding built on the dropped feed (`pkg/feeds/feeds.go`).
2. For an enforced policy that references such a binding, `policies_lower.go` returns the `__unsupported_address__` sentinel.
3. The Rust integrity preflight returns `UnrepresentableAddress` (`userspace-dp/src/policy.rs`) and rejects the **whole** snapshot. The previous-good state stays enforced (fresh boot: default-deny).

That is the #5645 retain-previous-good decision. It has three consequences that no setting lets an operator choose between:

- **An allowlist feed keeps permitting removed addresses.** For a denylist, retaining last-good keeps denying, which is the intent of #5645. For an allowlist (a permit policy), the addresses the feed stopped publishing stay PERMITTED past the operator's explicit `hold-interval`, for as long as the feed stays down.
- **Later commits do not reach the dataplane either.** Every snapshot built while the binding is unresolved carries the same unrepresentable rule, so it is rejected too. The userspace manager's one-shot warning says so ("Edit out the offending application/address and re-commit to restore enforcement"). An unrelated policy or NAT change committed during the outage is accepted by the control plane and not enforced until the feed recovers or the reference is removed.
- **The feed show surface disagrees with enforcement.** `show security dynamic-address` reads the cleared live set while the last-good set is enforced.

The reject is signalled: a Warn from feeds.go, the manager's snapshot-reject warning, and `ProcessStatus` reject reasons (#3261). So this is a design gap, not a silent defect. #9527 corrects the two rationale statements that described it wrongly; it does not change the behaviour.

## Decision needed

- A per-binding fail mode, `retain` (today) versus `drop`. In drop mode, the resolved overlay publishes the EMPTY row rather than omitting the binding, so an allowlist becomes permit-none and a denylist becomes deny-none, as the operator chose, and the rest of the snapshot is not blocked.
- Whether `show security dynamic-address` should show the enforced set alongside the live set.

## Acceptance (if taken)

- A hold-drop fixture asserts the configured mode end to end, for a denylist and an allowlist.
- In drop mode, an unrelated rule committed during the outage is enforced.
- The show surface agrees with the enforced snapshot.
- The #5645, #5282 and #3261 cells stay green.

Refs #9527, #5645, #3261.

## #9690 — test/incus: test-double-failover and test-chained-crash emit no throughput cell for a sub-Gbit iperf3 run, so the ledger records PASS with no throughput_gbps [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-11)

## What is wrong

`make test-double-failover` and `make test-chained-crash` look for a `Gbits` token only when they parse the iperf3

throughput block has a PASS arm (`>= MIN_THROUGHPUT`) and a FAIL arm guarded by `!= "0"`, and no `else`, so

The completion cell still passes on `iperf Done`, and the summary reads `N passed, 0 failed`. The `ha-smoke`
ledger adapter then records a PASS row: its headline is `cells_passed`, and it has no `throughput_gbps`.

had the identical defect (#6897). PR #7431 (`589671a56`) made its verdict total and did not touch these two

3. `test/incus/test-chained-crash.sh:539-540` and `:551-555` have the same parse and the same two-arm block,

4. The completion cell (`test-double-failover.sh:344-351`, `test-chained-crash.sh:542-549`) passes on

5. `test/incus/harness-result.sh:150-203` (`harness_adapt_ha_smoke`) works as follows:

`test-chained-crash`, `test-active-active` and `test-stress-failover`. They therefore measure destination port
5201.

The CoS test fixture classifies 5201 into `iperf-100m`, a `transmit-rate 100m exact` class. It does so on the
output filter of `reth0 unit 80`, which is the path to the loss userspace cluster's `IPERF_TARGET4`. So these gates
measure either capacity or the 100 Mb/s shaper, depending on whether an earlier lane left the CoS fixture applied
on the shared cluster.

With the fixture applied, on a healthy dataplane:

- `test-active-active` fails with "0 Gbps" and `test-stress-failover` fails at about 0.09 Gbps, both against a
  1.0 Gbps floor. Both read as forwarding regressions.
- `test-double-failover` and `test-chained-crash` hit their silent sub-Gbit throughput path and record PASS. That
  path is the companion issue from this review, about the missing throughput cell.

`test-failover.sh` had the same defect (#7673) and now measures the unshaped port 5211. Its siblings were not
changed. The selftest's port-to-class agreement cells read only `test-failover.sh`.

   - `test/incus/test-chained-crash.sh:248`

     `then forwarding-class iperf-100m`.

## #9692 — test/incus: test-ha-crash kills the established iperf3 streams of its hard-stop and daemon-stop phases unobserved, so the mandated HA crash gate cannot fail when established flows die [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-11)

## What is wrong

`docs/engineering-style.md:296` makes `make test-failover` plus `make test-ha-crash` the required gates for HA,
VRRP, session-sync and fabric changes. The pass criterion is "0 / very low packet loss across failover/failback".

`test-ha-crash` never measures that criterion. Phase 1 (hard VM stop) and phase 2 (`systemctl stop xpfd`, the #68
fail-closed path) each start a 4-stream, 120 s iperf3 client through the primary. After the takeover they assert
only three things: the takeover time, a new TCP connection and a ping. Then they `pkill -9 iperf3`. In phase 1 the
kill carries the comment "sessions are dead — fw0 hard-crashed". No phase measures loss, established-stream
survival or throughput recovery.

Two kinds of regression therefore pass the mandated gate, as long as new connections work:

- the survivor loses or refuses the synced sessions at takeover;
- the stopping node's teardown breaks established flows.

## Mechanism, at `a21c23ac70d02cc156ba898ff51855c1b8cd4bec`

1. Phase 1, `test/incus/test-ha-crash.sh:273-321`:
   - the client starts at `:276`;
   - `incus stop --force "$FW0"` runs at `:299`;
   - the takeover cell is `:302-307`, `test_new_tcp` is `:310` and the ping cell is `:313-317`;
   - the client is then killed at `:319-320`:
   ```sh
   # Kill iperf3 from phase 1 (sessions are dead — fw0 hard-crashed)
   incus exec "$CLUSTER_LAN_HOST" -- pkill -9 iperf3 2>/dev/null || true
   ```
2. Phase 2, `test/incus/test-ha-crash.sh:386-429`:
   - the client starts at `:394`, and a `pgrep` cell (`:397-403`) confirms only that it started;
   - `systemctl stop xpfd` runs on fw0 at `:407`;
   - the takeover cell is `:410-415`, `test_new_tcp` is `:418` and the ping cell is `:421-425`;
   - `pkill -9 iperf3` runs at `:427-428`.
3. The header (`:4-28`) scopes the checks to takeover, new TCP connections and recovery.
4. #73, the issue that asked for this gate, required "existing stream survival/recovery behavior" and
   "sustained throughput recovery" for both a hard-stop and a daemon-stop scenario
   (`docs/issues/issue-history.md:1636-1666`).
5. Two siblings do observe established flows:
   - `test/incus/test-chained-crash.sh:327-332`: a `pgrep` cell, "iperf3 survived fw0 hard-reset".
   - `test/incus/test-stress-failover.sh:268-281`: a budget of zero-throughput intervals over the iperf3 log.

## #9693 — [cohort] daemon: a failed next-table/rib-group/PBR ip-rule reconcile or route-leak snapshot republish has no re-assert owner, so stale cross-VRF policy persists until an unrelated apply [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-11)

**[cohort]** One re-assert owner is missing for two deferred apply-tail errors from the same routing step. Both are
Low. They are grouped because one debt record and one idempotent retry close them together.

## What is wrong

Every config apply first reconciles the kernel policy-routing rules: next-table, rib-group and firewall-filter PBR.
It then republishes the userspace route snapshot from that kernel state. #5844 and #5696 made failures in those two
steps visible, as deferred errors joined into the commit result. Nothing retries them.

A transient failure therefore leaves stale or missing cross-VRF rules in the kernel, plus a userspace FIB rebuilt
from that partial state. Both persist until some later, unrelated apply re-runs the reconcile. The code says so:
"This commit-tail reconcile has no dirty-retry engine".

On the applies nobody waits on (boot, DHCP lease callback, feed, config-poll), the joined error is only logged at
Warn.

   runs every rule type. Its comment says "a partial clear/add leaves stale-or-missing cross-VRF policy in the
   kernel", and that the following snapshot reconcile "canonizes that partial live kernel state". The next-table
   error is collected at `:250-253` and the PBR error at `:330-333`; the joined error is returned at `:339`.

   - `:520`: `routeLeakErr := d.reconcileRouteLeakSnapshot(cfg, commitOverlay)`;
   - `:542`: both go into `applyTailReconciles`, which joins them into the commit error
     (`pkg/daemon/daemon_apply_tail.go:495`).
3. `pkg/daemon/daemon_apply_routing.go` records the missing retry itself:
   - `:366-371`: "This commit-tail reconcile has no dirty-retry engine";
   - `:383-393`: the republish-failure arm contrasts itself with "the ip-monitoring actuator", which has a retry
     engine, and logs that "the userspace FIB may retain a stale inter-VRF leak until the next apply";
   - `:409-412`: the FIB-generation bump arm says "With no retry owner for this commit-tail path".
4. Outside tests, a search for `routingRuleErr` and `routeLeakErr` in `pkg/daemon` finds only the capture sites,

## #9694 — userspace-dp: the policy-tuple comment says static DNAT preserves the L4 port, but a port-mapped static rule rewrites it and policy matching uses the translated port [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-11)

## What is wrong

A comment above the session-miss policy tuple in `poll_descriptor/mod.rs` says static DNAT and NPTv6 preserve the L4
port, so policy matching sees the original port for them. That is false for a static rule with a mapped port. The
static-NAT lookup sets `rewrite_dst_port` from the rule's `mapped_port`, and the policy tuple reads that rewrite.

Runtime behaviour is correct; only the prose is wrong. The comment sits beside NAT and policy key derivation, the
class where a wrong reading of pre- versus post-DNAT ports has already caused real defects (#9388, #9403). A reader
who trusts this comment derives the wrong destination port for port-mapped static DNAT.

## Evidence, at `a21c23ac70d02cc156ba898ff51855c1b8cd4bec`

1. `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/poll_descriptor/mod.rs:1618-1621`:
   "Only port-based DNAT carries a destination-port rewrite; static-DNAT and NPTv6 preserve the L4 port, so the
   original port flows through for those."
2. `userspace-dp/src/nat/static_nat.rs:662-667`, the static-DNAT decision:
   ```rust
   NatDecision {
       rewrite_src: None,
       rewrite_dst: Some(entry.internal_ip),
       rewrite_dst_port: entry.mapped_port,
       ..NatDecision::default()
   },
   ```
3. `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/poll_descriptor/mod.rs:1646-1649`:
   `policy_dst_port = pre_routing_dnat.as_ref().and_then(|d| d.rewrite_dst_port).unwrap_or(flow.forward_key.dst_port)`.
   So policy matching uses the translated port when a static rule maps one, and the original port only when it does
   not. Whole-address static rules and NPTv6 do keep the port.

The same comment is at `:1526-1528` at the report base `5fafce23f`. Six post-base commits to the file (`2ee1de302`,
`e4cc769e9`, `df8c7588c`, `31614ea12`, `a943235ec`, `704fc7d69`) left it unchanged.

## Consequence (bounded)

This is documentation only; there is no forwarding or policy defect. The cost is a wrong premise for the next change
to NAT or policy key derivation around this site.

I checked #9388 and #9403, both closed, which are pre/post-DNAT port-key defects nearby. Neither changed this

## #9695 — [cohort] afxdp docs: the UMEM README says every XDP_PASS became a cpumap redirect, and two texts still assert the refuted mlx5 fill-starvation NAPI fallback [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-11)

**[cohort]** At the verification revision, three documentation statements about AF_XDP zero-copy behaviour on mlx5
contradict the source. One of them is the "mitigation stands either way" reassurance attached to the unverified #9043
premise. All three are Low. They are grouped because they cover one subject: what happens to an mlx5 zero-copy frame
on `XDP_PASS` or on fill-ring starvation. They rest on the same primary sources and need one documentation change.

This issue does **not** say whether the #9043 premise is true, that is, whether `XDP_PASS` permanently consumes a
zero-copy UMEM frame. That question is still unmeasured, and the section "Open validation item" below names it as an
open item, not as the defect.

## What is wrong, at `a21c23ac70d02cc156ba898ff51855c1b8cd4bec`

1. `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/umem/README.md:82-88` says: "The mitigation (#209), which stands either way: the XDP shim
   replaces every `XDP_PASS` path with a cpumap redirect (`USERSPACE_CPUMAP`), which frees the XSK frame immediately
   ..."

   The shim at the same revision keeps two direct `XDP_PASS` paths:
   - `userspace-xdp/src/lib.rs:484-486` sends every non-IP frame to `pass_non_ip_l2_direct()` (`:1289-1294`). That
     function returns `XDP_PASS` on purpose, because "cpumap redirect breaks ARP neighbor resolution".
   - `cpumap_or_pass` (`:1405-1415`) returns `XDP_PASS` whenever the cpumap control flag is unset or the redirect
     fails.

   So "stands either way" does not hold for the non-IP arm. That arm is the unrate-limited ARP/LLDP path #9043 was
   worried about.
2. `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/worker/lifecycle.rs:117-119` says: "Without this, fill ring starvation causes mlx5 to fall
   back to non-XSK NAPI, leaking packets to the kernel."
3. `docs/afxdp-packet-processing.md:330-334` says: "When no fill ring frames are available, mlx5 falls back to the
   regular (non-XSK) NAPI RX path. These leaked packets bypass AF_XDP entirely and reach the kernel TCP stack via VLAN
   sub-interfaces ..."

Items 2 and 3 contradict the tree's own later comment at `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/tx/rings.rs:180-182`: "Without
this, mlx5 increments rx_xsk_buff_alloc_err and silently drops all incoming packets". They also contradict upstream
Linux v6.18 mlx5e, which the product's kernel floor requires (`scripts/dist/install.sh:132`, "kernel >= 6.18"):

- `drivers/net/ethernet/mellanox/mlx5/core/en/rx_res.c`, `mlx5e_rx_res_xsk_update()`, points the channel's RSS and
  direct RQT at the XSK RQ while XSK is enabled. It selects the regular RQ only on disable (called from

## #9696 — userspace: the Go neighbor-replace ACK check cannot recognise a #6034 fence, so a fenced replace is recorded as applied [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-14)

**Severity: LOW** (latent). Pre-existing #6034 code. Found by the Codex round-6 review of #9173.

## Defect

The Go manager cannot recognise a fenced `update_neighbors` replace, so if a fence ever happens, it records a neighbor table the helper rejected.

- Rust: `apply_manager_neighbors` (`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/coordinator/mod.rs:694`, at `0b077cc6a`) fences a replace when `generation != 0 && generation <= applied_manager_generation` and returns false without touching the table. The ACK the handler then returns is `last_applied_manager_neighbor_generation()`, which is **>= the fenced generation**.
- Go: both senders treat the replace as fenced only when `status.ManagerNeighborGeneration != 0 && status.ManagerNeighborGeneration < gen`:
  - `RegenerateNeighborSnapshot`, `pkg/dataplane/userspace/manager_neighbor.go:123`;
  - `BumpFIBGeneration`, `pkg/dataplane/userspace/manager_generation.go:100`.

  A fence returns ACK >= gen, so that branch never fires on one. Go falls through to the success path: it writes `lastSnapshot.Neighbors = newNeighbors` and rebuilds the index. After that the regeneration diff sees no change and never re-sends, so the helper keeps the old table until the next neighbor change or a full apply.

## Reachability

A fence needs a Go generation at or below the helper's applied generation. `seedNeighborReplaceGenerationLocked` raises Go's counter from the helper's ACK (status tick and Compile), which normally keeps Go ahead, so this is latent rather than live. The exposure is any send that precedes seeding, for example a daemon restart while the helper keeps its state and its generation. The code comment ("a value below `gen` means it fenced the replace as stale") describes the opposite of what the helper returns.

## Fix direction

- Treat any nonzero ACK other than the generation just sent as unacknowledged: an ACK above `gen` means the helper is ahead and fenced this send.
- Seed `neighborReplaceGen` from that ACK before the retry.
- Add a cell with a helper ACK above the sent generation (for example 100 against 2) at both senders.

Not queued in lane-low-sweep; for lane-dataplane.

## #9697 — test: TestSessionSocketNamesTheResponseCap9322 fails with an i/o timeout under load: the 64 MiB oversize reply races the session socket's round-trip deadline [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-11)

**Severity: LOW** (test-only flake under load). Found while landing #9359, whose change is test-only in `pkg/daemon`.

## Observed

`make test` on branch `fix/9359-syslog-cells-loopback` (base `0b077cc6a`), with the host at load average ~38 from two mutation matrices and a review job:

```
--- FAIL: TestSessionSocketNamesTheResponseCap9322 (3.55s)
    response_cap_diagnostic_9322_test.go:181: the over-cap error does not name the cap.
         got: session helper unreachable: read session response: read unix @->/tmp/x9322.../userspace-dp-sessions.sock: i/o timeout
        want a message containing "control-response cap"
```

In isolation on the same tree, `go test ./pkg/dataplane/userspace/ -run '^TestSessionSocketNamesTheResponseCap9322$' -count=10` passes 10 of 10, each run 0.44–0.57 s.

## Why it is load-sensitive

- `oversizeReply9322` streams more than the cap in 4 MiB writes (`MaxControlResponseBytes/len(chunk) + 2` chunks). The cap is `const MaxControlResponseBytes = MaxControlRequestBytes`.
- The session socket is read under a fixed round-trip deadline: `requestSessionSyncLocked` in `process_control.go` sets `conn.SetDeadline(time.Now().Add(sessionSyncRoundtripDeadline))`, with `sessionSyncRoundtripDeadline = 400 * time.Millisecond`.
- The client has to receive and decode about 64 MiB of JSON before it reaches the cap. On a loaded box that takes longer than the deadline, so the cell reports the deadline instead of the cap.

That turns a cell meant to pin the cap message into a timing test. Under enough load it fails for the wrong reason, which is exactly the kind of red that trains people to re-run instead of read.

## Fix direction

Make the cell independent of the deadline, and keep asserting the cap message:
- give the cell a test-only lower cap, or a deadline seam;
- or size the oversize reply to just cross the cap.

The control-socket and boot-probe siblings in the same file stream the same reply and should be checked for the same exposure.

Not queued in lane-low-sweep.

## #9698 — userspace: the helper-status binding index multiplies the helper-supplied ifindex in uint32 before the cap check, so an ifindex of 2^28 or more wraps past the guard onto another interface's row [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-11)

## What is wrong

The Go manager computes the composed `userspace_bindings` index as
`uint32(binding.Ifindex)*bindingQueuesPerIface + binding.QueueID`, with `Ifindex` taken from helper status. It checks
that index against the dense cap only **after** the multiply. The ifindex has a lower bound (`<= 0` is skipped) but
no upper bound. With a stride of 16, an ifindex of 2^28 or more wraps the `uint32` product, so the wrapped index lands
inside the cap and writes, or later repairs, the row of a different (ifindex, queue).

The queue and slot dimensions each have an explicit fail-closed guard (#4894, #7497) because helper numbers are not
trusted. The ifindex dimension is the one left to the post-multiply cap check (#814), and a wrap defeats that check.

2. `pkg/dataplane/userspace/helper_status_apply.go` computes and checks the index in this order:
   - `:484` skips `Ifindex <= 0`;
   - `:508` bounds the queue (#4894);
   - `:514` computes `idx := uint32(binding.Ifindex)*bindingQueuesPerIface + binding.QueueID`;
   - `:520` checks `if idx >= dataplane.BindingArrayMaxEntries` (#814);
   - `:530` bounds the slot and `:538` rejects a duplicate composed index.

   (repair-only, log-and-skip).
4. `pkg/dataplane/constants.go:34`: `BindingArrayMaxEntries = MaxInterfaces * BindingQueuesPerIface`.
5. `userspace-xdp/src/binding_index.rs:41-58`: the Rust side's module doc names the same range, ifindexes at or above
   2^28 where the multiply overflows `u32`.

Present at the report base; no post-base commit changes these lines.

One of the three reviewers ran a hermetic Go cell at the verification revision:

- Control: `Ifindex = 65536` was refused with the cap error, and nothing was written.

## #9699 — [cohort] userspace: the owner-RG session exporters return collected deltas together with a status-apply error, contrary to the one-complete-window-or-error contract the #5085 receiver relies on [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-11)

**[cohort]** One export contract is broken at three Manager return sites and one runtime passthrough. All are Low.
They are grouped because a single all-or-error rule and one test shape close them together.

## What is wrong

The owner-RG export produces the bulk window that the peer reconciles authoritatively (#5085): any session missing
from a completed window is deleted on the peer. The exporter's documented contract is therefore "one complete window
or an error — never a partial one".

Three Manager return sites break that contract. When the request succeeds but applying the helper status that comes
back with it fails, they return the deltas collected so far **together with** the error. The runtime passthrough
then wraps those partial deltas into a snapshot and returns it with the error.

Both production callers at the verification revision discard the deltas whenever an error comes back. So no receiver
is fed a partial window today; the defect is the API shape.

## Mechanism, at `a21c23ac70d02cc156ba898ff51855c1b8cd4bec`

1. The contract is stated in two places:
   - `pkg/dataplane/userspace/owner_rg_export_paging_9344.go:74-79`, for `ErrOwnerRGExportUnterminated`: "It is a
     FAILURE, never a partial answer: #5085's receiver reconciles authoritatively against the delimited window and
     deletes every eligible session missing from it".
   - `pkg/daemon/daemon_ha_userspace_export.go:99-106`: "It returns ONE COMPLETE window or an error — never a partial
     one."
2. `owner_rg_export_paging_9344.go:91`, `ExportOwnerRGSessionsPaged`, has three exits:
   - a request failure returns nil deltas (`:123-124`);
   - the unterminated arm returns nil deltas (`:137`);
   - but after a page has been appended, a failed `applyHelperStatusLocked` returns `all, status, err`
     (`:129-130`).
3. The unpaged fallback, `exportOwnerRGSessionsUnpagedLocked` (`:144`), returns `resp.SessionDeltas, status, err` at
   `:159`.
4. `pkg/dataplane/userspace/manager_status.go:336`, `ExportOwnerRGSessions`, returns `resp.SessionDeltas, status, err`
   at `:357`.
5. `pkg/dataplane/userspace/runtime_delta.go:24-29`: the runtime passthrough returns
   `runtimeSessionDeltaSnapshot(deltas, status, max), err` at `:27`.
6. Consumers:
   - `daemon_ha_userspace_export.go:67-70` returns `0, err`, and `:126-129` returns an empty `BulkSnapshot`.
   - A non-test census of `pkg/` and `cmd/` finds nothing else that uses the export output. `ExportOwnerRGSessions`
     appears only in the runtime interface declaration (`pkg/dataplane/runtime/session_delta.go:83`) and in two

## #9712 — userspace-dp: after a backward clock step the SYN-cookie epoch latch either breaks HA cross-node validation (today) or, if it follows the clock, resurrects old cookies — pick a rollback policy [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-11)

**Severity: LOW.** Pre-existing: the latch has been non-decreasing since the userspace SYN-cookie wiring, 4c26c6a65. This needs a design decision rather than a mechanical fix, because the two obvious behaviours each fail a property. Both properties were raised in the #9173 hostile review (Codex rounds 8 and 9); #9173 keeps the original behaviour and leaves the trade-off here.

## Behaviour today

`ScreenState::current_syn_cookie_full_epoch` (`userspace-dp/src/screen/mod.rs:631` at `2c29dc14f`) latches the cookie epoch non-decreasing: `self.syn_cookie_last_full_epoch = self.syn_cookie_last_full_epoch.max(epoch)`. A validator accepts a cookie only within one epoch of its own current epoch (`SynCookieCodec::candidate_validation_epochs`: current−1, current, current+1; one epoch is 64 s).

## The trade-off

- **Keep the latch (today).** A node whose wall clock steps BACKWARD by more than one epoch keeps minting at its latched epoch until the clock catches up. An HA peer on the correct clock cannot reconstruct those cookie epochs, so a SYN-cookie handshake that straddles a failover to that peer is refused for the length of the step. The node's own cookies still validate locally, and no cookie from an epoch it has already left validates again.
- **Follow the clock back** (tried in #9173 round 8, reverted in round 9). The node rebases onto the stepped-back epoch, so a peer on that clock validates its cookies. But it RE-ACCEPTS cookies from epochs it had already left. A recorded ACK for a cookie minted before the node's clock moved forward validates again and re-installs its 64-second source-scoped whitelist entry. The active path does not rate-limit validation, and the standby limiter needs only one token per replayed cookie. If the backward step is itself the fault (the clock went into the past), the rebase breaks cross-node validation AND opens the replay window.

A node cannot tell locally whether its latched epoch or its new wall reading is the correct one.

## Options

1. **Keep the latch** and document the cross-node gap under a clock fault. HA already assumes node clocks agree to well within 64 s.
2. **Fail closed during a rollback**: refuse to mint and validate while the wall epoch is more than one below the latch. No replay and no unverifiable cookies, but SYN-cookie service stops for the length of the step.
3. **Peer-coordinated rollback generation**: mix a generation into the key derivation and bump it on a detected rollback, so pre-rollback cookies cannot validate. Both nodes must agree on the generation, which means control-plane coordination.

## Acceptance

Whichever option is chosen:
- a regression cell for the replay property (a cookie from an epoch the node already left does not validate after a backward step);
- a regression cell for the cross-node property under the chosen behaviour;
- the choice recorded in `docs/syn-cookie-flood-protection.md`.

Not queued in lane-low-sweep.

## #9714 — userspace-dp/HA: under dual primary, a peer session delete removes the kernel, DNAT and shared rows and every sibling worker's replica of a live local session; only the owning worker's entry is protected [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-14)

## What is wrong

Suppose both nodes are primary for the same redundancy group, a dual-primary split. A session-sync delete then
arrives from the peer for a flow this node is also forwarding locally. The helper handles it on its generation-zero
delete path. That path checks only generation recency before it deletes:

- the process-wide kernel session-map row;
- the DNAT steering row;
- the shared forward and reverse rows.

It then pushes `DeleteSynced` for the key and its reverse to every worker.

The #9048 refusal protects only the owning worker's local-origin entry. Sibling workers hold `WorkerLocalImport`
replicas of that local session, and `WorkerLocalImport` counts as peer-synced, so every sibling drops its replica.
No path re-creates the shared row for a session the owner still holds. The install direction has the same gap: it
publishes shared state before the worker's ownership refusal applies.

   - it removes the kernel session-map row (`:757-766`), the `dnat_table` row (`:776-785`) and the shared forward and
     reverse rows (`:787-809`);
   - `:847-857` pushes `DeleteSynced` for the key and its reverse to every registered worker's queue.
2. `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/session_glue/commands/delete_synced.rs:77-84`: the worker refuses only an entry that is
   not peer-synced and whose owner RG is locally active (#9048).
3. `userspace-dp/src/session/entry.rs:431-437`: `is_peer_synced()` is true for `WorkerLocalImport`. When a worker
   materializes a shared hit on a local entry, it gets `WorkerLocalImport` (`session_glue/mod.rs:1718-1745`).
4. `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/ha/export.rs:~140-160`: bulk export reads only the shared map and skips peer-synced
   origins.
5. Install direction:

   - `:628-638` gates only the BPF publish on `synced_entry_allows_local_replace`;

## #9715 — cluster: each fabric connection applies session-sync installs and deletes on its own receive loop with generation admission and the dataplane write in separate critical sections, so an older operation can overtake a newer one when the stream moves [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-11)

## What is wrong

`SessionSync` starts an independent `receiveLoop` for every installed fabric connection. Session installs and deletes
are applied by whichever loop reads them, with no per-key serialization across loops. The #2198 guard design assumes
a single-threaded apply (the "F3" note). At the verification revision, generation admission and the dataplane
mutation are separate operations:

- An install's guard and its generation record are separate `recvGenMu` sections, with the dataplane write between
  them.
- A delete's guard and tombstone run under the lock, but the dataplane delete runs after the lock is released.

When the sync stream moves between fabrics, through a fabric flap or a #9508 preferred-fabric switch, the old loop can
still be applying frames it has already read while the new loop applies newer frames for the same key.

1. `pkg/cluster/sync_conn.go:505-512`: each installed connection starts its own `receiveLoop`.

   - `:~168-184`: `syncMsgDeleteV4` calls `deleteClusterSyncedV4`.
3. In `pkg/cluster/sync_conn_gen.go`:
   - `installGenGuardV4` (`:292-305`) is a single `recvGenMu` section; the generation record is written in a later
     section, after the dataplane store.
   - `deleteClusterSyncedV4` (`:~683-697`) calls `deleteGenGuardV4`, which checks and tombstones under `recvGenMu`.
     It then calls `s.sessions.DeleteWithCompanionsV4(key, ...)` after the lock is released.
   - `:480-496`: the F3 note still asserts that no two installs or deletes for one key are applied concurrently.
4. The userspace helper's delete request carries generation 0
   (`pkg/dataplane/userspace/manager_sessionsync_request.go:105`). The helper therefore cannot re-check a stale
   delete that has already passed the Go guard.

Present at the report base. #9508 (post-base) adds a full re-prime on every stream move, which widens same-key

## #9716 — cluster: an unincarnated BulkEnd or between-bulks BulkStart still completes or restarts a bulk on epoch alone, so a delayed marker from a dead peer process can reconcile against a partial table and release the sync hold early [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-11)

## What is wrong

Since #5084 and #9174, bulk markers carry the peer's boot incarnation, and a `BulkEnd` or `BulkStart` from a retired
incarnation is refused. Both checks deliberately fail open when either side has no incarnation, to keep rolling
upgrades working. That happens when a peer on an older build sends the short form, or when a bulk was primed without
an incarnation.

In that case completion is matched on the epoch alone. Epochs restart at 1 in every process, so collisions are
routine. A delayed `BulkEnd` read from a dead peer process's still-established connection can therefore complete the
current bulk, while the replacement's live bulk is still arriving. The receiver then:

- reconciles stale sessions against a partly received set;
- latches `bulkEverCompleted`;
- releases the VRRP sync hold.

Nothing records that a completion was matched on epoch alone, and no version gate excludes a peer without an
incarnation.

## Mechanism, at `a21c23ac70d02cc156ba898ff51855c1b8cd4bec`

1. `pkg/cluster/sync_conn_read.go:395-420`: the `BulkEnd` arm drops the marker only when both incarnations are known
   and differ ("FAIL OPEN on either side being un-incarnated, which is a decision and not a default"). Otherwise it
   runs `reconcileStaleSessions()`, sends the ACK, stores `bulkEverCompleted` and fires `OnBulkSyncReceived`
   (`:~420-428`).
2. `pkg/cluster/sync_bulk.go:618` `bulkStartStaleLocked`: its doc says the between-bulks stale arm "REQUIRES AN
   INCARNATION ON THE FRAME".
3. `pkg/cluster/sync_boot_incarnation.go:~213-216`: a prime without an incarnation records nothing; it only counts
   `BulkPrimesWithoutIncarnation`.
4. `pkg/cluster/sync_conn_read.go:~337-344`: a stale-incarnation connection is evicted only when
   `switched && priorInc.known()`. That misses the upgrade edge from a process without an incarnation to one with
   an incarnation.
5. `pkg/cluster/sync_wire_version_7990.go:~80-86`: `peerVersion == 0` is permitted, so a pre-#7990 peer is admitted
   during rolling upgrades.
6. `pkg/cluster/sync_bulk_gaps_9174_test.go:168,186,373` pin the fail-open arms as intended behaviour.

- a marker without an incarnation, either from a peer build that predates #5084 during the first rolling upgrade or

## #9717 — cluster: after live keying, a session-sync stream admitted before the key stays unauthenticated unless the default-off strict-session-auth is set, while the status line says unauthenticated frames are rejected [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-11)

## What is wrong

A cluster that was running without `chassis cluster authentication-key` keeps booting (lenient load and peer sync)
and is keyed live by committing the key. #6628's in-place upgrade authenticates an established session-sync
connection whose peer answers. A connection whose peer stays silent looks exactly like a legitimate peer that is not
keyed yet, so it is kept unauthenticated for its lifetime. #7441 added eviction for that case, but only behind the
opt-in `set chassis cluster strict-session-auth`, which is off by default.

No operator surface shows whether an established session-sync connection has authenticated. The one
authentication line, `controlLinkAuthStatus`, reads "engaged (peer authenticated; unauthenticated frames rejected)"
from heartbeat evidence alone. The README and the function's comment do scope that line to heartbeat/fabric
(`pkg/cluster/README.md:2549-2555`). Even so, the status output itself gives no indication that a pre-key
session-sync stream may still be accepted without HMAC.

## Mechanism, at `a21c23ac70d02cc156ba898ff51855c1b8cd4bec`

1. `pkg/cluster/sync_auth.go:~363-387`: "A hostile stream admitted before the commit declines the upgrade by staying
   silent ... that residual is OPEN". The comment predates #7441 and does not mention it.
2. `pkg/cluster/sync_auth_strict_7441.go` evicts an established, never-authenticated connection after
   `strictSessionAuthGrace` (`:98`, 10 s). The posture is published by `SetStrictSessionAuth` (`:114`).
3. `pkg/config/compiler_system.go:2802-2806`: `StrictSessionAuth` is set only when the `strict-session-auth` leaf is
   present.
4. `pkg/cluster/status.go:716-744`, `controlLinkAuthStatus`: when a key is configured and `HeartbeatPeerAuthSeen()`
   is true, it returns "engaged (peer authenticated; unauthenticated frames rejected)". The comment above it says:
   "It does NOT track the session-sync channel ... it does not tell you whether an existing session-sync connection
   predates the key."
5. `pkg/config/compiler_validate_strict_cluster_auth.go:8-30` (#6611) makes strict commit reject an unkeyed cluster.
   Lenient load and peer sync still keep a legacy unkeyed cluster running. `pkg/cluster/README.md:2496-2507`
   documents the residual and names `strict-session-auth` as the way to close it.

## Reachability (bounded)

Every one of these must hold:

- the cluster was loaded unkeyed (legacy persisted config or peer sync);
- an attacker had control-segment connectivity and established a session-sync stream before the key commit;
- the operator neither sets `strict-session-auth` nor restarts the node.

A new cluster cannot strictly commit without a key.

- publishes to the shared map;
- pushes no worker command;
- is absent from the replay.

## #9719 — cluster: session-sync generation tombstones are never evicted on a long-lived connection, so after 200 000 closed sessions the receiver stops recording new keys and the #2170/#2221 ordering guards are off for every new session until the next bulk [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-11)

## What is wrong

The receiver's generation maps record each install's generation. Since #2221, every non-zero delete records a
TOMBSTONE, so an ordinary delete never frees an entry. Entries leave the map in only three ways: a generation-0
delete, the whole-map reset on an accepted `BulkStart`, or construction.

`putGenBounded` stops recording NEW keys once a map holds `genGuardMapCap` (200 000) entries. A busy, long-lived sync
connection therefore fills the receiver map with tombstones of closed sessions. After that, no new key's install or
delete is recorded, and the #2170/#2221 install/delete ordering guards do nothing for every new session until the
next bulk.

The sender echo map has a matching arm. Above 200 000 live stamped keys, a new install is not stamped, so its later
delete is sent with generation 0, which the receiver applies unconditionally.

## Mechanism, at `a21c23ac70d02cc156ba898ff51855c1b8cd4bec`

1. `pkg/cluster/sync_conn_gen.go:24-58`: `genGuardMapCap = 200000`. `putGenBounded` updates existing keys and skips
   new keys at the cap. The comment "Both are evicted on delete; the cap is a safety valve for keys whose delete never
   arrives" (`:24-27`) is true only for the sender echo maps (`delete(s.genSentV4, key)` at `:234,247`).
2. `pkg/cluster/sync_conn_gen.go:~372-392`, `deleteGenGuardV4`: a non-zero delete records a tombstone. Only
   `deleteGen == 0` removes the entry (`delete(s.recvGenV4, key)` at `:386`, and `:406` for v6).
3. The whole-map reset `resetRecvGen` has one production caller, the accepted `BulkStart`
   (`pkg/cluster/sync_conn_read.go:293`).
4. Sender arm:
   - `takeDeleteGenV4`/`V6` return 0 for a key with no `genSentV4` stamp (`sync_conn_gen.go:225-249`);
   - `stampInstallGenV4` records through `putGenBounded`;
   - `DEFAULT_MAX_SESSIONS = 131072` per worker (`userspace-dp/src/session/mod.rs:83`), so two workers already exceed
     the cap.

Present at the report base; no post-base change to the cap or tombstone handling.

## Executed evidence

One of the three reviewers ran a Go cell at the verification revision:

- Churn: 200 000 install+close cycles on one connection, with no `BulkStart`.
- State after churn: the receiver map held 200 000 entries while 0 sessions were live.
- Result: a new live key was not recorded, and a delete older than its install removed it.
- No-churn control: the same delete was refused.

## #9720 — [cohort] userspace-dp/HA: RG-transition worker commands dropped at a full worker queue are never re-driven, leaving stale worker-local origin, kernel-row and CoS-slot state [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-16)

**[cohort]** One queue policy loses three RG-transition commands: `DemoteOwnerRGS`, `VacateAllSharedExactSlots` and
`RefreshOwnerRGS`. All three are Low. They are grouped because one non-droppable path, or one per-worker transition
debt, closes them together.

## What is wrong

`update_ha_state` bumps the RG epochs and stores the new RG runtime. It then pushes the transition commands to each
worker with `push_bounded`, and ignores the `false` return when a queue is at capacity. Later calls compare against
the stored state, so a dropped command is never re-driven. The only signal is the global
`WORKER_COMMAND_QUEUE_DROPS` counter.

Forwarding converges regardless, through the epoch bump, per-hit HA re-resolution and fabric redirect. The affected
worker, however, keeps stale local origin, skips its kernel-row republish and keeps a stale CoS V_min slot. That lasts
until the next transition, expiry or an incidental republish.

## Mechanism, at `a21c23ac70d02cc156ba898ff51855c1b8cd4bec`

1. `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/ha/state.rs:55-72`: the epochs are bumped and the runtime is stored before the commands
   fan out.
2. The returns from the fan-out are ignored:
   - `ha/state.rs:85-95`: `push_bounded(... DemoteOwnerRGS ...)` and `push_bounded(... VacateAllSharedExactSlots)`.
   - `:149`: `RefreshOwnerRGS` is pushed the same way.
3. `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/worker_queue.rs:104-110`: at `MAX_PENDING_WORKER_COMMANDS`, `push_bounded` increments
   `WORKER_COMMAND_QUEUE_DROPS` and returns `false`.
4. What makes forwarding converge:
   - `afxdp/flow_cache.rs:1008-1018` evicts cache entries whose epoch changed;
   - `afxdp/forwarding/ha.rs:153-177` re-validates cached decisions;
   - `session/expire.rs:592-610` self-heals the standby.

Present at the report base. #9517 touched `ha/state.rs` post-base; no retry was added.

## Consequence (bounded; as traced by the reviewers)

- The worker-local origin is not flipped, so on that worker the entry is aged rather than held.
- The worker's kernel-row republish is skipped. The shim still steers to XSK, and every hit re-resolves HA state.
- The CoS V_min slot stays stale-low until the worker publishes again. The hard-cap suspension bounds the throttling.
- If `RefreshOwnerRGS` is dropped, the coordinator's prewarm and BPF republish still run.
- No forwarding, ownership or failover-correctness failure was found.

## #9721 — vrrp: in legacy no-private-rg-election mode, a vlan-tagging RETH whose addressed unit has no vlan-id binds its VRRP instance to the base member, which has no IPv4 source, so that RG sends no IPv4 adverts [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-11)

## What is wrong

The report claimed that VRRP-backed RETH members have no non-VIP IPv4 source. For ordinary shapes that claim is
refuted. Every VRRP-backed RETH member, and every sub-interface with a `vlan-id`, gets a `169.254.<RG>.<node+1>/32`
base address. The default private-RG election runs no RETH VRRP at all.

One shape that commit accepts is still affected: a RETH with `vlan-tagging` and an address on a unit that has no
`vlan-id`.

- `CollectRethInstances` binds the VRRP instance to the base member.
- The VLAN-parent render gives the base member no address, and renders sub-interfaces only for units that have a
  `vlan-id`.
- So the base member has no non-VIP IPv4, `resolveLocalIPv4` returns nil, and no IPv4 advertisement is sent.
- The unit's addresses are also never rendered, so this shape is broken beyond VRRP.

## Mechanism, at `a21c23ac70d02cc156ba898ff51855c1b8cd4bec`

1. `pkg/vrrp/vrrp.go:222-239`: when `ifc.VlanTagging` is set, each addressed unit gets an instance on
   `subIface := linuxName`. That name becomes `linuxName.<vlan>` only when `unit.VlanID > 0`.
2. `pkg/dataplane/compiler_iface.go`:
   - `:1314-1328` renders a VLAN parent with no addresses;
   - `:1330-1340` emits sub-interfaces, carrying the 169.254 base for a VRRP-backed RETH, only for `unit.VlanID > 0`.
3. `pkg/vrrp/instance_addr.go:100-124`: `resolveLocalIPv4` skips VIPs and returns nil when no non-VIP IPv4 exists.
   `pkg/vrrp/instance_send.go:139-153` then returns before sending.
4. The default rules this out:
   - `PrivateRGElection = true` (`pkg/config/compiler_system.go:2879-2883`);
   - `CollectRethInstances` returns no instances in that mode (`pkg/vrrp/vrrp.go:141-143`).

The code is the same at the report base and the verification revision.

## Executed evidence

One of the three reviewers ran strict `CompileConfig` with `no-private-rg-election` on
`reth0 vlan-tagging; reth0 unit 0 family inet address 172.16.50.8/24`:

- The config is accepted, with only an unrelated NTP warning.
- `CollectRethInstances` binds the instance to the base member `ge-0-0-2`.
- Control: `unit 50 vlan-id 50` binds to `ge-0-0-2.50`.

## #9722 — cluster: every config apply on an HA node restarts the heartbeat receiver and re-arms its 30 s startup grace, so a peer that dies within 30 s after a commit is declared lost up to 30 s late [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-11)

## What is wrong

On a chassis-cluster node that has any management interface (`fxp*`, `fab*`, `em*`, which is every reference HA
configuration), each config apply rebinds the management VRF and then calls `RestartHeartbeat`. That call replaces
the heartbeat receiver. The new receiver's `start()` resets `startedAt`. `checkTimeout` then suppresses peer loss for
`heartbeatStartupGrace` (30 s) after that reset. The suppression also covers a peer that **was** seen and then went
silent. The restart carries over the previous receiver's `lastSeen`, but not its start time.

So for 30 s after every operator commit, and after the peer-synced apply on the other node, a node cannot declare
its peer lost. In the default private-RG election mode, heartbeat loss is what promotes the surviving node. A
primary that crashes or wedges inside that window is taken over up to 30 s late, instead of after the configured
interval × threshold.

## Mechanism, at `a21c23ac70d02cc156ba898ff51855c1b8cd4bec`

1. The management-VRF set is built from the configured management interfaces and published by
   `publishMgmtVRFIfaces(mgmtSet)` at `pkg/daemon/daemon_apply_interfaces.go:276`. Names are classified by prefix `fxp`,
   `fab` or `em` in `pkg/config/ifname_class_6731.go:128-130`.
2. `pkg/daemon/daemon_apply_dataplane.go:485-497`:
   ```go
   if mgmtSet := d.mgmtVRFIfaceSet(); d.routing != nil && len(mgmtSet) > 0 {
       if err := d.rebindManagementVRFIfaces(); err != nil { ... }
       // Restart heartbeat after VRF rebind — networkd reconfigure moves
       // the control interface (em0) out of vrf-mgmt temporarily ...
       if d.cluster != nil {
           d.cluster.RestartHeartbeat()
       }
   }
   ```
3. `applyDataplaneAndHACore` runs inside `applyConfigLocked` (`pkg/daemon/daemon_apply.go:474`). Both the operator
   commit path and the peer-synced apply reach `applyConfigLocked` (`pkg/daemon/daemon_apply_commit.go:284,651`).
4. `pkg/cluster/heartbeat_manager.go:332` (`func (m *Manager) RestartHeartbeat() bool`) stops the receiver and
   starts a replacement. It seeds only `lastSeen`. Its doc says a peer whose sockets are down is detected "once the
   post-restart 30s startup grace expires".
5. In `pkg/cluster/heartbeat.go`:
   - `:79` sets `heartbeatStartupGrace = 30 * time.Second`;
   - `start()` sets `r.startedAt = time.Now()` (`:1541-1542`);
   - in `checkTimeout` (`:1777-1816`), for a peer that has been seen, `if time.Since(r.startedAt) < heartbeatStartupGrace {
     return }` runs before the staleness test that calls `handlePeerTimeout`.
6. `handlePeerTimeout` writes `peerAlive = false` (`pkg/cluster/heartbeat_manager.go:659`). The only other writer is

## #9723 — cluster: a negative redundancy-group id admitted on the tolerant load/peer-sync path saturates to wire byte 0 and aliases RG0 on the heartbeat, so peer RG0 state becomes nondeterministic [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-11)

## What is wrong

Strict commit rejects a redundancy-group id that falls outside the wire and dataplane ranges. The tolerant path
(persisted-config load and HA peer sync) downgrades that same error to a warning and keeps the group. `compileChassis`
parses the id with `strconv.Atoi`, so a numeric negative token such as `-1` is kept as -1. Only a parse failure
collapses to 0.

#8337 made the heartbeat saturate group ids at the wire boundary. That maps every negative id to byte 0, the same byte
as RG0.

On receive, `localRGIDForWireByte` returns the first local group whose saturated id matches the byte. It finds that
group by ranging over a Go map. A node that holds both RG0 and RG -1 therefore attributes the peer's RG0 entry to
either group, nondeterministically. RG0's election can then run on RG -1's peer state, or with no peer entry at all.

## Mechanism, at `a21c23ac70d02cc156ba898ff51855c1b8cd4bec`

1. `pkg/config/compiler_system.go:2921-2924`: `rgID := 0; if n, err := strconv.Atoi(rgInst.name); err == nil { rgID = n }`.
2. `pkg/config/compiler_uniformgates_cluster_zone.go:~74-82`: under `opts.lenientChassisRG` (load / peer sync), a
   `validateChassisClusterStrict` failure is appended to `cfg.Warnings` instead of being returned. The strict
   rejection itself is `pkg/config/compiler_validate_strict_chassis.go:237-264`.
3. `pkg/cluster/heartbeat_manager.go:458-466`, `wireRGID`: `id < 0` maps to 0, and `id > 255` maps to 255.
4. `pkg/cluster/heartbeat_manager.go:484-491`, `localRGIDForWireByte`:
   `for id := range m.groups { if wireRGID(id) == b { return id } }`. Go map iteration order is unspecified.
5. The #5694 comments (`pkg/config/compiler_chassis_identity.go:12-19`) describe only a token that fails to parse
   collapsing to id 0. A numeric negative token is not that case.

Present at the report base; no post-base change to these sites.

## Executed evidence

One of the three reviewers ran cells at the verification revision:

- Strict `CompileConfig` rejects `redundancy-group -1`.
- `CompileConfigLenient` keeps RG ids [0, -1] and emits two warnings. The cluster manager then holds groups -1 and 0,
  and `wireRGID(-1) = 0`.
- Over {0, -1}, `localRGIDForWireByte(0)` resolved to -1 in 46 of 400 lookups.
- After 200 peer heartbeats carrying both groups, the peer-group map lacked RG0 three times. The reviewer traced a
  missing entry into RG0's "peer has no RG info" election arm.

## #9724 — vrrp: in legacy no-private-rg-election mode the RETH VRID is fixed at 100 + RG with no cluster identity check, so any VRRP speaker on a member segment using VRID 101-115 can depose that RG's master, and no doc says to reserve those VRIDs [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-11)

## What is wrong

In legacy mode (`no-private-rg-election`), RETH VRRP instances use `VRID = 100 + rgID`, and that base is not
configurable. The receive path accepts an advertisement if it passes these checks:

- the arrival interface;
- TTL 255;
- the not-self address set;
- the VRID byte;
- packet integrity.

Nothing checks a cluster identity, source MAC, VIP list or subnet.

So any VRRP speaker on the same L2 segment that uses a VRID in 101-115 feeds that RG's election. That covers a second
legacy-mode cluster with an overlapping RG id, or a third-party router. The heartbeat rejects a foreign cluster id,
but VRRP has no equivalent check.

The documentation scopes RETH VRRP as an xpf-to-xpf mechanism between the two chassis of one cluster. No document
states the per-segment VRID reservation that this scope implies.

## Mechanism, at `a21c23ac70d02cc156ba898ff51855c1b8cd4bec`

1. `pkg/vrrp/vrrp.go:~222-260`: both the VLAN-unit arm and the base-member arm of RETH instance construction set
   `GroupID: 100 + rgID`.
2. `pkg/vrrp/instance_receive.go:~155-182` performs, in order:
   - an arrival-ifindex check;
   - a drop when `hdr.TTL != 255`;
   - the self-address set filter (#7334);
   - a drop when `payload[1] != uint8(vi.cfg.GroupID)`.

   No cluster identity is consulted. The reviewers traced the consequences in `pkg/vrrp/instance_rx.go`: a
   higher-priority advertisement makes a master step down, and a priority-0 advertisement makes a backup take over
   at once.
3. Private-RG election is on by default (`pkg/config/compiler_system.go:2878-2882`), and `CollectRethInstances` builds
   no RETH VRRP instance under it (`pkg/vrrp/vrrp.go:~135-143`).
4. `docs/feature-coverage.md:~268-281` describes RETH VRRP as "an xpf-to-xpf mechanism between the two chassis of one
   cluster". A docs search finds VRID mentioned in five documents; `100 + rgID` appears only in
   `docs/vpp-dataplane-assessment.md` and in bug history. None gives per-segment reservation guidance.

Present at the report base; no post-base change to these files.
