## #9725 — daemon: at boot the transit gate opens kernel forwarding and removes the #7191 barrier at dataplane Start, before any interface has an XDP program attached, so static non-VIP addresses and FRR routes forward unadjudicated until the first apply attaches [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-17)

## What is wrong

The #5275/#7191 transit gate is meant to keep kernel forwarding closed until the dataplane is armed: the forwarding
sysctls at 0, plus an nftables forward barrier. At the verification revision, "armed" is declared at
`rt.Start`/`LoadUserspaceShim`. At that point `markDataplaneArmed` writes the forwarding sysctls to 1 and removes the
barrier. Its own documentation says the per-interface AF_XDP attach happens later, inside the first `ApplyConfig`.

On a cold boot:

- networkd and FRR are already up, because the unit is ordered after them;
- the appliance image has already set forwarding to 1 in sysctl.d.

So from the sysctl apply until the first attach, static non-VIP addresses and FRR routes forward transit through the
kernel with no XDP program and no barrier. The boot policy also calls `enableForwarding()` before `rt.Start`.

Once a program is attached, the shim drops transit when the helper heartbeat is missing or stale, so the window ends
at attach. A crash or signal inside the window leaves forwarding open until the service recovers.

## Mechanism, at `a21c23ac70d02cc156ba898ff51855c1b8cd4bec`

1. `pkg/daemon/daemon_run_bringup.go:583-592`, `applyBootTransitPolicy`: the default arm calls `enableForwarding()`.
2. `pkg/daemon/daemon_run_bringup.go:609-626`, `armBootDataplane`: calls `rt.Start(...)`, then
   `d.markDataplaneArmed("boot")`. Only the Start-failure arm closes forwarding (`:613-625`).
3. `pkg/daemon/daemon_transit_gate.go:140-175`, `markDataplaneArmed`: stores the armed flag, writes the forwarding
   sysctls to 1 and removes the #7191 nft barrier. Its doc (`:~147-152`) says the per-interface attach "happens later
   inside the first ApplyConfig". The gate's contract (`:10-24`) is that no `hook forward` chain exists while armed.
4. `pkg/daemon/daemon_run_naming.go:225-230`: bootstrap exit follows the same order, enabling forwarding before
   arming.
5. `scripts/image/bake.py:93-99,419`: the appliance image writes IPv4 and IPv6 forwarding = 1 into sysctl.d.
6. `test/incus/xpfd.service:3`: `After=network-online.target frr.service`.
7. `userspace-xdp/src/lib.rs:598-645`: once attached, a missing or stale heartbeat drops transit.

Present at the report base; no post-base change to these files.

## Reachability (bounded)

- This affects every cold boot of a standalone node, and of any interface with a static non-VIP address, from the
  sysctl apply until the first per-interface attach.
- Cluster RETH members get only the 169.254 base address from networkd, and their VIPs are added at runtime, so
  VIP-addressed cluster data paths are mostly outside the window.

## #9726 — userspace-dp: the helper statically links the build host's libxdp/libbpf with no version pin, provenance record or semantic compatibility check; only ring-struct layout is gated (#4976) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-12)

## What is wrong

`userspace-dp` compiles its C bridge against `/usr/include` and statically links whichever `libxdp`, `libbpf`,
`libelf`, `libz` and `libzstd` are installed on the build host. Nothing records which versions went into a binary,
nothing constrains them to a supported range, and nothing tests the library behaviour the dataplane relies on. The
only guard is #4976's compile-time layout check of the ring structs.

The practical risk is build-image drift, not runtime drift. Static linking freezes the library into each helper
binary, so a target host's installed `libxdp.so` is never loaded. But two builds from differently provisioned hosts
can embed different library semantics, and neither the build nor the binary says so.

## Mechanism, at `a21c23ac70d02cc156ba898ff51855c1b8cd4bec`

1. `userspace-dp/build.rs:1-26`:
   - compiles `csrc/xsk_bridge.c` with `.include("/usr/include")`;
   - emits `cargo:rustc-link-lib=static=xdp`, `static=bpf`, `static=elf`, `static=z` and `static=zstd`;
   - reruns only when `csrc/xsk_bridge.c` or `/usr/include/xdp/xsk.h` changes (#4976: "an in-place libxdp header
     upgrade that reorders/resizes the ring structs must re-run the C `_Static_assert`s").

   No version is queried, recorded or bounded.
2. The code also depends on library *semantics* that the layout asserts cannot see. `userspace-dp/src/xsk_ffi.rs:1311-1313`
   passes `libxdp_flags: u32 = 1` ("XSK_LIBBPF_FLAGS__INHIBIT_PROG_LOAD = 1 << 0 — We manage our own XDP program; don't
   let libxdp load one"). The #4976 asserts in `csrc/xsk_bridge.c` check only ring-struct size, alignment and offsets.

## Consequence (bounded)

- There is no live incompatibility or behaviour regression at the verification revision, and no supported build
  image is shown to link an incompatible version.
- A deployed binary does not pick up a later target-host `libxdp`.
- The gap is provenance and reproducibility. A behaviour change in `libxdp`/`libbpf` between build images, beyond
  struct layout, reaches a shipped helper without any record or failing check, and a field report cannot be tied
  to the library version inside the binary.

## What does not cover it

- #4976 asserts ring-struct layout only.
- The UMEM field order (`umem` before `area`) is correct and is pinned by the in-tree `drop_order` test, so it is
  not a runtime drift path.

## #9727 — userspace-dp: a jumbo MTU commits clean on a userspace-dataplane interface although RX frames larger than the fixed 4096-byte UMEM frame cannot reach a worker, and a failed MTU apply only warns [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-11)

## What is wrong

The userspace dataplane receives into fixed 4096-byte UMEM frames and binds its sockets without multi-buffer support.
The interface `mtu` leaf accepts any value of 1 or more ("kernel/driver enforces its own ceiling"), and a failed MTU
apply is only logged as a warning.

Nothing at commit or bind time tells the operator that frames larger than one UMEM frame cannot reach a worker in
userspace mode. What the reviewers found in upstream AF_XDP:

- In copy mode such a frame is dropped and counted in the kernel's `rx_dropped`, which xpf surfaces as
  `kernel_rx_dropped`.
- A zero-copy driver may refuse the XSK setup instead, and the #7191 arm then fails closed.

A jumbo configuration therefore commits clean and quietly turns into drops or a refused bind.

## Mechanism, at `a21c23ac70d02cc156ba898ff51855c1b8cd4bec`

1. `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/mod.rs:280`: `const UMEM_FRAME_SIZE: u32 = 4096;`
   `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/umem/mod.rs:40-50` creates the UMEM with `flags: 0`.
2. `userspace-dp/src/xsk_ffi.rs:291-294` defines only the SHARED_UMEM, COPY, ZEROCOPY and NEED_WAKEUP bind flags, and
   `XDP_USE_SG` appears nowhere in `userspace-dp/src`.
3. `pkg/config/schema_interfaces.go:54-60`: the `mtu` leaf is validated by `ValidateIntegerMin(1)`, with examples
   `1500` and `9000`.
4. `pkg/dataplane/compiler_iface.go:927-933`: when `LinkSetMTU` fails, the apply logs `slog.Warn("failed to set MTU", ...)`
   and continues.
5. `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/binding_state/kernel_stats.rs:36-68` exposes the kernel XSK `rx_dropped` counter as
   `kernel_rx_dropped`.

These are unchanged between the report base and the verification revision.

## Consequence (bounded)

- This is an availability and operator-honesty gap only.
- The report also claimed that parsing could go wrong. That half is refuted: no multi-buffer or truncated descriptor
  reaches the parser.
- On a userspace-dataplane interface, a jumbo MTU either drops oversize frames, visible only in `kernel_rx_dropped`,
  or fails the bind.

## #9728 — test/results: seven of the eight HA smoke gates have no usable ledger baseline (six have never recorded a row, mandated test-ha-crash has two unattested rows), so harness-compare cannot judge them [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-11)

## What is wrong

`harness-compare` judges a gate against a robust band built from the last three green rows in the same environment.
With fewer than three it reports NO-BASELINE, which the ledger doc says is "Not a PASS".

At the verification revision the tracked ledger holds 68 rows:

| Gate | Rows |
|---|---|
| `test-failover` | 62 |
| `test-ha-crash` | 2 |
| `selftest` | 2 |
| `harness-result-selftest` | 2 |

Six HA gates have never recorded a row: `test-double-failover`, `test-active-active`, `test-stress-failover`,
`test-chained-crash`, `test-private-rg` and `test-restart-connectivity`. The mandated `test-ha-crash` has only two
rows, and neither carries the #9044 `exe_scope` provenance. The HA merges after the report base recorded only
`test-failover` rows.

So for seven of the eight HA gates, a gate run cannot be compared with earlier runs to show there was no regression.

## Mechanism, at `a21c23ac70d02cc156ba898ff51855c1b8cd4bec`

1. `test/results/ledger.d/` holds 68 shards. The only two `test-ha-crash` rows, `5643c509151bec05.json` and
   `aa6221768272ea7b.json`, have no `exe_scope` field.
2. `docs/harness-ledger.md`:
   - `:210`: `NO-BASELINE` means fewer than K green rows exist, "**Not a PASS.**"
   - `:223`: the band is built over the last `K = 3` green runs at the same env.
   - `:240-243`: fewer than three green rows is NO-BASELINE, "full stop".
3. `Makefile:953-998` runs all eight HA gates through `harness-result.sh --adapter ha-smoke`, so each would leave a
   row if it were run.
4. `docs/engineering-style.md:296` mandates `make test-failover` plus `make test-ha-crash` for HA changes. The other
   six are manual, destructive, self-locking gates.

## Consequence (bounded)

This is an assurance gap, not a product defect.

- A regression in one of these gates is noticed only if someone runs the gate and reads its absolute cells; there is
  no historical band to compare against.

## #9729 — [cohort] test/incus: the unreached persistent-NAT and DHCP-lease failover acceptance gates can pass without a failover, print summaries the ha-smoke adapter VOIDs, and leave accepted properties unasserted [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-11)

## #9736 — config: a one-line routing-instance run where an undeclared token extends a declared statement commits and takes effect nowhere (needs leaf arities declared first) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-17)

> **Re-scoped in place.** The original title and body claimed a brace-elided
> routing instance EVADES the #9323 closed-world check. That is wrong — it was
> measured against the wrong braced twin — and the full refutation is in the
> first comment below, kept because it corrects a class of reasoning rather than
> just this issue. What remains is real, narrower, and has a prerequisite the
> original acceptance omitted.

## What is wrong

A **one-line** routing-instance run where an undeclared token extends a declared
statement is accepted in **both** spellings, so

```
routing-instances { ri1 instance-type virtual-router firewall family inet filter f1 term t then discard; }
```

commits clean, emits no warning, and the filter takes effect nowhere. That is the
#9323 class — a subtree that compiles to NOTHING on a commit that reports
success — and `firewall` there carries security intent.

## What this is NOT: there is no spelling that evades the gate

Measured at `766da5332`:

| spelling | verdict |
|---|---|
| `ri1 instance-type virtual-router bogus-kw foo;` (elided) | accepted |
| `ri1 { instance-type virtual-router bogus-kw foo; }` (**one-line braced — the true twin**) | **accepted** |
| `ri1 { instance-type virtual-router; bogus-kw foo; }` (two statements) | REFUSED |

The elided spelling agrees **exactly** with its true twin. The original issue
compared it against the *two-statement* braced form — a different config, where
the token really is its own statement and the gate correctly refuses it.

`normalizeElidedRoutingInstance9620` already documents the rule that produces
this: *"An undeclared token after a declared statement extends that statement,
exactly as it does inside braces, where `ri1 { instance-type virtual-router
bogus-kw foo; }` also commits (#9736)."*

So this is **grammar completeness, not spelling evasion.**

## #9740 — syn-cookie: nodes with different screened zone sets derive different cookie keys, so cross-node validation fails after failover [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-11)

**Severity: LOW.** Pre-existing. Master's `buildSYNCookieMasterKey` already hashed the screened zones into the key. Found during the #9173 review (round 15). Not queued.

## What happens

The SYN-cookie key base is HMAC-SHA256 over three inputs (`deriveSYNCookieBase`, `pkg/dataplane/userspace/screens.go`):
- the secret;
- the cluster identity;
- the sorted screened (zone, profile) pairs.

The helper's SYN-cookie machinery is global, not per zone. So the zone set separates nothing; it only makes the key a function of the screen configuration.

That has two consequences:

1. **Nodes that screen different zone sets disagree on every key.** A node-specific configuration group, for example, could apply a syn-flood profile to a zone on one node only. The two bases then differ. A cookie minted by one node, in any zone, fails validation on the peer after a failover. The client has already sent its ACK, so it does not resend the SYN: the connection fails and the application must reconnect.
2. **A commit that adds or removes a screened zone changes the key immediately.** Cookies minted before the commit stop validating, even on the same node, until those handshakes are retried.

## Options

1. **Drop the zone set from the base.** The domain label and the cluster identity already separate the key.
   - Changes the base known-answer vector and the base-framing and zone-order tests.
   - A mixed old/new pair disagrees until both nodes upgrade.
2. **Keep it, and warn at commit** when node-specific groups make the screened-zone set differ between nodes. This does not address consequence 2.

## #9743 — config: `show configuration | display inheritance` omits the properties a group gives a brace-elided routing instance — the commit applies them [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-12)

## Summary

`ConfigTree.FormatInheritance` (pkg/config/ast_format.go) expands `groups` on the raw tree. Both compile paths run the #8662 compact normalizer first. The #9620 routing-instance change makes that normalizer rewrite a brace-elided routing instance into its braced shape before group expansion, so the compiled config inherits the group's properties for that instance. The inheritance display omits them.

## Measured

Measured on the #9620 branch head. `FormatInheritance` does not call the normalizer, so its output does not depend on that change. `CompileConfigLenient` and `FormatInheritance` were run on the same tree:

| Config | `display inheritance` contains `description inherited` | compiled instance has it |
|---|---|---|
| `groups { G { routing-instances { blue instance-type forwarding description inherited; } } } apply-groups G; routing-instances { blue { interface ge-0/0/0.0; } }` | **no** | yes |
| the same, with the group body braced: `blue { instance-type forwarding; description inherited; }` | yes | yes |

An operator reading the effective configuration does not see the inherited properties. `instance-type forwarding` is among them, and `forwarding` decides whether the daemon creates a VRF at all.

## Severity

Low. Only the display is affected, and the committed configuration is correct. But the display is wrong exactly where an operator checks what a group contributes.

## Fix direction

Normalize the clone that `FormatInheritance` expands, as both compile cores do, so the display and the commit expand the same tree. Check `FormatPathInheritance` as well.

Found by a Codex review of the #9620 routing-instance change and measured in that lane.

## #9751 — cluster: a heartbeat restart that fails during a config apply latches the heartbeat dead; later applies short-circuit on "not running" and the caller discards the result [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-11)

## What is wrong

On an HA node, every config apply that rebinds the management VRF calls `RestartHeartbeat`. If the heartbeat cannot bind during its five one-second retries, `RestartHeartbeat` returns false with the sender and receiver both torn down. Every later `RestartHeartbeat` then sees the heartbeat as "not running" and returns at once, and the apply caller discards the result. The heartbeat stays dead across later applies until cluster comms restart (a daemon restart, or a commit that changes the cluster transport key).

Meanwhile this node sends no heartbeats, so the peer declares it lost after its timeout, while this node has no receiver with which to notice anything about the peer.

## Mechanism, at `7b1cb4511c093ea965b6588bfa14f13ed76abad6`

1. `pkg/daemon/daemon_apply_dataplane.go:485-497`: after `rebindManagementVRFIfaces`, the apply calls `d.cluster.RestartHeartbeat()` and discards the returned bool.
2. `pkg/cluster/heartbeat_manager.go:332-345`: `RestartHeartbeat` snapshots `running := m.hbSender != nil || m.hbReceiver != nil` and returns false when `!running || localAddr == ""`.
3. `pkg/cluster/heartbeat_manager.go:363-391`: it calls `m.StopHeartbeat()` (which nils the sender and receiver and keeps `hbLocalAddr`, `:213-233`), then retries `StartHeartbeat` five times one second apart. On exhaustion it logs "heartbeat restart failed after retries" and returns false with both still nil.
4. `pkg/cluster/heartbeat_manager.go:269-304`: `ApplyCommittedHeartbeatTiming` returns early when `m.hbReceiver == nil`, so the timing-change path cannot revive it either.
5. The only other `StartHeartbeat` caller is `startHeartbeatWithRetry` (`pkg/daemon/daemon_ha_sync.go:~1200-1232`), which runs when cluster comms start. On the apply path, comms restart only when the transport key changes or a bootstrap restart is owed (`pkg/daemon/daemon_apply_tail.go:359-360`).

Executed at the pin with a bounded Go probe in a scratch worktree:

- A heartbeat started on 127.0.0.1, whose remembered address was then made unbindable, made `RestartHeartbeat` return false after about 5 s of retries.
- With the address bindable again, `RestartHeartbeat` returned false immediately (running=false), and `ApplyCommittedHeartbeatTiming` returned false.
- Control: `StartHeartbeat` with the same parameters succeeded, and `RestartHeartbeat` on a running heartbeat returned true.

This is present at the report base; neither `heartbeat_manager.go` nor `daemon_apply_dataplane.go` changed after it.

## Reachability (bounded)

- HA nodes with a non-empty management-interface set (fxp/fab/em, as in every reference HA configuration), on any apply that rebinds the management VRF.
- The trigger is a bind failure longer than the ~5 s retry window. Examples: the control interface's address, or its management-VRF membership, is absent after the networkd reconfigure in that apply; or the authoritative management rebind fails, which the apply reports but still follows with the restart.
- Recovery needs a daemon restart or a commit that changes the cluster transport key. An ordinary re-commit does not recover it.

## Consequence (bounded)

- This node sends no heartbeats. After its timeout the peer declares this node lost and elects, while this node, with no receiver, keeps its own view. That risks conflicting roles until comms restart.
- Neither the commit result nor a health field reports the dead heartbeat, because the return value is discarded.

## What does not cover it

- The #1792 protections (sync keepalives feeding the peer's suppression guard, and seeding `lastSeen`) apply only while a restart is in progress or after it succeeds.
- `ApplyCommittedHeartbeatTiming` (#7164) is gated on a running receiver.
- #9722 (OPEN) concerns a successful restart re-arming the 30 s startup grace on every apply. It does not change the `!running` short-circuit or the discarded return value.

## Dedup

## #9752 — userspace-dp: a PBR `then routing-instance` session does not keep its installing table, so synced hits, synced import and owner-RG refresh re-resolve it in inet.0 [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-16)

## What is wrong

A firewall-filter `then routing-instance X` (PBR) term steers a new flow. On the session miss, the dataplane resolves that flow in X's routing table and installs the session with the result. The table itself is not stored with the session.

Whenever the session's forwarding resolution is recomputed later, the recomputation has no table input and runs in the default table (`inet.0`/`inet6.0`). That happens:

- on every hit of a peer-synced session;
- on synced import and HA owner-RG refresh, which also write the new result back into the session;
- on a hit of a local session whose stored resolution is not a reusable ForwardCandidate.

The steered flow is then forwarded by `inet.0` instead of X. Either it goes NoRoute and breaks, or, if `inet.0` has a covering route, it leaves through the default instance under a policy verdict that was admitted for X's egress.

## Mechanism, at `7b1cb4511c093ea965b6588bfa14f13ed76abad6`

1. On the miss path, `ingress_route_table_override` produces `route_table_override` (`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/poll_descriptor/mod.rs:1740-1760`). That override is passed to `lookup_forwarding_resolution_in_table_with_dynamic(..., route_table_override.as_deref())` (`:1788-1793`).
2. The session stores only `SessionDecision { resolution, nat }` (`userspace-dp/src/session/entry.rs:11-14`), with no table.
3. `lookup_forwarding_resolution_for_session_with_cache` (`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/session_glue/mod.rs:82-162`) reuses a stored ForwardCandidate only when `allow_cached_fast_path` is true (`:136-140`). Otherwise it calls `lookup_forwarding_resolution_with_dynamic_for_flow(forwarding, dynamic_neighbors, target, &flow.forward_key)` (`:150-155`), which has no table argument.
4. Synced hits pass `allow_cached_fast_path=false` (`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/session_glue/mod.rs:164-177`), so every synced hit re-resolves in the default table.
5. Synced import re-resolves through `lookup_forwarding_resolution_for_session` and writes `entry.decision.resolution` (`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/session_glue/commands/upsert_synced.rs:75-92`). The owner-RG refresh does the same (`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/session_glue/commands/refresh_owner_rgs.rs:130-137`).

The post-base commit `e4cc769e9` (#9519) validates the arrival zone on a session hit; it does not change the resolution table.

## Reachability (bounded)

- Configurations with PBR `then routing-instance` steering into an instance whose egress is not a tunnel. A tunnel resolution is re-resolved by tunnel endpoint id (`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/session_glue/mod.rs:92-133`), so steers with a tunnel egress keep their egress.
- HA clusters: every hit on a peer-synced session (for example the new primary's sessions after a failover), and every synced import.
- Standalone: local sessions whose stored resolution cannot be reused, for example MissingNeighbor seeds. A stored ForwardCandidate is reused, so ordinary neighbor churn alone does not trigger it.
- No attacker is needed; an ordinary HA failover of a PBR/FBF deployment triggers it.

## Consequence (bounded)

- The steered flow is forwarded by `inet.0`. With no covering route in `inet.0` it goes NoRoute and breaks; with one, it egresses through the default-instance route.
- The flow's zone-policy verdict was decided at miss time against X's egress.

## What does not cover it

- `cached_session_resolution` covers only local hits whose stored resolution is a ForwardCandidate (`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/session_glue/mod.rs:136-140`).
- The tunnel branch covers only steers with a tunnel egress.
- #9519 adjudicates the arrival zone, not the table.
- #7924 rejects overlap combined with PBR at commit, which is a different root cause.

## #9754 — daemon/routing: a bare routing-instance member (`interface ge-0/0/0`) enslaves only the parent netdev, so its tagged VLAN units stay outside the VRF on the kernel path [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-12)

## What is wrong

A routing-instance `interface ge-0/0/0` written without a unit means every configured unit of that interface. The userspace route binder and the DHCP route map both read it that way.

The kernel VRF bind does not. It enslaves only the parent netdev. The 802.1Q sub-interfaces for the tagged units are created with no master and never enslaved. Kernel-path traffic, FRR's view of VRF membership and VRF-bound sockets therefore treat those units as default-instance.

## Mechanism, at `7b1cb4511c093ea965b6588bfa14f13ed76abad6`

1. `pkg/daemon/daemon_apply_interfaces.go:342-360` (`bindRoutingInstanceMembers`) calls `BindInterfaceToVRF(riMemberLinuxName(...), ri.Name)` once per member string. The post-networkd `rebindRoutingInstanceMembers` (`:385-387`, called at `pkg/daemon/daemon_apply_dataplane.go:483`) runs the same loop.
2. `pkg/daemon/daemon_run_routehelpers.go:77-95` (`logicalUnitDeviceKeyForRef`): a bare reference has no unit token, so it returns the base netdev (`:81-83`).
3. `pkg/routing/vrf.go:126-142` (`BindInterfaceToVRF`) does one `LinkByName` and one `LinkSetMaster`.
4. VLAN sub-interfaces are created with only `Name` and `ParentIndex` (`pkg/dataplane/compiler_iface.go:262-269`). The generated networkd `.network` files set `VRF=` only for management interfaces (`pkg/dataplane/compiler_iface.go:1398-1408`).
5. The other consumers read a bare reference as all units:
   - `InterfaceUnitRefKeys` fans it down to every configured unit (`pkg/config/host_inbound_effective_view.go:50-53,68-95`), and the userspace routing-instance binder consumes that (`pkg/dataplane/userspace/routes.go:537-560`).
   - The DHCP route map keys every unit of a whole-device member (`pkg/daemon/daemon_flow.go:104-122`).

Executed at the pin with a bounded Go probe in a scratch worktree. Strict `CompileConfig` accepts `routing-instances blue { interface ge-0/0/0; }` on a vlan-tagging port with unit 0 on vlan 10 and unit 1 on vlan 50. For that config:

- the kernel bind target is `ge-0-0-0`;
- the userspace binder keys are `ge-0/0/0`, `ge-0/0/0.0` and `ge-0/0/0.1`;
- the DHCP lease keys are `ge-0-0-0.10` and `ge-0-0-0.50`.

This was already present at the report base. #9132 (closed) added the bare fan-down to the userspace route builders only and did not touch the bind path.

## Reachability (bounded)

- Any routing instance whose member is a bare interface on a port that has tagged units.
- Strict commit accepts it, and no warning is emitted.
- Ordinary configuration triggers it; no attacker is needed.

## Consequence (bounded)

- Kernel-path traffic on the tagged units (host-inbound, kernel-delegated and XDP_PASS frames) is routed in the default instance, failing open to main.
- FRR/zebra takes interface VRF membership from the kernel master, so the units' connected prefixes land in the default VRF. VRF-bound daemons and sockets do not see the units.
- The AF_XDP transit fast path does not depend on the kernel VRF master.

## What does not cover it

- The #6805 late rebind re-runs the same single-target loop.
- networkd `VRF=` covers management interfaces only.

## #9755 — [cohort] frr: `StreamBGPRoutes` forks vtysh outside the #9143 funnel, so the funnel's invariant, its 19-read census and the process-wide four-child cap do not cover the stream path [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-12)

## What is wrong

#9143 made `Manager.vtysh` the single funnel for operational FRR shell-outs. It applies the process-wide admission bound `diagcmd.VtyshLimiter`, sized at four children across every control surface. Its doc comment says "nothing in this package can reach vtysh except through here" (`pkg/frr/vtysh.go:227-237`), and `pkg/frr/README.md:348` says the same.

`StreamBGPRoutes` does not go through the funnel. It calls the executor's `VtyshStream` directly, so it takes no `VtyshLimiter` slot, and `VtyshStream` does not apply the 15 s `vtyshTimeout`. The #9143 census test that covers "every operational read" has no row for it.

The only production caller bounds itself, so this is not a reachable over-admission today. The written invariant, the four-child aggregate and the census are still false for the stream path, and a second caller of `StreamBGPRoutes` would get neither bound.

## Mechanism, at `7b1cb4511c093ea965b6588bfa14f13ed76abad6`

1. `pkg/frr/vtysh.go:248-255` (`Manager.vtysh`) acquires `diagcmd.VtyshLimiter` (`:249`) and calls `m.executor().Vtysh`. `realExecutor.Vtysh` wraps the caller's context in `context.WithTimeout(ctx, vtyshTimeout)` (`:131-133`; `vtyshTimeout = 15 * time.Second` at `:39`).
2. `pkg/frr/status_parse.go:461-470` (`StreamBGPRoutes`) wraps the caller's context only in a private cancel (`:464`) and calls `m.executor().VtyshStream(ctx, bgpRoutesCommand)` directly (`:467`).
3. `pkg/frr/vtysh.go:153-172` (`realExecutor.VtyshStream`) runs `exec.CommandContext(ctx, vtyshBinary, "-c", command)` under the caller's context, with no timeout.
4. `pkg/diagcmd/limiter.go:312-342`: `MaxConcurrentVtyshShellOuts = 4` bounds "how many FRR `vtysh -c` shell-outs may run at once across EVERY control surface that exposes FRR status". The comment says the funnel caps the worst-case footprint at that many children.
5. `pkg/frr/vtysh_admission_ctx_9143_test.go:132-160` (`TestVtyshAdmissionCoversEveryOperationalRead9143`) enumerates 19 reads, and `StreamBGPRoutes` is not among them. `pkg/frr/README.md:367` describes the cell as driving "nineteen operational reads".
6. The only non-test caller is the REST BGP routes branch (`pkg/api/routing.go:355`).
   - It takes the REST-local `ribStreamLimiter` (`maxConcurrentRIBStreams = 2` at `:97`, declared at `:113`, acquired at `:303`).
   - It applies a 10-minute total budget (`bgpStreamTotalBudget`, `:91`, applied at `:317`).
   - The comment at `:99-112` says that limiter is deliberately local to the REST surface.

An independent reviewer ran a bounded probe at the pin. With a capacity-1 `VtyshLimiter` already held, the control `GetBGPRoutes` returned `ErrVtyshBusy`. `StreamBGPRoutes` reached the executor with no error and a context without a deadline.

## Reachability (bounded)

- Today it is reached only through `GET /api/v1/routing/bgp?type=routes`. The worst case is four funnelled plus two streaming vtysh children (six, not the documented four), and every one can be cancelled.
- A future caller of `StreamBGPRoutes`, for example a gRPC or CLI stream, would get no admission bound and no deadline.

## Consequence (bounded)

- There is no live over-admission. Both REST-side guards are in place, and the stream stops when the caller cancels. A budget longer than 15 s is deliberate for a large, progressing RIB stream.
- The process-wide invariant and aggregate cap are false as written, and the census gives the stream path no coverage. A regression in the REST guards, or a second caller, would therefore go unnoticed.

## What does not cover it

- #9143 (closed) bounds the buffered reads only; its census omits the stream path.
- #6809 (closed) created `ribStreamLimiter`, which is REST-local by design and does not share the process-wide budget.

## Dedup

- #9143, #6809 and #5056 are closed. No open issue owns the stream path's position relative to the funnel.

## #9757 — dataplane: deleting a unit's family mtu leaves the VLAN sub-interface kernel MTU, and the userspace egress MTU, at the old value [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-12)

**Severity: MEDIUM. Not queued.** Found while measuring #9395 on the loss userspace cluster.

## What happens

`pkg/dataplane/compiler_iface.go:805-817` applies a unit MTU to the VLAN sub-interface only when `unit.MTU > 0`, through `linkSetMTUSeam`. Nothing resets the device MTU when the statement is deleted. There is no other writer for a VLAN unit's MTU: `git grep -E "LinkSetMTU|linkSetMTUSeam|MTUBytes" -- pkg/` finds none.

The userspace dataplane reads its egress MTU from that kernel device (`pkg/dataplane/userspace/interfaces.go`, `buildLinkSnapshot(linuxUnit)`). So the stale value keeps driving `forwarded_egress_mtu_decision` as well.

## Measured (5f28e89ac)

1. Commit `set interfaces reth0 unit 80 family inet mtu 1400`. Both `ge-0-0-2.80` (fw0) and `ge-7-0-2.80` (fw1) go to 1400.
2. Commit `delete interfaces reth0 unit 80 family inet mtu`. `show configuration interfaces reth0` then has no mtu statement, but both devices stay at 1400 (read 9 s after the commit).
3. A DF-set 1450-byte ping through the box still draws `Frag needed and DF set (mtu = 1400)` from the firewall.
4. The only repair was to commit an explicit `mtu 1500` and then delete it again.

## Consequence

After an operator removes a lowered MTU, the box keeps enforcing the old value until the device is recreated or the box reboots:
- DF-set traffic between the old MTU and the link MTU draws PTB / Frag-Needed and is dropped;
- DF-clear traffic in that range still records the #9328 `egress_mtu_exceeded_forwarded_no_df` exception.

The committed configuration no longer describes the running state.

## Fix direction

When a unit has no MTU statement, restore the VLAN sub-interface MTU to the parent link's MTU (what a new VLAN child inherits). Add a cell that deletes the statement and asserts the reset. `family inet6 mtu` compiles into the same `unit.MTU`, so it has the same gap.

## #9758 — userspace-dp: no IPv4 egress fragmenter, so a DF-clear datagram larger than the physical egress link is submitted whole [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-17)

**Severity: LOW (enhancement). Not queued.** Split from #9395, which decided the policy for an oversized DF-clear IPv4 datagram: keep forwarding, counted.

#9395 measured the common case: a configured egress MTU below the link MTU. The whole datagram reaches the far side, so forwarding is correct there and a drop would regress it. The measurement: DF-clear 1450-byte datagrams over a 1400-configured `reth0.80` on a 1500-byte link. UDP arrived 10/10 and ICMP 5/5, with no reassembly at the receiver and no NIC TX error.

The case that stays open is a DF-clear datagram larger than the **physical** egress link MTU:
- It needs an ingress link that carries larger frames, for example a jumbo trust side toward a 1500-byte WAN. #9727 covers frames past the 4096-byte UMEM chunk; this is the range below that.
- The dataplane has no IPv4 transit fragmenter; the only MF/offset writers are NAT64's, which copy them from an existing IPv6 Fragment Header. So such a datagram is submitted whole and is expected to be dropped by the NIC driver or the next hop.
- It is counted as `egress_mtu_exceeded_forwarded_no_df`, but not delivered.

It could not be measured on the loss userspace cluster, whose ingress and egress share a 1500-byte physical MTU. `interfaces reth0 mtu 1400` did not change the RETH member link in the same run.

Options:
- RFC 791 fragmentation on egress: ID assignment, per-fragment checksums, multiple TX descriptors, and NAT / CoS / session accounting.
- Drop-and-count limited to the physical-link case. That needs the parent link MTU in the interface snapshot, which today carries only the unit's MTU.

## #9761 — dataplane: an interface-level mtu on a vlan-tagging interface with only tagged zone units never reaches the parent link [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-12)

**Severity: LOW. Not queued.** Found while measuring #9395 on the loss userspace cluster.

## What happens

`planPhysDesired` in `pkg/dataplane/compiler_iface_desired.go` is the single planner for a physical netdev's MTU write (#8119/#8120). It walks the zone interface references and skips every TAGGED one:

```go
if physName == "" || vlanID != 0 {
	// A tagged unit actuates its own sub-interface, not the parent.
	continue
}
```

The interface-level `mtu` is read only after that skip (`if ifCfg.MTU > 0 && mtuUnit[physName] == -2`). Take an interface with `vlan-tagging` whose zone references are all tagged units, such as the loss cluster's `reth0` with units 50 and 80. No plan is ever created for its parent link, so the interface-level `mtu` is never written. The commit is clean and has no effect.

## Measured (5f28e89ac)

`set interfaces reth0 mtu 1400` was committed. The RETH member `ge-0-0-2` on fw0 stayed at 1500, read back 13 s after the commit.

## Consequence

An MTU set on the parent of a VLAN trunk is silently ignored, for example a jumbo parent carrying tagged units. The VLAN children then stay bounded by the parent's actual MTU, so a unit MTU above it cannot take effect either. #9727 separately covers frames past the userspace 4096-byte UMEM chunk.

## Fix direction

- Plan the parent link's MTU for tagged references too. Address reconciliation stays with the sub-interface; only the MTU is new, and the interface-level leaf stays authoritative for the parent.
- Add a planner cell for a `vlan-tagging` interface whose only zone references are tagged units.
- For a RETH, confirm the member resolution writes the value to each member link.

## #9766 — HA: a FullResync export and the reconciliation drain queue session deltas without a shared lock, so a stale install can follow a close [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-11)

**Severity: MEDIUM. Not queued.** Pre-existing. Found in the #9630 design review and verified in code at e8d84dd75.

## What happens

- **The export path takes no lock.** `handleEventStreamFullResync` → `exportUserspaceOwnerRGSessionsWithConfig` (`pkg/daemon/daemon_ha_userspace_export.go:59-72`) first calls `ExportOwnerRGSessionsPaged`, a synchronous helper snapshot. It then passes the returned installs to `queueUserspaceSessionDeltas`, with no lock held between the two calls.
- **The fallback drain races it.** `eventStreamFallbackLoop` (`pkg/daemon/daemon_ha_userspace_stream.go`, the connected reconciliation arm) drains helper deltas under `userspaceDeltaSyncMu`, every 5 s while the stream is connected and every 100 ms while it is not. It queues them through the same `queueUserspaceSessionDeltas`.
- **Result:** if that drain queues `close(X)` after the export's snapshot was taken but before the export's batch is queued, the peer receives `delete(X)` and then the export's stale `install(X)`.

## Why the generation guard does not stop it

Generations are drawn per send (`stampInstallGenV4`, `takeDeleteGen*`, `pkg/cluster/sync.go`):
- the delete draws a generation greater than X's last install;
- the stale install queued after it draws a fresh generation, greater still.

The receiver's #2221 tombstone refuses only an incoming install OLDER than the tombstone. So it applies the stale install, and X is resurrected on the standby until it idles out.

## Fix direction

- Hold `userspaceDeltaSyncMu` across the whole export-and-queue transaction in the FullResync path. The fallback drain already takes it.
- Add a cell that interleaves a drained close with an in-flight export and asserts the peer ends without X.

Refs #9630

## #9767 — HA: a FullResync is ACKed even when its export was dropped by the full session-sync send queue or refused by the schema gate [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-11)

**Severity: HIGH by consequence, not measured on the cluster. Not queued; recommend queueing it before #9630's redesign.** Pre-existing. Found in the #9630 design review and verified in code at e8d84dd75.

## What happens

1. `handleEventStreamFullResync` (`pkg/daemon/daemon_ha_userspace_stream.go`) returns true whenever `exportUserspaceOwnerRGSessionsWithConfig` returns no error.
2. That function returns `(queueUserspaceSessionDeltas(...), nil)` and never compares the count with the export's size.
3. `queueUserspaceSessionDeltas` can admit less than it was given:
   - it returns 0 without queueing anything when the #7194 schema gate (`userspaceDeltaSchemaAdmits`) refuses the batch;
   - each install goes through `QueueSessionV4`/`V6` → `queueMessage`, which DROPS the message when the 4096-entry `sendCh` is full. It returns false (ignored), counts `Errors` and sets `syncBackfillNeeded`.
4. The event stream then marks the FullResync frame applied and ACKs it, so the helper trims the barrier.

## Why the backfill does not cover it

`syncBackfillNeeded`'s only consumers are in the background sweep. The sweep re-sends a session only after its timestamps move; `docs/session-sync-architecture.md` ("Background Sweep") gives its filter as `Created >= lastSweepTime`, so "once a session is behind the window it is never re-sent". A FullResync exports OLD sessions. An idle one dropped from the burst is never revisited, and the standby stays without it. That is exactly the gap the resync exists to repair.

## Arithmetic

An owner-RG export queues one message per session in a single burst, and the send queue holds 4096. A resync of a table with more than 4096 sessions can overflow the queue unless the sender drains faster than the walk queues.

## Interaction with #9630

Today every exported session also reaches the daemon a second time, as an event-stream open frame: the helper's export flushes through `drain_and_flush_all!`, whose consumers include the event stream. That second copy is queued later and partially masks this loss. Suppressing the echo, one proposal for #9630, would remove that copy, so this must be fixed first.

## Fix direction

- Make the export report complete admission (every install queued, schema gate passed), and return false otherwise so the resync is retried.
- Better: send the resync as an authoritative, acknowledged bulk window.
- Add a cell with a send queue smaller than the export that asserts the FullResync is not ACKed.

Refs #9630

## #9770 — userspace: the first ctrl-enable flush deletes steering rows the helper's live sessions still use [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-15)

**Severity: LOW** (pre-existing). Found by the hostile Codex code review of the #9560 branch; the mechanism was checked in source at `3dd5064fe`.

## Defect

`flushStaleBPFStateOnCtrlEnableLocked` (`pkg/dataplane/userspace/helper_status_apply.go`) runs on the first ctrl enable after daemon startup. The gate is `ctrl.Enabled == 1 && !m.ctrlWasEnabled && !m.initialCtrlCleanupDone` in the helper-status ctrl programming in `maps_sync.go`. It walks `userspace_sessions` with `NextKey` and deletes **every** row.

The flush exists for stale `PASS_TO_KERNEL` rows left by legacy-fallback windows. Its own comment states that at that moment the helper's session tables (`SessionTable` plus the shared maps) hold the authoritative synced sessions. The steering rows those sessions published are deleted along with the stale ones.

## Consequence

Until the helper writes a row again, the shim misses for that tuple. That happens on a worker's next publish for the session, or through `republish_bpf_session_entries_for_owner_rgs` on RG activation.

- Transit traffic is redirected to XSK on a miss anyway.
- A host-bound flow is passed to the kernel. With an `lo0` input filter, it skips the userspace filter evaluation, which is the consequence #9517 and #9560 address for aliased rows.

The flush is reachable whenever the helper already holds published sessions at the daemon's first enable:
- peer-synced imports (`sync_session` is served without the `ServerState` mutex, #7209);
- a bringup replay of preserved synced sessions before the first status-driven enable.

On the #9560 branch, the steering-row owner registry also keeps those owners after their rows are gone. That divergence causes no wrong delete: a later delete of an absent row is a no-op, and a republish rewrites it. But it cannot restore the row either.

## Fix direction (to settle in a plan)

- Restrict the flush to what it exists for. `PASS_TO_KERNEL` alone is not a sufficient discriminator: since #9517, the helper legitimately publishes `PASS_TO_KERNEL` for peer-synced host-bound sessions on single-instance nodes.
- Or ask the helper to republish its steering rows once after the flush (a single control request, not per tick).
- Or make the helper the only mutator of `userspace_sessions` and move stale-row cleanup into helper bringup.

HA startup path: needs `make test-failover` and a check that a live synced host-bound row survives the first enable.

Refs #9560, #9517

## #9778 — Architecture: is moving an established flow to another RX queue safe under AF_XDP per-queue UMEM ownership? (re-pin beats the RSS floor at HEAD, #9488) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-17)

## Question

Is it safe to move an **established** flow to a different RX queue, and so to a different worker, on this dataplane? The question has to be answered under AF_XDP per-queue UMEM ownership, and against #1748's barriered ownership-transfer protocol.

`docs/fairness-regimes.md` called that move forbidden, and the #1765 umbrella ended on that verdict. The verdict's empirical support was #1203's 49–55% per-flow CoV, a closed-loop controller's result. #9488 re-measured by hand at HEAD, and re-placing established flows beats the RSS floor by a wide margin (below). So "it would not help anyway" no longer answers the question. It needs an architectural answer of its own.

Correction to #9488's premise: #1203's final comment attributed its number to flow-fair MQFQ being off for `shared_exact` and to 1024 flow buckets. The code #1203 ran on, PR head `979482dff` (base `38881341c`), already had `queue.flow_fair = queue.exact` and `COS_FLOW_FAIR_BUCKETS = 4096`. That attribution does not hold, so why the controller stayed at 49–55% has not been established.

This issue asks for that answer. It does **not** ask to reopen #1748 or #1751. It does not ask to land `engineer/1748-ntuple-rebalance` or `engineer/1751-count-balance` either.

## The measurement (#9488)

**Setup**
- Build `e1cebdf8b` on `loss:xpf-userspace-fw0`, which held the LAN VIP. `ge-0-0-1` is an mlx5 VF with 6 RX queues, so 6 workers.
- 70 s `iperf3 -c 172.16.80.200 -p 5210 -P 12 -t 70 -i 1 -J` from `10.0.61.102` (iperf 3.20).
- Port 5210 maps to forwarding class `iperf-24g`, queue 10, `24g exact`. That makes it `shared_exact`, with flow-fair MQFQ on. equal-flow-enforcement is not configured.

**The two states**
- **re-pinned:** at about t=14 s, install one exact-5-tuple rule per established client socket: `ethtool -N ge-0-0-1 flow-type tcp4 src-ip 10.0.61.102 dst-ip 172.16.80.200 src-port <p> dst-port 5210 action <i mod 6>`. There are 13 rules (12 data sockets plus control). This is #1748 R1's recipe.
- **unsteered:** the same push with no rules.

**Runs:** 3 per state, all in one `with-cluster.sh` lock cell, with the order alternated (r1 unsteered first, r2 re-pinned first, r3 unsteered first). Every run is reported; none was dropped.

**Metrics**
- Per-flow CoV is the population CoV (`test/incus/fairness_cov.py`) of each stream's 5 s mean.
- Cstruct is `xpf_fairness_cstruct{queue_id="10"}` from the last 1 s scrape in each window.

Each cell reads per-flow CoV / Cstruct.

| run | state | t10–15 (re-pin starts about t14) | t45–50 | t55–60 | t65–70 | retransmits |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---:|
| r1 | unsteered | 50.6% / 0.507 | 49.0% / 0.447 | 50.7% / 0.447 | 55.4% / 0.447 | 2 |
| r1 | re-pinned | 44.3% / 0.563 | 6.7% / 0.000 | 9.0% / 0.000 | 7.6% / 0.000 | 2682 |
| r2 | re-pinned | 25.1% / 0.333 | 8.2% / 0.000 | 9.2% / 0.000 | 8.6% / 0.000 | 2854 |
| r2 | unsteered | 51.2% / 0.676 | 51.2% / 0.601 | 46.7% / 0.601 | 46.2% / 0.601 | 3 |
| r3 | unsteered | 41.5% / 0.542 | 41.7% / 0.471 | 41.5% / 0.471 | 42.7% / 0.471 | 0 |
| r3 | re-pinned | 35.9% / 0.471 | 10.0% / 0.000 | 13.7% / 0.000 | 13.9% / 0.000 | 4771 |

Aggregate over t45–70 was 22.05–22.74 G unsteered and 22.64–22.80 G re-pinned. After the re-pin, the per-worker queue-10 flow counts were `[2,2,2,2,2,2]` in every window.

## #9782 — nat: pool-mode source NAT to a proxy-ARPed pool address never completes a connection on the loss cluster, while interface SNAT on the same path works [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-15)

## What is wrong

On the loss userspace cluster, a LAN client's connection through **pool-mode source NAT** never completes. The same client, target and port connect normally through interface-mode source NAT. The pool is `pool-snat-pool` (`172.16.80.7/32`, proxy-ARPed on `reth0.80`), the pool #8573's accepted manual run (2026-09-04) translated to. Persistent NAT does not matter: pool mode fails with it and without it.

The fault surfaced because #9729 turned the persistent-NAT failover gate into a real verdict. The gate failed twice with no persistent-NAT binding minted. A discriminator then separated the gate from the product.

## Measurements

All runs were lock-celled and config-only. Rule `lan-to-wan/snat` was retargeted and restored afterwards; the restore was read back as `then source-nat interface`. The probe was `timeout 5 bash -c 'exec 3<>/dev/tcp/172.16.80.200/5201'` from `10.0.61.102` on `cluster-userspace-host`.

| rule `lan-to-wan/snat` | probe | notes |
|---|---|---|
| `source-nat interface` (the cluster's own config) | CONNECT-OK 3/3 | positive control |
| `source-nat pool pool-snat-pool` | CONNECT-FAILED 3/3 | sessions show only the client-side `In:` leg, with SYN retransmits |
| same, plus `persistent-nat permit any-remote-host` | CONNECT-FAILED 3/3 | `persistent-nat-table` holds `10.0.61.102:51594 -> 172.16.80.7:30004`, so allocation and translation happen |

**Prometheus deltas on the RG0 primary** (`127.0.0.1:8080/metrics`), across three probes in pool mode:
- `xpf_policy_denies_total` +20;
- `xpf_drops_total` +22;
- `xpf_userspace_event_stream_dataplane_events_total{type="policy_deny"}` +22;
- `xpf_zone_packets_total{direction="egress",zone="sfmix"}` +30;
- `xpf_userspace_source_nat_pool_live_lock_acquisitions_total{pool="pool-snat-pool",rule="snat"}` +23.

The interface-SNAT control showed session-table growth and no deny movement among its top deltas. So in pool mode something on the path is policy-denied, and some traffic leaves in the `sfmix` zone.

**Ruled out:**
- **Proxy-ARP identity looks correct.** On the RG0 primary, `ip neigh show proxy` lists `172.16.80.7`, pool GARPs are announced about once a second (`directSendGARPs: announced pool proxy-ARP addresses`), and the VLAN-80 sub-interface carries the RETH virtual MAC. The standby logs `proxy-arp: suppressing responder for an interface this node does not own`.
- **Not the local-address classifier change in #9646.** That change only preflights capacity. Pool addresses were never members of the shim's local-address set, including when #8573 passed.

## Suspects (not established)

The accepted run is from 2026-09-04. Changes on 2026-09-06 touch exactly this path:
- source-NAT keying: `052abd073` (source-NAT flow and allocator keyed on routing domain), `b12aebeb9` (teardown and HA reserve keyed on the post-DNAT port), `4c6f5dce4` (one pool, one allocator);
- proxy-ARP: `c50096251`, `0924a65c2`, `c9184b93c`.

## Next measurements

1. The 5-tuple, zones and rule of the `policy_deny` events emitted during a pool-mode probe (event stream or RT_FLOW deny records). That shows whether the denied packet is the client SYN leaving via `sfmix` or the reply to `172.16.80.7`.
2. If it is the reply, whether the reverse session lookup for `172.16.80.7:<port>` misses. Compare `worker_session_lookup_miss_*` for the probe's worker against the interface-SNAT control.
3. A bisect across 2026-09-04..2026-09-06 on the cluster with the same three-row discriminator.

`make docs-check` (`scripts/docs/check-upgrade-docs.sh`) exits 1 on current master (`e09f425dd`). Its phantom-symbol leg runs `grep -rnF -- "manifest.Managed" docs/`, and every hit is in a generated history archive that quotes the old symbol while describing its removal:

## #9788 — config: `security-zone <name> apply-groups G;` without braces commits clean and never applies group G to the zone [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-11)

A zone statement whose inline `apply-groups` is written without braces commits clean on strict, and the group is **never applied** to the zone. The braced spelling and the flat-set spelling of the same statement both apply it.

Measured at `e09f425dd` through `configstore.CheckText` (strict) and `config.CompileConfigLenient` (the boot and HA-sync path), with `groups { G { security { zones { security-zone <*> { tcp-rst; } } } } }`:

| Spelling | Strict | Compiled `trust.TCPRst` |
|---|---|---|
| `security-zone trust apply-groups G;` | accepts | **false** |
| CONTROL `security-zone trust { apply-groups G; }` | accepts | true |
| CONTROL `set security zones security-zone trust apply-groups G` (built with ParseSetCommandGrouped and SetPathQuotedGrouped) | accepts | true |
| `security-zone trust screen edge apply-groups G;` | refused: unexpected trailing token "apply-groups" | lenient: false |

`show configuration` renders the first spelling back unchanged, as `security-zone trust apply-groups G;`. A cluster peer therefore compiles the same loss.

**Not measured:**
- groups that set zone properties other than `tcp-rst`, such as `screen`, `host-inbound-traffic` or `interfaces`;
- other containers with an elided inline `apply-groups`;
- the normalized AST, which was not dumped.

If a group supplies a zone's `screen`, this path would leave the screen checks off on a green commit. That is inferred, not executed.

**Mechanism, as far as traced.**
- setSchema does not declare `apply-groups` inside a zone. The #9685 apply slot resolves only at wildcard slots.
- The #8662 scoped fold does not admit the `(security-zone, apply-groups)` pair.
- The parsed statement is one leaf, `Keys=["security-zone","trust","apply-groups","G"]`, and it renders back as one line. The zone compiler names the zone from `Keys[1]`.

**Relation to #9656 M40.** That change fans out statements naming two or more zones, and leaves a single-member statement to the scoped fold. This spelling was measured unchanged on that branch.

**Severity: Medium.** Group-supplied zone configuration is lost silently on a green commit. It fails open when the group supplies a screen (inferred).

**Suggested remedy.** Rewrite a single-member zone statement whose tail starts with an apply statement keyword into the braced form, in the zone hook `expandZoneGroups9656` added for M40. Alternatively, admit the pair in `compactNormalizeInScope` with its #8921 ratchet rows. Either way, group expansion must see `security-zone trust { apply-groups G; }`.

**Acceptance.** `security-zone trust apply-groups G;` compiles to the braced control's result on both strict and lenient, or strict refuses it with a message naming the spelling. A cell pins it and fails at `e09f425dd`.

**Queue.** After the #9656 M40 PR lands, since the remedy sits in its hook.

Refs #9656, #9685, #9620. Discovery credit: `model:claude-opus-5-1m`, found while adjudicating #9656 M40; `validated-by:research`.

## #9791 — dhcpserver/HA: after a failover the promoted Kea can name a reused address's previous owner, refusing the client that holds it [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-11)

## What is wrong

After an HA failover, a DHCPv4 client that holds a **reused** address can be refused its renewal by the promoted node. The promoted Kea's lease file names the address's **previous** owner, a client that is gone. So the current holder's REQUEST goes unanswered, and it falls back to DISCOVER and a new address.

## Observed: #9729's DHCP lease failover gate, run 6

The run was attributable (`exe_check=MATCH`, ledger row `4f3fcd62ccfeb31c`): deployed from the branch, lock-celled on the loss userspace cluster.

1. **Before the run.** An earlier run's client, MAC `42:52:86:7e:4e:37`, had held `10.0.61.100`. Leases in the lab pool are 86400 s.
2. **Lease.** This run's client A (a fresh MAC, `f6:c2:10:d9:73:69`) was granted `10.0.61.100` by the RG0 primary.
3. **Failover.** The primary was hard-rebooted. The standby was promoted, and its Kea logged a memfile lease-file load with no errors.
4. **Second client.** A second client DISCOVERed on the promoted node and got `10.0.61.103`, not `.100`.
5. **Renewal.** Client A's `DHCPREQUEST for 10.0.61.100` repeated with no ACK and no NAK. It then DISCOVERed and ended on `10.0.61.106`.
6. **The promoted node's lease file** held three rows for `10.0.61.100`, all for the OLD MAC `42:52:86:7e:4e:37`, and no row for client A's MAC:
   ```
   10.0.61.100,42:52:86:7e:4e:37,,86381,1789213076,2142673195,0,0,cluster-userspace-host,0,,0
   10.0.61.100,42:52:86:7e:4e:37,,86381,1789213076,2142673195,0,0,cluster-userspace-host,0,,0
   10.0.61.100,42:52:86:7e:4e:37,,86400,1789213148,2142673195,0,0,cluster-userspace-host,0,,0
   10.0.61.106,f6:c2:10:d9:73:69,,86400,1789214360,2142673195,0,0,cluster-userspace-host,0,,0
   ```

In run 4 the same property passed. That run did not reuse a previous client's address.

## Where the identity model admits this

- **`SyncLease.IdentityKey()`** (`pkg/dhcpserver/lease_sync.go`) is `4|<address>|<client-id or hwaddr>`. A rebind of one address to a new client is a DIFFERENT identity.
  - The sender's change detection is therefore not the gap: `dhcpLeaseSetFingerprint` includes the identity, so the rebind changes the fingerprint and pushes on the 2 s change poll.
- **`mergeLeasesByIdentity(local, peer)`** builds the takeover pre-seed (#5040). It dedups by that identity and lets a LOCAL lease win only an identity conflict.
  - A stale local row for `.100` (old client) and a peer row for `.100` (new client) do not conflict under that key, so the union carries BOTH.
  - They are written with the local rows first.
  - What a Kea memfile load does with two different-client rows for one address is not decided by xpf.

## Not established

The lease file showed no row for client A's MAC at all. So two mechanisms fit, and this report does not choose between them:
1. The held peer set carried client A's binding. The merge wrote both rows, and the new row was dropped or overridden on load.
2. Client A's binding never reached the held peer set before the takeover, and the stale local row alone was written.

**Next measurements:**
- the held peer lease set at the moment of takeover;

## #9793 — configstore: `deactivate` of one zone in a `security-zone [ a b ]` group deactivates every zone in the group, with no error [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-11)

`deactivate` addressed to one zone of a `security-zone [ a b ]` group marks the **whole grouped statement** inactive, and every zone in the group leaves the compiled candidate. The command reports no error. `delete` of the same path is already refused with #8992's re-author guidance; `deactivate` has no such refusal.

Measured through `configstore.Store` (`LoadOverride`, `DeactivateFromInput`, `DeleteFromInput`, `CompileCandidate`, `ShowCandidatePath`) at `e09f425dd` and on the #9656 M40 branch at `4a9ef6590`. The braced-group rows are identical at both:

| Candidate `security-zone [ zga zgb ] { tcp-rst; }` | Command result | Compiled zones |
|---|---|---|
| no edit | — | `zga zgb` |
| `deactivate security zones security-zone zga` | **no error**; the statement becomes `inactive: security-zone zga zgb { tcp-rst; }` | **none** |
| `delete security zones security-zone zga` | refused: *present in an ELIDED spelling packed together with other statements on one line … Re-author that line with braces around "zga", then delete it (#8992 …* | `zga zgb` |
| `delete security zones security-zone zgb` | refused: `path not found: no node matching "security-zone zgb"` | `zga zgb` |
| `ShowCandidatePath(… security-zone zga)` / `(… zgb)` | `zga` prints the whole group; `zgb` prints nothing | — |

**The leaf group `security-zone [ zga zgb ];` gives the same command results.** At `e09f425dd` it compiled only `zga`, which is #9656 M40. On the M40 branch it compiles both zones, so the same `deactivate` now removes two.

**Not measured:**
- `activate`;
- what a later commit does. A policy naming a lost zone would be refused on strict; unreferenced zones would vanish;
- the flat-set spelling of the group.

**Severity: Medium.** An edit addressed to one zone silently changes other zones.

**Suggested remedy.** Give `DeactivateFromInput` and `ActivateFromInput` the refusal `DeleteFromInput` already has, for a path that addresses one member of a grouped or packed node. The path-scoped `show` of a later member, `zgb` printing nothing, is the same addressing gap and may belong in the same change.

**Acceptance.** `deactivate security zones security-zone zga` against a group is refused with a message naming the spelling, or deactivates only `zga`. A cell pins it and fails at `e09f425dd`.

Refs #8992, #8794, #9656. Discovery credit: the #9656 M40 Codex review (`model:gpt-unknown`), narrowed by measurement, because its `delete` claim did not reproduce. `validated-by:research`.

## #9799 — configstore: a path naming a later member of a `security-zone [ a b ]` group finds no node — show prints nothing, delete and deactivate say `no node matching` [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-11)

## Defect

A path that names a **later** member of a grouped statement finds no node. Nothing changes, but every verb misreports it:

- `show ... security-zone zgb` prints nothing;
- `delete` and `deactivate` fail with `path not found: no node matching "security-zone zgb"`.

The zone is visible in `show configuration`. The error is true of the walk and false of the tree, which is the #9006 shape: it sends the operator to re-check a spelling that is correct.

The first member reaches the node, because the walk prefix-matches `Keys [security-zone zga zgb]`:
- `show ... security-zone zga` prints the whole group;
- `delete ... zga` is refused with #8992's re-author guidance;
- `deactivate ... zga` is refused with #9793's.

## Measured

Candidate `security { zones { security-zone [ zga zgb ] { tcp-rst; } } }`, through `configstore.Store`:

| Command | Result |
|---|---|
| `ShowCandidatePath(... security-zone zga)` | the whole group |
| `ShowCandidatePath(... security-zone zgb)` | nothing |
| `delete security zones security-zone zgb` | `path not found: no node matching "security-zone zgb"` |
| `deactivate security zones security-zone zgb` | `path not found: no node matching "security-zone zgb"` (measured on the #9793 branch) |

The `show` and `delete` rows are from #9793's measurement at `e09f425dd`.

**Not measured:** `activate` on an inactive group's later member; groups of other statement kinds; the flat-set spelling of the group.

## Why it matters

- Severity **Low**: every row either errors or prints nothing, and no candidate changes.
- The cost is diagnosis. The same zone is findable by one name and not by the other, and the message denies that a visible statement exists.

## Fix direction

When a path's key slot names a member that appears among a grouped node's names, resolve it against that node. Then do one of:
- refuse with the same re-author guidance #8992 (delete) and #9793 (deactivate/activate) give for the first member;
- or address the member itself.

## #9801 — config: a `<*>` group is not applied to a zone written as a leaf — `security-zone trust;` loses the group's screen, `security-zone trust { }` keeps it [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-12)

A wildcard group statement (`security-zone <*> { … }`) is merged into a zone written with braces, even empty ones, but **not** into the same zone written as a leaf. The two spellings name the same zone, yet only one of them inherits. Strict commit accepts both.

Measured at master `6cf4305ab` through `configstore.CheckText` (strict) and `config.CompileConfigLenient`, reading zone `trust` directly and listing every compiled zone. The configuration has one top-level `security` stanza, with `apply-groups G;` at top level.

| Group `G` supplies | Zone spelling | Strict | Compiled `trust` |
|---|---|---|---|
| `security-zone <*> { screen edge; }` | `security-zone trust;` | accepts | **`ScreenProfile=""`** |
| same | `security-zone trust { }` | accepts | `ScreenProfile="edge"` |
| `security-zone <*> { tcp-rst; }` | `security-zone trust;` | accepts | **`TCPRst=false`** |
| same | `security-zone trust { }` | accepts | `TCPRst=true` |
| `security-zone trust { screen edge; }` (named, control) | `security-zone trust;` | accepts | `ScreenProfile="edge"` |

No zone other than `trust` compiles in any row.

**Mechanism.** The wildcard branch of `mergeNodes` (`pkg/config/ast_groups.go`, under `keysContainWildcard(s.Keys)`) only visits destinations where `!d.IsLeaf && keysMatchWildcard(d.Keys, s.Keys)`. A leaf `security-zone trust;` is skipped. A named group path goes through the container branch instead and is merged.

**Severity: High.** In the screen row, the zone's screen profile is silently absent after a clean strict commit, so its IDS/DoS screen checks are off. #9620 rated that consequence High for member H1.

**Scope.** The guard applies to every wildcard destination, but zones are the only measured case where it loses configuration. In the same probes, a leaf `interfaces { ge-0/0/0; }` and a leaf `routing-instances { ri1; }` compiled no instance at all, so a skipped merge there changes nothing measurable. Other leaf-spelled instances were not measured.

**Suggested remedy.** When a wildcard source matches a leaf destination that the schema models as a named container, such as `security-zone <name>`, convert the destination to an empty container and merge into it, as the braced spelling already gets. A value leaf must not be converted.

**Acceptance.** `security-zone trust;` and `security-zone trust { }` compile identically under a `<*>` group on strict and lenient. A cell pins it and fails at `6cf4305ab`.

Related:
- #9788: its `apply-groups-except` control compiled `trust;` without the group for this reason.
- #9423: a partial glob adopted verbatim.
- #9656 M40: a zone group fanned out into leaf statements inherits exactly like the longhand leaf.

Discovery credit: `model:claude-opus-5-1m`, found while measuring #9788. `validated-by:research`.

## #9802 — config: a `<*>` group under a container the target lacks is adopted verbatim — strict commit compiles a zone named `<*>`, and zones in a second `security` stanza lose the group [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-12)

Suppose a group carries a wildcard statement under a container that the configuration it merges into does not have. The container is then adopted **wholesale**, wildcard key included. The result is a real compiled zone literally named `<*>` carrying the group's statements, and strict commit accepts it.

The same happens when zones sit in a second top-level `security` stanza. The group's `security` body merges only into the first stanza, so the real zones never see the group.

Measured at master `6cf4305ab` through `configstore.CheckText` and `config.CompileConfigLenient`, listing every compiled zone. The group is `groups { G { security { zones { security-zone <*> { tcp-rst; } } } } }`, applied with top-level `apply-groups G;`.

| Configuration | Strict | Compiled zones | `trust` |
|---|---|---|---|
| `security { screen { … } }` only, no `zones` | accepts | **`[<*>]`** | — |
| `security { zones { security-zone trust { } } } security { screen { … } }` (zones first) | accepts | `[trust]` | `TCPRst=true` |
| `security { screen { … } } security { zones { security-zone trust { } } }` (zones second) | accepts | **`[<*> trust]`** | **`TCPRst=false`** |

With `security-zone <*> { screen edge; }` instead, the zones-second row compiles `[<*> trust]`, and `trust` has `ScreenProfile=""`.

Split top-level stanzas are a supported spelling. #5691, fixed by #5741, made the AST pre-passes aggregate across all roots, and the compiler unions them.

**Mechanism** (`mergeNodes` in `pkg/config/ast_groups.go`, container branch):
1. A group container merges into the **first** same-keyed destination only (the `keysEqual` loop `break`s), so a group `security` body lands in the first `security` stanza.
2. With no same-keyed destination, the source container is appended wholesale (`*dst = append(*dst, s)`). Its wildcard-keyed descendants are never matched against anything and stay literal, so `security-zone <*>` becomes a zone named `<*>`.

**Severity: High.** In the zones-second shape, a group-supplied screen is silently absent from every real zone after a clean strict commit. That fails open, and #9620 rated the consequence High for member H1. The phantom zone's effect on zone IDs, the dataplane zone table and policy validation was not measured.

**Not a duplicate of #9423.** That issue was a partial glob (`<ge-*>`) failing to *match* and being materialised; its fix added glob matching. Here a bare `<*>` is never matched at all, because its parent container is adopted without recursing into it.

**Suggested remedy.**
- Never adopt a wildcard-keyed node verbatim. When a container is adopted wholesale, drop any wildcard-keyed descendant, which by construction matched nothing, or refuse it at strict with a message naming the group.
- Merge a group container into every same-keyed top-level stanza that holds a matching destination, consistent with #5741's all-roots aggregation.

**Acceptance.** No compiled zone is named `<*>`, and the zones-second row compiles `trust` with the group's statement, on strict and lenient. Cells pin both and fail at `6cf4305ab`.

Related: #9801 (the wildcard branch of the same function skips leaf destinations).

Discovery credit: `model:claude-opus-5-1m`, found while measuring #9788. `validated-by:research`.

## #9803 — userspace: update_fabrics stores plan-bearing fabric rows in the helper's snapshot without a replan, so the next full apply compares same-plan and skips the fabric rebind [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-17)

## What is wrong

`SyncFabricState` sends `update_fabrics` with freshly built fabric rows. Each row carries the plan half of its fabric: the parent netdev name, the parent ifindex and the RX queue count.

The helper's `update_fabrics` handler does two things with those rows, and neither is a replan:
- it re-resolves the fabric links;
- it stores the rows in its retained snapshot.

The binding plan key hashes exactly those fields. So once a row's parent ifindex or queue count changes:
- the helper's stored snapshot already carries the new values;
- the next full `apply_snapshot` carrying the same values computes an equal plan key and takes the same-plan path;
- the same-plan path reconciles only in one case: a registered, error-free binding is unbound or not XSK-registered, and the planned or live binding count is short. Otherwise, bindings planned for the old parent or queue layout are not replanned.

Go agrees with the helper that nothing moved. After a successful round trip, `SyncFabricState` writes the same rows into `m.lastSnapshot.Fabrics`, and Compile compares plan keys against `m.lastSnapshot`.

## Mechanism, at `fbc51cc02`

1. `pkg/dataplane/userspace/manager_fabric_sync.go:30`: `fabrics := alignFabricVerdicts(build(m.lastSnapshot.Config), m.lastSnapshot)`.
   - The builder samples `ParentLinuxName`, `ParentIfindex` and `RXQueues` from the kernel (`fabric.go:119-124`).
   - `alignFabricVerdicts` keeps only the stored device verdict.
2. `manager_fabric_sync.go:36` sends `update_fabrics`. `:84` writes `m.lastSnapshot.Fabrics = fabrics` after success.
3. `userspace-dp/src/server/handlers/mod.rs:200-236`:
   - `refresh_fabric_links(fabrics)`;
   - then `snapshot.fabrics = fabrics.clone()` on the stored snapshot, plus `content_digest.clear()` and `persist_state`;
   - no replan.
4. `userspace-dp/src/server/helpers/planning.rs:224`: the plan key hashes `fabric={name}/{parent_linux_name}/{parent_ifindex}/{rx_queues}`.
5. `userspace-dp/src/server/handlers/snapshot.rs:219-237`: `same_plan` is `snapshot_binding_plan_key(stored) == snapshot_binding_plan_key(next)`. On the same-plan path only `same_plan_apply_needs_binding_reconcile` (`planning.rs:31-60`) can reconcile.

## Reachability (bounded)

- It needs a fabric row's parent ifindex or RX queue count to change between full applies, while `SyncFabricState` keeps running. For example, the fabric parent netdev is re-created or reset, or its channel count changes.
- A lost `update_fabrics` response can leave the helper in the same state without Go writing `m.lastSnapshot` (#9684). A Compile built with the new values then compares same-plan on the helper.
- Not reproduced. It is not established whether the same-plan reconcile predicate fires in the common cases. For example, a binding on a vanished ifindex that reports an error is excluded from the predicate.

## Consequence (bounded)

Fabric bindings can stay on the previous parent or queue layout while the helper's snapshot describes the new one, and new queues can stay unbound. Cross-chassis fabric forwarding over those queues would be affected. Not measured.

## Fix direction

## #9804 — daemon: the #7191 arm-coverage gate never gates in production (LegacyDataPlaneAdapter does not expose ArmCoverageSummary), and switching it on as written would disarm every node with a GRE interface in a zone [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-17)

## What is wrong

`evaluateArmCoverage` (`pkg/daemon/daemon_arm_coverage_7191.go:92`) gates only when `d.dataplane()` satisfies `armCoverageSource`.

The production runtime is `dpuserspace.Boot()`, which returns `NewLegacyDataPlaneAdapter(New())` (`pkg/dataplane/userspace/manager.go:82-84`). `LegacyDataPlaneAdapter` (`legacy_dataplane.go:39-42`) embeds the `dataplane.DataPlane` interface and keeps the manager in an unexported field. The `ArmCoverageSummary` methods on `*userspace.Manager` (`manager.go:747`) and `*dataplane.Manager` (`armcoverage_publish.go:46`) are therefore not in its method set. The type assertion fails, and the function returns before it reads any proof.

So the #7191 claim does not hold on a production build: that an interface with no shim disarms the box and closes transit (`pkg/daemon/README.md`, "The per-interface attach is now part of the arm state (#7191)").

## Evidence

- **Probe at `fbc51cc02`.** A program asserting `dpuserspace.Boot().(armCoverageSource)` prints `runtime *userspace.LegacyDataPlaneAdapter satisfies armCoverageSource: false`.
- **Tests.** The #7191 cells in `pkg/daemon/transit_barrier_7191_test.go` drive `fakeCoverageDP`, which implements `ArmCoverageSummary` directly, so none of them exercises the published type. No test asserts that the production runtime satisfies `armCoverageSource`.
- **Live cluster.** The journal on `loss:xpf-userspace-fw0` and `fw1`, 2026-09-11 13:13-13:14 UTC:
  - every apply logs `dataplane arm-coverage proof ... ran=true direct=6 delegated=2 skipped=0 uncovered=1 would_gate=true did_gate=false`;
  - the uncovered surface is `gr-0-0-0` ("link-layer type none is not Ethernet");
  - both nodes stay armed.

## Why it cannot simply be switched on

The uncovered surface on the live cluster is the #8279 raw-L3 refusal: a non-Ethernet netdev in a zone is kept out of `pendingXDP` and recorded as an unarmed surface. If the adapter forwarded `ArmCoverageSummary` today, every node with a GRE or other non-Ethernet interface in a zone would disarm at its first apply. Transit would close and the #7178 RG weight would drop. On the loss cluster that is both nodes.

So before the gate can go live, someone has to decide how a recorded raw-L3 refusal counts.

## Consequence

- **An unattached interface still forwards.** A box where Start succeeded but an Ethernet interface failed to attach keeps transit open, with nothing adjudicating that interface. One example is a generic attach failure that is joined as a deferred commit error. This is the hole #7191 describes as closed.
- **The docs describe a gate that is not in effect.** Both `pkg/daemon/README.md` and the comments in `daemon_transit_gate.go` and `daemon_arm_coverage_7191.go` say it gates.

## Fix direction

1. Decide how the proof classifies the #8279 raw-L3 refusal, and any other surface that is recorded but cannot carry the shim, so that a healthy GRE node proves complete.
2. Then forward `ArmCoverageSummary` through `LegacyDataPlaneAdapter`, or have the daemon look through the adapter. Add a test that the published runtime type satisfies `armCoverageSource`.
3. Validate on the loss cluster that neither node disarms after a live apply, and pass `make test-failover`.

## Origin and dedup

- Found while working #9725, the boot window before the first attach. That fix needs a post-attach signal and does not use this proof.
- #7191 introduced the gate, and #8279 introduced the raw-L3 refusal.
- Searches for "ArmCoverageSummary adapter" and "arm coverage gate inert" found no issue.

## #9807 — api: TestLargeEventSurvivesASlowButProgressingReader7632 flakes under host load (60ms per-chunk margin) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-11)

`TestLargeEventSurvivesASlowButProgressingReader7632` (pkg/api) failed once inside a loaded `make test`. At the same head it passes 8/8 on its own.

## Observed

- Head `5e310ded1` (a pkg/cluster-only branch; nothing under pkg/api changed), `make test` with `GOFLAGS=-p=4`, while other lanes' `make test` runs and a cluster deploy build shared the host.
- Output:
  ```
  --- FAIL: TestLargeEventSurvivesASlowButProgressingReader7632 (0.11s)
      sse_slow_reader_pin_7632_test.go:652: a 262144-byte event to a CONTINUOUSLY reading client failed after 3842 payload bytes: EOF — the write budget is measuring elapsed time rather than progress, so one large event severs a healthy reader (#7654 review A,
  FAIL	github.com/psaab/xpf/pkg/api	55.789s
  ```
- `go test -count=8 -run TestLargeEventSurvivesASlowButProgressingReader7632 ./pkg/api` at the same head: ok.

## Why it is timing, not the defect

- The cell sets `sseWriteDeadline = 100ms`.
- Its slow reader moves 32 KiB per 40 ms window, so one `sseWriteChunk` needs 40 ms of a 100 ms window. That is a 60 ms margin, in wall-clock time, on a shared host.
- A scheduler stall longer than that inside one chunk expires the re-armed deadline, and the client sees EOF.
- The failure message then asserts the #7654 defect ("the write budget is measuring elapsed time rather than progress"), which is exactly what this run did not show.

## Suggested direction (not applied)

Keep the FAIL-ON-REVERT property: one window must still be too short for the whole payload. For example, a 400 ms deadline with a payload of 32 or more chunks (1.28 s or more at this rate):
- a single-window write still expires mid-payload;
- a chunked write gets 360 ms of margin per chunk instead of 60 ms.

The message could also name the per-chunk margin, so a load stall is distinguishable from the regression.

Severity: Low. Test-only, but it reds `make test` intermittently under load and misattributes the cause.

Refs #7632, #7654, #7655
