## #9809 — [cohort] config: the #7924 overlap-plus-PBR gate misses steered space written as a prefix-list, bare host, `any` or no-`from` term, and reads a bare member as unit 0, which also drops units >= 1 from the rib-group leak set [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-11)

## What is wrong

This issue covers three findings on one detector, `validateVRFOverlap`, and on the member resolver that `RibGroupConnectedPrefixes` duplicates from it. They share one corrective scope.

1. `SYN-CMP-01` (MATERIAL): the detector misses steered space in several spellings.
   - The #7924 gate refuses overlapping routing-instance address space combined with a PBR `then routing-instance` term.
   - It learns a steering term's space only from literal `source-address`/`destination-address` values that `netip.ParsePrefix` accepts. Anything else is skipped silently.
   - The PBR builder that installs the steers reads more: it expands prefix-lists, maps a bare host to `/32` or `/128`, and treats `any` as match-all. A term with no address match also steers everything.
   - Strict commit therefore accepts the same overlap, with no overlap warning, when it is written as a prefix-list, as a literal in one term and a prefix-list in the other, as a bare host, as `any`, or as a term with no `from`. Written as a literal CIDR, a `/32` or `0.0.0.0/0`, it is refused.
   - The tolerant path runs the same detector, so it records no tolerant admission and the admission metric stays silent.
2. `SYN-CMP-02` (MATERIAL): a bare member is read as unit 0.
   - The detector and `RibGroupConnectedPrefixes` both read a bare member (`interface ge-0/0/1`) as unit 0 only. Since #9132, the userspace FIB binds every configured unit of a bare member (`InterfaceUnitRefKeys`).
   - Rib-group arm (the consequence that stands):
     - An `interface-routes rib-group` leak for a bare member never includes the connected prefixes of units ≥ 1.
     - When unit 0 is addressed, those prefixes are silently missing.
     - When unit 0 is unaddressed, strict commit warns that the members are "DHCP-only or unaddressed" and installs no leak rule.
   - Detector arm: overlap on unit ≥ 1 of a bare member is not seen. Since #7160, that unit's native flows carry the instance's routing domain, so this arm is a gate-contract inconsistency with no demonstrated collision.
3. `SYN-C-CMP-07` (COHORT): the gate's rationale text predates #7160.

   - #9519 now re-evaluates policy on a hit from another zone, so "never adjudicated by any policy" is also stale.

## #9810 — [cohort] routing: the next-table window is counted per leak at commit and in the FIB/show verdict but spent per ingress interface by the applier; lo0 units add detached next-table and PBR rules [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-16)

## What is wrong

This issue covers two defects in how the next-table ip-rule window (`NextTableRuleWindow = 100`) is accounted. They share one corrective scope.

1. `SYN-WIN-01`: the counting unit.
   - Since #9420, the kernel applier installs one rule per default-instance ingress interface for each next-table leak, and draws the window down leak-atomically. A leak therefore costs N slots for N ingress interfaces.
   - The strict commit gate and `StaticRouteExclusions` still count one slot per leak. The userspace FIB builder and the `show` surfaces use the `StaticRouteExclusions` verdict.
   - For L leaks with L ≤ 100 < L·N:
     - the commit gate passes;
     - the FIB and `show` publish all L leaks;
     - the kernel installs only ⌊100/N⌋ leaks and reports the rest as dropped.
2. `SYN-LO0-02`: loopback.
   - The comment on the scoping set and two docs say loopback is deliberately excluded. `DefaultInstanceIngressIfaces` has no loopback filter.
   - An unclaimed `lo0` unit, as in the host-inbound filter idiom `interfaces lo0 unit 0`, therefore contributes the ingress name `lo0`.
   - No kernel device has that name. Each leak gets an extra rule that installs detached and never matches, and N grows by one per `lo0` unit.

## Mechanism, at `7b1cb4511c093ea965b6588bfa14f13ed76abad6`

- `pkg/routing/rules.go:244` drops a whole leak when `prio+len(ingressIfaces)` exceeds the window. `:280-296` installs one rule per ingress interface (`rule.IifName = iif`, `:286`) and advances `prio` by that count.
- `pkg/config/compiler_validate_strict_routing_rulewindows.go:34-54`: `nextTableRouteCount` counts one per next-table route. Its comment still says the applier feeds "one rule per next-table route" into the window. The gate compares that count against `NextTableRuleWindow = 100` (`pkg/config/types_system.go:1052`).
- `pkg/config/static_route_exclusion_reason.go:82-115`: `StaticRouteExclusions` admits one leak per `window++` (`:114`).
- The same one-slot verdict feeds the userspace FIB builder (`pkg/dataplane/userspace/routes.go:99-121`, called at `:103`). It also feeds the `show` surfaces (`pkg/cli/cli_show_routing.go:912,1018`; `pkg/grpcapi/server_show_routes_text.go:318`).
- `pkg/routing/rules.go:347-353` says "Loopback is deliberately EXCLUDED", and so do `docs/rib-group-route-leaking.md:252` and `pkg/routing/README.md:410-412`.
  - The function body (`:354-407`) excludes only claimed interfaces and units.
  - `pkg/config/compiler_derivations.go:100-106` reads the `lo0` input filter from `Interfaces["lo0"].Units[0]`, so `lo0 unit 0` is the configured idiom.
  - The unit resolves to the ingress name `lo0`, not the kernel `lo`: `LinuxIfName` (`pkg/config/types.go:12`) only rewrites `/` to `-`.

Executed on this host's kernel (7.0.13) in a private user and network namespace (`unshare -Urn`):

- `ip rule add pref 32000 iif lo0 table main` returned 0 and lists as `from all iif lo0 [detached] lookup main`.
- The control, `ip rule add pref 32001 iif lo table main`, returned 0 and lists attached.

Test coverage at the pin:

- `TestDefaultInstanceIngressIfaces_9420` (`pkg/routing/rules_9420_test.go:164`) has no `lo0` fixture.
- The #6467 cap and agreement cells use a single ingress interface (`testNextTableIifs`, `pkg/routing/rules_test.go:1115`), where the two counting units coincide.

## Cohort members (same fix pass)

- `LEAD-O4` (COHORT, Low): an `lo0` input filter with a `then routing-instance` term builds PBR rules scoped to the nonexistent `lo0`.

## #9811 — daemon: a commit-confirmed auto-rollback whose apply fails is only logged, so the node keeps enforcing the abandoned config with no retry and no degraded status [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-12)

## What is wrong

When a `commit confirmed` times out, the daemon promotes the rollback target (C1) in the store and then re-applies it. If that apply fails, the failure is only logged; nothing retries it.

- A dataplane-phase failure leaves the abandoned configuration (C2) enforced under the #5679 contract. A routing-phase failure leaves a mixed C1/C2 state.
- The store and `show configuration` report C1 in both cases, and the peer is re-synced to C1.
- `/health` keeps a healthy status.

On the commit path, the operator sees such an apply failure and re-commits. This timer callback has no caller to report to, so the node keeps enforcing C2 until some later apply happens to succeed.

## Mechanism, at `7b1cb4511c093ea965b6588bfa14f13ed76abad6`

1. `pkg/daemon/daemon_apply_commit.go:827` (`executeConfirmedRollback`) promotes the store first: `prevCfg, ok := d.store.PromoteRollback(gen)` (`:843`; `pkg/configstore/store_commit.go:1120`).
2. Its comment says the dataplane "MUST be brought into agreement unconditionally" (`:916-919`). The apply outcome is only logged: `if err := d.applyConfigLocked(context.Background(), prevCfg); err != nil { slog.Error("commit confirmed auto-rollback dataplane apply failed", ...) }` (`:928-930`).
3. `d.resyncRolledBackConfigToPeer()` then runs whatever the apply outcome was (`:953`; the helper is at `:966` and no-ops when no peer is eligible).
4. `pkg/daemon/daemon_apply_dataplane.go:174-195` (#5679): an ordinary full-apply failure calls `recordCompileFailure(err)` (`:176`) and leaves the old compiled policy live. The comment says an identical re-commit or the feed retry (#5646) self-heals it, because the applied config never advanced. The timer path has neither.
5. `pkg/api/health.go`:
   - it reports `degraded` only when the dataplane compile has never succeeded (`:35-39`) or config persistence failed (`:65-72`);
   - a failure after an earlier success sets only the non-fatal `compile_last_error_unix` timestamp (`:32-34`, fed by `pkg/daemon/daemon_health.go:110-129`, which logs a WARN);
   - a routing-phase error from the apply tail is not recorded there at all.

## Reachability (bounded)

- A `commit confirmed` whose rollback target is a real prior config (not a first commit on a fresh store) times out, and the rollback apply then fails. For example, a transient helper or control-socket error hits the dataplane publish, or an ip-rule or route-leak reconcile error hits the routing tail.
- No attacker is needed.

## Consequence (bounded)

- The node enforces C2, or a mixed C1/C2 state, while its store, `show configuration` and the peer hold C1. That is inter-node enforcement divergence, and on the dataplane arm it is a fail-open-to-stale sibling of #5679.
- The divergence lasts until a later apply of any kind succeeds, such as a commit, DHCP or feed callback, or peer sync.
- The only signals are an ERROR log line and, for a dataplane-phase failure, the `compile_last_error_unix` timestamp.

## What does not cover it

- #5679 (closed) makes a returning commit caller see the dataplane failure; this callback has no caller.
- The #5680 guard (`pkg/dataplane/userspace/manager_overlay.go:176-180`) refuses to publish an old-policy/new-route hybrid as applied. It does not retry the rollback.
- #9693 was closed after the pin by `a665e39f6`. Per its commit message, an apply now latches a routing-reconcile debt from the ip-rule and route-leak errors, and a loop re-runs that reconcile every 30 s while the debt is owed. That covers the routing-phase arm. It never re-applies the dataplane, so it does not cover a dataplane apply failure or the missing status.
- #9615 was closed after the pin by `f817593e9`, which pre-flights the rollback target at fire time, before `PromoteRollback`. A refused target is deferred or sent to the bootstrap safe state. An appliable target still "rolls back and applies exactly as before", so a transient apply failure of a validated target is still only logged.

## #9813 — daemon/HA: the #6791 fabric recovery loop re-creates fab0/fab1 outside vrf-mgmt, and nothing re-binds VRF members between applies, so VRF-bound session sync is stranded until the next apply [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-12)

## What is wrong

VRF devices and their slave bindings are created and bound only during a config apply. Nothing re-asserts VRF slave membership between applies.

The product's own recovery loop reaches this gap:
- The #6791 fabric reassert loop re-creates a missing `fab0`/`fab1` IPVLAN overlay between applies.
- It creates the device with only a name and a parent, so the re-created overlay is not a slave of `vrf-mgmt`.
- Session sync binds its sockets to the management VRF device, so sync over that fabric stays down until the next apply of any kind re-binds the management interfaces.

The same gap covers any netdev re-created outside an apply, for example by a driver re-probe, a VF reset or an operator `ip link set nomaster`. This includes tenant routing-instance members.

## Mechanism, at `7b1cb4511c093ea965b6588bfa14f13ed76abad6`

1. VRF membership is written only on the apply path.
   - The production callers of `BindInterfaceToVRF` are `pkg/daemon/daemon_apply_interfaces.go:277,316,353` and `pkg/routing/tunnel.go:1107`.
   - `ReconcileVRFs` is called only at `daemon_apply_interfaces.go:221`.
2. Management interfaces (`fxp*`, `fab*`, `em*`; `pkg/config/ifname_class_6731.go:127-131`) are bound to `vrf-mgmt` at apply step 0b (`daemon_apply_interfaces.go:257-283`). After networkd, `rebindManagementVRFIfaces` binds them again (`:309-323`, called at `pkg/daemon/daemon_apply_dataplane.go:485-488`). The step's comment records that `networkctl reconfigure` strips the master because networkd ignores `VRF=` for the daemon-created `vrf-mgmt` (`daemon_apply_dataplane.go:457-460`).
3. None of the always-on loops started in `pkg/daemon/daemon_run.go` touches VRF membership. Those are: proxy-ARP (`:591`), RA (`:605`), host-inbound conntrack (`:618`), management listener (`:633`), fabric IPVLAN (`:651`), service-reload debt (`:667`) and DDNS (`:679,691`).
4. `fabricIPVLANReassertLoop` exists because in-apply creation retries five times and then gives up. The motivating case is a parent NIC still being renamed after a power cycle (`pkg/daemon/daemon_fabric_reassert.go:38-47`).
   - Every 30 s (`:24`), `missingFabricOverlays` treats an overlay as healthy when it exists and is administratively up (`:79-101`).
   - `reassertFabricIPVLANOnce` re-creates a missing overlay through `fabricEnsureFn(ov.parent, ov.name, ov.addrs)` (`:165-195`, call at `:189`).
5. `ensureFabricIPVLAN` (`pkg/daemon/daemon_ha_fabric.go:24-66`) builds `&netlink.IPVlan{LinkAttrs{Name, ParentIndex}}` with no master (`:57-66`). It also deletes and re-creates an overlay it finds on the wrong parent (`:53-55`). Its comment says the overlay carries the fabric IP used for session sync (`:20-23`).
6. Session sync listens and dials through `vrfListenConfig(s.vrfDevice)` (`pkg/cluster/sync_conn.go:855,868,1037`). That device is set once, at `pkg/daemon/daemon_ha_sync.go:990`.

## Reachability (bounded)

- On HA nodes, a fabric overlay can be missing between applies in two ways:
  - in-apply creation exhausted its retries, which is the loop's own motivating case;
  - a parent netdev re-registration deleted the IPVLAN child.
- For tenant members, the trigger is netdev re-creation, or an out-of-band `nomaster`, outside an apply.
- RETH MAC programming, link down/up and device-map renames keep the kernel master, so they are not triggers.
- No attacker is needed.

## Consequence (bounded)

- The re-created fabric overlay holds the fabric address outside `vrf-mgmt`. Session sync over that fabric is down until an apply binds the overlay again.
  - A dual-fabric node keeps sync on the surviving link.
  - The window ends at the next apply of any kind (commit, DHCP callback, config poll, feed, cluster sync). Those applies are event-driven, not periodic.
- A re-created tenant member forwards in the default instance on the kernel path until the next apply.

## #9814 — [cohort] config: routing-instance `instance-type` is a free string, so a typo such as `forwardng` silently makes a VRF, and `vrf-target`/`vrf-table-label`/`route-distinguisher` are inert with no warning [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-16)

## What is wrong

This issue covers two routing-instance statements that commit clean and do something other than what they say. They share one corrective scope: value and closed-world validation of `routing-instances <name>`.

1. `DUP-CMP08` (MATERIAL): `instance-type` accepts any value.
   - The schema leaf has no validator, and the compiler stores the raw token. Every consumer tests only for the literal `"forwarding"`.
   - A mistyped or unimplemented type (`forwardng`, `no-forwarding`, `bogus`) commits clean with no warning, and so does an omitted type. In every case the instance is treated as a VRF.
   - The repository records that this is the harmful direction. Per `schema_routing.go:938-941`, `forwarding` is what makes the daemon skip VRF creation, so losing the value "creates a VRF the operator asked NOT to have and moves interfaces into it".
   - The originating report recorded this as a duplicate of a finding in an earlier review report. That finding was never filed and has no GitHub issue, so it is related work, not an owner.
2. `SYN-CMP-04` (COHORT): three L3VPN statements are accepted and inert with no warning.
   - `vrf-target`, `vrf-table-label` and `route-distinguisher` are deliberately accepted and inert (#9323), and their help text says so.
   - Unlike inert per-instance protocols (#9374), they draw no commit or load warning.
   - The consequence is an unmet VPN route-exchange expectation, not lost isolation.

## Mechanism, at `7b1cb4511c093ea965b6588bfa14f13ed76abad6`

- `pkg/config/schema_routing.go:990` declares `"instance-type": {desc: "Routing instance type", args: 1, placeholder: "<type>", children: nil}` with no validator.
- The compiler stores the raw token: `ri.InstanceType = child.Keys[i+1]` (`pkg/config/compiler_routing.go:614-617`) and `ri.InstanceType = nodeVal(prop)` (`:676-677`).
- Every consumer branches on the literal `"forwarding"`:
  - `pkg/daemon/daemon_apply_interfaces.go:198,348` (VRF creation and member binding);
  - `pkg/daemon/daemon_run_routehelpers.go:137,454,514,547`;
  - `pkg/daemon/daemon_ipmon.go:157`;
  - `pkg/config/junos_host_deny.go:976`;
  - `pkg/dataplane/compiler_iface.go:527,1561`;
  - `pkg/dataplane/compiler_filter.go:33`;
  - `pkg/cli/apply.go:323`;
  - the #9409 strict gate (`pkg/config/compiler_validate_strict_forwarding_protocols_9409.go:59`).
- `pkg/config/schema_routing.go:938-941` and `pkg/config/compiler_routing.go:586-589` state that `InstanceType == "forwarding"` makes the daemon skip VRF creation.
- Documented supported values:
  - `instance-type forwarding` for filter-based forwarding (`docs/multi-wan.md:314`);
  - `virtual-router` or `vrf` for a VRF (`docs/multi-wan.md:329`, `pkg/config/types_routing.go:776`).
- The three VPN statements are declared at `pkg/config/schema_routing.go:986-988` with the desc "accepted; xpf compiles no BGP/MPLS VPN state from it". The #9323 decision to accept them is recorded at `:951-968`.
- The #9374 precedent emits "... is ACCEPTED but NOT APPLIED" for inert per-instance protocols (`pkg/config/routing_instance_inert_protocols_9374.go:66-77`).

## #9815 — [cohort] daemon/routing: a routing-instance member spelled differently from its interfaces stanza (dash vs slash) binds the wrong netdev and stays in the default next-table scoping set [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-17)

## What is wrong

This issue covers two findings that share one root cause: routing-instance members are resolved using their raw spelling.
- `LEAD-F66` (MATERIAL): the kernel VRF bind misses a unit member whose spelling differs from its stanza.
- `SYN-VRF-02` (COHORT): the default-instance next-table scoping set misreads the same spelling split. It is described in its own section below.

The bare-member bind finding from the same report is #9754.

Interface references may be written with slashes (`ge-0/0/0.1`) or dashes (`ge-0-0-0.1`), and the repository supports both spellings (#8829).

To bind a routing-instance unit member to its VRF, the daemon looks up the `interfaces` stanza using the member's raw base spelling. When the member and the stanza use different spellings, that lookup misses and the unit's vlan-id is unknown. The bind then targets one of two wrong netdevs:

- `base.<unit number>`, which does not exist when the vlan-id differs from the unit number; or
- for a tagged unit 0, the parent netdev.

The real VLAN sub-interface is never enslaved, and the commit is strict-clean.

## Mechanism, at `7b1cb4511c093ea965b6588bfa14f13ed76abad6`

1. `pkg/daemon/daemon_apply_interfaces.go:342-360`: `bindRoutingInstanceMembers` binds the netdev returned by `riMemberLinuxName(cfg, tunMap, ifaceName)`.
2. `pkg/daemon/daemon_run_routehelpers.go:97-123`: `riMemberLinuxName` canonicalizes only the unit suffix (`config.CanonicalInterfaceUnitRef`, `pkg/config/schema_validators.go:253-263`) and returns `logicalUnitDeviceKeyForRef`.
3. `pkg/daemon/daemon_run_routehelpers.go:77-95`: `logicalUnitDeviceKeyForRef` looks up `cfg.Interfaces.Interfaces[baseRef]` using the raw base spelling (`:88-93`). On a miss, `unit` stays nil. `logicalUnitDeviceKey` then returns `base.<unitNum>` for a non-zero unit, or `base` for unit 0 (`:56-67`).
4. The same helper also keys the connected-prefix producer and the claimed-by-VRF set (`pkg/daemon/daemon_run_routehelpers.go:383,467`).
5. By contrast, the DHCP lease map matches the stanza by kernel name, `config.LinuxIfName(name) == base` (`pkg/daemon/daemon_flow.go:91-102`).

Executed at the pin with a bounded Go probe in a scratch worktree. The config was a vlan-tagging `ge-0/0/0` with unit 0 on vlan 10 and unit 1 on vlan 50, and strict `CompileConfig` accepts every row below.

- Member `ge-0-0-0.1` binds `ge-0-0-0.1`, which does not exist. The control `ge-0/0/0.1` binds `ge-0-0-0.50`.
- Member `ge-0-0-0.0` binds `ge-0-0-0`, the parent. The parent exists, so the bind succeeds silently. The control `ge-0/0/0.0` binds `ge-0-0-0.10`.
- Reverse spelling (dash stanza `ge-0-0-0`, member `ge-0/0/0.1`) binds `ge-0-0-0.1`. The control binds `ge-0-0-0.50`.
- In each row the DHCP lease map attributes the tagged unit to the VRF.

This was already present at the report base; `pkg/daemon/daemon_run_routehelpers.go` has not changed since then.

## Reachability (bounded)

- A routing-instance unit member whose base spelling differs from the `interfaces` stanza key, and whose unit number differs from its vlan-id. A tagged unit 0 is also affected.
- Strict commit accepts both spellings.

## #9818 — cluster: a new peer process's connection installed before any reboot evidence is evicted as a corpse by the later retirement [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-17)

Found while reconciling the two peer-reboot classifiers (#9636). This is pre-existing, and #9636 does not change it.

## Defect

A peer reboot is retired by one of two classifiers:
- `installConn` retires it on a raised heartbeat boot epoch, or on a supersession;
- the BulkStart switch retires it on a changed boot id.

Either way the retirement advances `peerIncarnation`, and `evictStaleIncarnationConnsLocked` then evicts every installed connection whose stamp is older.

A connection from the NEW process that installed BEFORE any evidence of the reboot arrived is stamped with the OLD incarnation. The later retirement evicts it as a corpse. That leaves a dual-fabric cluster on one fabric until the peer redials, and it owes another cold prime.

#9636 closes the orderings where one classifier has already retired the reboot and the other arrives later: each consumes the other's record. The shapes below have no earlier classification to consume. The install could not attribute the connection to either process:
- the epoch had not landed;
- nothing was superseded;
- an install after a full disconnect never advances the incarnation.

## Executed

Cells drive `handleNewConnection` and send frames on the stored connection. `A` is primed and acked on fabric 0, with epoch 100. Results are identical on `3cfc88ceb` and on the #9636 fix:

| ordering | advances | fabric 0 | fabric 1 | arms | OnPeerConnected |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A's sockets gone (full disconnect); B installs fab1, then fab0; B's BulkStart on fab1 | 1 | **empty (B's fab0 evicted)** | B | 2 | 2 |
| A still on fab0; B installs fab1 before its heartbeat; the epoch lands; B's fab0 supersedes A | 1 | B | **empty (B's fab1 evicted)** | 1 | 1 |
| full disconnect; B installs fab1 before its heartbeat; the epoch lands; B installs fab0 | 1 | B | **empty (B's fab1 evicted)** | 2 | 2 |

In the first row both `OnPeerConnected` dispatches are installs: B's first install after the full disconnect, then its fab0 install, which becomes preferred while the prime is owed.

## Why it is not a local fix

Nothing a connection carries at install time says which peer PROCESS dialled it:
- the boot id arrives only on a BulkStart, and a sibling fabric never primes;
- the heartbeat epoch is node-wide, not per connection, and it can land after either install;
- a sibling of the new process and a corpse of a flapped-then-rebooted old process look identical to the classifier.

So both the switch and the epoch arm treat every older stamp as a corpse.

Closing it needs a per-connection process identity, sent on every installed connection before either classifier acts. For example, the sender's boot epoch and boot id could be carried in the capabilities exchange that `handleNewConnection` already sends on each connection (an HA wire ADD). Retirement would then evict only connections whose announced identity is the retired process's, and would fall back to today's rule for a peer that announces none.

## #9819 — routing: a VRF table miss falls through to main and to rib-group leaked source tables because no per-VRF terminator is installed, so VRF-context kernel lookups leave the instance [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-11)

## What is wrong

This issue covers two findings about a kernel lookup that misses in a VRF table. They share one fix.

1. `SYN-MISS-04` (MATERIAL): no per-VRF miss terminator.
   - xpf creates VRF tables and binds members, but installs nothing that ends a lookup that misses the VRF's table.
   - The kernel `l3mdev` rule is a `lookup` rule, so a miss continues down the rule list, into `main` among other tables.
   - VRF-context kernel lookups can therefore leave the instance through the default table. On the default posture these are traffic arriving on a VRF slave that the userspace dataplane does not adjudicate, and traffic from VRF-bound sockets.
2. `SYN-RIB-03` (COHORT, inside the same fix): the rib-group band catches those misses.
   - The rib-group leak rule has no ingress scope and sits in the 30000 band, after `l3mdev` and before `main`.
   - A VRF-context lookup that misses its own table, for a destination inside a leaked prefix, therefore resolves in the leak's source-instance table.
   - Scoping the band by ingress interface is neither necessary nor sufficient: those lookups would then fall through to `main` instead. A terminal default in each VRF table closes both.

A documentation residual belongs to the same area.
- `docs/rib-group-route-leaking.md:259-264` says the AF_XDP fast path "was never exposed" because the userspace FIB is "instance-scoped by construction".
- That holds only for PBR-steered traffic. Without PBR, the fast path does no per-instance destination-FIB selection, as `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/forwarding/README.md:400-408` documents.
- This residual comes from the report's SYN-FWD-02 record. All three reviewers dismissed that record's forwarding claim as a documented limitation, and all three named this sentence as misleading.

## Mechanism, at `7b1cb4511c093ea965b6588bfa14f13ed76abad6`

- The rib-group leak rule sets only `Dst`, `Table`, `Priority` and `Family`, with no `IifName` (`pkg/routing/rules.go:634-638`).
  - Its band starts at `ribGroupLeakRulePriority = 30000` and spans 30000-30999 (`:66-67`).
  - That is after the kernel `l3mdev` rule at 1000 and before `main` at 32766.
- Nothing installs a miss terminator. The coordinator's census over non-test Go under `pkg/` and `cmd/` found:
  - no `RTN_THROW`, `RTN_PROHIBIT`, `FR_ACT_PROHIBIT` or `FR_ACT_UNREACHABLE`, and no `"throw"` or `"prohibit"`;
  - `RTN_UNREACHABLE` only as the label for `reject` statics (`pkg/routing/routes.go:240-242`).

  The FRR renderer's only default blackhole is the global `ip route 0.0.0.0/0 Null0 250` (`pkg/frr/config_render.go:578`).
- VRF slaves that the userspace dataplane does not adjudicate:
  - The AF_XDP exclusion classes cover `fxp`, `em`, `fab` and `lo0` names and route-based IPsec secure tunnels (`pkg/dataplane/userspace/ingress_exclusions.go:131-146`).
  - Management interfaces are bound to `vrf-mgmt` at apply (`pkg/daemon/daemon_apply_interfaces.go:257-283,309-323`).
  - Management DHCP routes go into table 999 directly (`pkg/routing/fibimport.go:92-103`), so a covering default exists only while a lease carrying a router does.
- Armed transit is gated only by the two global forwarding sysctls (`pkg/daemon/daemon_transit_gate.go:91-102`). The forward-hook barrier exists only while unarmed (`pkg/nftables/transit_barrier.go:18-39`).
- For contrast, a userspace NoRoute on an uncapped default-deny box evaluates zone 0 and falls to the default action (`userspace-dp/src/policy.rs:3018-3030`). Traffic bound to AF_XDP is therefore not the exposed arm.

Executed at the pin in a private user and network namespace (kernel 7.0.13):
- Topology:
  - `vrfa` (table 100) with slave `slavea` at 10.10.0.1/24;
  - `vrfsrc` (table 200) with slave `slavesrc` at 10.30.0.1/24;
  - `xmain` at 10.20.0.1/24, with the `main` default route via 10.20.0.254.

## #9820 — [cohort] frr: an IPv6 static route with an IPv4 next hop commits clean and renders inert, or with an interface as a line FRR cannot parse; backup-router family checks disagree on IPv4-mapped literals; OSPF area IDs render raw [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-14)

## What is wrong

This issue covers three render-path gaps that share one fix: a single address-family and area-ID predicate used by both the commit gates and the FRR render belts.

1. `SYN-FRR-02` (MATERIAL): an IPv6 static route with an IPv4 next hop commits clean and renders as an inert route.
   - The static-route renderer picks `ip` or `ipv6` from the destination alone. The commit validators accept a destination and a next hop of either family.
   - `routing-options static route 2001:db8::/32 next-hop 192.0.2.1` therefore renders `ipv6 route 2001:db8::/32 192.0.2.1 5`.
   - FRR's `ipv6 route` grammar has no IPv4 gateway alternative, so `192.0.2.1` can only fill the interface-name slot. The result is a route to a nonexistent interface, which installs nothing. The commit reports success.
   - With an interface (`next-hop 192.0.2.1 interface ge-0/0/1.0`, or a `qualified-next-hop` with an interface), the renderer emits `ipv6 route 2001:db8::/32 192.0.2.1 ge-0/0/1 5`. No FRR `ipv6 route` command parses that line, so it breaks the managed-section reload instead of installing nothing.
   - The opposite direction, an IPv4 destination with an IPv6 next hop, is a supported FRR form (`ip route ... <A.B.C.D|X:X::X:X>`) and is not part of this issue. The report's second row, a space-separated community member, is valid FRR grammar and is not part of this issue either.
2. `SYN-FRR-04` (COHORT): the three backup-router family predicates disagree on IPv4-mapped IPv6 literals.
   - The commit validator classifies by the presence of a colon.
   - The render belt classifies by `netip` and treats `::ffff:a.b.c.d` as IPv4.
   - The emission classifies by `strings.Contains(":")`.
3. `SYN-FRR-05` (COHORT): OSPF and OSPFv3 area IDs are rendered raw.
   - `ValidateOSPFArea` accepts an IPv4-mapped IPv6 literal, so a strict commit renders ` ip ospf area ::ffff:192.0.2.1`. FRR's area argument grammar takes only `<A.B.C.D|(0-4294967295)>`.
   - On the tolerant load and peer-sync path, a malformed area such as `"0 1"` renders raw too, as ` ip ospf area 0 1`. #9493's belt covers only the virtual-link transit area.

## Mechanism, at `7b1cb4511c093ea965b6588bfa14f13ed76abad6`

- `SYN-FRR-02`:
  - `pkg/frr/config_render.go:141` sets `isV6 := strings.Contains(sr.Destination, ":")` and picks `ip` or `ipv6` from it (`:142-145`).
  - The next-hop belt checks only that the address parses (`:233`; `validFRRNextHopAddress` is `netip.ParseAddr`, `pkg/frr/render_validate.go:119-126`). A next hop with both an address and an interface is rendered as `<address> <interface>` (`:241-242`). The route is emitted at `:263`.
  - `ValidateRouteDestination` is documented as family-agnostic (`pkg/config/schema_validators_routing.go:125-135`). `ValidateStaticNextHop` accepts any IP literal (`:170,188`).
  - No strict static-route gate compares the two families. The only family check found is the backup-router one below.
- `SYN-FRR-04`:
  - `natAddrFamily` returns `v6` for any spelling with a colon (`pkg/config/compiler_nat_helpers.go:28-36`).
  - `validateBackupRouterDst` returns before any family comparison when the destination is empty (`pkg/config/compiler_system.go:3680`).
  - The render belt compares `frrOperandIsV6`, i.e. `Is6() && !Is4In6()` (`pkg/frr/render_validate.go:224-232`), at `pkg/frr/config_render.go:512-520`. It warns that "FRR rejects a mismatched-family static route".
  - The emission picks the family with `strings.Contains` (`:527,537`) and renders at `:540`.
- `SYN-FRR-05`:
  - Both area keys carry `keyValidator: ValidateOSPFArea` (`pkg/config/schema_routing.go:335,385`). Its IP arm returns nil for any address whose `To4()` is non-nil, which includes an IPv4-mapped IPv6 literal (`pkg/config/schema_validators_network.go:207-211`).
  - The tolerant path downgrades a schema violation to a warning and continues (`pkg/configstore/store.go:683`).
  - The compiler stores the key raw (`pkg/config/compiler_protocols.go:81`). The renderer interpolates it raw at `pkg/frr/protocols_render.go:92,94` (area stanza), `:180` (` ip ospf area %s`) and `:193` (OSPFv3 ` interface %s area %s`).
  - #9493's `ValidateOSPFArea` belt guards only the virtual-link line (`:100-106`).

Upstream FRR stable/10.6 grammar, from the source files:
- `staticd/static_vty.c`:
  - `ip_route_cmd` accepts `<<A.B.C.D|X:X::X:X>$gate|<INTERFACE|Null0>$ifname>`;
  - `ipv6_route_cmd` accepts `<X:X::X:X$gate|<INTERFACE|Null0>$ifname>`;

## #9821 — [cohort] config/routing: a declared interface whose name contains a dot, used as a routing-instance member, is parsed as a unit reference by most consumers, so its instance attribution, kernel bind and warning disagree [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-15)

## What is wrong

Interface names may contain a dot. A declared interface such as `ge-0/0/5.0` can therefore also be used verbatim as a routing-instance member, and strict commit accepts it.

The config resolver follows #8994's rule that a declared name outranks a parse, so it resolves the member to that interface's device. Most member consumers ignore that rule and cut the name at the first dot, treating it as unit 0 of an undeclared `ge-0/0/5`. The consumers then disagree about the member:
- the snapshot puts the instance on the base row, not on the unit row that carries the address;
- the kernel bind targets a different netdev;
- the overlap detector and the rib-group prefix set skip the member;
- the commit warning says a declared interface is "not in interfaces config".

This is a cohort item. It shares its root cause with the member-resolver issues from the same report: #9809 (overlap detector and rib-group resolver) and #9815 (member spelling).

## Mechanism, at `7b1cb4511c093ea965b6588bfa14f13ed76abad6`

- A dot is an allowed interface-name character (`pkg/config/validate_interface_name.go:58-66`).
- `resolveKernelIfNameWith` applies the declared-name-first rule (`pkg/config/types.go:268-290`), so the member resolves to the declared device, `ge-0-0-5.0`.
- These consumers cut at the first dot instead:
  - the routing-instance member warning takes the text before the first dot as the base (`pkg/config/compiler_validate_warn.go:499-508`);
  - the strict unit-reference check validates the text after the first dot as a logical unit (`pkg/config/compiler_validate_strict_unitref.go:59-69`);
  - the overlap detector (`pkg/config/compiler_validate_vrf_overlap.go:143-158`) and `RibGroupConnectedPrefixes` (`pkg/config/compiler_routing.go:1662-1675`) look up the undotted base and skip the member when it is not declared;
  - `logicalUnitDeviceKeyForRef` looks the stanza up by the raw base (`pkg/daemon/daemon_run_routehelpers.go:88-94`), so the kernel bind targets `ge-0-0-5` rather than the declared device.
- `InterfaceUnitRefKeys` returns only the literal member key (`pkg/config/host_inbound_effective_view.go:72-77`).
- When two snapshot rows share one ifindex, the Rust forwarding builder handles their fields differently (`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/forwarding_build/interfaces.rs:236-251`):
  - it inserts the routing-instance name unconditionally, so the name comes from whichever row is processed last;
  - it inserts the routing domain only when the domain is non-zero.

  The name and the domain recorded for that ifindex can therefore come from different rows.

Executed at the pin with a bounded Go probe through strict `CompileConfig` and the userspace snapshot builder, re-run by the coordinator. The config declares `ge-0/0/5.0` with `unit 0 family inet address 10.55.0.1/24`, and routing instance `RA` names `interface ge-0/0/5.0`:
- Strict commit accepts the config, with the warning `routing-instance "RA": interface "ge-0/0/5.0" not in interfaces config`.
- `InterfaceUnitRefKeys` returns `[ge-0/0/5.0]`.
- The snapshot rows are `ge-0/0/5.0.0{ri="" dom=0 linux=ge-0-0-5.0}` and `ge-0/0/5.0{ri=RA linux=ge-0-0-5.0}`. Both rows name one kernel device, and the instance is on the base row.
- The undotted control `ge-0/0/6.0` gives `ge-0/0/6.0{ri=RA}` and `ge-0/0/6{ri=""}`: the instance is on the address-carrying unit row.

## Reachability (bounded)

- Only a config that declares an interface whose name contains a numeric dot and uses that name verbatim as a routing-instance member.
- Strict commit accepts it and emits only a misleading warning.
- No attacker is needed.

## #9822 — cluster: TestAStoreWalkRePrimeDischargesTheFence_9508 failed under a full make test (session sync disconnected during barrier wait) and passes alone [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-12)

## What happened

`pkg/cluster` failed during a full `make test` on `fix/9712-syncookie-rollback-policy` at `3b7b85af3`. That branch changes only docs and Rust test comments.

```
--- FAIL: TestAStoreWalkRePrimeDischargesTheFence_9508 (0.02s)
    barrier_connection_causal_9508_test.go:320: #9508: after the store-walk re-prime was ACKed, a barrier must complete: session sync disconnected during barrier wait seq=2
```

The log line just before the failure reports `ordered stream moved to another fabric connection; readiness barriers are fenced until a re-prime is acked fence_epoch=1 released_barrier_waiters=1`. In that run the package took 87 s.

On the same tree, the test alone passed five times in a row (`go test -count=5 -run 'TestAStoreWalkRePrimeDischargesTheFence_9508$' ./pkg/cluster/`, 0.08 s).

## Why it matters

`make test` gates every merge. An intermittent red in `pkg/cluster` blocks unrelated merges, and it reads like a regression in whatever the branch changed.

## Not established

- The failure rate, and whether it depends on load: the failing run was the full `make test`.
- Whether the race is in the test or in the code under test.

## Origin

- The test came in with `3d1dcdc3d` ("cluster: fence the readiness barrier when the sync stream changes connection").
- A search for the test name found no existing issue.

## #9824 — userspace: a partial update that lands while Compile builds leaves Compile's snapshot at an older generation, and the XSK-startup deferral then never publishes the new config [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-15)

## What is wrong

`Compile` reserves its snapshot generation, then builds the snapshot outside `m.mu`. A partial update that succeeds in that window advances the manager's generation, and when the last full snapshot was published, it advances `publishedSnapshot` too.

`applyCompiledSnapshot` then takes `m.mu` with a snapshot whose generation is below both. On the XSK-startup deferral branch it stores that snapshot as `m.lastSnapshot` without publishing it. From then on `syncSnapshotLocked` returns at its first check (`publishedSnapshot >= lastSnapshot.Generation`), so the compiled config is not published by the status loop.

## Mechanism, at `fbc51cc02`

1. `pkg/dataplane/userspace/manager_compile.go:256` calls `buildSnapshotWithSchedulerStateAndNATCounters(cfg, ucfg, m.bumpGeneration(), ...)`. `bumpGeneration` takes and releases `m.mu`, and the build runs without it.
2. A partial update succeeds in that window, and `advanceGenerationAfterPartialUpdateLocked` runs (`manager_generation.go:181-194`; callers `manager_neighbor.go:141`, `manager_fabric_sync.go:90`):
   - it bumps `m.generation` and sets `m.lastSnapshot.Generation` to it;
   - if the full snapshot was published, it also sets `m.publishedSnapshot` to the new generation.
3. `applyCompiledSnapshot` (`manager_compile.go:334`) evaluates `pendingXSKStartup` (`:358`). On that branch, `m.lastSnapshot = snap` (`:449`) stores the build's older generation, and the function returns without publishing.
4. `syncSnapshotLocked` (`process_status.go:15`) returns while `m.publishedSnapshot >= m.lastSnapshot.Generation`, which now holds.
5. A later successful partial update does not help. `advanceGenerationAfterPartialUpdateLocked` sees the full snapshot as published, and advances both generations together.

## Reachability (bounded)

- The deferral branch runs only while the XSK startup probe is pending after a helper start, and a partial update must succeed during Compile's unlocked build.
- A boot or helper restart that commits while neighbors churn is the plausible shape. Not reproduced.
- The compiled config still reaches the helper through another full publish, such as the next commit or a scheduler, overlay or worker-arm republish, since those copy `m.lastSnapshot`. How long that takes is not established.
- What the non-deferred publish of the older generation does on the helper is not established.

## Consequence (bounded)

Until another path publishes, the helper enforces the previous compiled config while the commit has succeeded. A tightening commit, such as a new deny, is then not in force.

## Fix direction

Reviewer's suggestion: under `m.mu`, rebase `snap.Generation` onto a new high-water generation before publishing or deferring.

## Origin and dedup

- Found by the Codex round-4 review of the #9684 branch, and verified by reading the code above.
- The generation reservation, the partial-update advance and the deferral branch all predate #9684. That change does not touch generation handling.
- Related: #9520 (apply_snapshot content identity) and #9803 (update_fabrics plan fields).

## #9831 — config: a group's leaf `security-zone X;` is dropped when the configuration has any inline leaf `security-zone Y;` — the override matches on the keyword, not the zone name [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-12)

Group expansion drops a zone statement that an applied group supplies as a **leaf**, whenever the configuration already has **any** inline `security-zone` statement written as a leaf, including one that names a different zone. Strict commit accepts the result, and the group's zone never compiles.

Measured at master `ed313e4c9` through `configstore.CheckText` (strict) and `config.CompileConfigLenient`, listing every compiled zone. Each configuration applies the group with top-level `apply-groups G;`.

| Group `G` supplies | Inline zones | Strict | Compiled zones |
|---|---|---|---|
| `security-zone zga;` | `security-zone trust;` | accepts | **`[trust]`**; `zga` dropped |
| `security-zone [ zga zgb ];` | `security-zone trust;` | accepts | **`[trust]`** |
| `security-zone zga;` | `security-zone trust { tcp-rst; }` | accepts | `[trust zga]` |
| `security-zone zga { tcp-rst; }` | `security-zone trust;` | accepts | `[trust zga]` |
| `security-zone zga;` | none (only another `security` statement) | accepts | `[zga]` |

The loss needs a group leaf **and** an inline leaf. A braced statement on either side merges correctly.

**Mechanism.** In the leaf branch of `mergeNodes` (`pkg/config/ast_groups.go`), the inline peer is found with `leafListPeer(*dst, key)`, where `key` is only `s.Keys[0]` (`security-zone`). When that finds the inline leaf `security-zone trust`, the code takes the inline-wins override path and skips the group leaf. The zone name is never compared.

**Severity: Medium.** A zone the group supplies silently disappears after a clean strict commit.
- A policy that names the zone is refused at strict commit, so that case is loud.
- A zone nothing references is simply absent, together with its interface bindings. Not measured.

**Related, not duplicates:**
- #7648 (closed) was a group's compact spelling dropped when a peer with the *same* name exists. Here the peer has a *different* name.
- #9801: a `<*>` group skips a leaf destination.
- #9802: a `<*>` group is adopted verbatim.
- #9656 M40: its commit-time check runs after group expansion, so it cannot see a statement that expansion discarded.

**Suggested remedy.** For a leaf whose schema declares instance args (a named instance such as `security-zone <name>`), match the inline peer on the keyword **and** the instance keys, so statements for different zones never override each other.

**Acceptance.** The first two rows compile the group's zones alongside `trust` on strict and lenient, with a cell that fails at `ed313e4c9`.

Refs #7648, #9801, #9802, #9656. Discovery credit: the #9656 M40 Codex review, round 5 (`model:gpt-unknown`); measured and scoped with `validated-by:research`.

## #9837 — config: a family mtu above the interface mtu on a vlan-tagging unit commits clean, and the kernel refuses it on every apply [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-15)

## What is wrong

On a `vlan-tagging` interface, a unit's `family inet mtu` / `family inet6 mtu` can exceed the interface-level `mtu`, and the commit accepts it. The lower of the two family values is the unit MTU (`pkg/config/compiler_interfaces.go`).

The two values land on different netdevs:
- the interface-level `mtu` is the parent link's MTU (`planPhysDesired`; since #9761 also for a parent whose zone references are all tagged);
- the unit MTU is written to the VLAN sub-interface (`mapZoneInterface`).

Linux refuses a VLAN child MTU above its parent's (`vlan_dev_change_mtu`, `net/8021q/vlan_dev.c`). So every apply logs `failed to set VLAN sub-interface MTU`, and the child keeps its old MTU. The committed config is never realised, and only the journal says so.

## Reproduce

```
set interfaces ge-0-0-2 vlan-tagging
set interfaces ge-0-0-2 mtu 1400
set interfaces ge-0-0-2 unit 50 vlan-id 50
set interfaces ge-0-0-2 unit 50 family inet address 172.16.50.8/24
set interfaces ge-0-0-2 unit 50 family inet mtu 9000
commit
```

The commit is clean. `ip link show ge-0-0-2.50` keeps its previous MTU, and every later commit logs the warning again.

## Fix direction

At commit, reject a tagged unit whose family MTU is above its interface-level `mtu` when both are set, and name both values. Two cases need no commit check:
- An untagged unit's MTU replaces the parent's, so it cannot exceed it.
- A tagged unit on an interface with no interface-level `mtu` is limited by the parent's running MTU, which the commit cannot see. That case can stay a runtime warning.

Severity LOW: a misconfiguration is silently not realised, and nothing forwards wrongly.

Found in the Codex review of #9761 (lane-low-sweep).

## #9838 — config: an interface or routing instance written as a leaf (`interfaces { ge-0/0/0; }`, `routing-instances { ri1; }`) compiles no instance, while its empty braced spelling does [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-15)

An interface or a routing instance written as a **leaf** compiles no instance at all, while the same statement with an empty braced body compiles it. Strict commit accepts both spellings.

Measured at master `36dfa8e5a` through `configstore.CheckText` (strict) and `config.CompileConfigLenient`. The check is whether the compiled configuration's JSON contains the instance name. A second interface, `ge-0/0/1`, is defined in the interface rows so the configuration is otherwise valid.

| Spelling | Strict | Instance compiled |
|---|---|---|
| `interfaces { ge-0/0/0; }` | accepts | **no** |
| `interfaces { ge-0/0/0 { } }` | accepts | yes |
| `routing-instances { ri1; }` | accepts | **no** |
| `routing-instances { ri1 { } }` | accepts | yes |
| `security zones { security-zone trust; }` (control) | accepts | yes, the same as `security-zone trust { }` |

A wildcard group does not change the leaf rows. With `interfaces <*> { description fromgroup; }` applied, `ge-0/0/0;` still compiles no interface, while `ge-0/0/0 { }` compiles one carrying the description. `routing-instances <*> { instance-type virtual-router; }` behaves the same way.

**Why it matters.** Two spellings that name the same statement compile differently, and nothing reports it. The consequence is not measured beyond the instance being present or absent. An interface with no units and a routing instance with no type may be inert either way.

**Severity: Low.** The divergence is silent, but its consequence is unmeasured.

**Scope note.** Found while scoping #9801. That fix lets a wildcard group apply to a zone written as a leaf. It is kept to zones because only a zone's leaf spelling already compiles as the instance. Extending it to interfaces or routing instances would create an instance only when a wildcard group applies, and leave none without one.

**Acceptance.** `interfaces { ge-0/0/0; }` and `routing-instances { ri1; }` compile like their empty braced spellings, or strict refuses the leaf spelling with a message naming it. A cell pins it and fails at `36dfa8e5a`.

Refs #9801. Discovery credit: `model:claude-opus-5-1m`, found while scoping #9801. `validated-by:research`.

## #9841 — dataplane: an interface MTU the apply cannot read or write is only logged, and the commit reports success [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-15)

## What is wrong

`mapZoneInterface`'s per-phys setup (`pkg/dataplane/compiler_iface.go`) writes each netdev's planned MTU (#8119/#8120). Two failures leave the netdev at its old MTU, and the apply still returns success:
- **The link lookup fails.** `cachedLinkByIndex` returns an error, and the MTU write is skipped with no log line of its own.
- **The write fails.** `LinkSetMTU` returns an error. The apply logs `failed to set MTU` and continues.

Nothing retries within the apply. No commit warning or `show` output reports the unconverged MTU; only the journal does.

Since #9761, a VLAN child whose unit MTU is above its parent's resulting MTU is skipped with a warning, instead of being written and refused. So a failed parent write also leaves that parent's jumbo children unconverged.

## Fix direction

Decide the policy for an MTU the apply could not realise. Either:
- fail the apply, using the #4960 host-mutation annotation for what already changed; or
- keep applying, retry the lookup once without the cache, and surface the unconverged MTU in a commit warning and a `show` field.

Severity LOW: a configured MTU is silently not realised. Nothing bypasses policy.

Found in the Codex review of #9761 (lane-low-sweep).

## #9842 — HA: a restarting node regains full RG weight at dataplane Start, before anything is attached, so it can win an election it cannot serve [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-17)

## What is wrong

The #7178 arm track demotes every redundancy group while the dataplane is not armed. `markDataplaneArmed` clears it at `rt.Start` (`applyDataplaneArmTrack(true)` in `pkg/daemon/daemon_transit_gate.go`). But Start only loads the shim; the per-interface XDP attach runs later, inside the first `ApplyConfig`. So from Start until that attach, the node carries full RG weight with nothing attached.

A restarting higher-priority node can therefore preempt a healthy peer in that window.
- With #9725, kernel transit stays closed until something is attached, so the traffic the node now masters is dropped.
- If the first apply never attaches (it fails, or nothing needs the shim), the node keeps mastership and keeps dropping.
- Before #9725, the same node forwarded that traffic through the kernel with no policy instead.

## Why it is not a one-line fix

Two properties are needed, and neither holds today:
- **The first election.** `cluster.UpdateConfig` creates each RG at weight 255 (`pkg/cluster/group_state.go`), before the daemon can apply any debt. The debt has to exist when the group is created.
- **RGs added later.** `applyDataplaneArmTrack` walks only the groups that exist when it runs, so an RG added by a later commit starts at 255 even while the node is demoted. The same gap already exists for an arm failure followed by a commit that adds an RG.

## Fix direction

- Keep dataplane readiness in the cluster manager as a node-level monitor debt, applied to every RG when it is created and whenever readiness changes.
- Clear the debt only while at least one shim XDP program is attached (the #9725 predicate, `AttachedXDPLinkCount`), and restore it when none is.
- Cells:
  - a node restarting into a healthy cluster does not preempt before its first attach;
  - an RG added while the node is demoted starts demoted;
  - an arm failure followed by an RG add stays demoted.

Severity MED: after a restart, a node can win an election it cannot serve.

Found in the Codex review of #9725 (lane-low-sweep), and left out of #9725's scope because it needs the cluster manager to carry the debt.

## #9844 — daemon: TestIPsecSASyncHotEnableStartsAndStops8967 reads loopCancel without loopMu and races the exiting publisher (flaky -race failure) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-12)

## What happens

`go test -race ./pkg/daemon` intermittently fails with a DATA RACE in `TestIPsecSASyncHotEnableStartsAndStops8967` (`pkg/daemon/ipsec_sa_hotenable_8967_test.go`).

- The test reads `d.ipsecSASync.loopCancel` directly, without `loopMu`. The reads are at lines 104, 122 and 134 at master `b44818428`.
- `ensureIPsecSASyncLoop(false)` cancels the publisher. Its goroutine then exits through `clearIPsecSALoopIfCurrent` (`pkg/daemon/daemon_ipsec_sa_sync_loop.go:172`), which writes `loopCancel = nil` under `loopMu`.
- The race detector reports the test's unlocked read at line 134 against that write.

## Reproduction

On master `b44818428`, in a clean detached worktree:

```
go test -race -count=40 -run '^TestIPsecSASyncHotEnableStartsAndStops8967$' ./pkg/daemon
```

That gave 1 DATA RACE in 40 runs. It was first seen in the `-race` gate for the #9766/#9767 change (head `0f209a4ac`), which touches no IPsec file.

```
Write at 0x00c0001582a0 by goroutine 4660:
  github.com/psaab/xpf/pkg/daemon.(*Daemon).clearIPsecSALoopIfCurrent()
      pkg/daemon/daemon_ipsec_sa_sync_loop.go:172
  github.com/psaab/xpf/pkg/daemon.(*Daemon).ensureIPsecSASyncLoop.func1()
      pkg/daemon/daemon_ipsec_sa_sync_loop.go:115
Previous read at 0x00c0001582a0 by goroutine 4659:
  github.com/psaab/xpf/pkg/daemon.TestIPsecSASyncHotEnableStartsAndStops8967()
      pkg/daemon/ipsec_sa_hotenable_8967_test.go:134
```

## Impact

As far as verified, the defect is in the test only: the reported read is in the test body. Any lane's `-race` run over `./pkg/daemon` can go red on it.

Not verified: whether every production read of `loopCancel` holds `loopMu`.

## Fix direction

- Read `loopCancel` under `loopMu` in the test, through a small accessor.
- For the disable half, either wait for the goroutine to exit or assert on a value the exiting goroutine does not write.

## #9845 — dataplane: a VLAN child's unit MTU is written before its parent's MTU in the same apply, so raising both converges only on the next commit [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-15)

## What is wrong

`mapZoneInterface` (`pkg/dataplane/compiler_iface.go`) writes a tagged reference's unit MTU to its VLAN sub-interface in the VLAN branch. That comes before the per-phys setup, later in the same call, writes the parent netdev's planned MTU (#8119/#8120).

Linux refuses a VLAN child MTU above its parent's current MTU (`vlan_dev_change_mtu`, `net/8021q/vlan_dev.c`). So a commit that raises both the parent and a unit, for example to 9000, has this effect:
- the child write is refused, and only a warning is logged;
- the parent is then raised;
- the apply succeeds, and the child keeps its old MTU until the next apply.

This is present on master for any interface that has an untagged unit, which plans the parent's MTU, plus tagged units. #9761 plans the interface-level MTU for tagged-only interfaces too, so it exposes the same order there.

## Constraints a fix must meet

#9761's review tried two shapes, and each introduced failures that a fix here must avoid:
- **An early parent write from the VLAN branch.** It ran ahead of the #5268 RX-VLAN offload gate. A once-per-apply guard then suppressed the parent's retry after a failed write, and a failed parent lookup still let the child write proceed.
- **Deferring child writes until after the zone loop.**
  - A failed parent read vetoed child writes the kernel would have accepted, reductions included.
  - The deferred child was re-resolved by name, so a foreign device renamed onto the VLAN's name could be modified.
  - A later zone error dropped queued safe reductions that master applies.
- **The kernel model itself.**
  - A VLAN over macsec is capped at the parent MTU minus `VLAN_HLEN`, and it starts that way at creation.
  - Newer kernels propagate a parent MTU change to VLAN children asynchronously (torvalds/linux `cd1c188db109`), so a child's clamp is not visible when the apply returns.

## Fix direction

Keep the child write inline, on the link and ifindex the VLAN branch already validated. If the kernel refuses it and the parent's planned MTU is not yet written, retry that same write once, right after the parent's per-phys MTU write in the same call. Let the kernel decide admission rather than modelling it.

A related gap: successful MTU writes record no #4960 host mutation.

Severity LOW: the MTU converges on the next commit, and nothing bypasses policy.

Found in the Codex review of #9761 (lane-low-sweep).

## #9847 — dataplane: every compile removes the XDP link pins and AttachXDP never re-pins a registered link, so a restart detaches the shim [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-15)

## What is wrong

`CompileUserspaceShim` calls `removeUserspaceShimXDPLinkPins()` on every compile, before the attach (`pkg/dataplane/loader.go`). This deletes every `xdp_*` link pin, so that the attach is fresh rather than a pinned-link reuse.

`AttachXDP` then returns "XDP already attached" for any ifindex already in `m.xdpLinks`, and the attach loop swallows that error. A link attached by an earlier compile is therefore never pinned again.

`Manager.Close` closes every XDP link handle (`for ifindex, l := range m.XDPLinks() { l.Close() }`), and its comment says hitless restart keeps the pinned maps. A bpf_link's program stays attached only while a handle or a pin holds the link. So once a second compile has removed the pins, closing the last handle detaches XDP from every interface.

## Consequence

- **On a stop or restart after at least two compiles**, including a hitless restart, the shim leaves every interface when the process exits. It does not stay attached until the new process re-attaches.
- **Kernel transit is exposed in that gap.** The forwarding sysctls outlive the process, so the kernel path forwards with no program until the next xpfd closes transit at bring-up (#9725) or attaches again.
- **The same holds** when the initial pin fails after a successful attach.

## Fix direction

- Never unpin a link that is still in the registry. Either re-pin a registry link on the "already attached" path, or remove only the pins of links no longer in the registry.
- Treat successful pinning as a precondition for hitless operation, and fail closed on shutdown when a link is not pinned.
- Cell: two compiles, then close every Go handle, then require the kernel attachment to survive, through a link seam or a namespaced integration test.

Severity MED: the loss is on a restart path and predates #9725, which only makes the resulting gap visible.

Found in the Codex review of #9725 (lane-low-sweep).

## #9848 — daemon: kernel transit stays open when every XDP-bearing device is unregistered between applies [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-17)

## Summary

With the #9725 change (branch `fix/9725-transit-closed-until-attach`, not yet merged), kernel transit is open only while two things hold: the dataplane is armed, and at least one shim XDP bpf_link is attached (`transitOpen`, `pkg/daemon/transit_closed_until_attach_9725.go`). Transit here means `ip_forward`, `conf.all.forwarding` and the #7191 forward-hook barrier.

The attached count asks the kernel: an XDP bpf_link whose device was unregistered reports ifindex 0 and is not counted. But the gate reads the count only at applies, after every `ApplyConfig` and at the apply tail.

Suppose every XDP-bearing device is unregistered while the node is armed: a driver reload, a VF re-creation or a NIC removal. The kernel detaches every program, and transit stays open until the next config apply. networkd can configure a recreated device, and FRR can restore its routes, without an apply. The kernel then forwards transit with no program adjudicating it.

Codex found this reviewing #9725 (round 5, HIGH). It is filed separately because it predates that change and needs a new mechanism.

## Pre-existing on master

Master has the same gap, and a wider one. At `fbc51cc02`, `markDataplaneArmed` (`pkg/daemon/daemon_transit_gate.go:162-164`) opens transit at `rt.Start()`. Only `markDataplaneArmFailed` and `markDataplaneNotArmed` close it. So master keeps transit open for the whole armed run, whatever is attached.

#9725 does not widen the gap. It closes the window from Start to the first attach, and closes transit again at any apply that leaves nothing attached.

## Why it is not part of #9725

The daemon has no always-on link lifecycle subscription to trigger a re-read from:
- `monitorLinkState` (`pkg/daemon/daemon_flow.go`) runs only while SNMP is configured. It is started from `startSNMPMonitorLocked` (`daemon_snmp_reconcile.go`), and the comment at `daemon_run.go:592` notes it is SNMP-gated.
- `monitorFabricState` (`daemon_ha_fabric.go`) runs only for an HA fabric.
- `pkg/vrrp/track.go` subscribes only for `track-interface`.

## Fix shape

Add an always-on netlink link subscription for the gate. It re-reads the gate on `RTM_DELLINK`, and again after every subscribe and resubscribe. The resubscribe case matters because a receive error such as ENOBUFS closes the vishvananda/netlink channel and drops notifications; `monitorLinkState` already resubscribes and resyncs for this reason (#3950).

In `net/core/dev.c`, `unregister_netdevice_many_notify` appears to run `dev_xdp_uninstall`, which clears the link's device, before it builds the `RTM_DELLINK` message. If so, a re-read on that event sees ifindex 0. Confirm this against the shipped kernel when implementing.

A recreated device carries no program until an apply attaches one, so the node's fast path is down too. Closing transit is the fail-closed choice the #9725 rule states.

Cells:
- an unregister, simulated through a seam with no apply, closes transit;
- a resubscribe after a lost notification closes it too;
- an unrelated link deletion while links remain attached leaves transit open.

## Severity

MED. It needs every XDP-bearing device to go away while the node is armed, which takes a root-level or hardware event. The consequence is policy-free kernel forwarding until the next apply.

## #9852 — boot: bridged transit forwards with no barrier from networkd bring-up until xpfd installs it [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-17)

## Summary

xpf writes bridge domains as systemd-networkd `.netdev` files (`pkg/networkd/networkd.go`; `buildBridgeDomainModels` in `pkg/dataplane/compiler_iface.go`). So on every boot, networkd recreates the bridge devices and enslaves their ports before xpfd starts.

Bridged frames do not consult `ip_forward`. The #7191 transit barrier (`xpf_transit_barrier`, in the inet and bridge families) is an nftables table, so it does not survive a reboot. Until xpfd's bring-up installs the barrier, a bridge domain forwards between its ports with no policy.

## Relation to #9725

#9725 (branch `fix/9725-transit-closed-until-attach`, not merged) adds `xpf-transit-closed.service`. It is a boot-only oneshot that writes both forwarding sysctls to 0 after `systemd-sysctl` and before networkd, FRR and xpfd. That closes ROUTED transit from boot until xpfd starts, but it does nothing for bridged frames. xpfd's bring-up then installs the barrier (`closeTransitUntilAttached`) and keeps it until the gate opens. Codex raised this while reviewing #9725 (round 7, HIGH).

The gap predates #9725. At `fbc51cc02`, nothing installs the barrier before `rt.Start()`, and `markDataplaneArmed` removes it at Start. So on master, the bridged window runs from networkd bring-up until an attached shim adjudicates the ports. #9725 narrows that window to the stretch between boot and xpfd's bring-up; it does not create it.

## Fix shape

- **Load the barrier at boot.** Extend the boot oneshot to load an nft file that creates `inet xpf_transit_barrier` and `bridge xpf_transit_barrier`, with the same forward-hook DROP chains `pkg/nftables/transit_barrier.go` builds. Order it before `systemd-networkd.service`.
  - xpfd's `InstallTransitBarrier` already replaces an existing table idempotently, and `RemoveTransitBarrier` deletes it when transit opens. So the daemon takes ownership with no new handoff.
- **Pin the match.** Add a check that the file's tables and chains match what the daemon installs (name, families, hook, priority, policy), so the two cannot drift.
- **Stage it in the test VMs too.** `test/incus/setup.sh` and `cluster-setup.sh` deploy raw binaries and do not install the package's units.
- **Accept the consequence.** A box where xpfd never starts (disabled, or a failed install) keeps bridged forwarding dropped. That is the fail-closed direction for a firewall appliance.

## Severity

MED. It needs a configured bridge domain and a reboot. The exposure is policy-free bridged forwarding between networkd bring-up and xpfd's bring-up.

## #9853 — dhcpserver: the takeover pre-seed re-injects a pure backup's stale memfile rows, re-leasing addresses the primary released [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-17)

## What is wrong

On a takeover, `PreSeedMemfileMerged4`/`6` writes the Kea memfile from the UNION of this node's local leases and the held peer set (#5040). The local read prefers Kea's control socket and falls back to the memfile.

On a node that was a **pure backup**, Kea is stopped (`systemctl is-active kea-dhcp4-server` = inactive), so the local set comes from a memfile last rewritten when that node was primary. The primary may since have released or expired rows in that file. The union re-injects them, and the promoted Kea loads them as live bindings.

## Measured (loss userspace cluster, #9791 lab run 3, 2026-09-11)

- **fw1 (promoted) memfile after takeover** held rows for `10.0.61.103`, `.104` and `.106`. Their `valid_lifetime` was about 72.4k–73k s, and their clients came from lease-failover runs about 3.9 h earlier.
- **fw0 (the primary until the reboot) memfile** no longer had those rows. Those clients had released at the end of their runs, and fw0's Kea processed the releases.
- **`.102`:** fw1 also held a stale row for `10.0.61.102` naming an earlier run's client. That address was reused the next time; #9791's one-owner-per-address pass resolves that collision by grant recency.
- **Addresses the primary had freed:** nothing resolves those. They stay leased to stale clients on the promoted node until expiry.

## Consequence (bounded)

- **Pool leakage.** After a failover, the promoted node refuses to allocate addresses that the primary had freed, until each stale lease expires, which can be up to a full `valid-lifetime`.
- **Stale identity binding.** A stale client that returns can renew an address the primary had released.
- **Where it happens.** Only on a takeover by a node whose local Kea was not serving. That is the common active/passive shape.

## Why the union exists, and the fix direction

#5040 added the union for per-RG active-active. There the taking-over node is already MASTER for other RGs, and their leases are live in its running Kea. A peer-only pre-seed wiped those.

So the local rows are authoritative only for subnets whose RG this node already masters. Rows for the RG being taken over should come from the held peer set, which the primary replaces on each push.

- `applyRethServicesForRG(rgID)` knows the RG being taken over.
- `filterDHCPConfigForMasterRGs` already maps DHCP groups to RGs through their interfaces.

A per-subnet authority rule could therefore drop local rows in the subnets of the RG being taken over, and keep the union elsewhere. A group whose members span several RGs cannot attribute its pools, and would keep the union.

A narrower alternative is to trust local rows only when they come from a live Kea socket. That would break a node whose Kea crashed while it mastered another RG.

## Acceptance

- **Unit cells:**
  - a pure backup's stale local row for a released address does not survive the pre-seed;
  - an active-active node's live local row for its own RG does survive;
  - a peer row always survives for the RG being taken over.
- **Lab:** the lease-failover gate with a released stale client pre-planted on the standby's memfile. The promoted memfile must not hold it.

## #9854 — config: two `system syslog host <addr>` statements for one address compile two syslog destinations [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-15)

## Defect

Two `system syslog host` statements naming one address compile as two destinations. Strict commit accepts each row.

Measured at master `ad2ba883a` through `config.CompileConfig`:

| Configuration | Compiled `System.Syslog.Hosts` |
|---|---|
| `system { syslog { host 10.0.0.1; host 10.0.0.1; } }` | two destinations for 10.0.0.1, both with no facilities |
| `system { syslog { host 10.0.0.1; host 10.0.0.1 any any; } }` | two destinations: one with no facilities, one with `any/any` |
| `groups { G { system { syslog { host 10.0.0.1 any any; } } } } apply-groups G; system { syslog { host 10.0.0.1 { } } }` | two destinations at master; one, with `any/any`, after the #9801/#9831 change (#7648 expands the group statement into the braced host) |

Zone statements are merged into one zone (#4818). Syslog host statements are not, so a message matching both would presumably be sent to the same address once per statement. The runtime delivery was not measured.

This is the #8436 duplicate-named-block class, disposition "append both". The #8436 conservation census lists `system syslog host` in `dupConservationSkipped8436` (`pkg/config/duplicate_block_conservation_inventory_8436.go`), the bounded set of sites whose duplicate its fixture cannot express. So the census does not measure this site. The rows above were measured by hand.

## Expected

One destination per address, with the statements' facilities merged, or a strict refusal naming the duplicate address.

Severity: Low (it needs duplicate host statements, authored inline or produced by group expansion).

## #9855 — config: a group's packed `system syslog host <addr> <facility> <severity>;` is dropped beside an inline leaf `host <addr>;` [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-15)

## Defect

A group's packed named-instance statement is overridden by an inline **leaf** naming the same instance, and the group's statements are dropped. Strict commit accepts the configuration.

Measured at master `ad2ba883a` through `config.CompileConfig`:

| Configuration | Compiled `System.Syslog.Hosts` |
|---|---|
| `groups { G { system { syslog { host 10.0.0.1 any any; } } } } apply-groups G; system { syslog { host 10.0.0.1; } }` | one host with `Facilities: null`; the group's `any any` is dropped |
| `system { syslog { host 10.0.0.1 { any any; } } }` (control) | one host, `any/any` |

## Cause

This is the leaf branch of `mergeNodes` (`pkg/config/ast_groups.go`). The inline peer `host 10.0.0.1;` is a leaf. The #7648 expansion of a packed group statement merges only into a container peer, so it does not run, and the inline-wins override skips the group statement.

For a `<*>` group, the #9801 change turns a leaf zone into the container its braced spelling is. There is no equivalent for a named-instance leaf peer.

Adopting the group statement beside the leaf is not a fix: `host 10.0.0.1; host 10.0.0.1 any any;` compiles two destinations (#9854).

## Scope

- Measured for `system syslog host` only. The mechanism applies to any named instance whose leaf spelling is an inline peer.
- Zones are excluded. After the #9801/#9831 change, a group zone statement carrying keys past the zone name is adopted beside a leaf zone and judged by the #9656 zone-statement check.
- Pre-existing: the #9801/#9831 change leaves this row unchanged.

Severity: Low (a narrow shape: the group supplies the body, and the inline configuration names the same host as a leaf).

## #9856 — userspace-dp: an owner-RG export's control response keeps only 4096 deltas per binding buffer, so a FullResync can ACK a partial export [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-17)

## Summary

A FullResync republish (`ExportOwnerRGSessionsPaged`) sends the owner-RG export to the daemon over two paths. Only the control response is checked for completeness, and it is capped.

- **The control response keeps at most 4096 exported deltas per binding buffer.**
  - During an export, `flush_session_deltas` (`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/session_delta.rs:306`) pushes each `bulk_resync` delta into the binding's RPC buffer, using `push_session_delta_bulk_export` (`:363`).
  - That buffer holds `MAX_PENDING_SESSION_DELTAS = 4096` (`afxdp/mod.rs:442`). Past the cap, `push_session_delta_inner` counts `session_delta_dropped` and returns without arming a resync (`afxdp/binding_state/session_delta.rs`; this is the #8593 non-arming push).
  - The worker drains, exports in chunks, drains, and only then acks (`afxdp/worker/loop_body/mod.rs:1476-1481`). The control thread collects the buffers only after every worker has acked (`wait_and_collect`, `afxdp/ha/export.rs`).
  - The response's `more` bit (`drain_session_deltas_from_live`, `ha/export.rs:372`) reports deltas still buffered past the drain budget. It says nothing about deltas already dropped at the push.
- **The event-stream copy is complete but lossy.** The same flush also emits every exported open onto the binary event stream. That copy is what makes the worker-loop comment true ("ships the COMPLETE bulk snapshot to the HA peer without dropping sessions 4097..N"). The daemon receives it in `handleEventStreamDelta` (`pkg/daemon/daemon_ha_userspace_stream.go:338`), which drops the delta when sync is not connected and otherwise hands it to the ordinary `queueUserspaceSessionDeltas` path.

## Consequence

#9767, fixed by PR #9850, acknowledges a FullResync only once the export batch is completely admitted (`queueUserspaceSessionDeltasComplete`, `pkg/daemon/daemon_ha_userspace_export.go:73`). That batch is the control response.

On a node where one worker owns more than 4096 sessions, the rest of the export reaches the peer only through the event-stream path. A drop on that path is invisible to the FullResync transaction, so the ACK can cover a partial export.

It also blocks the next step of #9630, which is to suppress the export's event-stream echo: suppressing it would drop sessions 4097..N outright.

## Evidence status

This comes from reading the code at `30c30ab6a`; it has not been measured. To confirm on a loaded node, check whether a binding's `session_delta_dropped` rises across a FullResync.

## Fix direction

- **An uncapped collection path.** Give the export a path that is not bounded by the incremental RPC buffer: either a per-export buffer handed to the control thread, or a chunked handoff in which the worker waits for the control thread to drain before it continues.
- **A completeness check.** Count every export delta that did not reach the response, and fail the export when that count is nonzero, so the #9767 transaction does not ACK it.
- **Then #9630 can suppress the echo** for export-sourced deltas. That needs a source tag that tells an owner-RG export apart from the #2442 loss-of-sync resync, which must keep echoing.

Cells:
- an export of more than 4096 sessions from one worker returns every session in the response;
- a forced drop fails the export.

## Severity

MED. It needs more than 4096 owned sessions on one worker, plus a drop on the event-stream path during a FullResync. The result is sessions the standby never receives, after a resync it acknowledged.

Refs #9630, #9767.

## #9859 — config: outside zones, a group's leaf `<keyword> <name>;` is dropped beside an inline leaf naming another instance (syslog host, CoS schedulers); the override matches on the keyword [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-17)

## Defect

In the leaf branch of `mergeNodes` (`pkg/config/ast_groups.go`), a group leaf finds its inline peer with `leafListPeer`, which matches on the keyword alone. So a group leaf naming one instance is overridden, and dropped, by an inline leaf naming a **different** instance. The #9801/#9831 change repairs this for `security-zone` statements only. Every other named instance keeps it.

Measured at master `ad2ba883a` through `config.CompileConfigLenient`. Strict commit accepts every row.

| Configuration | Compiled |
|---|---|
| `groups { G { system { syslog { host 10.0.0.1; } } } } apply-groups G; system { syslog { host 10.0.0.2; } }` | hosts `[10.0.0.2]`: the group's host is dropped |
| `groups { G { class-of-service { schedulers group-sched; } } } apply-groups G; class-of-service { schedulers inline-sched; }` | schedulers `[inline-sched]`: the group's scheduler is dropped |
| the same, with the group written `schedulers group-sched { }` (control) | schedulers `[group-sched inline-sched]` |

## Why the zone repair did not generalise

The #9801/#9831 branch first matched every schema container with instance args by keyword plus instance keys. Two Codex review rounds, each measured, found shapes where that is wrong, so the rule was scoped to zones. A fix here must handle each one.

1. **Value lists** (`valueList`: static-route `next-hop`, `system ntp server`, DHCP `interface`).
   - With identity matching, a group `next-hop 192.0.2.2;` beside an inline `next-hop [ 192.0.2.1 192.0.2.2 ];` was matched against the first member only. It was adopted and compiled `[.1 .2 .2]`, a duplicate hop. The reversed list did not. Measured at branch head `d64625101`.
   - These belong on the leaf-list path.
2. **`multi` named containers** (`class-of-service schedulers`). `multi` with children marks named containers (see `schema.go`), not value lists. Excluding `multi` wholesale restores the drop in the table above; measured at `9d1424e09`.
3. **Keys the compiler canonicalises.**
   - With identity matching, a group `ospf area 0 area-type stub;` beside an inline `area 0.0.0.0;` compiled areas `[0.0.0.0, 0]`: two entries for one area, and the packed `area-type` is lost (#9656 member M26). The braced group spelling at master also compiles two areas, `0` with `stub`.
   - `vrrp-group 01` beside `vrrp-group 1` canonicalises in its compiler and merges.
   - Raw key equality is therefore correct at some sites and wrong at others.
4. **Packed tails beside a leaf instance** stay overridden. That is #9855 (syslog facilities, and a VRRP priority).

## Expected

A group leaf naming a different instance survives, for every named instance, without duplicating value-list members or canonical aliases.

Severity: Medium. Group-supplied configuration is lost silently, and strict commit accepts it.
