## #14621 — [Y22-01] Session open/update encoder reserves 2 bytes after rule_id but writes 10; a 307–314 B (v6) / 367–374 B (v4) rule id panics the packet worker [CLOSED] (closed 2026-10-18)

## Summary
Session open/update encoder reserves 2 bytes after rule_id but writes 10; a 307–314 B (v6) / 367–374 B (v4) rule id panics the packet worker

Finding `Y22-01` from `claude-opus-5-5-review-full-firewall-hostile-001.md` (deep-review run `review-work.7YDz9xALDc`, audit `5b122dda5ebb23aec9c283ef7cbddca0874b9338`). Both independent re-review passes (opus `opus-ob*` + spark `spark-ob*`, in `/var/tmp/deep-review-work/research-work.jd4pLTefrR/`) gate this claim **MATERIAL** at their checked `origin/master` revisions, with the narrowed scope noted in the source where applicable. Verified again against `origin/master` `3d2f037ea4ceb2732aec3d8c8c3c67424d69aa1c` for filing (citations below are at origin/master as cited by the re-reviewers; audit citations in Evidence).

**Severity (source verifier):** Medium — Medium. A packet from an untrusted peer that matches the affected policy kills the worker that installs the session. That worker's queues fail closed (READY withheld) until the helper restarts. The window is narrow and needs a deliberate length: a `from->to/name` rule id of 307–314 bytes (v6) or 367–374 bytes (v4). Junos-length (63-char) names cannot reach it. (Reporter rated Medium.)

## Contract
The guard at `userspace-dp/src/event_stream/codec/session_sync.rs:414-421` exists to keep every write inside the frame (`EventFrame.data: [u8; EVENT_FRAME_CAPACITY]`, `codec/mod.rs:28` = 512). The encoder comment at `:411-413` says the trailing fields keep "a stable position". The #13965 commit text claims "append-only length-gated trailers … Risk: none new". A commit-accepted config should never be able to make the dataplane panic.

## Evidence (audit @ `5b122dda`, re-verified at master by both passes)
- `userspace-dp/src/event_stream/codec/session_sync.rs:414-416` (observed): the guard is `pos + 2 + rule_id.len() + 2 <= buf.len()`, which reserves 2 bytes after the id.
  - `:430`, `:434`, `:438` (observed): the code writes `tcp_handshake_state` (1 byte), `source_nat_provenance` (1 byte) and `pptp_call_ids.to_le_bytes()` (8 bytes), 10 bytes in total. The `+8` arrived only in 7c60f3d04f (`git log -S`).
  - `pos` before the length prefix is 194 (v6) or 134 (v4). The final write therefore needs `206+L ≤ 512` (v6) or `146+L ≤ 512` (v4), while the guard admits L ≤ 314 / ≤ 374. That arithmetic gives the panic windows [307,314] and [367,374].
  - `session/sync_attribution.rs:84-90` and `policy.rs:4574-4579`: the rule id is `stable_policy_rule_id` = `format!("{}->{}/{}", from, to, name)`. Go stamps the same id (`pkg/dataplane/userspace/policies_ids.go:100-110`). Global policies use `junos-global->junos-global/<name>`.
  - `afxdp/coordinator/supervisor.rs:86-120` (observed): `catch_unwind` sets `dead=true` and nothing respawns the worker.
  - No config-side cap (observed): a grep over pkg/config and pkg/configstore for `len(name) >`, `too long` and `exceeds` hits only login username, host-name, RI kernel name, commit description and config size. The same grep serves as the positive control, since it finds those caps.

### Decisive regression / re-review evidence at master
- | Y22-01 session encoder reserves 2B after rule_id, writes 10B → worker panic | **MATERIAL** | Cur verified `session_sync.rs:414-438`: guard `pos + 2 + rule_id.len() + 2 <= buf.len()` then writes handshake 1B + provenance 1B + `pptp_call_ids` 8B = 10B. Panic windows arithmetic: v6 pos=194 → L∈[307,314], v4 pos=134 → L∈[367,374] (guard admits, final `buf[pos..pos+8]` OOB). EXECUTED@audit z7 sweep: panicking lens exactly [307..314] @`:438`, L≤306 full 512B frame, L>314 silently stripped (separate D17-05). Rule id `format!("{}->{}/{}",from,to,name)` uncapped config-side (grep w/ positive control); Go probe commits 308B id. Supervisor `catch_unwind`→`dead=true`, no respawn; queues fail-closed un
- | Y22-01 session open/update encoder reserves 2 B after rule_id but writes 10 B — 307–314 B (v6) / 367–374 B (v4) rule id panics packet worker | **MATERIAL** | Cur `session_sync.rs:414-421` verified: guard admits the id iff `pos + 2 + rule_id.len() + 2 <= buf.len()`, reserving 2 trailing bytes; the code then writes handshake (1 B, :430) + provenance (1 B, :434) + `pptp_call_ids` (8 B, :438) = 10 B into the 512 B `EventFrame` (`codec/mod.rs:28` audit). The `+8` arrived with #13965 (commit `7c60f3d04f`, `git log -S`). Arithmetic: pre-prefix pos 194 (v6)/134 (v4) → final write needs `206+L ≤ 512` / `146+L ≤ 512`, guard admits L ≤ 314/374 → panic windows [307,314]/[367,374]. EXECUTED@audit: z7 R

## Probe / verification
- Source verification: EXECUTED. z7 ran the Rust encoder sweep, and the worker ran a Go probe showing a strict-committed config yields a 308-byte rule id. The worker-reachability chain (packet worker → encoder, supervisor behaviour) is STATIC. The v4 window is arithmetic only, because the v6 assert fired first. The configstore commit path was not exercised end to end.
- Confidence: High on the mechanism (executed). Medium on real-world likelihood.
- Probe: - z7 `z7_y22_rule_id_len_sweep` (`verify/z7/probes/event_stream_codec_codec_tests.rs.z7probe.rs`) sweeps L in 0..=600 through `encode_session_open_with_handshake_state` under `catch_unwind`.
    - Output (`verify/z7/run1.out`): `z7 y22 v6: panicking lens = [307, 308, 309, 310, 311, 312, 313, 314]; len0 frame=206 len100 frame=306 len600 frame=206`, panic at `session_sync.rs:438:12`.
    - Control: lens 0..306 and 315..600 encode. L=306 yields a full 512-byte frame, and above 314 the id is silently stripped (the separate D17-05 behaviour).
  - Worker Go probe `workers/y22/evidence/y22-01-go-ruleid-probe_test.go.txt` runs SchemaValidate + CompileConfig + snapshot build. Output `workers/y22/evidence/y22-01-go-ruleid-probe.out`: `rule_id len=308`. z7 did not re-run it.

## Why it matters
A commit-accepted config turns ordinary matching traffic into a persistent worker kill, i.e. a self-inflicted forwarding outage on the affected queues until the helper restarts. The narrow, deliberate-length name window bounds the risk. Global policies reach it with a 280–287-character name.

## Fix direction / acceptance
- Compute the reservation from the trailer actually written (`1 + 1 + 8`, ideally a named constant) and/or use checked slicing for every trailing write.
  - Consider a config-time or snapshot-time cap on the `stable_policy_rule_id` length.
  - Affected consumer: Go `decodeSessionEvent`.
  - Acceptance criterion: a sweep of L in 0..=600 for v4 and v6 never panics, every frame has `len <= 512`, the trailer decodes in Go `decodeSessionEvent`, and a mutation restoring `+ 2` turns the sweep red.
  - Remaining validation: execute the v4 leg and run the configstore `commit` path end to end.

Accounting invariant (cleared bit must be claim-reachable) violated. | Narrow: needs deterministic→PAT flip on live pool + cursor passing offsets while occupied (audit co

## Probe / verification
- Source verification: EXECUTED for the local-allocator path. The HA-synced variant (`synced.rs:769-779`) is plausible but not probed.

CGNAT pools are sized close to demand. A mode change on a busy pool silently removes up to the live-session count of ports, and the operator sees exhaustion while `show security nat source pool` shows free bits.

Production installs both halves (`forward_request.rs:31-39 should_install_local_reverse_session` unless FabricRedirect; `poll_descriptor/mod.rs:5393,6262`). EXECUTED@audit SNAT44 both-halves cell FAILS (`outer_src=10.0.61.102` vs expected SNAT addr) while shipped forward-only #6474 cell passes same build — explains gree

## Probe / verification
- Source verification: EXECUTED for v4 SNAT44 in the poll-descriptor fixture with both halves installed. STATIC for v6 SNAT66 and NPTv6.
- Confidence: High for v4 (executed). The v6, SNAT66 and NPTv6 twins are STATIC.
- Probe: - z7 `z7_y24_01_outbound_snat_icmp_error_with_reverse_companion_installed` (`verify/z7/probes/afxdp_tests_embedded_poll_filter.rs.z7probe.rs`) is the shipped #6474 v4 cell plus the reverse half, built exactly as in the #13772 fixture.
    - Output (`verify/z7/run1.out`): `y24-01 queued: target_ifindex=12 outer_src=10.0.61.102 quote_dst=10.0.61.102:12345`, then the assertion `outer src must be the SNAT address, not the internal host` fails (left `[10, 0, 61, 102]`, right `[172, 16, 80, 8]`).

The `TcpCloseClass::Reset` doc (`session/mod.rs:550-560`) says: once a RST is seen, both halves reap on the 2 s abort window and the reset is sticky ("a later graceful FIN cannot promote the entry back to a longer window"). One source can accumulate uncounted, unsheddable rows (one per aborted handshake) for 300 s each, or for the app inactivity timeout. ## #14631 — [Y26-01] `from is-fragment` matches IPv4 first fragments (MF=1, offset 0) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-10-17)

## Summary
`from is-fragment` matches IPv4 first fragments (MF=1, offset 0)

Finding `Y26-01` from `claude-opus-5-5-review-full-firewall-hostile-001.md` (deep-review run `review-work.7YDz9xALDc`, audit `5b122dda5ebb23aec9c283ef7cbddca0874b9338`). Both independent re-review passes (opus `opus-ob*` + spark `spark-ob*`, in `/var/tmp/deep-review-work/research-work.jd4pLTefrR/`) gate this claim **MATERIAL** at their checked `origin/master` revisions, with the narrowed scope noted in the source where applicable. Verified again against `origin/master` `3d2f037ea4ceb2732aec3d8c8c3c67424d69aa1c` for filing (citations below are at origin/master as cited by the re-reviewers; audit citations in Evidence).

**Severity (source verifier):** Medium — Medium. A network peer can bypass the stateless-filter accept idiom by setting MF on the first fragment. It is bounded by the stateful zone policy for transit, so the exposure is the stateless layer: interface filters, and lo0 host-bound in the Rust path. (reporter rated Medium)

## Contract
The Juniper "Firewall Filter Match Conditions Based on Bit-Field Values" and "service match conditions" pages make `is-fragment` the alias for `fragment-offset 0 except` (trailing fragments). Matching both kinds needs `first-fragment` plus `is-fragment` in separate terms. The IPv4 match-conditions page says "On MX Series Routers, `is-fragment` matches all fragments". So the any-fragment meaning is MX-specific, and the SRX/vSRX meaning (xpf's stated target) excludes offset 0. The IPv6 page says only "Match if the packet is a fragment". These sources were fetched by the verifier, not in-tree. In-tree, `userspace-dp/src/filter/README.md:613` asserts the any-fragment meaning without a citation.

## Evidence (audit @ `5b122dda`, re-verified at master by both passes)
- `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/frame/inspect.rs:1046-1059`: the predicates. IPv4 uses mask 0x3FFF, which includes MF. IPv6 uses `walk.fragment.is_some()`.
  - `inspect.rs:1196-1260`: `is_fragment` comes from `is_any_fragment`, and `l4_present` stays true for a first fragment.
  - `userspace-dp/src/filter/engine/matching.rs:56-58`: the term check.
  - `pkg/daemon/daemon_nft_term_lower.go:253-266,456-466`: the lo0 nft mirror now refuses IPv4 is-fragment (after #13955); IPv6 uses `exthdr frag exists`.
  - #2362 introduced the field with no Junos semantics analysis.

### Decisive regression / re-review evidence at master
- | Y26-01 `from is-fragment` matches IPv4 first fragments (MF=1, off 0) | **MATERIAL** (IPv4 only) | Cur `inspect.rs:1046-1059→` re-read: `ipv4_is_any_fragment (frag_off & 0x3FFF)!=0` incl. MF; `is_fragment=is_any_fragment`, `l4_present` stays true for first fragment so `matching.rs:404` gate doesn't save port terms. EXECUTED@audit: predicates `v4 first=true trailing=true unfrag=false`; filter `frags{is-fragment accept};no-ssh{tcp22 discard}` → `plain=Discard first_fragment=Accept`. SRX contract: `is-fragment`=`fragment-offset 0 except` (trailing only); separate `first-fragment` exists. Bounded by stateful policy for transit; exposure is stateless/lo0 layer. | Strongest refutation: MX documen

## Probe / verification
- Source verification: EXECUTED: predicate and filter-evaluation probes. The IPv6 atomic case is executed as code behaviour, but its contract is unresolved.
- Confidence: Medium. Juniper's documentation conflicts by platform.
- Probe: The probes are in `verify/z8/z8_rust_probes_inline.diff`, with output in `verify/z8/cargo_z8_probes.out`:
  - `z8_y26_01_predicates`: `v4 first=true trailing=true unfrag=false; v6 atomic=true first=true unfrag=false`. The controls (trailing true, unfragmented false) hold.
  - `z8_y26_01_filter` (`frags{is-fragment accept}; no-ssh{tcp 22 discard}`): `plain=Discard first_fragment=Accept`.

  The worker's draft is `workers/y26/evidence/y26-01_is_fragment_first_fragment_probe.rs`.

## Why it matters
The Junos idiom `term frags { from is-fragment; then accept; }` before port terms is safe on SRX because the first fragment, which carries the ports, still faces the port terms. On xpf, a peer that sets MF on the first fragment has the whole datagram accepted by the fragment term at the stateless layer.

## Fix direction / acceptance
Make the term predicate "fragment offset != 0" (reuse `is_non_first_fragment`), and keep any-fragment for internal uses. Optionally add `first-fragment`. Acceptance criterion (verifier): an IPv4 MF=1/offset-0 TCP/22 packet through `frags{is-fragment accept}; no-ssh{tcp 22 discard}` returns Discard, a trailing fragment still matches is-fragment, and README:613 and `tests_fragment_term_extra.rs:69-123` are corrected. The alternative is for xpf to document the MX meaning as a deliberate, cited choice. Remaining validation: the Junos inet6 atomic-fragment contract.

Acceptance: a regression test exercising the decisive check named by the re-reviewers for `Y26-01` fails on current `origin/master` and passes after the fix, with the cited controls still passing. Do not close on a nearby/already-fixed sibling mechanism.

## Dedup note
#2362 (CLOSED) introduced the field. #13955 / H13-06 (CLOSED) is the lo0 v4 defrag hook, a different mechanism. #3231 (nft v6 syntax) and #12528 (fused `then`) are unrelated. A grep of gh-issues.tsv and prior-titles.txt for is-fragment/first fragment/trailing finds no owner.
Re-checked open+closed by Y-ID and mechanism at filing time; no open owner found (nearest closed parents are narrower residuals, per re-review dedup). Y29-02 is a duplicate of Y15-01 and is filed only under Y15-01.

Juniper IPv6 match conditions (fetched by the verifier): `next-header` matches "the first 8-bit Next Header field in the packet". The MX note says `payload-protocol` matches the last Next Header.   - lo0 nft `pkg/daemon/daemon_nft_term_lower.go:148-150`: emits `meta l4proto`, which is also the transport protocol.

EXECUTED@audit: strict `next-header 43 ACCEPTED protocols=[43] warnings=[]` (name form rejected — control); Rust RH packet `outcome=L4(48,6)` — filter sees 6, never 43. Dead set 0/43/44/51/60/13

- Source verification: EXECUTED: the Go strict `CheckText` path and the Rust extension-header walk. Rust term evaluation against the walked protocol is a static read of `matching.rs` / `poll_descriptor/filter.rs`.
- Confidence: High
- Probe: - Go: `verify/z8/z8_y26_test.go` → `verify/z8/y26go.out`. `next-header 43`: strict commit ACCEPTED, `protocols=[43]`, `warnings=[]`. Control: `next-header routing` is REJECTED ("unknown protocol").

IPv6 extension-header filtering (RH/HBH/fragment/AH) is the main use of `next-header` in Junos IPv6 filters. Today every such term is dead with no diagnostic, its counter reads 0, and later accept terms admit the traffic.

EXECUTED@audit: Go `bit-length 4 range 0x4→{Offset:0 Length:1 Value:4 Mask:15}`, explicit Junos `match-mask 0xf`→identical (refutes "explicit mask avoids it" — only non-Junos pre-shifted mask works); Rust on `0x45…`: `version-nibble(4)=Accept ihl-nibble(5)=Discard` proves low nibble read.

## Probe / verification
- Source verification: EXECUTED: the Go strict `CheckText` lowering, including the explicit-mask and `bit-offset` variants, and the Rust filter evaluation.
- Confidence: High on the mechanism. Medium-High on the contract.

## Why it matters
Sub-byte header fields (IP version/IHL, TCP data offset, IPv6 traffic class/flow label) are the reason to use a non-byte-multiple bit-length. Each is evaluated against the wrong bits with a clean commit, and its counter silently reflects the wrong field.

## Fix direction / acceptance
Default mask `((1<<bits)-1) << (len*8 - bits)` with the value (and any explicit field mask) shifted the same way, or shift the read value right before comparing. ## #14635 — [Y27-01] SYN-flood attack-threshold (and alarm-threshold) is one per-zone aggregate, not per destination [CLOSED] (closed 2026-10-18)

## Summary
SYN-flood attack-threshold (and alarm-threshold) is one per-zone aggregate, not per destination

Finding `Y27-01` from `claude-opus-5-5-review-full-firewall-hostile-001.md` (deep-review run `review-work.7YDz9xALDc`, audit `5b122dda5ebb23aec9c283ef7cbddca0874b9338`). Both independent re-review passes (opus `opus-ob*` + spark `spark-ob*`, in `/var/tmp/deep-review-work/research-work.jd4pLTefrR/`) gate this claim **MATERIAL** at their checked `origin/master` revisions, with the narrowed scope noted in the source where applicable. Verified again against `origin/master` `3d2f037ea4ceb2732aec3d8c8c3c67424d69aa1c` for filing (citations below are at origin/master as cited by the re-reviewers; audit citations in Evidence).

**Severity (source verifier):** Medium — Medium (availability and operator contract). Busy zones get false cookie challenges (the first connect is reset) or, with cookies off, false drops. A single targeted service is under-protected until the zone-wide sum crosses the threshold. There is no enforcement bypass. (Reporter rated Medium.)

## Contract
- Current Juniper DoS guide (security-network-dos-attack.html): "SYN proxying only happens when a destination address and ingress interface port attack threshold is exceeded", and attack-threshold counts SYNs "to the same destination address per second".
  - Older ES 9.2 and Security 10.x docs: "same destination address and port number".
  - Neither says per zone.
  - In-tree, xpf presents the knob as a Junos clone: `docs/syn-cookie-flood-protection.md:15-35` ("Matching Junos SRX ... default of 200") and `pkg/config/compiler_security_screen.go:26-32` ("Junos SRX default").
  - The project's own #4112 rationale (`docs/syn-cookie-flood-protection.md:74-84`) calls per-zone aggregate keying a defect for ICMP and UDP ("two high-volume services in one zone ... SUM into one counter").

## Evidence (audit @ `5b122dda`, re-verified at master by both passes)
- `userspace-dp/src/screen/zone.rs:84-91` (observed): `syn_counter` and `syn_off_attack_bucket` are zone fields.
  - `zone.rs:488-490` (observed): the counter is incremented with no dst/port key.
  - `zone.rs:523-572` (observed): `MintChallenge`, a zone-wide active latch (`syn_cookie_active_until_secs`), and `DropAggregate`.
  - `docs/syn-cookie-flood-protection.md:172` says "the aggregate attack-threshold".
  - The worker adds `frame/tcp.rs:497-520`: a validated cookie ACK is answered with a RST, so every caught client loses its first connection.
  - No in-repo doc declares the zone aggregate a deliberate SYN deviation.

### Decisive regression / re-review evidence at master
- | Y27-01 SYN-flood attack/alarm threshold is per-zone aggregate, not per-destination | **MATERIAL** | Cur `zone.rs:87,91 syn_counter/syn_off_attack_bucket` zone fields (re-read; post-audit #14324 touched only cookie-ACK sketch); `:492 increment_and_classify` no dst/port key; `:523-572` zone-wide `syn_cookie_active_until` latch + DropAggregate. EXECUTED@audit cookie-OFF cell w/ controls: `one dst@150/s drops=0; two dsts@150/s each drops=802; one dst@300/s drops=801` — two under-threshold dsts drop at 2×-threshold rate, decisive keying proof. Junos (current+older): per destination addr (+port/ingress port), never per-zone; xpf docs claim Junos clone (`syn-cookie-flood-protection.md:15-35`, com

## Probe / verification
- Source verification: EXECUTED for the cookie-OFF cell. The cookie-ON cell (`y27_01b`) was not run by z7; the cookie-OFF cell suffices for the keying claim.
- Confidence: High (executed, plus vendor documentation).
- Probe: z7 `z7_y27_01_attack_threshold_keying_cookie_off` (`verify/z7/probes/screen_tests.rs.z7probe.rs`), threshold 200, cookies off, 10 s. Output (`verify/z7/run1.out`): `one dst@150/s drops=0; two dsts@150/s each drops=802; one dst@300/s drops=801`, then the assertion `two dsts each under threshold dropped as zone aggregate` fails (left 802, right 0). The single-destination under and over cells are the controls and behave as expected. Two under-threshold destinations drop at the same rate as one destination at twice the threshold.

## Why it matters
In cookie mode, a zone-wide false trip resets the first connection of every new client to every service in the zone. With cookies off, legitimate SYNs are silently dropped. Conversely, a flood against one service escapes challenge while the zone sum is low. Both directions contradict the documented Junos-clone behaviour.

## Fix direction / acceptance
- Key the attack/alarm measurement and the cookie-OFF drop bucket per (dst_ip, dst_port), or per destination plus ingress port as the current Junos docs say.
  - Activate cookies per key, and keep any zone-wide latch only as a secondary ceiling, as #4112 did for ICMP/UDP.
  - Acceptance criterion: two destinations at 0.75×threshold each give 0 drops and 0 challenges, and one destination:port at 1.5×threshold is still dropped or challenged.
  - Remaining validation: run the cookie-ON cell (`y27_01b`).

Acceptance: a regression test exercising the decisive check named by the re-reviewers for `Y27-01` fails on current `origin/master` and passes after the fix, with the cited controls still passing. Do not close on a nearby/already-fixed sibling mechanism.

## Summary
With an ingress BA classifier plus an input-filter `then forwarding-class`, the packet is queued as the filter's class but its DSCP is re-marked with the BA class's code-point (a regression from #13968)

Finding `Y28-01` from `claude-opus-5-5-review-full-firewall-hostile-001.md` (deep-review run `review-work.7YDz9xALDc`, audit `5b122dda5ebb23aec9c283ef7cbddca0874b9338`). **Severity (source verifier):** Medium — Medium. It affects every packet of the standard "BA on the unit plus an MF filter for exceptions plus an egress rewrite" design. Marking toward the next hop is corrupted, and a LAN host that picks the DSCP chooses which class's code-point leaves the box. There is no local enforcement bypass. (reporter rated Medium)

## Contract
A multifield (filter) forwarding class overrides BA classification, and the egress rewrite is keyed by the packet's final class and loss priority.   - `tx/cos_classify_ba.rs:249-251`: the class key is tried first, with the queue key as fallback. `:895-939` `reclassify_cached_cos_lp_rewrite`, the filter-pinned cache-hit path, also keys on the BA class first.
  - `git show b9f8b6fb7f`: before the fix the lookup was `resolve_cos_queue_lp_rewrite(queue_id)`, which is the filter queue. That is the inference that this is a regression.
  - The only #13968 test (`egress_dscp_rewrite_unmaterialized_fc_does_not_bleach_and_no_unmaterialized_guard`) has no filter. The worker also reports a secondary effect, static only and not separately verified: an unmaterialized filter class is never rewritten by its own class.

- Confidence: High

Control A, unit 6 with no BA: `queue=Some(5) rewrite=Some(46)`. Control B, unit 5 with no filter: `queue=Some(1) rewrite=Some(17)`. Witness, unit 5 with filter voice: `fresh queue=Some(5) rewrite=Some(17); cached queue=Some(5) rewrite=Some(17); hit=Some(17)`, where the expected value is 46. The worker's unexecuted draft is `workers/y28/evidence/probe_y28_01_filter_fc_rewrite.rs`.

## Why it matters
The MF classifier exists to override what the host marked. The egress marking now follows the host's choice, so upstream treatment can be wrong in either direction: EF-marked bulk, or MF-selected voice bleached. It is bounded to configs that use all three features together.

## Fix direction / acceptance
Pass the resolved filter forwarding class into the rewrite resolver, with key order filter class → BA class → clamped queue. Store the filter class in the cached descriptor for `reclassify_cached_cos_lp_rewrite`. Acceptance criterion (verifier): the witness above yields Some(46) on the fresh, cached-seed and cache-hit paths. Controls A and B and `egress_dscp_rewrite_unmaterialized_fc_does_not_bleach_and_no_unmaterialized_guard` stay unchanged.

An operator who renames or removes best-effort to cap bulk traffic gets the opposite: unclassified traffic uncapped at line rate, and rate-less priority classes starved behind it. ## #14639 — [Y30-01] WireGuard under-load handshake admission keyed on the full IPv6 /128 fails closed at 2048 entries; one /64 locks every legitimate peer out of rekey [CLOSED] (closed 2026-10-17)

## Summary
WireGuard under-load handshake admission keyed on the full IPv6 /128 fails closed at 2048 entries; one /64 locks every legitimate peer out of rekey

Finding `Y30-01` from `claude-opus-5-5-review-full-firewall-hostile-001.md` (deep-review run `review-work.7YDz9xALDc`, audit `5b122dda5ebb23aec9c283ef7cbddca0874b9338`). Both independent re-review passes (opus `opus-ob*` + spark `spark-ob*`, in `/var/tmp/deep-review-work/research-work.jd4pLTefrR/`) gate this claim **MATERIAL** at their checked `origin/master` revisions, with the narrowed scope noted in the source where applicable. Verified again against `origin/master` `3d2f037ea4ceb2732aec3d8c8c3c67424d69aa1c` for filing (citations below are at origin/master as cited by the re-reviewers; audit citations in Evidence).

**Severity (source verifier):** Medium — Medium. The attacker is unauthenticated and needs only the tunnel's public key plus IPv6 reach to the listen port. Every peer of the tunnel loses rekey, and existing sessions die at REJECT_AFTER_TIME (180 s). There is no confidentiality or integrity impact. (reporter rated Medium)

## Contract
WireGuard whitepaper §5.3: under load, a peer that completes the cookie round trip with a valid MAC2 must still be processed. The Linux reference ratelimiter keys IPv6 on /64 ("Only use 64 bits, so as to ratelimit the whole /64", `ratelimiter.c:102`) with a table of up to 65536 entries. wireguard-go keys on the full address but has no entry cap. xpf's own `wg/cookie.rs:133-135` doc says overflow evicts the least-recently-refilled bucket. That is true of the reply table and false of the handshake table.

## Evidence (audit @ `5b122dda`, re-verified at master by both passes)
- Observed: `wg/cookie.rs:103-136` sets `SOURCE_TABLE_MAX = 2048`.
  - Observed: `:448-497` `source_handshake_allowed` keys on the full `IpAddr`, refuses a new source at the cap, and garbage-collects only entries idle ≥1 s.
  - Observed: `wg/cookie_tests.rs:331-366` pins the refusal as intended behaviour.
  - Observed: the under-load trigger is 25 type-1/s per tunnel and counts junk too (`cookie.rs:374`, `engine.rs:665-668`).
  - Inference: an attacker who refreshes each /128 within 1 s keeps the table permanently full.

### Decisive regression / re-review evidence at master
- | Y30-01 WG under-load handshake admission keyed on full IPv6 /128, fails closed at 2048; one /64 locks out every peer | **MATERIAL** | Cur verified `afxdp/wg/cookie.rs:136` `SOURCE_TABLE_MAX=2048`; `:455-496` `source_handshake_allowed(src_ip: IpAddr)` full-address key, new source refused at cap `:476-480`, GC only idle ≥1s `:467-471`; pinning test `cookie_tests.rs:331-366` audit asserts refusal. Under-load trigger 25 type-1/s incl. junk (`cookie.rs:101` cur `INITIATIONS_UNDER_LOAD_THRESHOLD=25`). EXECUTED@audit: one /64 refreshing 2048 /128s → legit admissions `0/10`; control (attacker stops 2s) admitted. MAC2 bound to src IP:port so actor must own addresses — one SLAAC /64 suffices; valid 
- | Y30-01 WG under-load handshake admission keyed on full IPv6 /128 fails closed at 2048; one /64 locks out every legitimate peer | **MATERIAL** | Cur verified: `wg/cookie.rs:133-136` `SOURCE_TABLE_MAX=2048` with doc claiming overflow "evicts the least-recently-refilled bucket" — true of the reply table, false here: `source_handshake_allowed` (cur `:455-496`) keys `handshake_buckets` on the full `IpAddr`, returns `false` for a *new* source at cap (cur `:476-480`), GC reclaims only entries idle ≥1 s (`:467-471`). EXECUTED@audit probe with positive control: `legit admissions while one /64 refreshes 2048 /128s: 0/10`; after attacker stops 2 s the same legit source *is* admitted. MAC2 is source-b

## Probe / verification
- Source verification: EXECUTED. z10 ran a Rust probe with a positive control and fetched and confirmed the Linux and wireguard-go reference sources.
- Confidence: High
- Probe: `z10_probe_one_v6_slash64_pins_handshake_admission_table` in `wg/cookie_tests.rs` printed `legit admissions while one /64 refreshes 2048 /128s: 0/10`. Positive control: after the attacker stops for 2 s, the same legitimate source IS admitted (the assert passed). Saved at `verify/z10/probes_run1.out`. The worker's version is at `workers/y30/evidence/probe_y30_01_cookie_v6_prefix.rs`.

## Why it matters
The cookie mechanism exists to keep legitimate peers serviceable under a handshake flood. Here it becomes a lock-out primitive that one IPv6 host can drive, and it diverges from the reference's /64 aggregation.

## Fix direction / acceptance
Key IPv6 on /64 (IPv4 on /32, after canonicalising v4-mapped addresses), and/or replace the LRU entry instead of refusing when the table is full. Update the `handshake_source_bucket_burst_and_table_cap` test and correct the `cookie.rs:133-135` doc. Acceptance criterion: with IPv6 keyed on /64 (v4 /32) and/or LRU replacement instead of refusal, the probe admits the legitimate source while one /64 refreshes 2048 /128s, and one /64 receives at most SOURCE_HANDSHAKE_BURST admissions per refill.

## #14641 — [Y31-01] `enqueue_pending_forwards` recycles (and can publish to FILL) the ingress UMEM chunk before the staged port-mirror clone copies bytes out of it [CLOSED] (closed 2026-10-18)

## Summary
`enqueue_pending_forwards` recycles (and can publish to FILL) the ingress UMEM chunk before the staged port-mirror clone copies bytes out of it

Finding `Y31-01` from `claude-opus-5-5-review-full-firewall-hostile-001.md` (deep-review run `review-work.7YDz9xALDc`, audit `5b122dda5ebb23aec9c283ef7cbddca0874b9338`). **Severity (source verifier):** Low — Low. Port-mirroring on the ingress, a non-in-place forward path and a post-push FILL backlog of exactly 1024 are all required. The kernel must then consume about 1023 earlier entries and DMA into this chunk within the memcpy window, which is practically remote. If hit, the analyzer receives another packet's bytes from the same queue: wrong mirror content and cross-flow disclosure to the analyzer. Forwarding is not corrupted. (reporter rated Low)

## Contract
A chunk on the FILL ring is kernel-owned, and userspace must not read it after publishing. The worker cites kernel `net/xdp/xsk_buff_pool.c` `__xp_alloc`/`xp_alloc_new_from_fq` from a 6.19/7.0-rc tree, not the host's 7.2.8. The read site states the same invariant: `tx/dispatch/mod.rs:984-997`, "frame not yet returned to fill ring (that happens after this function completes)".

## Evidence (audit @ `5b122dda`, re-verified at master by both passes)
- `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/tx/dispatch/mod.rs:121-130`: `recycle_ingress_frame` drains at ≥1024.
  - `tx/dispatch/mod.rs:1674-1692`: recycle, then `commit_staged_mirror_clone(.., source_frame)`. `:1306`: the snapshot is taken only on the in-place branch.
  - `tx/rings.rs:175-262`: `drain_pending_fill` pops FIFO, then `fill.commit()`, then an optional wake.
  - `neighbor_dispatch.rs` commits before recycling (worker, `:887-889,936-953`), so only the dispatch site is exposed.

UMEM invariant stated in-tree (`tx/dispatch/mod.rs:984-997` "not yet returned to fill ring"). Audit EXECUTED w/ modelled-DMA hook: prequeued=1023 → mirror=`[a5…]`≠frame; control (tail drain) mirror==frame. `neighbor_dispatch.rs` commits-before-recycle = correct sibling.
- | Y31-01 `enqueue_pending_forwards` recycles (can publish to FILL) ingress UMEM chunk before staged mirror clone copies bytes | **MATERIAL** (Low, latent ownership-ordering) | Cur verified ordering: success path `tx/dispatch/mod.rs:1674-1676` `recycle_ingress_frame` *before* `:1677-1692` `commit_staged_mirror_clone(...,source_frame)`; `recycle_ingress_frame:122-129` pushes to `pending_fill_frames` and at `>=FILL_BATCH_SIZE` (1024) synchronously `drain_pending_fill` → kernel FILL ring. Only in-place branch snapshots first (`:1305-1307 snapshot_staged_mirror_clone`), so non-in-place (cross-UMEM/tunnel/NAT64) staged clones read live UMEM after possible publish — violates in-tree invariant `disp

## Probe / verification
- Source verification: EXECUTED, with a simulated DMA hook. The hook models kernel ownership; it is not a kernel observation. The reporter had marked this STATIC plus NEEDS_VALIDATION; the verifier executed it.
- Confidence: High for the ordering violation (executed with modelled DMA). Low for observed production impact.
- Probe: `z9_y31_01_mirror_clone_reads_chunk_after_fill_publish` with a temporary cfg(test) hook that scribbles 0xA5 over each chunk as `drain_pending_fill` publishes it (`verify/z9/probes/z9_y31_ptb_append.rs`, `z9_y31_rings_hook.txt`, in `z9_full_probe.diff`; output `verify/z9/run_z9.log`). Control: `prequeued=0 … fill_published=1 mirror == frame`, because the publish happens at the function-tail drain after the commit. Witness: `prequeued=1023 … fill_published=1 mirror_first16=[a5 …] equal_frame=false`. Worker draft: `workers/y31/evidence/y31-01_probe.diff`.

## Why it matters
A mirror/analyzer is an evidence and lawful-intercept surface. A clone carrying another packet's bytes is an operator-visible lie and a cross-flow disclosure. The in-code invariant comment is false. A future change (LIFO free list, smaller batch, an inline-NAPI wake) could make the window live.

## Fix direction / acceptance
Move `commit_staged_mirror_clone` above the success-path `recycle_ingress_frame`, as `neighbor_dispatch.rs` does, or make `recycle_ingress_frame` never drain mid-loop. Acceptance criterion (verifier): the armed cell yields mirror == frame (commit before recycle, or no mid-loop drain), and `successful_forward_commits_one_mirror_clone_11432` stays green.

Acceptance: a regression test exercising the decisive check named by the re-reviewers for `Y31-01` fails on current `origin/master` and passes after the fix, with the cited controls still passing. Do not close on a nearby/already-fixed sibling mechanism.

## #14645 — [Y34-01] Native GRE cannot receive an outer-fragmented GRE datagram: the head reaches the helper, which never reassembles and fails decap, and the tails go to the kernel (or are refused), which has no GRE terminator [CLOSED] (closed 2026-10-18)

## Summary
Native GRE cannot receive an outer-fragmented GRE datagram: the head reaches the helper, which never reassembles and fails decap, and the tails go to the kernel (or are refused), which has no GRE terminator

Finding `Y34-01` from `claude-opus-5-5-review-full-firewall-hostile-001.md` (deep-review run `review-work.7YDz9xALDc`, audit `5b122dda5ebb23aec9c283ef7cbddca0874b9338`). Both independent re-review passes (opus `opus-ob*` + spark `spark-ob*`, in `/var/tmp/deep-review-work/research-work.jd4pLTefrR/`) gate this claim **MATERIAL** at their checked `origin/master` revisions, with the narrowed scope noted in the source where applicable. **Severity (source verifier):** Medium — Medium. Any native-GRE deployment loses every GRE datagram that the peer or an underlay router fragments. Examples are a DF-clear inner at full underlay MTU, and xpf's own `clear-dont-fragment-bit` or DF-copy encap crossing a smaller-MTU hop. The loss is silent and has no xpf counter. It is an availability/interop gap, not an enforcement bypass. (reporter rated Medium)

## Contract
A tunnel endpoint is an IP host for the outer datagram and must reassemble it before decap. The worker cites RFC 1122 §3.3.2 and RFC 4459 §3; whether they were fetched is not recorded. `docs/userspace-native-gre-plan.md:181`: xpf itself emits DF-clear outers "allowing downstream fragmentation". `docs/bugs.md:1306-1310` (#10677) and the comment at `userspace-xdp/src/lib.rs:981-987` say native GRE tails stay on the helper path.

## Evidence (audit @ `5b122dda`, re-verified at master by both passes)
- `userspace-xdp/src/lib.rs:707-708`: `native_gre` is keyed on the parsed protocol. `:1876-1884`: a non-first fragment's protocol is set to 255, so `native_gre` is false for tails.
  - `lib.rs:887-1000`: a tail to a local destination takes `cpumap_or_pass` (kernel). On the interface-NAT arm, `userspace-xdp/src/tunnel_frag.rs:90-109` steers the tail to the helper, which refuses a proto-255 tail (`docs/bugs.md:1306-1310`).
  - `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/gre.rs:124-150`: `packet_trimmed_len` returns None when the inner Total Length exceeds the bytes present, which is always true for a head. `:1078-1198` has no fragment handling (grep `fragment` in gre.rs finds only the encap DF line).
  - `pkg/routing/tunnel.go:588-592`: the native-GRE tunnel netdev is a TUN anchor. Inference: even if the kernel reassembled, nothing terminates the GRE, and a kernel-side decap would bypass the helper anyway.

### Decisive regression / re-review evidence at master

Audit EXECUTED helper leg: whole-decap contr
- | Y34-01 Native GRE cannot receive outer-fragmented datagram: head→helper never reassembles/fails decap, tails→kernel (or refused), no GRE terminator | **MATERIAL** (Medium) | Cur verified split ownership: shim `lib.rs:709-710 native_gre = protocol==PROTO_GRE && flag`; non-first frag protocol substituted 255 (`:984-988` comment, audit `:1876-1884`) so tails aren't native-GRE — local-dst arm `cpumap_or_pass` (kernel), IFNAT arm steered to helper which refuses proto-255 (audit `tunnel_frag.rs:90-109`, `docs/bugs.md:1306-1310` — comment accurate only for IFNAT arm). Helper: `gre.rs:124-149 packet_trimmed_len` returns `None` when inner total-len > bytes present (always for head), `:1198` propaga

## Probe / verification
- Source verification: EXECUTED (helper decap) / STATIC (shim steering, kernel).
- Confidence: High that the helper never decaps a head (executed). Medium for the exact tail and kernel disposition (static).
- Probe: `z9_y34_01_outer_first_fragment_never_decaps` (`verify/z9/probes/z9_y34_append.rs`, in `z9_full_probe.diff`; output `verify/z9/run_z9.log`). Control: `control whole decap some=true`, byte-identical inner. Witness: `witness first-fragment decap some=false`. The shim and kernel legs were not executed; the worker notes that `unshare -Urn` cannot load ip_gre. Worker draft: `workers/y34/evidence/y34-01_tests_gre_outer_fragment_probe.rs`.

## Why it matters
xpf's own default GRE encap (DF copied from an IPv4 inner, `pkg/config/types_routing.go:759-761`; `gre.rs:1389-1391`) produces DF=0 outers for most UDP. A receiving xpf drops any of them that an underlay hop fragments. The only signal is the kernel's reassembly-timeout counters, while the in-tree comment and docs say tails stay on the helper. The verifier noted that the `lib.rs:981-987` comment is accurate for the interface-NAT arm it sits in; it only gives a false impression about the local-destination arm.

## Fix direction / acceptance
Keep the head and tails of a native-GRE outer on one path, for example by keeping proto-255 tails whose wire protocol is GRE on XSK when native GRE is armed. Then reassemble in a bounded pool before `try_native_gre_decap_from_frame`. Until then, count the drop. Acceptance criterion (verifier): a native-GRE outer split into head and tail (IPv4 MF/offset, and an IPv6 Fragment header) yields exactly one byte-identical decapsulated inner. A shim truth-table cell asserts that a native-GRE local tail is not sent to `cpumap_or_pass`. Until that is fixed, the drop is counted. Remaining validation: the shim and kernel legs.

Acceptance: a regression test exercising the decisive check named by the re-reviewers for `Y34-01` fails on current `origin/master` and passes after the fix, with the cited controls still passing. Do not close on a nearby/already-fixed sibling mechanism.

## Probe / verification
- Source verification: EXECUTED. z10 ran a Rust probe that mirrors the delta_recovery macro over 3000 owner-RG-1 sessions, with a connected positive control. Outage duration was not measured.
- Confidence: High for the mechanism. Medium for how long outages last in practice, which was not measured.
- Probe: `z10_probe_loss_resync_rearms_while_event_stream_disconnected` in `afxdp/session_glue/tests.rs`, release profile. Control (connected handle with room): `connected pass: out_of_sync=false candidates=3000 frames=3000`. Defect: `disconnected pass 0/1/2: out_of_sync=true re-exported=3000` on every pass, with the wedge latch reset per pass as worker_loop does. The test PASSED as written. Saved at `verify/z10/probes_run1.out` (diff in `verify/z10/probes_run1.diff`). The worker's unrun sketch is at `workers/y35/evidence/probe_y35_04_resync_rearm.rs`.

## Why it matters
A routine event-stream reconnect on an HA primary turns into repeated whole-table export work on every worker while the control plane recovers. The effect is reduced throughput and added latency. It is bounded by the outage duration, which was not measured.

## Fix direction / acceptance
(1) On the event-stream leg, treat a failed `bulk_resync` delta like the RPC leg does: count it but do not arm. Alternatively, skip the #2442 resync while `!connected`, since reconnect already triggers FullResync. (2) Optionally carry the wedge latch across passes. Acceptance criterion: with the stream disconnected for N worker passes, the LossResync export runs at most once (or not at all until reconnect), the probe's disconnected passes 1..N report no re-export, and a genuinely new incremental drop still re-arms. Remaining validation: real outage durations on the loss cluster.

## Summary

Finding `D2-01` from `gemini-4-argon-high-review-high-security-hostile-experts-100-001.md` (deep-review audit `0c5f646c`). ## Narrowed material core (both passes)
- Opus: .** Fragment leg: master `try_native_gre_decap_from_frame_with_input_filter` (`gre.rs:1078ff`) checks only `meta.protocol != PROTO_GRE` then proceeds; no `ipv4_is_any_fragment` / `ipv6_is_nonatomically_fragmented` guard anywhere in the function (grep confirms absence on master). Stage order confirmed: stage 6 GRE decap (`poll_stages.rs:369`) precedes session-flow/screen/IPsec stages. XDP walker: for IPv4, first fragment (offset 0, MF=1) keeps protocol 47; for IPv6 the walker (`ipv6_ext_walk.rs` FRAGMENT arm) sets `non_first_fragment` only when offset≠0 — a first fragment (M=1, offset=0) walks through to GRE and emits protocol 47. So an outer first fragment whose inner packet fits is decapsulated without reassembly/screen — bypassing `ip_frag` screen and overlap tracking for the outer layer. (Inner packet still faces full inner-packet pipeline, bounding impact.) **Strongest refutation/alternative.** AH leg is weaker than claimed: XDP `eh_class(AUTH)=EH_CLASS_AUTH` and the walk advances past AH to GRE, emitting protocol 47 — that part holds. But the claimed harm is bypass of Stage-11 `PROTO_AH` drop (#10729), which is a fail-closed policy for *unverified AH on transit traffic*; a GRE tunnel endpoint is a configured trust boundary — decapsulating AH-wrapped GRE arguably mirrors kernel GRE-over-IPsec behaviour. The defect is real as an *inconsistency* (non-GRE AH traffic dropped, GRE-wrapped AH silently stripped, no AH verification anywhere) but "authentication bypass" overstates: GRE itself has no authentication being bypassed; no IPsec SA is circumvented because GRE decap doe
- Spark: `try_native_gre_decap_from_frame_with_input_filter` gates only on `meta.protocol == PROTO_GRE` and contains no AH-sighting or fragment check at all. The XDP walker advances past `NEXTHDR_AUTH` (51) unverified (`EH_CLASS_AUTH` arm) and, for a first fragment (offset 0, M=1), leaves `non_first_fragment=false`, so `meta.protocol` stays 47. Stage 6 decap therefore runs before Stage 10 screen / Stage 11 (`stage11_raw_protocol_requires_drop`, ESP/AH) ever see the *outer* packet. The non-GRE path explicitly re-derives AH identity (`inspect.rs` `ipv6_ah_sighted`, #10729) — the GRE path is the asymmetric hole. A first fragment whose inner packet fits is decapsulated with no outer reassembly/overlap screening.

## Summary
`fragment_nat64_ipv6_frame` Floors `mtu` to `1280` (`mtu.max(1280)`), Emitting Oversized 1280-Byte IPv6 Fragments and Gratuitous Atomic Fragments That Are Dropped on Sub-1280 Tunnel Underlays

Finding `D2-05` from `gemini-4-argon-high-review-high-security-hostile-experts-100-001.md` (deep-review audit `0c5f646c`). Both independent re-review passes gate this claim **MATERIAL** at their checked `origin/master` revisions — opus: ; spark:  — with the narrowed scope below. ## Narrowed material core (both passes)
- Opus: .** MTU leg confirmed verbatim on master: `fragment_nat64_ipv6_frame` (`frame/mod.rs:475`) `let mtu = mtu.max(1280);` after the `total_len <= mtu` early return. For caller MTU 1200 and total 1240: emits one 1248-byte "atomic" fragment (larger than input); for 1400: 1280-byte first fragment — both exceed the egress MTU the caller explicitly passed, and the sibling `tcp_segmentation.rs` (#5159) comment explicitly forbids this floor for tunnel underlays. Downstream `wg_encap_frame_with_commit` MTU guard then drops — silent blackhole, no PTB (DF=0 path). **Strongest refutation/alternative.** Non-8-octet leg is NEG as stated: master loop computes `max_data = mtu.saturating_sub(48)/8*8` (multiple of 8), `len = min(remaining, max_data)`; only the *final* chunk can be non-multiple-of-8, and final chunk has `more = original_more || offset+len < data.len()`. If `original_more` and the incoming fragment's data length is non-multiple-of-8 — but a *non-final incoming* fragment with non-multiple-of-8 payload is itself RFC-invalid input; NAT64 translating it at all is questionable, and the emitted sub-fragment's non-8 length is inherited, not created. The audit's Case 3 (data_len=1350, second fragment chunk=118 with M=1) requires max_data not multiple of 8 or misaligned base — `base_offset` from existing frag header is in 8-byte units (`word>>3)*8`, checked `absolute % 8 != 0 → None`), so the arithmetic on master does not produce it for valid inputs. Also note RFC 8200: sub-1280 MTU tunnels are themselves non-conformant underlays; the floor has a defensible reading ("IPv6 min MTU") — but 
- Spark: `fragment_nat64_ipv6_frame` early-returns when `total_len <= mtu`, then executes `let mtu = mtu.max(1280);` — so for a sub-1280 tunnel egress (e.g. 1200) a 1240 B translated packet is emitted as one 1248 B atomic fragment (`max_data=(1280-48)/8*8=1232 ≥ data 1200`), 48 B over the egress MTU, and `wg_encap_frame_with_commit`'s exact outer-MTU guard drops it with no ICMP to the sender. Larger packets fragment at 1280, equally over-MTU. The IPv6-minimum-MTU comment confuses a *link* floor hosts must accept with the *configured egress* MTU the caller already computed.

## #14664 — [Y39-01] `tcp-mss all-tcp` is not a ceiling on tunnel egress when no `gre-out` is set: the MTU-derived GRE/WG MSS replaces a smaller `all-tcp` [CLOSED] (closed 2026-10-18)

## Summary
`tcp-mss all-tcp` is not a ceiling on tunnel egress when no `gre-out` is set: the MTU-derived GRE/WG MSS replaces a smaller `all-tcp`

Finding `Y39-01` from `claude-opus-5-5-review-full-firewall-hostile-001.md` (deep-review run `review-work.7YDz9xALDc`, audit `5b122dda5ebb23aec9c283ef7cbddca0874b9338`). Both independent re-review passes (opus `opus-ob*` + spark `spark-ob*`, in `/var/tmp/deep-review-work/research-work.jd4pLTefrR/`) gate this claim **MATERIAL** at their checked `origin/master` revisions, with the narrowed scope noted in the source where applicable. Verified again against `origin/master` `3d2f037ea4ceb2732aec3d8c8c3c67424d69aa1c` for filing (citations below are at origin/master as cited by the re-reviewers; audit citations in Evidence).

**Severity (source verifier):** Low — Low — an accepted knob is not applied to tunnel-bound SYNs; the derived value never exceeds the local tunnel budget, so loss only bites when the bottleneck is downstream of the tunnel peer (reporter rated Low).

## Contract
`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/forwarding/mss.rs:6-19` ("`all-tcp` ... applies to every forwarded TCP SYN regardless of tunnel context") and `docs/feature-gaps.md:413` ("all-tcp — clamps every forwarded TCP SYN"). These contradict `select_tcp_mss`'s own doc (`mss.rs:203-207`, "Falls back to all-tcp only when that yields 0"). Junos (fetched security-edit-tcp-mss page): a GRE-specific value overrides `all-tcp` only when configured; no precedence is given to an implicit MTU-derived value.

## Evidence (audit @ `5b122dda`, re-verified at master by both passes)
- `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/forwarding/mss.rs:194-232` — `select_tcp_mss` tunnel branch returns the tunnel value if > 0, else `tcp_mss_all_tcp`.
  - `mss.rs:66-99` — `native_gre_tcp_mss` min-s `gre-out` with the derived value; `all-tcp` is never min-ed in.
  - Callers `frame/build/mod.rs:107`, `tx/dispatch/mod.rs:1304`, `poll_descriptor/flow_cache_hit.rs:765`, `neighbor_dispatch.rs:988` all use `select_tcp_mss`, so the gap is uniform across paths (observation).

### Decisive regression / re-review evidence at master
- | Y39-01 `tcp-mss all-tcp` not a ceiling on tunnel egress when no `gre-out` (derived MSS replaces smaller all-tcp) | **MATERIAL** (Low, narrow) | Cur `mss.rs:194-232` re-read: `select_tcp_mss` tunnel branch returns `tunnel_tcp_mss` if >0 else all-tcp; `native_gre_tcp_mss:66-99` mins `gre-out` with derived but never all-tcp. Header `:6-19` claims all-tcp "applies to every forwarded TCP SYN regardless of tunnel context" — internal contradiction with `:203-207` fallback-only doc persists. EXECUTED@audit: derived=1416, all-tcp=1200 → returns 1416 (assert fails); controls non-tunnel→1200, gre-out 1200→1200 pass. Callers uniform (frame/build, dispatch, flow_cache_hit, neighbor_dispatch). | Explici

## Probe / verification
- Source verification: EXECUTED (verifier's Rust cell, debug build).
- Confidence: High
- Probe: Verifier cell appended to `afxdp/tunnel_tests.rs`, `cargo +1.98.1 test --bin xpf-userspace-dp z13_y39 -- --nocapture` (CARGO_TARGET_DIR=tmp/z13-target). Diff `verify/z13/rust-probes.diff`, output `verify/z13/rust-probes.out`: `derived=1416 plain_all_tcp=1200 gre_out_1200=1200 all_tcp_1200_tunnel=1416 all_tcp_1200+gre_out_1300=1300`, assertion failed. Controls: non-tunnel all-tcp → 1200 and explicit gre-out 1200 → 1200 show the cell can pass. The 1300 cell is consistent with Junos precedence and is not a defect. Worker's unexecuted draft: `workers/y39/evidence/probe_y39_01_all_tcp_tunnel.rs`.

## Why it matters
Operators set `all-tcp` below the tunnel budget precisely when a downstream link is smaller; tunnel-bound flows then advertise a larger MSS and depend on PMTUD, the blackhole the knob exists to prevent. Scoped to tunnel-bound flows with no `gre-out`.

## Fix direction / acceptance
Min only the implicit derived tunnel value with `all-tcp`; keep explicit `gre-out` as min(gre-out, derived) irrespective of `all-tcp`. Acceptance criterion (verifier): `select_tcp_mss` with all-tcp 1200, no gre-out and a GRE decision whose derived MSS is above 1200 returns 1200; with all-tcp 0 it returns the derived value; with gre-out set it returns min(gre-out, derived) irrespective of all-tcp (pinned and documented); the WG arm has the same cell; `mss.rs:8-10` and `select_tcp_mss`'s doc agree.

Acceptance: a regression test exercising the decisive check named by the re-reviewers for `Y39-01` fails on current `origin/master` and passes after the fix, with the cited controls still passing. Do not close on a nearby/already-fixed sibling mechanism.

## #14665 — [gemini-hostile D4-02] Missing Outer-Destination Validation and Composed SNAT+DNAT Private-IP Leak in Embedded ICMP N… [CLOSED] (closed 2026-10-18)

## Summary
Missing Outer-Destination Validation and Composed SNAT+DNAT Private-IP Leak in Embedded ICMP NAT Matchers and Rewriters

Finding `D4-02` from `gemini-4-argon-high-review-high-security-hostile-experts-100-001.md` (deep-review audit `0c5f646c`). Both independent re-review passes gate this claim **MATERIAL** at their checked `origin/master` revisions — opus: ; spark:  — with the narrowed scope below. Coordinator re-checked the cited anchors against current `origin/master` `09c6b9ed9f62e389081b8ecc3a9df7bce23da7c9` for filing (line numbers as cited by the re-reviewers; re-anchor before fixing).
## Narrowed material core (both passes)
- Opus: Grep-verified: `outer_dst` appears *only* in `nat64_match.rs` (`hdr.src != outer_dst_v4` :165, `hdr.src_wire != outer_dst_v6` :291); `nat_match_v4/v6.rs` and `session_match.rs` have zero outer-destination checks, so a quoted tuple matches regardless of the ICMP error's actual outer destination. `outbound_snat` (v4 :222) requires `rewrite_dst.is_none()`, excluding composed SNAT+DNAT from the outbound-error rewrite path. The NAT64 sibling proves the check is the house pattern, omitted here. - Strongest refutation/alternative: The quoted-tuple match itself is a strong authenticator (attacker must know live 4-tuple + ident), and builders do rewrite some outer fields (`builders.rs:72` writes `pkt[16..20]`) — so "any destination, no crafting" overstates ease, and the leak leg depends on which builder a composed flow actually reaches, not fully traced here. Still, destination-blind acceptance defeats egress-destination policy for the error's delivery, which tuple knowledge does not justify. - Gate: MATERIAL for adding the NAT64-style outer-dst gate to v4/v6/session matchers; validate the leak on the composed builder path before filing it. - Decisive check: claim's NoMatch unit test + SNAT+DNAT outbound builder byte assertion.
- Spark: `match_outer_v4` (nat_match_v4.rs:12ff) and the v6/session_match counterparts build the embedded key purely from the *quoted* header and proceed to session lookup/rewrite; no step binds the ICMP error's outer destination to the quoted flow's source (or its translated equivalent), and the SNAT builders named in the claim do not rewrite the outer destination. A quoted tuple therefore authorizes delivery/rewriting toward an outer destination the original flow never involved. The composed SNAT+DNAT leg follows from `outbound_snat`'s `rewrite_dst.is_none()` precondition excluding exactly the twice-NAT sessions whose errors then fall through unrewritten, leaking pre-NAT addresses.

## Summary
`handle_upsert_synced` Evaluates `allow_replace_local` Before Re-Resolving `owner_rg_id`, Short-Circuits Cached `LocalDelivery` Across Nodes, and Leaks Replaced Pool/NAT64 Port Reservations

Finding `D4-05` from `gemini-4-argon-high-review-high-security-hostile-experts-100-001.md` (deep-review audit `0c5f646c`). Both independent re-review passes gate this claim **MATERIAL** at their checked `origin/master` revisions — opus: ; spark:  — with the narrowed scope below. ## Narrowed material core (both passes)
- Opus: Verified verbatim at master: `let allow_replace_local = synced_entry_allows_local_replace(ha_state, entry.metadata.owner_rg_id, ...)` and `is_active` are computed *before* the re-resolve block that later does `if new_owner > 0 { entry.metadata.owner_rg_id = new_owner; }` — so the replace/active decision uses the peer's stale `owner_rg_id` (incl. the #9714 `owner_rg_id==0` case). It also calls the cached `lookup_forwarding_resolution_for_session` though a `..._without_cache` variant exists for exactly this distrust. A standby/active misclassification therefore either overwrites a live local session or enforces HA snapshot on the wrong node state. - Strongest refutation/alternative: `enforce_ha_resolution_snapshot` is still applied when `is_active`, and the packet path revalidates HA via flow cache, so a wrongly-stored session may not forward on an inactive RG — impact may be session-table churn/foreign ifindex retention rather than traffic bypass. The reservation-release gating (`!new_entry_reserves` only) was not fully re-traced; cross-pool leak is COHORT until shown. - Gate: MATERIAL for reorder (compute owner from local re-resolve first, use without-cache lookup); validate leak leg separately. - Decisive check: claim's split-RG upsert test + cross-pool reservation-release assertion.
- Spark: In `handle_upsert_synced` the replace/activeness decision (`allow_replace_local`, `is_active`) is computed from the *peer's* stamped decision before the local re-resolution that yields the local `owner_rg_id` — so the guard is evaluated against the wrong node's ownership. The resolution helpers in `session_glue/resolution.rs` then trust cached `LocalDelivery`/neighbor-fallback resolutions, which on a receiving node can carry a foreign `local_ifindex`, delivering transit traffic into the wrong node's host stack. Both are order-of-evaluation defects visible in the control flow, at both revs.

## Summary
Deterministic NAPT64 (`allocate_deterministic_v6_at`) Omits Expired-BIB Garbage Collection and Activation-Rollback Bookkeeping, Enabling Permanent Per-Subscriber Port-Block Exhaustion and HA Standby BIB Destruction

Finding `D5-01` from `gemini-4-argon-high-review-high-security-hostile-experts-100-001.md` (deep-review audit `0c5f646c`). Both independent re-review passes gate this claim **MATERIAL** at their checked `origin/master` revisions — opus: ; spark:  — with the narrowed scope below. ## Narrowed material core (both passes)
- Opus: In `allocate_deterministic_v6_at` the only expired-lease handling is for the *candidate's own* `bib_key` (`persistent_by_source.get(&bib_key).filter(expired)`); when `claim_in_block` returns None there is no `gc_expired_for_addr_locked` sweep of the subscriber's block (that helper is called on other paths, e.g. :3237), so a block full of expired idle BIBs still reports exhaustion. The minted lease sets `activation_had_previous_lease: false` (master :4460 in the deterministic ctor) without the `0→1` promotion bookkeeping other paths set (:3423, :5002), so `rollback_flow`'s `activation_had_previous_lease` branch treats a promoted/imported BIB as fresh and removes it. - Strongest refutation/alternative: Expired BIBs for the *same* src_port are reclaimed inline, so a subscriber reusing one port is fine; exhaustion needs `block_size` distinct ports — but that is ordinary browsing behaviour over 300s, as claimed. Memory-cap sub-leg (max_tracked bypass on reuse branch) plausible from the branch structure but secondary. - Decisive check: claim's fill-expire-allocate allocator test + rollback-preserves-BIB test.
- Spark: In `allocate_deterministic_v6_at`, the block claim (`occupancy[ip_idx].claim_in_block`, allocator.rs:4303 at both revs) has no preceding `gc_expired_for_addr_locked` sweep — the only GC call sites are in the sibling PAT path — and the claim-failure branch consults only the *new flow's own* `persistent_by_source` key. Once a subscriber's block is fully occupied by expired idle BIB leases under *other* source ports, every new allocation fails `AllocatorExhausted` with no in-path reclamation, indefinitely (until unrelated pressure GC happens to run). The secondary legs (bitmap claimed before BIB-existence check; `max_tracked_flows` skipped on the full-block reuse branch; missing `0->1` activation-rollback bookkeeping that `rollback_flow`/`release_flow` expect) are consistent with the #14091 retrofit having bolted persistent-lease storage onto a path that never got the PAT path's lifecycle machinery.

## Summary
Same-Allocator Address-Only Source-NAT Admission Ignores `persistent_address_only_owner_counts`, Allowing Duplicate `(translated_ip, port)` Leases That Blackhole Inbound Persistent-NAT Traffic for Both Subscribers

Finding `D5-02` from `gemini-4-argon-high-review-high-security-hostile-experts-100-001.md` (deep-review audit `0c5f646c`). Both independent re-review passes gate this claim **MATERIAL** at their checked `origin/master` revisions — opus: ; spark:  — with the narrowed scope below. ## Narrowed material core (both passes)
- Opus: Bounded check of the three reserve functions shows they consult `address_only_owners` (live) but not `persistent_address_only_owner_counts` / `address_only_owns_wire_identity` in their admission heads, while PAT/deterministic/idle-import paths do call `address_only_owns_wire_identity` (:3049, :3253, :4436...). After H1's flow releases, the live owner is gone but the idle PersistentLease + owner counts remain for 300s, so H2 with the same src port admits the same `(translated_ip, port)`; `persistent_inbound_lookup` then sees two permitted source keys for one wire identity and returns Denied for both. - Strongest refutation/alternative: The scan window (first ~4000 chars per fn) could miss a later guard, and pool rotation in roundrobin may usually pick a different IP, making collision probabilistic on multi-IP pools (deterministic on single-IP / same-start pools). - Spark: The contention state exists and is used inconsistently: `persistent_address_only_owner_counts` (allocator.rs:1002) with `address_only_owns_wire_identity` is consulted by the PAT allocation path, the deterministic path, peer-pool contention, and idle-lease import — but the three same-allocator address-only admission functions (`reserve_address_only_persistent`, `reserve_address_only_roundrobin`, `reserve_address_only_maybe_persistent`) admit on live `address_only_owners`/`pat_owns_wire_identity` alone. An idle/expired-but-counted owner therefore does not block a second subscriber from being minted the same `(translated_ip, port)` wire identity, and `persistent_by_translated` then holds two source keys for one identity, which inbound persistent-NAT lookup treats as contended (`Denied`) for both.

A daemon restart would clear state, but that is not a defence of an explicit revoke verb violating its own doc ("Revoke every persistent source-NAT lease owned by the current forwarding snapshot"). - Gate: MATERIAL (clear + display + fence legs). - Decisive check: as in table.
- Spark: Verified asymmetry in one file: `export_idle_persistent_leases` DOES iterate `nat64.prefixes` with `nat64-deterministic-{idx}` and import handles that prefix (so HA sync leg is covered), while `export_display_persistent_leases` and `clear_persistent_nat_leases` iterate only `forwarding.source_nat_rules` pool_mode — no nat64 prefix loop. ## Summary

Finding `D6-05` from `gemini-4-argon-high-review-high-security-hostile-experts-100-001.md` (deep-review audit `0c5f646c`). ## Narrowed material core (both passes)
- Opus: Verified end-to-end. `stop_workers::handle` (the `PrepareLinkCycle` verb) calls `guard.afxdp.stop()` → `stop_inner(true)`. `stop_inner` defaults `self.forwarding` and `self.validation` unconditionally, and `if clear_synced_state` (mod.rs:1197-1211) clears `sessions.nat`, `sessions.forward_wire`, and — via `SharedSessionOwnerRgIndexes::clear(&sessions.synced)` at `types/mod.rs:256-275`, which locks and `sessions.clear()`s the primary synced map itself — every HA-synced session. That destroys: the synced map `rebind`'s `replay_preserved_sessions` is supposed to replay, the `PortAllocator` instances holding persistent-NAT leases (previous-forwarding migration in the later `reconcile` then sees an empty baseline), and the `tunnel_owners` baseline for the remap purge. The `rebind.rs` comment states these exact side effects are "wrong for a rebind" and asserts the link-cycle path is unaffected because Go sends a separate `stop_workers` — which is precisely the call that performs the wipe. Go side confirmed: `PrepareLinkCycle`/`NotifyLinkCycle` are the RETH MAC link-cycle hooks in `pkg/daemon/daemon_apply_dataplane.go`. - Strongest refutation/alternative: One could argue a full stop is *supposed* to wipe and the HA peer will re-sync afterwards. But `rebind`'s documented contract is replay-from-memory, a standby node may have no peer to re-sync from (or only at bulk-export cost), and persistent-NAT leases are local allocator state no peer holds in identical form. No preservation snapshot is taken in `stop_workers` before `stop()`. - Gate: MATERIAL. Fix shape (preserve synced/forwar
- Spark: `stop_workers.handle` calls `guard.afxdp.stop()` with comment “Used by PrepareLinkCycle… subsequent rebind recreates workers”. `Coordinator::stop → stop_inner(true)` (mod.rs:772/1016) and at 1251 `if clear_synced_state { …clear(&self.sessions.synced) }`. `rebind.rs:18-36` comment explicitly documents stop_inner(true)'s side effects as “wrong for a rebind: wiping in-memory synced session map (should be replayed), defaulting forwarding/validation, blinding tunnel-owner remap purge” — and Go sends separate stop_workers before link cycle, so rebind's avoidance does not save the stop_workers leg. Persistent NAT/tunnel baseline wipe follows same stop_inner path per claim.

## #14678 — [gemini-hostile D8-02] SocketReinjectSubmitter.DrainReinjectCompletions Destroys In-Flight Completions by Closing s.c… [CLOSED] (closed 2026-10-18)

## Summary
`SocketReinjectSubmitter.DrainReinjectCompletions` Destroys In-Flight Completions by Closing `s.complete` on Idle 5ms Read Deadlines while `CapturePipeline` Unboundedly Buffers Per-Flow Frames

Finding `D8-02` from `gemini-4-argon-high-review-high-security-hostile-experts-100-001.md` (deep-review audit `0c5f646c`). Both independent re-review passes gate this claim **MATERIAL** at their checked `origin/master` revisions — opus: ; spark:  — with the narrowed scope below. Coordinator re-checked the cited anchors against current `origin/master` `09c6b9ed9f62e389081b8ecc3a9df7bce23da7c9` for filing (line numbers as cited by the re-reviewers; re-anchor before fixing).
## Narrowed material core (both passes)
- Opus: Verified verbatim. `DrainReinjectCompletions` sets a 5ms read deadline (`s.timeout=5ms`, :135) and on *any* `isTimeout(err)` — including 0-byte idle — does `Close(); s.complete=nil; return nil,nil`. My probe (unix socketpair, audit tree): two consecutive idle drains both return `(nil,nil)` with `s.complete==nil` after each, confirming close-on-idle (not in packet). Rust `serve_complete_conn_with_target` does `write_all(&response)` then `core.ack_ready(&ids)` with only a 100ms write timeout, and on write error `release_ready`+break — i.e. Rust commits removal on socket-buffer write, not on Go application ack. So a completion written in the window [Go deadline expiry, Go `Close()`] is acked in Rust and destroyed unread in Go; the Go `pendingReinject` then expires in `Poll` (`pipeline.go:1116-1145`) → `p.uncertain("ack timeout")` → fail-closed quarantine. Mid-frame arm also real: `readReinjectMessage` returns timeout after partial `io.ReadFull`, same close+`nil,nil`, so `Poll` never calls `failPending("completion drain error")`. Unbounded queue arm verified: `enqueueFlowLocked` (pipeline.go:640-657) appends unconditionally and `return nil` always, despite `consumeFrames` expecting drop-returns (`drops = append(drops, p.enqueueFlowLocked(frame)...)`); `p.flows` map and per-flow slices have no cap while `handoff` is capped at 16384 and `Enqueue` is try-or-drop — so memory growth is bounded only by Drain rate vs pending-head stall (`ackDeadline` default 5ms, but follower frames behind a pending head accumulate until retire). - Strongest refutation / alternative: (1) The race wind
- Spark: Verified identical both revs. `DrainReinjectCompletions` (`reinject_socket.go:224-237`): 5ms deadline (`:135` default), on *any* timeout — including 0-byte idle — closes `s.complete` and returns `nil,nil` (silently, unlike non-timeout errors which `Poll:pipeline.go:1096-1098` turns into `failPending`). Comment at `:228-230` admits partial consumption is possible, so close-on-timeout is stream-safety, but it is applied indiscriminately. Rust side (`reinject_9506.rs:266-285`): `peek_ready → write_all → ack_ready` — ack is on socket-buffer write, not Go read. So a completion written after Go's deadline expiry but before `Close()` executes is acked/purged in Rust and destroyed unread in Go; pending entry then hits `ack timeout → uncertain` (`pipeline.go:1116-1126`). Mid-frame partial timeout is additionally misreported as `nil,nil` instead of drain error. Mechanism is real and in code.

## #14686 — [gemini-hostile D10-01] RBAC Command Authorization Bypass via Cross-Form Longest-Match Maximization and Argument/Pipe… [CLOSED] (closed 2026-10-18)

## Summary
RBAC Command Authorization Bypass via Cross-Form Longest-Match Maximization and Argument/Pipe Keyword Smuggling

Finding `D10-01` from `gemini-4-argon-high-review-high-security-hostile-experts-100-001.md` (deep-review audit `0c5f646c`). Both independent re-review passes gate this claim **MATERIAL** at their checked `origin/master` revisions — opus: ; spark:  — with the narrowed scope below. Coordinator re-checked the cited anchors against current `origin/master` `09c6b9ed9f62e389081b8ecc3a9df7bce23da7c9` for filing (line numbers as cited by the re-reviewers; re-anchor before fixing).
## Narrowed material core (both passes)
- Opus: Exactly as claimed and reproduced. `EvaluateForms` takes an independent global max per side over three projections of different lengths (matched = command+pipe, command, prefix). An end-anchored deny (`^show version$`) is capped at the short form's length while a wildcard allow (`^show.*`) grows with the piped form, flipping tier 2 to allow. Separately, `longestMatchLen` matches anywhere, so an unanchored allow phrase placed inside user-controlled pipe filter text (`| except show interfaces`) satisfies the allowlist for a command (`show configuration`) that never matched it. Both are complete RBAC bypasses for the affected (plausible, Junos-idiomatic) class shapes. - Strongest refutation / alternative: Requires the class to combine a wildcard allow with end-anchored denies, or to use an unanchored allow phrase — a class with only anchored allow+deny, or deny-only, is unaffected. Junos longest-match tier-2 semantics are upstream-documented, so part of the behavior is parity; but Junos does not measure the allow side against pipe-filter text the operator appends, and the in-code rationale (#9022/#9628) only considered narrow literal exceptions (`^show log 100$`), not wildcard allows. Parity does not cover the smuggling arm at all. - Decisive unresolved check: regression test asserting piped/arg-suffixed forms of an anchored-deny command stay denied (packet's `TestEvaluateFormsPipeAndArgDoNotDefeatAnchoredDeny` shape), run against a fix that keeps the documented `^show log 100$` exception working.
- Spark: Behaviourally confirmed on master (clean tree): `EvaluateForms("show version | match .","show version","show version")` with allow `^show.*`/deny `(^show version$)|(^show log$)` → **ALLOWED**; unanchored allow `show interfaces` + `show configuration | except show interfaces` → **ALLOWED**. Mechanism exactly as claimed: `EvaluateForms:292-365` pools matched/command/prefix into one max per side (`login_regex.go:185-209,292-407`), caller passes pipe-bearing `matched` (`permissions_regex.go:165-181`). Pipes/args inflate only the allow side vs `$`-anchored denies. This also moots the deliberate #9628 comment at `permissions_regex.go:178-180` ("pipe-less command is measured as well") — measuring more forms widens allow too.

The packet conflates the two arms' strength. - Decisive unresolved check: Go tests — `Canonicalize` must return non-OK for trailing `parentTyped` (packet's table), and handler tests asserting dangling `filter`/`ids-option`/`zo

## Summary
RBAC Command Authorization Bypass via Post-Dynamic Sibling Traversal and Repeated-Key Argument Overwrite in `cmdtree`

Finding `D10-03` from `gemini-4-argon-high-review-high-security-hostile-experts-100-001.md` (deep-review audit `0c5f646c`). Both independent re-review passes gate this claim **MATERIAL** at their checked `origin/master` revisions — opus: ; spark:  — with the narrowed scope below. ## Narrowed material core (both passes)
- Opus: After a dynamic value is consumed, `current` still points at the node's Children, so mutually-exclusive siblings (`terse`, `queue`, `name`) resolve after a positional value; handlers then ignore the extra tokens (`showInterfaces` checks `args[0]` for subcommands and last-token `detail`/`extensive`, otherwise `filterName=args[0]`) — judged string ≠ executed command again. The CoS arm is the cleanest: the packet's own code comment ("A later explicit name keyword wins over the bare positional", #6858/#11834) documents the overwrite; RBAC sees the allowed positional (`public-cls`), the handler renders the overwritten value (`secret-cls`). Prefix-scoped allow (`^show class-of-service classifier public-cls.*`) is thereby defeated with no deny involved. - Strongest refutation / alternative: The interfaces/zones arms need an anchored exact deny (`^show interfaces ge-0/0/0$`) to be *defeated*; with prefix-style allows the extra tokens are arguably legitimate Junos-ish syntax (`show interfaces ge-0/0/0 terse` is a real Junos command), and `SplitModifiers` handling of `terse` is deliberate. So those arms are a judged-vs-executed mismatch only against exact-anchored denies, whereas the CoS repeated-key overwrite has no legitimate reading — two different names in one command cannot both be the filter. - Decisive unresolved check: Go tests — `ParseCoSNameTypeArgs` must reject duplicate `name`/`type` (packet's test); `showInterfaces` must reject `len(args)>2` / non-`detail|extensive` second tokens; and RBAC tests for the exact-anchored interface deny forms.
- Spark: Confirmed: `show interfaces ge-0/0/0 terse`, `… queue detail`, `show class-of-service classifier public-cls name secret-cls` all CanonicalOK; `ParseCoSNameTypeArgs([public-cls name secret-cls])` → `secret-cls` (overwrite at `cos_filter_topic.go:62-86`). Root: dynamic consumption leaves `current=currentNode.Children` (`canonicalize.go:81-180`), so mutually-exclusive siblings/`name` re-resolve after the positional value; handlers (`cli_show_interfaces.go`, SplitModifiers for zones `terse`) ignore the smuggled token and serve the denied target.

## #14692 — [gemini-hostile D11-02] Unvalidated security ssh-known-hosts Rendering in applySSHKnownHosts Enables OpenSSH @cert-au… [CLOSED] (closed 2026-10-18)

## Summary
Unvalidated `security ssh-known-hosts` Rendering in `applySSHKnownHosts` Enables OpenSSH `@cert-authority *` / Wildcard Trust Poisoning and Newline File Injection into `/etc/ssh/ssh_known_hosts`

Finding `D11-02` from `gemini-4-argon-high-review-high-security-hostile-experts-100-001.md` (deep-review audit `0c5f646c`). Both independent re-review passes gate this claim **MATERIAL** at their checked `origin/master` revisions — opus: ; spark:  — with the narrowed scope below. Coordinator re-checked the cited anchors against current `origin/master` `09c6b9ed9f62e389081b8ecc3a9df7bce23da7c9` for filing (line numbers as cited by the re-reviewers; re-anchor before fixing).
## Narrowed material core (both passes)
- Opus: `applySSHKnownHosts` renders `fmt.Fprintf("%s %s %s\n", host, sshType, key.Key)` with no validation of any field: `host` is the raw map key, `sshType` defaults to the raw `key.Type` for anything outside the five mapped Junos spellings, and `key.Key` is unvalidated. The compiler copies name/type/first-token verbatim and the schema node is `closedWorldOpaque` with no `keyValidator`. So `host = "@cert-authority *"` or `host = "*"` renders a line OpenSSH honors for *every* host — directly defeating #10298's `StrictHostKeyChecking=yes` + `UserKnownHostsFile` design for `scpArchiveTransfer`, whose payload is the unredacted active config. The reachability precondition is also plausible as an RBAC-crossing: `security` config permission is a lesser grant than `system`/super-user, yet it controls trust used by a `system archival` (system-permission) feature. - Strongest refutation / alternative: The newline/multi-line *injection* arm is much weaker: Junos-style config values come from tokenized stanzas (`nodeVal(kp)` = first token), so embedding `\n` or spaces via normal CLI/commit is not obviously reachable — it needs a lenient DB/peer-synced load or quoted-string path the packet asserts but does not demonstrate. The wildcard/CA arm needs no injection at all (single tokens `@cert-authority`, `*` are exactly what the config grammar accepts as a host name), so the claim stands on that arm alone. Also note OpenSSH still requires the attacker to present a key *certified by / equal to* the injected entry and to be on-path for the archive host — MITM positioning is required, as with any k
- Spark: `applySSHKnownHosts:1004-1053` renders `fmt.Fprintf("%s %s %s\n", host, sshType, key.Key)` raw; unknown types fall through verbatim; compiler (`compiler_security.go:71-81` — note: append/merge code, zero validation) and `closedWorldOpaque` schema (`schema_security.go:1559-1561`) validate nothing. Host `@cert-authority *` or `*`, or newline in any field, writes attacker lines into root `/etc/ssh/ssh_known_hosts` (0644), which `scpArchiveTransfer` trusts with `StrictHostKeyChecking=yes` — defeating #10298 and enabling MITM capture of unredacted archival config. `security`-only RBAC suffices to author `security ssh-known-hosts`.
